article:
Baby among four killed in bomb attack in western Colombia, official says

Baby among four killed in bomb attack in western Colombia, official says
- Published
At least four people were killed when a lorry laden with explosives detonated in Tolima province, western Colombia, on Sunday, a local official has said.
A two-month-old baby girl was among the dead, Tolima governor Adriana Magali Matiz wrote in a post on X.
The lorry exploded near a military base in the town of Planadas, damaging a nearby hospital and several other buildings.
It is not yet clear who was behind the bombing, but armed criminal groups have recently stepped up attacks against the security forces in what appears to be retaliation for an offensive ordered against them by the new right-wing President, Abelardo de la Espriella.
Governor Matiz called the attack in Planadas "a vile and criminal act that we reject with absolute forcefulness".
"Attacking the civilian population and putting at risk the lives of our soldiers and the Tolima families is crossing a line that we will not tolerate," she added on X, external.
President de la Espriella, who campaigned on a tough-on-crime platform, wrote on social media that "we will not retreat, not even a millimetre".
Since he was sworn into office in August, the right-wing former defence lawyer has put an end to peace talks with some of Colombia's illegal armed groups, negotiations which had been started under his left-wing predecessor Gustavo Petro.
"In my government, criminals will have no political status, no leniency, and no impunity," de la Espriella wrote in a post on social media at the time, external.
At the start of his presidency, Petro had advocated for a "total peace strategy", arguing that only talks could lead to an end to the violence perpetrated by Colombia's many armed groups.
But after repeated breaches of the terms of the negotiations, Petro put some of the peace talks on hold.
De la Espriella has gone further, expanding his crackdown on all of the country's illegal groups, including bombing their camps.
These groups have in turn stepped up their attacks on the security forces, in some instances using drones - rather than cars or motorcycles - to transport the explosives.
In one of them, carried out on 23 October, a marine infantryman was killed and four others were injured aboard a Navy boat in Cauca province.
Writing on X after Sunday's bombing in Tolima, the president directly addressed what he said were "the narco-terrorists who continue to assassinate innocents".
"We're going to carry on with the bombings against legitimate military targets and we will step up our special operations," he stated, adding that those responsible would be "hunted down".
"This government will confront you, dismantle your organisations and restore security for Colombians."

article:
Major study into 'forever chemicals' in people's bodies launched in UK

Major study into 'forever chemicals' in people's bodies launched in UK
- Published
The government is launching its first study into the levels of so-called 'forever chemicals' in the UK population.
By taking blood and urine samples, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) hopes to gain a better understanding of any potential health risks caused by the substances also known as PFAS, as well as other potential contaminants like lead and arsenic.
It said current evidence suggested the possible health impacts associated with PFAS are likely to be limited, but said the strongest links found in large population groups have been to raised cholesterol and lower birth weights.
The first results are expected next year.
PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) have been used prolifically since the 1940s and 1950s because they are resistant to water, oil and heat.
It is why they have been placed in thousands of items such as pots and pans, clothing and foams used to fight fires.
But because they do not break down easily in the environment - hence the name 'forever chemicals' - they have raised health concerns in recent years.
Two are already banned in the UK - PFOA and PFOS - because prolonged exposure to them can increase the risk of cancer, according to the World Health Organization., external
But the study of PFAS is an emerging field with more than 15,000 types to research.
The UKHSA will take blood and urine samples collected through the existing Health Survey for England, external to establish baseline levels of PFAS, lead, arsenic, bisphenols, phthalates and flame retardants in the population.
Inside Health: What we do and don't know about PFAS
Listen on R4 at 09:30 or on BBC Sounds
In an exclusive interview with BBC Radio 4's Inside Health, Dr Edward Wynne-Evans, director of radiation, chemicals, climate and environmental hazards at the UKHSA, said there are gaps around "what different levels of exposure mean for an individual's long-term health".
There are growing concerns among people living near sites where there has been contamination from the two known toxic PFAS, and they have chosen to get individual blood tests.
In September, blood tests found "really high levels" of one of the cancer-causing forever chemicals (PFOA) in dozens of people living near a major chemical factory.
But the UK government does not recommend individuals get routine PFAS blood testing because there is no "established clinical intervention" if they have elevated levels, Wynne-Evans said.
"If you are going to do a test where you cannot recommend an action to follow, we would not normally recommend a test."
He said that this study would help "build an evidence base to better understand what might be happening".
Speaking before this study was announced, Prof Tony Fletcher from the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine said he believed there is a low level of PFAS in everyone's blood.
"If we tested a random sample of anybody's blood, we would measure [PFAS] in low levels."
"We are not all dying because of this but at higher levels [and in larger populations] they have been associated with adverse health effects."
For the two banned PFAS - PFOA and PFOS - the known risks, external include increased cholesterol, an increased risk of cancer, reduced antibody levels following childhood vaccinations and a range of endocrine effects linked to the thyroid and lower birth weights.
"I have met with people living in an area with contamination - they are angry," Fletcher said.
"What I try and explain to them is we have found these causal associations between exposure and effect in studying large populations. Although at an individual level, the chances of you getting some bad disease or some adverse health effect is quite low."
He stated the important thing is to stop ongoing exposure, to avoid any long-term effects.

article:
Indonesia's toxic haze is giving its neighbours a political headache

Indonesia's toxic haze is giving its neighbours a political headache
- Published
The haze billowing out from wildfires in the Indonesian regions of Kalimantan, Papua and Sumatra knows no borders.
Carried by winds to nearby Singapore and Malaysia, the toxic smog has in recent weeks impacted populations across maritime South East Asia, triggering respiratory illnesses and headaches.
It's also giving the region's governments a different kind of headache - split between the mounting frustrations of their citizens and the risk of souring diplomatic ties with Indonesia.
"People are fed up, angry and anxious," Eugene Tan, associate professor of law at the Singapore Management University, tells the BBC. "The governments have to respond to them, or else what is more an external issue has become an internal one with ample headroom for politicisation."
Indonesia's wildfires are a yearly occurrence, widely associated with industrial-scale land clearing to make way for crops like oil palm.
But the blazes this year have been particularly difficult to tame due to a strong El Niño, which has exacerbated drought conditions in the country's forests and peatlands.
Whereas previous haze episodes in Singapore and Malaysia have typically lasted for a few days, this time it stretched into weeks.
In Malaysia, locals started a boycott of Indonesian products in protest against the haze, after lawmaker Syed Saddiq called for sanctions on companies linked to the wildfires and said Malaysians should "treat them as an outcast in the region".
There have also been complaints in Singapore, a country that has come to expect seamless efficiency from its leaders.
"There appears to be the view that the government dropped the ball in dealing with the haze, given that it was known that the El Niño weather phenomenon would be severe and that early warning was given," says Tan.
"Clearly, Singaporeans expect the government to decisively deal with the polluters."
A diplomatic dilemma
Singapore's government, for its part, has made it clear that the haze problem is a priority.
Hundreds of haze shelters have been set up across the island, and masks are being distributed to children, the elderly and other vulnerable residents.
Authorities have also said they're looking to strengthen existing haze legislation and are investigating 10 Singapore-registered companies for potential links to the wildfires in Indonesia.
Last week, Singapore's foreign minister Vivian Balakrishnan met Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto in Jakarta for what the former described as "honest" and "sincere" conversations that produced "constructive approaches".
The meeting came as both countries announced they would set up a joint task force to deal with the haze - an apparent détente after weeks of simmering bilateral tensions.
As the haze spiralled into yet another crisis for Prabowo's beleaguered administration, some officials pushed back against criticism.
One senior official ruffled feathers when he said the wildfires were out of human control and that oxygen in neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia "also comes from our forests".
That remark was "disappointing" and "not right", according to Singaporean senior minister K Shanmugam - a rare rebuke from the city state, which prides itself on its diplomatic prowess.
"The haze is affecting our health seriously, and it's really unacceptable," Shanmugam told reporters. Since the haze impacts citizens on both sides of the border, there should not be "any bilateral issues" in addressing it, he added.
"The Indonesian public is suffering as well, and it is in Indonesia's interest as much as ours to deal with the companies that are causing these problems."
Days later, Indonesia announced it would reduce gas exports to Singapore, citing domestic energy needs - a move that many saw as retaliation to Singapore's rhetoric.
To be sure, Indonesia has faced recent electricity shortages in parts of the country. Singapore also says the reduction, which amounts to less than 2% of its total daily demand, will have little impact on its gas supply.
But the abrupt announcement came just days after Indonesia's energy minister warned that they could halt gas exports to countries that don't "respect Indonesia". That same day, Prabowo made reference to "countries that like to insult Indonesia" when talking about the wildfires.
"It's a tired playbook of using Singapore as the bogeyman, driven by the 'abang-adik' [big brother-little brother] syndrome," Tan says, referring to a historical dynamic that Singapore's leaders have long tried to shrug off: the expectation that it should defer to its larger neighbours.
"Singapore leaders expressing concerns about the haze and how it affects the people of both countries have been taken to mean that Singapore has been disrespectful to its neighbour."
Waiting for winds to change
In contrast, Malaysia's official rhetoric on the haze has been relatively muted.
Its foreign minister Mohamad Hasan has ruled out lodging a formal diplomatic protest with Indonesia or taking legal action, saying such actions "would mean we were prepared to sever relations".
For now, Malaysia has agreed to explore a memorandum of understanding with Indonesia to strengthen wildfire prevention efforts.
It would also rely on diplomatic mechanisms, Mohamad said - like the Asean Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution.
The agreement, which came into effect in 2003, commits members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) to collaborate on tackling the recurring haze.
But many see it as toothless, as it is unable to punish agricultural companies linked to wildfires or to force individual governments to do so.
The agreement has turned out to be "just not worth the paper it was signed on", says James Chin, professor of Asian studies at the University of Tasmania.
"The moment the haze disappears, the moment the political pressure's off, it's back to business as usual."
In 2016, Asean countries had set a goal to eliminate haze in the region by 2020. When that deadline drifted quietly by, they set a new target of achieving the goal by 2030 instead.
Complicating Malaysia's position is the fact that it is also a major palm oil producer. The commodity is often linked to commercial "slash-and-burn" practices that are widely blamed for the region's wildfires.
Malaysia has at times dealt with acute haze stemming from blazes on local land.
In 2019, when Malaysia pointed to hotspots in Indonesia's peatlands as the cause of the haze shrouding the region, Indonesian authorities pointed the finger back at Malaysia, claiming the smog came from their side.
"As long as we place a lot of importance on oil palm planting, [the haze] is going to recur," says Ei Sun Oh, principal adviser at the Pacific Research Centre of Malaysia.
And even if Malaysia were to speak up, Oh adds, it's unlikely to wield the same "leverage" over Indonesia as Singapore, which is Indonesia's largest foreign investor and an offshore financial hub for many wealthy Indonesians.
For now, Malaysia "doesn't want to unduly provoke Indonesia", says Oh.
"The government is just wringing their hands till the wind blows [the problem] over. Because eventually it will blow over."

article:
Boulders dropped off coast to disrupt deep fishing

Boulders dropped off coast to disrupt deep fishing
- Published
Greenpeace has dropped nine boulders off the east coast of England to create a barrier that disrupts bottom trawling by fishing vessels.
The environmental campaigners' ship Arctic Sunrise released the rocks, without a licence, over the weekend about 50km (30 miles) east of Great Yarmouth, Norfolk.
Bottom trawling involves dragging weighted nets along the seabed to catch fish, although it can harm underwater vegetation.
Greenpeace claimed it had "effectively closed 116 sq km (45 sq miles) of the Southern North Sea Marine Protected Area (MPA) to bottom trawling". The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said "activities at sea should be carried out lawfully".
When asked if it had permission to drop the boulders, Greenpeace said this was a "last resort" for it, and it did not have a licence.
It said that after years of meeting with politicians and the government to try to protect marine protected areas, progress had been "at a glacial pace".
Greenpeace added that bottom trawling could leave harbour porpoises, external, marine mammals which are found all over the UK's coast, with low fish stocks to feed on.
It added that the noise pollution of trawling disrupted the porpoises' ability to hunt and that the MPA had been designated to protect the animal.
A Defra spokesperson said: "We have strict legislation in place to protect our marine environment while supporting sustainable fishing and coastal communities.
"All Marine Protected Areas are safeguarded by legislation, with damaging fishing activities banned in more than 100 sites, and we are also considering further restrictions where there may be benefits in doing so.
"Activities at sea should be carried out lawfully and with due regard for the safety of other sea users."
Greenpeace said that, external after dropping the two-tonne boulders, it had called "the authorities to tell them the co-ordinates of each placement, and they update maps to inform other vessels".
The Southern North Sea MPA covers an area stretching from north of Dogger Bank (due east of Tyneside) to the Straits of Dover in the south.
The MMO has issued a notice to give the grid references for the reported positions of the nine boulders, external.
In 2022, activists dropped 18 boulders off the coast of Cornwall.
After this, the government body responsible for managing coastal waters, the Marine Management Organisation (MMO), said: "As England's marine regulator, we are very disappointed that Greenpeace has chosen to take this action to drop boulders to form a barrier, as we don't believe it is justified or will help protect our marine environment."

article:
Bute House protested by environmental campaigners

Bute House protested by environmental campaigners
- Published
Environmental campaigners have staged a Halloween themed demonstration outside the first minister's official residence over "scary" fossil fuels.
Climate groups gathered outside Bute House in Edinburgh to protest against the Scottish government's decision to give the go-ahead for a new, gas-fired, power station at Peterhead in Aberdeenshire.
The decision has been branded a "catastrophic failure" by environmental campaigners, who said burning fossil fuels is the key driver of extreme weather such as recent storms, record heat and flooding.
The Scottish government said it remained committed to tackling climate change.
The protest also comes after the announcement from the UK government that the Jackdaw gas field near Aberdeen would be allowed to go ahead.
Protesters wearing Halloween themed masks and holding placards with messages such as "fossil fuel ghouls" and "this decision will haunt you" gathered on Charlotte Square.
Kate Whitaker of Friends of the Earth Scotland said fossil fuels are "scary" because of the harm they are causing "millions of people".
"When politicians make disastrous decisions to approve new oil or gas, people get even more terrified about our collective future," she said.
"Giving the go ahead for a new fossil-fuelled power plant at Peterhead is a catastrophic failure from the Scottish government to protect people from both climate breakdown and the increasing burden of household energy bills.
"Politicians could instead help allay our fears by focusing on climate solutions that improve people's lives such as warmer homes, reliable bus services and creating green jobs."
A Scottish government spokesperson said: "We remain unwavering in our commitment to tackle climate change, delivering positive climate action to achieve net zero by 2045.
"The full grounds for the ministers' decision are set out in the decision letter.
"Potential impacts on communities, nature and cultural heritage, including the cumulative effects of developments, were important considerations in the decision-making process."

article:
Charity warns about damage of over-foraging fungi

Charity warns about damage of over-foraging fungi
- Published
The impacts of over-foraging natural spaces, particularly in protected areas, can damage habitats, a Devon charity has said.
The Woodland Trust said unsustainable harvesting of plants - and particularly fungi - could put wildlife under pressure.
Joe Middleton, site manager for the Woodland Trust, said he had seen commercial mushroom pickers "wiping out everything on the path edges they can find".
Under Section 4 of the Theft Act 1968, it is "perfectly legal to forage for fruit, foliage, flowers, and fungi on any land, provided they are wild and collected strictly for personal use", but "foraging becomes criminal theft if you pick wild plants for commercial sale or reward without permission".
Middleton said: "I have seen commercial pickers, dropped off in mini buses with bags for life, laden heavy with mushrooms and they are going through and they are wiping out everything on the path edges they can find, trampling the forest floor."
The majority of mushrooms are not edible to humans, so picking them can be potentially dangerous.
In the autumn they are an essential source of food for animals such as deer and badgers, all the way down to things that live in the soil such as worms and woodlice.
Middleton said: "If we start decimating the population, it takes their food source away.
"They can't just get up and move, a lot of our wildlife is dependent on this fungi. We just need to be a bit more sustainable in what we are doing."
Entering private property without a landowner's consent to forage is a civil rather than criminal offence. However, foraging is heavily restricted or illegal in local Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs) or protected areas like Woodland Trust sites.
Using ingredients from local areas is very fashionable on social media at the moment.
John Dobson, from the Refectory restaurant near Ugborough, said he thought there were other factors too.
He said: "The rising cost of ingredients; they're getting really, really expensive, so I think that could be encouraging people to go out and source things from other places. There is also a lack of education about the impact."
Dobson added he made sure to forage responsibly, only taking a third of what he found, and doing so with any landowner's permission.
Middleton said foraging was a great way to connect with nature, but he wanted to encourage people to enjoy woodlands without taking any of it home with them too.
He said: "We've gone a long way from Victorian times in terms of taking everything we see and pinning it and netting it.
"Now we are in a technological age. We can just use our phones, take great pictures; we can look without touching - particularly in a protected place."
Penzance-based forager, wild food guide and founder of Wild Walks South West Rachel Lambert said: "It's always an issue.
"It's one of the fundamental rules, guidelines of foraging, is to consider who else is foraging in the area, and that includes all the other non-human beings - the wildlife in the area."
She said people should only take what they needed and only select things which were abundant.
She added foraging "takes time" and people should think about their impact on nature.

article:
Building boom puts 300,000 people in the path of potential Himalayan disasters

Building boom puts 300,000 people in the path of potential Himalayan disasters
- Published
At least 300,000 people in parts of the Himalayan region could now be living in the path of potential disasters, a new study suggests.
Researchers found that the amount of built-up land in high-risk zones in northern Nepal, parts of south-eastern Tibet and a corner of India's Uttarakhand had grown by about 45% between 2016 and 2023.
In areas particularly threatened by flooding from glacial lakes, development increased even faster, rising by almost 78% over the same period, according to the peer-reviewed study published in Scientific Reports.
The team of scientists behind it said the true number of people under threat could be much higher, as they only analysed a specific territory and not neighbouring areas which face similar risks.
The study was carried out before August's devastating mass floods which left more than 1,400 dead and thousands missing in Nepal. More recently there have been several smaller incidents, including flooding along the Budhi Gandaki river on 11 October that damaged 200 houses, swept away five bridges and left five people missing.
Nine researchers from the UK, Nepal and India looked at areas up to 50km (30 miles) downstream from Himalayan rivers, as well as around 1,360 glacial lakes.
They found significant development in these areas - including an expansion of tourism facilities, infrastructure development and real estate.
It's clear in Pokhara, a major tourism hub at the foot of the Himalayas that's grown significantly in the past 30 years to cater for a massive increase in visitors.
Mayor Dhana Raj Acharya says it's a huge challenge to deal with the risk posed by the Seti Gandaki River, which stems from the Annapurna mountain range and flows right through the city. Many old buildings are just 5m (16ft) from river banks, he says, despite new rules requiring them to be further away.
"Where we move them, and how we do that, is the real challenge."
To the north is the world-renowned Annapurna trekking region that has also seen a major increase in settlements along river banks - some hit by recent floods and landslides.
Phurpa Chhiring Lama, who runs a homestay there, feels helpless. Normally all of his 20 rooms are occupied at this time of year - the peak trekking season - but now only five are. "We have been doing this business for more than 40 years, but we've never seen this kind of disaster."
Krishna Gauchan, whose hotel is close to the glacier-fed Modi river, is worried too. "This river can flood if the glacier collapses or if the glacial lake bursts out and we are living in constant fear."
Tourism investors promote some of these spots as destinations without factoring in the risks, suggests Khagendra Poudel, a geographer at a local campus of Tribhuvan University. It's similar to what's happening in parts of north India's Himalayan valleys which host major pilgrimages.
The president of the Hotel Association Pokhara admits tourism businesses have expanded "without any proper planning" in the region and been promoted "haphazardly".
"By the time disasters hit, it is too late," says Laxman Subedi. "As a professional body we are trying to create awareness among tourism entrepreneurs and investors."
But it's not just tourism. The regions surrounding the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers have seen a significant rise in the construction of hydropower plants.
"As river valleys become increasingly populated, development decisions being made today will shape disaster risk for decades to come," warns the study's lead author, University of Leeds glaciologist C Scott Watson.
And even more buildings may be under threat than those identified by the researchers.
The study categorised buildings at risk as all those that were within 50 vertical metres (164ft) of a river or glacial lake's surface.
But during the catastrophic flooding on 26 August, locals in Rasuwa district say the river level had risen by 70m (230ft) at some points - so even buildings that were relatively far from the river banks were hit and buried by debris-sludge.
The risks in all of these areas are largely driven by warming in the Himalayan region, which scientists say is happening at twice the global rate. This has sped up the melting of glaciers, icefields, snowpacks, and ground that's normally frozen all year.
This can, in turn, destabilize mountain slopes which are also frequently shaken by earthquakes, unleashing devastating disasters downstream.
The rapid melting is also filling up and expanding glacial lakes until they burst, causing deadly floods. Nepal alone has documented around 30 of these events since 1940.
Another issue is that rising temperatures cause rain to reach high altitudes where it used to only snow, leading to slope failures, rock and ice falls, and other disasters.
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah raised the dangers of climate change at his recent UN General Assembly speech, where he said his country was paying a "colossal price" for a crisis it did not create.
"Every major disaster threatens to erase years of development. And it forces a poor country to borrow money to repair damage it did not cause."
Alton Byers, a mountain geographer at the University of Colorado who was not involved in the study, says it should serve as a "springboard" to bring about more effective early-warning systems and other precautionary measures.
But achieving that will be a challenge. Campaigners say building regulations aren't implemented on the ground and through the years, development has been haphazard in too many places.
Roads, hydropower projects, hotels and market towns have expanded on the low, flat land along rivers, which is accessible and buildable, says Prof Surya Raj Acharya, an urban planning expert and registrar at the University of Nepal.
Those responsible have often ignored safeguards including keeping off the river bank, he adds.
"A fragile ecosystem like the Himalaya demands stricter planning and building regulations than elsewhere, yet these rules have been weak and poorly enforced."
Authorities in Nepal say they are working to address these issues. Settlements within 15m (49ft) of the riverbank along the recently devastated Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi corridor will soon be banned, according to the national disaster agency. Similar rules are being introduced in other river corridors soon.
"It is a challenging job because people in many places have sentimental attachments with their land and property but we cannot ignore the increasing risks," says chief executive Dharam Raj Uprety.
A similar story has unfolded across Nepal's western border in India's Uttarakhand state, where maximum tourism limits and environmental regulations have been bypassed in the name of economic growth, claims activist Anoop Nautiyal.
On paper there are zoning rules prohibiting the construction of houses and infrastructure too close to river banks, "but on the ground we see no implementation of such rules.
"You can see rampant construction all over."
The Uttarakhand government on 12 October approved new floodplain zoning rules to regulate land use and development. "Its objective is to protect life, property and important infrastructure from possible flood damage while maintaining the natural flow of flood waters," the state's cabinet decision read.
But Basanta Raj Adhikari, director of the Centre for Disaster Studies at Tribuvan University, thinks it will not be possible to mitigate such threats completely.
Insurance grades, he suggests, could be another way to encourage people to build in less risky areas. If authorities were to map places as high, moderate and low risk, he believes insurance coverage would "follow accordingly" ensuring people who build homes in safer areas get better protection.
But for now, the pace of construction across the region shows no signs of slowing.

article:
Global nature talks reach deal but money remains an issue

Global nature talks reach deal but money remains an issue
- Published
In Armenia's capital this week a fight between politicians broke out - not the mass brawl in its parliament that was so widely documented on social media - but between delegates from nearly 200 countries.
The world's nations have been gathered in Yerevan for nearly two weeks negotiating, and arguing, over a new agreement on nature.
Early on Saturday morning, hours after talks were due to finish, they finally agreed the key parts of a new action plan.
"And that's it. Perfect," said the meeting president, Hambardzum Matevosyan.
Four years earlier the same countries had signed a landmark deal committing to "halt and reverse" the decline of nature.
That global deal in 2022 - the Global Biodiversity Framework - contained 24 targets including putting 30% of the world's land and seas into protection by the end of the decade.
They agreed that action was urgent.
The world is currently in a sixth mass extinction event with species becoming extinct at 100 times the natural rate because of human activities, scientists say.
But according to the UN this week,, external the world is on track to achieve just one of those two dozen targets.
As part of this week's deal, countries acknowledged they were falling behind.
"While not particularly exciting or detailed, it's good news that countries could reach agreement," said Catherine Weller, from environmental charity Fauna & Flora.
"We cannot just plod on to 2030 without a course correction; nature is critical to all life on Earth: to our economies, to our wellbeing," she added.
This was echoed by Craig Bennett, CEO of The Wildlife Trusts, who told BBC News: "We are still seeing an appalling loss, threatening the collapse of ecosystems globally. We run out of words really about how serious this is."
But he added "the better news is there are so many examples worldwide about how... to turn things around".
Countries have put 623 million acres (252m hectares) of degraded land into protection, external - an area bigger than Greenland.
Just last month the WWF praised conservation efforts which had achieved the recovery of key species including elephants, green sea turtles and tigers.
Countries have recognised the main barrier to accelerating those efforts is money.
In 2022, they agreed they would put $30bn (£22.4bn) towards nature recovery efforts by the end of the decade, and mobilise a further $170bn from private sources.
But years later many nations have been redirecting international aid to defence budgets and to deal with repeated energy shocks, such that pledges are not at the rate required to reach those targets, according to the UN. , external
At this meeting, more than $1bn was pledged, with half of that coming from philanthropists including Leonardo DiCaprio's Re:wild organisation.
Anna Ducros, a researcher at the International Institute for Environment and Development, said there had been some progress on countries committing to reducing subsidies for industries harmful to the environment.
"A concrete example is that governments subsidise large-scale fishing that is especially harmful for nature - for example, trawling."
Ducros, who was in attendance at the talks, added: "Right now, we have the situation where governments are paying twice.
"So they know that they need to increase spending on nature and climate, but at the same time, they're damaging nature."
A specific funding pot, the Cali Fund, was previously set up for private companies that profit from using genetic material found in the environment to donate to. It was estimated up to $3.6bn could be raised annually - at the start of the meeting just $10,000 had been pledged.
Little progress was made on that issue - its voluntary nature makes it difficult to put pressure on companies, Bennett acknowledged.
"When you have countries that have rich biodiversity in them and you have companies trying to make money out of the genetic material found in those countries they should be paying those communities," he said. "That should not be controversial."
'Blatant political move'
One of the easier issues on the agenda was meant to be the approval of scientific reports into the state of nature.
But a small group of countries, including Saudi Arabia and Russia, were reported to have frustrated that process.
"The attacks on science have bothered me a lot," French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut was reported as saying by the AFP news agency.
Next month countries will gather for the annual climate conference - COP31. Its own science body, the IPCC, has faced similar challenges in the past month with passing its own scientific reports and securing funding.
"This is such a blatant political move...and the IPCC is no such place for such political manoeuvring since the outputs are in humanity's interest," said Prof David Lee, from Manchester University, who has worked on previous reports.

article:
Young child injured by firework on Halloween night

Young child injured by firework on Halloween night
- Published
A toddler was taken to hospital after being burnt by a firework in County Tyrone on Halloween night.
It was one of numerous Halloween-related incidents that the emergency services responded to across Northern Ireland on Saturday night and into Sunday.
Fireworks were deliberately directed at fire crews in six separate incidents.
The injury to the toddler - a girl under two years old - happened outside a filling station on Main Street in Carrickmore at about 20:30 GMT.
Insp McDonagh of the Police Service of Northern Ireland said the firework was thrown on the road by teenage boys and "partially exploded" before bouncing back and "exploding for a second time" beside the child, who was with her parents.
The girl sustained a burn to her forearm, which required hospital treatment.
"It's only by sheer luck that the consequences of this reckless act weren't even more serious," said Insp McDonagh.
"The irresponsibility of throwing fireworks near a petrol station is shocking."
Halloween celebrations took place in Northern Ireland over the weekend, with the biggest festival being held in Londonderry on Saturday evening.
Across Northern Ireland, the fire service responded to 89 incidents, many of which were Halloween-related with 23 of them involving bonfires, between 18:00 on Saturday and 01:00 on Sunday.
Fireworks were directed at fire crews in Drumquin in County Tyrone, Enniskillen in County Fermamagh and Kilkeel in County Down.
"No damage or injuries resulted and operational response for local communities was maintained throughout," said a Northern Ireland Fire and Rescue Service spokesperson.
"We cannot emphasise enough how dangerous fireworks are as they can result in life changing injuries if used inappropriately.
"We acknowledge these incidents were isolated to a small minority of individuals, but this antisocial behaviour could have had devastating consequences."
'Perfect storm' in Dublin
In the Republic of Ireland, the Dublin Fire Brigade reported the highest number of Halloween calls in more than a decade.
Chief fire officer Greg O'Dwyer said that, as of midnight the service had received 558 calls, an increase from 320 calls last year.
O'Dwyer described it as a "very busy night" resulting from a "perfect storm" of dry weather and Halloween falling on a Saturday.

article:
Europe on alert after supermarket freezers hit by cyber-attacks in 10 countries

Europe on alert after supermarket freezers hit by cyber-attacks in 10 countries
- Published
A spate of cyber-attacks that hit supermarket chains across at least 10 European countries on Monday has prompted European Union officials to warn of a deliberate attempt to disrupt the food supply chain.
Supermarkets have reported problems in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Germany and Sweden, and the significant increase in freezer temperatures has forced retailers to discard food.
Temperatures in chains across Europe reportedly rose as high as 50C (122F).
No-one has yet admitted carrying out the cyber-attacks.
The European Union has raised concerns about the attacks, which come three weeks after a cyber-attack disrupted as many as 700 French grocery stores, causing food losses estimated at tens of millions of euros.
The security of refrigeration systems as well as other devices that can be monitored remotely has heightened concerns about government-backed hybrid attacks.
The EU's food and agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, said the bloc was taking the incidents very seriously and warned of further disruption in the future.
Commission spokesman Thomas Regnier was careful not to attribute blame, but said: "These incidents of course show once again how cyber-attacks can disrupt essential services and affect citizens' daily lives."
"These are not isolated incidents and of course we have to be collectively resilient and prepared for such cyber incidents."
In Italy, Giorgia Meloni's government called a meeting with intelligence chiefs, but said the impact was "currently very limited" and most of the food distribution chain had up-to-date security systems able to fend off such attacks.
At least four Co-op supermarkets in Sicily and one business in Tuscany were affected, according to the national cybersecurity agency.
Meloni's office said those businesses affected were "mostly still equipped with obsolete security systems, with interfaces directly exposed to the internet and inadequate authentication mechanisms".
Belgian supermarkets were among those hardest-hit, with dozens of stores reporting refrigeration failures. Federal prosecutors have opened an investigation.

Mathieu Tilman, a manager at a Delhaize supermarket in Belgium, said he was shocked by this kind of attack: "I don't even understand how anyone could do this... How can we end up throwing away so much food? I find it truly distressing. In moments like these, you just feel like quitting your job."
In Ireland, 13 SuperValu stores were impacted by what the chain's owner, Musgrave Group, called a cyber-incident. "Replenishment of chilled and frozen ranges in the affected stores is well under way," a spokesman said on Monday.
A small number of corner shops in the Netherlands also suffered disruption. Last month, supermarket chain Albert Heijn had to take several services offline because of a separate cyber-attack.
There was disruption to refrigeration systems at the Rewe Büsken supermarket in western Germany after a cyber-attack on system provider Danfoss, the company told the BBC. Its systems have been back in operation since Monday afternoon.
In Portugal, the Mosqueteiros group said that incidents at seven Intermarché stores had been linked to a cyberattack, which "appears to have targeted an external service provider responsible for managing the refrigeration systems".
Swedish chain ICA also said "a limited number" of its stores had experienced refrigeration problems, without confirming a cyber-attack, and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.
In Finland, irregular temperatures were detected in a few smaller grocery stores belonging to the Kesko group, which said it was investigating the issue.
In Estonia, at least one supermarket was attacked by hackers who raised the temperature in the refrigeration units to 50C, public broadcaster ERR reported.
In the UK, the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has warned British retailers to update the software on fridge temperature controls.
The agency said the country was likely to suffer an AI-powered cyber-attack on critical national infrastructure within two years.
Richard Horne, the head of the National Cyber Security Centre, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme there were a couple of instances in the UK where "vulnerable technology has been exploited" after the cyber-attacks.
"We don't know the full impact, but we do know there are a couple of instances where vulnerable technology has been exploited and we're working with those organisations."
Asked if there was any evidence that supermarkets in Britain or freezers of the same make or model had been targeted, Horne said: "It's not just supermarkets, it's through the whole food supply chain, and we've been working through the night alerting organisations where we can see they've got exposed technology that's vulnerable in this way."

Motorists angry as car problems shut Asda petrol station pumps

Motorists angry as car problems shut Asda petrol station pumps
- Published
Some motorists are angry after they said their cars developed problems after refuelling at an Asda petrol station.
Sandra Reid is among the people who have reported issues with their vehicles after buying fuel from the same Asda-owned forecourt.
She said her car started to "chug along and struggle to accelerate" and eventually broke down, after leaving the filling station.
Asda has apologised for any inconvenience and removed some pumps from service at the site in question while an investigation is carried out.
Reid said she noticed issues with the car shortly after topping up at the garage in Coleraine, County Londonderry, in Northern Ireland.
"I eventually managed to get the car started again and it again was struggling, but I nursed it to a car park in Long Commons area of Coleraine and there it has stayed ever since," she told BBC News NI.
"It's a paid car park so I have had to top up the parking app for four days now just to keep my car there until I can get someone out to look at it.
"I think I am down about £20 already on parking as I can't move the car."
Reid said not being able to use her car has been a "disaster", especially as she usually uses it to get to and from work, which is a 45-minute walk away.
Reid added that to get the fuel removed from the vehicle, it could cost more than £500.
It is not yet known what may have caused the reported vehicle problems or just how many cars are affected.
Asda said the "isolated incident" affected some - but not all - fuel purchases made at the Coleraine site between 25 and 29 October.
"We're working with customers who may have been affected and asking anyone experiencing issues with their vehicle following a purchase during this timeframe to contact us so we can put things right," a spokesperson said.
"We've safely reopened the majority of pumps following a full investigation, while some remain out of use as we work to resolve the issue."
'Sister and girlfriend's car both broke down'
Dean Law said two cars belonging to his girlfriend Courteney and sister Emma broke down after they had filled up at the petrol station.
He said he and his girlfriend had now spent about £1,000 on mechanic bills after her car broke down on Monday when she was driving to work.
"She told me the car felt different and started to vibrate when she was driving, but she managed to get it to work.
"After work, she then went out and tried to start the car and it wouldn't move."
"It was only after we spoke to my sister, who had also filled up her car at the same petrol station on Sunday and whose car had also broken down, that we eventually realised the issue could be linked to the fuel," he said.
"I actually put up a Facebook post asking if anyone else had experienced the issues that we had and I couldn't believe the response.
"So many people started commenting and messaging me about it, so it seems to have impacted a number of people."
Law said the car was bought a year ago and that it was really frustrating to have to spend so much money on it.
David Jardine, from Belfast, said he was on a family holiday on the north coast at the weekend and filled up his car at the petrol station on Sunday night and broke down shortly afterwards in Portstewart.
"We were just heading up for a few days and filled up at Asda and I remember turning to my son in the car and saying the car doesn't feel right," he said.
"It was like jumping a bit and sounded strange.
"We got to Portstewart where we were staying and the car just completely died on us."
Jardine said his partner and two sons were fortunate that they had another vehicle to rely on during their stay.
"Thankfully my other son was driving his car up as he wanted to go off and meet up with his friends and we had two cars, but a lot of the plans we had were obviously impacted because we were down to the one car."
He said his car had to get towed back to Belfast and cost about £225 to fix.
East Londonderry assembly member Claire Sugden said she had received a number of messages from constituents at the beginning of the week who had raised concerns after filling up their cars at the petrol station.
"One constituent had fuelled up and then, the following day, his car wouldn't start and he then took it to a mechanic, and it is still there. He is now without a car so it is concerning," Sugden said.
"He had seen on social media that others had experienced similar issues after filing up at this station so it seems to be a pattern which has seen Asda conduct an investigation."
Sugden said anyone who may have filled up their cars at the petrol station should be made aware of any potential issue.
"It is pleasing that Asda have responded quickly in relation to this, but it is important that other people who have fuelled up at this station are made aware that this issue could potentially affect them too."

Girl who rescued injured boy from bonfire acted 'on instinct'

Girl who rescued injured boy from bonfire acted 'on instinct'
- Published
The 17-year-old girl who rescued an injured teenage boy from a bonfire said she reacted on instinct.
The boy, also 17, fell into the bonfire in Strabane, County Tyrone, after being knocked unconscious by a punch.
A local councillor, who spoke to his mother, said he had been left with "severe burns" to his face and hands.
Tianna Patterson said she saw him collapse and fall into the fire and her first thought was to try to help.
She had witnessed him being assaulted only moments earlier.
"I just reached for him by the neck and pulled him out of the bonfire," she said.
"I then got a friend's phone and called the emergency services."
The A Level student at Holy Cross College in Strabane said she had been at the bonfire with friends when the incident happened on Saturday night.
Her mother Alex praised her actions.
"We are all very proud of her as this could so easily have been a terrible tragedy," she said.
"But thankfully she acted quickly and rescued the young lad and got him help from the emergency services."
'Destructive'
Independent councillor Paul Gallagher has spoken to the boy's mother and said she is "distraught".
"Young people have gone to the bonfire and in the chaos of it, a young 17-year-old got knocked unconscious, fell onto a fire which at best can be described as white hot," Gallagher told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme.
"I've spoken to his mother who was very distraught, to say the least."
Gallagher said the boy will now require extensive medical care and it will take a long time for him to recover.
"The chaos around a bonfire is madness and it should never have happened that a young boy gets knocked out and put on a fire.
"Bonfires bring very little benefit, they are destructive, they are a serious danger to young people."
The police are stepping up their hunt for the boy's attacker but no arrests have been made.

article:
'Fascinating' rare beetle found in Wales again after 60 years

'Fascinating' rare beetle found in Wales again after 60 years
- Published
A rare species of beetle has been found in Pembrokeshire after not being seen in Wales for 60 years.
The Short-Necked Oil Beetle is named after the adult beetles' stubby shape and its ability to secrete an oily yellow-orange substance from its knee joints when alarmed.
They were not reported in the UK for almost 60 years after 1948 as habitat loss brought the species to the brink of extinction.
Anne Hobbs, from the Bumblebee Conservation Trust, said it was "very exciting" that the evidence suggested the species was breeding in Wales again.
The Short-Necked Oil Beetle is classed as nationally rare within Great Britain and listed as vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, external.
It is dependent on solitary bees for its lifecycle and needs a particular habitat to survive, with thick vegetation for shelter and dense flower coverage both essential.
The larvae of Short-Necked Oil Beetles lurk among flowers, waiting for a passing bee to carry them back to its nest, where they feed on the pollen the bee has collected.
In 2025, the survey at Castlemartin found only dead adults of this particular beetle, raising concerns about the future of this species and its continued presence on the site.
But this year, after three years of searching, experts discovered larvae of the beetle on a small area of the site, suggesting that surveyors had managed to find some of the hatchlings from a larger batch of immature beetles.
The number and distribution of the beetle larvae seen also supported this, according to Natural Resources Wales (NRW).
They can typically be found from March to June in flower-rich coastal grassland and sand dune habitat, and are most active on warm, sunny days.
Adults can grow up to 24mm (0.9in) in length and the life span of an adult is approximately one year.
NRW said these conditions mean there are only a handful of suitable sites in the UK.
They were rediscovered in Devon in 2006 and on the Isle of Coll, in Scotland, in 2009. Since then, populations have been found on Tiree, Islay, Barra and Uist.
Castlemartin Range, in Pembrokeshire, is currently the only place in Wales where the species can be found and it is being consistently surveyed by conservationists.
The project is part of Wales's "flagship species recovery programme", said NRW, which works to conserve the Short-Necked Oil Beetle Sand other species that share similar habitats.
Hobbs described the Short-Necked Oil Beetle as an "amazing creature" and said their work needed to consider the "needs of several species to be effective".
She thanked their partners and volunteers for their continued support, despite having two years without a larval sighting.
"We look forward to the continued management of the site so that this amazing species can survive now and into the future."

article:
Oil tank vandalism results in waterfowl park 'nightmare'

Oil tank vandalism results in waterfowl park 'nightmare'
- Published
Recovery efforts are continuing after an oil spill caused by the vandalism of a nearby home heating oil tank resulted in the death of 13 birds from Broughshane Waterfowl Park.
More than 20 birds were transported to the USPCA's headquarters last week for urgent specialist care, but the death toll has continued to rise.
The popular attraction in County Antrim has been forced to close while efforts continue to remove oil from the pond.
Police have appealed for anyone with information to come forward.
Broughshane Environment Wildfowl and Wildlife Trust's chairman, Gary Hayward, said they incident had been a "nightmare".
"We are devastated," he told BBC News NI.
"One of our volunteers appeared on the Thursday morning to feed [the birds], and walked down through the park and smelt this kerosene smell and saw the black swans completely oiled."
The park is home to 120 "collection birds", as well as wild birds, he explained.
"So far we have lost 13 birds, some of which are really close to us."
Hayward praised the efforts of the USPCA and Northern Ireland Environment Agency (NIEA), who have been instrumental in treating the sick birds and clearing up the spillage.
The Northern Ireland Environment Agency (NIEA) was first alerted to the incident on Thursday 22 October and have been involved in trying to remove the oil waste.
"The incident was quickly confirmed as having had a significant impact on the ponds and NIEA inspectors deployed oil absorbent booms and other countermeasures as mitigation," a spokesperson said.
The agency said the substance involved had been identified as home heating oil, or kerosene, and that the source had been traced to a nearby tank.
The waterway is noted to be much improved but further works will be carried out as long as is deemed necessary.
Hayward hopes that the incident will be an deterrent to those engaged in vandalism.
"People need to be fully aware of what impact it can have if somebody vandalises a heating containers and tanks."
Siobhan Hawthorn, wildlife supervisor at the USPCA, has been a key part of the rescue operation.
"It's massively frustrating when these kind of incidents occur, especially when it's caused by carelessness and us humans and these poor birds have suffered because of it," she said.
"There's no reason for them to have died needlessly for that reason."
Siobhan and the team have been working tirelessly to help revive the birds which include geese, ducks and swans.
"It's been a case of getting them all bathed and treated as soon as we could because of the level of contamination they suffered," she said.
"We've given them all doses of charcoal to help combat some of the toxins that they would have ingested.
"Unfortunately not all of them got to us as quickly as we would have liked and they have ingested too much," she added.
Siobhan and the team said the incident has also placed their staff under considerable pressure "emotionally and mentally".
The centre is unsure just how long they will have to care for the remaining birds.
"We would like to think that they're over the worst of it, but you just don't know exactly how much they have potentially ingested," she explained.
"Birds are extremely good at hiding illnesses and ailments, so sometimes you don't see the symptoms until it's a little bit too late because they're just so good at hiding it.
"The majority of these birds that have come into us are actually not native species so they can't be returned until the pond is 100% fully cleaned and cleared."

article:
Mining giant joins fight to stop killer toad march across Australia

Mining giant joins fight to stop killer toad march across Australia
- Published
Rio Tinto is ploughing millions of dollars into stopping the poisonous cane toad reaching the Pilbara region of western Australia, where the mining giant has a vast iron ore operation
The firm, alongside Curtin University in Perth and others, will spend A$28m (£14.5m) building a "toad containment zone" to prevent the pest travelling south.
While the cane toad is not a direct threat to Rio Tinto's business, it produces toxins lethal to native wildlife and poses a threat to Pilbara's ecosystem.
Rio Tinto has previously faced criticism for destroying two sacred Aboriginal rock shelters in Pilbara which sat above tonnes of iron ore.
The decision cost the former chief executive his job, provoked a widespread backlash and saw Rio Tinto commit to rebuilding trust with Indigenous communities.
Commenting on the proposed containment zone, Roberta Hunter, a ranger in Australia's Nyangumarta Warrarn Indigenous Protected Area, said: "Cane toads destroy the water and animals.
"When toads come close to our country, we want to be there to stop them because we don't want the country to be destroyed."
The plan is to cut off the toad's water supply by building a barrier across 7,500 sq km (2,895 sq m) of land between the Great Sandy Desert and the Indian Ocean.
In drier months, the cane toad needs water every few days to survive.
If there are no natural water sources, the toad relies on artificial water points normally used for cattle and irrigation.
The funding will be used to stop the toad accessing dams, storage tanks or other ground-level water sources. The five-year project will begin in 2027.
A number of native species are at risk if the toad gets into Pilbara. These include the northern quoll, whose numbers have been decreasing, the goanna lizard and the ghost bat.
The toads were introduced into Australia in 1935 to control beetles within the sugar cane industry.
Since then, they have been on a slow march west across the country's northern landscape, according to the Australian government, travelling between 40 km and 60 km a year.
There are no predators or diseases that control the toads, which defend themselves using poison.
Ben Phillips, a professor at Curtin University, said the toads would reach Pilbara within two decades without action.
He said: "The toad containment zone is a once in a lifetime opportunity to stop one of the world's worst invasive species in its tracks and protect the region's unique wildlife."

Wage protests force hundreds of Bangladesh garment factories to close

Wage protests force hundreds of Bangladesh garment factories to close
- Published
Hundreds of garment factories in Bangladesh have been forced to close after days-long protests by workers demanding higher wages.
On Sunday, protests in the capital Dhaka turned violent with protesters blocking roads, vandalising factories and setting vehicles on fire. They also clashed with police, who fired tear gas to disperse them. Police later said that dozens of protesters had been arrested.
Workers are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka ($242; £180), more than double the current standard, citing rising costs of living.
Bangladesh's textile industry employs around four million workers and manufactures garments for major global brands including H&M, Primark and Uniqlo.
There are fears in the industry that the prolonged unrest could disrupt production and affect international buyers, state news agency BSS reported.
The garment industry generates nearly $40bn every year for Bangladesh, accounting for around 10% of its GDP.
The South Asian nation is the world's second-largest garment exporter after China - but its workers are among the lowest-paid in the world, taking home around 13,000 taka ($105; £78) a month.
"We want the government to accept our demands and increase our wages. [And] they need to instruct landlords and homeowners not to raise rent and ensure that the prices of essential commodities remain affordable," one female worker told BBC Bangla.
"Food prices, cooking gas and electricity bills have all gone up," Mamun, a 28-year-old factory worker, told AFP. "The government must either bring down the prices of essential commodities or raise our wages."
The government announced on Sunday that it had established a board to review workers' wages, and Prime Minister Tarique Rahman held an emergency meeting with ministers to address the unrest.
But demonstrations continued on Monday in Dhaka and nearby manufacturing hubs including Ashulia, Gazipur and Narayanganj.
Around 670 factories suspended operations on Monday, according to reports by Reuters and AFP, and hundreds in these areas will remain shut on Tuesday.
At least 29 protesters were arrested as of Monday, according to Dhaka police Deputy Commissioner Mohidul Islam, who said that those who created an "unstable environment in the garment factories" would come under the law.
Authorities have accused the Awami League, the banned political party of former leader Sheikh Hasina, for taking advantage of the protest movement to instigate violence - though they did not provide any evidence of this.
Home minister Salahuddin Ahmed threatened punitive action against protesters who were trying to "destabilise the country" "under the guise of labour protests".
Babul Akhter, a workers' representative on the wage board, urged protesters to go back to work on Monday, promising to "fight for [their] fair wages".
"I tell my fellow workers, return to work. Don't give in to anyone's incitement."

article:
'Campsite ban could be the end of our business'

'Campsite ban could be the end of our business'
- Published
A farmer fears plans to tighten rules for pop-up campsites in a national park could spell the end of her business.
The Lake District National Park Authority (LDNPA) wants to make it compulsory for temporary campsites to require planning permission. Current rules allow sites operating for fewer than 60 days to be set up by simply notifying the authority.
Ruby Cardiff runs Newlands Valley Campsite, near Keswick, during the summer to supplement income from her Keskadale Farm. She said the ban would "strip away a crucial source of income" from farmers who depend on diversification "for their survival".
The LDNPA said the proposal aimed to "prevent unneighbourly or harmful sites".
Cardiff started using one of her fields as a pop-up site after the coronavirus pandemic, when travel bans meant more people holidayed in the UK.
She said the site's popularity helped her business plug the gap left by the phasing out of EU funding following Brexit.
"This has been absolutely perfect for us because obviously it's just seasonal so it doesn't take away from our other farming operations, we can still lamb and we can still have cows in the winter, because obviously there's only so much we can do."
Cardiff said when she tried applying for permission to run the campsite for up to 80 days to have more flexibility in operations, the LDNPA turned down the proposal because of the visual impact on the landscape.
She said: "We live in the valley, we live in the Lake District, there's fells all around us so the visual impact, we were never going to mitigate that, so we could never get around it."
If plans to ban pop-up campsite are confirmed following the LDNPA consultation, Cardiff said she feared she would not get planning permission again.
"It could be the end of our business and many other businesses."
Data from Pitchup.com, a campsite booking service, showed pop-up campsites in Cumbria generated about £1.6m in revenue this year, with a further £800,000 being spent in local businesses such as pubs, shops and attractions.
Cardiff has launched a petition opposing the LDNPA's proposal, which garnered hundreds of signatures.
Those in favour of pop-up campsites argue they help to deal with the Lake District's popularity and tackle issues such as fly camping.
However, critics have said the unregulated nature of them means residents are left to deal with potential problems such as noise, anti-social behaviour and impacts on the environment alone.
Bowness-on-Windermere resident Sarah Wilson campaigned with neighbours for the LDNPA to tighten rules.
She said the campaign asked for "the same planning scrutiny as everyone else" and sought to protect the national park, which is a Unesco World Heritage site.
"What we don't want to do is create pop-up campsites that damage the very environment that these visitors are coming to see."
She said she was in favour of farms diversifying, but oversight was needed to ensure heritage and landscape protections were in place.
"We're just trying to make sure that the Lake District National Park is kept as beautiful as it is already."
The LDNPA's head of development management Andrew Smith said greater control of pop-up sites would help manage problems.
"Many temporary recreational campsites are well operated, but they can also be poorly sited and have negative impacts – for example there is currently no minimum separation required between a permitted development campsite and a neighbour's house."
He added a consultation on the proposal was open until 16 November and any comments were welcome.

article:
Shop freezers in seven European countries hit by cyber-attack

Shop freezers in seven European countries hit by cyber-attack
- Published
Dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their refrigerators and freezers.
Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up, in what is believed to be the same method used in last month's incident that hit hundreds of French supermarkets.
Millions of euros worth of food had to be thrown away in October, local media reported at the time.
Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's systems, on Monday told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyber-attack and that the company had been "working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network".
He said since the French attack in early October, the company had been working to "protect our customers fridges against this vulnerability" but that the units needed physical modifications, not just software updates.
Most supermarkets across Europe are linked to the internet, and maintenance and troubleshooting can be done remotely.
"The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection. Most of our customers switched to that after the attack in France," Moelans added.
The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C (122F).
It is unclear who is behind the latest apparent attack.
In the US, authorities are investigating what caused refrigeration malfunctions at a number of American military bases in August and working together with French officials to examine whether the incidents could be linked.
Both Belgium and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre said it was working with international partners and industry to "fully understand details of an incident". No incidents have been reported in the UK.
In Flanders, northern Belgium, a Delhaize branch in Hoeilaart told news website Het Laatste Nieuws it had lost €100,000 (£83,500) worth of produce.
The manager said that estimate did not even take into account further losses that would result from closing the shop.
Carrefour, a French-owned supermarket, said the incident had only affected 15 of its Belgian stores, adding that measures had been taken immediately to ensure all shops remained open.
A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, told Reuters news agency five shops had their fridge systems attacked.
Sweden's budget furniture retailer Ikea said refrigeration systems of its store in the western Belgian city of Mons were affected, with a spokesman quoted by Reuters as saying "we cannot rule out that additional locations may be affected".
In Sweden, several ICA and Coop shops were hit.
A spokesperson for ICA confirmed the incident had affected a "small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA's central network".
"ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation," they said.
One of the ICA branches located in Sjöbo, southern Sweden, wrote on social media: "Our refrigerators and freezers have been hacked overnight and they have set the temperature to 50 degrees."
The store was closed earlier but has now reopened to customers.
Seven out of the 800 Coop stores in Sweden were also affected but the "situation is currently contained and under control", the company told the BBC.
In neighbouring Finland, refrigerator malfunctions were detected in some K-stores.
The owner of the supermarket chain Kesko was quoted by Finland's Helsingin Sanomat newspaper as saying its security experts were investigating what caused the problem.
The attack is also affecting shops in Ireland, the Netherlands and Estonia.
In Ireland, it impacted 13 SuperValu supermarkets. A spokesman for the owner of the chain, Musgrave Group, confirmed to The Irish Times that a "cyber incident" affected its refrigeration systems, but added that the impact was limited to a "specific model" of refrigerator.
A spokesperson for Danish manufacturer Danfoss told Dutch public radio channel NOS that the freezing and cooling systems of at least 17 companies in the Netherlands were attacked overnight, affecting butchers' shops and small neighbourhood stores.
A Selver supermarket in Estonia was also affected and there are reports of other affected companies in the country, according to ERR.

Plane may have broken apart ahead of deadly Florida jet crash, say investigators

Plane may have broken apart ahead of deadly Florida jet crash, say investigators
- Published
The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) says it will investigate whether parts of a jet that crashed in Florida broke off before it nose-dived and exploded, killing all nine people on board.
The Learjet 60, which was travelling from Austin, Texas to the Bahamas on Sunday, crashed on a street nine miles (14 km) from President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago resort.
A tech entrepreneur and his young family, as well as the 20-year-old copilot, were among those who died.
The NTSB said on Monday that it would also investigate to what extent ice and turbulence may have been contributing factors.
- Who are the victims of the deadly Florida jet crash? 
  - Published1 hour ago
It confirmed that, after the jet took off from Austin, the crew transmitted to air traffic control that they were encountering ice and moderate turbulence.
"We are picking up precipitation, requesting to climb to 37,000 feet if able," the crew said.
NTSB member Tom Chapman said that less than 30 seconds later, the plane began to descend and the crew issued a mayday call.
The transmission then became "unintelligible", he said, adding that: "Sadly, all aboard were lost."
The NTSB said that ice and turbulence were factors in the crash but that determining its probable cause will be a "lengthy investigatory process".
Thunderstorms had been reported in the area at the time.
Officials are also trying to find out whether a cockpit voice recorder was on board at the time of the crash and if it can be recovered.
As part of the investigation, the NTSB is working with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), representatives from Learjet as well as meteorologists and air traffic control experts.
Recovering the wreckage from the crater on the roadway will be a "daunting challenge", said Timothy Monville, an air safety investigator with the safety board.
Flight analysis indicates the jet was plummeting hundreds of feet per second before crashing.
In air traffic control audio, a crew member can be heard declaring an emergency, shouting "we are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute", before saying, "we are going to crash into the ground".
About 35 seconds after the initial mayday announcement, the last remark from the cockpit appears to be "we're out of time".
The seven people killed who were travelling as passengers were identified in a joint statement from their families as tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp, and their two children - Emma and Charlie - as well as Rachael Reed, Charmi Fehr and Anita Maria Cetina.
The pilot was named in media reports as Jeffery Gregory, while Nathalia Filgueiras, who earned her pilot's licence when she was 17, was reported to be the copilot.
As well as those killed, one man on the ground sustained a leg injury when the plane nosedived onto the street.
The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said the crash happened on Military Trail, a six-lane road lined with businesses and restaurants.
Images from the crash scene show a large fiery crater in the middle of a residential suburban street.
The debris was scattered across sports fields, businesses and homes in the area, officials told a news conference on Monday, possible evidence that the plane broke up before it hit the ground.
Unverified footage posted on social media shows what appears to be a dash-camera recording of the moment of the crash.
Trump was at Mar-a-Lago on Sunday morning, and departed from an airport nearby on Air Force One about an hour before the crash.

article:
Crypto giant Binance hit by $6.3bn hack suspected to be largest in history

Crypto giant Binance hit by $6.3bn hack suspected to be largest in history
- Published
Cryptocurrency giant Binance said on Thursday that $6.3bn (£4.7bn) of digital assets have been impacted by what is thought to be the biggest crypto hack on record.
The world's biggest crypto exchange said about half of those assets had been frozen but that many remained in the hands of the hackers, adding that it will "cover all losses".
The firm said while initial checks suggested an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals, "our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach".
Two analytics firms have attributed the incident, which eclipses a record-setting $1.5bn hack on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor.
Cyber-security firm Check Point said the unit is also known in the industry as Lazarus Group, which has been blamed for the 2025 hack.
Check Point's chief information security officer Jayant Dave said the losses estimated by Binance made it "the largest crypto theft on record".
AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said in a report that several elements of the Binance attack resemble earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack.
The lab's global head of policy Ari Redbord told the BBC the Binance hack is a "watershed moment" that is unlike anything the industry has seen.
The attacker still holds an enormous sum of stolen assets, meaning efforts to trace and recover the funds are far from over, Redbord added.
Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.
The company said in 2024 that it has more than $160bn in assets under its custody.
The exchange has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world.
Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, also said it has "high confidence" that the North Korean group are linked to the hack.
For the last few years North Korea-linked operatives have focussed on attacking cryptocurrency companies for large thefts of digital tokens.
Western security agencies have previously said stolen funds are used to finance North Korea's nuclear weapons and missile development programs.
The regime has denied any involvement in hacks in the past.
Eric Jardine, Chainalysis' Head of Research, urged every exchange to remain vigilant as the platforms are attractive targets for hackers due to the sheer value of assets.
Binance did not directly respond to BBC questions about the incident's potential links to North Korea but said: "We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice."
The incident concerns Binance.com - while much smaller crypto platform Binance.US, which provides trading services specifically for American residents - said its platform is not affected by the issue.
Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said the company's initial investigation suggested the hack started with a compromised engineer's laptop.
"That gave an attacker access to a service container, where they submitted unauthorized withdrawal transactions," he said in a statement.
"To be clear: the attacker did not simply use one engineer's permissions, and this was not a single 'one-click' action. It involved a more complex attack process. Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual. So far, we have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak."
He said a detailed "post-mortem" would be shared once the investigation was complete.
In an update, the company said in a statement on X that another investigation found there had been other breach points: "We are still gathering the facts, and will share more directly as we have them."
Check Point's Dave said this attack also resembled a hack on crypto exchange platform Bitget in September in which $388m (£289m) was lost: "This implies that attackers no longer need the vault keys. They target the systems and people with authority to use them."
In a series of posts, Yi He, Binance's co-chief executive, thanked various cryptocurrency issuers for freezing the assets.
"Safety first: withdrawals are currently disabled until the environment is confirmed to be secure," she said.
Two other major crypto platforms, Tether and Circle, said they had frozen a total of about $2.4bn of assets in response to the potential Binance hack.
World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to US President Donald Trump and his family, said it has worked with its partners to freeze stolen funds.
Crypto exchange Coinbase said it was unaffected by the incident and was monitoring the situation.
Several crypto industry observers had flagged concerns about a potential hack on Binance hours before the exchange confirmed the security issue.
Bitcoin dropped by more than 4% following the alerts. The price of other major cryptocurrencies including Ethereum and Solana also fell sharply.
