article:
Fake nuclear warnings issued after Ukrainian and Russian air alert apps hacked

Fake nuclear warnings issued after Ukrainian and Russian air alert apps hacked
- Published
Ukraine and Russia have both said air alert apps were hacked on Sunday night after fake messages warning of attacks, including nuclear, were sent to users.
Ukraine's widely used app sent red-level air raid warnings across the country, with additional warnings of radiation, chemical attacks, and street fighting sent to some residents in areas including Kyiv.
A few hours later, Russian authorities said a similar app was hacked after fake alerts, some of which contained foul language, were triggered.
It was unclear who was behind the cyberattacks or whether the two incidents were connected.
Many Ukrainian citizens are used to receiving almost nightly alerts warning of incoming Russian missile and drone attacks. Some told the BBC that, four and a half years into the war, they have disabled the app altogether.
After Sunday night's hack, the country's air force urged people to consult other official channels.
In a post on Telegram, the air force said: "The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our [Telegram] channel."
The government said it had temporarily disabled the app for maintenance, saying it had "apparently been compromised".
Some of the fake warnings were written in Russian, which would have alerted many users to the fact they were not legitimate.
But Olena, a Kyiv resident, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme she had been alarmed, saying: "The first thought was 'oh my god, I'm not prepared for this'.
"I'm prepared for blackouts, for a cut in central heating and water supply, but not for nuclear attack."
Olena says her husband then received alerts for "street fighting attacks in Kyiv" and another alert, written in Russian.
"After that I understood that somebody had attacked the app, because all notifications we get in Ukrainian."
In Russia, the government said one of its air raid alert apps had also been targeted by "a massive cyberattack", which sent "fake information to the public".
A purported screenshot of a fake alert was shared on Telegram by Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating inside Russian-held territory.
It warned some users that "nuclear warheads mounted on P1-Suns [a Ukrainian attack drone] had been launched at all regions of Russia".
The alert, which included profanities, opened with a message telling residents there was a "risk of [things] getting lively" and told them to "stock up urgently on food for three weeks and hide".
On Monday morning there was no sense the messages had caused widespread panic in Russia and the incident did not feature prominently on media outlets.
Asked about the breach, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov did not address it specifically but said all Russian government internet resources were "one way or another... under constant cyberattacks", including the presidential site, which is targeted "round the clock".
He said the proliferation of AI technology was contributing to an increase in cyberattacks.
Russia's emergencies ministry said on Monday that the app's "full functionality will be restored by the end of the day" and the hack had not impacted the wider alert system.
While both Russia and Ukraine are widely believed to carry out cyberattacks against one another, the informal language used in the hoax alerts on Sunday pointed to so-called hacktivist groups, which could be aligned to Moscow or Kyiv but are not formally directed by either government.
Those responsible for the hack on Russia's system have likely had the capability to launch such an attack for some time but decided to hold off until Ukraine's alert app was compromised, cyber experts told the BBC.
Oleksander Merezhko, chair of the foreign affairs committee in the Ukrainian parliament, said the attack did not cause panic or extreme reactions.
Merezhko told the BBC that Ukrainians, especially in Kyiv, were used to "practically non-stop alerts", adding "this message was in Russian language which immediately aroused suspicions".
He continued: "It's a very unpleasant fact but it is part of cyber war and people in Ukraine understand that. It is possible and we are quite prepared for such possibilities."
Herbert Lin, a senior research scholar for cyber policy and security at Stanford University, told BBC World Service's Newsday programme: "I think it's the first time [a hack of this kind] happened to an official Ukrainian information app, but I suspect it won't be the last."
The alerts in Ukraine were sent minutes before the end of a localised ceasefire in Ukraine's frontline Kherson region, which was implemented last Tuesday. It had been brokered in part by US First Lady Melania Trump to allow civilians to evacuate the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.
Fighting continued elsewhere while the Kherson ceasefire was in place. In the city of Dnipro alone, 15 people were killed in an attack on a train platform on Thursday.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Additional reporting by Jamie Whitehead and Helen Davidson

Developers behind plans for a £2bn data centre in southern Scotland are calling for feedback from the public as the project takes another step forward.

article:
'Absolutely disgusting and sick': Police investigate pigs' heads in public park

'Absolutely disgusting and sick': Police investigate pigs' heads in public park
- Published
An incident where pig heads were put in a public park early on Saturday morning has been described as "disgusting and sick" by a local councillor.
The heads, including one impaled on a wooden stick, appeared in Kilbroney Park in Rostrevor, County Down, accompanied by a sign that said "here piggy piggy".
Independent councillor Mark Gibbons said it was "absolutely disgusting and sick" that somebody would go to "great lengths" to do this, especially on a weekend where young families would be enjoying the Halloween break.
The PSNI confirmed they are investigating the incident and are keeping an open mind as to the motivation behind this report and considering all potential lines of enquiry.
Sinister and disturbing
Newry, Mourne and Down District Council said they were aware of the incident and are working with the PSNI and relevant partners.
"It is just awful for this to be done in a public park and a lot of people are horrified," Gibbons said.
"I'm just completely shocked by it."
The Crotlieve councillor added that he does not think it was children who would have done this because of "the huge big stake posts" that were driven into the ground. He added that the pigs heads were quite large.
"It's very sinister, very disturbing and hopefully there will be CCTV cameras being looked at through the village...and hopefully they're caught."
Gibbons had this stern message for the culprits:
"Just why on earth would you do this? If it was a prank, you've taken it too far, people need to take a good look at themselves.
"It's just horrific prank that would have scared the life out of children and people passing...and if they think this is some kind of joke that they're enjoying, then they may think again because it's been very disturbing for a lot of people."
He added he hoped no children saw it and if they did, he hoped they would be convinced by parents that the heads were fake.
"It's just vile."
'Extreme attempt at a prank'
One resident, called Jack was walking his dog early on Saturday and was shocked at the sight.
"It's a very extreme attempt at a prank in a public space which is very busy at weekends with families, the Parkrun, and the couple of planned Halloween activities in the village for kids today," he said.
"This is a public space used daily by families, young children and people walking their dogs. Whatever the intention behind it, leaving animal remains on display like this is completely unacceptable."
He added whether it was Halloween prank or not, "it's crossed the line from harmless fun to something disgusting".
"There's absolutely no need for this in a public park. It's disturbing, unhygienic and shows a complete lack of consideration for everyone else using the space."

Six flights across Europe searched after suspected bomb threats

Six passenger planes across Europe, two of which departed from the UK, have been inspected following a series of suspected bomb threats.
Two Ryanair flights, one originating from Dublin and the other from Lisbon, were searched after landing in Rome following anonymous tips but no explosives were found, sources at the city's Fiumicino airport told the BBC.
The Dublin flight was escorted by the Italian air force until landing.
Meanwhile, authorities have also searched planes in Poland, Spain and Bulgaria. It is unclear if the incidents are connected.
In Rome, sources at Fiumicino airport told the BBC police bomb disposal experts carried out standard security protocols to ensure the safety of all passengers and crew.
Inspections of the passengers, luggage, and the aircraft yielded negative results, and the alert has since been cleared.
One plane which landed in Murcia, southern Spain - a Ryanair flight coming from Manchester - was also found not to have any explosives on board, Spanish authorities said.
Two flights heading to Warsaw were also affected, including one from London Heathrow.
The Heathrow flight was originally meant to land at the Polish capital's main airport, Chopin, but was diverted instead to the smaller Modlin airport, briefly forcing its closure.
A Scandinavian Airlines flight from Copenhagen to Warsaw-Chopin landed as planned.
Bulgarian media reported a flight landed in the capital Sofia after a bomb threat was received by email. A Bulgarian interior ministry spokesperson told AFP the flight came from Bergamo in Italy. Bulgarian local media earlier reported that the plane flew from Israel.
These four incidents come a day after a Wizz Air flight from London Luton made an emergency landing in Budapest, escorted by a Hungarian fighter jet, after a bomb threat.
Wizz Air said later that security checks had been made and nothing was found.

article:
Shock and anger in India after eight-year-old beats six-year-old in classroom

Shock and anger in India after eight-year-old beats six-year-old in classroom
- Published
Warning: Some details in this story could be distressing for some readers.
There has been shock and anger in India over video footage from the CCTV of a school that shows an eight-year-old boy brutally beating a six-year-old girl.
The girl, who was seriously injured, is recovering in hospital and is now out of danger but remains traumatised by the assault in Haryana state, her family has said.
Police say they have registered a case and the eight-year-old has been sent to a home for juvenile offenders where he is undergoing psychiatric evaluation.
The school principal and two other teachers have been suspended for suspected negligence, police say.
The incident that took place in a government school in Panchkula in the northern state of Haryana on 28 October came to light at the weekend after the CCTV footage went viral on social media.
The motive of the boy is not known.
The horrific assault has sent shock waves through the country. Many people expressed anguish over the little girl's injuries - and the brutality displayed by the boy.
Police say the eight-year-old, who is studying in third grade, told the girl that her father was waiting for her in a classroom where he assaulted her.
The family of the girl, who studies in kindergarten, reached the school after being informed by an auto-rickshaw driver that he had gone to pick her up but could not find her.
"When the girl was not found even after school ended, we went in to look for her. No one there knew where she was," her father told BBC Punjabi.
He said the boy who assaulted his daughter told him that she was in a classroom upstairs, where he found his seriously injured daughter.
"When I saw her, I almost screamed. Looking at her condition, I thought they'd killed my daughter. If a child isn't safe in school, then where will she be safe?"
The girl was initially taken to a local hospital but later moved to the multi-speciality PGIMER hospital in the nearby city of Chandigarh.
A statement from PGIMER said the six-year-old girl was "brought to the hospital with critical injuries".
She is under the care of a multidisciplinary team of specialists, which is closely monitoring her condition and providing all necessary medical attention, the hospital said.
"The circumstances involving this little child are deeply concerning. We want to ensure that she receives the best possible medical care, along with all the support and comfort she needs," the statement quoted hospital director Vivek Lal as saying.
The hospital later shared a photo of Dr Lal with the girl sitting in her father's lap and smiling.
In a video statement on Saturday, senior police official Aditi Singh said they had registered an FIR (first information report) against the school management for "negligence" and were investigating what happened.
"The boy is being evaluated by mental experts under the Juvenile Justice Act and further action will be taken accordingly," she added.
Under Indian law, an eight-year-old cannot be punished or sent to jail so the child has been sent to an observation home run by the Juvenile Justice Board, another senior police official Amarinder Singh said.
The emphasis in cases involving minors is on reformation and counselling, he added.
Meanwhile, the Haryana state government has formed a committee to investigate what happened and whether there was any negligence in the case.

Binance users withdraw $3.6bn after largest-ever crypto hack

Binance users withdraw $3.6bn after largest-ever crypto hack
- Published
Binance customers withdrew $3.6bn (£2.7bn) of assets from the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange as it reopened on Sunday following what is believed to be the largest hack in history.
The firm suspended all transactions in the wake of the incident, which impacted $6.3bn worth of digital assets.
Major organisations, including the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), have accused North Korea of being responsible for the cyber-attack.
The company said it has covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach but the remaining amount may take longer to source. Binance has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack.
Binance said on X: "Between 06:00 and 15:30 [GMT] on November 1, we processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of approximately $3.64 billion."
There was an "initial spike" in withdrawals, which later declined and "are stabilising as expected", it added.
Sunday's net withdrawals account for just over 2% of the $171bn of assets under its management, said Binance.
The firm said last week that it has reserved more than $6.3bn in funds, to deal with the fallout of the attack.
Binance also said withdrawals of more than two dozen major cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum have resumed and that more services will resume in phases once security checks are completed.
Funds linked to the Binance hack continue to be laundered, according to Alec Zebrick, senior manager in global services at Chainalysis, which has been working with the firm and governments to get the stolen money back.
"We continue to see funds being laundered quite actively," he told the BBC's Today Programme.
"The attackers are layering these funds across many thousands of addresses, across thousands of deposits," he added.

  - Published22 October
The attack on Binance has been attributed to TraderTraitor, a North Korean cybercrime group also known as the Lazarus Group, which stole a then-record $1.5bn from crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.
The FBI on Saturday published a list of cryptocurrency wallet addresses linked to the group and urged partners in the industry to help by blocking transactions involving them.
The exchange scrambled to urge cryptocurrency issuers to freeze affected assets.
Binance said last week that early checks suggest the incident may have started with a compromised laptop that belonged to an engineer, allowing hackers to find a way to make unauthorised transactions.
The hack hit Binance's global centralised exchange, Binance.com, while its US-facing platform has said it was not affected by the issue.
Binance said it had replaced customers' assets using a combination of sources, including its corporate treasury as well as its futures insurance and emergency reserve funds.
"Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident," the firm said.
Cryptocurrencies are digital assets traded on exchanges such as Binance. Unlike cash, they do not exist in physical form and are managed on computers, smartphones and other digital devices.

article:
Why North Korea's 'elite' hackers are the prime suspect in major Binance hack

Why North Korea's 'elite' hackers are the prime suspect in major Binance hack
- Published
Two major blockchain analytics firms say they have robust intelligence pointing to a North Korean state-backed group as the likely culprits in the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange.
The Lazarus Group, a North Korean hacking unit also known as TraderTraitor, was identified "with high confidence" by TRM Labs, as well as Chainalysis.
This incident is just the latest linked to the country, one of the poorest in the world and where access to the internet is severely restricted.
Experts accuse the government of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un of relying on cybercrime to finance itself, something Pyongyang has long denied.
Though not financial, the nation's most spectacular suspected hack took place in 2014. The target: Sony Pictures, which had made the Hollywood film The Interview. The film involves a plot to assassinate Kim.
The resulting hack exposed thousands of embarrassing emails exchanged among the studio's top executives.

  - Published4 days ago
Last year, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said North Korea was responsible for the theft of $1.5bn on the Bybit exchange.
In the aftermath of that incident, the agency said TraderTraitor had moved to quickly launder and disperse the stolen assets, converting them to Bitcoin and other digital assets with a goal of eventually turning them into hard currency.
The FBI has broadly accused North Korea of "illicit cybercrime and virtual asset theft activities".
The nation has systematically developed its cyber operations, recruiting the most promising students from universities and channeling them into hacker groups overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, according to reports.
Some of the cyberwarfare conducted takes place just over the nation's border in China, according to analysis from tech groups.
Much of its hacking activity has centred on monetary gain.
North Korean hackers are also suspected in the theft of $620m worth of cryptocurrency in 2022.
In this most recent heist, North Korean agents are accused of using a special authorisation to turn a Binance hot wallet, which is connected to the internet, into one that moved funds automatically to the attacker.
TRM said it's likely the attacker gained access to Binance's hot wallet signing system as part of the scheme.
Binance has not directly responded to the BBC's queries about the incident's potential links to the area.
The company had initially said it thought an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals, but later said the attack was wider.
"Our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach," Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said.
Some 80% of stolen assets have been secured, a Binance spokesperson said on Friday, but the rest remains unaccounted for.
If the accusations are true, the record-making heist shows how powerful suspected North Korean hackers have become – a sign that the tools of the hacking trade have grown sharper.
Experts say the rise of artificial intelligence has also given threat actors new ways to carry out crime, through automation and other means.
In this case, it's plausible that AI was used to infiltrate Binance's systems.
As Chainalysis put it, the attacker used laundering patterns "we have not seen before".

article:
The people saving hundreds of pounds by dumpster diving

From scooters to shampoo - the people saving hundreds from dumpster diving
- Published
Darryl Baker was shocked to see piles of clothes dumped beside the recycling bins outside her local supermarket.
On several trips to the dumpsters she has also found a host of other items, such as "a perfectly decent" Ikea picture frame and children's scooters.
Always on the lookout for ways to save money and appalled by the waste, the thrifty mother-of-two from north London asked supermarket staff if she could take some of it.
Permission granted, "I got my children entire new wardrobes," says Darryl, 39, adding that she's stuff put away for years to come.
During a six-month stint this year, "I have probably saved hundreds of pounds," says the freelance journalist.
Darryl reels off the names of brands she has salvaged - Ralph Lauren, Nike and The North Face, among others. "My mind was blown," she says. "This stuff is just strewn all over the floor."
In addition to finding clothing for her children and her nephews and nieces, she keeps some for herself. Others she donates or sells, including recently getting £30 for a men's Barbour jacket.
Darryl has joined the ranks of so-called dumpster divers – people who rummage through commercial bins for treasures. Motivations include saving money, giving items to charity and disgust at how often perfectly usable items are being consigned to waste - or a combination of all three.
'I'm a bit of a Robin Hood'
Texan Jeff Ferrell has been rooting around in trash for more than 50 years.
"I still dumpster dive every day by bicycle," says the 72-year old, who lives in Fort Worth, and has written books on the topic. "I still enjoy it as much, or more, than ever."
Jeff considers himself a "bit of Robin Hood mixed with anarchist direct action", only scrounging in more affluent neighbourhoods and giving away many of his finds.
"Almost everything in our home is scrounged, and I never buy, for example, soap or toiletries or medical supplies, or shoes and clothes and tools and garden supplies," he says.
Jeff looks for discarded metal to sell at a scrapyard which, he says, earns him around $150 (£110) every two weeks. His wife sells his other finds, such as "an antique or piece of jewellery", on eBay.
Through savings and selling the more valuable items, he estimates his finds are worth "tens of thousands of dollars a year".
'If something catches my eye, I'll grab it'
While dumpster diving may have been considered taboo in the past, it's now something many people are proud to do and post about online.
Millie Diamond, a London-based stylist, posts videos on Instagram of her rummaging through bins. But she has a very specific aim - to unearth fabrics and clothing that she can salvage and refashion into new items, some of which she then sells.
She estimates that one dress she found was worth £600.
"I'm a bit of a magpie. I like collecting things off the street or anywhere that there's a freebie. If I see something that catches my eye, then I'll grab it."
Millie, 36, began bin diving after spotting some fabrics discarded by a business that had shut down. "I literally clambered into the bin. It turned out it was loads of vintage clothes."
'I haven't bought shampoo for years'
For Charlotte Bayford in Essex it's all about timing. Her best finds come when students at Essex University head home for the summer and ditch anything they don't want to take with them.
This includes half-filled toiletries. "I haven't bought shampoo for eight years," says the 44-year-old sales assistant. "I'd say that has saved me some money."
Like other dumpster divers, Charlotte gives a lot of her finds to charity. But she has also filled her house with salvaged objects, and sells on some valuable items.
Food, as long as it remains sealed, is fair game too. "I've found tins of Heinz baked beans, perfectly fine. I'm quite happy to eat those," Charlotte says.
But is taking things out of bins and keeping them acceptable in the eyes of the law?
Jeff, who is professor emeritus of sociology at Texas Christian University, says many US cities have made the practice illegal, including New York, Cleveland and Wichita.
"Dumpster diving is considered illegal [in such places] because that which is thrown away now belongs to the city... or to the private company that provided trash services," he explains. Any dumpster diver also risks trespass charges.
In Fort Worth, where Jeff lives, items can only be removed from bins if they are on public land, external.
In the UK, Sunjay Versani of Duncan Lewis Solicitors says it depends on the circumstances.
"In many cases involving genuinely discarded goods, prosecution is unlikely," he says.
"But there is no general rule that something is free to take simply because it has been put in a skip or bin. If in doubt, the safest approach is to ask the owner or business for permission."

Huge data centre plan sees hundreds attend meeting

Huge data centre plan sees hundreds attend meeting
- Published
More than 400 people were at a public meeting to share concerns about plans to build what would be one of the UK's biggest data centres and accompanying solar farms.
The Longmarsh Green Energy (LGE) project would cover 4,695 acres (1,900 hectares) of farmland across two sites south of King's Lynn in Norfolk.
Dr Martin Little, who leads the Stop Longmarsh Energy (SLE) campaign group, said the proposal would "destroy" farming land.
LGE, which revealed the plans last month, said they "welcome comments during this consultation period".
The hall at Tilney St Lawrence was full on Monday evening, with locals even following proceedings from the car park.
Farmer James Kitchen grows wheat, barley and oilseed rape on land that would neighbour the data centre.
He said he was "gobsmacked" to hear about the project.
Natural England, a public body which advises the government, classifies the affected area as grade one - meaning it is "excellent quality agricultural land".
"We've got some really good heavy silt land here - it's very good at producing good quality produce," said Kitchen.
Despite this year's drought, he said his yields were still high because of the way the soil in the Fens retains moisture.
Resident Amanda Naish said the project would ruin the countryside views she currently enjoyed.
"I just feel like I'm living in a nightmare," she said.
"I'm not against AI. I think it's a necessity for us all going forward. I just think that there needs to be thought, there needs to be balance."
David Rutter, who lives in the village, has been researching data centres since receiving a letter from LGE explaining the plans.
He fears the noise will be heard up to a mile away and will effect human health and the environment including birds.
Little, who lives in the village, said he was proud to be a so-called nimby - an acronym for "not in my back yard".
"Everybody - and I do mean everybody - is a nimby when the time comes.
"If anyone out there thinks they aren't a nimby, come and buy my house from me and live surrounded by glass for the rest of time."
Little echoed the views of those who spoke at the meeting, saying they were not against data centres or solar farms, but that they should be smaller in scale and on brownfield sites.
Referring to the potential loss of farmland, he added: "Is it dinner or data? It's as simple as that."
- How has community reacted to major data centre plan? 
  - Published17 October
LGE was invited to the meeting - which was organised by the local parish council - but declined.
In a statement, it said: "We have already received helpful feedback during the community consultation.
"We are committed to working with residents nearest to the proposals to develop site-specific mitigation measures, including appropriate planting, screening and landscape treatments prior to submission."
South West Norfolk MP Terry Jermy said the meeting turnout had been "amazing".
"Food security is absolutely crucial," he said. "We cannot have improving energy security but worsening food security."
The Labour politician said he would be pushing for a ban on solar farms being built on farmland which is classed as grade two or higher.
Parts of Europe already have restrictions on placing solar farms on high quality farming land, including across Italy and in parts of Spain.
In last week's Budget, the chancellor announced a Data Centre Covenant, requiring operators to invest in local communities, create jobs and protect water supplies in return for the best grid connections.
The scale of the proposal deems it a nationally significant infrastructure project, so the ultimate decision rests with the government rather than the local council.
A public consultation is open via the project's website, external until 26 November. An application is due to be submitted by April 2027.
It could take six months for the plans to be examined by the Planning Inspectorate. A decision could be made by July 2028.

Indian tourist killed after two helicopters collide near Everest base camp

Indian tourist killed after two helicopters collide near Everest base camp
- Published
An Indian tourist has died after two helicopters collided while attempting to land near the base camp of Mount Everest, two officials have confirmed to the BBC.
Verified footage of the crash showed the helicopter blades of the two aircraft clipping each other as they came into land at around 08:15 local time (02:30 GMT) in Pheriche, approximately 12km (7 miles) south of Mount Everest Base Camp.
Helicopter company Fishtail Air named the man killed in the crash as Vasanth Kumar Balaramudu.
The helicopter company said one of its vehicles was involved in the collision and that another passenger and the helicopter's captain had been injured.
The injured passengers and crew members on board were rescued and taken to Kathmandu, Fishtail Air added in a statement.
The injured passenger was a tourist from New Zealand, an official of Solukhumbu district, Bhupendra Thapa, told BBC Nepal.
The other helicopter involved was operated by Air Dynasty and had been carrying cargo, the company said.
It was operated by one crew member who sustained no injuries, it added.
A spokesman for Nepal's Civil Aviation Authority, Gyanendra Bhul, said: "It appears the accident happened when two helicopters... attempted to land at the same spot."
In the video footage of the incident, the weather conditions look clear and no strong wind effects are visible. One helicopter appears to be making a more rapid descent than the other.
Helicopters are widely used for transport in the Himalayan nation due to its challenging terrain. But its rapidly changing weather conditions and high altitude often make aviation operations hazardous.
The village of Pheriche, located on the trekking route to the summit of the world's tallest mountain, Mount Everest, is just over 4,000m (13,120ft) above sea level.
Climbing expeditions to Everest and Ama Dablam mountain are currently under way in the region, as autumn is a popular climbing season.

article:
Ex-Tory MP admits altering image of passport to access gambling website

Ex-Tory MP admits altering image of passport to access gambling website
- Published
A former Conservative MP has admitted illegally altering a date on an image of her passport in order to access a gambling website.
Katie Wallis, who uses female pronouns and was formerly known as Jamie Wallis, was due to stand trial on two charges of possessing a false passport and possessing a false passport with improper intention.
Wallis, who represented Bridgend from 2019 to 2024, has been found formally not guilty of those charges after agreeing to plead guilty to a new charge under the Computer Misuse Act.
She was given a conditional discharge for nine months in a hearing at Cardiff Crown Court.
Prosecution barrister Richard Posner told the court that Wallis had a "recognised gambling problem" and had "taken action" to deal with the issue by registering with Gamstop, a service that bars someone from accessing gambling websites.
In April 2022, while suffering "acute psychiatric distress", Wallis used her own computer to digitally edit the date on an image of a passport to access an online gambling site.
The court heard that Wallis had a genuine physical passport which had "not been altered or tampered with" and that she had not "attempted to use an image of anyone else".
The judge was told that Wallis deposited money onto a gambling website which was subsequently lost, but that no-one else suffered any financial loss.
The court heard this was on a single occasion and that Wallis had acted on an "impulse".
Subsequently Wallis has reapplied to be blocked from using gambling sites.
The court heard that, at the time of the offence, Wallis was suffering from a "serious mental disorder" after coming out as transgender while a sitting MP, having become separated from her family and having publicly disclosed having been a victim of rape.
Posner told the judge that Wallis had co-operated with the prosecution to reach a conclusion in this case.
Judge Shomon Khan said he accepted this was a "single impulsive" act in a "period of psychological distress" and that Wallis had provided "compelling personal mitigation".

Train attacker said 'I am the baddest', trial hears
- Published
A man accused of a mass train stabbing was heard saying "I am the baddest, no-one is as bad as me", on a different train the day before the attack, a court has heard.
Anthony Williams is accused of attempting to murder 10 people on a London-bound train which had to make an emergency stop in Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire on 1 November last year.
A passenger texted the British Transport Police reporting a male behaving erratically the night before, Cambridge Crown Court heard.
Williams, 33, of Langford Road in Peterborough, denies 14 counts of attempted murder over events on the train, and beforehand in Peterborough and London.
He is accused of trying to kill three people in Peterborough during the evening of 31 October. Later that night he boarded a train from the city's railway station, headed towards London.
In a statement read to jurors, another passenger, Keirah Lee-Oakman, said a male entered the train, sat down and "appeared to be talking and mumbling to himself".
She said he began walking up and down the carriages stating "boom and power", repeatedly saying things like "I haven't got it" as well as referencing the devil, jurors were told.
Lee-Oakman said he was "acting in an aggressive and intimidating manner... I felt unsafe" and while on the train she sent a text to the British Transport Police.
Jurors heard police officers attended Stevenage station but the male dropped down on to the tracks and officers eventually deemed it unsafe to continue following him.

Abbie Harrison-Evans was on the train with her partner Ethan Daniels. She said there was a "male shouting from the front of the train" who was "playing spooky Halloween music on his phone".
His behaviour was "erratic" and her "first impression was he was suffering from a mental condition", the court heard.
She sent a Snapchat to Daniels stating "we going to get attacked or what?".
Harrison-Evans said Williams had a black rucksack on the seat next to him and "kept grabbing it and saying 'I'm going to do it'."
"It looked like he was reaching for something inside the black rucksack," she said.
Daniels said he heard the man state: "I am the baddest, no-one is as bad as me."
Williams is also accused of attempting to murder Isaiah Idris on a Docklands Light Railway train in London in the early hours of 1 November.
In a video recorded interview played to jurors, Idris said: "Only a couple of seconds after the train started moving, he sliced my face.

He said the man repeatedly asked "are you beefing the devil?", and tried to attack him again, before the victim blocked him with his hand.

article:
No more washing up: How Airbnb's new house rules have divided hosts and guests

No more washing up: How Airbnb's new house rules have divided hosts and guests
- Published
When Lisa Clewes returned to her Welsh holiday let after a group of guests checked out, she was horrified by the mess.
Just days earlier, she had met the group in person and helped with their luggage.
But after a dinner party, the house was left "in a complete mess" with broken glasses, drinks cans on the floor, pans full of food on the table and fish guts left in the garden.
"It was really unbelievable. Had I had another booking the same day, I would have had to cancel or delay check-in," says Clewes.
She charges a cleaning fee that covers around 75% of the cost of a cleaner and asks guests to empty the fridge, put rubbish in the bins and load the dishwasher.
But Airbnb's new rules mean hosts can no longer ask guests to do jobs normally carried out by cleaners, including washing and putting away dishes, stripping beds and taking rubbish off site.
The updated guidelines, which apply to bookings made globally from 20 November, state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules and add other "reasonable" requests.
Clewes says it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her three-bedroom property. She fears guests leaving more mess could mean hiring extra cleaners and increasing costs – expenses that may ultimately be passed on to her guests.
The changes have come as a relief to guests like Jessica Newhook, who says she has been faced with lengthy checkout lists, often on top of hefty cleaning fees.
She booked an Airbnb in Florida for a family reunion of 11 guests and says they had to "leave the property move-in ready for the cleaners", despite paying a $250 (£187) cleaning fee.
Newhook says the host told them to wash and fold towels, clean the bedding and kitchen, and sweep and mop the floors. She was also warned by the host that their behaviour needed to improve or they could be told to leave, because they had left chairs blocking bins.
"We had rules about everything and it was not relaxing at all."
While Newhook likes the home comforts of staying in an Airbnb, she says the combination of relentless rules and rising cleaning fees has taken away much of its appeal.
"It is getting to the point where a hotel is cheaper and I know what to expect."
Krissi Foskett, 46, from Glasgow, runs a national cleaning company and regularly stays in Airbnb properties so "can see the issue from both sides".
During a recent stay in Stafford, she paid a £35 cleaning fee but was still asked to strip the beds, put on a wash, empty bins and carry rubbish down a long track to a recycling area.
"I don't particularly mind doing those things, but it did make me question what exactly I was paying the additional cleaning fee for," she says.
For Foskett, there is a difference between being a considerate guest – "putting your dirty dishes in the dishwasher" – and being "expected to prepare the property for the next guests".
Through her cleaning business, she has also seen the other extreme, with teams arriving to find broken furniture, vomit and pet urine.
While she sympathises with hosts facing tight turnarounds and rising cleaning costs, these should not be passed on to guests, she says.
"If you're running an Airbnb as a business, professional cleaning is a cost of doing business."
Anthony Marsh, who co-owns a cabin retreat in North Yorkshire with his husband, used to list five of their 12 properties on Airbnb, but says the new rules have prompted him to reduce this number to just two.
His concern with the changes is that "Airbnb has effectively given guests permission to come and leave properties a tip, and a host can't do anything about it".
He believes asking guests to wash their pots and put out the bins is hardly unreasonable and, with a small cleaning team and tight turnaround times, he worries extra mess could leave properties unready for the next arrivals.
"It's common sense and common decency," he says.
His company does not charge a cleaning fee, and Marsh says most guests are respectful. But fees are more common than not. Some 63.2% of Airbnb listings charge a cleaning fee, with an average cost of £55 according to data from AirROI, external.
Laura Lewis runs a directory that helps holiday-let owners market their properties and connect with potential guests.
Many of her clients also list on Airbnb and she says most are unhappy with the new rules, arguing that asking guests to wash up is a matter of basic respect.
"Some people say it's factored into the cleaning fee, but I wouldn't leave a holiday let with all the washing-up to do. It's not the right thing," she says.
The announcement has added to growing frustration among owners following increases in Airbnb's commission rates last year. Many are investing in their own websites and social media to attract direct bookings and avoid platform fees.
Lewis has taken the same approach with the three treehouses on her farm – most of her bookings are already direct and she now plans to remove her listings from Airbnb altogether.
Not all hosts are concerned about the changes, however. Matt Porsz, who hosts and manages other Airbnb properties full-time, believes the update will improve the guest experience without changing how most people behave.
Guests at his property in south-west London are asked only to lock up and return the keys. "People sometimes strip the beds or do things without me asking, and that's nice for my cleaners, but I don't expect it."
Porsz doubts the changes will lead to guests leaving properties in a worse state, pointing to Airbnb's mutual review system.
"If I put a big chore list, I wouldn't expect a five-star review and vice versa – if a guest leaves the place in a state, you're not going to give them a good review."
He believes the system encourages both sides to behave reasonably, and that most guests will continue to treat properties with respect.
"Airbnb is trying to cut out the silly stuff because it's not a good guest experience."

article:
'Dissident republicans may be responsible' for hotel explosive device

'Dissident republicans may be responsible' for hotel explosive device
- Published
Police believe dissident republicans may be responsible for a "viable postal device" which was delivered to a hotel in Londonderry.
Ammunition technical officers were sent to the hotel at Ebrington Square in the Waterside after the package was discovered at about 15:20 GMT on Tuesday.
They carried out a controlled explosion on the device, which was later taken away for a forensic examination.
Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) Ch Supt Gillian Kearney condemned it as "shameful and utterly abhorrent", adding that "those responsible clearly do not care who or what they harm".
"We are keeping an open mind as to who is responsible and we are working through a number of lines of inquiry, one of which, at this time, is that dissident republicans may be responsible," Kearney said.
She said the investigation was at an early stage and she appealed to anyone with information to contact police as "it could make all the difference".
A number of people were evacuated from The Ebrington hotel, along with staff from neighbouring premises.
The chair of a local policing watchdog said he believed the incident it may be linked to the Ministry of Defence (MoD) having a stall at a careers fair at the hotel last month.
A Halloween funfair had been taking place a short distance away from the hotel.
It remained open during the security alert.
Toni Collins said the targeting of The Ebrington was a "disgrace", particularly in the run-up to Halloween when thousands of people would be in the city.
"No-one wants it and no one supports it," she said.
Teresa Boyle from Enniskillen is visiting the city. She said the community had moved on and no-one wanted to return to the conflict of the past.
"That's what people want, peace," she added.
Mayor of Derry City and Strabane District Council Grace Uí Niallais said her "thoughts are with the staff and anyone impacted".
"This was a serious and reckless incident which has no doubt caused trauma to all involved," she said.
"We will not go back to the past but instead look forward to the fantastic four days of Halloween celebrations ahead."
Justice Minister Naomi Long condemned the incident, calling it "abhorrent".
"The viable device was placed in the vicinity of families and young people celebrating Halloween," she said.
"It was an utterly shameful and dangerous act and the people behind it have shown absolutely no regard to the community or businesses affected."
She paid tribute to the police officers who responded to the incident, "once again putting themselves in harm's way to ensure the safety of the public".
Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant said the incident was "very worrying".
He added: "This is absolutely despicable. Whoever has been involved in this, I very much hope that we'll be able to track down who it is and they should face the full force of the law."
'No justification whatsoever'
Ulster Unionist councillor Darren Guy, who chairs the local policing and community safety partnership, believes the incident was timed to cause maximum disruption.
He also said it may have been linked to the MoD being represented at a careers event at the hotel in September.
"Recently, there was a careers event held in that hotel where I believe an RAF [Royal Air Force] stall was there," said Guy.
"This was specifically done this week to cause as much disruption as possible during the 40th Halloween celebrations with thousands of international visitors visiting the city and the amount of families, especially young families, going out to enjoy the many things on offer.
"It is totally reckless and these people don't think about anyone else but themselves."
Sinn Féin councillor Christopher Jackson said it was too early to "speculate" about any link between the alert and the jobs fair.
"We need clarification from those responsible," Jackson said.
He said this was "a disgusting attack on the city and the people of Derry".
"There is no justification whatsoever for carrying this out and putting people in danger, especially when the city is gearing up for the 40th anniversary of the Halloween festival," he added.
"Derry is a warm and welcoming place and it's disgusting why someone or some organisation did this."
SDLP MP Colum Eastwood told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme that the incident must have been terrifying for those members of the public in the vicinity of the hotel.
"This was clearly a viable device which is really frightening for the staff and the visitors to the hotel and to the hundreds, probably thousands of kids who were at that funfair yesterday and have been over the past number of days," Eastwood said.
"I don't know what entered someone's head to think this was a good idea.
"It is appalling, reckless and achieves absolutely nothing."
Julie Middleton, Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) assembly member for Foyle, told BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme that she was "deeply disturbed and disgusted".
"There is no excuse to leave a viable device anywhere at all, but in the middle of Ebrington Square, where you have people at their work, families out enjoying some half-term fun and tourists visiting and unfortunately this was designed to cause disruption and with any viable device, it was obviously designed to cause harm," she said.
'Innocent lives put at risk'
The Police Federation for Northern Ireland (PFNI) described sending a viable device to a hotel as "the height of madness".
"If this device had detonated, there's no knowing the damage it would have done," PFNI chair Liam Kelly said.
"Not for the first time at the hands of these reckless fools, innocent lives were put at risk."
Kelly said those responsible were "reckless thugs" who wanted to "kill and maim", but that there was an "utter futility to their efforts to destabilise society".

Valuable bust 'found in shed' could still be sold overseas, says council

Valuable bust 'found in shed' could still be sold overseas, says council
- Published
An 18th Century sculpture valued at more than £3m could be sold to an overseas buyer if a museum fails to raise the funds to buy it.
The bust of Highland landowner and MP Sir John Gordon was made by Edmé Bouchardon, whose other works have been exhibited in the Louvre in Paris and J Paul Getty Museum in Los Angeles.
It lay forgotten in local authority storage for years - and was claimed to have been found propping open the door of a garden shed - before it was put up for sale by Highland Council.
Invergordon Naval Museum and Heritage Centre wants to buy the artwork, but a new report said if it did not have funds needed by 1 December the council could proceed with a sale to an overseas buyer.
The profits of the sale are to go to Invergordon, a town named after the Gordon family.
There is a temporary ban preventing the marble bust from going abroad to give the museum the chance to purchase it.
But the report, external to next week's meeting of Highland Council's Black Isle and Easter Ross committee said the sale to a prospective overseas buyer could go ahead if the museum's bid was unsuccessful.
Highland Council looks after the sculpture on behalf of Invergordon Common Good Fund.
Councillors approved the sale in 2024 with the money raised to be put towards a community fund.
Invergordon Naval Museum and Heritage Centre must raise £3.1m by 1 December under the terms of a sale agreement, but in August it said it was struggling to secure grants.
- 'Serious buyer' for council's £3.1m marble bust 
  - Published30 April
- Objection to overseas sale of council's '£2.5m' bust 
  - Published8 August 2025
"Highland Council's rush to monetise a common good asset has completely broken the system," a spokesperson for the museum said.
"The council has created a nightmare scenario where the community is punished for the council's own unethical sales process."
The spokesperson added: "We are expected to raise more than £3m to buy back our own property, while being barred from the very grant funds built to preserve national treasures."
Trustees are urging Scottish ministers to intervene and have launched an online crowdfunding campaign.
Highland Council said it had followed all relevant legal, governance and decision-making processes.
It said it had carried out a statutory public consultation, adding that "a majority of respondents" had been in favour of the sale.
The council added that it had made an application to a sheriff court seeking authorisation to sell the bust.
It said no objections were received during that process and the sheriff approved the proposed sale.
The Scottish government said it was aware of concerns raised regarding the Bouchardon Bust.
A spokesperson said: "Common good assets are administered by local authorities under their own statutory responsibilities, though we take seriously the duty to ensure consultation requirements under the Community Empowerment (Scotland) Act 2015 are properly observed."
"We are engaging with the relevant parties to get the full information to determine the appropriate next steps."

The bust depicts Sir John Gordon whose family owned large areas of land in Sutherland and Ross-shire and established the town of Invergordon on the Cromarty Firth.
Gordon was a young man travelling through continental Europe when he met the renowned artist Edmé Bouchardon in Rome in 1728 and the sculpture was made.
Invergordon Town Council bought the marble bust for £5 in 1930, but it was later placed in storage at an industrial estate.
It was claimed it was used to prop open the door of a shed.
When the value of the bust eventually came to be fully appreciated, Highland Council decided to sell it with the funds raised to go towards helping the community of Invergordon.

article:
If hackers can take control of a supermarket freezer, how vulnerable is other tech?

If hackers can take control of a supermarket freezer, how vulnerable is other tech?
- Published
Supermarkets across Europe have been hit by a suspected cyber-attack affecting their fridges and freezers, and raising concern about the vulnerabilities of internet-connected hardware from industrial machinery to humble domestic appliances.
Smart devices which are connected to the internet can include fridges, central heating, and even washing machines.
And while that makes them easier to control remotely, in theory, any device which goes online can potentially be exploited by malicious actors.
However, that doesn't mean hackers can easily take control of it, and big brands generally go to great lengths to make sure their tech is secure.
Exploits have been found before in some devices. In 2015, researchers demonstrated how a vulnerability in a Samsung smart fridge could allow them to intercept internet traffic.
But there's no evidence domestic appliances are being targeted in the cyber-attacks which targeted supermarkets in November.
Ciaran Martin, former chief executive of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says manufacturers needed to do more to make connected devices secure.
"There's a lot more that we need to demand of big tech to give us safer devices and products in the first place," he said.
He advised consumers to keep devices updated and enable multi-factor authentication wherever possible.
"I know it's a pain, but it only takes a few seconds," he said.
Since April 2024, UK law has required manufacturers of certain consumer smart devices to meet minimum cyber security standards, including requirements around passwords and security updates.
The NCSC said it was working with international partners and industry to understand the supermarket incidents, but it was unaware of any impact on the UK.
However, researchers from UK Cyber Defence have identified more than 800 refrigeration and building-control interfaces associated with British retailers that can be accessed over the public internet.
That doesn't necessarily mean they can be hacked, but it could leave them exposed to attackers exploiting weak passwords or software vulnerabilities.
The government has already held talks with senior food retailers about cyber resilience, following earlier attacks on supermarkets.
Helen Dickinson, chief executive of the British Retail Consortium, has said cyber incidents are a major concern for retailers, with businesses working alongside the NCSC to share intelligence and strengthen their defences.
It would not be the first time that hacks have raised concern about impact on food supply.
When UK supermarkets M&S and the Co-op were targeted by ransomware hackers in May 2025, the retailers struggled to stock some shop shelves with fresh deliveries.
Customers across the UK complained of empty shelves in the days following the attack.
Tom Hegel, a researcher at cyber-security firm SentinelOne, said retailers must be clearer about responsibility.
"The question retailers need to answer is who owns the security of that equipment, not just who repairs it," he said.
He said internet connectivity can make everyday technology more convenient, but security needed to keep pace.
"Once an attacker can operate those controls, legitimate functions such as defrosting become tools for disruption," he said.
"Changing a setting can destroy physical stock, not just interrupt a computer system."
Could cars, power plants and water supplies be vulnerable?
Outside of the home, connected tech is used to remotely manage industrial machinery and vehicles.
Cyber security expert Ken Munro pointed to a 2015 demonstration in which researchers remotely hacked a Jeep through its internet-connected entertainment system, prompting improvements in vehicle security.
"Fortunately, the vehicle industry woke up to this and fixed the problem," he said.
Mobile connections are also widely used to monitor equipment in power plants and water networks, allowing engineers to manage systems remotely.
Munro said UK utilities were generally good at securing these connections, but standards varied around the world.
His biggest concern was smaller, poorly funded utility companies which may still be relying on older, vulnerable equipment.
Without proper protections, "any factory or equipment" connected to the internet - ranging from carmakers to electricity or transport infrastructure - could face similar risks, said Olivier Daloy, a cybersecurity expert at Zscaler.

article:
Couple hope D-Day boat bought on eBay will sail again

Couple hope D-Day boat bought on eBay will sail again
- Published
A couple who bought a World War Two D-Day boat on eBay are trying to restore it in time to sail it back to Normandy for the 85th anniversary of the landings.
Simon and Gemma Robins saved the vessel from the scrap heap when they bought it in 2021.
"We never planned on buying a World War Two boat, especially one that was so rotten and so big," Gemma said.
"But my husband likes a challenge and I fell in love with the history of it."
The boat now sits on the banks of the River Dee in Heswall, Wirral.
Known as Motor Launch 1392 during the war, it was one of 464 navigational launches built for the war effort.
During the D-Day landings in 1944, its role was to guide British troops towards Gold Beach in Normandy.
"There's not many of these boats left and if people don't step up to save our history, things are going to get lost and forgotten," said Gemma, who is from Huyton.
During the restoration, the couple discovered the wartime diary of crew member Frank "Curly" Capstick, who was just 17 when he served aboard the vessel.
With permission from his family, Gemma published the diary, which records the boat's day-to-day movements and offers a rare first-hand account of life at sea during World War Two.
"We know exactly where this boat was and what was happening every day during 1944," she said.
The couple, who work full-time restoring the vessel, hope one day to see it sail again along the same route taken by its wartime crew.
Now known as Sarinda, a name given by a former owner, the boat has been made watertight and can generate its own electricity.
"We would love to be able to take Sarinda back to Normandy and follow the route they took in 1944, hopefully alongside her sister ship, Medusa," Gemma said.
The couple have been documenting the restoration on their YouTube channel, Ship Happens, which has attracted support and advice from around the world.
"It's hard work, but we love it," Gemma said.
"Most people ask whether we're going to sell her when she's finished, but she's part of our family now.
"We've got no desire to ever part with her."

North Korea denies being behind record $6.3bn Binance hack

North Korea has denied claims that it was behind the record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance, calling the allegations "absurd rhetoric".
Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said on Tuesday that the accusations are another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage Pyongyang's public image.
The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Secret Service and cyber analysts have said North Korea orchestrated the hack, which has been described as the largest in history.
This is the latest hack to be linked to North Korea, which has been accused of relying on cyber-crime to help finance its sanctioned economy.
Blockchain analysts and the FBI have said the attack was led by state-backed hacking group TraderTraitor.
The FBI has called on industry partners to help block transactions involving cryptocurrency accounts linked to the group.
"The US has made a trite provocation of linking it with the Democratic People's Republic of Korea again," Kim Yo-jong, the director of North Korea's General Affairs Department, said in a statement.
"It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads the international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds," she said.

  - Published4 days ago
But Pyongyang has been blamed for a number of major cyber attacks in recent years - accusations that it has denied.
The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.
Pyongyang has systematically built its cyber operations, recruiting promising students from universities and sending them to hacker units overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, research groups like the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies think tank have said.
The country has consistently denied such claims.
Kim Yo Jong said "it is the consistent policy stand of the DPRK government to resolutely oppose all sorts of malicious acts in cyberspace".

The net outflow represents a "relatively limited portion" of Binance's total assets, which stand at approximately $157bn, the spokesperson told the BBC on Tuesday.
That figure reflects the impact of the hack, subsequent withdrawals and market price changes.
"Withdrawal levels are stabilising to what we would consider normal and expected on-chain activity," she added.
The company said last week that initial checks indicated that an engineer's laptop had been compromised, enabling an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals.
Trading in major cryptocurrencies on Binance has since resumed after the exchange worked with issuers to freeze assets impacted by the hack.

article:
UK meat industry hit by cyber-attack which targeted European supermarket freezers

UK meat industry hit by cyber-attack which targeted European supermarket freezers
- Published
Businesses in the UK's food supply chain have been impacted by the cyber-attack which hit supermarket fridges and freezers across Europe on Monday.
The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says it is aware of "a couple of instances where vulnerable technology had been exploited in the UK."
The NCSC's chief executive Dr Richard Horne told the Today programme, on BBC Radio Four, that it had "worked through the night" to alert potentially affected organisations in the UK.
The British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers (AIMS) told the BBC some of its more than 300 members had unexpectedly become what it called "collateral" as part of the hacks.
Two members saw their fridges begin to defrost, AIMS said, while another saw their cold units rise up to 100C (212F) in temperature.
AIMS spokesman Tony Goodger said the affected devices were empty at the time so no produce was lost - but urged businesses to be vigilant.
The incident "must act as a reminder to all in the food industry at whatever point in the supply chain they are that their businesses may be seen by some as targets," he said.
On Monday, supermarkets in countries including Ireland, Sweden, Estonia, and Belgium reported fridges and freezers being hiked in temperature.
The events followed attacks targeting supermarkets and food suppliers across France in early October.
Hundreds of stores were targeted by the overnight hack, which spoiled fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.
Those attacks exploited vulnerabilities in some systems used to remotely control and manage cold refrigeration units that had been surfaced by cyber-security researchers months prior.
Horne told the BBC on Tuesday that it was still "too early to say" who was behind the hacks.
But he said it pointed to an urgent need for organisations and businesses to ensure the technology underpinning a whole range of applications we use and need daily was secure and up-to-date.
"That technology base we rely on as a society has not been invested on to the extent it needs to be," Horne said, noting many firms had extended systems beyond their end of life, not upgraded them nor kept them in secure compartments disconnected from the internet.
Such actions can create vulnerabilities that many cyber-security experts say amounts to low-hanging fruit for hackers, and can be easily exploited.
But the UK's cyber chief said that they could be found and exploited more quickly and easily via "AI in the hands of our adversaries".
"We do need all organisations to look at what they rely on, to invest in renewal," he said.
"We intervene where we can. But, at the end of the day, it's your business. It's your charity. It's your life. You need to make the choice and choose wisely."
Thrown away food
Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected in Monday's cyber incident, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up.
The same method was thought to have been used in last month's incident that hit hundreds of French supermarkets.
As with that incident, many of the retailers affected on Monday said they had no choice but to throw away spoiled food - some saying this amounted to hundreds of thousands of euro in lost produce.
Mathieu Tilman, who runs a Delhaize supermarket in Belgium, told the BBC he found it "truly distressing".
"There's so many people starving, people who don't have enough to eat. How can we end up throwing away so much food?"
"In moments like these, you just feel like quitting your job."
So far, there have been little to no signs of any such impact in the UK.
But the BBC has approached major UK supermarkets for comment and asked what action, if any, they are taking to safeguard against any similar hacks attempts.
"Retailers invest heavily in their cybersecurity and are currently working with the NCSC to ensure their fridges and freezers are secure as possible against potential attacks," said Graham Wynn, assistant director of regulatory affairs at the British Retail Consortium.
Asda, Lidl, M&S, Sainsbury's and Tesco are among the retail trade association's members.
Paul Chichester, director of operations at the NCSC, said at the launch of its annual report on Tuesday it was continuing to work with and monitor UK organisations affected.
"At the moment, the impact is minimal," he added.
"We're working with organisations identifying existing vulnerabilities in the UK and trying to get those closed before somebody exploits them."

article:
Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far

Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far
- Published
Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, has been hit by what is believed to be the largest crypto hack ever at $6.3bn (£4.7bn).
Crypto is a type of digital asset which does not exist physically like cash or coins. Instead, people use digital wallets on their smartphones or computers to access and manage it.
Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, said it is working with the authorities to work out what has happened and it will cover all losses.
Here's what we know so far.
What is Binance?
Binance is the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange by trading volume, where people can buy, sell and trade digital currencies, like Bitcoin, as well as deposit and withdraw them.
It was founded in China in 2017 and has hundreds of millions of registered users worldwide.
The exchange has come under scrutiny over the past few years - notably in 2023, when its then-chief executive, Changpeng Zhao, resigned after pleading guilty to money laundering violations.
Last year, a lawsuit in the US accused the company of helping send millions of dollars to US-designated terrorist organisations.
In 2024, the company said it has more than $160bn in assets.
- From Bitcoin to blockchain: Key cryptocurrency terms and what they mean 
  - Published4 days ago
How did the hack happen?
The hack happened to Binance's global centralised exchange, Binance.com.
Binance.us, which provides trading services specifically for US residents, said it has not been affected by the issue.
In an initial announcement, Teng said: "Our initial investigation suggests this security incident may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop.
"That gave an attacker access to a service container, where they submitted unauthorised withdrawal transactions."
He said the hack "was not a simple 'one-click' action" but a "more complex attack process".
Raghu Nandakumara, vice president of industry strategy at cybersecurity platform Illumio, said this could mean an engineer was "talked into taking a test" and malware - malicious software – "landed on their laptop while they did it".
Because the laptop already had sufficient security privileges, Nandakumara said early reports suggest it became "the attacker's route straight into production, and from there to the wallets".
Teng has since said the hack was "not carried out by one person" and the hackers used sophisticated methods to hide their tracks, such as a "self-destruct mechanism".
"You can build a vault with mathematical firewalls, but if the individual holding the keys can be duped, the vault is opened," said Dr Clive Summerfield, head of FARx, a biometrics in AI security company.
Who is behind the hack?
It is not yet known who is behind the attack, but some analytics firms have pointed to North Korea - though this has not been confirmed.
AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said in a report several elements of the Binance attack resembled earlier incidents linked to the territory, including a $1.5bn (£1.1bn) hack on the ByBit exchange in 2025.
These previous attacks have been linked to a cluster of cyber-criminals accused of working directly for the regime called the Lazarus Group - also known as TraderTraitor.
North Korean foreign policy expert Dr Edward Howell, from the University of Oxford, has told the BBC that Pyongyang "has a long history of using cyber warfare to extract cash".
Howell said North Korea "basically has a state-run cyber warfare agency", which it uses "to fund its weapons of mass destruction programmes" and as a "slush fund" for its leader Kim Jong Un's regime.
Howell added that as of the current day "about 40 – 50% of North Korea's weapons of mass destruction programmes are funded by cyber and crypto-currency warfare".
North Korea has always denied any involvement in these attacks; Binance has not directly responded to BBC queries about the incident's potential links to the area.
What does it mean for Binance users?
In his earlier statement, Teng said Binance users' funds are safe and, as a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals had been temporarily suspended.
He said the firm would cover all losses from its emergency reserve set up for such situations, and make up the rest with company funds.
Binance said it had been working with partners to freeze the affected assets, with around $3bn reportedly located so far.
Teng said concerned users can check funds on their Binance accounts. Experts suggest doing so through the official app and website, and to reach out to the company's customer service with any questions.
Users from other crypto platforms have also been warned to be wary of hackers seeking to exploit the situation.
Marijus Briedis, NordVPN's chief technology officer, said people should be on the lookout for things such as "an email claiming your funds are at risk", "a fake support account offering help" or "a message urging you to move your cryptocurrency to a 'safe' wallet".
"Check updates through the Binance app or a website address you already trust," he said.
"Avoid links in unsolicited messages, and never give anyone your password, verification codes or wallet recovery phrase."
What does this mean for cryptocurrency and the wider financial system?
Jennifer Craven, an international commercial fraud expert at the law firm Pinsent Masons, said the repercussions of the hack could "extend well beyond Binance".
"More broadly, the incident exposes the fragility of parts of the crypto ecosystem," she said.
"If a platform as sophisticated as Binance can suffer a serious attack, regulators will inevitably ask what that means for smaller, less mature platforms and currencies."
She said the attack would likely accelerate scrutiny of how the sector protects both its infrastructure and its customers.
Although there is no evidence yet that AI was used in this attack, it fits into a much wider concern in the financial industry of whether AI agents could potentially identify weaknesses in software and work out how to exploit them much faster than human hackers.
The Bank of England has warned, external this could leave institutions struggling to fix vulnerabilities before attackers take advantage of them.
How many people use cryptocurrency?
Crypto has become an increasingly popular way of investing and transferring money online, partly because, unlike traditional currencies, it is not controlled by central banks or governments.
This makes it popular for people who think decentralisation can bring financial freedom.
But it also makes it extremely volatile, with it rising and falling in value at the whim of buyers and sellers.
According to Solcard, a crypto-funded prepaid payment and virtual card platform, somewhere between 560 million and 741 million people own crypto worldwide in 2026.

Men jailed for throwing Molotov cocktails at homes

Men jailed for throwing Molotov cocktails at homes
- Published
Two men have been jailed after throwing Molotov cocktails through the windows of three separate homes in south Wales over the course of less than six hours on the same day.
Yasin Hussain, 18, and Adam Taylor-Morris, 19, were driven down from Scotland by Taylor-Morris' sister on 1 June 2026, thereafter travelling in taxis between the three targeted houses.
At one home, the petrol-filled bottle ignited on impact and could have caused "serious injury or loss of life", police said.
Taylor-Morris and Hussain were sentenced to nine years and nine months in prison at Cardiff Crown Court on Monday, after previously pleading guilty to three counts of arson with intent to endanger life.
The two teenagers arrived at Porcher Avenue, in Glyncoch, Pontypridd, at about 04:00 BST on 1 June this year, after being driven to Wales by Danni Taylor.
The family in the house was woken by the sound of their living room window being smashed by a brick.
A Molotov cocktail was then aimed at the hole in the broken window, but missed and smashed on the floor outside.
Taylor-Morris and Hussain fled the scene.
The pair then caught a taxi to the Caerphilly area where, at about 07:00, they launched a brick through the window of a home on Wallis Drive.
A glass bottle full of petrol was thrown through the window and ignited on impact. The fire was subsequently extinguished, according to South Wales Police.
In the third such incident, on the same day, Taylor-Morris and Hussain caught another taxi to a location on Pearson Crescent in Glyncoch.
At about 09:00, the two teenagers approached the house, where Taylor-Morris filmed Hussain putting a Molotov cocktail through the open window of a living room, which set the room alight.
Det Con Connor Michael said: "These were deliberate and dangerous arson attacks which could have had devastating consequences, including serious injury or loss of life."
"The sentences handed down reflect the severity of the offenders' actions, and we hope they serve as a warning that such reckless behaviour will not be tolerated."
Danni Taylor, 24, from Perth and Kinross, has pleaded guilty to participating in the criminal activities of an organised crime group, and will be sentenced at a later date.
