article:
AI data centres could undermine UK's emissions goals

AI data centres could undermine UK's emissions goals
- Published
The UK government's ambition of achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2050 could be undermined by its new deal on AI data centres, according to BBC research.
During Wednesday's Budget speech, Chancellor John Healey said data centres would be allowed to build onsite power generation while they wait for a grid connection.
BBC File on 4 Investigates has discovered that four planned "hyperscale" data centres - including three in the south of England - are already considering using gas-fired power to meet their electricity needs, creating more CO2 than the cities of Manchester, Liverpool and Southampton combined.
Labour MP Toby Perkins, who chairs the Environmental Audit Select Committee, said a substantial increase in the use of natural gas "can't be the future".
"Government absolutely shouldn't be in the business of just saying anyone who wants to bring it here, can do whatever you like to power it, because that is not acceptable," he said.
The government said data centres were "essential to Britain's economy" and that its new Data Centre Covenant set clear expectations for developers to pay a fair share of the costs they impose on the energy system and deliver benefits for local communities.
Data centres are warehouses full of powerful computer servers used to run a vast range of digital services, including streaming, banking and public services and have been part of the British landscape for more than two decades.
But a new generation of data centres due to come on stream in the next few years will operate on a much larger scale to cope with the growing computing demand needed for increasingly sophisticated artificial intelligence technology.
They will consume considerably more energy than their predecessors at a time when the National Grid is already struggling to meet demand.
Ofgem, the energy market regulator, says data centre developers are seeking connections totalling 72 gigawatts. The peak electricity demand across the whole country last year was 45 gigawatts.
Such is the demand for access to the already under-strain national electricity grid, some data centre developers have been told they could be waiting up to 10 years for the system to be upgraded to provide them with a connection.
Nathan MacWhinnie, head of market intelligence and oversight at Ofgem, said: "In a lot of places, the grid is at capacity. I think sometimes it's easy to forget the scale of the demand of these connections. These projects are sometimes the size of cities."
In last week's Budget, the chancellor announced a British Data Centre Covenant, requiring operators to invest in local communities, create jobs and protect water supplies in return for priority grid connections.
But he also said that where grid connections were unavailable, developers would be permitted to generate their own power on-site.
BBC File on 4 Investigates has discovered that four data centres are already looking at using gas-fired power stations to meet their electricity needs.
If continuously running at full capacity, our calculations show they would require 1.3 gigawatts of power and could produce an estimated 4.1 million tonnes of carbon emissions a year. This could be more than the cities of Manchester, Liverpool and Southampton combined.
Oliver Hayes, head of campaigns at environmental charity Global Action Plan, said: "If we're powering by gas that means local communities are going to have huge gas turbines on their doorstep, and they are going to be generating a huge amount of local air pollution and a huge amount of noise and they will be using a huge amount of water from the local water supply."
The developments already considering on-site gas vary in scale.
At Acre Slough, west of London, developers say they could use gas engines with a generating capacity of up to 49.5 megawatts while waiting for a National Grid connection, something they expect could take at least 10 years.
At Wapsey's Wood, next to the M40 in Buckinghamshire, a proposed 200-megawatt gas power station could operate until sufficient grid capacity becomes available, currently not expected until 2040.
"It would be a disaster for us environmentally," said Buckinghamshire independent councillor Ed Gemmell, who also leads the Climate Party.
"If allowed, it sets a precedent that we could be getting gas-fired power stations all over the country and that would make it extremely difficult for us to hit any of our environmental and net zero targets."
Is it time to press pause on AI data centres?
An increasing number of large AI data centres are waiting in the UK energy supply queue - but will meeting that demand derail the road to net zero?
3 November
Quest Park has proposed building a data centre on the site of a quarry pit next to the planned Universal theme park in Bedfordshire. It would have a power load - the total amount of electrical power drawn at any given time - of 1 gigawatt, the equivalent to 200,000–250,000 average UK homes.
David Kohler, director of Quest Park, has previously told the BBC the company's energy mix was still a "work in progress" and that incorporating renewable power was "sensible" but had to be "feasible".
He said creating 1 gigawatt of solar electricity would require an area equivalent to 15% of Bedfordshire, and that wind power was "intermittent and expensive".
He said the company was considering alternative technologies that did not rely on gas combustion.
In Cardiff, a data centre developer is also seeking permission to build a temporary energy centre that has turbines with a maximum generating capacity of 49.9 megawatts.
Planning documents say it could operate for up to five years if the site cannot secure an electricity grid connection quickly enough. Developer Curtis Hall has described the turbine plan as a "worst-case scenario".
All four projects say they intend to connect to the national grid when it can meet their electricity needs, reducing their reliance on fossil fuels.
The government said its priority was connecting data centres to the grid so they could benefit from the UK's rapidly decarbonising power sector.
It said any behind-the-meter power generation would be tightly controlled, time-limited and allowed only for exceptionally strategic projects where sufficient capacity could not be secured by other means.
A government spokesperson added: "Data centres are essential to Britain's economy, supporting everything from online banking to NHS services.
"Pausing development would send jobs, investment and data overseas and leave us more reliant on other countries for critical digital infrastructure. That's why we're backing their growth while making sure it's done responsibly.
"Our new Data Centre Covenant sets clear expectations for developers to minimise water use, pay their fair share of energy costs and deliver benefits for local communities."

article:
How Kenyans got caught in $130m US ghost student scam

How Kenyans got caught in $130m US ghost student scam
- Published
In May 2024, Francis Mogambi arrived in the United States after winning the Diversity Visa lottery, a programme that gives people from around the world a chance to become permanent residents.
Just over two years later, the Kenyan national found himself at the centre of a US investigation into an alleged nationwide scheme to defraud the federal student aid system.
On 19 October 2026, a grand jury in Nebraska indicted Mogambi on five counts of theft of government money and five counts of aggravated identity theft.
Prosecutors allege that, between November 2025 and May 2026, he worked with associates in Kenya to steal the identities of US citizens and use them to fraudulently enroll fictitious students in American colleges.
Once the fake students were enrolled, Mogambi allegedly diverted their financial aid payments to himself, keeping 30% and sending the remainder to his associates in Kenya.
The intended loss in his case was $20,000 (£15,000), according to prosecutors.
Court documents say Mogambi received $2,000 a week and attempted to recruit another person into the scheme. He allegedly told the individual he needed a business that would allow him to cash larger cheques without paying taxes.
Mogambi was arrested shortly after the indictment was returned and is being held in custody pending trial. He has not yet commented on the allegations against him.
His case forms part of a wider US investigation, dubbed Operation Ghostbusters, into the alleged use of stolen identities to enrol fictitious students at colleges and claim federal financial aid that resulted in a loss of $130m in taxpayers funds.
US authorities say the investigation has so far resulted in five indictments that involved Kenyan nationals, while a further 40 investigations remain open. Hundreds of people have been affected after fraudsters allegedly stole their personally identifiable information (PII) and used it to access federal student aid.
The stolen personal information was sometimes sold online for between $4 and $8, with fraudsters targeting low-income Americans who had never had the opportunity to attend college.
At a news conference on 29 October announcing the first charges in the investigation, Assistant Attorney General Colin M McDonald, who heads the Justice Department's National Fraud Enforcement Division, vowed to pursue those involved.
"If you steal taxpayers' dollars, if you exploit a programme meant to help students, we are resolved to find you and prosecute you," he said.
The Justice Department says those behind the fraud use what is described as "super intelligence" to place fake students in classrooms and complete coursework, creating the impression that they are attending college and allowing financial aid payments to continue.
"The goal is to keep the ghost student in school as long as possible. Semester after semester after semester stealing money from the taxpayers," McDonald said.
But the consequences extend beyond the financial losses suffered by the US government.
People whose identities are stolen can find themselves facing unexpected student loan debts, even if they have never enrolled in college.
"His identity was stolen, his credit is now at risk, and his name is on the bill," McDonald said, describing the impact on one victim.
He also said that nearly a third of community college applicants in California in 2024 had been identified as fraudulent.
The scale of the suspected fraud is significant.
Investigators identified 830,840 potentially fraudulent Federal Student Aid identification numbers associated with nearly $130m in September and October 2026. They recommended that the Department of Education disable them.
The figure represents financial aid associated with potentially fraudulent accounts, not confirmed losses.
"In a flash, the money vanishes, often overseas in places like Kenya," McDonald said.
The investigation has also exposed alleged financial links between the US and Kenya.
In September, US officials travelled to Kenya to work with local law enforcement on extraditions, prosecutions and the recovery of money allegedly stolen from American taxpayers.
With the help of Kenyan investigators, US authorities seized more than $750,000 from a cryptocurrency account belonging to a Kenyan national connected to the wider scheme. The Justice Department described it as the first international seizure of its kind in Kenya.
The seizure was not connected to Mogambi's individual case.
In a separate case in Virginia, prosecutors allege that a Kenyan national received more than 700 fraudulent student-aid refunds totalling approximately $1.44m. At least $1.3m was subsequently transferred through thousands of transactions to accounts in the US and Kenya.
Meanwhile, in New Jersey, three people have been charged with allegedly acting as money mules in a scheme to obtain more than $1m in federal student aid.
Prosecutors say they received the funds through US bank accounts, kept a portion for themselves and transferred the remainder to alleged co-conspirators in Kenya linked to a purported safari company.
If convicted, Mogambi faces a mandatory prison term of at least 10 years, according to the Justice Department.
Authorities say those convicted will also face appropriate orders for forfeiture of assets and restitution to victims, in addition to any prison sentences.

M&S worker trying to stop shop theft hit by e-bike

M&S worker hit by e-bike trying to stop shop theft
- Published
A man was injured when a suspect rode an e-bike into a shop, picked up about £200 worth of children's clothes before knocking a staff member to the ground.
Nottinghamshire Police said it was informed at about 11:45 GMT on Sunday that the suspect had ridden into the Marks and Spencer (M&S) in Giltbrook, Nottinghamshire.
A member of staff went to block the exit, but was struck by the bike and dragged along the ground before managing to halt the rider and bring them and the stock back inside.
The suspect then fled after a struggle, before police detained a 36-year-old man at an address in Eastwood on suspicion of robbery.
Police said the shop worker suffered minor injuries during the incident.
PC Luke Cutts said: "Having spotted an apparent shop theft in progress, staff went to confront a suspect at the exit.
"Rather than stop, the individual instead rode an e-bike directly into and over the staff member, causing minor injuries as a result.
"That use of violence and aggression meant that, when we located a suspect, he was arrested for robbery - as opposed to shop theft.
"It really should go without saying but nobody should ever be subjected to something like this when they're just trying to do their job.
"This type of behaviour will never be viewed as anything other than completely unacceptable, so we're pleased to have made this arrest."

Dutch police offer record €2m reward in hunt for drug lord

Dutch police offer record €2m reward in hunt for drug lord
- Published
Dutch authorities have offered a record award of €2m (£1.7m/$2.24m) for information leading to the arrest of Jos Leijdekkers, one of Europe's most-wanted men.
The 35-year-old, who is also known as Bolle Jos (Chubby Jos), was previously accused of being "one of the key players in international cocaine trafficking" by Dutch police.
Commenting on the decision to increase the reward ten-fold, Dutch justice minister David van Weel said it was "necessary given the threat that Leijdekkers poses to national security, our democratic rule of law, and the international legal order".
Dutch prosecutors said capturing Leijdekkers was their "highest priority" and any information shared would be kept secret.
He is listed by Europol, the EU's law enforcement agency, as among their most-wanted fugitives.
In January 2025, Dutch police said he was believed to be living in Sierra Leone and going by the name Omar Sherrif.
Images apparently showing Leijdekkers in the company of President Julius Maada Bio and other officials have previously emerged.
Dutch prosecutors have demanded his extradition but Sierra Leone has refused to cooperate, prompting the EU to cut some aid to the country.
West Africa is a major transit point for cocaine trafficking from Latin America.
In 2024, a court in Rotterdam sentenced Leijdekkers in absentia to 24 years in prison after finding him guilty of smuggling more than seven metric tons of cocaine.
Several other police investigations in the Netherlands are ongoing.
Leijdekkers has also been sentenced to 79 years in prison in Belgium.
Dutch authorities estimate he has made tens of millions of euros from cocaine smuggling, and accuse him of money laundering and involvement in the use of extreme violence.

article:
France launches attempted murder investigation after petrol bomb thrown at police

France launches attempted murder investigation after petrol bomb thrown at police
- Published
Prosecutors in France have launched an attempted murder investigation after petrol bombs were thrown at police during unrest, French media reported.
An image of a police officer with his leg on fire during a clash with protesters in Paris on Saturday has prompted outrage and follows weeks of street protests in France that have also seen demonstrators injured.
The officer, who suffered burns to his ankle and minor injures to his hand, told French newspaper Le Figaro it was a "particularly sophisticated" incendiary device.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said throwing a molotov cocktail at a police line was "what I call a murder attempt", adding officers were working to find the perpetrators.
Hundreds of thousands of people demonstrated across France in largely peaceful protests on Saturday, the latest in a series of youth-led protests that began in late September demanding action on the high cost of living and poor public services, especially schools.
Following previous clashes and looting, thousands of police officers were deployed across the country over the weekend, and officers fired tear gas at demonstrators in some cities.
There were more than 770 arrests on Saturday, roughly half as many as the previous week's protests, the French interior ministry said.
But police said no one had been arrested for the attack caught on camera that set a police officer on fire, AFP reported.
The officer - part of the National Gendarmerie, a national law enforcement force that is technically part of the military but under the control of the interior ministry - said his unit "suddenly found ourselves facing several hundred hostile, well equipped adversaries".
Speaking to French newspaper Le Figaro, he said police were yet to identify the liquid used but that the incendiary device "had a far greater burning capacity than a standard Molotov cocktail".
"We faced hostile individuals who are not protesters," he said. "These adversaries are there with the intent to harm those who represent the state."
Fourteen other officers sustained wounds ranging from minor to serious, he said, adding some were struck by paving stones. The unit was supposed to be on leave but had been urgently recalled to police the weekend protests, he said.
French protest organisers, the Gilets Jaunes, or Yellow Vests, have said dozens of protesters have been seriously injured during recent demonstrations across the country, with many hurt by "grenades".
France suspended the use of one type of stun grenade while policing student protests in early October after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off, but French newspaper Le Monde has reported that police have continued to use a different model in subsequent protests.
Protests also took place in Germany and Italy over the weekend, as mainly youth-led protests continue across parts of Europe, with varying demands but broadly linked to a focus on cost-of-living issues and public services.

article:
Dramatic clifftop rescue of bride and groom-to-be

Dramatic clifftop rescue of bride and groom-to-be
- Published
A couple who went for a beach walk shortly after getting engaged had to be rescued by the Irish Coast Guard after an incoming tide trapped them against a coastal cliff.
The bride and groom-to-be were hauled approximately 150m (490 ft) to the top of the cliff to safety because rescuers could not reach them by boat or by helicopter.
The dramatic rescue took place during gale-force winds on Achill Island, off the west coast of Ireland, on Monday afternoon.
Coast Guard volunteer Peter McManamon, who coordinated the operation, told BBC News NI: "They were two very lucky people."
It is believed the pair are originally from overseas but live in Ireland and were on a visit to Achill Island, off the County Mayo coast, when the incident happened.
McManamon said the couple had gone for a walk along Keel Beach when the tide began to come in behind them - at one point reaching above knee-level.
"They got engaged in Achill and they were just walking along [the beach] and they went out too far on the rocks," he explained.
"The weather conditions were atrocious there, and in that particular area the tide has come in very quick."
Unable to get off the sand because of the towering cliff behind them, the couple called 999 and asked for a coast guard rescue.
"It was too rough for a rib (rigid inflatable boat) to be tasked - it was blowing Force 8 to 10 at the time and the wave conditions wouldn't let us," McManamon said.
"We tried to walk out along the rocks to them but... the waves were just coming in and it was just too dangerous to put the crew in, so the helicopter was tasked."
'Hypothermia was beginning to set in'
Coast Guard helicopter R118, based in County Sligo, flew to the scene but the force of the winds meant its crew were unable to help the stranded couple.
"When the helicopter came, they tried to move in to winch them but there was too much down draft off the mountain for it to happen," McManamon explained.
So he then deployed climbers from Achill Island Coast Guard's cliff rescue team who abseiled down the cliff to pluck the couple out of the rising tide.
"The water was coming in around them - the water was roughly just above their knees," McManamon recalled.
The couple were taken to safety in stages. The woman was brought to higher ground first while her fiance waited with "waves crashing" around his legs.
Once they were both out of immediate risk, the climbers used ropes to separately haul both casualties a further 150m to the clifftop.
"They were very cold - hypothermia was beginning to set in," McManamon said.
However, the remote beauty spot could not be reached by vehicle so the casualties then faced a 2km (1.2 mile) walk down the hill to a waiting ambulance.
There, they were treated by paramedics before being taken to hospital for checks, but they did not need to be admitted.
McManamon said it is never a safe decision to walk along coastal cliffs in such weather conditions.
"It can be a dangerous spot, the locals don't really go near it at all," he said, explaining that other parts of the beach are more suitable for walking or swimming.
McManamon has been a member of the Irish Coast Guard for 20 years, the last seven of which he has spent at "officer in charge" at Achill Island Coast Guard Unit.
The role is voluntary.
Monday's rescue operation took more than seven hours, with his crew finally leaving cliff at about 21:30 local time.
"I didn't get a chance to talk to them [the couple] properly, I was too busy organising my own team," McManamon said.
"We were that wet and hungry, we just wanted to get tidied up and get our equipment back and to get to our own homes and families."
Popular site to pop the question?
McManamon agreed that it was one of the most dramatic engagement stories that he had come across.
Having celebrated his own 25th wedding anniversary earlier this month, he has some affinity with the couple - in fact Keel Beach was the setting for his own marriage proposal.
However, he was quick to point out that he popped the question "on the safe side of the beach".

Ryanair says it may freeze workers' pay and raise airfares

Ryanair says it may freeze workers' pay and raise airfares
- Published
Ryanair is considering a temporary wage freeze for staff and confirmed airfares will be "materially higher" next summer because of a sharp rise in fuel costs following the US-Israel war with Iran.
The airline said it expects fuel prices to remain high "well into 2027" unless there is a "swift resolution" to the conflict.
Ryanair said its fuel bill is forecast to be €2bn (£1.6bn) higher in the short-term and its boss, Michael O'Leary, said airfares would have to rise by "double-digits" to help cover the cost.
But the firm said that was unlikely to be enough and it is looking into pay freezes. Unite, the union representing Ryanair staff, said it had not been told of "any such proposals".
O'Leary also said the company would slow down hiring as airline's costs rise.
The airline said its pre-tax profits fell by 16% to €2.4bn during the six months to the end of September, largely due to fuel costs jumping by 15%.
The company said that although 80% of its fuel bill had been "hedged" – in effect, bought in advance at fixed prices – the cost of the remainder was elevated.
O'Leary reiterated forecasts from earlier this year Ryanair would "need a 20% fare increase" to cover the cost of jet fuel.
"I'm not sure we'll get to 20%," he said. "But we're certainly looking at double-digit fare increases across Europe from all airlines in 2027."
Aviation fuel prices have surged this year as a result of the US-Israel war with Iran, which has dramatically reduced the supply of refined products coming from the Gulf and increased competition for those produced elsewhere.
Ryanair also said it was weighing up whether to freeze pay, as multi-year wage deals with unions come to to an end. The policy could be implemented from April next year.
Oliver Richardson, national officer at Unite, said the union "hasn't been advised of any such proposals and we have a multi-year pay deal in place which covers next year. A number of Unions across Europe have the same".
He said: "Our pay agreement was not attached to, nor dependent on company performance. This was something that the Ryanair was at pains to emphasise. As such we would expect it to be honoured."
Ryanair also said it would increase its use of artificial intelligence within its back office and support functions.
Meanwhile, Ryanair has cut back on winter flights and said on Monday there would be more to come. It said this was happening across the airline industry, particularly with short-haul carriers.
O'Leary said: "We believe those cuts will continue into the summer of 2027. Over the medium term, we expect short-haul capacity will remain constrained out to the early 2030s."

article:
Warning as scammers use real police phone number

Warning as scammers use real police phone number
- Published
Scammers are impersonating police officers to try to persuade their potential victims to pay them money over the phone, a force has warned.
Merseyside Police has urged the public to be vigilant after scammers also used a technique called ID spoofing to make it look like they were calling from the force's switchboard.
The warning has been issued after people on Merseyside reported they had received calls from the force's genuine number 0151 709 6010.
Merseyside Police, which said an investigation was under way to find the scammers, stressed that no officer should ever ask someone for their PIN or bank account details.
"Impersonating a police officer is a criminal offence and it's something we take extremely seriously," Det Ch Insp Alan Nuttall said.
"We will not hesitate to investigate any reports whether on people's doorsteps, on the phone or online so that we can take action and bring offenders to justice.
"Shamefully, offenders like this often deliberately target the most vulnerable in our community.
"I would ask people to take a few minutes to speak to friends or relatives who may be vulnerable to such a scam so they are aware of the risks and have the right advice and guidance.
"There are a number of steps you and they can take to try to prevent this from happening: You can always ask a police officer for identification. All our officers have a collar number and a warrant card.
"If in any doubt, you can always check the name, collar number and crime reference numbers provided are genuine by calling 101.
"If you suspect someone is impersonating a police officer please contact police."

article:
Man jailed after causing crash that killed his wife

Man jailed after causing crash that killed his wife
- Published
A man whose wife died three years after sustaining injuries in a crash he caused has been jailed.
Sylwia Borychowska was a front-seat passenger in a vehicle being driven by Haseeb Ahmed, when it left a 20mph (32km/h) road and hit a tree in Mapperley Road, Nottingham, on 3 August 2019.
Borychowska, 25, sustained injuries and underwent surgery to remove a section of her bowel, spending two months in hospital. The surgery left her vulnerable to infection and in 2022, she contracted pneumonia and died on 27 October of that year. A post-mortem examination concluded the crash injuries led to her death.
Ahmed, 34, was jailed for three years at Nottingham Crown Court on Monday.
Nottinghamshire Police said in relation to the crash, Ahmed had already received a two-year prison sentence - suspended for two years - after admitting causing serious injury by dangerous driving, driving while disqualified, driving without insurance, two offences of driving while unfit through drink or drugs, and taking the vehicle without consent.
But following Borychowska's death, the case was reopened and Ahmed was charged with causing death by dangerous driving, and causing death by driving while disqualified, which he admitted.
Ahmed, of Stockhill Circus in Basford, then pleaded guilty to causing death by dangerous driving on the opening day of a trial earlier this year.
As well as being handed a custodial sentence, Ahmed was also disqualified from driving for three years and eight months, and must pass an extended driving test before he can regain his licence.
Police said Ahmed admitted at his sentencing hearing that he had consumed both alcohol and ecstasy before the crash.
A victim impact statement from Borychowska's family, read out in court, said she was a "happy and talkative person with so many plans", and that her death had left "an empty space in our family and in our hearts".
"It has been over four years since her passing, but the family is still struggling to make sense of this situation," the statement said.
"She was a bright, beautiful young lady with dreams. She was studying and working to support others and was so proud to have completed her degree and graduated.
"A sense of emptiness, meaninglessness and uncertainty accompanies us every day."
Following sentencing, police collision investigator Sarah Butler said Ahmed "got behind the wheel with both alcohol and drugs in his system", and caused "unimaginable pain and devastation".
"His manner of driving in a 20mph zone demonstrated a complete disregard not only for his own safety, but for Sylwia's as well," she said.
"No family should ever have to go through what Sylwia's family has endured and continues to endure every day, and Ahmed will have to live with his own pain and guilt for the rest of his life."

Jewellery thief jailed after gun and fake cash found in Gucci bag

Jewellery thief jailed after gun and fake cash found in Gucci bag
- Published
A man has been jailed for more than five years after he was found with a gun, ammunition and counterfeit cash in a Gucci bag.
Jason Britton was arrested after he was chased near to Glasgow's Hilton hotel on 2 December.
The High Court in Glashow heard that the 35-year-old from Salford, near Manchester, had been in a car with Cade Johnson, 28, of Manchester, who was previously jailed over a firearms plot.
Britton was previously jailed for five years and 10 months in 2015 after he was part of a gang who committed a £230,000 armed heist at Glasgow's Argyll Arcade.
The gang made off with high value watches from the Rox store, but they were caught after two friends were seen wearing the stolen watches.
'High risk of re-offending'
Britton previously pleaded guilty to two charges of having the firearms without a reasonable excuse or lawful authority.
He also admitted acquiring and possessing £10,285 of criminal property.
Britton was jailed for five years and three months.
The Judge Lord Scott told him: "These offences were motivated wholly or in part with the objective of committing serious organised crime.
"This makes each charge more serious. You are assessed as being at a high risk of re-offending due to the serious risk of harm you pose to the public.
"Having regard to the circumstances, gravity of the crimes and your previous convictions only a custodial sentence is appropriate which is necessary to punish you and deter others."
Johnson was previously jailed for five years and nine months in December 2019 for his involvement in serious organised crime and reset - possessing property acquired dishonestly.
He was caught alongside two others after officers discovered a fake parcel, designed to conceal a pistol, which was addressed to a vet practice at the Forge Retail Park in Glasgow's Parkhead.
Armed police stopped their Mercedes car and recovered a balaclava, £1,000 of counterfeit money, two full cans of petrol, as well as Royal Mail uniforms and bags.
Johnson was given a serious crime prevention order at the sentencing in December 2019 - which he flouted by failing to tell police about his journey to Scotland with Britton in 2025.
He was jailed for two years and seven months during his latest court appearance, after he admitted breaching the order.
The court heard that police did a check on a BMW on 2 December last year which came up as being registered in the Manchester area.
Officers spotted that three people in the vehicle had their hoods up.
The driver was asked to stop the vehicle after sirens and lights had been put on by police.
Prosecutor Adrian Stalker said: "Britton exited from the passenger door and ran towards the Hilton Hotel with a brown Gucci bag.
"He dropped a quantity of £20 notes and proceeded on foot."
Meanwhile, the BMW drove off but stopped again when ordered to by police who turned their lights and sirens back on.
Stalker said: "The constable chased Britton towards the A804 when he fell over a metal railing and dropped another quantity of £20 notes.
"Britton got up and fell again and was apprehended."
Officers found Johnson in the rear passenger side of the vehicle.
Stalker told the court: "No information was given [to police] about his intended travel to Scotland before he was apprehended."
Britton was found still in possession of the Gucci bag which was opened and found to contain a handgun and a quantity of cash.
Counterfeit cash
The handgun was found to be a Turkish manufactured Zoraki model 917-B self-loading pistol.
Officers also discovered modified .380 bulleted cartridges which were "suitable for use with the handgun."
"The handgun was in working order capable of discharging cartridges and self-loading when fired," Stalker added.
The Gucci bag contained £1,060 in cash - most of which was £20 notes.
Britton dropped £3,000 during the pursuit which was also found to be in £20 notes.
A further £6,225 in mixed notes was recovered from an Asda bag under the rear passenger side of the BMW.
Stalker said that the banknotes were examined and "all were found to be counterfeit."
Marco Guarino, defending Britton, told the sentencing: "The sentence is inevitable here and he accepts that.
"There is a reference in his background report saying that he is the victim - this is not quite how the conversation went.
"He was attempting to say there was no direct victim in this particular matter and was referencing himself as he means he got himself into this problem due to the decisions that he made."
Rhonda Anderson, defending Johnson, said: "This is a man who does regret his actions - when the car was stopped, he made no attempt to move.
"He remained with the police and co-operated fully with them.
"His intention was not to become involved in committing any crime but to go for the ride."

article:
'My legs buckled when I opened my exam results during Covid'

'My legs buckled when I opened my exam results during Covid'
- Published
A student whose exam results were downgraded during Covid says she still wants answers from education bosses after their decisions changed the trajectory of her life.
Erin Bleakley's plans were ruined after she was awarded Bs, Cs and Ds in her highers in 2020 after an emergency marking system was introduced.
Despite her results being eventually adjusted, she never got the A grades her prelims suggested she would get and she had to change course.
As former SQA head Fiona Robertson prepares to give evidence to the Scottish Covid Inquiry later, Erin wants someone to take accountability for what happened.
After lockdown came into force in March 2020 and schools were closed to pupils, teachers were instructed by the Scottish Qualifications Authority (SQA) to estimate exam grades for pupils.
A later review, external found there was no consistency with how this was carried out around the country.
In June, the SQA then lowered 125,000 of these grades using an algorithm, saying the grades did not tally with the outcomes of previous cohorts at the same schools.
Public outrage grew when it became apparent that pupils who had gone to schools in deprived areas formed the bulk of students who had their results downgraded from teacher estimates.
Grades were then restored to teacher estimates for those who had been downgraded.
But by then it was too late for some pupils who had already lost their chance of a specific university course, because they had entered clearing.
Plus, some students were surprised that the restored teacher estimates didn't match prelim results.
Erin, who is from Glasgow, can't forget the moment she opened her exam results in August 2020.
She'd been studying for six Highers and after getting A grades at prelim, was hoping to study veterinary medicine.
"I remember being quite excited," she said. "I didn't think anything was going to go wrong. I thought I'd set myself up really well."
Then the postman arrived and Erin remembers opening the envelope, receiving three Bs, one C and two Ds.
"My legs buckled beneath me, I remember feeling I just couldn't believe this had happened," she said.
"It did not reflect anything that I'd done over the last two years."
Timeline of the exams saga
Erin had never failed a class in her life. She said: "I was crying uncontrollably. I remember my mum just didn't know what to do and my dad came home from work early. It was a horrible experience."
The story was repeated on social media and among her school friends.
Then she opened Twitter and saw a post from a private-school pupil from an affluent area who was delighted that despite failing all their prelims, they'd just got five A grades.
"I remember thinking, something's not right here," Erin said.
"All of my friends and people I know that wanted to do medicine weren't getting the grades that they got in their prelims."
Erin organised a Facebook page and set up a protest in Glasgow's George Square.
"It felt like my full life had disappeared in front of me. And when I started reading into it, I realised it wasn't anything to do with me. It was bigger, systematic inequality."
She added: "I'd read about the algorithm they used, I didn't know too much about it at the time but I just knew it wasn't right the way we'd been treated and that it was pupils from deprived communities that had been disadvantaged with the marking."
The week after the protest, John Swinney, who was education secretary at the time, said he was sorry for the "feeling of unfairness" caused by the downgrading, adding that it was "deeply regrettable we got this wrong".
Erin's adjusted grades were not enough. She pivoted to studying human geography.
Erin says she still wants answers. "It was a massive injustice that people faced. I think I would like to know if anybody in any of these deprived areas was consulted before these decisions were made.
"I think there needs to be some sort of accountability in the system.
"It has still left an impact on people to this day. So I do think it's important, even just for acknowledgement, to take accountability of what happened and what went wrong."
The experience set her off on a different path.
She is now a PhD student at the University of Glasgow, studying environmental research and community work.
Her research has looked into automated algorithms and the effect on lived experiences, looking at decisions about people which have been based solely on statistics.
"I've kind of built my full research around making sure that communities are involved in any work that I do because of the inequality that I faced, that a lot of us faced," she said.
Just over a year after the exams fiasco, it was announced that the SQA would be scrapped.
It took another four years for its replacement Qualifications Scotland to take over many of its responsibilities.
Critics called the change a "superficial rebrand", especially as the new body has many of the same staff as the old one, but its stated aim is to "reset relationships with learners and teachers" in order to "win back trust".
A spokesman for the new Qualifications Scotland agency it was committed to supporting the work of the Scottish Covid-19 Inquiry and continues to engage fully with the inquiry's work.
"It would not be appropriate to comment further while the inquiry is ongoing," he said.
A spokeswoman for the Scottish government said: "The unprecedented Covid pandemic had an enormous impact across society, including in education, where the removal of exams for the first time in 100 years created a unique and very challenging situation.
"The SQA developed an alternative certification model in March 2020. In August 2020, the Scottish government instructed the SQA to revert any downgraded results to teacher and practitioner judgement.
"The Scottish government is a key participant in both the UK and Scottish Covid Inquiries and will follow all the evidence given at the Scottish Inquiry's implementation hearings closely."

article:
Footage of Seoul crush to be removed from Call of Duty after backlash

Footage of Seoul crush to be removed from Call of Duty after backlash
- Published
Video clips showing the aftermath of a deadly crush in Seoul will be removed from the latest Call of Duty game after an angry reaction from victims' families.
Real life news coverage of the 2022 disaster which killed almost 160 people was included in an opening scene of Modern Warfare 4 to illustrate a fictional invasion from North Korea.
Bereaved families said they were "appalled" to see the footage - which included people being removed on stretchers, body bags on the street and resuscitation efforts - repurposed for the game.
Activision, which makes Call of Duty, has since apologised and confirmed it would be removed in the game's next update on 12 November.
The crush happened in the narrow alleys of Seoul's Itaewon district when more than 100,000 people went to the area to celebrate Halloween four years ago.
The streets became so tightly packed that people could not move and some were unable to breathe.
In a statement on Thursday, the families of those who died said the disaster "was a tragedy that caused hundreds of casualties, and citizens who took part in the rescue or witnessed it have suffered from trauma until now".
"We cannot help but be appalled that the chaotic and desperate scene, in which many citizens at the site performed CPR to save one another and victims lay on the freezing street, was used to create a scene in a game.
"Using such an event as material for a game made for entertainment is in itself highly inappropriate and senseless."
'Not intended to trivialise'
Activision confirmed it had used real news coverage of the disaster "to establish the game's fictional narrative" but insisted it had "not intended to reference or trivialise the Itaewon disaster or any other real-world tragedy in any way, shape or form".
Confirming on Friday that the footage would be removed in a statement, the company offered its condolences and apologised to the bereaved families and victims who have been hurt by this incident.
The decision was welcomed by the 10.29 Itaewon Disaster Bereaved Families Association, however the group told the BBC they had not received a direct apology from Activision.
Modern Warfare 4, which was released last week, had already faced criticism for basing the game on North Korea invading South Korea, as the two countries have been technically at war for decades.
Fighting stopped in the Korean War in 1953, but the two countries never signed a peace treaty and conflict is a very real worry in that part of the world.
At the launch of the game, Call of Duty's chief marketing officer, Tyler Bahl, told BBC Newsbeat: "We have to understand this is entertainment".

article:
Council pulls support for future jobs fairs with Army

Council pulls support for future jobs fairs with Army
- Published
Derry City and Strabane District Council has voted to withdraw any involvement in the organisation or marketing of any future jobs fair that includes the UK's armed forces.
Proposed by Sinn Féin councillor Christopher Jackson, the motion stated that their presence at a recent jobs fair organised by the Department for Communities (DfC) had acted as a "barrier" for some people seeking employment opportunities.
Jackson said the legacy of the armed forces in Londonderry had been one of "trauma, hurt and destruction".
However DUP councillor Niree McMorris said the motion would limit employment opportunities and accused the council of politicising employment opportunities.
A Ministry of Defence (MoD) spokesperson said it was disappointed by the council's decision and said it would "continue to work openly and cooperatively with councils across Northern Ireland".
The MoD welcomed opportunities to attend jobs fairs across Northern Ireland and "share the wide range of careers available to potential recruits".
Previously, the Army pulled out of a jobs fair at the council-owned Foyle Arena last year following opposition from nationalist councillors after the MoD, which had initially registered as an employer for the event, decided not to go ahead with a stall.
Speaking in support of his motion, Jackson said: "The legacy of the British armed forces in this city has been one of trauma, hurt and destruction of many people."
He added: "To have the British armed forces present at a jobs fair has become a barrier for many people who are seeking employment or looking to advance their careers."
"It has caused hurt to families and victims," he said.
Jackson told the full council meeting on Wednesday that preparations were already underway for a council-run jobs fair without the presence of the military.
"We as a council have an opportunity to hold our own jobs fair and preparation to host a jobs fair is already underway," he said.
"We can't have people who are resident in this council area who want to seek and further their careers be intimidated out of it."
SDLP councillor Rory Farrell said his party fully supported the motion.
"We do not support any organ of the British military being invited to a jobs fair anywhere across this city and district," he said.
"In the event that they are present, there should be no council role whatsoever in facilitating that jobs fair."
'Jobs fair should be inclusive not selective'
DUP councillor Niree McMorris opposed the motion, arguing that jobs fairs should provide equal access to a range of employment opportunities.
"A jobs fair should be inclusive not selective," McMorris said.
"Whatever our individual political perspectives may be, employment fairs should be about opportunity, choice and equal access to careers.
"Excluding the British armed forces from participating sends entirely the wrong message and denies local people the chance to hear about a legitimate and respected career path."
McMorris said many former members of the armed forces lived in the city and district and "deserve neither discrimination or exclusion".
"This council should not be in the business of deciding which lawful employers are politically acceptable and which or not," she said.
"If we start excluding organisations because some disagree with their role, where does that end?"
She added that residents deserved access to a range of employment opportunities and said "they can make informed decisions for themselves".
UUP councillor Darren Guy also raised concerns about the motion, while acknowledging the reasons some councillors opposed the armed forces' presence at jobs fairs.
He said he could understand opposition given "what happened on the streets in our city and in their homes", but stressed that "a jobs fair is all about choice".
"The armed forces is a legitimate employer," he said.
'High levels of poverty in our city'
Guy questioned whether the motion could go "against the equality and good relations policy of this council".
He also criticised what he described as the removal of an employment option for people who might lack the qualifications or skills needed for other jobs advertised at the fair.
"The constant shouts of oppression of the Irish people and the high levels of poverty in our city and district yet all we hear now is elected representatives looking to remove an avenue of employment that may be the best option for someone who doesn't have the skills or qualifications for other jobs on offer at the fair," he said.
"If this council excludes the armed forces from a jobs event for political reasons there is a credible argument that the decision is inconsistent with section three, four and five of our equal opportunities policy because it limits opportunities available to those seeking potential employment."
A senior solicitor at council told members at the meeting that, as with any motion passed, it would result in a paper being brought before all elected members, "where relevant matters would be addressed and considered".
Communities Minister Gordon Lyons said it was a "deeply disappointing" decision by the council adding "it is not fair, it's exclusionary and shows a complete disregard for inclusivity".
"Due to the intolerance of some councillors, people interested in a career in the Royal Air Force, Royal Navy or Army will be denied the opportunity to learn more about those professions," he said.
He said no one should have "the right to dictate which lawful career opportunities are showcased".
"But that is exactly what has happened," he continued.
"Shame on them. Yet again those who claim to champion equality have demonstrated that this is only extended when it is on their terms. That hypocrisy will not be lost on the public."

article:
Man guilty of stealing cash from farm owned by South African president

Man guilty of stealing cash from farm owned by South African president
- Published
A court in South Africa has found a man guilty of stealing more than $580,000 (£432,000) in cash from a farm owned by South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, in a case that mired the head of state in an impeachment saga.
Imanuwela David was found guilty of theft on Monday, as well as conspiracy to commit housebreaking with intent to steal at Phala Phala farm in the Limpopo province in 2020.
Froliana Joseph, a cleaner at the property, was also found guilty of conspiracy to commit housebreaking with intent to steal.
Her brother, Ndilinasho Joseph, was acquitted on all charges.
David was accused of breaking into the cattle farm in February 2020 and taking the cash from a sofa on the property. David then went on a spending spree, buying a range of cars including three Mercedes - among them one for his girlfriend - a Porsche, two Volkswagens as well as diamond-encrusted Rolex watches and a house.
David told the court he had made the money through businesses including diamonds and Bitcoin, claims the court rejected. The court also found that David was the only one of the two convicted who had any of the stolen cash in his bank account.
Pre-sentencing will take place on 13 November.
There have been many twists and turns in what is known as the Farmgate scandal.
The theft was largely unknown until 2022 when it was brought to light by Arthur Fraser, South Africa's former intelligence chief and an ally for the former president Jacob Zuma, when he claimed that Ramaphosa hid the theft from the police and tax authorities.
Ramaphosa admitted the theft took place but denied any wrongdoing.
An independent panel that same year found Ramaphosa could have questions to answer over the burglary. MPs voted against establishing an impeachment inquiry.
In May this year, the constitutional court ruled that parliament had acted unlawfully by shelving the panel's report, and in July Ramaphosa blocked the parliamentary inquiry through a provincial court.

article:
Shock of rail tragedy gives way to sorrow and outrage in politically divided Spain

Shock of rail tragedy gives way to sorrow and outrage in politically divided Spain
- Published
The chaos and horror of Spain's second rail tragedy this year has been conveyed vividly by survivors of Wednesday's high-speed crash that has left at least 69 people dead.
But as Spain holds three days of mourning, revelations from leaked audio recordings of the apparent human error in a control room in the minutes before this disaster happened have given way to public disbelief and outrage, in a highly politicised climate, exactly a month before Spaniards go to the polls.
"You don't know what's happening, you don't know what has happened, you just know that you're being thrown around in a matter of seconds," said Iñaki García, 60.
He was on the stationary Iryo train that was rammed from behind by a Renfe train on the Madrid-Seville line near Urda, around 140km (87 miles) south of the capital.
"There were people injured, walking around, there were dead people," he said. "In the next carriage along there were a lot of dead people."
Recalling the horrific scenes around him, one young man told the BBC in a quivering voice: "I don't know if that's something I'll ever recover from."
Stories of tragedy have continued to emerge. A pharmacist from Urda was one of the first to reach the scene, bringing with him first aid supplies and medicine.
"One of [the passengers] was saying goodbye to his wife and children. His last words were 'God is good'," Antonio García told Spanish radio.
Similar scenes of grief played out only nine months ago in the southern village of Adamuz, when a collision on the same Madrid-Seville route killed 46 people.
Now, in the town of Urda, just like Adamuz, awful stories are combined with acts of kindness and solidarity.
Locals turned out to help the injured, bringing blankets, food and water to a nearby sports hall that was converted into a makeshift hospital for much of the day.
"We all started to turn out to help and we organised ourselves as best we could," said Rosa María Domínguez, a local woman, who described the scene as "a horror film".
Spain Train Crash: What Happened?
We look at how the deadly train crash happened, the rescue operation and the aftermath.
However, the overriding sentiment that these two tragedies have generated is one of confusion and a failure to comprehend how this could have happened.
Not long ago, the speed, efficiency and safety of Spain's high-speed rail system, the largest in Europe, was the envy of its neighbours.
The Adamuz crash triggered a nationwide debate about whether the network was fit for purpose.
This latest incident intensifies pressure on the left-wing government of Pedro Sánchez, in the middle of an election campaign where his Socialist PSOE is behind the conservatives in most opinion polls.
On Wednesday night a demonstration protesting at the government's handling of the rail network saw far-right groups turn out and clash with police.
Although the main parties, other than the far-right Vox, have suspended campaigning, Sánchez has twice visited the scene of the crash and his People's Party rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo came to Urda on Thursday.
Sánchez's transport minister, Óscar Puente, made clear from the start that a computer failure followed by human error was the likely cause of the crash. By late evening, leaked audio recordings of a control-room operator talking to train drivers appeared to back that up.
Puente has long been a hate figure for the right, and with two of the worst rail tragedies in Spanish history taking place on his watch, the criticism is only going to increase.
Spain's biggest train drivers' union Semaf condemned the leak of audio recordings as irresponsible and slanted. The union had already called a strike for Thursday in a bid to ensure that "urgency to travel is never prioritised over safety".
One train driver, Vicente Almenar, told Spanish media: "They always look for the last link in the chain, where it's weakest, but here the entire procedure failed because we don't even know what our colleague was seeing on the screen," he told Spanish media.
Sánchez had not been expecting rail safety to dominate his campaign, but that now looks increasingly likely.
After two accidents and more than 100 deaths on the same high-speed line, Feijóo told reporters in Urda on Thursday: "The Spanish people need answers. They are wondering what is happening to high-speed rail in their country."
And he emphasised that politics was not about talking - it was about acting.

article:
Secondary school teacher to crofter - life on the UK's most remote island

Secondary school teacher to crofter - life on the UK's most remote island
- Published
Katy Phenix's new life as a crofter on the UK's most remote inhabited island is a far cry from her previous life as a history teacher in a secondary school.
The 33-year-old relocated to Fair Isle from Redcar, North Yorkshire, with her partner Josh Moore, 35, and their children Teddy, 11, and Hetty, six, in July.
They had never visited the island before moving there but were seeking more family time and a better quality of life.
Four months on, they say they have settled in to their "completely different" island life and feel "really lucky".
Fair Isle lies half-way between Orkney and Shetland and has a population of about 60 people.
It is three-miles (5km) long and owned by the National Trust for Scotland (NTS).
Since moving to the island, Katy has begun working as a part-time crofter - a crofter is a person who shares pasture land to raise livestock.
She said the family mainly moved to Fair Isle for more time together.
"We weren't living the lives we wanted," she said. "We were snatching time together over weekends and holidays.
"You get a mortgage, you get a car and you have to work to keep that up. Moving to Fair Isle has cut all of that out."
Fair Isle has a primary school and nursery, a local shop, post office and a community hall.
Katy has also taken up a post in early years education.
Her children are two of only five pupils at the local primary school.
Josh is in high demand as a self-employed electrician because Fair Isle is off-grid with its own energy system.
The island's homes are powered by a combination of wind and solar power.
A diesel generator provides a back-up supply.
Josh is working on a large battery replacement project.
"We're switching to new lithium ones," he said. "I'm also fixing people's lights and sockets."
He said friends and family had been supportive of the family's move.
The couple have been engaged for several years and are planning a wedding on the island in 2027.
"The church is literally next door", Katy said.
The pair said they hoped another family with children would move to Fair Isle early next year.
The National Trust for Scotland has advertised a further opportunity, with a five-bedroom house and 12-acre (5ha) croft available to rent.
The trust said it was encouraging applicants with crofting and land management experience, trade skills such as plumbing or anyone looking to develop a craft business on the island.
Angus Murray, NTS operations manager for Fair Isle, said: "We're inviting applications from hard-working and enthusiastic people who will bring skills, creativity and care to this special place."
The deadline, external for applications is Sunday 8 November.
Eileen Thomson, who chairs the Fair Isle committee, said everyone had a role to play.
"You'll see people working in the fire service, the shop and the school," she said.
Eileen said the new tenants should be multi-skilled.
"A lot of the really big jobs need every single person to turn up and help, whether it's gathering all the common grazing sheep or doing the hay bales in summer," she added.
She said creative people could also support the famous Fair Isle knitwear - a textile developed on the island in the early 19th Century.
Eleven-year-old Teddy hopes more children will move to the island so he can start a football team.
"We do a lot of outdoor activity," he said.
His six-year-old sister Hetty added that their seven pets from North Yorkshire were "loving" island life.

article:
Adventurer completes 400-mile expedition after losing contact with team

Adventurer completes 400-mile expedition after losing contact with team
- Published
An adventurer has completed the first leg of his latest challenge after losing contact with his UK team for almost 24 hours.
Ash Dykes, 35, from Old Colwyn, Conwy, holds five world records but his most recent quest was the first of six back-to-back expeditions he will take on in extreme environments.
Dykes encountered elephants, gorillas and was chased by "killer" bees as he rowed more than 434 miles (700 km) along rivers in the Congo Basin, central Africa.
Towards the end of the journey, Dykes' portable satellite kit lost power. He said: "My parents and fiancée were worrying but as soon as I had a bit of signal I made sure I got in touch".
In his latest Project 6 challenge, Dykes will attempt six expeditions in very different locations.
He has previously walked 4,000-miles (6,437km) along the length of China's Yangtze River in 2019 and kayaked the length of the Coppename river in Suriname from source to sea in 37 days
On "going missing", Dykes said his "power bank just shut down".
"We were underneath the jungle canopy, because we were staying with a small community, and then it took me about 20 hours before I could get out the first message," he said.
As the adventurer is sharing expeditions "live", he said he had learned lessons from the experience going forward.
He said: "I don't think the world's ready for a truly live expedition so I've learned from that...
"If I lose contact again with the team, we have to keep it within the team because I do know that that hit alarms and a lot of people were stressed and panicked. So it's important to make this as live as possible, but moving forward, it can't be that live anymore."
During the adventure, Dykes said his biggest fear was not the danger posed by wildlife or disease, but the extreme heat during many hours of kayaking in rivers home to crocodiles and hippos with no shade.
He said: "We took the warnings seriously. Experience means listening to local advice, reading the conditions and making the decisions that get your team through safely."
For the explorer, the main highlight was spending time with the Baka tribe, a semi-nomadic indigenous ethnic group.
They demonstrated their hunting prowess which involves trapping animals in netting set up around the jungle.
"They were amazing, they took us under their wings, they showed us how they survive, how they hunt, how they gather," Dykes said.
"They took us to an area where we saw a group of gorillas within Sanga National Park. I was about five metres away from silverback."
Dykes was joined on his trek by local guide Obed Temba Tuyumvire as well as videographer Will Perez, who has been helping chart the journey with regular social media posts.
His popularity on TikTok has soared following his latest adventure.
Dykes said: "It felt like the world was on the river with us."
But he added some followers were disappointed in the lack of drama.
"Everyone wanted that excitement, that danger, but if something was to happen, I'd be criticised: 'this is dangerous'.
"Now that I've made it unscathed, everyone's like: 'It's easy, there were no crocs'.
"So there's no true winning when you go that viral."
He said he lost 11lbs (5kg) during the trip, as he was relying mostly on ration packs of food.
In a social media post to mark the end of the first stage of Project 6, Dykes said: "It's been a lot. We've faced ups and downs - seen some crazy wildlife, but more importantly we've survived."
Dykes said he would reveal the second stage of Project 6 next week, and hinted it would be somewhere "a lot colder" than the Congo Basin.

Plans unveiled for open air swim and sauna complex at old dock

Plans unveiled for open air swim and sauna complex at old dock
- Published
New details have been announced of a swim and sauna complex that could transform an old dock in Cardiff.
Waterfront developers Nordic Urban revealed plans to transform the old grade-II Mount Stuart Graving Docks in Cardiff Bay into a 12,400 square metre year-round outdoor swimming and sauna complex.
It will include a 25 metre outdoor heated swimming pool, along with hot and cold pools, four saunas, changing and relaxation rooms as well as a cafe, restaurant, terraces overlooking the water and a rain garden.
The planning documents read that the main vision is to transform the "under-utilised docks" into a "year-round public swimming, wellness and cultural destination."
The project is "rooted in Nordic values of inclusion and social connection" and is "aiming to create a modern outdoor bathing culture in the heart of the city."
The complex is based on, and named after, the Allas Pool in Helsinki which opened in 2016.
The development is proposed to provide both a "premium wellness offering" alongside "open-access public swimming".

article:
Healey provides some breathing space but things still set to get worse for most

Healey provides some breathing space but things still set to get worse for most
- Published
John Healey talked of charting a new course for Britain, but this Budget was more about course-correcting than charging down a new path.
It was abundantly clear that the financial fallout from that conflict in the Middle East has hampered the finances of households and businesses – and the government's ability to help.
While the government targeted those impacted by higher energy and fuel bills, the "breathing space" it aimed to provide was limited; it is a pill that doesn't fully alleviate the pain.
The most telling evidence was that official forecasters predict that while earnings will rise, that is not compensating for higher prices and taxes.
Even after the extra help is taken into account, households' incomes after inflation and tax are set to be typically lower across the next two years than the start of the parliament. On that basis, it could be the second worse parliament for living standards, after the last one, since the 1950s - a sign of how far the war has blown prosperity off course.
But it can't be all be blamed on the war. Taxes haven't helped. Although there were few major measures aimed at households, the policy of previous chancellors of freezing the thresholds at which different rates of tax on income apply - fiscal drag - has been maintained in the background, scooping more money out of pay packets.
Overall, this Budget has the tax burden - the proportion of the nation's income going to the tax office - rising to a new historic high of 38.6%
However, a more generous package of help would have been hard to pull off. The impact of higher inflation and debt have increased borrowing costs by £14bn in the past year alone.
The Chancellor had to prove to the markets which lend the government money that he has a plan to bring down future debt to avoid those costs climbing further.
As it stands, debt interest repayments are due to be £160bn in 2032, more than double the amount spent on schools in England.
And the plans Healey has unveiled already eat into wiggle room he has within the public finances. He says he was right to do so - that's what such safety margins are there for - in times of strife. But the great uncertainty that remains made going further very risky. Energy prices remaining high, for example, could easily chew up all the spare cash.
So the result was what some have termed a beige, safe Budget. As Healey strove to prove his fiscally sound credentials, there wasn't even the customary rabbit pulled out of the hat, the end-of-speech sweetener.
The markets seem reassured – even if some of his tax raising plans involve clamping down on loopholes and those not paying the right tax, which is always highly uncertain.
- Budget 2026: Key points at a glance 
  - Published5 days ago
- Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you 
  - Published5 days ago
So the chancellor appears to have bought himself some breathing space. But that means some big questions have been postponed until another day, not least on public services.
Higher-than-expected inflation may mean that if areas such as health and defence are prioritised, budgets for some other "unprotected" areas – justice and higher education for example – are set to lag behind inflation after 2028.
There was a hint too from John Healey that he'd tap into some of those budgets to help out defence spending. To maintain those budgets in 2030 would means finding tens of billions of pounds.
And issues around the other big area of spending – welfare – remain unresolved. Between 2025 and 2032, spending there is set to increase by £100bn.
The official forecasters also noted the rapid rise in sickness and disability caseloads since the start of the pandemic. They warn if that trend continued, spending on such benefits would rise by a further £13bn.
Any suggestion of welfare reform has been postponed until the forthcoming review into the plight of workless young people.
Then there's the issue of boosting growth. There was a bit more detail on the plans for devolution – but there is much to be fleshed out.
And on another key part of the growth strategy, housebuilding, there was disappointing news. Even though first-time buyers are set to get more help, their first home may be more elusive.
Between regulation and higher costs – in part, related to the war - the OBR estimates that 190,000 fewer homes will be built by 2032 compared to what it thought in March, a significant setback.
So the chancellor may have unveiled 98 (relatively small) measures but the to-do list gets longer.
With his official forecasters warning that, in a very uncertain world, his finances face exceptional risks, playing a wait-and-see game feels like a prudent move.
The risks go both ways: the OBR points out that a swift resolution to the war and an improvement in the economy could spell a significant boost to the public finances.
So the chancellor has more reason than most to keep his fingers crossed that happens rapidly.
For as it stands, the official forecasters say incomes after inflation, living standards, are set to be only 1% higher at the end of the decade than at the start.
A series of economic shocks outside out control could thwart plans to turbo-boost prosperity . And as today shows, breathing space only extends so far.

Man and boy arrested after allegedly attacking One Nation volunteer with bat

Two people have been arrested after a volunteer for Australia's right-wing populist party One Nation was allegedly assaulted with a baseball bat.
A man, 37, and a boy, 14, were arrested on Sunday night after an incident outside the volunteer's home in Torquay, about 100km (62 miles) south-west of Melbourne.
The man was charged with assault offences and remanded in custody while the boy was issued with a caution. The volunteer was hospitalised with non-life threatening injuries, police said. He remains in a stable condition.
One Nation's Victorian leader Warren Pickering claimed the attack happened after the pair "interfered with" election signs on the volunteer's property.
Police haven't provided any detail about a motive, but Pickering said the alleged assault was "un-Australian and unacceptable".
"Political violence or intimidation of any kind against anyone is unacceptable in this country," he said.
"If you don't like someone's politics, you vote accordingly. You don't assault them."
On Tuesday, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson visited the injured volunteer at University Hospital Geelong where he is recovering, praising his "resilience" and "belief" in her party.
"He wants to go right back out there and put the signs up," she said outside the hospital.
The party has said the man has serious injuries, and shared a photo of him with severe swelling and bruising to his face.
Victorian Premier Ben Carroll described the attack as "shocking".
"Whether you're wearing a red, a blue, an orange, or a green T-shirt, they are volunteers," he said.
"They are out there doing what they believe is right, and no one should be coming under attack."
The alleged attack comes during a state election campaign in Victoria, and amid a reckoning in the country more broadly over the tone of political debate, after the attack on Federal MP Helen Haines last month.
Police have not detailed a motive for the incident - which left Haines needing both of her legs amputated - but politicians, law enforcement, and experts have said heated public discourse is heightening the threat of political violence in the country.

Major test for Australia's social media ban begins in High Court

Major test for Australia's social media ban begins in High Court
- Published
Australia's rush to put in place a landmark social media ban for children led to "ill thought out" reforms which have robbed them of their right to free communication, the country's top court has been told.
In a major test for the world-leading policy, online forum Reddit and a digital rights group argued at a hearing on Tuesday that the law should be struck down as it is unconstitutional.
Introduced last December, the ban is among a number of online safety reforms the Australian government has spearheaded in recent years.
Supporters say it protects children from harmful content, but critics say it is too blunt an instrument and efforts should focus on improving online safety.
Speaking outside the High Court in Canberra, Communications Minister Anika Wells said the question of what society is willing to accept from tech platforms is "the most compelling policy question of our time".
"We are here to defend a fundamental tenet of Australian democracy, which is an Australian's right, and particularly an Australian child's right, to be free from harm," Wells said.
"We seek to defend that from sustained ideological attack."
The constitutional challenge was filed by the Digital Freedom Project a few weeks before the ban started on 10 December last year. The group is led by New South Wales parliamentarian John Ruddick, who told reporters outside the court the policy amounted to "censorship".
Two teens who originally spearheaded the case, Noah Jones and Macy Neyland, have since withdrawn as plaintiffs. The teens have yet to publicly state their reasons for doing so.
But Jones told media outside the court that children deserved to have their voices heard.
"If the children aren't collaborating and sharing their own views, then they're just spectators in their own world," he said, according to Nine newspapers.
Reddit also launched a High Court challenge to the ban, arguing the policy has serious implications for privacy and political rights.
The company said it shared Australia's goal of protecting young people online "but there are better and more effective ways" than a ban.
"As we challenge this law in court, we'll continue to comply with it and advocate for more effective youth safety measures," said Reddit's chief communications officer Adam Collins.
Inside the courtroom, the company's lawyer Perry Herzfeld argued the law breached the freedom of political expression implied in Australia's constitution by restricting children from the most important means of communication in the modern world.
He said the ban was "ill thought out" and contradicted the advice of Australia's online safety tsar, and was rushed through without true public consultation - pointing out they had only 24 hours to make submissions about the law.
Meanwhile government lawyer Joanna Davidson SC, began outlining for the full bench of the High Court why the government believed social media harmed children. She will continue presenting her case on Wednesday.
Under the ban, ten platforms - Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Reddit, Snapchat, X, Kick, Threads and Twitch - must take "reasonable steps" to ensure no one under 16 years old can access its site.
Platforms risk fines of up to A$99m (US$70m, £52m) for serious or repeated breaches, but since the ban started, no company has been fined.
The eSafety Commissioner - the body tasked with enforcing the ban - has launched several investigations into alleged non-compliance by Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube.
WhatsApp and online gaming sites like Roblox and Discord were not included in the ban, nor were educational platforms like YouTube Kids and Google Classroom.
In the first few days of the ban, Meta - which owns three of the banned platforms - said it had closed about half a million accounts.
Some children said they were booted off their accounts in the days before and when the ban started - but many have said they were able to easily circumvent the age checks which included uploading credit card details, photo IDs or a selfie.

Lib Dems and Reform UK in war of words over alleged shove
