A war of words has broken out between Lib Dem MP Caroline Voaden and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage over an alleged physical altercation in the House of Commons.
The row was triggered when Farage, explaining why he had not attended Wednesday's Budget, said he had been involved in a "physical altercation" with another MP at the State Opening of Parliament in May and had wanted to avoid a similar incident.
Voaden revealed herself to be the MP Farage had been referring to, writing on social media that she had been left "shocked and bloody angry" by the confrontation.
The Lib Dems have claimed that Farage "attempted to shove" their South Devon MP but a Reform source accused the party of "lying".
The Reform insider added: "The Lib Dems were claiming Nigel shoved her and that she was shaken, the video disproves that clearly."
Footage, first unearthed by the Daily Telegraph, shows the pair leaving the chamber together at the state opening of Parliament but there is no visible evidence of a major altercation.
However, Voaden has said the incident between herself and Farage was not shown in the clip originally posted by the Telegraph, external.
The incident does not appear to have been captured on the official feed of the state opening provided by Parliament.
Voaden said Farage had been ordered to apologise to her after she complained to Commons authorities. The House of Commons would not comment on this.
In a statement, Voaden said: "The truth is that on the day of the King's Speech, Farage missed his chance to process with the other party leaders to the Lords, and rather than queue with the rest of us, he shoved me out of the way to barge past.
"Such behaviour is unacceptable in any workplace, and it has no place in the House of Commons.
"Shoving a colleague out of the way on a staircase just shows the complete disdain he has for Parliament and for other MPs."
Asked about the incident on Sky News, Lib Dem deputy leader Daisy Cooper said: "My understanding - I didn't see it, I wasn't there – but my understanding is that he physically shoved one of our female MPs out of the way, and that one of our male MPs then challenged him on that."
Reform MP Robert Jenrick told Sky: "I am sick to death of these pathetic Westminster debates."
The issue has only now emerged, nearly six months after the alleged incident, because Farage was pressed on why he had not been in the House of Commons chamber for the Budget on Wednesday.
In response he said: "At the State Opening of Parliament, I got involved… I didn't want to… but I got involved in a physical altercation with an MP in the chamber.
"I didn't make a fuss about it, I didn't complain, but I could see given that my prayer card had been removed, I was heading towards another physical altercation.

article:
No windows and steel doors - life at NI's 'most-attacked Orange hall'

No windows and steel doors - life at NI's 'most-attacked Orange hall'
- Published
Orangemen whose hall has been targeted dozens of times in sectarian attacks say the fear and intimidation has damaged their community and left them unable to properly celebrate their heritage and culture.
Rasharkin Chosen Few Orange lodge believes its hall is "the most-attacked Orange hall in Northern Ireland" and says there have been 51 incidents in 30 years.
Police recorded 17 hate crimes in the past year against Orange and Apprentice Boys' halls across Northern Ireland - an increase on the previous two years and the second highest in five years.
Rasharkin Orangemen say they have lost confidence in police, particularly after CCTV showed a patrol car driving over freshly-painted graffiti.
Leigh Gerrow, a member of the lodge, said attacks ranged from graffiti to attempts to set fire to the hall and meant the building now had steel doors and no windows, with members unable to park their cars outside in case they were attacked.
"Sometimes you need to take a step back and realise that's not a normal way to be living," he said.
The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) said it had a "robust and comprehensive policing plan in place" to prevent further attacks in Rasharkin and it condemned sectarianism, intimidation and hate crime.
Gerrow said the attacks on the County Antrim lodge were "an attempt to incite, intimidate, threaten and at times provoke a reaction as well".
"It's not just an attack on an Orange hall, it's an attack on what that hall represents and what it stands for and the community that it represents," he said.
"It sends a very clear message from the perpetrators to the members of my community: 'You are not wanted here.'"
Gerrow said members of the lodge wanted people from all sections of society to be allowed to express their culture and traditions in peace.
He added that the lodge was frustrated by the response of the police.
CCTV footage shared with BBC News NI by the lodge showed an incident on 12 July 2025 - the height of the Orange Order's marching season - when masked figures painted "INLA" on the road outside.
At about 01:15 the figures disappear from view - with one seen running away - seconds before a PSNI patrol vehicle drives over the graffiti without stopping.
Moments later vandals threw paint at the hall.
Other CCTV footage from June 2026 showed a masked figure spraying sectarian slogans on the hall.
'Handled really badly'
Gerrow said the footage of both incidents was given to police but they declined to share it publicly.
"Sadly and disappointedly, I'd say the police have handled this really badly," he said.
The PSNI said officers were on patrol in the Rasharkin area about 10 minutes before "the reported criminal damage" to the hall on 12 July 2025.
A spokesperson said officers responded from Kilrea as soon as a report was received at 01:22, about seven minutes after the timestamp on the CCTV footage showed the patrol vehicle driving past the hall.
They said no-one was present when patrols were in the area.
The spokesperson added that CCTV of both the July 2025 and June 2026 incidents was examined by officers and was "unsuitable" for a public appeal.
The lodge's senior officer, worshipful master Rodney Cubitt, said the attacks had an affect on its charity fundraising efforts, which had to be run during the day to avoid the risk of attack.
"We would like to run some events here at night but we feel it's more safe to have them during the day," he said.
Cubitt said the lodge had a long history going back to 1796 and it was important for members to keep a presence in the village.
"It makes us harder to promote and to encourage people to come and join our ranks," he said.
"We feel that the vast majority in this area would have great tolerance for us and respect and we appreciate that.
"It's only a very small minority in this village that has an aggressive approach to our culture."
Democratic Unionist Party MLA Cheryl Brownlee said the rise in attacks on halls was worrying and unacceptable.
"If you cannot have your traditions and your culture respected without being petrol bombed, graffitied, attacked, what sort of society do we have?" she asked.
Brownlee, who is an Orangewoman, said there needed to be community confidence in the police but that at the moment that was "a struggle".
"The PSNI need to be active on the ground," she said.
"When communities are showing confidence in them and reporting [incidents], they need to be able to see the officers there, reacting and and investigating to the fullest extent.
"We need to see that brought through to justice."
Brownlee added she was concerned over rhetoric about the Orange Order.
"Over the past few weeks I've seen images of Orangemen crossed out, I have seen some horrific things in Belfast saying 'shoot your local Orangeman'," she said.
"To see that is absolutely devastating."
PSNI district commander Supt Yvonne McManus said she recognised the serious affect the incidents had on members of the Orange lodge.
She said repeated attacks must not be viewed as an isolated series of incidents.
"As such, we looked at the wider pattern of offences this year in relation to the Orange hall and adopted a different policing approach," McManus said.
She said the impact of attacks on halls went beyond individuals and that sectarian incidents could generate fear and damage relationships within a community.
"Often, this is due to the senseless actions of what is actually a very small minority," McManus said.
"Collaboration, engagement, respect and mutual understanding are therefore vital elements to countering polarising narratives."

Welsh public sector unlikely to meet net zero plans by 2030, say auditors

Welsh public sector unlikely to meet net zero plans by 2030, say auditors
- Published
A spending watchdog has strongly criticised the lack of progress made by public sector organisations in tackling climate change.
Audit Wales says since a Welsh government "climate emergency" was declared, external in 2019, "decarbonisation" has become a lower priority for public bodies.
It says there are many examples of positive changes but the "collective ambition" for a net zero public sector in Wales by 2030 is unlikely to be met.
It has been estimated that it would cost at least £2.3bn to decarbonise Welsh council buildings alone.
The Welsh government said its 2030 ambition had "driven action and leadership, but it's clear that there is more work to do".
Net zero means balancing the amount of planet-warming "greenhouse" gases produced by human activities with the amount being actively removed from the atmosphere.
Effectively this means no longer adding to the total amount of these gases in the atmosphere to limit climate change.
- Wales 'to go further' on climate target 
  - Published12 June 2019
- Wales facing unrecognisable future, warns commissioner 
  - Published29 April 2025
In its new report, the spending watchdog said public bodies in all sectors recognise decarbonisation is important.
But it said: "Since 2022, financial and political pressures have caused decarbonisation to fall down the priority list.
"Public bodies told us their overall financial pressures mean they are struggling to invest in decarbonisation."
It criticised the Welsh government for not defining the "collective ambition" for net zero by 2030 as a "target".
"There are also no penalties or incentives to drive compliance. Some public bodies told us this had added to uncertainty around the level of priority to attach to carbon reduction."
On spending, it added that public bodies had made "limited progress" overall in understanding how much it will cost to decarbonise in the near or longer term.
"Where public bodies have estimated the longer-term cost, some described it as unaffordable."
Ann-Marie Harkin from Audit Wales said: "We can list positive examples, but not enough progress has been made overall, and we owe it to future generations to do better."
In 2017, the then-Labour Welsh government called for a net zero public sector by 2030, saying that public bodies were "uniquely placed" to influence emissions in areas such as buildings and transport.
The thinking was that if government-backed bodies made the switch and invested in infrastructure like electric vehicles and charge points, renewable power and heating systems, it would make it easier and cheaper for the public to follow suit.
The "collective ambition" does not require every public body to reach net zero individually by 2030 but it is meant to provide a shared direction of travel and an expectation that all public bodies contribute towards reducing emissions.
Responding to the report, a spokesperson for the Welsh government said: "A net zero public sector is a priority for Welsh government.
"We want to continue to support the decarbonisation of the public sector to lower emissions, energy bills and strengthen energy security.
"The 2030 ambition has driven action and leadership, but it's clear that there is more work to do on decarbonisation across and beyond the public sector in Wales."
The current Plaid Cymru government's ambition is for Wales, as a whole, to reach net zero by 2040 - which is ten years sooner than the current legally binding target for Wales and UK.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham's call for governments to hand more powers down to regions and cities "just doesn't work" in Wales, a former Welsh government minister has said.
Lee Waters is one of two ex-Labour ministers who have criticised the UK government's push for Wales to hand more powers to local councils.
The other, Alun Davies, accused his Labour colleagues in Westminster of putting him through "hell" when he tried to reform councils in 2018.
Burnham appealed to Welsh and Scottish governments for "deeper devolution" when he met their first ministers last week, and said the UK's four nations must "move together" to devolve more to regions and cities.
- Burnham promises more devolution and public control of essential services 
  - Published1 September
Waters, who stepped down as Welsh transport minister in 2024 before leaving the Senedd at the last election, commented on Friday after former Manchester mayor Burnham's meeting with Welsh First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth in Glasgow.
Waters wrote on LinkedIn: "The term 'region' in an English context typically refers to an area covering between 1.5 and 3 million people. In Wales, regions cover much less dense areas.
"Transposing an English mayoral worldview onto a very different political geography just doesn't work. Wales may be a similar population size to the PMs old manor but that's where the parallel ends.
"His argument for England is that powers should flow from Westminster to city regions because they operate at an economically meaningful scale. Yet when the PM turns to Wales, he seems to suggest that powers already devolved to Cardiff Bay should be dispersed further down the system."
Waters said Burnham was not calling on his successor as Manchester mayor, Bev Craig, "to fragment the powers of the Greater Manchester Combined Authority".
He added Burnham wanted Wales to move "in the opposite direction" to Greater Manchester.
Following the meeting with Burnham on Friday, ap Iorwerth welcomed a "step forward" on more spending powers for the Welsh government.
But the first minister said further devolution within Wales is a matter for the Senedd, which controls local government.
However, ap Iorwerth had also promised to draw up a green paper on the powers local authorities have, and how they can work together regionally, with potential legislation after the next election in 2030.
'Crumbs off the table'
Former Welsh local government minister Davies told Radio Wales Breakfast on Monday he was also not sure that Burnham's plans to devolve more powers to English councils would work in Wales.
Davies, who lost his seat at May's Senedd election, had attempted to force mergers between Wales' 22 councils in 2018 in an attempt to reorganise and empower the local authorities.
After robust opposition from the Labour-dominated Welsh Local Government Association, Davies ditched the plans.
Davies said on Monday that he had been "stopped at every step of the way" by Labour MPs.
Davies said he was also disappointed by the recent £30m rail investment for Wales announced at the UK government budget, suggesting they were "crumbs off the table".
He said Burnham had brought in a new "approach", and he urged the current Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock to "read that memo and to understand what it means, because it doesn't mean delivering the same powers of a Manchester mayor to my local authority Blaenau Gwent".
Davies said that "you cannot pretend... that you can equate the tiny local authorities that we have in Wales with the big mayoral regions of England".
In a later interview with Dros Frecwast on Radio Cymru, Davies said: "In the same way that Stephen Kinnock's dad stood up to negative attitudes in the Labour party in the '80s and transformed the party, the son has to do the same thing today."
He said Kinnock should "stand up to his fellow members and say that Wales will be part of the process [and] part of the devolution journey".
"The important thing for me is that devolution doesn't come to an end at Offa's Dyke, and that Wales is treated the same as Northern Ireland, Scotland and England and we have the same powers as exists in the other countries of the UK," he added.
It was the last time the Welsh government tried to reform local government, which has a structure that dates back to the 1990s and includes some very small local authorities.
On Sunday Kinnock told Radio Wales' Sunday Supplement that the UK government fully respected the devolution settlement.
"We are absolutely not in the business of prescribing how this should work in Wales," he said.
"That's up to the Welsh government to draw that map, if you like.
He said that it was a "collaborative process".
"It's got to be UK government, Welsh government, local authorities working together to figure this stuff out." he said.

UK-EU deal could see NI suppliers import products 'without all the red tape'

UK-EU deal could see NI suppliers import products 'without all the red tape'
- Published
The UK and EU's draft deal on food and plant products could allow suppliers in Northern Ireland to import products "without all the red tape".
If passed, the deal could benefit exporters based in Great Britain as it would reduce the extra costs and paperwork they face when selling goods to EU states and Northern Ireland.
It should also remove many of the post-Brexit goods checks between GB and Northern Ireland.
Robin Mercer, who runs the Hillmount chain of garden centre stores in counties Antrim and Down, said: "Honestly, all gardeners and plant suppliers are going to be so happy that, if we can get rid of all this red tape, it will be amazing.
"We can go back to the old days where you can bring in roses, you can bring in shrubs, you can bring in your sweet potatoes, without all the red tape and bring in the varieties you want."
Garden centres and plant importers in Northern Ireland have been particularly hard hit by post-Brexit restrictions in recent years.
However, the deal would not cut all Brexit red tape entirely because Northern Ireland would still be the only part of the UK that must follow EU customs rules.
Critics of the plan argue that in return for a relaxation on trade rules between GB and the EU, the UK government is agreeing to adhere to EU goods standards without any say in how those standards are set.
Those critics include some unionist leaders, who also object to the fact that Northern Ireland would continue to be treated differently to the rest of the UK.
- UK and EU agree draft deal to scrap Brexit red tape over food exports 
  - Published3 hours ago
What is the Irish Sea border?
The Irish Sea border was the term coined for checks and controls on goods entering Northern Ireland from the rest of the UK.
It came about as the result of an initial Brexit deal between the EU and UK in 2019.
The deal was revised in 2023, and is now known as the Windsor Framework.
It was agreed that the most practical way to keep the border open between Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland after Brexit was for Northern Ireland to follow many EU laws on the regulation of goods.
However this means that goods coming from the rest of the UK into Northern Ireland face paperwork and other restrictions to ensure they meet EU rules.
Food products and plants face the most bureaucracy and this continues to cause problems for retailers.
For many nationalists in Northern Ireland, this is a necessary compromise to minimise the impact of Brexit on the island of Ireland.
For many unionists it is a "constitutional affront" which undermines Northern Ireland's place in the UK.
The largest unionist party, the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP), prevented Northern Ireland's power-sharing government from operating between 2022 and 2024 in protest at the Irish Sea border.
How could an agri-food deal change things?
Agri-food deals from the EU fall into two broad categories: New Zealand-style or Swiss-style.
The EU's deal with New Zealand means that each party recognises the other has high food standards and so the frequency of checks on products and paperwork is reduced.
However, New Zealand still sets its own standards and a proportion of goods are still checked as they enter the EU.
By contrast there are no regulatory border controls for trade in agri-food products between Switzerland and the EU.
But the Swiss only have this deal because they agreed to follow EU rules almost to the letter, without much say in setting those rules.
Switzerland is obliged to modify its laws in response to changes in EU legislation - what is known as dynamic alignment - and accept oversight from the European Court of Justice.
It is a Swiss-style deal which the UK and EU are now on the verge of finalising.
Such a deal would mean the Irish Sea-border controls on GB food products entering Northern Ireland could be effectively ended.
Border control posts built at Northern Ireland ports would become largely redundant, although pre-Brexit checks on livestock would continue.
The 'Not for EU' labels seen on GB food products sold in Northern Ireland would no longer be needed.
What border processes would remain?
The Irish Sea is really two borders.
One deals with products' standards - making sure goods can be legally sold.
The other deals with customs - making sure the correct tariffs have been paid.
An agri-food deal would go a long way to removing the standards border, but it would leave the customs border untouched.
Businesses in GB would still have to make customs declarations for goods going to Northern Ireland with the risk that goods would be delayed if the paperwork is incorrect.
What have traders said?
The President of the Ulster Farmers' Union, John McClenaghan, gave a cautious welcome to proposed UK-EU agreement.
"Initially, we would be very welcoming of what we see in draft form at the minute," he told the BBC's Good Morning Ulster programme.
"Now we do need to see more of the detail but certainly for some time now we've been calling out this higher level of bureaucracy and red tape which has been adding cost to our industry and that frictionless trade, particularly between east-west (GB to NI) trade.
"So very, very keen to see more of the detail but broadly speaking it sounds very positive."
What has the political reaction been?
Agriculture Minister Andrew Muir, of Alliance, welcomed the draft agreement as positive first step in reversing some of the "damage" Brexit did to the UK economy.
"I'm confident this will be good for consumers, good for businesses and good for our farmers.
"It's won't resolve everything. I've always been clear that cleaning up the mess caused by Brexit is a big job and I'll continue to constructively represent Northern Ireland, ensuring further and deeper collaboration with the European Union."
Stormont's Economy Minister, Caoimhe Archibald from Sinn Féin, pointed out that Northern Ireland already had its own arrangements in place "which mitigate the impact of Brexit".
She said the current rules "give the North a unique competitive advantage, being able to sell into both the British and EU markets".
But Archibald added that her party welcomed "anything that is going to minimise the friction for trade, for businesses."
DUP leader Gavin Robinson accused the UK government of negotiating a deal that would disregard the result of the Brexit referendum in order to "follow suit with the European Union".
"My question to them is this - if they are willing to ignore 2016, ignore the referendum and agree alignment in so many areas of life – why do they continue to keep Northern Ireland separate from the rest of the United Kingdom?" he asked.
"It's a constitutional affront to keep us separate from the rest of our country when they are accepting alignment in so many facets of trade and life."
Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) leader Jim Allister said the UK should have "taken back sovereignty" over food and plant trade in Northern Ireland but "chose not to".
"They've chosen to leave us under the sovereignty of the EU and instead to align the rest of the United Kingdom with EU rules – as a rule taker – for which then the United Kingdom will have to pay a significant contribution."
Allister added: "It does not take us out of the Customs Union and it is the Customs Union which decrees GB to be a 'foreign country', which then requires customs declarations and paperwork, etc. None of that will go."

article:
Schoolboy unlawfully killed in 1984, new inquest concludes

Schoolboy unlawfully killed, new inquest concludes
- Published
A schoolboy who was last seen when he left his home on his bike to fly a kite in September 1984 was unlawfully killed, a coroner has concluded.
The body of 15-year-old Mark Billington was found two months later hanging in a tree in woodland on the edge of Meriden, near Coventry, nearly seven miles (11km) from his home in South Yardley, Birmingham.
Police at the time treated the death as a suicide, but it became a murder inquiry in 2002. No-one has ever been charged. Mark's family has fought for four decades for answers.
Following a two-day inquest, senior coroner Louise Hunt told the court on Tuesday she was "satisfied that Mark was murdered and there was no evidence that he took his own life".
"It remains an unsolved murder", the court heard.
Warning: This story contains distressing details
Delivering her conclusion at Birmingham and Solihull Coroner's Court, Hunt said she was satisfied the evidence provided showed that the teenager went missing on 1 September 1984 and would have died at some point that day.
Addressing his family, Hunt displayed a picture of the smiling schoolboy as she described Mark as a "quiet" and "happy" boy who loved going to Butlins, his stamp collection and model railway kits.
The inquest heard the teenager had a "keen interest in cooking, and cheesecake was a regular on the menu" and was looking ahead to his future by writing to caterers about employment opportunities once he left school.
His father and mother Royston and Winifred Billington, who adopted Mark as a baby in 1971, had no concerns about any mental health issues and said going missing was "completely out of character"
The court heard the boy's body was found on 11 November by four men who were ferreting in the woodland in Meriden.
The court previously heard from consultant forensic pathologist Dr Brett Lockyer who said the rope found at the scene was "tied unusually" in an "elaborate arrangement" and it was unlikely that Mark would have been able to secure the knot himself.
Describing the last time he was seen, Hunt told the court Mark carried out his usual morning paper round, before he returned home where his parents last saw him sitting on their kitchen step before they left to go shopping at around 09:30.
He said goodbye to his grandfather and brother Russell Billington at about 11:00, before heading to The Rec, a park near their family home, with his bike and a blue kite with a crimson pink tail.
Witness sightings placed him in a number of locations near his neighbourhood that morning, including the Birmingham and Bridgewater Building Society on Church Road where he deposited his £8 wages.
A "comprehensive" missing persons investigation was launched when his parents called police after the newsagent where he worked alerted them he had not turned up for his evening shift at Allen's News.
That day, his jumper and building society passbook were found in the shed where his bike and kite were normally kept, the court heard. His kite was found in a hedge behind the family home two weeks later.
During the relaunched police investigation, three people were arrested but later released due to a lack of evidence.
The coroner's court heard West Midlands Police was satisfied Mark Billington was unlawfully killed.
Detectives continue to have a theory that Mark's death was linked to a bottle scam in which people took fizzy drink glass bottles to shops in exchange for a deposit, then stole them back to return again.
It is thought the teenager uncovered the involvement of one or more of the suspects and they "were trying to scare him".
The coroner told the court this remained West Midlands Police's main theory.
Hunt said Mark was "either a willing or duped victim or murdered".
She added that "it was extremely unlikely that he tied the knot" in the way he was found at the scene.
Due to the condition of his body it was not able to determine how he died and his medical cause of death was recorded as unascertained due to decomposition.
As the conclusion was delivered, Mark's family were tearful following a 42-year battle for answers.

article:
US tech stocks see sharp falls as AI spending nears $1tn

US tech stocks see sharp falls as AI spending nears $1tn
- Published
Tech stocks tumbled for the second day in a row as concerns rise over the hundreds of billions of dollars firms are investing in artificial intelligence (AI).
Shares in Intel plummeted by 28% on Friday, while Google owner Alphabet saw its stock price continue to fall another 1.4% after a 12% plunge on Thursday.
Other tech stocks, including Reddit and Amazon also fell, while the Nasdaq index of the largest tech firms listed in the US, ended October with its worst monthly slide since March 2025.
While tech firms are spending big on AI, their earnings are not always meeting analysts' expectations, spooking investors and creating fears of an AI bubble.
Major tech companies have ramped up artificial intelligence spending, with Meta, Alphabet, Oracle, Amazon, and Microsoft committing to spending $800bn between them in 2026.
Alphabet's stock market value fell sharply on Thursday, taking more than $500bn (£374bn) off its market value after it revealed the AI summaries it now provides as the top answer to search queries were affecting its core search advertising revenue.
At the same time, Alphabet expects to spend up to $205bn this year on investments, almost entirely related to AI.
The bigger losses on Friday were elsewhere however, with Intel shedding more than $130bn in value.
The chip maker said it planned to increase spending on AI despite weaker demand for computers, a major source of demand for its micro-processors.
On Thursday, Intel's finance chief David Zinsner said the firm did not expect to bring in more cash than it spent this year and forecast lower-than-expected revenue for its fourth quarter.
"Looking ahead, we see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," he said in the chip maker's third quarter earnings report.
In the earnings call, he said the firm had significantly ramped up investment in equipment in the third quarter and expected that to be "even more significant" in the following three months.
Amazon and Reddit down
Amazon on Thursday revealed it had also spent more cash than it was making, and that spending had increased six-fold over the span of three months.
The company has committed to spending $220bn this year, putting the money towards investments such as AI data centres, network equipment, and servers.
Amazon shares recovered some overnight losses, but were still down by 1.4% at the end of Friday trading.
Reddit stock plunged by 29%, after the social media platform revealed weaker-than-expected daily user figures and warned that Google's growing AI-driven search was hurting referral traffic.
Stock in online game platform Roblox also fell, down by 18%, as its daily active user numbers dropped.
Several major tech firms have reported earnings this week, including Microsoft, and analysts said there were questions about the payout from the huge investments in AI.
Chris Low, from investment management firm FHN Financial, said the bulk of what was happening in the stock market was in reaction to some of the biggest tech players such as Amazon and Google.
He told Reuters the companies were "showing some pretty significant growing pains as they aggressively pursue the AI build-out".
"The thinking is that these signs suggest that the entire sector is going to slow down."
'Investors have turned ruthless'
Many analysts have been debating the possibility of an AI bubble in the stock market.
The worry is that some tech firms will not be able to justify their sky-high valuations because the cost of building AI data centres and developing the software will end up being greater than the money they can make from it.
Kathleen Brookes, research director at trading firm XTB, said there have been many ups and downs in AI trade in recent months.
"Investors have turned ruthless, punishing any signs of disappointment in [third quarter] earnings," she said.
"The AI trade has had a good run in recent years, but now investors want payback, and companies like Alphabet and Intel are in the crosshairs."
However, stock market values for many of these companies remain well above where they were a year ago.
While the Nasdaq closed 2.8% lower, it is up 7.8% over the last year. Similarly Amazon is up nearly 8% over the past 12 months, while Alphabet is down 1.3%.
Brookes noted that November is typically a strong month for stocks.
"If we see AI stocks continue to struggle in the coming days, it could suggest the AI trade is past its peak, and investors will be looking for a new theme to drive markets," she said.

article:
How Clarkson's Farm is attracting young people to farming

How Clarkson's Farm is attracting young people to farming
- Published
Ellie grew up in a farming family and had planned to pursue a different career, until she was drawn back to agriculture by what her college has called "the Clarkson effect".
The 17-year-old is one of a growing number of young people choosing a career in farming, with Myerscough College in Lancashire putting a rise of 30% in applications down to the impact of Jeremy Clarkson's reality show on Amazon Prime Video.
First broadcast in 2021, it has followed the broadcaster attempts to run a farm in the Cotswolds.
For Ellie, Clarkson has put agriculture "in front of everyone in the country" and inspired her to follow the same path as her parents and grandparents.
Ellie's grandparents run a dairy farm near Garstang in Lancashire and her parents keep sheep and cattle, but she had decided to take a different path.
"I was doing A-levels for a year but that didn't suit me," she said.
"So I decided to come here and get back into farming.
"Jeremy Clarkson has put agriculture in front of everyone in the country.
"He has shown why agriculture is important in Britain for food production.
"There is a lot of people want to come into agriculture now."
Fellow student Oliver is not from a farming background, but said he had been equally influenced by watching the ups and downs at Clarkson's Diddly Squat Farm.
The 17-year-old said he believed the series had inspired a lot of his classmates to pursue a career in the industry.
"Interest in farming has spiked because Jeremy Clarkson is such a massive influence and isn't from a farming background himself," he said.
"It shows the side of farming that a lot of people do not see, including the harsh reality.
"It's a way of life.
"It's not for the money, it's for the life."
Course tutor David Singleton said the college had seen a rise in applications for farming courses since Clarkson's Farm first aired.
"It has had quite a big influence on student numbers," he said.
"We're finding a lot of people from outside the industry coming into agriculture and deciding to give it a go at 16 or 17.
"We've probably gone up about 30% since Clarkson's Farm [began]."
Singleton said it was not only Clarkson who had had an influence, as other programmes, such as former Emmerdale actor Kelvin Fletcher's ITV show Fletcher's Family Farm, had helped encourage young people to consider a career in agriculture.
Some female students at Myerscough have also said they have been inspired by farming influencer Harriet Cowan, who joined the fourth series of Clarkson's show as his main sidekick.
Melina, whose parents run a farm in Bacup, said Cowan "went on there like a girl boss, nails and lashes, proving the stereotype wrong".
But, for all the media influence, there are still students at the college for whom a life in farming felt like an inevitability.
Connie said all she could remember was "going out with my dad and doing work".
"I couldn't see my future any other way," she added.

article:
'An annoying buzz': The search for stealthier drones

'An annoying buzz': The search for stealthier drones
- Published
Nature lover Ashley Schmidt no longer spends much time in her garden, in the Dallas suburb of North Garland.
She's also given up on cycling to the local parks where she previously enjoyed taking close-up photos of the bugs, lizards and toads.
It's all because she can't stand the sound of the delivery drones that fly overhead, depositing her neighbours' online orders.
"They emit this very annoying buzz. It triggers my fight or flight response," says the 44-year-old administrative assistant.
"You can hear the drones on approach and you can hear them inside your home when they pass directly overhead and then you hear them as they leave," she says.
Schmidt is one of a growing number of people living with the noise of drones dispatched by companies including Amazon and Walmart as they seek to speed up home deliveries.
Delivery drone services, not long ago a novelty, are becoming part of everyday life for many people in the US.
Among them, Amazon Prime Air is in the process of expanding deliveries to nearly 500 cities and towns, delivering items that fit into a space the size of a shoe box. It has also launched to customers in and around Darlington in the north of England.
Smaller drone delivery services are popping up too: in some US cities, customers can order flying treats from their local pizza joint or ice cream parlour.
Even in cities where noise is already a steady part of life, the sound of drones seems to irk in a particular way.
While the steady passing of traffic might blend into the background, the sudden whine of a drone's rotors can pierce the everyday hum.
The sound tends to be "particularly noticeable, even when overall sound levels are relatively low," says Antonio Torija Martinez, professor in acoustic engineering and psychoacoustics at the University of Salford.
Unlike planes, drones operate at low altitudes and may fly directly over residential areas.
"They can expose communities that have not previously experienced significant aircraft noise, and who may therefore be more sensitive to changes in their local soundscape," says Torija Martinez.
He points to research showing that people respond strongly to a noise when they consider the source to be "novel, intrusive or frequent". People who benefit from a drone delivery service, for example, may be less bothered by the noise.
However, complaints about the sound of drones are likely to grow, he warns: "At the moment we are seeing some of these problems localised in some areas, but… as the drone sector expands, more and more of these complaints will happen."
In the US, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) regulates commercial drones, but it has come under fire for allowing noisy drone delivery operations. The FAA says operators and local community leaders have primary responsibility for addressing any community concerns.
Might better technology muffle the irritating buzz?
One startup, Greenjets, set out to tackle both "noise level and the frequency of that noise," as Darren James, future technologies lead at the company, puts it.
The London-based business has designed a propulsion system it claims can reduce drone noise by at least two thirds.
While standard drones use spinning propellers that slice through open air, creating that high-pitched buzz, Greenjets encloses spinning blades inside a pod, to muffle the sound and direct the noise away from the ground.
Its system also quietens things down through slower rotor speed and by using materials that reduce vibration noise.
Making quieter drones isn't just about keeping the noise down for neighbours who are already sick of airborne deliveries.
Greenjets' low-noise tech has been used by police and harbour security teams in Germany. It has also helped conservationists in Africa, who are seeking to track poachers from above without being detected.
Battlefield drone operators also have good reason to keep the noise down, to avoid alerting the enemy of the approach of their unmanned vehicles.
"There are some efforts to reduce the sound of drones. The US Special Forces are interested, at an experimental stage," says Robert Tollast, a research fellow at Whitehall think tank The Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).
But he stresses that drone speed, rather than stealthiness, tends to come first for larger drones used in the war between Russia and Ukraine. "Make it faster, not less quiet, seems to be the approach," says Tollast.
For Detroit-based entrepreneur, Greg Sharrow, it was the challenge of broadcasting a classical music performance back in 2012 that set him on the path to quieter drone design.
He needed to film a violinist from a tricky angle and a drone seemed the only solution – except that it would be far too noisy.
As a starting point, "I knew that most of the noise from the drone was coming from the propeller, not the motor," he says. Specifically, it was the tips of the blades that he realised were creating the noise as they swiped through the air.
"I asked myself a very simple question, what would a tipless propeller look like and how would it function?"
The result was to create a propeller with twisted loop-shaped blades with no points.
It turned out it was easier to test his propeller in water than it was to repeatedly fly a drone, which led Sharrow to initially develop a less noisy boat propeller. Now, however, his company, Sharrow Engineering, is focusing on developing "ultra-quiet" drone rotors.
"We have validated that the technology works in drone applications and that it is dramatically quieter," says Sharrow.
Companies at the forefront of drone deliveries say they are also working to reduce the noise of their fleets. A spokesperson for Amazon says it has made "measurable sound improvements" to its drones and its latest designs use custom-designed propellers "that produce almost half the perceived sound of the prior generation, with a milder tone".
Drone maker Wing, which provides its vehicles for Walmart deliveries, says its propellers are designed to minimise noise. It also varies its flight paths to prevent repeated overflights over any single home or neighbourhood.
For Schmidt, fed up with the noise of drones, the only truly satisfactory solution would be to halt drone deliveries in her area. "I would like them to completely stop until they figure out how their services stop being a nuisance," she says.

article:
Scotland needs to embrace AI for its potential to be realised, minister says

Scotland needs to embrace AI for its potential to be realised, minister says
- Published
Scotland needs to embrace AI technology and trust the country's planning system to allow its potential to be realised, Innovation Minister Alyn Smith has said.
The Scottish government said AI could generate an additional £23bn in annual GDP for Scotland by 2035 with the right investment and leadership, citing independent research, external.
It comes at a time of widespread debate about the technology's value, as well as opposition to a number of proposed AI data centres in Scotland.
Smith told the BBC: "People are up for these developments but we need to see the planning system augmented to take due note of the significant implications of some of these projects, particularly on energy use."
The minister is due to attend a meeting in Edinburgh to hear from businesses about what they feel is holding back AI adoption and what is helping.
The event will also discuss the role of Scotland's universities and colleges in developing the AI and data skills the economy needs.
In September, the Scottish Greens led a debate calling for a pause on planning applications for large-scale AI data centres until national guidance had been published.
The Scottish government officially rejected this, though ministers said consent for such sites was "highly unlikely" to be granted before guidance is updated by the end of this year.
The government said that while there were "legitimate concerns" about large data centres, ministers were increasing oversight of the planning process.
Smith said some of the arguments surrounding the building of large data centres had been leading the conversation about the future of AI in Scotland.
"Some of the discourse we have seen on this is wild," Smith told Radio Scotland Breakfast.
"You'd think there wasn't a planning system at all. Comparing a really bad data centre in the middle of the Utah desert doesn't track through to what we're going to have in Scotland."
BBC Scotland has previously heard from people living near proposed data centre sites who worry about the appearance of developments, potential noise and the amount of land required to build them.
Experts have also warned MSPs that these data centres could push up electricity prices for consumers and challenge climate change targets.
Meanwhile the Scottish Greens say an unregulated expansion of data centres would "enrich giant AI companies and their super-rich owners".
Smith said the Scottish people were "pro-technology", pointing out that the IT industry in Scotland currently employs 87,000 people compared with the 21,000 people employed by the mining industry in 1979.
"Lets just get a grip on this," he said. "The people of Scotland are serious about technological developments. We've got a great industry right now."
He said there needed to be "confidence-building measures" in AI going forward.
"I want to see us get a grip on this debate - focus on the actual facts," he said. "We could get significant community benefit out of these things."
- How could AI change Scotland's public services? 
  - Published21 March
Smith said data centres were "the whisky bonds of the AI sector".
"They're an integral part of what the sector needs to be and for tech sovereignty in a really interconnected, but unstable world, I think it's quite important that if you're using a smartphone you ask where your data is being kept. Is it somewhere reliable? Is it somewhere trustworthy?"
Smith admitted that there were not a great deal of jobs created by data centres but emphasised the benefits AI could bring to businesses and the community.
Speaking about the concerns raised over data centres, he said: "Everything will be judged on its merit. People who are expressing concerns about particular developments, so they should. We have a planning system in Scotland that the people are in charge of.
"Not all of these applications are going to go forward because not all of them are suitable or have sufficient community engagement.
"We are a tech-heavy nation. We have got a lot of great jobs in this sector and I want a debate on the merit of these AI data centres."
The minister said a new Workplace Jobs Observatory - led by STUC - could examine in real time how AI was impacting on the workplace.
"This is a technology that is developing at pace," he said. "I want to see ethical guard rails put on it by legislation and want to align with the EU norms."
He said Tuesday's meeting would look at what the Scottish government was doing to adopt the technology and to make sure people had the relevant skills.
"Where there are opportunities for AI I want us to be all over it," he said. "And where there are things that people need to be reassured about I also want to be all over it because I'm here to represent the interests of the people of Scotland."
Julian David, chief executive of techUK, who is also attending the meeting, said: "The opportunity AI offers Scotland is significant, but it will only be realised if businesses and government pull in the same direction.
"Today's roundtable is a chance for industry to share what is working on the ground and for government to listen and act.
"By collaborating, we can help more businesses of every size make the most of AI."

Police investigate alleged assault after Enoch Burke confronts church leader

Police investigate alleged assault after Enoch Burke confronts church leader

Police are investigating a report of an assault following an incident involving Enoch Burke and the head of the Church of Ireland.
A video posted on social media by former teacher Burke shows him confronting and grabbing the arm of Archbishop of Armagh and Primate of All Ireland John McDowell.
A spokesperson for the church said Burke and members of his family approached the archbishop following a funeral service at St Patrick's Church of Ireland Cathedral on Thursday.
Burke has been in a long-running legal battle for defying court orders to stay away from a school that dismissed him for gross misconduct.
The dismissal arose out of his refusal to obey a direction of the school that a transgender pupil be addressed as 'they' and "because of his gross misconduct at a school religious service (and other events) and the manner in which he conducted his objection to transgenderism", according to the legal judgement.
The school also obtained an injunction restraining Mr Burke from trespassing on the school premises, which he has defied a number of times.
The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) confirmed it was investigating a report of an assault on a member of the clergy.
"Police enquiries are ongoing," a spokesperson added.
In the video, Burke, along with another man, confronts McDowell and grabs his arm before the Archbishop says "you are assaulting me".
He accuses McDowell of staying "silent" after Burke said he was in a "prison cell for 700 days".
McDowell continues to tell Burke that he is "assaulting" him and "preventing me from going about my lawful business".
He then says: "If you keep assaulting me, I am going to report you to the police."
Another member of the church tells Burke "you are in the grounds of a cathedral at a funeral".
A Church of Ireland spokesperson said it was a matter of "deep concern and sadness" that the Burke family had confronted the archbishop in a "particularly hostile and aggressive manner" following the funeral service for a rector of the diocese who died last week.
"No respect was shown for the occasion or the sanctity of the cathedral grounds," they continued.
"Entry onto the See House property, which is a private residence, is a further concern."
The Church said it would assist police with their enquiries and would make no further comment until the investigation was complete.

article:
UK and EU agree draft deal to scrap Brexit red tape over food exports

UK and EU agree draft deal to scrap Brexit red tape over food exports
- Published
The UK and EU have agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports, ahead of the UK-EU summit later this month.
The BBC understands the 200-page draft text for this so called "SPS" [sanitary and phytosanitary] agreement has been circulated to EU nations in Brussels for consideration at a meeting on Wednesday.
Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated alongside a 15-page draft joint statement for UK and EU top leaders.
The food deal is the most significant part of the so-called Brexit reset agreed so far, removing checks and red tape that hit exporters after the UK exited the EU's single market.
As a result of the agreement, the government claims the UK economy will eventually see £5.1bn worth of annual benefits.
The deal could have the following impact:
- Exports to the EU of fresh sausages, burgers, shellfish from domestic waters and seed potatoes would be able to resume
- It should remove the need for £200 Export Health Certificates, which confirm the product meets the health requirements of the country it is heading to
- It should also end the need for £25 Phytosanitary certificates, which show that plants or plant products are free from pests and diseases
- Inspector fees, organic certificates, some port fees and other checks for exports and imports to and from the EU could be removed
- It will bring back passports for British pets being taken into the EU
In return, the UK is expected to commit to observing and adapting to existing EU regulations on plant, animal and food trade standards - a process called "dynamic alignment".
Each of the elements on the table was up for discussion under Sir Keir Starmer, and the summit would have taken place by now had Labour not replaced its leader in July.
Under Andy Burnham, Britain's approach to post-Brexit relations with the EU have shifted significantly. Sir Keir said the UK would not rejoin the bloc in his lifetime, while Burnham has said he would like to see Britain back in the EU in his.
Jon Walsh, the chief executive and co-founder of Bio&Me, which makes granolas, mueslis and yoghurts, told BBC 5 Live the draft deal sounded like "really good news".
"We're just a small company but when we were trying to export our yoghurts before, every time we'd send a pallet we had to pay a vet to inspect it and that was £140, and that meant that you'd lose money... so we had to stop."
The company also had problems exporting granola and overnight oats, with some shipments being returned.
"It was so frustrating because it was the same person filling out the same form and yet half would make it through and half wouldn't," Walsh said.
"You just kind of give up because you're losing money."
In an interview with ITV, Burnham said "public opinion has changed nationally" since the 2016 Brexit vote, but added he would "not run ahead of public opinion" on the issue.
"The public need to be the boss when it comes to whatever happens with Brexit," he added.
Burnham also said he had not proposed the return of freedom of movement between the UK and EU.
Asked by the BBC about the UK's relationship with the EU, Tory Leader Kemi Badenoch said that while we should "work closely", "dynamic alignment" with the EU would be a red line and "actually take us backwards".
Liberal Democrat Europe spokesperson Al Pinkerton said the draft deal was a "patch, not a fix".
"The real solution is to rejoin the single market and to establish a customs union with the EU," he added.
Reform UK's business spokesman Richard Tice said: "One of the key benefits of Brexit was that Britain no longer had to adhere to ridiculous EU rules.
"Returning to any form of alignment with Europe would crush Britain's competitiveness and force us to surrender sovereignty over trade policy, putting trade deals worth hundreds of billions of pounds at risk."
While UK rules remain mostly aligned with EU ones, there are some areas where England has diverged from the EU rule book, for example on "precision breeding" of plants, previously known as gene editing. In recent weeks, agreement has been struck on transition arrangements while the EU's new regulations come in to force.
The government has already announced a European Partnerships Bill which will provide a legal mechanism for the application of new EU rules and regulations. This will also allow for the necessary alignments for the linking of the UK emissions trading scheme with the EU's, and save the need for UK exporters to pay the EU's new carbon border tax.
The draft agreements will be discussed at a meeting of EU ambassadors called Coreper on Wednesday, with some key details on the planned numbers in a Youth Experience Scheme to be finalised at a political level in the coming days. A discount on full foreign student fees for EU students is likely to be pushed to next year alongside a plan to reconnect electricity markets.
The BBC understands the draft agreements will also include some references to UK involvement in defence co-operation schemes, access to law enforcement databases and some reassurances over the EU's "Made in Europe" plans.
A food deal will have particular significance for Northern Ireland, radically reducing the impact of the post-Brexit Irish Sea border.
Northern Ireland's Brexit deal kept it inside the EU's single market for goods. That means food products from elsewhere in the UK require paperwork and some physical checks when arriving at NI's ports. A deal will ultimately end those requirements.
While the food trade plans have been backed by supermarkets and farmers representatives, some pro-Brexit campaigners have criticised the reapplication of EU rules. The post-Brexit trade deal signed by Boris Johnson's government prioritised regulatory freedoms for the UK over avoiding new regulatory red tape, checks and delays.
But William Bain, the British Chamber of Commerce's (BCC) head of trade policy, told the BBC's Today programme that business overall thought it was a "price is worth paying" to follow common rules, as companies would benefit from "lower costs, reduced delays [and] increased market access".
At the moment, he said, the requirement for Export Health Certificates can add thousands of pounds of costs to each truck carrying goods, in addition "to the delays that people find at the ports or at the borders".
"So we get lower exports because of the delays and the massive increases in costs that have come into the supply chain."
The BCC has released a new analysis of its members' views suggesting options for a closer relationship.
The business lobby group says the current trade relationship is "failing to deliver", leaving firms "struggling with a thicket of Brexit red tape" nearly six years after the UK's exit from the bloc.

article:
Parents' concerns to trigger urgent checks in A&E

Parents' concerns to trigger urgent checks in A&E
- Published
A new early warning system is being introduced in hospital emergency departments in England to help busy NHS staff identify sick children who are dangerously deteriorating.
A high overall score means a child needs more urgent attention. Concerns from staff, parents, carers or the child themselves will trigger an immediate escalation of care.
It comes after Health Secretary Yvette Cooper promised to stop "corridor care" for sick children because of long waits for hospital beds.
The new National Paediatric Early Warning System (PEWS) asks staff to check, log and grade vital signs, such as blood pressure, heart rate and oxygen levels.
Early warnings to save lives
The initiative is designed to save lives ahead of winter, when pressure on the NHS is at its highest.
On the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Cooper recently talked about the case of two-year-old Finlay Roberts, who died in 2024 after spending hours in a hospital corridor before being discharged.
Cooper apologised to Finlay's parents on behalf of the NHS, saying: "No child should be treated in a corridor. No patient should be treated in a corridor."
Whittington Health NHS Trust, where Finlay waited for treatment, extended its condolences to the family and said it continued to experience periods of exceptional demand across emergency care and, at times, some patients may receive care in temporary clinical areas, including corridors.
A coroner raised concerns about a lack of basic observations done by busy staff, external.
Every moment matters
A similar "early warning" system to identify acutely ill adults, including those with sepsis, is already in use in emergency and general NHS hospital wards.
More than 90 hospitals across England have been using the alert system in children's wards, with different age-appropriate assessments available for babies through to teenagers.
The NHS has already said it will expand Martha's Rule to all hospital emergency departments in England. The rule gives patients, families and carers the right to request a rapid review if they are worried that a patient's condition is getting worse and their concerns are not being responded to.
The initiative is named after Martha Mills, who died aged 13 in 2021 after developing blood poisoning, or sepsis, in hospital following a bike accident.
A coroner ruled that her family's concerns about her worsening condition were not listened to and she would probably have survived had she been moved to intensive care earlier.
Martha's parents Merope and Paul came up with the idea of the rule in a bid to change the culture that contributed to her death.
A&E units will have a dedicated phone number that can be called to trigger an urgent review of a patient's care.
Duncan Burton, chief nursing officer for England, said the new early warning system for children in emergency departments was an "important next step in improving care for children and young people across England for this winter - and beyond".
He added: "In fast-paced emergency departments, staff need to spot quickly when a child's condition is deteriorating.
"This standardised approach will help them recognise the warning signs, communicate concerns, and make timely decisions when every moment matters."
The early warning system for children, PEWS, is a collaboration between NHS England and the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health and the Royal College of Nursing.

article:
Police admit unlawful home entry and assault of couple

Police admit unlawful home entry and assault of couple
- Published
A couple have been awarded £9,000 in damages after police admitted its officers unlawfully entered their home and assaulted them nearly four years ago.
Andrew and Sabrina Fearn had a house party in their home in December 2022. Earlier, Sabrina had called police and officers attended before leaving. They then returned, believing someone was injured inside and wanted access.
Sabrina refused, but officers forced entry and used physical force on her, according to legal documents. Andrew then stepped in before "unnecessary force" was used on him.
Both were arrested and charged with assaulting an emergency worker, but their trial was halted when police admitted the forced house entry was unlawful.
Andrew and Sabrina, from Alvaston in Derby, pursued a civil claim against the force, and the case has now been settled for £9,000, the Local Democracy Reporting Service (LDRS) said.
According to the legal claim submitted by the couple, a gathering at their home ended when they discovered one of the guests had a knife.
Sabrina called the police, which attended and then left shortly after.
But soon after, several officers returned wanting to gain entry, believing someone was injured inside and needed urgent medical attention.
Sabrina, 31, refused to let police in, saying the party had finished and no guests remained. She tried to stop police from entering her house, before officers forced entry and used physical force on her.
Andrew, 40, stepped in to protect his wife, fearing she was being hurt, before "unnecessary force" was used on him, according to the legal papers.
Extracts from police bodycam footage describes Andrew being held by the throat against a wall, while Sabrina was held by the neck as officers forced entry.
Andrew was warned he would be Tasered if he did not comply, was sprayed in the face with an incapacitant spray, handcuffed, taken away in a police van and held for 15 hours.
According to the LDRS, as the couple made physical contact with officers during the incident, both were arrested and charged with assaulting an emergency worker.
However, the pair were found not guilty in the middle of their trial, after police gave evidence to admit the forced entry to the home was unlawful.
'Held accountable'
Sabrina said: "It has caused an awful amount of stress. My mental health was so bad that whenever anyone came to my door, I would lock it.
"I've been terrified. I have awful PTSD [post-traumatic stress disorder].
"If I entered someone's property unlawfully and harmed people, I would be done for assault. I would have a criminal record.
"Not one of those police officers have been held accountable for what they have done."
Sabrina and Andrew, who according to their lawyers were acquitted at Southern Derbyshire Magistrates' Court in December 2023, then submitted a civil claim for damages over trespass, Andrew's unlawful arrest, and assault and battery on both parties - which Derbyshire Police accepted.
In a statement, the force apologised for the distress caused, and said officers had acted on a "honestly held belief" someone inside may have been injured, but later accepted the legal grounds for entering the property had not been met.
No disciplinary action was taken against the officers involved, the force added.
A spokesperson said: "We would like to take this opportunity to apologise for the distress and harm that was caused by this incident.
"It was later found that, due to the time that elapsed between the initial call and officers entering, that the grounds under section 17 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act were not met and that the entry, and all other matters following it, were unlawful.
"There were also claims, which were not accepted by the force, that the woman was unlawfully arrested, she was not handcuffed or detained at any point and the necessity for arrest was not met due to her suffering a medical episode, during which the officers provided immediate first aid.
"It was also not agreed that the man had suffered a dislocated shoulder during the incident. It was also not accepted that a malicious prosecution had taken place - or that officers were negligent.
"As a force, we always expect the highest possible standards of conduct from our officers and staff.
"However, they are also human and may make errors, as has occurred in this situation and we will always seek to learn from incidents to improve our response."

article:
Trump to remove Rwanda and South Africa from US trade deal

Trump to remove Rwanda and South Africa from US trade deal
- Published
US President Donald Trump has notified Congress of his intention to remove South Africa and Rwanda from a preferential trade programme, from 1 January 2027.
The African Growth and Opportunity Act (Agoa) allows eligible African countries to export thousands of products to the US duty-free.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement that an annual review had found that both countries were engaging in practices inconsistent with the programme's eligibility requirements.
He added that the Trump administration had additionally notified the two countries of the decision.
The Trump administration cited barriers to US trade and investment, as well as concerns over national security and foreign policy interests in the region.
For South Africa, the US pointed to corruption.
In a letter to South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, Trump said Pretoria's actions on international security and its relations and cooperation with governments of concern to Washington risked undermining US national security and foreign policy interests.
He also accused South Africa of maintaining significant barriers to American trade and investment, including restrictions affecting agricultural market access, regulatory requirements, investment protections and intellectual property.
"The Trump administration is working to ensure our African partners take the necessary steps to meet the eligibility criteria," Greer said.
South Africa's Trade Minister Parks Tau described the decision as "unfortunate", saying Washington was raising new issues that had not featured in trade negotiations between the two countries, which began in 2025.
"We will continue to accelerate the diversification of South Africa's export markets to protect jobs," Tau said.
- South African white genocide does not exist, new ambassador to US tells BBC 
  - Published26 September
- Is there a genocide of white South Africans as Trump claims? 
  - Published2 June 2025
South Africa has also sought to put the potential impact of losing Agoa benefits into perspective, arguing that the country's broader trade relationship with the US extends well beyond the programme.
Government figures show that about 89% of South African exports to the US entered under ordinary World Trade Organization most-favoured-nation terms in 2025, while around 10% benefited from Agoa, down from 28% in 2024.
"The value of South African exports under the programme fell to about $1.7bn (£1.3bn) in 2025, from $4bn the previous year," Tau said.
Bilateral trade between the two countries reached $28.8bn in 2025, while more than 600 American companies operate in South Africa, supporting about 134,600 jobs.
Pretoria says the two economies have complementary trade interests. South Africa supplies 12 of the 50 minerals considered critical by the US, as well as 70% of American isotopes used, among other things, in cancer treatment.
South African manufacturers also use American inputs in products exported to the US under Agoa, including vehicles and boats.
Oxford Economics senior economist Jee-A van der Linde said Washington's move will put further pressure on South Africa's manufacturing sector, warning that affected exports may be difficult to redirect to other markets.
"This decision comes as global trade flows remained disrupted and South Africa faces growing competition from cheap Chinese imports, particularly in the automotive industry," he said.
However, he noted that South Africa had previously managed to redirect some tariff-affected exports to markets including Europe and China.
US Ambassador to South Africa Leo Brent Bozell III said it was regrettable that South African policies led to its termination from Agoa.
"This was a predictable and preventable outcome resulting from the rejection by South Africa's government of real concerns raised by the US," he wrote on X.
The announcement comes amid strained relations between Washington and both countries, with the proposed termination threatening their access to preferential trade arrangements with the US.
Last year, Trump accused South Africa of persecuting its white minority and launched a programme for white Afrikaners to get asylum in the US.
Trump also repeated widely discredited claims of a genocide of South Africa's white population.
In Rwanda's case, Washington also raised concerns about human rights, political pluralism, the rule of law and workers' rights.
The move comes barely a week after Rwanda's defence ministry was hit with sanctions by US Treasury for its alleged role in the armed rebellion in eastern DR Congo.
The US Treasury said Rwanda's defence ministry directed thousands of troops to fight alongside M23 rebels in eastern DR Congo, providing weapons, equipment, logistics and training.
Rwanda has denied backing the M23 despite overwhelming evidence.
Rwanda saw its exports to the US rise to $43.3 million in 2025, up from $13.1 million in 2024, according to US import data.
Alexander Venter, an Oxford Economics economist, said Washington accounted for about 2% of Rwanda's merchandise exports in 2025, with only around 4% of its exports to the US benefiting from Agoa preferences.
Neighbouring African countries and Asian markets continued to dominate Rwanda's trade, Venter added.

article:
Man finally freed from prison housed miles from home

Man finally freed from prison housed miles from home
- Published
The mother of a man released from prison after 21 years says she feels she has "lost him again" after he was housed in temporary accommodation miles from home.
Luke Ings, 38, from Bracknell, was freed last month after judges quashed an indefinite sentence he was given as a 17-year-old in 2006.
But his reunion with his family was short-lived as he has been housed in east London, because there was reportedly nowhere appropriate in his hometown.
A Ministry of Justice (MoJ) spokesman said: "Prison teams assess every prisoner's needs before release, working with local services to help secure housing and other support."
Ings was originally convicted in 2006 after admitting offences including a robbery in a Bracknell underpass and an assault on a teenager in a fast-food restaurant.
He received a detention for public protection (DPP) sentence, which allowed him to be held beyond his minimum tariff until he was considered safe to release.
DPP and imprisonment for public protection (IPP) sentences were abolished for new cases in 2012, but people already serving them remained subject to the regime.
Ings told the Local Democracy Reporting Service: "I feel like I'm back in prison again to be honest."
He said he was living in supported accommodation where staff re helping him adjust to life outside prison, including learning how to manage Universal Credit, banking and other day-to-day tasks.
But he said being so far from his mother, sister and brother once again has been difficult, adding: "I can only contact my family on the phone again. At least this time we can video call."
'Terrible condition'
His mother, Sam Ings, said the family had been delighted to have him home but was devastated when he was told he would have to move away.
She said: "It has been great to have him home for a week but the Probation Service couldn't find him anywhere local to live and they placed him in a maisonette in east London.
"It was in terrible condition when he first arrived. It's been a real shock for him to be out of prison, reunited with family and now suddenly living somewhere he doesn't know and he has none of his family or support network around."
A Bracknell Forest Council spokesman, which manages social housing in the area, said: "We are not able to comment on individual cases."
The MoJ said release teams worked with probation and local authorities to plan prisoners' returns to the community, including arranging accommodation and referrals for employment, benefits, health and other support.
It said prison leavers at risk of homelessness who are supervised by probation can be offered up to 12 weeks of temporary accommodation.
The Criminal Cases Review Commission, which referred Ings' case back to the courts, said his was one of 25 IPP and DPP cases it had referred since the start of the year.
A CCRC spokesperson said the cases represented "only a fraction of the people who remain caught up in this abolished sentencing regime".

article:
MSPs 'unable to say' if Scottish government spending plans are affordable

MSPs 'unable to say' if Scottish government spending plans are affordable
- Published
A Holyrood committee says it has been unable to determine whether the Scottish government's tax and spending plans are affordable due to a lack of transparency from ministers.
MSPs on the Finance and Public Administration Committee said in a report that the government must provide "much greater transparency" on its progress in closing a forecasted £5bn gap in the nation's finances.
The committee warned of "substantial risks" to next year's Budget if ministers fail to deliver on plans to reform public services, boost economic growth and increase the tax take.
The Scottish government said it would consider the recommendations of the report, adding it had delivered a balanced budget every year.
The finance committee had taken evidence from public bodies, local authorities and economic experts to determine the affordability of the government's tax and spending plans, but said it was unable to do so due to a lack of answers from ministers.
The committee noted that the country faces "significant financial pressures".
It highlighted an anticipated budget shortfall of £2.6bn for day-to-day spending, such as paying public sector wages, and £2.1bn in capital funding, to pay for long-term infrastructure projects, by 2029-30.
- Scottish ministers to work with councils on £100 energy payment rollout 
  - Published5 days ago
- More than £700m to be cut from Scottish Budget next year 
  - Published25 August
The Scottish government has announced plans for major overhauls of public services, including proposals to drastically shrink the number of NHS boards and regional councils, in a bid to make savings and improve efficiency.
However, the committee noted that the country is facing economic pressures from inflation and rising energy prices.
Meanwhile, the Scottish government must contend with a £720m reduction in next year's Budget because of weaker-than-expected income tax receipts compared with the rest of the UK.
The finance committee also highlighted that the UK government's prioritisation of defence spending could reduce capital funding for Scotland by £87m.
As they deal with difficult financial conditions, the committee urged ministers not to "routinely" use cash from the ScotWind project - generated by the leasing of offshore wind farm options - as a "second reserve".
Finance committee convener Clare Haughey, an SNP MSP, acknowledged the "scale of the pressure on the Scottish Budget", which is due to be announced on 3 December.
"However, we have insufficient evidence to determine whether the Scottish government's tax and spending plans are affordable and sustainable," she said.
"We are also concerned that the Scottish Budget faces substantial risks if the three pillars of its Fiscal Sustainability Delivery Plan (FSDP) – including ambitious public service reform targets – are not delivered in full and on time.
"We therefore call on the Scottish government to provide much greater transparency on progress in closing the fiscal gap and meeting reform targets."
Haughey said "as a first step" the Scottish government should publish an updated FSDP alongside the Budget and resume the annual publication of the medium-term financial strategy while committing to regular spending reviews.
"We also urge the government to update its public sector pay policy and tax strategy at the earliest opportunity," she added.
'£5bn funding gap'
Scottish Conservative finance spokesperson Craig Hoy said: "Even one of their own backbenchers who leads this committee says it is typically shrouded in SNP secrecy."
He added: "This reeks of more economic incompetence from the nationalists, who are already presiding over a £5bn funding gap in Scotland's finances."
A Scottish government spokesperson said: "This government has delivered a balanced budget every year and a comprehensive strategy and delivery plan has been published which sets out how we will close the gap between funding and spending by 2029-30, whilst ensuring spending is focused on frontline services such as the NHS, action to eradicate child poverty and other priorities.
"We are also taking forward a public service reform strategy to deliver services that are preventative, better joined up and more efficient."
The Scottish government has said that its funding package from the UK government in 2027-28 will suffer a real-terms cut of £650m as a result of the measures announced in the chancellor's UK Budget.
The spokesperson said this would reduce "the money we have to spend on public services and supporting people with the cost of living".
They added: "Ministers note the committee's report and will consider the recommendations within our current fiscal constraints."
The government said it would respond to the report after Finance Secretary Jenny Gilruth announces the Budget next month.
