article:
Sandie Peggie loses discrimination case against nursing union

Sandie Peggie loses discrimination case against nursing union
- Published
A nurse has failed in her claim of discrimination against a union about her beliefs on biological sex and gender.
Sandie Peggie alleged the Royal College of Nursing (RCN) had failed to adequately support her during a dispute with NHS Fife and Dr Beth Upton.
The RCN disputed the claim, arguing that it had acted "reasonably" throughout the process.
It is the second employment tribunal brought by Peggie over the dispute with Dr Upton, a transgender woman - that is a biological male who identifies as a woman.
The RCN said it welcomed the tribunal's decision and that it would "support all of its members".
A spokesperson for Peggie said her legal representatives were considering the judgement before recommending any "further legal steps available to her".
Peggie objected to sharing a changing room with Dr Upton at the Victoria Hospital in Kirkcaldy and a number of disagreements over the subject came to a head in December 2023.
The nurse was suspended in January 2024 and took both Dr Upton - who has since left the NHS - and the health board to a long-running and high-profile tribunal.
Peggie partially won a claim for harassment against NHS Fife last December, but her other allegations of discrimination and victimisation, including those against Dr Upton, were dismissed.
Peggie holds what are described as "gender critical" or "sex realist" beliefs that people are born male or female and cannot change sex.
- Closing arguments heard in Sandie Peggie nursing union tribunal 
  - Published1 October
- Sandie Peggie says union did not take her case seriously 
  - Published23 September
The second tribunal, which finished hearing evidence in Dundee last month, centred around whether Peggie should have been provided with legal advice after the union contacted her over her suspension.
Employment judge Melanie Sangster found the RCN had not shown "conscious or subconscious discrimination" towards Peggie during the case.
In a written decision, Judge Sangster said Peggie did not "request legal assistance", following her suspension, during a call with RCN representative Stuart Fraser.
The tribunal ruled that Fraser's approach during the call was "in line with the approach he would take in other cases".
Peggie subsequently received funding for legal representation in her case against NHS Fife and Dr Upton from campaign group Sex Matters.
Legal assistance bid
She was formally refused legal assistance by Norman Provan, associate director of employment with RCN, in January 2025.
In written reasons issued by Provan to Peggie, he said that she had already sought independent legal advice and her claim had been submitted prior to Peggie seeking RCN assistance.
Peggie was told Fraser and the RCN would continue to represent her in internal disciplinary matters.
The nurse also raised a claim over the fact a union official had not "copied" a letter from Peggie requesting assurances over protections for staff with sex realist beliefs in an email to all RCN members.
The tribunal found an RCN official, Gillian Tait, had sought those assurances from NHS Fife, but had only responded to Peggie as she understood her role was to support her individually in her return to work.
Judge Sangster agreed that the email would have been circulated wider if others had raised similar concerns, but none of the RCN's 55,000 Scottish members had done so.
Peggie, who has not returned to work since her initial suspension due to stress, was cleared of misconduct by NHS Fife in July 2025.
A spokesperson for Peggie described Judge Sangster's decision as "worrying" for union members.
They said the judgement entitled the union to "characterise" female staff's concerns over sharing spaces with colleagues born as biological males as a "disagreement" rather than "an expression of her protected belief".
They added: "It raises serious questions about the value of trade union membership if, when members report workplace concerns, the responsibility falls on them, rather than on experienced and trained union officers supported by internal and external legal teams, to identify the correct statutory basis for potential legal claims."
An RCN spokesperson said: "The judgment is comprehensive and we welcome the decision that we did not discriminate against our member based on her protected beliefs. RCN staff followed agreed processes that apply to all members and we acted fairly and impartially.
"We are sorry these matters were aired before the tribunal."
They added: "The RCN is an anti-discrimination organisation, supporting all of its members."

article:
Is Ebola under control in Kenya after nine cases confirmed?

Is Ebola under control in Kenya after nine cases confirmed?
- Published
As fears grow that the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo could spread further, Kenya, which announced its first Ebola case three weeks ago and has since had eight more cases, is hoping for the opposite.
Nine cases and two deaths have so far been confirmed.
With the first 20 of the people who came into contact with the first Ebola patient being released, the government has described it as a "milestone worth celebrating".
The government expects the outbreak to be declared over in less than two months, if efforts to contain the spread holds. But that is assuming there are no more cases, including from the 98 people still in quarantine and due to be freed next week.
Should Kenyans still be concerned?
Despite the initial release of the people in quarantine, Kenya's Health Director-General Patrick Amoth has reiterated that the focus was "firmly on the finish line".
The outbreak can only be declared over after 42 days from the time the last confirmed patient twice tests negative for Ebola, he said on Monday.
"We cannot afford to drop our vigilance until we reach that point," he said
In the days after the first case was announced, concerns had been rising that the virus could start spreading further, even as the government sought to assure citizens.
The US warned it citizens against travelling to Kenya, while neighbouring countries such as Uganda, Ethiopia and Somalia remain on alert.
Concerns remain among Kenyans that the disease could still spread more widely.
Nearly 5,000 people have died since Ebola was confirmed in DR Congo in May, making it the second most deadly outbreak of the disease.
With more than 10,000 cases in DR Congo, Kenya faces a steady risk of new cases arriving across borders, according to the International Rescue Committee, which has been working alongside both governments to contain the spread.
The latest outbreak has been caused by the Bundibugyo species, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
Kenyans raised questions from the outset, about how the first patient was able to spend time in the region worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified. He died days after his arrival in Kenya.
As a regional transport hub, the risk of the outbreak spreading remains a big concern.
The doctors' union in Kenya expressed concerns at "lapses" at various border points, including with neighbouring Uganda and Tanzania, as well as at Kenya's main airport.
Dennis Miskellah, the union representative, told the BBC that border and port facilities were grossly understaffed.
In the latest update on Monday, Amoth says that "each milestone brings us closer to the end of this outbreak, and together we will get there".
What is being done to stop it spreading?
When the first case was announced, the authorities urged people not to panic, assuring them of heightened surveillance at airports and border crossings.
Kenya has since introduced enhanced screening for travellers arriving from 10 countries it considers to be at high risk: DR Congo, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, Angola, Zambia, Ethiopia, South Sudan and the Central African Republic.
Travellers arriving from those countries are required to complete a digital surveillance form before boarding their flights, and to present a QR code to port health officials on arrival.
Kenya also ordered enhanced public health screening of aircraft arriving from those countries, as authorities seek to prevent further imported cases.
Within the country, the government has been sharing public messages to create awareness about Ebola, including encouraging people to promptly report any suspected cases and seek care at a hospital.
It has also focused on hygiene and safety measures, such as washing hands and avoiding close contact with sick people.
The government has additionally designated treatment and isolation facilities across the country, and health workers have been trained to deal with the disease.
Amoth also said that a dedicated laboratory had been set up at the Kenyatta National Hospital Infectious Disease Unit to handle Ebola tests, to ensure that the hospital's laboratory was not contaminated.
Following confirmation of the first Ebola case on 6 October, the health ministry conducted "robust contact tracing of anyone who may have been exposed", the World Health Organization (WHO) says. By 22 October, all contacts had been traced, both in Kenya and internationally, and placed in quarantine, it adds.
The government says that the confirmed cases so far are connected and there is no evidence that the virus has spread to the community.
Earlier, the International Rescue Committee noted that with all of those infected having links to the first victim, it showed Kenya's early response was working.
The government has been working with international partners, including Africa CDC and the WHO to support its response, including surveillance, communication and community engagement.
A toll-free emergency hotline, 719, has been provided to the public to report suspected symptoms.
Is Kenya prepared in case it starts spreading further?
Amoth earlier said that none of the contacts of the first patients had showed symptoms before going into quarantine "and therefore the potential to spread to another person is very minimal, literally non-existent".
The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks. The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
Despite that, Kenya's health ministry said nearly 5,000 healthcare workers have been trained to deal with Ebola at the national and local levels, besides the facilities that have been designated to handle the virus.
The ministry urged people to remain calm and vigilant. It also asked Kenyans not to stigmatise people identified as contacts of Ebola cases.
The ministry, along with the WHO, have produced posters to help people understand Ebola and support its containment. One message reads: "Stop stigma, choose support. Stigma can discourage people from reporting symptoms or cooperating with response teams."
In addition, the government has procured supplies of protective equipment.
Is enough being done to protect health workers?
Not according to the Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentists Union (KMPDU).
With three health workers and a hospital cleaner among those infected, questions have been asked as to whether the government could do more to protect workers.
Health workers and carers can face a higher risk of Ebola infection because caring for infected patients may bring them into contact with blood and other bodily fluids.
- What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? 
  - Published15 September
Dennis Miskellah, the KMPDU deputy secretary general, told the BBC that protective equipment should be provided to hospitals so that they were fully protected, especially in case patients with symptoms do not declare that they have been in areas with Ebola.
He suggests the government ought to conduct proper health education to destigmatise the virus, so that people do not seek to hide their symptoms.
The International Rescue Committee also called for continued funding for contact tracing, border screening and training of frontline health workers in Kenya.
Will there be any restrictions, like a travel ban?
Kenya remains open with no restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings.
Despite confirming nine cases, the authorities have explicitly ruled out a national lockdown or general travel ban for Kenyans.
The US on 19 October issued an advisory asking citizens to reconsider travelling to the country over Ebola concerns. Other countries have issued health alerts, including the UK, which warned its citizens that they may encounter enhanced health screening, and Canada, which has asked citizens to monitor their health for 21 days.
No country has issued an outright ban against their nationals visiting Kenya, nor have Kenyans been blocked from entering other countries over Ebola fears.
Has business and tourism been affected?
Analysts have raised concerns over the potential impact of public health fears on international travel and tourism but there is no evidence this has happened yet.
But the situation could change if the outbreak were to spread into the wider population.
How many Kenyans are there in DR Congo?
The exact number of Kenyans living in the DR Congo is not clear.
A report authored last year by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) think-tank put the number of Kenyans living in eastern DR Congo at about 2,500, including about 50 investors. It also noted that there were about four times as many Congolese living in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, alone.
The Kenyan embassy in the Congolese capital, Kinshasa, which represents Kenya's interests in four countries - DR Congo, Central African Republic, Congo-Brazzaville and Gabon - has in the past urged Kenyans living in the region to formally register so that it is able to serve them better.
How have neighbouring countries responded?
Several countries in the region have announced tightening of surveillance measures and enhanced screening for visitors.
One man who came into contact with the man who died in Kenya is under quarantine in Somalia and samples have been sent to Kenya for testing.
Somalia has also said it was taking precautionary measures, including enhancing surveillance measures at border points "given the evolving regional situation and the movement of people between countries".
The suspected case in Somalia had travelled through Ethiopia, which has also said it had tightened surveillance to prevent an outbreak
In Tanzania, visitors are expected to undergo daily health monitoring for 21 days, through an automated tracking system, which was announced after Kenya confirmed multiple cases of Ebola infections.
Uganda said after Kenya's first Ebola case that it was continuing to "maintain strong surveillance measures to protect public health". It later said that 60 people who had
The Kenyan businessman had travelled through Uganda on his way home from DR Congo.
Uganda later said 60 people who were being monitored after coming into contact with the Kenyan patient had all been discharged.
Uganda had reported two Ebola deaths shortly after the outbreak was reported in DR Congo, but the WHO has since declared it to be free of the disease.
On 20 October, Nigeria confirmed a case of Ebola in a female patient who travelled from Uganda to Abuja. Nigeria is the first West African state to report a case linked to the current Ebola crisis in East and Central Africa.
The woman, a 42-year-old Ugandan-born national is a wife of a Swiss diplomat who had travelled to the Ugandan capital for a holiday.
The health ministry stressed she did not have symptoms while transiting through Uganda and only developed them after arriving in Abuja.
She has since been evacuated from Nigeria to Switzerland.

Mayors will be free to use share of tax to give residents grants

Mayors will be free to use share of tax to give residents grants
- Published
English regional mayors due to be handed a share of tax revenues by central government will be free to use it to give cash grants to individual residents and businesses, it has emerged.
In his Budget, Chancellor John Healey unveiled plans to allow mayors to keep some cash from income tax and business rates collected locally, describing it as "the most radical act of devolution in a generation".
Prime Minister Andy Burnham wants local leaders to be given more control over how money is spent in their areas to boost economic growth and services.
But Conservative Tees Valley Mayor Ben Houchen says he has been given assurances that he will be able to give grants to local residents instead.
Lord Houchen told the BBC he is working on a voluntary scheme that would give local residents the opportunity to apply for a share of the tax distributed to his region.
He said Treasury officials had told him this would be acceptable within the government's rules around the devolution of funding.
"It's a technical point around spending decisions," Lord Houchen told the BBC.
He said devolution of funding was a "good thing" and "means mayors are able to decide spending commitments, which includes rebates".
The BBC has been told mayors could choose to use the tax revenues they received from the government to offer grants to individual residents or businesses.
But any mayor who decided to use the money in this way would have less for other local priorities, such as housing and transport.
Lord Houchen has described his proposal as a "tax rebate scheme".
The Treasury would regard these payments as grants, because His Majesty's Revenue and Customs (HMRC) is the only government authority in the UK that can issue income tax rebates.
Most of England's 14 strategic authorities are led by Labour mayors who have welcomed the move to give them a portion of income tax receipts.
Sources close to Reform UK's Greater Lincolnshire Mayor Andrea Jenkyns, and her counterpart in Hull and East Yorkshire, Luke Campbell, say they are waiting for more details to fully understand how they could use these tax revenues to benefit their regions.
The government published its broad approach, external to reforming funding for local and regional government in England after Wednesday's Budget.
As it stands, mayors of English strategic authorities receive most of their funding from ring-fenced grants, allocated by central government to be spent on specific policy areas.
From April 2028, all mayors of strategic authorities in England will be assigned a share of basic-rate income tax generated in their areas.
Each mayor will receive a bespoke funding allocation that takes into account regional inequalities in tax bases, with the exact amounts to be set at the government's spending review next year.
"The government is not devolving the power to set income tax rates or thresholds to mayors but will be granting significantly more flexibility as to how assigned revenues are spent locally," the government's plan says.
"Mayors will be able to choose where to target funding, for example whether to maintain funding for local transport or prioritise other interventions."
From next year, mayors will also receive a 20% share of locally retained business rates.
This will be the first step towards allowing local and mayoral authorities to retain 100% of their business rates income before the end of the decade.
From 2028, strategic authorities led by mayors will also be given the power to introduce an Overnight Visitor Levy, often dubbed a "tourist tax".
This charge will be an uncapped levy as a percentage of the cost of hotels, bed and breakfasts and other types of accommodation.
Labour mayors in 10 city regions said they would voluntarily limit the charge to 5%, but others - such as Lord Houchen - said they would not introduce the levy.
Burnham - who used to be a mayor himself in Greater Manchester - argues that funding and decision-making powers are too centralised in the UK.
The share of national taxes collected at a local level in the UK is 5.8%, the lowest in the G7, according to the OECD, external, a global policy forum.
That share is far below that of other countries with large economies such as France (20.4%), Japan (36%) and the US (45.7%).
But critics of fiscal devolution raise concerns about local capability, and inequalities between areas.
The Centre for Cities think tank says some areas may not have the expertise to manage developed powers effectively, risking deeper economic inequalities between areas.
The think tank supports fiscal devolution and believes it can offer significant benefits, if the challenges are managed effectively.
The Tees Valley Combined Authority (TVCA) led by Lord Houchen is facing a government inspection into its finances, after Local Government Minister Jim McMahon said he had concerns about its "long-term financial sustainability".
The authority said it welcomed the scrutiny and would continue to make improvements where needed.

article:
Labour ends power-sharing with Greens in 11 councils over Zionism row

Labour ends power-sharing with Greens in 11 councils over Zionism row
- Published
The Labour Party has pulled out of power-sharing agreements with the Green Party in 11 local councils, after the national party adopted a policy defining Zionism as a form of racism.
Labour councillors will no longer be in coalition with the Greens in areas including Sheffield, Warwick and Lewes.
Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson said: "Labour has been clear from the start that the "Zionism is Racism" policy crosses a line and we cannot work with any party that supports it – at any level of government."
Green leader Zack Polanski said the move would "backfire" on Labour and accused the party of wanting to "interrupt your local services and impose genocide support from its local councils".
In October, Green Party members backed a motion, entitled "Zionism is racism", which said Zionism was an ideology that supported an "ethnonationalist Jewish State in historic Palestine". Israel has denied committing genocide in Gaza.
The motion also backed a "single democratic Palestinian State", including in modern-day Israel.
Having been backed by party members, the motion became Green Party policy, but it has left senior figures bitterly divided. Jewish groups and opposition political parties have condemned it.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham told MPs in October that Labour would not partner with the Greens over the "antisemitic" policy.
Labour then issued an ultimatum from Labour's head office to Labour-Green councils, demanding that local Greens disown the motion passed by members at their national party conference.
Green groups were also asked to call on their party's national leadership to reconsider the policy.
Labour said there were local agreements in place in 18 authorities. Of those, Labour said 11 had not met the criteria it demanded.
The areas are:
- Arun District Council
- Derbyshire Dales District Council
- Havant Borough Council
- Lewes District Council (The Green Party announced last week it was "mutually" ending its alliance with Labour)
- Runnymede Borough Council (Labour says local co-operation had already ceased)
- Sheffield City Council
- Stafford Borough Council
- Warwick District Council
- Wealden District Council
- West Devon Borough Council
- West Suffolk Council
Labour said its conditions had been met in Broadland, Monmouthshire, North Somerset, Rother, West Oxfordshire and West Sussex. The party said that Coventry City Council does not have a formal arrangement in place and that no such deal will be made in the future.
It will continue co-operating with the Greens in the West of England mayoralty, where the deputy mayor is a Green member.
Green Party leader Zack Polanski has said the motion was "imperfect" but has defended its central premise, arguing that Israel's actions towards the Palestinian people are "clearly underpinned by racist ideology".
The collapse of co-operation at the local level could impact hundreds of thousands of residents through budgets and policy decisions taking longer to get voted through.
Green and Labour councillors in the impacted areas will now have to seek alternative coalition partners or try to govern as a minority administration.
In a joint statement, the Green Party and the Local Government Association Green Group said it was "hugely disappointed" that Labour had forced local leaders into "jeopardising successful progressive partnerships that are delivering benefits for residents".
'At the end of the road'
One of the biggest councils to be affected is Sheffield, where 25 Labour councillors formed a power-sharing agreement with 20 Green councillors after the May 2026 elections for the Yorkshire city's 550,000 residents.
Responding to Labour's ultimatum, leader of the Sheffield Greens Angela Argenzio did not mention the motion in a letter but insisted local Green councillors "are not antisemitic".
Argenzio told local Labour representatives they were being "directed by your national party leader" rather than local concerns.
In a statement on Monday, the council's Labour leader Cllr Fran Belbin said her party would propose on Wednesday that it proceeds as a Labour minority administration.
"We now feel we are at the end of the road with the joint administration," she said.
"Our trust in Sheffield Greens is completely broken," she added, accusing them of a "refusal to stand up for Jewish citizens".
'Complete disaster'
Green Party co-deputy leader Rachel Millward, also the leader of Wealden Council, said: "It is ironic that a Labour prime minister who made a promise to solve problems, not score points, has now shown he is willing to disrupt well-run councils for fear of Green success."
She added: "It is utterly irresponsible to conflate criticism of the actions of the state of Israel with antisemitism. Many Jewish people strongly reject the illegal actions of the current Israeli government."
In Warwick, the local Green party said: "We refuse to condemn a democratically decided policy because of political intimidation."
It urged Prime Minister Andy Burnham to "reflect his own words in his actions and allow local Labour groups to decide for themselves".
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Green group leader in Havant Netty Shepherd accused Labour of "performative politics" and said the end of their coalition would be a "complete disaster for residents".
"I am a local government councillor, I worry about people's bins, I worry about generating town centres - foreign policy is nothing to do with my remit," she added.
The Liberal Democrats are also in partnership with the Green Party in some local councils.
Last week, the party leader Sir Ed Davey ruled out entering into a national partnership with "any party that is committed to a dangerous and antisemitic policy like the Green Party's".
He added that he had asked those of his local leaders in coalition with the Greens to urge Green councillors to reject the motion and commit to campaigning for its reversal.

article:
A bust-up between mathematicians is fuelling fears that AI could undermine science

A bank of white freezers hums away at a former watch factory in central London. Inside: dozens of small boxes with barcoded glass tubes, collectively containing one hundred billion genes. Just two boxes may hold 10 times more information than all the text on the internet, says Dr Oliver Vince, the facility's co-founder.
His firm, Basecamp Research, plans to collect as much DNA as possible to create an artificial intelligence that can speak the language of biology, in the same way that US and Chinese tech firms have hoovered up written material online to create Large Language Models (LLMs), the basis of current AI systems.
Vince, like many in business and academic research, believes AI will supercharge scientific research. But increasingly, it also comes with controversy.
Last month, OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, said it had solved one of maths' great unsolved problems, relating to the famous Navier–Stokes equations. The company said its AI agents had cracked it in 88 hours. The body that runs a prize for whoever can solve the problem said it had "apparently been settled", but that its review would take time.
But hours before the announcement, Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician at New York University, went public with concerns. He formed an independent team with Levent Alpöge, a mathematician employed by day by the rival company Anthropic.
They had been working towards the same goal, and kept their drafts in OpenAI's coding tool, Codex. Buckmaster said that his co-researcher was tipped off that news of their progress had "reached" OpenAI, though he did not specify how. He asked whether his research, stored in Codex, could have fed into OpenAI's own work, though he stressed he was "not accusing anyone of anything".
OpenAI said that nobody at the company, human or AI, saw the other teams' work before it was published. Initially it said that while unlikely, it could not "rule out" that anonymised data from use of its products may have helped improve its models. Days later, it said Buckmaster's Codex prompts from the two months before the announcement "could not have influenced the system in any way".
It's a complicated story; we still don't fully know what happened. But it highlights a growing issue about the use of AI in science. Usually, those words make us conjure up images of robots building terrible genetically-engineered viruses, or chemical weapons, to wipe out humanity. But there's a more subtle problem that hasn't attracted the same headline-grabbing attention: that AI could undermine faith in the scientific process, raising questions about the novelty and accuracy of research.
And there's another concern. It's well known that AI chatbots like Claude or Gemini can sometimes hallucinate things that simply aren't true. They will tell you about a film that never existed, or a quote that was never said. Now there is evidence that this is increasingly happening in science. Eventually, it's feared, it will become difficult to separate true scientific discovery from AI-generated fiction.
And all of this could threaten to erode - if not explode - the rock on which scientific research rests: trust.
A 'watershed moment'
One threat is to scientific journals, the guardians of scientific integrity, which are seen to be failing to deal with a tsunami of AI-generated distortions.
"Generative AI has basically disrupted the whole scientific process," says Dalmeet Singh Chawla, a science journalist who has spent a decade reporting on research misconduct.
He tells the BBC that publishers' integrity staff - the people who screen submissions for accuracy and reliability - will need to "drastically increase [in number and effort] if they're anywhere near the fight". He says: "Right now, it seems like they're not."
On the face of it, AI seems just the right tool to power scientific research. Scientists deal with huge amounts of information. Telescopes and particle accelerators, for example, collect billions of data points – too large for the brain to comprehend. AI can pick the scientific highlights from the surrounding humdrum.
The poster child of scientific AI is the UK-based firm Google DeepMind, which in 2020 solved one of biology's biggest problems: how proteins in living things fold into their precise shapes.
It may sound dull, but proteins are the tiny machines that make life work, and the shapes they fold into determine what they can do; from building cells and fighting infection to helping form the tissues and organs of the body.
Before AI, scientists had to conduct time-consuming experiments in the lab. Then, Google DeepMind developed an AI model called AlphaFold that accurately predicted 200 million protein folds in just one year.
The equivalent experimental work would have taken hundreds of millions of years in laboratories. The firm gave the results away for free to researchers. The head of DeepMind and the project's lead scientist were both awarded the Nobel Prize for Chemistry.
It was big hugs all round.
Dr Pushmeet Kohli, who leads DeepMind's science work, told me that AlphaFold could be seen as a "watershed moment".
Questions over AI's work
But elsewhere, the use of AI in science has come with accusations of hype. Some computer models are accused of exaggerating the significance of their findings, with the human researchers that oversee them then believing some of the claims without enough scepticism.
Basking in its success over AlphaFold, for example, DeepMind turned its attention to predicting the structure of new materials. The work could lead to the development of better batteries, cheaper solar cells and electronic components that are not dependent on rare earth elements. (In theory, no-one would need to argue about mining rights ever again, and Greenland would be safe from invasion.)
A DeepMind model came up with what the firm claimed were more than two million new crystal structures, announced as "nearly 800 years worth of knowledge" released in one go. Of those, some 380,000 were considered promising enough to make in a laboratory.
But then came a warning sign from two chemists at the University of California. Anthony Cheetham and Ram Seshadri went through a random sample of the supposed new crystals. Writing in the journal Chemistry of Materials, they concluded that they had "yet to find any strikingly novel compounds", arguing that many were "trivial adaptations of known materials". Their verdict was not that the method was wrong, but that the results need more scrutiny and validation from human chemists.
DeepMind rejects the charge, saying it tested each compound for novelty. Dismissing a new structure for looking familiar misses the point, the company argues: swapping a single atom is how many of today's most useful materials arrived, from phone components to sunscreen.
Research 'slop'
In those cases, at least, the science was mostly real and the issue was just AI potentially exaggerating its importance.
Arguably of even greater concern is the growing risk that scientific journals will become polluted with so-called AI "slop" - where a computer, not a human scientist, is writing the research, leading to fake citations and phantom papers.
In 2024, computer scientist Prof Dmitry Kobak, of Ghent University, searched more than a million biomedical research papers for trigger words favoured by the LLMs that generate AI writing. His team found that by December last year, nearly 90% had AI fingerprints on them. AI detection technology is not perfect; some forms of the software have labelled the US Constitution, written in the 1780s, as "AI-generated". But still, Kobak said he was shocked by the scale of apparent AI use. There is a risk, he told Nature, that "whatever bias the LLM may have will just suddenly permeate the (scientific) literature".
Kobak is among many researchers who worries that AI is slowly killing scientific journals.
And it matters: research papers are the lifeblood of scientific advance. When a discovery is published, another team in another part of the world might obtain funding to build on the results.
The process of peer review - in which research papers are checked by other scientists before they are published - is also being compromised.
A team led by Weixin Liang and James Zou at Stanford University analysed referee reports submitted to four major computer science conferences, and found up to 17% of the text had been substantially modified by a language model.
A critical part of a scientific paper's integrity involves lead scientists listing earlier research in order to show what they have done is genuinely new. These are called citations. A separate team at Cornell University found that researchers were using AI to compile citations, and that it was inventing bogus research, with around 147,000 pieces of phantom research cited last year.
If AI continues to distort the integrity of the academic process in this way, then researchers will be sent up blind alleys, public money will be wasted, and the fruits of valid research - such as new drugs or green technologies - will be slowed or not realised at all.
'Research-grade AI'
Some publishers of scientific journals, such as Elsevier, are taking steps to avert this growing crisis of confidence.
Elsevier's research integrity team has developed some 100 signals that flag a paper for closer human scrutiny. Nature's journals forbid AI-generated images and tell referees never to upload a manuscript into an AI system. The website arXiv, where scientists share their early-stage results, bans researchers for a year if they submit invented references.
Prof Sarah Main, an Elsevier vice-president, is among those at the firm trying to work out how to responsibly use AI in research. "What we're calling research-grade AI would focus on ensuring the researcher is in the driving seat," she says.
As AI agents process the mass of data emerging from particle accelerators, the cosmos and the natural world, how do we know they are getting it right?
And there's another worrying question: how do we know that AI agents are not dismissing an important result as an anomaly? The discoveries of penicillin, radioactivity and weird stars called pulsars all came from odd results that could easily have been dismissed. Hunches by humans made them into some of the biggest scientific moments of the last century.
Can AI really replicate that sense of serendipity and human ingenuity?
Kohli of DeepMind does not think the answer is to turn our backs on AI. That would be "like saying you should be computing without using calculators", he told me. But he accepts there should be human guardrails: "The agents today are imperfect. Somebody has to take accountability."
His test is a simple one: "You have to understand what the agent has done, and you have to take responsibility. You can't just specify the problem and let the machine write the paper and submit it as true."

  - Published11 October

  - Published10 October 2025
Prof Andrea Pauli of the Vienna BioCenter in Austria has followed that test. She spent almost 10 years on a question no-one has yet been able to answer: how a sperm gets into an egg. Responsible use of AI helped her toward an answer. Her lab found a protein on the surface of zebrafish eggs which pointed to a lock-and-key mechanism for allowing the sperm in.
Hers is a case for hope, in a sea of AI scientific slop. It shows that AI can help.
This is also a story about humans. Soon after the formation of Basecamp - the lab I visited in a former London watch factory - its co-founder, Oliver Vince, was ill in hospital with leukaemia (from which he has recovered). It motivated him to develop an AI system that stood a better chance of curing cancers. It might not work, he says, but it's worth a shot.
"We have a technically feasible path to curing cancer," he says.
Not a promise from Vince, but a direction. The big question is whether AI carries the science there, or quietly erodes the bricks it is built on.

MI5 will not face contempt of court charges despite admitting its evidence was a lie

MI5 will not face contempt of court charges despite admitting its evidence was a lie
- Published
MI5 and its staff will not face contempt of court proceedings despite the spy agency admitting that its evidence to three courts was a lie, senior judges have ruled.
The three judges, including Lady Chief Justice Baroness Sue Carr, say a contempt case would be too complex for the court to manage, meaning it is not in the public interest to proceed.
The police have the right "investigatory powers and resources" to handle the case, they rule, with individual MI5 officers now potentially facing investigation for misconduct in public office.
MI5 gave false evidence to three courts in a case concerning an abusive informant known as Agent X.
The false evidence was about conversations between MI5 and the BBC concerning the agent, someone we had investigated and were seeking to expose.
MI5's chief Sir Ken McCallum said the court's decision was welcome and its judgment "underlines MI5's serious failures in this case".
"I repeat my apology for those failures, and for the additional distress they caused to Beth," he added.
In July 2025, the three judges asked MI5's watchdog to investigate how the security service came to give false evidence. At the time, they deferred any decision on contempt proceedings until after the investigation had reported.
In July this year, an investigation by Sir John Goldring - which had been ordered by the prime minister - concluded that one senior MI5 officer lied repeatedly while another misled his own colleagues and lied about what he was told. It also criticised other senior spies and found "serious and systemic failures in MI5's conduct".
In September, MI5 said it accepted the report's findings "without reservation".
The two MI5 officers who have been most criticised both deny any dishonest conduct. One has resigned from MI5, while the other is facing internal disciplinary proceedings.
Last week, the watchdog's boss, investigatory powers commissioner Lord Leveson, said the case was as "serious as anything" he has faced in his role.
- MI5 lied to courts to protect violent neo-Nazi spy 
  - Published12 February 2025
- How I exposed MI5's lie about its violent abusive agent 
  - Published12 February 2025
Despite this, the High Court has now decided not to take any further action, either against the two individual MI5 officers, or on a corporate basis against MI5 and its director general.
The judgment proceeds on the basis there is enough evidence to initiate contempt of court proceedings against the two senior MI5 officers, but concludes it is not in the public interest to do so.
A contempt process could "not realistically be undertaken by the court on its own" and the "investigative aspects of the task would be likely to be unmanageable", the judgment states.
"No purpose would be served by contempt proceedings, which are unlikely to do more than duplicate Sir John's findings," it concludes.
Instead, the judges say if there is to be further action, it should "follow an investigation by the police, who have the appropriate investigatory powers and resources," with the Crown Prosecution Service as the appropriate body to decide whether to prosecute.
The three judges - Baroness Carr, Dame Victoria Sharp and Mr Justice Chamberlain - suggest that the criminal offences of misconduct in a public office, or perverting the course of justice, may be more straightforward to prove evidentially.
The judges have already made serious criticisms of MI5 and said the way it gives evidence to courts in future has to change.
In Tuesday's ruling, they say it is "obvious" that Sir John Golding's findings are serious and "will inevitably affect the confidence" that courts will have in evidence from MI5.
But their decision will raise concerns about soft treatment for the security establishment, at a time when barrister Rajiv Menon KC is facing an unprecedented contempt of court process for a speech he gave in defence of his client, a one-time activist with the now banned group Palestine Action. Menon denies any wrongdoing.
Tuesday's judgment does not resolve disputed issues of law about whether MI5 and its director general are able to face contempt of court proceedings.
The judges said "nothing would be gained by contempt proceedings against MI5 as an entity" and that they "have already made trenchant public criticisms of MI5's conduct".
"We have underlined in this judgment the seriousness of those findings. A criminal investigation into the conduct of individual officers may follow," they added.
- MI5 court evidence based on lies, report says

Sir John Goldring's investigation examined how MI5 gave false evidence to three courts about having kept to its core secrecy policy - known as 'neither confirm nor deny' (NCND) - about the agent status of the violent neo-Nazi informant.
He coercively controlled his partner, known by the alias Beth, and attacked her with a machete. MI5 then helped him go abroad to continue intelligence work while he was under police investigation.
The government took the BBC to court in 2022 in a failed attempt to block our investigation into Agent X, but won him legal anonymity. Beth then sued MI5 at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal, and in 2024 she sought a review of a ruling at the High Court.
MI5 claimed to all three courts it had maintained NCND and, consequently, the courts allowed it to keep information secret from Beth and everyone else, leaving her at a serious disadvantage.
But what MI5 said was untrue. It had in fact disclosed the man's agent status in phone calls to me, as it tried to persuade me not to investigate him in 2020.
A senior MI5 officer had tried to cover up for the man, falsely saying he was not an abusive misogynist nor a real extremist. He even wanted me to meet the agent. In doing so, he repeatedly departed from the NCND policy.

'Mogging' is Collins' word of the year... but do you know what it means?

'Mogging' is Collins' word of the year... but do you know what it means?
- Published
"Mogging", a word used playfully to mean outshining, outperforming or upstaging someone or something, has been named as word of the year by the Collins English Dictionary.
A fast-growing slang word among members of Generations Z and Alpha - both online and in everyday conversation - mogging went mainstream in 2026 with a 210% increase in its usage.
Collins' managing director Alex Beecroft said its lexicographers look at "how often words are used" and also "analyse patterns of usage" that reveal the latest linguistic trends.
The selection of mogging as word of the year, he said, "shows how each generation leaves its mark on language".
He added: "It's a great example of how Gen Z and Gen Alpha have adopted a word and turned it into humorous slang, making the language their own and 'mogging' the rest of us!"
Mogging - not to be confused with mugging or mugging someone off - refers to outshining or dominating someone, most often in looks.
You may even have mogged someone or been mogged yourself over the past 12 months.
The word is often traced back to the acronym AMOG, standing for Alpha Male of the Group, and has been variously associated with bodybuilding forums in the mid-2010s as well as the manosphere and Incels.
But it now has a much more mainstream usage, as a playful put-down or a compliment, depending on the context.
It can be seen and heard in looksmaxxing communities - online groups where people swap advice on how to maximise their physical attractiveness.
Collins - one of the UK's major dictionary publishers - draws from a range of sources, including social media, to reflect how the English language is evolving in the UK each year.
Its word of the year for 2025 was "vibe coding" - the art of making an app or website by describing it to artificial intelligence (AI) rather than by writing programming code manually.
Other definitions that made the dictionary's 10-strong shortlist this year include ghost job, something frustrated jobseekers will be familiar with - when an employer posts a position with no intention of appointing someone.
Another, Hydration break was of course made famous by this year's Fifa Men’s World Cup, while P(doom) is the estimation of probability of an AI-aided collapse of civilisation.

Treasury accepts role in staff member's death

Treasury accepts role in staff member's death
- Published
The Treasury has accepted it contributed to the death of a personal assistant and said "immediate steps" have been taken to tackle outstanding risks.
Chloe Moffat, 26, took her own life in May 2025, the day after managers told her of allegations that she had shared sensitive confidential information, which she denied.
A coroner found a practice within HM Treasury of "informal fact-finding" meetings with employees accused of misconduct had no basis in the ministry's policy and posed a risk of future death.
Responding, the Treasury and the Cabinet Office wrote that they "accept the concerns identified" and "take them extremely seriously".
The Cabinet Office said it would also undertake a wider review of workplace conflict and resolution across Whitehall within a year.
At Moffat's inquest in August, the Treasury was found to have "materially contributed" to her death by not telling her that the likely penalty if allegations against her were proven would be a written warning and not dismissal.
In a response to the coroner's report, external, the Treasury "accepted the findings in the report in full" and said it had taken immediate action to mitigate the concerns raised.

Strengthened "wellbeing safeguards" had been introduced and the use of informal fact-finding meetings had been stopped while a full policy review was conducted, the department said.
Employees facing misconduct allegations would be informed of the possible outcomes before being asked to respond and a suicide prevention framework was being developed, it added.
"HM Treasury has considered these concerns carefully and has taken immediate steps to mitigate the identified risks," according to the department's response.
"While this work introduces some enhancements, much of it is intended to strengthen, clarify and build on the procedures and support already in place."
A Treasury spokesperson added: "The Treasury's deepest sympathies continue to be with Chloe's friends and family, and the department continues to mourn our colleague.
"An independent review found staff acted in good faith and with a duty of care throughout."

article:
Armed police start patrols in Sydney after Bondi Beach attack

Armed police start patrols in Sydney after Bondi Beach attack
- Published
Heavily-armed police officers have started patrolling Sydney's streets, as part of heightened security measures following last year's deadly shooting at Bondi Beach.
The Armed Response Command (ARC) will see specially trained officers in busy tourist areas carrying long-arm rifles – an unfamiliar sight for most residents.
New South Wales police say the officers will also patrol major events like sports matches and places of worship "to prevent, deter and rapidly respond to serious threats, including active armed offender incidents".
Fifteen people - including a 10-year-old girl – were killed in December when two gunmen opened fire on an event marking the Jewish festival of Hanukkah at the popular beach.
The attack was Australia's worst mass shooting in almost three decades and prompted sweeping gun law reforms and a crackdown on hate speech.
One resident told ABC news that the sight of armed police was "unnerving".
"They are just everywhere. Those guns are huge."
But another woman told the broadcaster that seeing police with weapons made her feel safe.
ARC is specifically designed to be "highly visible across Sydney, driving specialist vehicles and carrying rifles," New South Wales police said in a statement.
Its role "is built on a simple principle - preserving life," Detective Superintendent Andrew Evans said.
The shooting on 14 December put huge pressure on Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government, with calls for immediate action on antisemitism.
Jewish communities have welcomed the new police operation, which will eventually consist of 250 officers, but others have called for safeguards to protect human rights.
"No Australian wants to see officers with military weapons on our streets, but the sight of body bags is far worse," Alex Ryvchin, co-CEO of Executive Council of Australian Jewry, said.
But Amnesty International Australia said it was concerned about the "militarisation of policing", and asked for assurances from the state government that ARC will not be used to suppress peaceful protests.
"Any expansion of police powers and capabilities must be accompanied by clear, publicly accessible rules, robust independent oversight and accountability," said the organisation's Andrew Witheford.
The New South Wales administration defended the new measures.
"Our world changed forever. That's just the truth of it, right across this country. And I said it at the time, we will never be the same again," the state's Police Minister Yasmin Catley told the ABC.
One of the alleged gunmen, Naveed Akram, has been charged with 78 offences including 15 counts of murder, 40 counts of attempted murder, and one count of committing a terrorist act.
His father, Sajid Akram, 50 - who was also armed and shot at the crowd on Bondi Beach - was killed by police at the scene.

Man cut shop CCTV wires during 'terrifying' robbery bid

A man who tried to rob a shop in an Aberdeenshire town at knifepoint has been jailed for two years.
Jamie Dingwall, 34, admitted assault and attempted robbery after the incident at Oasis Vape in Banff in July.
Aberdeen Sheriff Court heard he was armed with what was described as a large knife and cut CCTV wires when he entered the shop.
Sheriff Lesley Johnston told Dingwall it must have been a "terrifying" incident for the victim behind the counter.
Fiscal depute Brian Young told the court a man was in the Strait Path shop alone and saw Dingwall enter with a large silver knife.
He cut CCTV wires at the entrance then pointed the knife at the victim and started shouting.
The court heard the man felt "instant fear" at the aggressive approach and backed away.
The serial criminal becoming irate before he left and the victim raised the alarm.
Dingwall admitted a charge of assault, presenting a knife, making threats of violence, and the attempted robbery of cigarettes and money.
'Psychological harm'
Defence solicitor Leonard Burkinshaw said his client had an "unenviable" record of previous convictions and accepted the court only had one option.
He said drugs had become a coping mechanism for the former welder, and he had taken a "heap of tablets" before the robbery bid, which he could not remember.
Burkinshaw said Dingwall accepted his behaviour had been "totally unacceptable" and could only apologise.
Sheriff Johnston said it must have been an "absolutely terrifying incident" for the victim and she was sure it would have caused "considerable psychological harm".
She said Dingwall had related previous convictions and jailed him for two years.

article:
Killer's string of driving offences before dragging cyclist to death

Killer's string of driving offences before dragging cyclist to death
- Published
News of the death of much-loved head teacher dragged to his death for more than a mile while trapped under the wheels of a car has left a community shocked.
The man responsible, Simon Richardson, crashed into Michael Mullins, 56, as he cycled home from his job at Stretford Grammar School on 20 April in the village of Warburton in Trafford, Greater Manchester.
Richardson was sentenced to life in prison for murder and ordered to serve a minimum of 25 years at Manchester's Minshull Street Crown Court on Monday.
But this was not the first time he had committed a driving offence with Judge Mrs Justice Brunner saying he had an "appalling" record including dangerous driving the day after the murder.
Warning: This article contains distressing content
The trial heard Richardson, of no fixed address, had driven through "give way" markings at a junction before colliding with the father-of-two on Paddock Lane, Warburton.
The cyclist fell on to his bonnet and windscreen before he was drawn under the car and became entangled in the suspension of Richardson's Volvo XC90, the trial heard.
Richardson then drove off before stopping in a country lane and twice getting out of his 4×4 vehicle in attempts to pull Mullins free, the jury was told.
He then mounted the grass verge and finally dislodged Mullins more than a mile away from Paddock Lane before reversing over the head teacher, causing "crushing" chest injuries.
Richardson, who was also found guilty of a separate dangerous driving charge on 21 April, had numerous previous motoring offences, the court heard.
Prosecution counsel Phil Barnes KC told the court Richardson had previous convictions for 28 offences with a "significant history" of driving-related crimes.
This included careless driving and failure to stop or report an accident in 2011, driving with excess alcohol and driving whilst disqualified in 2012 and driving whilst disqualified and uninsured in 2013, the court heard.
In 2023, he was convicted of driving without a licence and insurance.
In mitigation, defence barrister Jaime Hamilton KC said the absence of premeditation was a "significant feature" in the case, and that Richardson had not intended to use his vehicle as a weapon.
He said: "This defendant did accept that his actions did lead to the death of Mr Mullins and through me, he expresses his remorse."
The judge said Richardson would face a whole-life disqualification from driving as he was a driver with an "appalling" record.
She said: "You took away a life and in doing so you caused devastation to a family and a community.
"I find that you would be a danger to other road users indefinitely."
She added: "You deliberately used your car as a weapon over a prolonged period.
"You have repeated convictions for a range of serious driving offences over a 15-year period.
"This demonstrates the complete contempt you have for the law."
The judge also said Richardson drove dangerously the day after the murder, at a time when "you knew you had seriously injured or killed a man with your driving".
Mrs Justice Brunner imposed a concurrent sentence of 18 months for dangerous driving.
She said Richardson had limited leeway in the way of mitigation, but accepted he did not "deliberately kill someone to cover your tracks".
She said the crime was aggravated by his persistence and Mullins' vulnerability, and his motivation after the incident.
Richardson was also on bail at the time of the murder for offences including affray and assault occasioning actual bodily harm.
The judge said: "You heard [Mr Mullins] moaning for many minutes [under the car] and I am sure you knew he was alive and thought he was conscious.
"You knew that you were dragging a man who you believed was conscious against an abrasive road surface for four and a half minutes.
"You performed manoeuvres you must have known would have caused further injuries."
'Left a void'
Michael Mullins' family described him as a beloved husband, father and grandfather, who "truly excelled" in his "role as grandad".
He was a lover of sport and remained physically fit, regularly cycling the 19 miles between the school and his home in Northwich, Cheshire.
Elizabeth Baxter, the acting head teacher at Stretford Grammar School, told the court it was an "honour and a privilege" to work alongside Mullins, who led the school for 17 years.
Describing him as an inspirational leader, she said: "He has left a void and a gulf at every level of our school."

Four charged with attempted murder after South African farmer shot and tortured

Four charged with attempted murder after South African farmer shot and tortured

Warning: This article contains graphic details that some people may find distressing
Four people have been charged with attempted murder in South Africa over a brutal attack on a cattle farmer, who was assaulted and tortured in what has been described as a "senseless and barbaric" act.
Donovan Marx, 50, was attacked during a house robbery on his farm in Ventersdorp, a small town in South Africa's North West province, last Wednesday.
Marx was ambushed as he returned home, shot and stabbed and had his ears cut off in the horrific ordeal, police said.
Five people were arrested over the weekend but only four appeared in court on Tuesday.
The suspects, aged between 26 and 56, were charged with attempted murder, robbery and illegal possession of firearms and ammunition.
The fifth suspect has since turned state witness, the North West police chief confirmed on Tuesday.
The horrific attack has caused widespread outrage in a country which is used to high levels of violence.
Police last week explained how the attack on Mark happened.
A group of masked men armed with guns approached a worker at Mark's house as he was mowing the lawn, they said in a statement.
The attackers then demanded to know where Marx was before tying the worker's hands and feet with cable ties.
When Marx returned home, police said two of the suspects allegedly approached him and shot him in the upper body.
"They [then] dragged him inside the house, tied his hands and feet with cable ties, and allegedly stabbed him."
The suspects then ransacked the house and took three firearms from a safe before escaping with Marx's van.
The ordeal ended after the farm worker managed to free himself and call for assistance.
Marx was rushed to hospital, where he remains, but may need prosthetic ears after surgeons were unable to save his own, local news site IOL reported.
South Africa's Agriculture Minister Willie Aucamp condemned the attack on Marx, adding there was no "place in our country for such senseless and barbaric acts".
The chair of parliament's police committee, Ian Cameron, praised police for the swift arrests and called for a "strong, properly investigated case" to follow.
Some right-wing groups have used such attacks on white farmers, who are often from the Afrikaner community, to say there is a genocide against white people in the country - a claim that has been widely discredited.
Although the claims have been dismissed by every political party in the country, including those representing Afrikaners, US President Donald Trump has repeated them and has offered white Afrikaners asylum in the US.
South Africa's latest crime statistics, covering the period between April and June 2026, do not specify how many attacks took place on farms and only recorded one robbery in a rural area.
However, police data show most victims of crime in South Africa, including on farms, are black.

article:
Nomadic life for Irish Travellers 'at risk' over site shortages

Nomadic life for Irish Travellers 'at risk' over site shortages
- Published
The nomadic life of Irish Travellers is "at risk" in Northern Ireland with members of the community feeling pressured to move into "bricks and mortar" housing, a support group has said.
The number of sites and pitches in Northern Ireland has "reduced drastically" in the past 20 years, according to the Craigavon Travellers Support Committee.
It added that the issue was "compounded" by "well below par" provisions on remaining sites.
The Northern Ireland Housing Executive (NIHE), which is responsible for the accommodation needs of travellers, said it is investing in and future-proofing their way of life.
It is currently consulting the public on a draft strategy for the next five years, external on traveller accommodation.
Meanwhile, the Craigavon Travellers Support Committee also criticised Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly for contacting the police over roadside travellers during the summer, suggesting she should have found them somewhere suitable to stay instead.
One traveller at a site in Craigavon, who wanted to remain anonymous, told BBC News NI that "no one cares" about them.
They added: "It's got to the point where we just put up with it.
"We feel pressured to move into a house but that isn't our way of life. That would be horrific for mental health.
"Personally I feel no one improves it because we're travelling people."
Lisa Hogg, from the Craigavon Travellers Support Committee, described some families using shower units on sites with sewage coming up from under the shower tray.
She added that provisions have led to families becoming homeless or displaced.
"It has been frustrating, it has impacted health and mental health. We've seen a huge number of families moving off, out of the area because of the provision here, they just can't do it.
"I think there's a huge misconception that travellers don't pay rent and rates if they're in social housing. They are liable for rents and rates and it is claimed for and paid in the way that all social housing is."
Hogg added that nomadic traveller families were having their ability to maintain that lifestyle "slowly eradicated".
"The right to travel is a protected characteristic of Irish travellers, but there are no provisions in the north to allow that to happen."
Who is responsible for Irish Traveller sites?
The Housing Executive oversees accommodation needs for that community, as well as providing, managing or leasing caravan sites for travellers, who pay rent like social housing tenants.
As of June 2026, the NIHE provided and managed a range of sites including two transit/emergency halting sites, two serviced/permanent sites and seven grouped, social housing sites.
Three sites - based in Londonderry, Strabane and Belfast - have closed in the last decade.
In a statement, the NIHE explained this was due to "specific circumstances" in those locations including health and safety concerns, site viability issues and the proposed acquisition of land for major infrastructure projects such as the A5.
"We recognise that every site matters. When a site is lost, it can reduce accommodation choice for Irish Traveller families and communities," the NIHE said.
Currently under consultation, the draft Irish Traveller Accommodation Strategy 2026–2031, external sets out the NIHE's objectives, including "to improve the provision and standard" of sites.
"The Housing Executive remains committed to exploring opportunities to maintain and increase accommodation choice for Irish Travellers where feasible and where needs are identified," NIHE added.
"Our ambition is not simply to provide accommodation. It is to support the Irish Traveller way of life by ensuring that accommodation choice, cultural identity and community connections are recognised and respected."
In a response to the consultation, the Equality Commission said, external the strategy was an important opportunity "against a backdrop of declining traveller-specific accommodation and evidence of poor conditions on existing sites".
It said that at the time of writing only four Housing Executive sites were operational compared to seven in 2018 and 16 in 2009.
The Equality Commission also called on "stronger commitments" around Irish Traveller accommodation as well as "clear targets, timescales and resource commitments".
Meanwhile, the Craigavon Travellers Support Committee has criticised Northern Ireland's deputy first minister over her comments she made during the summer.
In August, Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly posted a video on social media, external to say she had contacted the police over travellers parked at Sprucefield Centre, outside Lisburn.
In the video, she said: "Just to reassure people we have been in contact already with the PSNI and Translink who operate the site, raising those concerns about what is happening.
"It is not legal to camp here overnight," the Lagan Valley assembly member added.
While she said in the video she had contacted Translink and the PSNI, it is not known whether she also took steps to find alternative accommodation for the travellers.
Speaking to BBC News NI, Kelly Laverty from Craigavon Travellers Support Committee was critical of this, and said "she should have contacted the statutory authority to highlight these people have nowhere to go".
BBC News NI has approached Emma Little-Pengelly through both the Executive Office and Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) for a response.
Are Irish Travellers moving into houses?
Prof Michelle Norris, from University College Dublin, has been on an expert panel for the Irish government looking at accommodation in the Republic of Ireland. She said accommodation is central to Irish Travellers' "identity as an ethnic group".
"So having access to accommodation that will facilitate their nomadic tradition is central to their identity as a traveller," she added.
Norris said it's not just about having "adequate" accommodation.
"It's also about accommodation that's appropriate for their ethnic identity and traditions.
"Demand for traveller specific accommodation, halting sites and group housing schemes, is falling."
Each year, local authorities in the Republic of Ireland undertake an assessment of social housing need, which are then compiled into a nationwide report, external.
"We found in the latest figures from 2025 that around 95% of travellers actually want standard housing in a housing estate," Norris said.
"I think that reflects changing aspirations among younger households.
"But that doesn't mean that travellers who want traveller-specific accommodation shouldn't be facilitated and we know that lots of households who do want that type of accommodation can't get access to it."

article:
Do the Shetland Isles need Cold War-style military protection?

Do the Shetland Isles need Cold War-style military protection?
- Published
Calls are being made for the defence of the Shetland Isles to be strengthened after increased sightings of Russian trawlers off the coast of Scotland.
Recent analysis by the Daily Telegraph, external also revealed that there have been more than 500 incidents where Russian boats have been stationed above undersea cables linking Britain with Europe and the US.
These cables carry the majority of telecoms data abroad.
The growing importance of undersea infrastructure prompted a parliamentary report, external last year to warn of security vulnerabilities in areas including transport and supply chains, financial services and payment systems.
There are also concerns that the £30m SaxaVord Spaceport in Shetland could be a Russian target.
But do the Shetland Isles really need better protection by the military?
Why are there concerns now?
In recent years there have been a number of incidents in the Baltic Sea where underwater cables have been damaged or completely cut.
In December last year, Finnish police detained a vessel sailing from Russia, which was suspected of damaging an undersea telecoms cable running from Helsinki to Estonia, across the Gulf of Finland.
In 2022, Shetland was cut off from the mainland after a nearby subsea cable was damaged.
And last year there were two cable breaks in Shetland, which disrupted internet services and, in one case, took weeks to repair.
There has been no suggestion that there was any Russian involvement in the Shetland incidents but they demonstrate how fragile the cables are and show the devastating effect on the islanders when they are damaged.
In July, Royal Navy warships and helicopters spent 21 days monitoring Russian activity in UK waters and the North Atlantic - this was a 25% increase on previous time spent monitoring.
The recent Telegraph revelation of more than 500 incidents where Russian boats have been stationed above undersea cables has also caused concern.
What is the history of Shetland's defences?
Jon Sandison, a high school history teacher and Shetland tour guide, said there were real concerns that Shetland could be attacked after Germany invaded Norway in 1940, during World War Two.
"Shetland could have been a stepping stone towards Orkney and mainland Scotland," he said.
There were many army, naval and RAF personnel stationed across the isles and coastal defences were built to defend Lerwick and the rest of the archipelago.
The SaxaVord Spaceport sits on a former RAF base and RAF Skaw played an important role in efforts to detect enemy aircraft from 1941.
RAF Saxa Vord was later involved in Nato's radar network to monitor Soviet activity during the Cold War.
The radar station closed in 2006 but it was revived in 2018 for Arctic surveillance as an automated remote radar head.
Sandison said that while military presence reduced in the second half of the 20th Century, Shetland's geographical position would never change.
"Where we are in the UK is always going to be a pivotal geographical location in relation to the North Sea, the Arctic Circle and wider scope of Britain," he said.
He added that coastal infrastructure was built very quickly during the Second World War.
"Air raid shelters, anti-aircraft defences - it's remarkable how much was built in a short space of time," he added.
"Not much of the infrastructure remains. It's part of our history, and part of our past."
What are the politicians saying?
First Minister John Swinney has accused the UK government of leaving "Scotland's vast coastline dangerously exposed".
He pointed to waters off Shetland as an area of significant Russian activity.
"I don't think we've got nearly the presence in those areas that we require today," he told BBC Scotland News.
Liberal Democrat MP Alistair Carmichael, whose constituency covers Shetland, has urged the UK government to step up efforts to protect critical infrastructure.
He told the BBC's Radio Scotland Breakfast programme: "This is something we do need to be taking seriously.
"We're not expecting an imminent problem here but this is a time where the government is already telling us that we should all be keeping baked beans and a wind-up torch in a cupboard."
- UK plans emergency powers to protect undersea cables 
  - Published22 October
- I do not have confidence UK is safe from Russian threats - Swinney 
  - Published14 October
- Damaged cable cuts Shetland off from mainland 
  - Published20 October 2022
Carmichael added that if the world had changed so much, some of the decisions made by the UK government to remove military presence from the northern isles may now need to be looked at again.
He said that over the last 20 years, there had been just one local full-time soldier running a reserved unit in Shetland but they were now managed from the Scottish mainland.
Carmichael said there should be restoration of a full-time presence to support the unit and more reserves should be recruited in the northern isles as numbers were low.
But he added: "If the signal that the government is sending the community is that we don't even think its important enough to send one full-time solider to run these units then you can't expect the community themselves to be particularly enthusiastic about it."
What is the significance of the spaceport?
SaxaVord in Unst is the UK's first fully-licensed spaceport with several companies interested in using the site to launch small satellites into orbit.
In September, the UK government announced investment of £30m in the project, as part of a new £7.8bn space strategy.
Alistair Carmichael said the spaceport would draw more attention to Shetland as a significant asset.
The German and UK governments plan to use SaxaVord to deepen their co-operation on space.
In October, Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Chancellor Friedrich Merz met in Berlin and announced plans to work more closely on economic growth, defence and technology.
SaxaVord Spaceport was identified as a focus for immediate work on European launches.
Two German companies are currently in a race to be the first to test a rocket in Shetland.
Chief executive Scott Hammond said: "The space strategy is absolutely critical.
"We're at the heart of the UK government's plans for assured access to space.
"That's also for our economic and Nato partners."
He added that the UK government had joined as one of its majority investors, with a member on the board, but stressed that SaxaVord Spaceport was still a private commercial company.
What has the MoD said?
A Ministry of Defence spokesperson said: "We are clear-eyed about the threat Russia poses.
"Through the UK-led Joint Expeditionary Force, we are leading allied activity across the High North, strengthening Nato's northern flank and increasing our ability to respond rapidly to emerging threats.
"This government is also investing in the capabilities needed to meet those threats, with £1.5bn backing Atlantic Bastion to deliver a next-generation Hybrid Navy and a further £330m to strengthen the protection of critical undersea infrastructure."
