Reform council leader quits after staff comments leaked

Reform council leader quits after staff comments leaked
- Published
The Reform UK leader of Leicestershire County Council has announced he is standing down after comments he made about staff redundancies were leaked online.
Dan Harrison announced on Monday that he would be stepping down from the role he has held since May 2025.
He said he had made the decision after taking advice from senior Reform colleagues, and added deputy council leader Kevin Crook had taken over as acting leader.
It comes after Harrison had apologised after being recorded saying 76 council solicitors would be made redundant, branding them "incompetent", before saying "what I want to look at now is the women", in remarks which were then released on social media.
In a statement, Harrison said it had been the "honour of his life" to lead the county council's first Reform administration.
Harrison has said he will remain as a councillor, representing the Ashby-de-la-Zouch division.
The Conservative opposition at County Hall had called for Harrison to resign after his comments about staff were leaked.
In the recording, Harrison said: "There's 76 solicitors will be made redundant.
"We'll buy in the service, because [they are] incompetent. They're not doing a good job.
"What I want to look at now is the women so it is ongoing, I would like it to be at great pace but I can tell you now if we suddenly drove massive redundancies the liberals would walk away."
Earlier on Monday, Harrison had told the BBC he would not be stepping down - but he later said he made his decision after talking to Crook and group whip Andrew Hamilton-Gray.
He had apologised over the remarks, which were made on Tuesday during a Reform party meeting.
Despite his apology, Harrison had insisted his remarks had been taken out of context.
Harrison said: "I would like to apologise unreservedly to the staff and officers of the county council for any hurt, distress or offence caused by the publication of these comments, which were made during a heated meeting with the expectation of privacy and confidentiality.
"However, I would like to stress that these discussions were just that, and I have not given any instruction or direction to officers in these matters and that there has not been any discussion nor agreement on these issues with officers."
He added: "I unequivocally reject any suggestion that staffing decisions are being taken based on gender.
"The comments made in that meeting were taken completely out of context."
Position 'untenable'
Before Harrison's resignation, the council's 15 Tory councillors had called for an emergency vote to try to remove him from the leader's role.
Group leader of the Conservative group, Deborah Taylor, said: "That was not a decision we took lightly.
"The serious concerns raised over recent days, particularly around the treatment of council employees and the comments contained in leaked recordings, left us feeling that his position had become untenable.
"His resignation brings an end to his leadership, but it does not mean those concerns should simply be forgotten.
"There are still questions that deserve answers, and it is important that the council learns from what has happened."
The Reform group remains the largest party on the authority, and runs it as a minority administration.
In a statement, Jeevun Sandher and Amanda Hack - Labour MPs for Loughborough and North West Leicestershire respectively - said: "Since taking office in 2025, the Reform UK administration has become increasingly embroiled in controversy and scandal, rather than focusing on delivering for the residents of Leicestershire.
"This is far from an isolated incident. Just last week, councillor [Joseph] Boam was found to have breached the council's own code of conduct through his actions against the former monitoring officer, while other Reform councillors have also been forced to apologise to residents over their behaviour. All of this in less than two years.
"Leicestershire residents deserve better."

Flávio Bolsonaro calls himself 'leader of Brazil' after election loss

Flávio Bolsonaro calls himself 'leader of Brazil' after election loss
- Published
The defeated candidate in Brazil's presidential election, Flávio Bolsonaro, has referred to himself as "leader of Brazil" in a letter he published on social media after leaving the country for the United States.
Bolsonaro lost to his left-wing rival, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, in the run-off on Sunday by a difference of 4.4 million votes, but has not conceded defeat.
In the letter, Bolsonaro alleges, without offering evidence, that he was the victim of "electoral fraud" and says that he will lead the opposition from the US.
He left Brazil on Tuesday after failing to comply with an order to surrender his passports, a decision which Lula described as "a shameful act".
Bolsonaro starts his letter, which he posted on his X account, saying "I address the Brazilian people and the international community as the leader of Brazil".
However, he had posted a previous version, that was later deleted, in which he wrote: "I address the Brazilian people and the international community as the rightful president of Brazil."
Both versions repeat the allegation that Bolsonaro first made on election night, that an extension of polling hours on Sunday had benefited his rival.
In the letter, he says it was "an electoral fraud unfolding before my eyes".
The extension was requested by both Lula's and Bolsonaro's campaign teams, and the head of Brazil's electoral authority has said that the vote proceeded normally and in full accordance with the country's laws and constitution.
An analysis of election data conducted by BBC Brazil and BBC Verify has also found that only around 34,000 people voted during the extended hours - far lower than the 4.4 million votes that separated Lula from Bolsonaro.
In his letter, Bolsonaro also addresses his departure from Brazil - which caused confusion after he disappeared for more than 24 hours.
It later emerged that he had gone across the land border to Argentina, and from there flew on to Florida, following a brief refuelling stop in Ecuador.
Bolsonaro left after failing to hand in his passports to police - in defiance of a Supreme Court order, which had been issued as part of an investigation into alleged money laundering.
He has not been charged as part of the money laundering probe and denies any wrongdoing, calling the investigation a "politically-motivated witch hunt".
Bolsonaro added that he had never intended to leave Brazil, but argued that he was the victim of "political persecution".
He ended the letter by saying: "I left Brazil but I haven't abandoned Brazilians".
While Flávio Bolsonaro said that he planned to lead the opposition from the US, it was not clear how he planned to do that.
His party recognised the election result and while some of its politicians have described Bolsonaro as a "political exile", his campaign manager, Rogério Marinho, stated on Wednesday that "there is no evidence" of the electoral fraud that Bolsonaro alleges took place.
It is also not yet clear where Bolsonaro intends to stay or for how long.
His younger brother, Eduardo, has been in self-imposed exile in the US since March 2025, saying he was the victim of political persecution. The two siblings posted a photo of themselves holding a Brazilian flag on Wednesday.
The Trump administration has provided visas for Flávio Bolsonaro and his family but did not say what kind of visas they were.
The US president did not explicitly endorse Bolsonaro in the run-up to the election and told reporters he "won't get involved" when asked about Bolsonaro's allegations of election fraud.
Earlier in the week, he had said that "it looked like another rigged election," without providing any evidence.
And on Thursday, Trump told reporters that "the election was a very great embarrassment to the people of Brazil".

Extremely rare red rainbow spotted in County Antrim

Extremely rare red rainbow spotted in County Antrim
- Published
An extremely rare red rainbow has been captured on camera in County Antrim.
Pete Kirk spotted the sight in Mallusk on Friday morning and sent the photos to the BBC.
Rainbows form when sunlight is bent and reflected by water droplets in the air, splitting the light into different colours.
Red rainbows form in the same way, but appear at sunrise or sunset when the sun is low in the sky.
At these times, sunlight travels through more of the atmosphere.
Colours such as blue and green are scattered away, leaving mostly reds and yellows, giving the rainbow a reddish glow.
It is essentially the same phenomenon that causes red sunsets.
Unlike a red sunset, red rainbows are uncommon, people who study the skies may only ever be lucky enough to see a red rainbow once or twice in their lifetime.

Two boys arrested after Halloween party stabbings

Two teenage boys have been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder after five teenagers were stabbed at a Halloween party.
Officers said they were called shortly after 22:30 GMT on Saturday to Park Road in Chandler's Ford, Hampshire, where an "unknown group" had gained entry to the event.
Police said two boys remain in hospital having suffered serious injuries, with one 17-year-old victim in a life-threatening condition. The others have been discharged from hospital.
A 17-year-old and 16-year-old, both from Southampton, have been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder and remain in police custody.
Two witnesses told the BBC a fight started after a group came in over a garden fence, although they said the motive for the stabbings was unclear.
One of the teenagers said: "I was [standing] in the hallway near the exit and I saw someone I know pull up their shirt and say 'I've been stabbed'.
"And then I later saw him lying outside the front of the house with someone compressing his wound."
Police cordoned off parts of Park Road and the adjoining Valley Road.
Det Ch Insp Elizabeth Pirie said: "Whilst the two arrests are a significant development in our investigation, which has moved at pace since the incident was first reported to us, we still urge our communities to contact us with any information, no matter how small it may seem."
She added: "If you were at the party and have not spoken with officers yet, or you have any CCTV, mobile phone, dash cam or doorbell camera footage covering Park Road and the surrounding area, then please get in touch."
The force said throughout the coming week, local officers from the Neighbourhood Policing Team are visiting local schools and colleges to offer further advice and reassurance, as well as to support those directly and indirectly affected by this incident.
The vicar of Chandler's Ford, the Reverend Duncan Hollands, said: "It's awful, it's shocking, it's sad. Chandler's Ford is a very peaceful place. These sorts of things don't happen."
He said churches had opened their doors for people to pause for reflection or seek support.
St Boniface Church in Hursley Road will be open 09:00-17:00 through the week, while St Martin in the Wood in Queen's Road will be available Monday and Wednesday between 15:00 and 17:00.

Hunt on for 'exceptional' nature island manager

The hunt is on for a new manager to care for a wildlife reserve on a Cornish island.
Cornwall Wildlife Trust said it was is recruiting for the post on Looe Island in the Whitsand and Looe Bay Marine Conservation Area.
Visitors are only allowed in organised trips and the island has Cornwall's largest breeding colony of the great black-backed gull, as well as being home to grey seals.
The trust said it was looking for an "exceptional" person and the job, with an application closing date of Sunday 15 November, offered "an opportunity to combine your passion for conservation with practical leadership, people management and a flair for creating a truly special visitor experience".
Accommodation was provided for the manager and the role included caring for wildlife, leading a team of volunteers and welcoming visitors, the trust added.
Looe Island was given to the wildlife trust in 2004 by sisters Babs and Evelyn Atkins, who lived there and wrote two books about island life.
It was also known as St George's Island during World War Two.
It sits one mile (1.6km) off Looe and covers just over 22 acres (8.9 hectares) , including woodland, grassland, shingle and a rocky reef teaming with wildlife.
The trust said: "The island is a sensitive habitat and provides important sanctuary for marine life, seabirds and other coastal species. Nesting birds include cormorants, shags and oystercatchers.
"There are a mix of habitats which, in such a small space, means it provides a really important space for wildlife."

Streeting denies 'kicking can down the road' in defence spending row

Streeting denies 'kicking can down the road' in defence spending row
- Published
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has denied "kicking the can down the road" over how much the UK spends on defence.
The government has faced criticism for not setting out a pathway at Wednesday's Budget to hit its target of spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.
Streeting is at odds with MPs on the Commons defence committee over the issue.
It comes as Chancellor John Healey and Streeting announce that foreign firms which are awarded defence contracts of more than £50m will need to invest an equal value back into the UK.
Under the new investment rules, described as an "offset strategy", these companies will need to spend an equivalent amount on British factories, jobs and training.
The Ministry of Defence will apply the rules on a "case-by-case" basis from April 2027, the government said. Healey and Streeting will unveil the policy on a visit to UK defence contractor BAE's shipbuilding site in Glasgow later.
Countries including Poland, Norway and the Netherlands have mandated similar rules to "boost the economic benefit from defence procurement", the government said.
While ministers hope the rules increase investment in Britain's defence industry, they appear designed to do so in a politically palatable way rather than committing to spending cuts.
Tan Dhesi, Labour chair of the cross-party Commons defence committee, said on Wednesday that decisions had been "kicked into the long grass" to next year's government spending review, rather than announced in the Budget.
He warned that without building capabilities now, "we risk leaving ourselves seriously vulnerable in the event of a major conflict".
Streeting hit back at these comments as "unfair" and "unfounded".
Speaking on Thursday, Dhesi said the committee stands by its criticism.
"We had hoped to see that the chancellor would set out a precise pathway to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030," Dhesi told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
"But instead some of those key decisions on defence have lamentably been delayed until next year's spending review."
He praised the government for plugging a £4.7bn hole in the Defence Investment Plan in the Budget, through asking government departments to cut their capital budgets by 1%.
Responding on Thursday, Streeting told Today: "I like Tan very much, he's a friend and I respect him, but I strongly disagree with him.
"And I don't think the charge he makes of delaying or kicking the can down the road stacks up against the extra money that is already going into defence and the capability we're funding right now."
Streeting told BBC Breakfast the new rules, aiming to create "bang for the British buck", would help achieve this target given increasing defence spending "does come at a cost to the country and other things we'd like to spend money on".
He said waiting for the spending review, which does not have a fixed date and could come in the second half of 2027, was "the right thing to do" so ministers can look at "spending in the round".
He added that the UK was ready to deal with hostile threats, but "we're not where we'd want to be".
"There's no sugarcoating the fact that our Armed Forces were under-invested in for more than a decade," he told Breakfast.
Defence analysts have questioned the government's ability to deliver on its 2030 target and the Nato-wide target of 3.5% by 2035. UK defence spending is at an estimated 2.6% of GDP this year.
Some estimates have suggested the government will need to spend an additional £10bn annually to reach its targets.
Tory leader Kemi Badenoch said on Wednesday that Healey "failed his own test" by not setting out a "plan for 3%".
Healey resigned as then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary in June over not spending enough on defence.
In the Budget, Healey said the UK was negotiating with Finland, Poland and the Netherlands to set up an international bank - the Multilateral Defence Mechanism - to boost defence investment and joint procurement.
But Conservative shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge said this amounted to "turning to borrowing at a time when the national debt is over £3 trillion".
"The answer is not more borrowing – it's to cut welfare to fund defence," he said.

article:
He questioned Thailand's monarchy dressed as Harry Potter. Now he's in jail for 34 years

He questioned Thailand's monarchy dressed as Harry Potter. Now he's in jail for 34 years
- Published
Even before they come through the door, you can hear the prisoners walking towards the courtroom, the shackles round their ankles clinking with each step.
The five who walk into the courtroom are familiar with the routine; they are facing multiple criminal prosecutions and have spent much of the past five years going back and forth to court.
One of them, a small, bespectacled man with greying hair, opens his arms to hold his three-year-old son, who has been brought to court by his partner to see him.
This is Arnon Nampa, a 42-year-old human rights lawyer. His offence was to call for Thailand's powerful monarchy to be scrutinised and held accountable. He did this dressed as the eponymous young wizard at a Harry Potter-themed demonstration in central Bangkok in 2020.
On Friday a court in Bangkok sentenced him to two years and eight months for violating Thailand's lèse majesté law, or article 112, under which more people have been jailed for perceived insults against the royal family than in all the other countries that have such laws combined.
This is just one out of 14 cases brought against Arnon under the same charge, bringing the cumulative sentence he has received so far to more than 34 years. The verdict in two cases is still pending.
"To me, this isn't a surprise," he later told reporters. "If the country was more open, we would be able to talk about these issues freely."
The past six years have seen the most extensive use of lèse majesté in Thai history, in response to unprecedented student protests in 2020 which for the first time called for a public discussion of the role of the monarchy. Two hundred and ninety-four people, including 20 under the age of 18, have been prosecuted, receiving prison sentences of up to 50 years. Dozens of them are still on trial.
Most of those charged under this law are denied bail and kept in jail, even though their court cases can last several years. The standard defence of the law given by Thai officials is that it "reflects the culture and history of Thailand, where the monarchy is one of the main pillars of the nation, highly revered by the majority of Thai people".
Article 112 of the Thai criminal code simply reads, "Whoever defames, insults or threatens the King, the Queen, the Heir-apparent or the Regent, shall be punished with imprisonment of three to 15 years."
In practice, though, the law has been interpreted to cover a much wider range of comment about the monarchy, and a much wider range of figures. Saying anything negative about any member of the royal family, about the institution of the monarchy, even about long deceased kings, or in one case, the king's dog, has resulted in prosecutions.
"If you ask me what the text of the law says, I can tell you," says Akarachai Chaimaneekarakate, assistant director of Thai Lawyers for Human Rights, which helps defend those accused of breaking it. "If you ask me how the courts interpret the words "defame" or "insult", I don't think I can give you a definition, because it's so ambiguous, it's so vague. Even questioning the law itself, for example, can constitute lèse majesté under Section 112."
From his cell in the Bangkok Remand Prison, where he has been for the last three years, Arnon has been writing to his young daughter and son.
"Dear Pran and Karl, my beloved children," one of his letters reads, "The winter wind has not only brought us cool weather, but also brings back stories from the past. I miss the time we travelled outside Bangkok that first winter after Karl came into this world. It was such a magical time for me. I shall miss it every winter I spend here until I regain my freedom."
Hearings like the one Arnon attended weeks before Friday's verdict are the only times he has seen Karl since he was a baby.
Karl is shy at first, but soon he's happy to be picked up and shown off to the other prisoners. His 10-year-old sister Pran sometimes visits their father in prison, and often draws and paints him.
But Arnon and Lookwa, his partner, think Karl is too young to visit. For now, Karl thinks the court is just where his dad works. A group of supporters has come too, filling the little courtroom. They mingle cheerfully with the prisoners, laughing and exchanging gossip before the judges walk in to start the hearing. It is an improbably informal setting for men facing one of the most feared charges in Thailand.
The effect of the law has been to smother any public discussion about the monarchy. Until six years ago, opinions on it were only ever whispered in private. In one notorious case a taxi driver was jailed because a passenger reported what he had said while riding in his cab.
That changed on 3 August 2020.
That year younger Thais had become increasingly frustrated with the conservative government led by coup-leader Gen Prayuth Chan-ocha. The year before millions had given their votes to a new party, Future Forward, which promised sweeping reforms, but in February 2020, the Constitutional Court dissolved the party on a technicality. The arrival of the Covid pandemic prevented any protests for three months, but as infections in Thailand started to fall, students began holding rallies calling for an end to the military's role in politics. Arnon Nampa argued this did not go far enough.
In the garb of Harry Potter, he gave a speech saying it was time to talk about the opaque power and wealth of the monarchy. He criticised King Vajiralongkorn's decision to take personal control of the vast assets held by the Crown Property Bureau, and over important units of the army.
In a single speech Arnon shattered a taboo which had hung over Thai society for the whole of its modern history. For the rest of that year the student-led protests continued, with increasingly bold demands for changes to the monarchy.
At the time, the use of the lèse majesté law had been suspended for three years. Sources close to the palace have in the past acknowledged that the negative publicity generated by lèse majesté convictions might do more harm than good.
But the protests forced a hasty reassessment. From the end of 2020 prosecutions under the law restarted and accelerated. Dozens of young activists have fled into exile to avoid being jailed.
One of them is Supitcha "Melinn" Chailom. The 24-year-old from Chiang Mai in northern Thailand lives in Montreal, a fugitive from four 112 charges which have been filed against her.
She was an 18-year-old school girl when she stood up and made a speech at a protest in Chiang Mai University, just three weeks after Arnon Nampa's call for reform of the monarchy.
A local photographer captured the moment she raised her hand in the three-finger Hunger Games salute, eliciting loud cheers from the crowd. It became one of the defining images of the protests, and propelled Melinn to nationwide fame.
She travelled up and down the country as one of the leading voices in the movement, demanding changes to Thailand's old-fashioned education system, conducting polls on what people thought of the monarchy.
"I love playing games, and I dreamed of being a game designer," she told me from Canada. But her parents did not approve.
"I felt that, as a young person, I could not question, or have a discussion with people older than me. The monarchy gave me the same vibe."
In November 2020 Melinn joined a protest in the southern city of Hat Yai, where she gave a speech comparing the royal treatment given to the king's dog with that of ordinary people. Nine months later the police delivered a summons to her home charging her with lèse majesté.
"It was a shock. I wasn't expecting it because I only talked about the dog. It was during Covid when the police came to my home with the summons, so they knew my parents would be there with me. They tried to stay calm, but I nearly lost my mind."
Her family tried to persuade her to co-operate with the authorities, to admit her wrongdoing. But Melinn refused.
She joined a movement calling itself Thalu Wang, which translates as "breaking through the palace". Instead of giving speeches, they came up with stunts like holding polls on the street, asking people what they thought of royal motorcades holding up the traffic, or whether they believed the monarchy had too much power.
"We knew the risks, but we thought it would be safer just conducting a poll. It turns out it was not."
She was given two more lèse majesté charges in 2022, and detained before being released on bail. She had to wear an electronic monitor on her ankle and was barred from leaving her home between 4pm and 6am. Her parents were forced to sign a document promising to inform on her. She was facing decades in jail.
Melinn decided she had no choice. With a friend she fled Thailand and eventually got asylum in Canada.
Article 112 is on paper just a law, like any other, passed by the Thai parliament, which can, theoretically, be amended by elected MPs. In fact it has been amended in the past, notably in 1976 when the punishment for breaking it was increased to between three and 15 years in prison.
But today the Constitutional Court has decreed that the law itself, like the institution it protects, is untouchable. The reformist Move Forward party - the successor of Future Forward - was dissolved in 2024, and its leader banned from politics, merely for proposing that the punishments be less harsh. And the courts make it very difficult for those charged under it to defend themselves.
"In many cases, like the one against Arnon Nampa, prosecutors accuse the defendant of lying about the monarchy," says Chaimaneekarakate, the lawyer. "But when we ask the judge to subpoena documents or witnesses who could show the truth of what the defendant says, the judge refuses to do it. When one lawyer protested against the court deciding that the trial would be held in secret, she was warned by the judge to be quiet or face a contempt of court charge."
He says judges sometimes criticise the young activists over their alleged actions even before the trial has started.
As the one who ignited the debate about the monarchy Arnon appears to be getting the harshest punishment. Despite the formidable odds stacked against him he still prepares carefully for every court appearance, taking part in his own defence and helping other inmates with theirs.
This isn't easy; he is not allowed to bring any of his written notes, and must memorise all his arguments.
The judges object to him playing the part of a lawyer in his regulation-brown prison shorts, his feet bare and shackled. But it does give him an opportunity to see his family.
The letters he writes are the only other way he stays in touch with them. He may spend his entire life in prison. He wants his children to know him, and to understand, when they are older, why he chose to challenge the system and lose his freedom.
"Since the first day that we made up our mind to take up this mission, we knew of the dangers. Speaking the truth is not difficult. What is difficult is speaking a forbidden truth. I remember well that on the evening of 3 August 2020, after speaking at the Harry Potter event, I felt very good, content, and relieved to have finally begun speaking about the truth, in public," he wrote to his family last year.
Earlier this year, he wrote: "Living here is a struggle. But it is just a dot in the bigger picture of our movement's struggle. We must play a part in writing our own history. Become a drop of water that will one day become an ocean."

article:
Ofcom outlines age check methods ahead of social media ban for under-16s

Ofcom outlines age check methods ahead of social media ban for under-16s
- Published
Ofcom has set out its recommendations for the most effective ways to identify which of the UK's millions of social media users are aged over 16.
Under the UK's social media ban - which is due to come into force in March next year - those under that age will be prevented from accessing ten of the biggest platforms, including Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat.
Many UK adults are also likely to have to confirm that they are not under-age by using one of the proposed measures, which are subject to government approval.
A similar ban was introduced in Australia last year but many children there have found ways to get round it. The UK says it intends to take a tougher approach.
Age verification below 18 is challenging because 16 and 17 year olds don't have credit cards or full driving licences, and may not have passports either. They can also look significantly older or younger than they are.
To address that challenge, Ofcom has - in addition to traditional forms of ID - recommended four methods that it says would be "highly effective" at gauging people's ages:
- photo ID matching, where relevant information on a photo ID document such as a passport is checked against a live image taken during an age check
- banking-based checks, which involves using the information a financial institution has on record regarding a user's age
- face age estimation technology (which the regulator argues has recently improved)
- digital ID services, which enable people to digitally prove who they are or provide information about themselves, such as their age
The BBC has asked three of the UK's biggest banks whether they would have a process for assisting with social media requests for age verification if it did become an official measure.
However, ultimately it will be up to the tech companies to figure out how to implement the checks: the onus is on social network providers to come up with their own solutions and comply.
Ofcom CEO Dame Melanie Dawes said the regulator was drawing on its experience in introducing tougher age checks for porn sites last year:
"What we've learned in introducing age checks across the porn industry is that actually what a lot of countries did before us was say you need to do it this way and they were very prescriptive and it didn't work," she told the BBC.
"So what we've said all along is here are things that can work, they must preserve privacy, they must protect people's data, but it's on you to put in place what you think works for you."
Some of the tech companies, including Meta, have called for age verification to be applied at device level, so that someone under-age would be automatically blocked from installing social media apps via app stores.
Meta told the BBC it already applies some methods recommended by Ofcom to enforce its user age requirements or place users in Teen Accounts settings.
But it said applying age checks at device-level, via app stores, could reduce the burden on people to have to repeatedly verify their age across multiple platforms.
This would place responsibility with Apple and Google, who between them operate most of the world's smartphones. Apple has already introduced age verification in the UK.
However Ofcom says that would not absolve the social network providers from doing their own checks as well.
The regulator said it didn't have a firm number for how many adults would need to prove they were not under age, but conceded that it would be a "large number of accounts" that social media companies would need to "deal with."
It has also acknowledged that "the risk of circumvention cannot be entirely eliminated", and some children would succeed in bypassing the age checks.
Dawes said making the ban work would be a joint effort.
"At Ofcom, what we will do is make sure that the services that the social media companies put in the checks that they need to," she told BBC News.
"That's our job, but the wider question about how everybody engages with this, it is for everybody, really.
"I actually think the real prize here is going to be for today's eight to 10-year-olds entering secondary school without it being the norm to go on Snap in your class group chat, without it being the norm to have all your sports fixtures organised on Instagram."
Ofcom's age verification report will now be considered by the government, with a decision due by the end of the year.
Australia ban lessons
Child safety campaigners including the Molly Rose Foundation and NSPCC welcomed Ofcom's guidance.
But both said there were lessons to be learned from how Australia's social media ban had been implemented, after it was found many under-16s could still access social platforms.
"That's why, as we prepare to embark on our own social media ban in the UK, we need to make sure we accurately know the age of child users," said Rani Govender, head of child safety online at the NSPCC.
She said the government and Ofcom must ensure tech firms are held accountable for meeting age check standards "to help keep children safe online and ensure the ban delivers change in practice".
But Andy Burrows, the Molly Rose Foundation's chief executive, said Ofcom had shown a "dire track record" of enforcing the Online Safety Act - raising questions over how effectively it would help deliver a social media ban.
"Andy Burnham must deliver a ban that learns the lessons from Australia and that incentivises safety-by-design as the price of admission to the UK market, with a ban as the starting point in a proper plan to give children a safe and happy online life," he said.
Jonny Bunt, corporate affairs director of BT's consumer division, said families should "prepare children for life online after the ban and highlight the risks of trying to dodge the restrictions".
"Having those conversations now and giving young people time to prepare for the changes in March will be crucial in helping them adapt to a significant change for a whole generation," he said.
"The restrictions have the potential to change the way young people interact with the digital world for the better, but only if regulators, tech companies, families, and educators come together to make it a success."

article:
Car finance compensation payments explained

Car finance compensation payments explained
- Published
Millions of drivers who were mis-sold car finance agreements must wait until at least 2027 to receive compensation, although some may be offered an early settlement.
Average payments of about £829 are expected under the rules published by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA).
However, legal challenges to the scheme - which will be heard in February 2027 -mean compensation calculations and payments have been delayed.
Who could receive car finance compensation?
The vast majority of new cars, and many second-hand ones, are bought with finance agreements. Customers pay an initial deposit to secure the vehicle, then a monthly fee with interest.
Compensation could be given to many of those who took out a car loan between April 2007 and November 2024.
The decision by the FCA, the financial regulator, applies to about 12 million car loans - about 37% of the total number during the period.
In 2021, the FCA banned deals where car dealers received commission from lenders, based on the interest rate charged to the customer. These were known as discretionary commission arrangements (DCAs) and customers were often not told about them.
The FCA said this provided an incentive for a buyer to be charged a higher-than-necessary interest rate, leaving them paying too much.
Other car buyers were also judged to have signed unfair contracts because the commission paid to the dealer was so high - accounting for 39% of the total cost of credit and 10% of the loan.
Some customers were not given accurate information about the best finance deal because of exclusive arrangements between car dealers and lenders.
How much compensation could victims receive?
Under the latest proposals, the FCA expects average payouts of £829 per mis-sold agreement.
The total cost of the compensation, including administrative costs, could hit £9.1bn.
How much individual consumers receive will depend on the degree of harm suffered.
The FCA has announced some claimants might be offered an early settlement, but only if it as good as what would be paid under the current proposed central scheme.
What do victims need to do to claim compensation?
Complaints have already been made about four million finance agreements. Those people do not need to do anything.
The regulator urged anyone who has not yet complained to contact their car loan provider directly, rather than using a third-party claims management company.
The regulator's central compensation scheme allows people to complain and potentially receive compensation for mis-sold deals without the need for a lawyer or to go through the courts.
Motorists have also been warned to be on the alert for scammers posing as car finance lenders offering fake compensation.
The FCA has published this guidance on how to complain, external.
Under its plans:
- lenders will respond to claims, explaining if you are owed compensation and how much – but timing of those letters is now uncertain owing to the legal challenge
- those who complain before the scheme gets up and running are likely to receive compensation faster
- some people who complained by 30 June and are not owed compensation should be told by 18 November, if the agreement began on or after 1 April 2014 and you complained by 30 June 2026
- some of those who complained by 31 August will be told if they are not owed compensation by 18 January 2027, if the agreement began before 1 April 2014
- there are exemptions, external, and anyone who does not hear from their lender by the dates set out, isn't necessarily owed compensation
- those who have not complained will be contacted by their lender. People will be asked if they want to opt in to the scheme to have their case reviewed
- those motor finance borrowers who do not receive a letter - for example because lenders no longer have their details and cannot trace them - can still make a claim
Regulators have warned claims management companies and law firms involved in motor finance commission claims to make sure consumers do not have multiple representatives for the same claim and are not charged excessive termination fees.
FCA boss Nikhil Rathi told the BBC's Today programme there are "many law firms out there who would like to get 30% of any compensation", stressing that the regulator's scheme was "free to use" for consumers.
When will drivers receive compensation and who will pay?
Millions of drivers were in line to receive compensation this year, and most of the remainder should have got compensation by the end of 2027.
But the FCA has confirmed that no compensation will be paid before 2027 as a result of legal challenges to the scheme.
Consumer Voice said the scheme left "too many people short-changed". The FCA has also received challenges from three lenders: Volkswagen Financial Services, Mercedes Benz Financial Services, and Credit Agricole Auto Finance.
The UK's Upper Tribunal has agreed to hear legal challenges to the scheme, with a hearing scheduled for 16 February to 3 March.
It means that lenders will no longer need to calculate or pay compensation to people owed money under its scheme, until the legal process concludes.
The FCA said it would need to decide what to do next if the courts decided to overturn the programme. Without a scheme in place, the FCA has estimated that up to 19 million complaints would need to be handled individually, taking three years and costing lenders £6bn more.
It said it would "defend the scheme robustly as lawful and the best way to resolve such a widespread, long running and complex issue".
Ultimately, the industry is expected to cover the full costs of any compensation scheme, including any administrative costs.
Lenders - including some of the UK's biggest banks and specialist motor finance firms - have already set aside billions of pounds for potential payouts.
Can drivers get an early settlement?
The FCA said a minority of claimants will be made early offers, but most will have to wait for the outcome of next year's court case.
With huge compensation payouts inevitable, Barclays will offer early settlements to some claimants, with others expected to follow suit.
The FCA has published a factsheet to help drivers, external work out whether they should accept early settlements from lenders.
Accepting would mean quicker payouts but remove them from any changes to the central scheme.
What's been the reaction to the payout plan?
The body that represents the lending industry, the Finance and Leasing Association, said it had "concerns" about the central programme but that it was choosing not to raise a legal challenge.
Santander, Barclays and Lloyds also accepted the scheme, despite raising concerns that the level of redress is disproportionate to those who suffered harm.
Even if drivers are entitled to compensation from these lenders they will need to wait.
There were some concessions made to lenders in a scaled-down final compensation plan from the FCA.
The Supreme Court considered three test cases which influenced the FCA's decision and, ultimately, limited how broad the compensation programme could have been.
It focused on whether the car dealers had a duty to act on behalf of their customers, rather than in their own interests. The test case which was upheld was that of Marcus Johnson, who bought his first car - a Suzuki Swift - in 2017.
In his case, the Supreme Court said the terms of his finance deal were unfair due of the size of the commission payment, and the fact he appeared to have been misled over the relationship between the finance firm and the dealer.

article:
Toddler heads to US for cancer treatment as family given 'glimmer of hope'

Toddler heads to US for cancer treatment as family given 'glimmer of hope'
- Published
A mother who is preparing to take her three-year-old son to the US for a vaccine trial says it has given her family a "glimmer of hope" for his future.
Almost a year ago, doctors warned Teddy Sloman's parents that he might not survive life-saving surgery after being diagnosed with high-risk neuroblastoma, external, a rare, aggressive childhood cancer.
But recent scans showed no active disease, and the family are preparing to fly to New York next month for what his mum Sarah hopes will be "the final chapter" of his treatment and "the end of this ridiculous nightmare".
"We've now given him the absolute best chance that we could possibly have in the world of medical science," she said.
Sarah, from Pontypool, Torfaen, said the process since Teddy's diagnosis had been "incredibly difficult" as they were often dealing with problems they could not have anticipated.
As a paediatric nurse herself, she previously said her medical knowledge had been both "a blessing and a curse".
An experimental treatment aimed at preventing the return of the type of cancer Teddy has was no longer available in the UK, so his family raised £250,000 to access the vaccine trial in New York.
Sarah said the scan results felt like "Christmas came early" after months of fearing Teddy would relapse, and they were finally "moving forward to the next step".
But she added they had to "mentally navigate all of these things" when all they "really want to do is stay at home and enjoy being a family for once".
The Welsh government said improving cancer care was a top priority and it was "acutely aware" how much it meant to people.
Teddy was diagnosed in July 2025 after months of symptoms that were initially thought to be teething, illness and constipation.
He stopped eating and drinking, was sleeping for hours in the day and night, and began vomiting.
Sarah felt a mass in his abdomen and was first told "it was just faeces".
With Teddy still feeling unwell, Sarah took him back to The Grange Hospital in Cwmbran in July.
A locum doctor in charge of the children's assessment unit said it was "not normal" for Teddy to have these symptoms and ordered a scan, later finding out that the mass was "actually a significant tumour".
Sarah said hearing the diagnosis was "surreal".
"I, as a student nurse, had been in that exact situation sort of 20 years ago... and it just felt so surreal, like an out-of-body experience.
"This is my work world. This is not supposed to be my personal life."
Teddy's tumour was so large it filled his entire abdomen, pressing on his organs and making it hard for him to eat or even breathe, and the cancer had spread to his bone marrow.
Sarah said: "Everything that we didn't want it to be, it was. So it's the most aggressive, the most rare, the most everything else."
Aneurin Bevan University Health Board said it recognised how "distressing it can be for parents when their child is seriously unwell, particularly when symptoms are complex and difficult to diagnose".
It added that it welcomed the family to contact them to discuss any concerns so they could be "reviewed fully".
The family spent 10 months in Noah's Ark Children's Hospital for Wales and also had to travel to Birmingham and London for specialist treatment.
This led to long-term implications, and Teddy now receives his food entirely through a tube and has to learn how to eat and drink again after already having to learn to walk three times due to being in bed for long periods.
Sarah said she felt "mum guilt" as her youngest son Joey, who is nearly two, spent most of his time with grandparents and relatives while Teddy was in hospital.
"We started running on fumes a long time ago, but you just do what needs to be done," she said.
Sarah said due to a measles outbreak in New York, they had made the "heartbreaking decision" to leave Joey in the UK during their first trip.
Over the past few months at home, the pair had been playing together and telling each other "they love each other", she said.
"It's those little things that you don't want to lose, you don't want to let go of.
"You want them to grow up together, looking out for each other and doing all the things that all the siblings [do]."
She added: "All of those things now feel like they're possible, whereas this time last year they didn't."
In June, the family found out that maintenance drug difluoromethylornithine, external (DFMO), which could prevent Teddy relapsing, had been withdrawn from the NHS, external, by the US-based company which owns it following a clinical trial.
Those who were already receiving the drug were allowed to continue for two years, but it was not available to new patients, such as Teddy.
Sarah said they were the only family they knew of going through the private treatment process.
To get an official referral for the clinical vaccine trial, Teddy's family had to send a urine sample, get a bone marrow aspirate and for his scans to declare "no active disease".
"To have the results come back... and for them to say that there's no active neuroblastoma cells, it was Christmas come early. It was everything that we'd hoped for for so long," said Sarah.
Teddy has officially been accepted as a patient for the vaccine trial in New York, and will have his initial appointment in November - but it comes at a hefty price.
"If he relapses the survival rates drop to single figures. So if there's a tiny chance that this vaccine can do some good [it's worth it]," Sarah said.
"At one point we were looking at selling the house and getting loans and all sorts because we just didn't see [another option].
"There's nothing in the world you wouldn't do for your children."
Friends launched a campaign to raise £250,000 and reached their target in 12 weeks, with Sarah admitting she thought "we'd never make it in a million years".
The fundraiser has since been increased to £350,000 to help with ongoing costs, and more than £300,000 has been raised so far.
She added: "It's absolutely incredible and there are not enough words in the world to thank people."
Despite everything, Sarah described Teddy as a cheerful "social butterfly" who had remained positive throughout.
"His friends are learning how to jump in muddy puddles and do climbing frames and Teddy's learning how to take blood pressures and use a stethoscope."
Sarah said more focus, support and research was needed for childhood cancers and that funding was "harrowing" compared to adult cancers.
"We shouldn't need to be raising all this money to fly the other side of the world for drugs," she said.
"I just want Teddy's story to be known so that the next person coming behind us doesn't have to go through this excruciating journey that we have."
The Welsh government said improving cancer care was a "top priority", with a 10-year strategy focused on better prevention, diagnosis and treatment aimed at improving services and outcomes for patients of all ages.
It added that, through Health and Care Research Wales, external, there was funding for "early stage clinical trials for children and young people" through a partnership with Cancer Research UK.

article:
What we know so far about deadly Spain train crash

What we know so far about deadly Spain train crash
- Published
Two trains crashed south of the Spanish capital Madrid on Wednesday morning, on the high-speed line to Seville.
At least 69 people were killed and dozens injured in the collision, when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of a stationary train operated by the Iryo company near the town of Urda.
It is one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013. Three days of national mourning have been declared in the country.
Here is what we know about the crash so far.
Where and when did the crash happen?
The crash happened at 08:53 (07:53 GMT) between municipalities Mora and Orgaz, and about 140km (100 miles) south of Madrid, according to an account given by the Spanish government.
The privately run Iryo train was stationary on the state-run Renfe train barrelled into the back of it at high speed. Iryo said its train was "struck from behind" by a Renfe train "due to causes that are still unknown".
The crash caused some carriages to fall down an embankment.
All train traffic on the line was stopped at stations along the route.
Renfe said services between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia were suspended.
A passenger on board one of the trains told local media there was a heavy impact about 40 minutes into the journey.
What caused the crash?
Spanish Transport Minister Óscar Puente said a computer failure at about 08:30 on Wednesday morning led to the initial halt of six moving trains, including the two trains that subsequently collided.
"In the event of a system failure, the control centre takes over," he said, adding it was the control centre that decided to allow the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions.
That decision, Puente said, was made "under inexplicable circumstances". It resulted in the Renfe train crashing into the Iryo train, which was stationary on the tracks about 25km (15 miles) ahead.
Audio recordings obtained by Spanish media between train controllers working in Madrid for a rail infrastructure company in Adif in Madrid and the train drivers appear to show that one high-speed train was given clearance to move at 08:36 even though another one ahead had stalled.
In one recording, the controller tells the driver of the Renfe train to disconnect and reconnect the LZB mechanism that monitors train speeds, and then resume the journey at normal speed.
"Disconnect and reconnect LZB. Continue your journey and then proceed under [Lateral Signalling Block], at normal speed with normal operation," the control centre operator says to the driver.
The driver replies, "At normal speed?" To which the controller says: "Yes."
- Young athlete and former minister among victims 
  - Published4 days ago
- Bloodied, dazed and angry - how passengers' rail journey turned to disaster 
  - Published5 days ago
Under normal protocols, the driver would be expected to continue moving at a maximum of 40km/h according to their line of sight, and not at normal speed on a track designed for speeds of up to 200km/h.
The Lateral Signaling Block is a back-up or alternative train system used when the automatic signalling or data transmission system fails.
In a second audio recording between the driver of the Iryo train in front and the control centre, the driver says the train "is stationary in front of the entry signal at Urda". After some exchanges, the control centre operator tells the driver to "resume the journey" normally.
The Iryo driver then contacts the control centre again, according to a later recording, saying they cannot start the train. "The train won't allow me to control the [security] system. That's why I am still stopped in front of the entry signal," they say.
The latter recording suggests that the controller had been notified that the Iryo train remained stationary as the Renfe train approached.
How many passengers were on board?
More than 540 people were on board both trains.
Esther Padilla, spokesperson for the government of Castilla-La Mancha region, told TVE that one of the trains - managed by the Iryo company - was carrying 146 passengers plus one baby, while the Renfe-managed train had 397 passengers on board.
Julieta Gallego, a 24-year-old Spanish female long jumper, and former government minister Fátima Báñez, 59, were among those killed in the crash.
More than 100 people were treated for injuries, according to Spanish authorities, and by the next day 50 of them were still in hospital, 15 in a critical condition.
How have the authorities responded?
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has said "the whole of Spain is grieving" and that "lives have been shattered, families have been torn apart".
"The pain is immense," he said on a visit to the crash site.
The government was "trying to determine what was the origin of this tragedy, of this terrible accident," he added.
"We will get to the bottom of this, and if there has been any negligence, it will come to light.
"If there have been failures in the security system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness."
Opposition conservative leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, whose People's Party leads most opinion polls ahead of 29 November elections, said it was not the day to talk about political responsibility, but insisted "Spain has the right to know what is going on with its infrastructure".
Most Spanish politicians cancelled all public engagements on Wednesday and suspended their election campaign.
However, Santiago Abascal of the far-right Vox refused to take part in what his party described as attempts to "use mourning to silence criticism" of the country's rail infrastructure.
Three days of official mourning began on Thursday.
Spain's royal family posted on X that it was "shocked and concerned" and expressed condolences for the relatives of the deceased and those affected by the crash.
A spokesperson for the EU said the bloc was ready to help Spain if needed.
A huge emergency response was under way with fire crews and helicopters at the scene.
Hospitals in the area suspended planned surgeries as they deal with an influx of patients from the crash, Spanish media have reported.
A blood transfusion centre in Madrid appealed for "urgent" donations. In a post on X, Centro de Transfusión said it made the request "in the face of a possible sudden increase in care needs".
It reported that facilities in Toledo, Ciudad Real and Alcázar de San Juan had cancelled procedures as casualties from the crash begin to arrive.
The Spanish Civil Guard set up bureaus in Madrid, Toledo, Seville and Córdoba to investigate reports of missing persons.
"The top priority is the identification of the missing persons and the taking of DNA samples to be able to locate their relatives," the civil guard wrote in a post on X.
This is the second high-speed rail tragedy in Spain this year.
In January a high-speed train derailed in southern Spain, its rear carriages going into the path of a state-run Renfe train, claiming the lives of 46 people.

article:
King visits Guyanese slave rebellion site on Caribbean tour

King visits Guyanese slave rebellion site on Caribbean tour
- Published
The King has made a poignant visit to the site where a Guyanese slave rebellion was violently resisted by British authorities, making the stop during his tour of the Caribbean.
He visited Independence Park in Georgetown to remember the Demerara Slave Rebellion of 1823, which saw an uprising by thousands of enslaved people.
Accompanied by Guyana's Culture Minister, Steven Jacobs, he was told how hundreds of slaves were killed by colonial leaders during the rebellion and many of those who survived were executed close to where the King stood.
Above the King was a sign that he took time to read.
"This ground was used as a public execution site," it said, "where enslaved persons...were condemned to death and hung."
The moment of reflection was what Buckingham Palace had described as the King "not shying away from the UK's colonial legacy" and described today as a chance for the King to reflect on Guyana's history of slavery and resistance.
In 2022, the King described how he was on a personal journey of discovery and was continuing to "deepen my own understanding of slavery's enduring impact", in a speech at the opening of a Commonwealth summit hosted by Rwanda.
Independence Park, which is now a sports ground, drew a crowd of dozens of schoolchildren. The King stopped to talk to many of them asking them about their homework, their holidays and if they'd had a day off school.
Outside one of the King's engagements later in the day, a small but noisy group of protesters gathered.
Many held placards saying "no apology will return what was stolen, reparations now" and "justice must not depend on wealth status and connections".
"This great wealth was built on the backs of slavery," said protester, Guyanese politician, Terrence Campbell.
"I do not want the British public to think that by me saying reparations can take various forms, it means that they do not have responsibility for reparations. They do, because the United Kingdom benefited tremendously from slavery."
The King will not be apologising for the UK involvement in the slave trade during the visit, nor will he offer reparations - compensation from those countries who benefited from the slave trade - in line with the position of the UK government.
This tour has seen a number of demonstrations so far but none have seriously disrupted the King's programme.
Royal tours often include cultural exchanges and the King's trip to Guyana saw an unusual mix up of musical styles.
On the bandstand of Promenade Gardens in Georgetown, the bagpipes of the National Piping Centre could be heard alongside traditional Guyanese drummers in a collaboration of musical styles.
Seven pipers from the National Piping Centre have been touring Guyana over the past week to learn more about the Guyanese musical traditions.
As part of his visit on Friday, the King also shared a moment with a veterans from Guyana who fought for Britain in the Second World War during an event at the Commonwealth War Graves in the capital Georgetown.
King Charles met Donald Grant, 99, who will celebrate his 100th birthday next week on November 3.
He also spoke to James Samuel, 100, who is in a wheelchair, with the the King hearing how aged 19 he enlisted in the British Guiana Volunteer Force in 1943.
"What a great pleasure it is to see you on this occasion," the King told him.
The King was waved off at the end of his state visit by Britain's High Commissioner to Guyana, Joseph Fisher, Guyana's Prime Minister Mark Phillips and a number of other dignitaries.
His departure had a small ceremonial element with the Guyana Defence Force providing a guard of honour at Cheddi Jagan International Airport.

article:
Scientists detect signals from the zeptoverse - the smallest scale of nature ever explored

Scientists detect signals at the smallest scale ever explored
- Published
Scientists have picked up signals from the smallest scale of nature ever explored – 100 billion times smaller than an atom.
A world so small that some physicists have nicknamed it the zeptoverse.
The research, led by scientists based in Cambridge, was obtained from an experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC).
This vast machine at the European Laboratory for Particle Physics (Cern) on the Swiss-French border smashes atoms together to break them apart and discover what is inside them.
The result is important because it could help researchers develop a new, more complete theory of how the Universe works.
'Knocking on the door' of the zeptoverse
Dark matter makes up a large part of our cosmos, and yet researchers have struggled to detect it.
Scientists know it is there because its gravitational force influences normal matter, but in all other respects it has remained completely invisible.
So in this experiment, particles were smashed together at high energy and scientists studied the material that was thrown out - the shrapnel of collisions.
One of these is a sub-atomic particle - smaller than an atom - called a beauty quark.
The particle is unstable and exists for just one and a half trillionths of a second before breaking down into other forms - decaying.
Despite its short lifetime, researchers managed to detect it interacting with other tiny particles at a scale of a billion-trillionth of a metre.
Some theories suggest that at these scales particles are more sensitive to dark matter and it could influence how the quarks interact and break down. So, detecting activity in this tiny world could help scientists detect dark matter.
"We're knocking on the door of this zeptoverse," Dr Harry Cliff, of Cambridge University who led the analysis of the data, told BBC News.
He said this sub-atomic dance provided researchers with a ringside seat to the behaviour of possible new particles.
"And what we want to do now is go in and explore and find what new particles are waiting there. And to do that, what we need is more data," Cliff added.
The 28 countries involved in the project have agreed a £150m upgrade to this detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHCb), which would increase the frequency of these decays tenfold.
"With that we can probe inside the zeptoverse and see what's waiting," Cliff said.
But last year the UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) agency, the government body in charge of research funding, announced that it was withdrawing its share of the money for the planned upgrade.
It later announced cuts to several other particle physics and astronomy projects this Summer, including Jodrell Bank's iconic Lovell telescope.
Although this research was led by scientists based in Cambridge, because of the cuts, Prof Tim Gershon, who leads the LHCb international collaboration, told BBC News that the UK's full involvement in the research would be in doubt.
"The UK is at risk of not being involved and making really major discoveries," he told BBC News.
"But I think the biggest long-term impact comes from the fact that the UK won't get the benefits from training young people who really are our greatest product."
Among those early-career researchers is Dr Mary Richardson-Slipper, who is part of the team that made the zeptoverse discovery. She is reconsidering her future in light of the physics cuts.
"I love being here in the UK, but I am looking at jobs abroad because that seems to be where there are more opportunities at the moment," said Richardson-Slipper.
She added that "lots" of her fellow researchers working in fundamental physics had already moved.
The cuts are being made despite an overall record increase in the science budget.
Prof Brian Cox, TV presenter and particle researcher at the University of Manchester, who is not part of the research team, described the result as "important".
But he condemned the recent decision to cut UK funding for the Cern project.
"It would be extraordinary to walk away from UK scientific leadership at this moment, damaging the future research programme and seriously damaging our hard-won international reputation," Cox said.
The UKRI told BBC News that it remained a fully engaged member of Cern as its second largest funder at around £175m per year.
A UKRI spokesperson said: "We sought independent advice and have taken forward an exciting portfolio of new infrastructure investments, which include projects in clean energy, medical imaging and cultural heritage.

article:
Who is the newly independent unionist MP Carla Lockhart ?

Who is the newly independent unionist MP Carla Lockhart ?
- Published
Carla Lockhart has resigned from the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) over its handling of the fallout of a parading dispute.
The MP is to sit as an independent unionist in the House of Commons.
Her resignation was widely expected after a clash with the DUP leadership over its failure to remove Sinn Féin's Michelle O'Neill from her role as first minister.
O'Neill and several other senior Sinn Féin figures have been interviewed by police for taking part in a protest which prevented an Orange Order parade from going down the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road in Portadown last month.
Responding to her resignation, the DUP said the only winner out of further divisions within unionism was Sinn Féin.
Who is Carla Lockhart?
Lockhart represents the Upper Bann at Westminster, a constituency covering towns and communities including Lurgan, Portadown and Craigavon.
She was first elected to the House of Commons in December 2019 and retained her seat at the 2024 general election.
Lockhart grew up on her family's farm outside Aughnacloy in County Tyrone. She has said her upbringing taught her "the importance of hard work, respect and being a good neighbour".
She attended Aughnacloy College before studying business studies at Ulster University.
On her parliamentary website, Lockhart says she joined the DUP while at university, inspired by Ian Paisley's "conviction politics" and Peter Robinson's "confident, coherent unionist message".
Political career
Lockhart entered the political arena in 2007, when she became a local councillor representing Lurgan. She went on to become the youngest mayor of Craigavon Borough Council, serving as its final first citizen before local government reorganisation.
In May 2016, she was elected as an MLA (member of the legislative assembly) for Upper Bann in the Northern Ireland Assembly. During her time at Stormont, she served on the education committee and the public accounts committee.
Her time in the assembly was relatively short. She resigned her assembly seat in December 2019 after winning the Upper Bann constituency at the general election, succeeding David Simpson at Westminster.
Lockhart was re-elected in 2024 as an MP and has continued to represent Upper Bann at Westminster since then.
Irish Sea border
The DUP blocked a functioning executive and assembly from February 2022 for about two years, in protest against post-Brexit trade arrangements.
Unionists said checks on goods entering Northern Ireland from the rest of the United Kingdom weakened Northern Ireland's place in the union.
When the DUP did a deal over the Irish Sea border to get Stormont back in 2024, Lockhart was critical of it.
In her resignation letter, she cited her concerns over the implementation of the Irish Sea border as another reason.
Role in the Drumcree dispute
As Upper Bann MP, the Portadown-based dispute has played out within her constituency.
She has been one of the DUP's most vocal supporters of the Orange Order's efforts to march along the Garvaghy Road.
The dispute returned to the headlines in 2026 after a court challenge overturned a Parades Commission decision restricting the parade.
The commission subsequently allowed the march to proceed under stricter conditions, but the planned procession was prevented from taking place after residents blocked the route.
The debate intensified when elected nationalist MLAs including First Minister Michelle O'Neill joined protesters on the road.
Lockhart publicly backed the Orange Order's position, arguing that its members should be allowed to complete the traditional route.
At a rally in Portadown on 30 September, she said, "there'll be no capitulation on the part of the Portadown district".
She also criticised a proposed resolution document put forward by Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant, describing it as "not acceptable".
The document was part of efforts to resolve the dispute between the Orange Order and the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition.
How has her response differed from the DUP leadership?
On 9 October Sir Chris banned the Orange Order parade at Drumcree.
Sir Chris said the PSNI chief constable advised him "it would not be possible to enable the procession to happen without a major intervention which would carry an unacceptable risk of serious injury, disorder and a wider contagion effect across Northern Ireland".
Following the ban, Lockhart called for a tougher response from the DUP over O'Neill's involvement in the protests.
Speaking the day after the parade ban outside Drumcree Church she said her constituents were angry with O'Neill, accusing her of "thumbing her nose at unionism and at the Orange Order and at this community".
Lockhart said: "It cannot be business as usual at Stormont", adding that the DUP must take action against O'Neill.
Lockhart stood down as party officer on 22 October.
On 24 October, she attended a rally in Portadown in support of the Orange Order, where she repeated her challenge to the DUP leadership: "Profound consequences must mean profound consequences. Michelle O'Neill must go."
The MP had called on her party to withdraw its Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly from her office – a move that would automatically force O'Neill from her role.
On Thursday, DUP leader Gavin Robinson said Little-Pengelly would not participate in joint engagements with O'Neill and permission would not be granted for the first minister to operate on a solo basis.
A controversial appearance in Scarva
In June, Lockhart rejected criticism of her after she was pictured at a protest standing near masked men.
She was attending a counter-demonstration in Scarva against a Palestine solidarity walk.
The MP defended her presence at the protest, saying she would "never apologise for standing with my community". She said she had been there with other unionist representatives and community leaders to help the protests pass without incident.
In a social media post Lockhart said: "Throughout the day we engaged with senior police officers, relayed concerns, encouraged restraint and worked to ensure calm heads prevailed. We were not there to inflame tensions. We were there to prevent them escalating."
However, her appearance drew criticism from politicians across several parties. SDLP leader Claire Hanna described the images as "bleak and disturbing", while the Sinn Féin MP for the area, Chris Hazzard, challenged Lockhart over her presence alongside masked men.
Writing on X, Hazzard challenged Lockhart to look into what the area has to offer "rather than standing with masked men intimidating women & children".
Alliance deputy leader Eóin Tennyson said at the time: "MPs should be challenging intimidation and sectarianism wherever it appears, not standing with masked men while vile abuse is hurled."
Northern Ireland Justice Minister Naomi Long also criticised Lockhart, accusing her of playing to a crowd wearing masks and shouting abuse.
Lockhart, in turn, condemned the "abuse directed at [her]" and accused her critics of commenting without having been present at the scene.

article:
Drivers may get compensation offers before car finance saga ends

Drivers may get compensation offers before car finance saga ends
- Published
Drivers may be offered compensation from lenders ahead of the next legal battle in the car finance mis-selling saga.
Regulator the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) said it would welcome lenders making settlement offers as long as customers were not given a worse deal than under its proposed central scheme.
That scheme is facing a legal challenge, to be heard in February, with resulting compensation unlikely to be paid until late next year.
But Barclays has confirmed it will make early compensation offers from now, with others expected to follow suit.
The FCA said it would still only expect a minority of claimants to be made early offers, with most having to wait for the outcome of next year's court case.
Stephen Braviner Roman, the FCA's general counsel and co-lead on the motor finance project, said: "Fair settlement offers could result in some people getting money sooner. It's clear they want the choice.
"Anyone who wants to wait can, and there's no obligation to agree to the offer. We'll closely monitor firms making offers and expect them to be clear what accepting an offer means."
Why drivers will receive payouts
The vast majority of new cars, and many second-hand ones, are bought with finance agreements. Customers pay an initial deposit to secure the vehicle, then a monthly fee with interest.
But millions of drivers who took out a car loan between April 2007 and November 2024 will be entitled to compensation after the loans were mis-sold.
They mostly related to when car dealers received commission from lenders, based on the interest rate charged to the customer. These were known as discretionary commission arrangements (DCAs) and customers were often not told about them.
Average compensation payouts of about £829 are expected to be made related to about 12 million car loans - about 37% of the total number during the period.
- Car finance compensation payments delayed until next year 
  - Published2 hours ago
Compensation will cost the industry up to £9.1bn, including administrative costs. Individual payouts will vary, depending on the degree of harm each driver faced.
With huge compensation payouts inevitable, some lenders have already set aside millions of pounds to cover the cost.
Barclays has decided to start making compensation payments early, potentially to start clearing the cost off its balance sheet. It pointed out that claimants had already faced "a considerable wait".
"By making these early settlement offers, we are giving some customers the option of receiving redress sooner, rather than waiting for the legal challenges and any subsequent FCA action to conclude," said a Barclays Partner Finance spokesperson.
"Each offer will be calculated using the FCA's redress scheme methodology. We will clearly explain how it has been calculated and what accepting a full and final settlement means, so customers can decide whether accepting the offer is right for them."
The lender said claimants would start to be contacted directly "in the coming weeks".
But it stressed not all customers whose complaints were acknowledged on or before 1 October 2026 would receive an early settlement offer.
Guidelines on whether to accept an offer
The FCA has published a factsheet to help drivers, external work out whether they should accept early settlements from lenders.
It will include a list of lenders who are making early offers, to ensure claimants with other lenders are not scammed.
The regulator said lenders will need to be clear with people about what accepting any offer means. This includes:
- Being able to keep any payment, even if the final settlement under the central scheme after the legal challenges proved to be smaller
- Claimants would not be able to claim more later if the outcome of the legal challenge meant they would have been paid more
- Accepting an offer takes you out of the scheme and stops any further input from the financial ombudsman
The Finance and Leasing Association, which represents lenders, said: "We want to see consumers receive the fairest outcome in as timely a way as possible and recognise that, in some cases, that may point to early settlement, while in others it may be appropriate to await greater legal certainty."
But Kevin Durkin, solicitor advocate and director at HD Law, who represented Marcus Johnson who won his case in the Supreme Court, said he had "real reservations" that fair compensation would be offered.
"These are only heightened by reports that just a small number of claimants will receive what could be lowball offers. I fear this is crumbs from the table, for some customers who are highly likely to be owed more, while the vast majority will receive no offer at all," he said.
The main proposed FCA scheme remains partially suspended, pending legal challenges in February.
Consumer group Consumer Voice said the proposed compensation scheme left "too many people short-changed". Three lenders - Volkswagen Financial Services, Mercedes Benz Financial Services, and Credit Agricole Auto Finance - are also challenging the scheme.
The UK's Upper Tribunal has agreed to hear legal challenges to the scheme, with a hearing scheduled from 16 February to 3 March.
Anyone who is concerned about their car finance deal and has not yet complained can still complain directly to their lender. There is information on the FCA website on how to complain for free, external.

article:
Cabbie who helped stranded driver gets 'taxi hero' award

Cabbie picks up regional 'taxi hero' award
- Published
A Peterborough taxi driver who gave up a fare to help a stranded motorist fix a puncture has been given an award.
Shafiq Ahmed, who has been driving cabs for more than 30 years, spotted the stranded woman while he was on his way to a pick-up.
He stopped and contacted his office to transfer the booking to another driver so he could help change the woman's tyre.
Ahmed, who has been named the East of England winner of the Acorn Taxi Hero Award, said: "When I saw the woman with a punctured tyre, I knew I could lend a hand... I never expected anything in return."
He added: "For me, it's important to look out for people, whether they're in my taxi or not."
According to Ahmed's nomination, he is known for helping people who are distressed or short of money, helping to ensure they can make their trips.
"I'm very grateful for the nomination and proud to receive this recognition," said Ahmed.
"It's wonderful to see taxi drivers celebrated for the things they do beyond their everyday work."
The Acorn Insurance awards "celebrate the unsung heroes of Britain's taxi industry".
Ash Coakley, of Acorn Group, said: "Giving up a fare to assist a stranded motorist, while making sure his passenger was collected on time, shows real consideration for everyone involved.
"His willingness to help passengers who are struggling financially speaks to that same generosity."
The national winner will be announced on 11 November.
