article:
Jet may have broken apart before Florida crash, officials say, as family named among victims

Jet may have broken apart before Florida crash, officials say, as family named among victims
- Published
Investigators believe parts of a private jet that crashed in Florida and killed all nine onboard may have broken off while it was in the air.
The Learjet 60 had been bound for the Bahamas from Austin, Texas when it nosedived into a multi-lane highway and exploded on impact.
A tech entrepreneur and his young family, as well as the 20-year-old co-pilot, were among those who died on Sunday.
The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said weather conditions would be a major focus of the investigation but that it was struggling to access the wreckage due to the huge crater created by the jet on the road in Palm Beach.
The plane crashed on Military Trail, a six-lane road that features businesses and restaurants, at around 12:50 local time (17:50 GMT).
"The biggest obstacle that we're going to have is recovering the major wreckage from the impacted crater on the roadway," lead investigator Tim Monville said at a news conference on Monday.
The NTSB said the crater, near the entrance to a mobile home park, had become partially filled with water because of severe storms. Heavy rainfall and thunderstorms had been reported in the area at the time of the crash.
Debris was scattered across sports fields, businesses and homes in the area.
"We do have some evidence that there was some breakup of the aircraft before impact," the NTSB's Tom Chapman said.
"We may find parts of the aircraft some distance away from the actual impact site."
Officials are also trying to find out whether a cockpit voice recorder was onboard at the time of the crash and whether it can be recovered.
Flight analysis indicates that the jet was plummeting hundreds of feet per second before it crashed.
In air traffic control audio recordings, someone in the cockpit can be heard reporting "moderate turbulence" and that the crew was "managing the ice".
They can then be heard saying the plane was "picking up precipitation" and "we need to climb". Moments later, the same voice said the plane was descending at a rate of 10,000ft (3,048m) per minute.
An emergency was declared and they can be heard yelling "we are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute", before saying, "we are going to crash into the ground".
Seven passengers died on board, named in a joint statement as tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp, and their two children - Emma, four, and Charlie, two - as well as friends of the family Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, and nanny Anita Maria Cetina.
The pilot was named in media reports as 55-year-old Jeffrey Gregory, while Nathalia Filgueiras, 20, who earned her pilot's licence when she was 17, was reported to be the co-pilot.
One man in a car on the ground sustained a leg injury.
Who are the victims?
Robinson and Sharp's family described them as "devoted parents" and said their children were "the light of their lives".
"Helen and Adam were the love affair that will last forever. Their warmth, generosity and gift for making people feel welcome touched so many lives," the statement read.
Robinson described himself on his LinkedIn page as the founder and CEO of RB2B and Retention.com, and the CEO of Moltsets - all technology companies. Helen Sharp was an artist, according to media reports.
Robinson previously worked at the global financial services business Lehman Brothers and the banking group Barclays. The BBC has contacted the companies.
The joint statement also named nanny Anita Maria Cetina and said she "cared for Emma and Charlie with tenderness and devotion, and she was truly part of the family".
It added: "She showed us a legacy of unconditional love and devotion."
Rachel Reed and Charmi Fehr were described in the joint family statement as "full of joy and adventure".
"They loved their people fiercely, fully and without hesitation. From the moment they met, they were all in on each other and the life they were building."
Nathalia Filgueiras's mother, Camila Corteleti, confirmed to US media that her daughter had died in the crash.
Corteleti told the New York Times: "She loved the freedom. It was completely different seeing the world from the top."
Filgueiras had spoken of her pride at receiving her pilot's licence while still a senior in high school in an interview with a local affiliate of CBS News in 2023.
"I like being different than everyone," she said. "Some people think that it's weird that I can fly planes but I can't drive a car - I mean, I can, but a lot of people think it's funny."
A spokesperson for East Coast Jets, where pilot Jeff Gregory used to work, said: "We are deeply saddened to learn that Capt Jeff Gregory was among those who lost their lives in yesterday's tragic aviation accident in Palm Beach."
He was married with two children, US media report.

article:
These firms you've never heard of are feeding fears the AI bubble could burst

These firms you've never heard of are feeding fears the AI bubble could burst
- Published
A once-obscure corner of the AI ecosystem finds itself in the spotlight – and investors don't all like what they see.
Names like CoreWeave and Nebius are familiar to the tech set in San Francisco and Silicon Valley.
These data centre companies, known as neocloud firms, run large warehouses packed with expensive computers, which they lease to major AI developers like Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta.
They're now the subject of one of Silicon Valley's most heated debates.
Many question whether neocloud firms are financially sound and what their recent stumbles tell us about the state of the AI economy.
Analysts at Gartner predict by 2030, 80% of neocloud firms will "cease independent operations", while Forrester's experts expect at least three of them to be imminently acquired "as finances get shaky".
On Thursday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent tried to downplay recent concerns about neocloud firms, calling them "a small component of the overall ecosystem, external" on CNBC.
Debt worries
Neocloud firms often finance themselves by signing long-term lease contracts with major tech customers who need quick access to computing power.
Firms can then borrow money using those contracts – plus the AI chips they purchase – as collateral, explained analyst Cory Johnson of "The Quiet Period" IPO research outfit.
He said debt is common across neocloud firms because the hardware has to be paid for up front.
Take the industry leader: CoreWeave. It's a fraction of the size of some of the Big Tech companies it serves.
But Johnson believes lenders sometimes consider the creditworthiness of CoreWeave's customers, like Microsoft or Meta, more than the company's when they lend.
"This helps explain how CoreWeave accumulated $35.1bn (£26.3bn) in debt," he said.
Some jittery investors appear to be having second thoughts.
CoreWeave stock has lost a quarter of its value over the past month, and it's not alone.
Shares in other neocloud firms like Nebius, IREN, and Applied Digital have all shed about that much if not more during the same period.
Debt investors also appear spooked, and are demanding ever-higher returns from several firms in the sector.
CoreWeave's CEO Mike Intrator has said that the market is acting "irrationally" and has expressed confidence in its business model. Some of the world's most consequential companies are queuing up for CoreWeave's infrastructure and other AI services.
Origins in crypto
Several neocloud firms have their roots in the volatile crypto mining industry, made of companies that generate cryptocurrencies, like Bitcoin.
Crypto miners use some of the same kind of physical infrastructure that is used to develop AI.
CoreWeave was founded in 2017 with a focus on mining Ethereum.
IREN, Core Scientific and Applied Digital also started in crypto mining.
Their infrastructure left them well-positioned when AI exploded in 2022 with the introduction of OpenAI's ChatGPT.
One outlier is Nebius, which was known as Yandex NV when it was part of Russia's version of Google before splitting off and changing its name in 2024.
Now, the success of these firms hinges on the fate of major AI developers and hyperscalers – even larger data centre operators which neocloud firms often count as key customers.
"There is just an enormous amount of spending getting injected into the system," said Melissa Otto, head of Visible Alpha Research at S&P Global. "It's an arms race."
And neoclouds have benefitted.
But the trade-off of their model is "greater financial risk" in the face of change, said Forrester VP and principal analyst Charlie Dai.
That includes any adjustments that their Big Tech customers might make to their spending plans.
This past week, when Microsoft and Google forecast less AI spending than Wall Street analysts had projected, shares in several neocloud firms tumbled.
Much is also riding on Anthropic and OpenAI, which are both expected to start selling shares to the public in the months ahead.
If AI proves to be a bubble – and bursts – neocloud firms "are definitely going to face collateral damage," said Bradley Tusk of Tusk Ventures.
'Guppy-level death'
The future of the neoclouds also depend on their ability to keep borrowing, which gets more expensive as interest rates rise.
In a recent social media post, Elon Musk suggested this challenge could lead more than 200 neoclouds to "see guppy-level death and consolidation", with the smallest firms being the most vulnerable.
"Some will make it through, but not many," he added.
For now, analysts at Yorkville Ives said demand for computing power still exceeds supply, adding that neoclouds are filling an important gap that larger data centre companies cannot fill.
But to some, the neocloud sector's recent wobbles are concerning.
Microsoft recently cancelled a deal with a British neocloud outfit called Nscale amid power supply issues which could last through to 2030.
Australia's Firmus just shelved plans to start selling shares to the public.
These developments come amid a public backlash against data centres and questions about how much value AI can add to worker productivity.
"There's reason to worry," said Johnson.

article:
'I was too worried to use the bus before training'

'I was too worried to use the bus before training'
- Published
"My parents are really proud of how far I've come," says Zak, who has a learning disability and can can now travel to college independently thanks to a training programme.
He is one of a growing number of teenagers receiving one-to-one support to help them use public transport to get to their place of study.
"I was really worried about crowding and [thinking] what if the bus is late or it's cancelled," says 16-year-old Eloise, who has autism.
"I struggled with my confidence getting on the bus," she said. "I was unsure about my route and how to get to the bus stop."
Earlier this year, Wiltshire Council voted to reduce the amount it spends on private taxi transfers for 16-19-year-olds with SEND, meaning more young people would have to rely on carers or public transport.
It was hoped the change would save the council £400,000 a year.
But it also expanded its travel training programmes, so more teenagers could learn the skills to use public transport independently.

Zoe Rankin, who leads the Intensive Travel Training programme, said: "For some, the alternative really now is to ask for that parental support and that's not always a viable option for families.
"But it also doesn't give the young person the chance to explore their own independence."
During the last academic year, the scheme supported four young people. Since expanding in September, 18 teenagers have been through the programme, with 21 more due to follow.
Zak, 18, received help when he was at secondary school.
"I'm not a big people person. My concern was the bus being really busy," he said.
He now travels to college by himself, and has learned to drive, making his parents proud.
The trainers take the bus with the young people to and from college, until they feel safe and confident to travel by themselves.
For some, they will be met at their front door by a trainer who will show them to a bus stop, help with understanding timetables, tickets, and how to ask for help if something goes wrong.
All of the young people have an Education, Health and Care Plan (EHCP) due to having autism, Asperger's or a learning or sensory disability.
"The young people we're working with are very vulnerable," said Rankin. "The speed at which our young people learn and process means they are not always able to see things in a clear way."
Building confidence
Sixteen-year-old Deanna said: "I used to feel nervous because of the other people on the bus."
She was taught how to make her journey to college by herself, and said one day she would like to use the bus to socialise in her spare time.
Rankin said often learning to travel without a parent or carer can open up confidence in other areas of the young person's life.
"You meet someone and they can barely say hello and are facing so many challenges. It's a massive transformation and it's wonderful to see."
Local authorities are not legally obligated to provide free or subsidised transport to education settings for children after they are 16, and as councils face budget pressures, many are reducing what they offer.
Swindon Council has consulted on reducing its provision.
Wiltshire Council's Community Connecting services run a range of travel training options, including helping young people to move safely as pedestrians in rural areas.
"There's noise, busy-ness, lots of people, changing weather," says the scheme's manager Marnie Kemp.
She said the changes to post-16 SEND transport provision were worrying for some parents, but that it could give some young people the chance to increase their independence.
"The council have seen the value of what we're doing," she said. "If that means there's less of a need for other services, that's a wonderful byproduct".

article:
Celebrity loses injunction bid but will stay anonymous pending appeal

Celebrity loses injunction bid but will stay anonymous pending appeal
- Published
A celebrity who asked the High Court to permanently prevent two news organisations from publishing his identity and allegations of sexual misconduct has lost his case, with the court saying the man's claim for an injunction was denied.
But the judge Mr Justice Nicklin said a temporary injunction preventing the man from being named and the allegations published should remain in place, in order to allow the celebrity to appeal against the judgment, with anonymity and reporting restrictions remaining in force during the period allowed for any appeal.
ITN and the Guardian have said they believe it is in the public interest to publish allegations that the man abused his status to attempt or attempt to engage in "inappropriate sexual activities with a large number of girls and young women".
The man, who denies the allegations, said any publication would be "highly likely" to lead him to kill himself, and that the court should prevent any publication or broadcast.
In a judgment on Tuesday, Nicklin rejected the injunction request and said in a summary of his ruling: "The claimant's claim for an injunction was dismissed.
"The court did not determine whether the allegations, or any of them, were true, and the dismissal of the claim does not amount to approval of any publication the defendants may decide to make."
He added that the man will remain anonymous to allow any appeal to be lodged.
During a two-day trial last week, the court heard that the man denies abusing "his power and position as a celebrity to contact and forge relationships with young women and teenagers to try to have sex with them".
The celebrity's lawyers told the court that his high suicide risk was not because of any wrongdoing, but because of the fear of "trial by media".
Sara Mansoori KC, representing the man, told the court that any publication "would have a potentially fatal impact".
The barrister told the court: "The only reason they would not be fatal is because the claimant would be locked up and prevented from his desire to end his life."
She said the man had made a suicide attempt after receiving letters from ITN and Guardian News and Media (GNM) asking for his response to the allegations, and later absconded from hospital and attempted suicide for a second time.
She added in written submissions: "This is not a case where an individual has spuriously raised 'mental health' concerns in the face of an impending publication that they do not wish to occur.
"The claimant has attempted suicide twice as a result of these matters, been hospitalised for months, been the subject of involuntary detention and been examined by multiple - now more than 10 - doctors."
Mansoori also said the man "has no intention of returning to public life".
Gavin Millar KC, for ITN and GNM, said in written submissions that "numerous allegations" had been gathered during "a wide-ranging and rigorous investigation" and that there was a "strong" public interest in publishing them.
He said reporters had spoken to more than 100 people, and that the resulting allegations "indicated a pattern of behaviour".
Millar later said many of the women "have been traumatised by the claimant's alleged conduct and have suffered mental health crises and mental illness as a result".
He argued that while the state may have a responsibility to protect life, applying that principle to this case would require the state to intervene in "lawful journalistic activities" to prevent "an autonomous act by the claimant himself".
A medical report carried out for the court said inpatient treatment could provide "significant, but not complete mitigation of the risk", but that treatment, perhaps for months, had "a realistic potential to reduce the risk".

article:
Google value plunges by $500bn as its own AI search hits ad sales

Google value plunges by $500bn as its own AI search hits ad sales
- Published
Google-owner Alphabet lost just over $500bn (£374bn) in value on Thursday after it revealed its own artificial intelligence (AI) summaries were hitting search advertising revenue.
Chief business officer Philipp Schindler said Google's "AI mode", where it answers questions conversationally, was eating into the money it makes from ads which appear next to results to traditional search questions.
Yet, Schindler said he felt "very good about our trajectory" with an AI-focused version of the search engine.
Google's role in answering the world's questions has been challenged by the AI boom, with millions of people using programs such as ChatGPT and Claude instead.
Kim Scott, who formerly led Google's advertising business, told the BBC's Today programme that the company would "rather eat its own lunch than allow someone else to eat their lunch" by having its own AI summaries hit its search revenue.
She said that Google was founded on the idea of making long-term bets on technology – even if they hurt the firm in the short term.
"I think they're making a long-term bet on AI," she said.
In its results published on Wednesday, Alphabet revealed that total revenue grew 25% in the three months to the end of September, compared to the same period last year, hitting $127.6bn.
However, the firm did not make as much money as analysts had predicted, particularly in its advertising arm, which spooked many investors.
Shares in the company plummeted over 12% to a six-month low following the release of the results.
By the end of Thursday, the company's total stock market value had fallen to $3.46 trillion from $3.97 trillion the day before.
Tracy Woo, a principal analyst at Forrester, said Alphabet's disappointing Search business results "highlights the challenge of funding massive AI investments while maintaining the strength of established businesses."
Amazon shares hit
Microsoft and Amazon also issued updates this week, and joined Google in plans to keep spending huge sums of cash in the ongoing AI race.
But investors appeared dismayed at the impacts these plans are having on the ability of each to keep growing their core lines of business.
Amazon's stock took a hit on Thursday , with its shares falling 6% in after-hours trading.
Alongside quarterly sales growth of 11%, hitting $201bn, the company shared a staggering cash flow figure of negative $42bn.
That number shows that Amazon is not only spending more money than it makes, but that spending has increased six-fold over the span of three months.
Chief executive Andy Jassy claimed the business was spending in part because it had the chance at, not one, but two businesses that could end up bringing in $1 trillion for Amazon the future.
Jassy noted that Amazon's cloud services business, as well as retail stores, may be those businesses. During a call with financial analysts he also repeatedly mentioned the financial opportunity presented by Amazon making and selling its own computer chips, as well as its AI developer platform Bedrock, which offers paying users access to most major AI models and tools.
"One of the lessons we've learned over 20-plus years is that there is not one tool to rule the world," Jassy said. "People always assume whatever is in the lead early on will be the only thing that people use - it's never true."
As Jassy was asked several times to explain the company's spending, he admitted it "would be more convenient" if it were spread over the next 25 years. "That's not the world we live in," he added.
"We can fund this plan, and I think it will forever change the size, the revenue, the free cash flow of Amazon."
Microsoft cuts AI spend
Wall Street's reaction to Microsoft's update was more muted, with shares falling by less than 1% on Thursday.
The company, which is also one of OpenAI's largest investors, spent around $5bn less on investments dedicated to AI. It also revealed earlier this week plans to cut thousands of workers, which will further reduce the company's costs.
Meanwhile, its revenue grew 19% from a year earlier, hitting $92.3bn for the quarter. Its crucial cloud business grew by 30% to $63bn.
Chief executive Satya Nadella said the use of Copilot, Microsoft's AI chatbot and tool, has seen "automated tasks nearly double since July" as daily users grew by 500% from a year ago.
Usually lower spending and growing sales earns a positive reaction from investors.
But Woo said Wall Street is trying to look farther into the future when it comes to which businesses will truly make good on their big promises around AI.
"Microsoft's results reinforce that enterprise demand for AI remains strong, but they also highlight a much bigger question facing the technology industry, where AI value will ultimately be captured," Woo said.

article:
City of London chief tops UK Black Powerlist

City of London chief tops UK Black Powerlist
- Published
Ian Thomas, chief executive of the City of London Corporation, has been named the UK's most influential Black Briton in this year's Black Powerlist awards.
The 57-year old is the first Black person to oversee the Square Mile's governing body in its more than 900-year history.
The City of London Corporation is an administrative body with responsibility for London's central financial district, headed by its own Lord Mayor.
Thomas tops the 2027 Black Powerlist, which recognises the most powerful people of African and Caribbean heritage in the UK.
The award body said he was "a respected public-service leader with over 30 years' experience in local government".
Other influential names in this year's top ten include entrepreneurs Emma Grede and Steven Bartlett, as well as actor and filmmaker Sir Idris Elba.
Comedian Sir Lenny Henry has also been recognised, with a Lifetime Achievement award, for co-founding Comic Relief, which has raised over £1.6bn since 1985.
Now in its 21st year, the Black Powerlist celebrates people who have broken through barriers to reach leadership roles, thereby inspiring future generations.
"It exists to show young people of African and Caribbean heritage what is possible, in fields they might never have considered," said Michael Eboda, the list's publisher.
Thomas said he secured the role at the head of the City of London Corporation in 2022 only following seven interviews and an election.
'When I started my journey in public service, I never, ever thought, [not] in a million years, that I'd be recognised in this way," he told the BBC.
'Discipline and respect'
As chief executive, he oversees around 5,000 staff with responsibilities including the City of London Police, 11,000 acres of open spaces such as Epping Forest and Hampstead Heath, and advocacy for the UK's financial and professional services sector.
Thomas was born in Sheffield to parents who made the city their home after leaving Jamaica as part of the Windrush generation.
"They worked incredibly hard and instilled that sense of discipline and respect, and that's the core of how I do business," he said of his upbringing.
Growing up, Thomas aspired to be a footballer and took part in trials alongside Alan Shearer.
Reflecting on his own change of direction, Thomas joked it was about "following dreams and if they don't come true… there's always something else".
Before joining the City of London Corporation, Thomas served as chief executive of the Royal Borough of Kingston upon Thames where he oversaw public services and a £1.2bn regeneration programme.
He was appointed a CBE in the 2019 New Year Honours in the wake of the Rotherham Abuse scandal for transforming children's services during his time as strategic director for children and young people at Rotherham Metropolitan Borough Council.
Thomas replaces last year's incumbent, Afua Kyei, the Bank of England's chief financial officer and executive director, and is joined on this year's list by Comfort Ero, the President and chief executive of the International Crisis Group, who takes second place.

article:
US strikes Iranian island ahead of midterm elections

US strikes Iranian island ahead of midterm elections
- Published
The US has carried out strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, US officials have told CBS, the BBC's US partner.
The officials described the strikes as limited and defensive, and said they were in response to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) firing on a US aircraft.
Iranian state news agency Irna reported explosions on Qeshm on Monday. The IRGC did not comment but said its forces had shot down two US MQM-170 drones south of the island and a US MQ-9 drone east of the Strait of Hormuz.
The US military has not commented on the strikes, which came as mediators stepped up their efforts to prevent a return to all-out war after the US midterm elections on Tuesday.
Trump has been facing falling polling numbers and pressure from within his Republican Party to end the war, which began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in February.
Earlier on Monday, the president told reporters that he was in "no rush" to ramp up strikes on Iran.
"One way or the other, we will do something, but there is no rush. We crippled them financially," he told news outlet Axios. "They have no money, no gasoline and their people are getting very tired of it."
He also said the US "might need to go after Pickaxe [Mountain]", an underground site linked to Iran's nuclear programme, in an interview with Fox News on the eve of the midterms.
This was "not a big deal" and could be done in "one hour", Trump added.
There has been mounting speculation in the last few days that the US may resume significant strikes in Iran again after the midterms. But asked by a reporter on Monday if that was the case, Trump said "no".
Meanwhile, the Associated Press cited two regional officials as saying that, during a weekend phone call, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had pushed Trump for another wave of strikes on Iran following the midterms.
On Tuesday, Iran's chief negotiator with the US, parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, stated: "The ball is now in America's court to prevent war."
"Just as the Islamic Republic of Iran stands ready for battle with its finger on the trigger, it has also given the American side a powerful and rational response," he said in a televised speech.
It was not immediately clear what Ghalibaf was referring to, but Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Irna on Monday that "very intensive" talks to try to end the war were under way with the US via Qatari and Pakistani mediators.
Qatar's foreign ministry spokesman said on Tuesday that both sides were "reviewing the ideas and proposals we have presented" and that it remained hopeful of a deal being agreed.
"Both parties remain committed to the negotiation process... We are facilitating the real-time exchange of proposals between them," Majed al-Ansari told reporters in Doha.
Last week, Iranian negotiators discussed with mediators a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days once the US met its seven conditions. They reportedly include lifting a naval blockade of Iranian ports and releasing frozen Iranian assets.
The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and the US naval blockade.
The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.
Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.
To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz.

article:
University of Cambridge scientist among those who died in Spanish train crash

Cambridge scientist dies in Spanish train crash
- Published
An award-winning University of Cambridge researcher died in the Spanish train disaster while on her way to collect a prize for scientific excellence.
Dr Marta Shahbazi was travelling to an awards ceremony on Wednesday when the train she was on crashed into another near Urda, south of Madrid, killing 69 people.
The mother of two was an affiliate associate professor leading a group of researchers at MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB) in Cambridge and had earned several awards for work on human embryos and cell biology.
In a statement, the LMB paid tribute to the "inspiring, talented and passionate scientist" and described her death as a "profound shock and a huge loss".
The expert in cell biology ran the Shahbazi Laboratory at the LMB, based on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus.
She had been announced as the winner of a Spanish Society for Developmental Biology award for her contributions to the study of early human development and was due to collect the award at a conference in El Rompido in Andalusia.
The LMB said: "As a wife and mother of two young children, Marta wrote eloquently about balancing her family and career, serving as a much-admired role model for a 'mother scientist', a term she used to describe herself.
"Marta was an inspiring, talented and passionate scientist whose research shed light on the earliest steps in the development of human embryos and how errors occur that lead to failed pregnancies," the LMB said.
The institute said her death was "a profound shock and a huge loss for LMB".
Her work had been recognised with "many awards and prizes", the laboratory added.
Shahbazi is listed on the University of Cambridge website as a principal investigator at its Stem Cell Institute (CSCI).
Institute director Prof Bertie Gottgens said its community was "shocked and deeply saddened" by her death.
"Marta led her primary research group at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB) alongside her roles as an affiliate principal investigator and affiliate assistant professor at the CSCI," he said.
"Across both institutes, she was highly respected for her pioneering research on early human development and valued for her collaborative spirit.
"Her creativity, passion, and generosity will be greatly missed."
The news of her death was first confirmed in a social media post, external by the CiMUS, based in Santiago de Compostela where Shahbazi's aunt works.
Shahbazi undertook her PhD at the Spanish National Cancer Research Centre, before joining the University of Cambridge as a post-doctoral fellow and then the LMB in 2020.
The crash in Spain happened when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of a stationary train operated by the Iryo company.
It is one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013.
Three days of national mourning were declared in the country.
More than 540 people were on board both trains.

Work finishes at rail junction near power plant
- Published
Work to improve a rail junction near a new nuclear power plant has finished.
The upgrades to the Saxmundham junction on the east Suffolk line were carried out over nine days.
Network Rail said the manually operated junction needed to be replaced with a powered system, along with the installation of modern railway equipment, in order to improve freight services to the Sizewell C construction site.
It would help improve "operational flexibility and railway performance" across the route, a spokesperson said.
The construction of Sizewell C on the Suffolk coast officially got under way in 2024, two years after the government granted permission for the project.
The rail junction connects the Leiston branch line to the east Suffolk line.
Sizewell C managers have already committed to transporting 60% of bulk construction materials by rail or sea.
Buses replaced trains while the works were carried out and Network Rail has thanked passengers for putting up with any disruption.

article:
Proposal for free bus service scrapped

Proposal for free bus service scrapped
- Published
Proposals for a free bus service in Guernsey will no longer be considered for next year's budget, deputies who suggested the move have said.
Deputies Sally Rochester and Ross Le Brun put the plan forward as an amendment to the 2027 budget, asking the Policy and Resources Committee for £1.9m to "enable the existing public transport service" to be made free of charge in a one-year pilot.
They have now pulled the plans after "concern from [operator] Stagecoach" that increased passenger numbers could mean certain routes not coping with the additional demand.
Rochester said she and Le Brun were committed to working with the Environment and Infrastructure Committee to explore plans for the future.
Rochester also acknowledged the pilot would not be possible if buses were "at capacity".
Speaking to BBC Radio Guernsey, she said: "This amendment was all about supporting those in our community that are facing cost of living challenges.
"It was about delivering the transport strategy so you could have access to a free bus service - make their lives easier, make their lives better.
"Now we're not going to be able to do that if the bus service is at capacity."
She said the "logical conclusion is that we would need more buses" while Stagecoach's contract "would need to be expanded" to provide the additional capacity.
Rochester said these elements are "what we'll be looking into and hopefully bringing this back some time in the future".
'High demand'
A spokesperson for Stagecoach said it welcomed "any initiative that encourages more people to use public transport and recognise the potential benefits of making bus travel more accessible".
But it said it was important that "any proposal to introduce free bus travel is carefully considered to ensure that sufficient capacity is available across the network to accommodate the additional passenger demand such a scheme could generate".
The company added: "Our priority is to ensure that bus services remain reliable, accessible and able to meet the needs of all passengers, particularly on routes that already experience high levels of demand."
The proposal was one of 30 changes put forward to next year's budget, scheduled for consideration on Tuesday.
Other amendments put forward include efforts to secure money for States' committees faced with budget cuts, attempts to freeze fuel duty and cuts to overseas aid.

article:
Government making up China policy as it goes along, say MPs

Government making up China policy as it goes along, say MPs
- Published
The government has failed to deliver on its promise to pursue a consistent approach towards China and is instead making up policy "as it goes along", MPs on the business committee have said.
The committee said in its report, external that decision-making had been characterised by "inconsistency" and was heightening national security risks.
It called on ministers to block the transfer of sensitive data to China, give businesses clear rules for doing trade with the super power and ban imports made using forced labour.
The business department said it disagreed with the report's conclusion adding: "Our approach to China is consistent - we will co-operate where we can and challenge where we must."
"We have placed our relationship on a more stable, balanced, long-term footing, and based it on a clear-eyed assessment of both the opportunities and the risks.
"Our trade strategy makes clear that we will capitalise on every opportunity to grow our economy while never compromising on our national security, and our increased discussions with China allows us to directly raise concerns where they arise."
Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer had sought to pursue a closer relationship with China, arguing that the UK could not afford to ignore economic opportunities, while insisting that should not mean compromising on national security.
However, efforts to build ties were criticised by some MPs concerned about China's alleged spying activities in the UK.
An audit of the two countries' relationship was carried out last year , externalbut the government has not published the document in full, saying it contained classified information.
Sir Keir's successor Andy Burnham has yet to set out his position on relations with China.
In its report, the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee said successive governments had "failed to reassure" the public they had taken "adequate measures to defend UK national security and economic resilience".
The MPs said the unpredictability of government approaches and a lack of clear guidance had hindered businesses ability to trade with China.
It proposed setting up "red" and "green" zones to clearly defining where trade and investment would be encouraged and the areas which were "off limits".
The committee said that the government should insist on fair trade with China and advised preparing tariffs that could be imposed if the country continued to subsidise its industry or failed to offer "fully reciprocal" market access.
On protecting sensitive technology and data, the report said there should be a ban on connected technology devices being used in critical national infrastructure.
The committee said "low-cost" Chinese connected technology had become wide-spread in the UK and that in this area the government had "prioritised diplomatic politeness over the UK's national security".
Universities should also get "faster advice" on conducting research with Chinese bodies, it said.
Committee chair and Labour MP Liam Byrne said: "Britain's businesses cannot plan for the future when the government keeps making up its China policy as it goes along.
"Ministers promised clarity and consistency. Instead, we have opportunities missed, risks unmanaged and decisions left until the eleventh hour.
"Britain must shape its own relationship with China, or risk having that relationship shaped for us in Washington or Beijing."

article:
Musk pumps $446m into US midterms, as campaign spending set to 'shatter' records

Musk pumps $446m into US midterms, as campaign spending set to 'shatter' records
- Published
The US midterms campaign is set to be the most expensive on record - with the total cost projected to reach nearly $12bn (£9bn), according to Open Secrets, an independent organisation that tracks campaign finance.
Most of the spending is driven by outside political groups - known as Super Political Action Committees (Super Pacs) - pouring large sums of money into some key races ahead of election day on 3 November.
The top individual donor is billionaire businessman Elon Musk, who has spent almost half a billion dollars backing Republican candidates, particularly in Texas where many of his companies are based.
BBC Verify has looked into the figures and where the money was spent.
How much has been spent?
There are rules on how much people, parties and political action committees (Pacs) can give directly to candidates.
But Super Pacs can accept unlimited contributions from individuals, corporations, labour unions, and other political committees. They can't give that money directly to candidates but they can spend it supporting them indirectly.
According to the latest Federal Election Commission, external (FEC) filings which run to mid-October, more than $9.5bn had been spent in this midterms cycle.
Pacs and Super Pacs make up more than half of that - at about $5.5bn - with their spending in the last couple of months almost doubling.
Candidates, parties and outside groups have to report their spending to the FEC, but the full totals won't be available until after the midterm elections.
However, Open Secrets has projected the total will be $11.9bn based on trends in past cycles.
This would be about 30% more than what was spent during the last midterm elections in 2022.
Which donors have spent the most?
The top 40 donors gave $2.4bn up until 14 October, according to the liberal-leaning think tank Brennan Center for Justice, external, which is a record high for that point in a midterms cycle.
"Spending in the 2026 midterms is shattering records, with more of the money coming from the wealthiest donors and groups this election," says Michael Beckel, a US campaign finance expert.
As well as individuals, organisations can also give to Pacs. For example, Geosor Corp and Fund for Policy Reform, both founded by the billionaire financier George Soros, have given a combined $102m to liberal groups.
Aside from Soros, former New York City mayor and businessman Michael Bloomberg has been the biggest Democratic donor, giving more than $60m.
Several billionaires including Jeff Yass, who runs one of the world's largest trading firms, and Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein, the owners of a US business supply company, have given over $100m this campaign to Republican causes, according to FEC filings.
But Musk has given by far the most of any individual, donating almost half a billion dollars as of October.
Musk has given most of this to a Super Pac he set up in 2024 called America PAC, as well as to the Republican-aligned Senate Leadership Fund.
Most of his money has been spent on the Texas Senate race, supporting Republican candidate Ken Paxton, who is running against Democratic candidate James Talarico.
America PAC's investments in the Texas race total more than $45m. It has also invested around $10m into both of the Senate races in Michigan and Ohio.
"Crypto companies have also been very active this cycle, with Ripple and Coinbase combining to give $63 million to fund Super Pacs promoting the crypto industry's interests," says Brendan J Glavin of Open Secrets.
What has the money been spent on?
Campaigns and political groups spend money trying to reach voters in a variety of ways - including hiring staff to do on-the-ground voter outreach and hosting campaign events like rallies. They also spend money to conduct internal polling.
However, the majority of funds are spent on advertising - especially on TV.
In this cycle, $11.15bn has been spent on advertising up until the end of October, according to ad tracking firm AdImpact, external.
"Traditional broadcast television remains the top beneficiary of advertising expenditures, though expenditures on digital ads continue to increase," says Beckel.
Similarly to Musk's spending, AdImpact tracked that most of the money has been spent on advertising in the Senate races in Michigan, Texas and Ohio, followed by Iowa and Maine.

article:
Mother told to book appointment to give birth to baby who had died

Mother told to book appointment to give birth to baby who had died
- Published
Warning: This article contains themes and images some readers may find upsetting.
A seven-month pregnant woman whose unborn baby died after she was discharged from hospital while suffering from a life-threatening condition was told by staff to make an appointment to give birth.
Danielle Brown, 31, from North Tyneside, said she was devastated to have to return home knowing the baby she was carrying was no longer alive.
She said no family should be put through the same experience and wants hospitals to offer alternatives for those grieving.
After she was discharged from hospital suffering with pre-eclampsia, Danielle insisted on returning to the maternity unit as she felt so unwell and was seen by doctors.
She was told her daughter had died but, instead of delivering the baby, the hospital sent her home and told her to ring to book a slot to give birth.
Her partner Anthony Miller, 34, described it as "horrible... lying in bed and holding that belly" knowing their baby was not alive.
The Newcastle Hospitals NHS Trust said it fully accepted "aspects of the care we provided fell short" and offered a "heartfelt apology".
Danielle and Anthony had been delighted to learn they were having a baby girl, who they decided to call Maisie.
"I was just over the moon, I couldn't be happier," Anthony said.
But in February 2023, seven months into her pregnancy, Danielle woke up feeling unwell.
Her face was swollen, as were her hands and feet - all potential signs of pre-eclampsia, external, which can be life threatening to both mother and baby.
The couple went to the Northumbria Specialist Emergency Care Hospital in Cramlington, Northumberland, but medics found problems with Maisie's heart rate and told Danielle her baby needed to be delivered immediately via emergency caesarean section, external.
"Maisie's heart rate had dropped and a midwife ran in and said 'don't panic, but I need to pull the emergency cord - you're having your baby'," Danielle said.
The midwife told her space was being found for her at the Royal Victoria Infirmary (RVI) in Newcastle and doctors there "were going to do the section", she said.
She was transferred by ambulance but, once in Newcastle, Danielle did not have the operation and was instead put on a ward.
"A consultant came to see me and he said I am staying in hospital until Maisie was born," she said.
But, the following day, another doctor reviewed her and sent her home.
Within 24 hours, again feeling unwell, Danielle called the maternity unit and said she was told she probably had a stomach bug. But she insisted on being seen.
"When I finally had a scan, the screen was turned away and there was no sound," Danielle said. She remembers turning to her partner and saying: "I think she's gone."
Doctors were unable to find Maisie's heartbeat and they told Danielle her baby had died.
But instead of delivering the baby, as she expected, Danielle was given a phone number, and sent home. She said they told her to "give us a call on Friday morning, and book a slot to come in and have Maisie".
At home the couple struggled to cope.
"It was horrible," Anthony said. "Lying in bed and holding that belly, and still being able to feel Maisie but knowing she wasn't alive."
Two days later, after 10 hours in labour, Danielle gave birth.
"When Maisie was born the room was silent," she said. "Seeing Maisie was bittersweet. She was perfect. I told her she was beautiful and I loved her.
"It was devastating that my first experience of holding a baby was holding my stillborn daughter."
Speaking publicly for the first time about what happened, Danielle said no-one should be sent home still carrying a baby who has died.
"Don't," she said. "Just take that family and help them. Help them.
"When we left hospital, we gave Maisie one last cuddle and kiss and told her we loved her and were sorry things couldn't have been different."
After saying goodbye to their daughter, the couple faced further distress. To leave the hospital they had to walk past other parents holding their babies.
"We should have been leaving with our baby too, but we were leaving with a memory box," Danielle said.
"All the new mums were walking out carrying their babies. That will stay with me forever."
The couple want every hospital in the UK to provide an alternative way out for grieving mothers, to "make a different route for a parent who has just lost a child".
The trust's executive director of nursing and midwifery, Ian Joy, said: "We fully accept that aspects of the care we provided fell short of the standards the family had every right to expect and offer a heartfelt apology for this.
"Following a detailed review in 2023, we improved urgent assessment for women who come to our maternity services with unexpected symptoms or suspected complications and introduced quicker escalation procedures when there are concerns."
Legal executive Faisal Ali, from the law firm Irwin Mitchell, said pre‑eclampsia could be life‑threatening without appropriate care.
"What happened to Danielle and Maisie vividly highlights the human cost of care failings," he said.
"The trust admitted Danielle should not have been discharged on either the 14th or 15th of February 2023. Had she remained in hospital, monitoring would have shown the need to speed up delivery and Maisie would have been born alive."
An NHS England spokesperson said: "These failings in care are unacceptable and should never have happened.
"Anyone experiencing the loss of a baby should be fully supported by a specialist maternity team so they can make choices about their care that are right for them."

Reform UK councillor charged with rape and sexual assault

Reform UK councillor charged with rape and sexual assault
- Published
The leader of Reform UK in Hampshire has been charged with 35 offences against four victims over a 13 year period, including 12 counts of rape.
The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said it had charged George Madgwick with the offences, which it said took place between 2008 and 2021 in Portsmouth and Wales.
It said the 37-year-old faced charges including rape, sexual assault, controlling or coercive behaviour, and making indecent images of a child against four victims - who were aged 16 and 17 at the time.
Reform UK said Madgwick had been suspended "with immediate effect". He is due to appear at Portsmouth Magistrates' Court on 25 November.
Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary said its investigation into Madgwick began on 24 July 2025, after receiving a report of a sexual offence.
The force said it first arrested him on 6 January 2026, before he was charged by the CPS on Tuesday.
In total, Madgwick, who is from the the Anchorage Park area of Portsmouth, has been charged with 12 counts of rape, two counts of assault by penetration and two of sexual assault.
Madgwick has also been charged with two counts of making indecent images of children, two of controlling or coercive behaviour and eight of assault occasioning actual bodily harm.
He faces one charge each of causing or inciting sexual exploitation of a child, distributing an indecent image of a child, stalking, making threats to kill, false imprisonment, theft and criminal damage.
A spokesperson for the CPS said: "Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence and that it is in the public interest to bring the case to court.
"We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are now active and that he has the right to a fair trial. There should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information which could in any way prejudice these proceedings."
The 37-year-old councillor represents North East Havant on Hampshire County Council and Paulsgrove on Portsmouth City Council.
Last month, he was featured in the the ITV News Exposure documentary Undercover: A Year In Reform - after which he accused the broadcaster of "electoral interference".
In the programme, he was featured voicing support for the Portsmouth Patriots anti-immigration group.
He subsequently issued a statement saying the undercover reporters potentially had an "impact on the result" of council elections.

article:
Many Cubans voted for Trump - now they're turning on Republican immigration policies

Many Cubans voted for Trump - now they're turning on Republican immigration policies
- Published
Since the Trump administration launched its crackdown on undocumented immigrants two years ago, the waiting room of Cuban-born immigration lawyer, Ismael Labrador, in Miami is never empty. His appointment book is packed with relatives of detained immigrants trying to secure their release before they're deported back to their countries of origin.
Although business is booming, Labrador wishes it wasn't.
"We have relatives living in fear right now, we've had relatives who have been deported back to Cuba, unfortunately," he explains.
Cubans have traditionally enjoyed favoured immigration status in the United States under provisions enshrined in 1960s-era legislation called the Cuban Adjustment Act. But widespread arrests across Florida by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents have left the Cuban American community more vulnerable in the US than they'd ever imagined, says Labrador.
"The way I put it is that if you don't have a Green Card in the United States, you may be a target."
Countless mobile phone videos have recorded such arrests in places previously considered off-limits: parents detained outside schoolyards, at bus stops, youth sporting events and even inside courthouses at pre-arranged immigration hearings.
Few have had the impact of the footage of 39-year-old Ecuadorean immigrant, Grace Calero, and her 19-year-old daughter, Giulianna Carriel, being arrested in a hospital ward.
Two months ago, the pair were driving to work in Kissimmee, central Florida when they were hit by another car and taken to hospital in an ambulance. While they were being treated for their injuries, ICE agents burst in and arrested them. They were deported back to Ecuador within days.
Labrador's cousin has also been caught up in the dragnet of ICE detentions. Despite his best efforts, the immigration lawyer was unable to prevent his own relative from being deported back to Cuba.
"It's hard when you're fighting against a lot of resources," he laments.
The Trump administration has repeatedly said the president was elected on a promise to deliver mass deportations and is delivering on that. "He stopped the invasion of our country and as a result of his policies more than 3 million illegal aliens have left the US," a White House spokeswoman told the BBC last week.
ICE, meanwhile, has said it is targeting anyone who has broken American immigration law and is in the country illegally.
Labrador was among the 68% of Cuban Americans in Florida who voted for Donald Trump two years ago, a decision he roundly regrets today.
Few could accuse Trump of hiding his plans on immigration. On the campaign trail in 2024, he touted his policy of mass deportations of undocumented migrants.
"On Day One, I will launch the largest deportation programme in American history", he said repeatedly at rallies, including in Florida.
Labrador – and many thousands of disillusioned Latino voters like him – thought the administration would only deport people with criminal records.
"I think we got blindsided by the administration," he argues.
"Personally, I voted for Trump because I wanted to get criminals out of the country," he says, alleging that "communists came in from Cuba under Biden."
"We wanted to have a safe America. We never thought that he was going to go after everybody."
"This isn't what I voted for," he insists.
Labrador is far from the only Cuban American in Florida to experience buyer's remorse over President Trump.
Congresswoman Maria Elvira Salazar, who represents Florida's 27th Congressional district, recently released a video filmed outside the White House in which she distanced herself from his deportation policy saying it had gone "too far".
"The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today," she said, addressing President Trump.
Salazar is locked in a tight race against another Cuban American, the Democratic Party's candidate, Eliott Rodríguez. Her close association with Trump on immigration could potentially cost Salazar her congressional seat.
Florida remains a Trump stronghold. At a recent gathering of Cuban American entrepreneurs in Miami, the atmosphere remained staunchly pro-Trump. "Miami loves Trump, Cuban Americans love Trump," says real estate businessman, Juan Omar Sixto, motioning at the other guests behind him.
"They agree with Trump that anyone who crossed the border illegally should be out," he says, despite acknowledging he illegally entered the US himself six decades earlier.
A poll released on Thursday, external by Florida International University found that not all South Florida Cubans agree - 76% said they disapprove of the Trump administration's deportations of Cubans with no criminal record. But their support for the Republican Party remains steadfast, with 68% saying they plan to vote Republican in November.
In other parts of the country, support amongst Latinos is declining.
In the last election, Trump beat Kamala Harris by 56.1% to 43% - the biggest margin of victory for a candidate in the state since 1988 - in part because of the support of Latino communities. But a recent NBC News/Telemundo poll of 8,000 registered Latino voters showed nearly 60% favour seeing Congress come under Democratic Party control to just 35% wanting a Republican victory.
The high cost of living is a big factor for people's discontent, as residents feel supermarket and petrol prices are impossibly high for working families.
But for many Hispanics, it's also partly because of stories like Heydi Sanchez's.
Sanchez left Cuba in 2019 as the island spiralled into economic collapse and illegally crossed the border from Mexico into the US. After nine months in a detention centre, she was released under an i-220B Order of Supervision which grants the right to remain in the US but carries the constant threat of deportation.
Sanchez settled in Tampa where she worked with autistic children and the elderly. After a complex and expensive fertility struggle, she and her husband had a baby girl called Kailyn.
Most i-220B holders try to normalise their immigration status via 'humanitarian parole' and must check in with ICE agents at regular scheduled appointments. Last year, President Trump revoked temporary humanitarian parole to about 300,000 Cubans. Sanchez knew something was wrong in her case when her regular ICE meeting was brought forward without warning.
At the appointment, she was detained. Kailyn was taken from her arms and passed to her father, a US citizen. Within a day, Sanchez was on a deportation flight back to Havana in shackles with no recourse to appeal.
I met her in Cuba where she now lives in a one-bed apartment in Mayabeque, a rural province outside Havana.
"It's like the sky fell in and crushed me", she says of being separated from her daughter.
"When we have video calls, she says: 'Mummy, come home.' And I say: 'darling, Mummy is away working.' What else can I tell her? How can I explain it?'", Sanchez asks, unable to hold back the tears.
Despite expressions of support from several US politicians, including Maria Elvira Salazar, more than a year has passed since her deportation and Sanchez remains in limbo in Cuba.
In a statement, ICE said that "in this case, the parent stated they wanted to be removed without the child and left the child in the care of a safe relative in the United States".
While the Trump Administration has rolled back Cubans' special immigration privileges, it has sent thousands of people back to an island Washington itself describes as a "failed state". Cuba is in the grip of its worst ever energy crisis amid a months-long fuel blockade imposed by the US.
Since overwhelmingly voting for Trump in 2024, Cubans in Florida now realise they are just as vulnerable to deportation as any other diaspora. His Republican colleagues may feel the brunt of their frustration at the ballot box.

No10 defends flight to Manchester to collect Andy Burnham

No10 defends flight to Manchester to collect Andy Burnham
- Published
Downing Street has defended sending the official UK government plane to Manchester to pick up Andy Burnham, rather than the prime minister travelling to London in advance of the flight.
The Airbus A321neo departed London Stansted Airport for Saint John's, the capital of Antigua and Barbuda, at about 06:00 on Monday without the prime minister on board.
Half an hour later it landed in Manchester to collect Burnham, before taking off again to cross the Atlantic for the Commonwealth heads of government summit (Chogm).
The trip sparked a backlash on social media with some questioning the value for money, but Number 10 said security, cost and "operational requirements" were all factored in.
The official UK government plane, carrying the registration G-GBNI, is often used by British prime ministers and royals for overseas trips.
Flight tracking data shows the jet made a 35 minute flight on Monday morning to Manchester, where it spent an hour and a half on the tarmac, before taking off at 08:00 to head to St John's.
In response, Tory MP and shadow cabinet minister Neil O'Brien accused Labour of managing to "waste taxpayers' money and jet fuel so they can posture".
"You have to pay through the nose for energy and fuel to pursue their Net Zero obsession... But when it's them, the rules are different," he added.
Asked why Burnham had not travelled to London instead, his official spokesperson told reporters: "The prime minister's travel arrangements reflect where he was carrying out official government business at the end of last week.
"As you know, he spent the day in Scotland on Friday; returned to Manchester to work from Number 10 North on Friday evening."
Burnham will meet Commonwealth leaders on Tuesday, coming at the end of the King's Caribbean tour, with the prime minister saying he is "open" to the possibility of the UK formally apologising for its role in slavery.
It is unclear how much the London to Manchester trip cost, or whether there is a precedent for it, as the Cabinet Office's transparency data for the plane only lists overseas trips.
None of Burnham's trips are listed yet, as the data is published quarterly.
The latest data for April to June 2026 shows then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer made four round trips on the jet, including a £121,000 trip to Armenia with 21 officials for the European Political Community Summit.
A trip from the UK to Paris in April cost £39,000.
The precise cost of each flight can depend on how many officials were with the prime minister, fuel costs and other factors such as landing fees.
It is also unclear whether transporting the prime minister, his security detail and officials by train or road transport from Manchester to Stansted would have been much cheaper.
A previous version of the UK government official plane, an RAF Voyager, was given a £900,000 repaint job in 2020 before being replaced with a different plane.

article:
Burnham's Number 10 North goes on multi-million pound hiring spree

Burnham's Number 10 North goes on multi-million pound hiring spree
- Published
Andy Burnham's Number 10 North has gone on a multi-million pound hiring spree with dozens of new jobs being advertised.
The office in Manchester, set up by the prime minister in July, has launched 50 external job adverts, including a "rewiring the state deputy director".
It is the latest sign of how pivotal the government outpost - designed as a sister office to London's Downing Street - may prove to Burnham's aim to devolve power across the country.
Government sources say the roles will be paid for out of existing budgets.
The new recruits "will work with mayors and councils to identify barriers holding places back", but the Conservatives have described the office as a "gimmick".
There will be no redundancies elsewehere in the civil service as a result of the hiring spree, the BBC has been told, with some jobs expected to be relocated and other vacant roles closed.
The new roles, all based in Manchester, cover areas including strategy, communications, engagement, private office and policy.
BBC News has calculated they total up to £2.8m for basic salaries alone, excluding employer pension contributions in the civil service of 28.97%.
No10 North now has 120 members of staff, nearly half of the 280 staff who work in No10 London.
Among the highest paid of the roles are a "rewiring the state deputy director", with a salary band of £86,000 to £117,000, who will "lead the Rewiring the State Unit... shaping the government's approach to devolution across departments".
The government said it was launching a recruitment campaign for staff who would "bring fresh perspectives and knowledge of the places they serve, moving decisions closer to the people they affect".
No10 North "is driving the most significant transfer of power out of Westminster in a generation," the government added in a statement.
Some apprenticeships and secondments are also being advertised.
It comes as the government confirmed on Friday that No10 North would move from its current temporary home in Heron House, on Manchester's Albert Square, to a new government office on First Street in spring 2027.
No10 North will share the city centre building with other government departments spanning business, education, local government and the Cabinet Office.
Burnham made opening No10 North one of his first acts as prime minister, describing it as "the nerve-centre of a rewired Britain" that would help bring growth to more areas of Britain.
No10 North's deputy director Duncan Parish said in a speech last week that officials faced "institutional challenges" with delivering on these aims and called for a "mindset shift" across the UK's central government.
Conservative Party deputy leader Alex Burghart said: "He [Burnham] promised to streamline the civil service, but now he is hiring extra staff and, once again, won't say where the money is coming from.
"Manchesterism is just more bureaucracy at taxpayers' expense."
Meanwhile, Tory shadow cabinet minister Mike Wood has said there is "so little transparency" around No10 North after ministers told him they could not reveal figures on headcounts and office attendance.
According to the new job adverts, the Office for the Prime Minister - with exceptions for certain roles - expects No10 staff to be in the office a minimum of 60% of the time.
Since opening, No10 North has hosted summits of regional mayors, at least two of which have been partly held as video calls on Microsoft Teams. At one of these meetings, ministers unveiled controversial powers for mayors in England to charge new fees on visitors' overnight stays.
It has also hosted an education summit of school leaders and Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin met Burnham for the first time as PM at No10 North in September.

'We grew up around this historic Delhi mosque - now we have been forced out'

'We grew up around this historic Delhi mosque - now we have been forced out'
- Published
In the heart of Delhi, a short distance from the Indian prime minister's residence, a small mosque stands amid piles of rubble. Its pale walls and pointed arches remain intact, its courtyard still lined with green-and-white tiles.
But the people who gave life to the place are gone.
Mohammad Wasim, 50, points across the rubble to the spot where his house once stood.
"My father was married there, and, decades later, so was my daughter," says Wasim, a driver.
Wasim and his family were among hundreds of people who lived around the mosque in a patchwork of modest homes tucked between military compounds, exclusive clubs and sprawling bungalows in Race Course, one of the Indian capital's wealthiest and most heavily guarded neighbourhoods. Many of them had lived here for generations, working as drivers, cleaners and gardeners in the wealthy houses around them.
On 7 October, the authorities demolished their houses across three settlements, saying they had been built illegally on government land. They also raised security concerns because of the houses' proximity to military installations. Some 717 families were relocated to Savda Ghevra, a colony nearly 31 miles away, on the city's outskirts.
Residents had challenged the evictions in the Delhi High Court, arguing that moving so far from their jobs, schools and communities would upend their lives. But in August, the court allowed the relocation, accepting the government's security concerns and noting that alternative housing had been provided.
Only the mosque and a nearby Hindu temple were left standing. But their water and electricity supplies were cut off that day, and access to the compound has since been restricted. Worshippers are generally turned away at the gates, though some are occasionally allowed through after pleading with guards.
The government says it owns the land on which the mosque stands, but mosque authorities say it was registered in 1977 as waqf property - land or buildings set aside under Islamic law for religious or charitable purposes - and is listed, external as a heritage structure. The Delhi Waqf Board says it is nearly 300 years old, though other estimates put its age at 125-150 years.
The board has written to the authorities seeking restoration of the mosque's water and electricity and raising concerns about its future. Separately, a worshipper has petitioned the high court over restrictions on prayers and fears that the mosque could be demolished.
1 of 5
On 29 October, the government told the court it would take no action against the mosque for four weeks while considering the board's objections. It opposed restoring access for prayers, citing safety concerns during demolition work, a position disputed by the worshippers' lawyer. The court declined to intervene and scheduled another hearing for 16 December.
While the mosque's future remains uncertain, for Hindus and Muslims who lived around it for generations, the question now is what can be salvaged of the lives they built there.
Wasim still returns to the mosque to pray when he can, though guards sometimes turn him away. On a recent afternoon, he was among just four or five worshippers inside. A generator chugged loudly outside, supplying electricity after the power had been cut off.
"Our hearts and entire lives are tied to this place," he says. "How can we let it go, when our childhood was spent playing here?"
Rekha, a widow, remembers the colony with longing. She washed dishes in nearby homes, raised her family and performed seva (voluntary service) at the local temple.
To her, the word rehabilitation seems painfully inadequate: "How can a life built over decades be uprooted and planted somewhere else?" she asks.
Since the move, she has lost the work she depended on. Her 19-year-old son is struggling to find a job. She has been allotted a third-floor apartment but climbing stairs is painful because of a metal rod in her leg after an operation.
"I may have a house but my home was snatched away."
Critics say these experiences are part of a longer history of displacement in Delhi, where working-class communities have repeatedly been pushed, external to the city's distant edges because they lack documents proving legal ownership of land they have lived on for decades.
"Relocation disconnects them from both jobs and networks, resulting in livelihood and income loss," urban researcher Mukta Naik told the BBC.
As families scatter in search of work, she says, the informal support systems they once relied on become harder to rebuild.
"This leaves families to fend for themselves," she says.
The Delhi government's housing agency, the local municipal council and the central government's land office did not respond to requests for comment.
Savda Ghevra was established in 2006 on farmland near Delhi's border with Haryana state, to house families displaced from elsewhere in the city.
The first arrivals found little more than bare plots, without roads, running water or electricity. Over time, they built homes, opened shops and fought for basic services. By the early 2020s, an estimated 50,000 people lived here, external, having made a neighbourhood out of a place they had little choice but to inhabit.
Now the families from Race Course have begun the same slow work.
They have traded the lush tree-lined avenues of central Delhi for rows of nearly identical concrete blocks, with open fields stretching beyond. Life is going on, but much of what sustained these families remains on the other side of the city.
Every day, Babloo leaves home at 5am to take his children by metro to their old school in central Delhi, changing trains three times along the way. He waits out the six hours until classes finish at a tea stall outside his former neighbourhood. When he has work his wife makes the journey.
Their new home is too far away, he says, to return between the school runs. By the time the family reaches Savda Ghevra, it is around 4pm.
Babloo once worked at a club in Race Course. He has now found work in Meerut, a town to the north-east of Delhi. Residents knew they might have to leave, he says, but they hoped they would be relocated somewhere close enough to continue their jobs and their children's schooling.
The government says suitable apartments were unavailable closer to Race Course. In court, it cited Savda Ghevra's schools, dispensaries and transport links as evidence that the area could accommodate the displaced families.
But the presence of these facilities offers little reassurance to Naeem Khan, 63. His two grandsons have hearing and speech disabilities and need specialised care and schooling that he says are unavailable in the area.
The move has also scattered Naeem's family. One son and a divorced daughter share his tiny one-room apartment, while his two other sons had to move elsewhere due to lack of space.
"We have been thrown 20 years backward," he says.
The distance has been especially costly for women. Naik says childcare responsibilities, transport costs and safety concerns make long commutes to work particularly difficult for them.
At Race Course, the wealth surrounding the settlements offered small but vital ways to earn money - dishes to wash, gardens to tend, discarded bottles to collect and sell.
Akhtari, an elderly widow, collected mineral-water bottles for about 100 rupees (about $1.05; £0.80) a day and dried leftover rotis, or flatbreads, to sell as cattle feed.
Now even these modest sources of income have disappeared.
"Everyone living here was evicted; everyone is poor, broken, and struggling themselves," Akhtari says. "Who will hire someone else for housework?"
At Race Course, when she had nothing, the mosque's imam or a neighbour might give her money for flour. Her neighbours checked on her. In the new apartment, she has a roof over her head, but few people to fall back on.
She has begun to worry about what will happen if she falls ill.
"If I collapse and die inside, no one will even know," she says. " Hopefully someone will break down the door and find me."

'Siesta a day' credited for woman's long life

Woman's 'siesta a day' credited for long life
- Published
A woman whose "siesta a day" is credited as her secret to a long and happy life has celebrated her 105th birthday.
Dora Horsfall, who was born on 2 November 1921, was joined by family earlier as she marked her special day at Flowers Manor Care Home in Chippenham, Wiltshire.
Describing her grandmother Dora as a "beautiful soul" who "likes to sleep", Mandy Cheeseman said: "I think that could be why she's so preserved, because she has a siesta every day, even when we were little ones."
Dora said the "the great thing" from her birthday celebrations had been "rejoicing" with her loved ones.

Violinist Sue Lord played songs such as Danny Boy in the morning, before the birthday group gathered for afternoon tea later in the day.
After everyone had sung Happy Birthday to her, Horsfall thanked them for coming to the "very nice" celebrations.
Born in London, Dora and her brother Jack were sent to West London District boarding school. The facility looked after children who were orphaned, abandoned or - as in the siblings' case - living in poverty.
The family then moved to Salisbury when Dora was 13.
Dora later decided to return to the capital where she met her husband Reg, who she married in Croydon on 23 December 1941.
Soon after, the couple moved back to Salisbury, where Dora had various jobs including as a bus conductor - also known as a clippy - and in production at one of the secret Spitfire aircraft factories.
Reg and Dora would later move to Spain, where they lived up until his death.
Dora, who has two daughters, seven grandchildren, nine great grandchildren and four great great grandchildren, moved to Flowers Manor Care Home in 2022.
Describing her grandmother as her "favourite person" and "magic", Cheeseman said: "I wish I could be half the lady she is."
"She's fun, she's got a wicked laugh," she added.
Her family said whenever Dora was asked her age, she would often respond: "I am the same age as my little finger and slightly older than my teeth."
Dora also credits elastic as the most exciting invention of her lifetime "because it was used in knickers" and they "hadn't perfected" underwear before then.
She added: "Sometimes it [underwear] fell down so you had to quickly pick them up and put them in your handbag!"
