Budget 2026: Key points at a glance

Budget 2026: Key points at a glance
- Published
Chancellor John Healey has set out the government's tax and spending plans in his Budget – the first since Andy Burnham became prime minister.
Here is a summary of the main points.
- One-off £100 payment for up to 20 million households in council tax bands A-D in England to help deal with rising energy bills, with equivalent funding for Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
- Standing charges – fixed daily fees customers pay regardless of usage – to be removed from household gas bills in England, Scotland and Wales, with costs added to the unit rate instead
- VAT cut on electricity bills extended to July
- A green levy - the Gas Shipper Obligation to fund hydrogen projects - to be removed from energy bills and put on to general taxation
- Freeze on fuel duty extended again to July
- Import taxes to be removed on more than 100 food products, including gherkins and marmalade, as well as kerosene and fertilisers
- A 55p per mile tax-free mileage rate for those driving up to 10,000 miles for work made permanent, with the rate rising from 25p per mile to 35p above that distance
- A new scheme taking 25% off electricity bills for 10,000 energy-intensive businesses to launch in April, with payments backdated for energy costs this year
- An extra 2% tax on income from savings and property rental from April
- Amount people can put into tax-free cash Isas (Individual Savings Accounts) to remain at £20,000 a year, with plans to lower the limit to £12,000 for under-65s scrapped
- Surcharge banks pay on their profits to rise from 3% to 6% for 15 months, starting in January
- Threshold at which High Street shops start paying business rates in England to be increased from £12,000 to £18,000, meaning businesses would pay no rates on properties with a rateable value below this level
- Adult games centres and vape shops will no longer qualify for certain business rates relief
- Taxes on gambling machines with stakes over £1 to rise from 20% to 25%
- Online marketplaces like Amazon, eBay and Temu to be made responsible for collecting VAT owed by sellers using their platforms
- New, flat-rate state pension to rise by £488 a year from April – equivalent to 3.9% - under the triple lock policy, with old basic state pension to rise by £374.40
- A new tax-free allowance for low-income pensioners, to ensure those with income up to the value of the full new state pension will not pay income tax
- Legal minimum wage to rise by 3.9% in April
- Unpaid carers will no longer lose their entire Carer's Allowance if they earn more than £204 a week after tax, with a taper rate introduced instead
- Parental pay extended to self-employed fathers and parents in same-sex couples

- A new First Time Buyer ISA to be introduced from April 2029, to replace the Lifetime ISA and help people save a deposit for their first home
- Lifetime ISA holders buying a property above the £450,000 cap will pay a reduced withdrawal charge of 20%, down from 25%
- An extra £1bn for social and affordable housing in England, taking total funding for the 10-year programme to more than £40bn

article:
Chris Mason: Budget needs to go some way towards delivering PM's promises

Chris Mason: Budget needs to go some way towards delivering PM's promises
- Published
Two quotes from the chancellor and the prime minister get to the heart of this Budget.
"The money New Labour had in the 90s is simply not there now… Britain has it harder now," Chancellor John Healey said last month.
And from Andy Burnham, days before he became prime minister: "This change... is the most significant change moment in our politics for 40 years."
So what happens when the economic realities confront the political ambitions of this new government?
As Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS), puts it, external: "We have a relatively new government with seemingly big ambitions but facing a long list of constraints.
"Some of those constraints… are self imposed, others are being worsened by global events, most noticeably war in the Middle East."
Let's be clear, plenty in Westminster in all parties will say that the amount of money around isn't everything – how well taxpayers' money is spent and where it is spent matters too.
And spending less and taxing less, plenty argue, should be a priority.
But in the bones of many in the Labour Party is an instinct that the government, the state, can and should be a vital agent in driving change and improvements in people's lives – a world-view grounded in a sense that governments should proudly step in, rather than one that believes they should get out of the way.
And how do you deliver a proudly proactive state, delivering for people in a noticeable way, when the tax burden is generationally high, the national debt is sky high, energy bills are rising and inflation is higher than expected?
In short: it is not easy.
But ministers argue all of this doesn't mean the government is powerless.
Many are expecting support on the cost of living, and in particular energy bills, to be targeted at the most vulnerable. On the eve of the Budget, Healey said he wants to "start the long-term action needed to get energy costs down for good".
The banks are braced for a levy or surcharge that may pay for this.
There will be an announcement about further spending on defence, but not yet how spending 3% of national income on our security will be delivered by 2030 – that will come in next year's Spending Review.
And one of the prime minister's key ideas - handing power away from Westminster and closer to you, devolution - will be central too.
There will be, the chancellor told BBC Newscast, a "really radical devolution of powers and resources to local leaders that are often better placed to get beyond the departmental systems."
But some at Westminster fret extra money for mayors and others in local government are not yet accompanied by adequate checks and balances to ensure that money is well spent.
The chancellor will argue the economy is becoming more robust – and yes, there are some economic indicators that are more positive than forecast: growth is better than expected, as is productivity and unemployment is down.
But as the Resolution Foundation think tank points out, external: "John Healey's problem is that conflict in the Middle East has once again pushed up energy prices and interest rates.
"So, despite the signs that the UK economy is becoming more resilient, household and public finances are in for another shock."
- Four ways Labour could raise money in the Budget without hiking income tax 
  - Published25 October
- Chris Mason: Jackdaw approved but tricky energy trade-offs remain 
  - Published21 October
In essence, we can expect a smaller Budget this time, compared to some in recent years, when it comes to the scale of tax and spending changes.
The chancellor has been talking up a desire to offer "breathing space" and "hope" - a tacit acknowledgement that there is a limit to what the government can do given the constraints it faces.
It has promised not to raise income tax, national insurance or VAT, a self imposed constraint, as the IFS put it. And there are the international ones beyond its control too.
The big question for many will be whether the Budget is – or can be - big enough to meet the moment? Opposition parties will argue it amounts to tinkering.
Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith argued the public finances are "on a cliff edge" and wants Healey to use the Budget to "take tough decisions, instead of continuing to kick the can down the road".
For the Liberal Democrats, Daisy Cooper warned a "steady as she goes" Budget is "not going to cut it", while Reform UK's Robert Jenrick said the chancellor "can't keep fiddling while the economy burns".
Green Party MP Ellie Chowns wanted a "bold" approach but fears it will be "business as usual".
The government will try to convince you it is one of many moments in the coming weeks and months that will attempt to deliver the scale of change the prime minister has promised.

Fireworks and fancy dress at Derry's 40th Halloween festival

Fireworks and fancy dress at Derry's 40th Halloween festival
- Published
The 40th anniversary of Londonderry's Halloween festival has come to a spectacular close, with a carnival parade and fireworks display lighting up the skies over the River Foyle.
From its humble beginnings in the 1980s, the festival has grown to become what organisers have called Europe's largest Halloween celebration.
This year, Derry marked four decades of the festival with events inspired by folklore, mythology and the traditions of Samhain, the ancient Celtic festival from which Halloween has its roots.
Now a major fixture in the city's calendar, the final day of the festival attracted visitors from around the world, who joined in the celebrations with all of the ghosts, ghouls and goblins.
Saturday's programme featured events across the city and district, culminating in the traditional carnival parade with costumes, floats, music and dance performances.
Thousands of revellers then lined up along the riverfront to watch the dazzling fireworks display to mark the close of the festival's 40th year.
Strabane also hosted trick-or-treat trails, live performances and interactive activities before a fireworks display at the Melvin Sports Complex.
A number of spooky events also took place in neighbouring Artigarvan, Castlederg, and Newtownstewart.
The festival is now promoted across the UK, North America, Europe and Australia, while international broadcasters and media organisations regularly feature Derry Halloween.
In 2015, a USA Today readers' poll named Derry the world's best Halloween destination, while the New York Times later included it in a list of leading spooky-season travel destinations.
About a quarter of the 120,000 people estimated to have attended the festival over the past four days are thought to have travelled from outside Northern Ireland.
Tourism Northern Ireland chief executive Laura McCorry praised the importance of Derry Halloween in attracting visitors to the north west and boosting its economy.
"Tourism is really important for Northern Ireland," she said.
"It supports over 70,000 jobs and currently contributes £1.2bn in revenue to the economy.
"We have ambitions to double [that figure] so events like this provide a much-needed boost for the local economy," McCorry said.
"They give visitors a reason to come here and spend longer in our cities - that's really crucial for Northern Ireland as a whole."
Derry City and Strabane District Council spent about £800,000 on this year's Halloween festival.
Festival and events manager Jacqueline Whoriskey said the last estimate of the economic return was about £7.4m.
"For every pound spent there is a significant return and that's great for the whole area," she said.
Visitors from across the globe
Izzy and Duana arrived in Northern Ireland on Saturday morning from Seattle in the US.
Duana first heard about Derry Halloween last year after seeing a video of the parade on social media.
"We just had to make the trip over and we are loving it," she said.
Closer to home, the Toye family from Derry brought a little Scooby-Doo magic to the celebrations.
Dressed as the Mystery Inc gang, they said they enjoyed a frightfully good night in the city.
The family dress up every year and love going to the carnival.
Their plans tonight included grabbing hot chocolate, a spot of trick-or-treating and watching the fireworks.
Aoife Thomas, the sales manager at Holiday Inn Express in Derry, said guests from around the world stayed at their hotel throughout the week.
She said the hotel staff dress up in colourful costumes every year and have great craic with the international visitors.
Businesses in the city also heard the sound of tills ringing out over screams of terror this Halloween, as many workers got into the spooky spirit during one of their busiest weeks of the year.
Caroline Casey, the store manager at O'Neill's Sportswear, said their shop was transformed into a spooky graveyard, complete with three skeletons - including a mischievous one that interacted with the crowds.
The performance in the upstairs window of the store was created especially for this year's festival, which has the theme "It's in our Bones".
Bar manager Paul Ansell loved seeing all the fantastic costumes throughout the Halloween festival and said his bar had done a roaring trade across the four days, serving drinks to crowds of revellers.
"If you aren't dressed up for Derry Halloween you are the odd one out here," said Ansell, of Castle and Cove Bar on Magazine Street.
"It is brilliant how the whole festival has developed and grown over the years."

Poundland's former owner offers to invest as minister prepares to meet board

Poundland's founder offers to invest in firm
- Published
Poundland's founder has said he would invest in the firm and a government minister said she would meet the firm's board amid its administration fears.
Steve Smith, who set-up the Walsall-based business, said he had attempted to contact owners Gordon Brothers having been "really surprised" to learn about them filing for administration when sales were up 11% on last year.
The BBC understands that Business Minister Kate Dearden will meet with senior Poundland executives later this week to discuss the company's threatened insolvency.
US-based Gordon Brothers said it was evaluating interest for the whole business and formal and indicative offers for significant viable parts of it.
Gordon Brothers, who bought the firm from Polish retail group Pepco last year for £1, has stopped funding the business and rejected a takeover offer from Irish firm Martin Property Group (MPG).
The retailer has given the business until Thursday to find a rescue deal, putting up to 12,000 staff at risk.
It's understood the meeting with Deardon will be predominantly a "fact finding" meeting with government sources conceding there is limited scope for the government to intervene in a commercial transaction albeit one that puts over 10,000 jobs and hundreds of stores at risk.
The meeting was first reported by Sky News.
There is no current meeting planned between the government and executives from current owners, US private equity group Gordon Brothers.
Concerns have been raised that Gordon Brothers have declined an offer from another buyer to keep Poundland afloat in order to ensure repayment of £30 million loan it inherited after buying the company for £1.
More on Poundland
- 'Poundland closure would leave a void in our town' 
  - Published3 days ago
- How Poundland grew from a market stall to a high street giant 
  - Published4 days ago
- Poundland staff protest after chain approach administrators 
  - Published4 days ago
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the government was "ready to support" staff as he also called for answers over why an offer to buy the business had been rejected.
Smith, from Wolverhampton and who set up the firm in 1990 with a store in Burton-upon-Trent, Staffordshire, said he contacted the owners over the last three months but had no reply. He had thought that was good news as he assumed the firm must have had offers on the table.
"And maybe I was a bit too late, but I'd certainly... with talking to the staff and how Poundland's performing at the moment, I'd certainly, if there's an opportunity, I definitely want to put some money back in there."
He said he was still in touch with staff there at levels within the business and "even last week" sales were 11.2 % upon last year.
"Although Poundland made a loss last year, they're going to make a good profit this year, so it's just crazy."
He warned that the two or three thousand suppliers to the firm only worked for Poundland so they would be directly affected by its collapse.
"This is not just about 12, 000 jobs. I'm estimating more like 20 or 30,000 jobs," he added.
The company has 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, and Smith said it had between four and five million customers a week, so with Poundland not being present on high streets would "cause a lot of other retailers to fall as well".
Liam Byrne, chair of the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee and Labour MP for Birmingham Hodge Hill and Solihull North, said he felt the company could be saved and "the whole deal stinks to high heaven right now".
"Because I think the issue that we've got is, you've got an owner that could well be trying to cut and run, to sell a business that is in fact a going concern in order to maximize their own profits and put in jeopardy 12,000 British jobs on the high street."
'Get on the case now'
"Our message today to government and to ministers is, do not leave this to the last minute, which is Thursday... please get on the case now to get everybody around the table to maximize every option to save as much of the business as possible," he added.
In a statement, the board of Poundland Limited said it had been "working on a formal sale process for Poundland" and despite "enormous efforts it had not been possible to identify an acceptable offer for the business as a whole".
"We recognise any sale process creates uncertainty and particularly when set against a challenging UK economic environment."
Gordon Brothers said: "While Martin Property Group had been identified as the preferred bidder by Poundland's management team, attention must now turn to other active bids."
The interest, formal and indicative offers were being evaluated "with a view to minimising uncertainty for Poundland's people and all relevant stakeholders."

Third teen arrested after Halloween party stabbings

Third teen arrested after Halloween party stabbings
- Published
A third teenage boy has been arrested after five teenagers were stabbed at a Halloween party.
Police said they were called shortly after 22:30 GMT on Saturday to Park Road in Chandler's Ford, Hampshire, where an "unknown group" had gained entry to the event.
One 17-year-old boy remains in hospital in a life-threatening condition. The others have been discharged from hospital.
A 16-year-old from Bristol has been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder. He remains in custody, as do two boys arrested on Monday.
Two witnesses told the BBC a fight started after a group came in over a garden fence, although they said the motive for the stabbings was unclear.
One of the teenagers said: "I was [standing] in the hallway near the exit and I saw someone I know pull up their shirt and say 'I've been stabbed'.
"And then I later saw him lying outside the front of the house with someone compressing his wound."
Police cordoned off parts of Park Road and the adjoining Valley Road.
Hampshire Police said officers were continuing to review video footage and information provided by witnesses to piece together the movements of those involved on the night.
Det Ch Insp Elizabeth Pirie, senior investigating officer, said: "I want to thank everyone who has already come forward to speak about what they saw on the night, or share with us any footage they have.
"Our team are working incredibly hard to understand what happened and identify anyone who may have been involved.
"We now have arrested three boys, but we still want to hear from you if you have any information which could assist us. However small it may seem to you, it may be key to our enquiries."
'Extremely distressing'
The force said throughout the coming week, local officers from the Neighbourhood Policing Team are visiting local schools and colleges to offer further advice and reassurance, as well as to support those directly and indirectly affected by this incident.
Ch Insp Rachel Noble, district commander for Eastleigh, said: "The violence witnessed on Saturday night will have undoubtedly been extremely distressing and concerning for everyone who was at the party.
"It is really important to us that everyone knows what support is available for them, should they want to talk about, and how they can report anything to us so the investigation team can continue with their enquiries.
"Local officers will also continue to be out in the area of Park Road, so if you do have any concerns or need to speak about anything then do not hesitate to do so when you see them."

'No nation left behind' says Burnham after meeting first ministers in Glasgow

'No nation left behind' says Burnham after meeting first ministers in Glasgow
- Published
The prime minister has said the UK's four nations must "move together" to devolve more power to regions and cities, following a meeting with the Scottish and Welsh first ministers in Glasgow.
Andy Burnham said he wanted to ensure no nation was "left behind" after the sit-down, which also included representatives from Northern Ireland.
SNP leader John Swinney said he welcomed recognition that "Westminster is not working for Scotland" and pledged to work "constructively and collaboratively" with Burnham, while Plaid Cymru leader Rhun ap Iowerth said the meeting was "positive".
Both first ministers have called for a wider conversation about independence but Burnham has ruled out referendums.
- Scotland 'not like Manchester', Swinney says in dig at PM Burnham 
  - Published17 October
- Burnham invites Swinney to work together on 'deeper Scottish devolution' 
  - Published16 October
- First minister says Budget not serious about Wales ahead of meeting with PM 
  - Published3 days ago
Speaking after the first National Economic Council for the nations in Glasgow, Burnham highlighted plans for devolution at the regional level, saying he wanted to ensure no nation was "left behind".
"It's really important we all move at the same pace together, and I won't allow anything to delay that," the prime minister said.
"Growth can't wait. People need to see improvements in employment and in living standards in all parts of the UK."
Northern Ireland was represented by officials at the meeting amid the political fallout from the Drumcree parade dispute.
Ministers and representatives at the summit discussed handing regions more powers to control employment support and funding for reindustrialisation.
"It's about creating those structures at a regional level and that is matter for Scotland and Wales to decide what that looks like in both countries," Burnham said.
He urged the Scottish and Welsh governments to "work jointly" with the UK government on "a model of deeper devolution".
In the context of reindustrialisation, Burnham added this could be more devolution of innovation funding.
Swinney, ap Iorwerth and Burnham also agreed during the meeting there are too many young people out of work in the nations.
The prime minister said the UK government would look at "arrangements for further devolution of employment support for young people in both Scotland and Wales".
Devolution has been at the heart of Burnham's policy agenda since he took his place in Downing Street this summer.
He claims "rewiring the state" and handing more control to regional mayors and authorities across England will boost economic growth.
The prime minister's devolution at the national level has so far been less clear but Burnham has said he will listen to the administrations' calls for further powers while advocating that they share more responsibilities with local authorities.
'Welcome start'
John Swinney said while he and Burnham disagree on independence, the meeting was "a welcome start" on further devolution.
"When the people of Scotland take issues into their own hands, the best outcomes will about," Scotland's first minister said.
"To that end, I will work constructively and collaboratively with the prime minister to devolve more powers from Westminster to Scotland - as long as those proposals drive economic growth that is felt in higher wages, better jobs, more opportunities for business to start and expand, and support with the cost of living."
A Downing Street spokesperson said the UK government would review issues raised by the first minister but this would not include a second independence referendum in Scotland.
Rhun ap Iowerth said: "I was pleased to meet with the prime minister in Glasgow today where I once again pressed the need for Wales and the Welsh government to have the necessary tools to better serve our communities.
"I also reiterated the point that further devolution within Wales is a matter for the Senedd and only the Senedd."
He added he welcomed the prime minister's "step forward" on the Welsh government's fiscal and borrowing powers and gave his "full support" in pushing for a stronger relationship with the EU.
The prime minister had "positive discussions" with the Welsh leader, Downing Street said.
A spokesperson added: "The first minister of Wales agreed to start a process to explore how each government could contribute to regional empowerment, reindustrialisation and achieving good growth in every postcode."

article:
MP Carla Lockhart quits DUP in Drumcree row

MP Carla Lockhart quits DUP in Drumcree row
- Published
Carla Lockhart has quit the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) in a row over its response to the Drumcree parading dispute.
The MP for Upper Bann had been calling for the party to withdraw Stormont's deputy first minister to force First Minister Michelle O'Neill from their joint office.
Lockhart said she was leaving the DUP on a "point of principle" and would continue in the House of Commons as an independent unionist.
The fall-out comes after unionist anger over Sinn Féin's involvement in protests on Garvaghy Road, which blocked a contentious Orange Order parade from passing along the mainly nationalist street in Portadown, County Armagh.
O'Neill and several other senior Sinn Féin figures have been interviewed by police investigating the demonstrations, with unionists accusing the party of acting unlawfully.
Last week the DUP, which shares power with Sinn Féin in Northern Ireland's devolved government, announced it would block official engagements involving O'Neill in response to the fall-out.
The Sinn Féin vice-president has defended her involvement in the protests, saying it was the "right thing to do".
DUP leader Gavin Robinson stopped short of Lockhart's call to force O'Neill from office.
In an open letter to colleagues last week, Lockhart said it was the "only one credible option" and any kind of "graduated response" would be "insulting to those who have trusted us".
In a statement posted on her Facebook page on Monday, the MP said: "My first responsibility remains to the people of Upper Bann.
"You placed your trust in me, and I will continue to work every bit as hard for you, your family and our community."
Lockhart said it was a "sad day and a deeply personal decision" but her departure from the DUP was "on a point of principle".
"I cannot stand idly by whilst Sinn Féin wilfully ignores the rule of law and the promised profound consequences fail to materialise," she added.
Lockhart concluded that she would "look forward to working with all shades of unionism, elected or not, to advance the cause we love".
In a statement, the DUP said: "We regret Carla Lockhart's decision to resign from the Democratic Unionist Party. We thank her for her service to the party and recognise her work on behalf of the people of Upper Bann.
"The only winner out of further divisions within unionism is Sinn Féin."
It added: "We share the anger felt across unionism at Michelle O'Neill's actions. Our disagreement is over the course of action that will secure accountability and best serve Northern Ireland."
In a statement, Traditional Unionist Voice leader Jim Allister congratulated Lockhart on her decision.
"Having myself resigned from the DUP almost 20 years ago, I know this was not an easy decision. But for honest politicians principle matters more than position.
"The DUP's preference for 'O'Neill Must Stay' caused them to choose Michelle O'Neill over Carla Lockhart. Little wonder their electoral base is deserting them."
Allister added that he looks forward "to working closely with Carla" and said it is "a hopeful day for unionism".
Analysis: Lockhart has been on a collision course for weeks
BBC News NI political editor Enda McClafferty
Cutting links with a party she first joined as a teenager was a big call for Carla Lockhart.
Her family ties to the DUP run deep prompting one colleague to say, "Carla bleeds the DUP".
But not anymore.
She has been on a collision course with the DUP leadership for weeks and now the "profound consequences" are being felt by the party.
Though she had some support within the DUP, she became a lone voice in her battle with the leadership.
She had the backing of Portadown Orangemen and many unionists, but Gavin Robinson crucially had the full support of the DUP officer and assembly teams.
He was able to face down the demands from his Upper Bann MP safe in the knowledge he had the numbers on his side.
Collapsing the executive without a budget agreed and running the risk of his party being blamed for a nurse's pay dispute strike was not a gamble he was willing to take.
But it has come at a cost for Robinson as he has now lost an MP from the DUP benches leaving just four for a party which once boasted ten members of parliament.
It has been a bruising time and one he needs to recover from quickly with just seven months until the assembly election.
The party has lost seats in the last two elections and now its losing seats in between elections.

article:
How do you navigate Halloween with food allergies?

How do you navigate Halloween with food allergies?
- Published
Like a lot of other holidays, food often plays a big part in how people celebrate Halloween, but it can be a more complex to navigate if you have a food allergy - especially if you want to go to parties or take children trick or treating.
How do people with allergies ensure they can take part in the fun and stay safe? And how can you help make sure that everyone is included in the celebrations?
Ciara, 15, is allergic to milk and eggs.
"You have to make sure you read every packet of everything, and you couldn't eat anything until you got home so that you were safe and you were sure of what was happening," she said.
When it comes to Halloween, she said people having more awareness would mean that everyone could be included in the fun.
She says that her friend group really help her by knowing about her allergies and what to do if she was to have a reaction.
Whilst she said it "wasn't easy" or a "particularly enjoyable" thing to do, she taught her group what to do in an emergency situation.
Ciara carries EpiPens. These are adrenaline injections that can help to save people's lives in a serious allergic reaction.
The 15-year-old explained that Halloween can be a bit more difficult to navigate.
She described how a lot of people are helpful and understanding about allergies but sometimes, "there are other people that just don't seem to fully understand the consequences" of what would happen if she was exposed to what she's allergic to.
'Trying to prevent the harm'
Her mum, Claire McGuigan, said she is proud of how well Ciara deals with her allergy.
She explained that parents of children with allergies have all the usual worries but "first and foremost is your allergy".
"As a parent, you carry all that worry and you just hope that they go out and they have a nice time and they come back safe, full of fun, and they can forget about their allergies as much as they can for that night".
"I think having a good circle of friends who understands the allergies is important.
"Trying to prevent the harm rather than relying on the rescue medication is really, really important," she continued.
'Don't let it define you'
Ciara's mum described the emotional burden on families and called for a national conversation about it.
She said people who have children with allergies or have allergies themselves have to do their "best to navigate a whole world that wasn't designed for you".
"I think take your wins everyday that you're safe and that you're happy and don't let it define you. You can be who you want to be," she continued.
She believes that with "a bit of careful planning" children with allergies can feel included.
'Understood but not made to feel different'
Caolán has just turned 11. His mum Colette Donaghy said he does all the "school activities that you could name" and he's "mad into scooting".
Caolán is allergic to nuts, dairy and eggs and has had, in the past, a very serious anaphylactic reaction that resulted in him being in an induced coma in intensive care.
"He has an awareness and a knowledge and probably a risk awareness that many other children of his age wouldn't have," his mum said.
She thinks it's important that children with allergies are "understood" but not made to feel "really different".
When it comes to Halloween, Donaghy explained that when Caolán trick or treats, he waits until the end when all the other children have been given their sweets.
"Then he will explain to the people at the door that he has allergies and there's only certain things he can have. And then, of course, before he would eat anything, we would have to check it," she said.
Donaghy advised giving out individually wrapped sweets to help avoid cross-contamination.
She also suggested looking at alternatives to sweets like fruit or little toys "that don't cost very much".
"There's loads of different options for people and that would take away another layer of anxiety for parents," she said.
Donaghy also explained how some people use teal pumpkins to indicate that a house will offer treats that are suitable for any trick-or-treaters who have any food allergies or intolerances.
Niamh Kennedy has three children who have food allergies and she is the chair of Food Allergy NI. It's a group aiming to build a safer and more inclusive society for everyone affected by food allergies.
She said special occasions are often centred around food.
"For families living with food allergies, these celebrations can bring an extra layer of planning and worry that many people never have to think about."
She explained that "every item may need to be checked and every situation assessed for risk".
How can you make sure everyone's included?
Kennedy suggests that everyone should "think ahead" to consider how they can make celebrations inclusive.
She said this may include "offering non-food alternatives, providing clear ingredient information, communicating with families in advance and being mindful of the risk of cross-contact".
"Being thoughtful and understanding can make a real difference to whether someone feels left out or included in these occasions."

Biggest fibre boost could be scraps in your bin, experts say

Biggest fibre boost could be scraps in your bin, experts say

Eating fruit and vegetable scraps such as peels and stalks could provide a health boost that most of us are missing, say UK researchers, external.
They say scraps are an overlooked source of dietary fibre and are encouraging people to try "root-to-tip" eating, including watermelon rind, pineapple core and butternut squash seeds.
Most adults do not get enough fibre. Official figures, external show only 4% meet the recommended 30g a day, despite its well-known benefits for gut health.
Fibre aids digestion, helps you feel fuller for longer and is linked to a lower risk of heart disease and bowel cancer., external
Stalks, pips and rind on
As a rule of thumb, the skins of fruit and veg pack more fibre than the insides.
Eating a kiwi with the skin on, external provides 50% more fibre than having a peeled one, for example.
For their study, the scientists at King's College London analysed 12 raw or uncooked fresh foods - beetroot, bell pepper, broccoli, butternut squash, cauliflower, celeriac, curly kale, fennel, kiwi fruit, leek, pineapple and watermelon.
They found many discarded parts contained more fibre than the sections people typically eat.
For example:
- watermelon rind contained 2.10g of fibre per 100g – roughly equivalent to the fibre in a slice of wholemeal bread
- butternut squash skin and seeds contained 9.25g per 100g – nearly as much fibre as a bowl of bran flakes
- pineapple skin and core contained five times more fibre than the flesh
- broccoli stalks contained fibre, although a bit less than the florets
Fibre is essential for your gut to work properly and helps prevent constipation.
Project lead Dr Rachel Gibson said the findings suggested people are throwing away a significant amount of fibre.
"This isn't just a nutritional loss, it's also a financial one - you're effectively throwing away a substantial portion of what you've paid for."
Banana peel curry?
King's College London has been experimenting in its canteen, external, offering staff and students root-to-tip meals, such as banana skin curry.
At home, people might want to try leaving skins on kiwi fruit, using broccoli stalks in stir-fries or adding bell pepper seeds to dishes, the researchers suggest.
While cooking can change the fibre content, it doesn't usually destroy it all.
Steaming, microwaving or quick sautéing tends to preserve nutrients best.
Gibson said: "This isn't about perfection and this isn't about forcing people to eat unpalatable food – it's about recognising the nutritional value in components we've been conditioned to discard."
She acknowledges some may be hesitant to try it.
Some diners raised concerns during the canteen trial.
Over the nine-week period, "root-to-tip" dishes made up a third of total daily hot menu sales at the university.
Those choosing the new dishes were less likely to finish their meals than diners eating from the conventional menu.
Kirsten Jackson, a dietitian with the British Dietetic Association who specialises in irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), says the food hacks are useful as long as produce is washed thoroughly.
She suggests blending pineapple cores into smoothies, but says the tough skins are not something she would recommend.
Some stalks may need to be cooked or finely chopped to make them more palatable, she adds.
"Just because a broccoli stalk doesn't fit into tonight's meal doesn't mean it needs to go in the bin. Chop it up, freeze it and add it to a soup or stir-fry another day," she said.
She advises increasing fibre intake gradually to avoid bloating, noting that people who have IBS may find it harder to tolerate.
And there are some things to avoid entirely, said the British Nutrition Foundation.
Green potatoes and rhubarb leaves contain toxic compounds, while tough stalks and seeds may not be suitable for young children.

Police question Steve Wright about unsolved cases

Police question Steve Wright about unsolved cases

Serial killer Steve Wright has been questioned about a series of cold cases but is "not currently a suspect" in any of them, the police have told the BBC.
The 68-year-old was jailed for life in 2008 for the murders of five women in Ipswich between October and December 2006.
In February, he was given a further life sentence after pleading guilty to the kidnap and killing of 17-year-old Victoria Hall, from Trimley St Mary, in September 1999.
Suffolk Police said his admissions prompted the force to consider whether Wright may have been involved in other unsolved disappearances or murders.
"Following his sentencing for the murder of Victoria Hall earlier this year, he has been interviewed in prison about other unsolved cases," a spokesperson said.
"In the cases where we have DNA we have sought to use it to eliminate him from inquiries."
Victoria had left the Bandbox nightclub in Felixstowe with her friend at about 01:00 BST in September 1999, and they went their separate ways at about 02:30.
After being reported missing the next day, her body was found five days later in a ditch 25 miles (40km) away in Creeting St Peter.
Wright was due to stand trial at the Old Bailey in London in February charged with murder and kidnap of Victoria, and of attempting to kidnap 22-year-old Emily Doherty.
However, he unexpectedly changed his plea to guilty, prompting gasps in the courtroom.
Prof David Wilson has suggested Wright may consider coming clean about potential links to other unsolved disappearances.
The prominent criminologist highlighted the cases of Kellie Pratt, 28, last seen in Norwich in 2000, and Amanda Duncan, 26, who went missing in Ipswich in 1993.
Police said they would not provide the details of the cases that officers quizzed Wright on when asked by the BBC.
"He is not currently a declared suspect on any unsolved case, but the potential for his involvement is always considered as we review cold cases," the police added.
The killer's admission to Victoria's murder came as a particular surprise given he has never admitted murdering any of the five women for which he was jailed nearly 20 years ago.
Wright was found guilty of murdering Tania Nicol, 19, Gemma Adams, 25, Anneli Alderton, 24, Paula Clennell, 24, Annette Nicholls, 29, on 21 February 2008.
He was sentenced at Ipswich Crown Court to a whole life order the following day.
The forklift driver, from Erpingham in Norfolk, appealed against the convictions before later deciding to drop the appeal.
The BBC asked police if officers asked Wright to confess to the murders of the five women from Ipswich in light of his guilty plea regarding Victoria.
"He was not asked again about the five murders in 2006 for which he has already been convicted," the police spokesperson responded.

'Fully loaded' All Blacks out to preserve Scotland record

'Fully loaded' All Blacks out to preserve Scotland record

New Zealand assistant Mike Blair says the All Blacks will come to Murrayfield "fully loaded" as they seek to preserve their unbeaten record against Scotland on Saturday.
With recent meetings between the sides decided by single-digit margins, Blair says there is a respect for the threat the Scots will pose in the Nations Championship meeting.
"When I played, New Zealand played their second-string team. They gave guys opportunity against us," he said.
"Times have changed from that. We're fully loaded. We're ready to go."
In 33 attempts and 121 years of trying, Scotland have never beaten the All Blacks, and as desperate as they are to end that barren run, New Zealand are just as keen to protect their unblemished record.
"It's really important," said Blair, who played 85 times for Scotland and was head coach of Edinburgh from 2021 to 2023.
"We've got a couple of long-standing records. The Eden Park record [the All Blacks have not lost a Test there since 1994], every time we play there, there's an extra edge to it because you don't want to be the team that loses that record. It's definitely a huge motivation.
"We're really proud of that record [against Scotland]. We know over the last four matches it's been close, so it's going to be a tough contest for sure."
Having worked under Scotland head coach Gregor Townsend with both Glasgow Warriors and Scotland, Blair retains a strong relationship with his former international team-mate.
"We've been in touch this week," Blair said. "When I was over after the fourth Test [against South Africa], I was over for a couple of weeks and caught up with them and make a point to do that.
"We're just a little bit more cagey around certain things, how we believe the game's developing now and what we can do, because obviously we're up against each other now and I think we play each other before the World Cup as well.
"You need to be aware of certain plays the opposition might do over shape, but you've really got to trust what you're trying to do. I certainly feel like that with attack, you'll make little tweaks in your detail depending on what the defence offer, but if we get our game right then we can impose ourselves.
"So there's a bit of inside knowledge but I don't think it carries a huge amount of weight."
Blair says the squad and staff are still coming to terms with the shock death of the All Blacks head of security, Logan Cadwallader.
Cadwallader passed away suddenly on Sunday following the squad's arrival in Edinburgh, with head coach Rennie saying "we are all devastated".
"It's been a tough couple of days," said Blair.
"Logan was a big part of the All Blacks for 10 years and very close with players and management and obviously a huge, huge shock and it's taken time to deal with."

Election rules for foreign nationals should be reconsidered, MSPs say
- Published
A law allowing foreign nationals with temporary permission to stay in the UK to stand in Scottish elections should be reconsidered, a Holyrood committee has said.
It follows the election in May of Green MSP Q Manivannan, whose visa was due to expire at the end of the year.
The Standards, Procedures and Public Appointments Committee said the "rationale" for allowing people with limited leave to remain and stand for election to councils and Holyrood was "simply not clear".
The Greens said reversing the law change would be a "regrettable backwards step" for Scotland.
MSPs voted to extend candidacy rights for foreign nationals in 2024 as part of wide-ranging reforms, though some have since acknowledged that they did not consider the full implications of the changes.
Critics have argued that the Greens should not have selected a candidate who did not have indefinite leave to remain - an immigration status allowing a successful applicant to live and work in the UK in perpetuity.
- John Cleese urges St Andrews students not to elect Q Manivannan as rector 
  - Published13 October
- MSP apologises for hurt caused by rape 'demonisation' comments 
  - Published10 August
Manivannan, who is originally from India and identifies as non-binary, was elected to Holyrood on the Edinburgh and Lothians East regional list.
At the time, the Green politician was on a student visa.
The MSP confirmed last month that they had been granted a three-year graduate visa - though they are yet to secure leave to remain for the duration of the Holyrood term, due to end in 2031.
"This is my home and I'm not going anywhere," Manivannan said.
Rationale 'not clear'
The rules for foreign nationals are being re-examined by MSPs after ministers tabled the Scottish Local Government Elections (Candidacy Rights of Commonwealth Citizens) Bill.
It is designed to correct an error in earlier legislation that accidentally excluded Commonwealth citizens from extended election candidacy rights.
Committee convener Jenni Minto MSP warned that the new bill risked "entrenching a policy that instead needs looked at again".
She said: "The changes that allowed people with limited leave to remain to stand for election should be reconsidered.
"They appear to have run ahead of what the public want and the rationale for making the change is simply not clear."
MSPs across the chamber voted to reform Scotland's electoral system in 2024, passing the Scottish Elections (Representation and Reform) Bill.
This included new rules on who could stand, how parties are financed and how votes are run.
Crucially, it included permission for foreign nationals without indefinite leave to remain to run for council and Holyrood elections.
Many of the MSPs who voted for the bill, including Minto, have since voiced concerns about that rule.
Another, Conservative MSP Stephen Kerr, said earlier this year that he "took on board" arguments that he and other MSPs had not properly considered the implications of the legislation they passed.
However, he insisted he had particular concerns about Manivannan because the Green was elected while on a visa that is due to expire by the end of the year.
'Backwards step for democracy'
A spokesman for the Scottish Greens said: "There are thousands of people with limited leave to remain who live and work in Scotland and have made a home here, including Commonwealth citizens.
"They should be able to stand for our parliament and councils."
He added: "MSPs backed this change unanimously at the time, including the convener and co-convener of the committee.
"It would be a regrettable backwards step for representation and democracy if Scotland was to roll back on this commitment."

article:
Burnham 'open' to calls for slavery apology but not reparations

Burnham 'open' to calls for slavery apology but not reparations
- Published
Prime Minister Andy Burnham says he is "open" to the possibility of the UK formally apologising for its role in the transatlantic slave trade, but has ruled out financial reparations.
He said he wanted a "dialogue with those affected" and was open to "calls for an apology", but said reparations were "not the right answer".
The statement was welcomed by the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) for Afrikan Reparations, with its chairwoman Bell Ribeiro-Adday telling BBC Radio 4's Today programme the issue was not just about money.
It comes ahead of next week's Commonwealth leaders summit in the Caribbean. As King Charles III tours the region, there have been renewed calls for an apology.
During the first leg of his tour in the Bahamas, the King made reference to the "suffering of the past". Later, in Guyana, he visited the site of a rebellion of enslaved people against British authorities.
On Saturday, Burnham described the transatlantic slave trade, when Africans were trafficked to the Americas, as a "brutal and barbaric violation" and said Britain must "face up to the past".
The British government has never formally apologised for slavery or offered to pay reparations. Burnham has stuck with the policy of his predecessors, and has stopped short of offering any consideration of reparation payments.
"I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part," Burnham wrote in a piece for the Guardian, external.
He said Commonwealth countries had for years been asking for an "honest conversation".
He said he wanted to offer a "structured dialogue", adding: "Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process. I am open to them."
Chancellor John Healey told the BBC that Burnham was "open to a discussion" about an apology because it was "the right thing, particularly ahead of the Commonwealth heads conference".
The Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting starts on 1 November in Antigua, and will be opened by the King as part of his tour.
Speaking to Laura Kuenssberg, Healey said the prime minister does not think reparations are the right approach.
He added that a formal apology doesn't mean British people should now "accept the financial liability for any part in things that happened hundreds of years ago in which they had no role".
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said there was "no reason British taxpayers today should be held financially responsible for things that happened generations before any of us were born."
In a post on X, Badenoch wrote that Labour was "already spending too much on Britain's welfare state, now is not the time for Andy Burnham to be providing global welfare."
Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey said: "I do think we have a duty there and saying sorry is always quite a good thing."
Bell Ribeiro-Addy said that while her parliamentary group welcomed the government's acceptance of the role it played, it had "still fallen short of a formal state apology and that actually costs nothing".
"Acknowledgement is not the same as understanding," she told Today, adding: "Until we apologise, we are never going to be on equal footing… it's meant to be a family of nations - a Commonwealth - and it's simply not the case."
Ribeiro-Addy, who is MP for Clapham and Brixton Hill, said that, to her knowledge, an invoice for financial reparations has not been given to the UK, and so discussing "reparative justice" on those ends, was missing the point.
"My worry is the focus on financial reparations, and I think that is deeply problematic and has not quite listened to what people have said," Ribeiro-Addy said.
Downing Street believes it is in the UK's interest to strengthen the Commonwealth, in a world where China and Russia are seeking to exert influence.
Only this week, President Vladimir Putin hosted a Russia-Africa summit in Moscow.
Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley, who has sought reparations, welcomed Burnham's statement, saying she would engage in good faith while still seeking reparatory justice.
Denis O'Brien, founder of The Repair Campaign, said Burnham's statement was disappointing and did not go far enough.
"The British government must stop obfuscating and give a full and formal apology now," he said.
"This would be a significant and symbolic first step towards reparatory justice."
From the 16th Century, English authorities and the monarchy were prominent participants in the centuries-long slave trade.
Burnham is not first UK prime minister to address the issue.
In 2007, the then PM Tony Blair said the UK's role in the slave trade was a matter of "deep sorrow and regret".
David Cameron ruled out making reparations for Britain's role in the historic slave trade in 2015, urging Caribbean countries to "move on" during a visit to Jamaica.
Rishi Sunak dismissed a call for the government to apologise and pay reparations for the UK's historical role in slavery in 2023 after Bell Ribeiro-Addy asked if he would make a "full and meaningful apology" and "commit to reparatory justice".
Sunak replied with a "no", and said: "Trying to unpick our history is not the right way forward."
In 2024, Sir Keir Starmer ruled out compensation for the UK's historical role in the slave trade.
At the time, he said he wanted to focus on the future of the Commonwealth.
Britain had a key role in ending the trade, through Parliament's passage of a law to abolish slavery in 1833.
As part of that law, British plantation owners were paid for the loss of people they had enslaved.
The UK only finished paying off the debt it incurred to cover the payments in 2015.

article:
James Blunt on Traitors: I tried - and failed - to get banished

James Blunt on Traitors: I tried - and failed - to get banished
- Published
He may have made it to the final episode of this year's Celebrity Traitors, but James Blunt says he did his best to get banished from the show.
The singer-songwriter became a fan favourite for his 1980s leisurewear, outlandish conspiracy theories and military-style approach to tasks.
A dominating presence at the round table, he characterises himself as the "yapping terrier" to actor Michael Sheen's "mature labrador", as they sniffed out the traitors.
Behind the scenes, however, he was playing a different game.
"We all get paid the same, whether you're there for day one or day 23," he tells the BBC.
"So for most of the time, I was trying to... get the hell out of dodge. But no-one was killing me and no-one was banishing me!"
Blunt's cavalier approach informed his gameplay. He knew that outspoken players are often snuffed out first, and that his best bet was to keep a low profile.
"But that's also really boring," he says. "And so for me, I just thought, 'Let's just go around and come up with theories.'
"You don't see it in the edit, but I was telling everyone, 'It doesn't matter [who goes], just kill them all!'
"It's fine, as long as you're apologetic when you get it wrong."
He was wrong more often than he was right. But in the penultimate episode, Blunt and Sheen stumbled on to a theory that the quiet contestants were more suspicious than their outspoken brethren.
In a pivotal round table, they turned their attention towards comedian James Acaster, and picked apart his story of a "murder in plain sight" that had occurred nights earlier.
Caught in the crosshairs, Acaster simply confessed.
"I was made a traitor without wanting to be," he revealed, as the others gasped.
Blunt says there was more to the sequence than viewers realised, hinting that Acaster was caught in a fib about a perfume bottle used in the murderous act.
"He didn't fall on his sword. That's what you saw, that's what you feel, but he didn't.
"You didn't see the full extent of the interrogation. It was heavy in there and it was clear-cut. He was pinned to a post. We got him. We really, really got him.
"I think how that played out hasn't really been revealed to you, but he didn't just say, 'Oh guys, you got me'."
In his exit interview, external, Acaster admitted the round table had been intense, but laughed off his uncloaking.
"It was sprung on me. It was a surprise," he said. "But I was glad that they caught me."
Blunt says the editing of the TV show is crucial to people's understanding of events.
And, with days and days of footage to sift through, not everything that happens makes it to air.
"There are elements [of the show] where I was screaming at the screen for a different reason than you," he laughs. "No matter what really went on in that castle, you're a victim to the edit."
Still, some of his favourite moments made it into the show, including actress and model Jerry Hall calling him "smooth like butter dripping off of hot corn".
"That was a very special one," he laughs. "And she also said, to my face, 'I'll take you home in your wetsuit'".
And what about Blunt's confession that he greased his nipples with butter before every physical task?
"I'm amazed you don't do that yourself, Mark," he shoots back.
In the end, however, he was voted off the show in its dying moments, when comedian Romesh Ranganathan couldn't shake the idea that Blunt was in cahoots with the traitorous Maya Jama.
Blunt maintains he was blindsided by the accusation, but bears no grudges.
"The ending was perfect. It had all the twists and turns. I wouldn't have wanted it any other way."
Still the question remains. If he wasn't that keen to go the distance in the castle, why did he enter in the first place? Was it simply for the experience, or did he simply want to promote his new music?
"I think you may have hit the nail on the head with the latter," he grins.
"I don't think otherwise I would have signed up to be imprisoned in a castle in Scotland."
There's a method in his madness, though.
In Blunt's own estimation, his eighth album, Airplane Mode, is his best work in years.
Now, musicians make that claim all the time. Blunt himself basically told me the same thing about his last album, 2023's Who We Used To Be.
But this time, he might have a point. After years of chasing radio hits and commercial success, he's gone back to writing from the heart.
The results are much more downbeat than you might expect from a man who's renowned for hilarious social media slapdowns and crowd surfing in inflatable dinghies.
Across the album's 12 tracks, he frequently sounds adrift, fretting about the state of the world and wrestling with "monsters in your head that you can't turn off".
"Darkness came like a tidal wave," he sings on the concerningly titled Reason To Die. "I'm paralysed by my body keeping score," he adds, over the portentous drums of Weight of it All.
The lyrics are informed by those negative, late-night thoughts that prey on your mind when you should be sleeping. Blunt says finally acknowledging them was a relief, after years of "trying to write happy upbeat radio singles".
"I don't have a therapist. I write songs as an exercise in voicing nostalgia and melancholy and the things I struggle with in the world.
"And, you know, the person you talk to the most in the world is the voice in your head. That's the truest conversation you're ever going to have, and that's who I was arguing with in the writing of this.
"I was going over the things that all of us struggle with: the burdens of growing up, growing older, having more responsibilities, having bills to pay, not knowing what the state of the world will be next year."
For all of his flippant humour, Blunt's demons are real.
In his 20s, he was an army captain stationed in Pristina during the brutal Kosovo war, and lost several close friends during the conflict.
Even after he left active service and became a successful musician, he was ostracised and ridiculed by his peers. He was later targeted in a tabloid newspaper sex sting, and was one of the many victims of the News of the World phone-hacking scandal.
The honesty of his new music reflects those experiences. And you can hear the rawness in his voice, too.
The musician who once quipped, "I sing like a girl, external", has a new depth to his vocals. On the new song Oh Daisy, there's even a Rod Stewart-esque rasp.
That, he says, is the result of a punishing 21-month tour celebrating the 20th anniversary of his debut album, Back To Bedlam (17.5 million copies sold and counting).
"I really damaged my vocal cords," he says. "I was pushing it too much, and my voice changed as a result.
"I actually now take singing lessons with different people – with an opera singer, even – and the [whole experience] has given my voice a bit of grit.
"Either that or my balls have dropped."
It's a typically self-deprecating jab. If anyone can laugh at themselves, it's James Blunt. And, however dark his new album gets, there's always a silver lining.
"This is not forever," he counsels himself on the closing track. "It's just for now."
"That song's a fist in the air saying, 'Yeah, we will endure'," says Blunt.
"I think I've been around long enough to know that I don't have to prove anything.
"The record label released my greatest hits album a couple of years ago, so if my greatest hits are already out, what am I doing now?
"I'm a guy on his own, writing songs with nothing to prove. That's a pretty good place to be."

Can a photo capture London's cultural appetite?

A world food photography competition, which last year had nearly 9,000 entries from more than 50 countries, has added a new category to capture the diversity of London's culinary delights.
Organisers said they hoped images would be shared "which tell stories of how the city feeds itself - from Michelin-star restaurants to street markets, corner shops, delis, delivery bikes and soup kitchens."
The 'London Museum London Taste' category of the World Food Photography Awards is open to both amateur and professional photographers, wherever they live.
The launch comes as London Museum prepares to open its new home in Smithfield on 28 November, which has been central to London's food history.
The museum is restoring two former market buildings in an area which has been home to a market since medieval times.
London Museum director Sharon Ament said: "At our new home in Smithfield, food and drink will be part of how we tell London's story and bring people together.
"Food is an essential part of our daily lives, it can tell us a lot about people, places, attitudes, trends and values. The grit and glitter of our city."
Caroline Kenyon, founder of the World Food Photography Awards, added: "We want to see images of the people behind the vast and complex food system of the city, from delivery bikes to washer-uppers and chefs, as well as those shopping, cooking and eating."
The awards are open to professional and non-professional photographers, with 27 categories spanning everything from growing and harvesting, cooking and eating, to selling and celebrating.
Entries close on 7 February 2027, with all finalist photographs due to be exhibited at the Mall Galleries in London in May 2027.

El Salvador sends 2,000 troops to Haiti to rescue four missing soldiers

El Salvador has deployed more than 2,000 soldiers to Haiti as part of a mission to retrieve four nationals who went missing in the Caribbean country almost two weeks ago.
The "robust deployment" was communicated by El Salvador President Nayib Bukele to the Prime Minister of Haiti Alix Didier Fils-Aime earlier this week, the foreign ministry of El Salvador said in a statement on Wednesday.
Bukele said the soldiers would also assist ongoing "security efforts against gangs in Haiti", the statement continued.
Tensions between the two central American countries have escalated over the disappearance of the four air force technicians working as part of a UN-backed anti-gang organisation in Haiti.
The four soldiers with the Gang Suppression Force (GSF) were travelling back to their base in an armoured vehicle when they were ambushed in an area of the Caribbean island nation controlled by armed groups called Croix-des-Bouquets.
No gang has so far claimed responsibility.
The Salvadoran foreign ministry said the "large-scale operation" was "supported by various countries and international organisations".
Earlier this week, Haiti handed four bodies over to special forces claiming they belonged to those of the missing servicemen, but Bukele said they did not match.
He said one of the corpses was a child's and another was wearing a different country's military uniform.
Bukele threatened last week in an X post to wipe out Haiti's gangs, saying he will replicate action he has taken in El Salvador, if they did not release the Salvadorans.
In October last year, the UN Security Council approved expanded powers for the GSF to tackle worsening gang violence in Haiti.
The multinational force has struggled to penetrate areas where gangs hold sway. More than 5,700 people were killed in gang-related violence in Haiti this year, the UN says, and armed gangs control much of the capital.
Haiti has been ravaged by gang violence for years, but the situation has worsened in the political vacuum that followed the assassination of President Jovenel Moïse in 2021.

article:
First minister says Welsh spending powers takes step forward after Andy Burnham meeting

First minister says Welsh spending powers takes step forward after Andy Burnham meeting
- Published
Welsh First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth says there has been a "significant step forward" with regards to his country's spending and borrowing powers after meeting the prime minister.
Andy Burnham held a meeting of his National Economic Council with the first ministers of Wales and Scotland on Friday, after which ap Iorwerth said it was a matter of "how and when" a loosening of financial restrictions will take place.
At the summit in Glasgow, Burnham lobbied the government leaders to devolve "deeper" to the regions of Wales and Scotland.
The prime minister said the two first ministers had agreed to work with him on "regional empowerment".
No timescales were announced for changes to Wales' finances.
Friday's meeting followed rows between the Welsh and UK government over the chancellor's Budget on Wednesday, which ap Iorwerth had said was "not serious about Wales".
His party Plaid Cymru said the budget left the Welsh government with a real-terms cut in funding, which the UK government denied.
Ap Iorwerth had set out a range of demands to the prime minister in a letter sent at the start of October.
As well as calling for powers over policing and justice, and for more funding for rail projects, he called for an end to restrictions on access to the Wales reserve - spare funding that the Welsh government can store in one year to use in another.
It is capped at £385m, and the Welsh government can only draw down £137.5m and £55m for resource and capital spend respectively per year.
The Welsh government can also borrow up to £1.1bn for infrastructure, with a limit of £165m a year.
Ap Iorwerth said: "There were some real positives here.
"On fiscal flexibility, the ability for us to use our funding better in Wales, use our reserves better in Wales - and on borrowing powers, I was told clearly that its now was a matter of how and when. That is a significant step forward."
He said there was "clearly an interest" for the prime minister to "really understand that sheer injustice of underfunding of rail in Wales that we have seen for many years".
"That is a particular issue we will be taking forward now between my office and his," he said.
On policing, the first minister said: "I think instinctively the prime minister wants to go there and there's still work to do."
At a speech this month the first minister called for "practical agreement" on how the two governments could work together on the economy, calling for Westminster to avoid duplication in areas that are devolved already to the Welsh government.
Burnham said Friday's meeting was "positive", and that both first ministers had agreed to "work together jointly on regional empowerment in Scotland and Wales as well".
"We now have a process where we have detailed work by officials on both sides to see if we can come to a set of arrangements that are right for Scotland and right for Wales," Burnham said.
"We had a good discussion today on two fronts, one around reindustrialisation and the offer of more devolution of innovation funding to the regional level."
He said it was for Scotland and Wales to decide how that looks.
Burnham also said the UK government will now look at arrangements for further devolution of employment support.
Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock said fiscal flexibilities and borrowing was on the agenda for future Welsh government discussions with No 10 North.
"It is going to take some conversations on how that would work in practice.
"I can't give you a specific time frame as things stand," he said.
Following Wednesday's Budget, which saw an extra £450m announced for Wales over the next three years as well as funding for individual projects, the Welsh government claimed the extra money would represent a real-terms cut to its own finances.
A £30m funding pledge for a new railway station in Cardiff was also described as "an insult" by Wales' transport minister.
On Radio Wales Breakfast on Friday before the summit, ap Iorwerth said there were "paltry sums of money coming on rail, when they've said there's £14bn on the way" and a "real terms cut in the money we have to spend on public services".
"The Budget was not serious about Wales," he said.
He said in another interview he could "only assume that the prime minister is holding something back".
After the meeting, Downing Street said ap Iorwerth had "agreed to start a process to explore how each government could contribute to regional empowerment, reindustrialisation and achieving good growth in every postcode".
"This would be a policy sprint led by No 10 North, involving officials from each government, to take this agenda forward," they said.
Ap Iorwerth said in a statement: "There was an encouraging consensus that the fiscal and borrowing powers which have for so long put Wales at a disadvantage compared with other UK nations must be revised as a matter of urgency.
"I welcome the prime minister's comments that this is now a matter of how and when."
Welsh ministers had called for changes to their borrowing rules and assurances that child poverty payments it wants to introduce would leave recipients' tax and benefits allowances unaffected.
None of that was addressed in the Budget, although Kinnock said "positive" talks were continuing regarding the child poverty payments.
Friday's meeting of the National Economic Council - a summit to help boost the UK economy - was due to be attended by the prime minister and all the devolved leaders.
However, it emerged on Thursday that Northern Ireland's First Minister Michelle O'Neill would not be there after her attendance was blocked by her Democratic Unionist Party (DUP).
Since he became prime minister, Burnham has consistently spoken in favour of devolution.
He has said he is "open" to transferring powers over policing and justice to Wales and, during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, he said he was "ready to make an offer" on the devolution of employment support.

article:
Demands for post-poll justice as Tanzania accused of weaponising counterterrorism laws

Demands for post-poll justice as Tanzania accused of weaponising counterterrorism laws
- Published
Families affected by election-related violence in Tanzania that led to the deaths of at least 500 people a year ago have told the BBC they want justice for those killed in the protests and help with medical expenses for those injured.
"We can no longer afford to pay hospital bills," Meshack Sane, who was shot in the leg, told the BBC.
On the eve of the anniversary of the poll that saw President Samia Suluhu Hassan elected with 98% of the vote, rights group Amnesty International also accused her government of "weaponising counterterrorism laws to silence critics and instil fear".
The opposition dismissed the result as a "mockery" of democracy as Samia's two main challengers were excluded.
Tundu Lissu, the 58-year-old leader of the main opposition Chadema party, had been put on trial for treason ahead of the poll - preventing him from standing.
He had been demanding electoral reforms and a verdict in his case is due next week.
Earlier this week, Lissu went on a hunger strike as he was not being allowed access to his lawyers - an allegation the prison authorities denied.
His lawyer Dickson Matata told the BBC on Wednesday he had now been granted a meeting and would be eating again.
In its statement, Amnesty said it had documented how over the past year security agencies had committed human rights violations with impunity against government critics, opposition supporters, media organisations and dissenting members of the ruling Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM) party.
"Not a single official has been criminally investigated, let alone prosecuted and punished for the excessive force that Tanzanian security forces used against protesters," said Tigere Chagutah, the group's regional director for East and southern Africa
"In fact, the situation has only deteriorated since the crackdown began. In a classic tactic pulled out of the authoritarian playbook, the authorities are increasingly weaponising counterterrorism laws to silence critics and instil fear."
The authorities in the East African nation have repeatedly denied accusations of widespread abuses and say the government is committed to respecting human rights.
Samia, 66, has insisted the election was fair and transparent and blamed foreigners for the unrest, saying it was part of a plot to overthrow her.
Last year, the BBC verified multiple videos of police shooting towards protesters. Footage posted online showed demonstrators being confronted by heavily armed units blocking their progress and firing tear gas to disperse crowds.
The BBC has since spoken to families of some of the victims of the electoral violence, who are still seeking answers.
Many, like Mwajuma Hamisi, have been left destitute. Her husband George Kisivani was shot in the northern city of Arusha on 29 October 2025, the day of the vote, and died two days later.
"I lost my husband, upon whom we, a family with five children, depended. We now have no other source of support. I am left to fight for the family on my own. We have no other assistance," the 32-year-old told the BBC.
She now sells vegetables at a nearby market to support the family - and would like help from the government.
Sane, who shot in the leg in Arusha, has been suffering physically and financially.
The father of three says he has undergone more than five major operations to deal with the gunshot wound. He still needs further surgery but says he can no longer afford treatment.
"We have done everything within our means, but we have reached our limit," the 33-year-old told the BBC.
"The government should look into the situation of those of us who have suffered these tragedies, so that we can receive medical treatment, as some of us are still very sick."
He explained how in the wake of the violence hospitals initially refused to treat injured people.
In the intervening months, his relatives have sought help from local officials and the district commissioner, but he says they were told the government had not allocated a budget for victims of the violence.
The BBC has not independently verified his account of those conversations.
A commission of inquiry's report into the violence was handed to President Samia in April, officially recording 518 deaths.
But Amnesty has criticised the fact that the full report has not yet been made public, saying it "entrenches a culture of secrecy".
The president has since set up another commission to inquiry to identify those behind the violence.
"It is imperative that this new commission comprehensively address the role of security forces in the election-related crackdown," Chagutah said.
The rights group says that between 3 and 17 September 2026, it interviewed 17 people who gave details of a continuing crackdown by the authorities.
Some of them were targeted after demonstrations were called for 7 July to demand democratic reforms and justice for those killed last year.
These marches were banned by the authorities. A 26-year-old man who had expressed support told Amnesty how he was arrested on 24 July in Dar es Salaam and held without charge for 47 days.
He said he was blindfolded by his interrogators who wanted to know who was funding the protests and threatened to kill him.
"On the first day, they didn't give me food. When I asked for water, they urinated on my blindfolded face and said, 'That is the price for those of you opening your mouths to make noise'," he said.
"On the second day, I was taken to Gogoni police station where they beat your legs until they get numb but then insist that you must stand."
The right groups also cites other "acts that may amount to torture... arbitrary arrests, enforced disappearances and abductions".
The authorities did not respond to the BBC's or Amnesty's request for comment.
Many of those who lost relatives a year ago want the government to acknowledge their suffering and address their questions about justice, like 40-year-old Neema Munuo.
She says her grief over the death of her 18-year-old daughter Maria Chami, who had gone out to buy phone credit in Arusha when she was shot, has often left her too distraught to leave the house.
"It is a date I will never forget for the rest of my life, because whenever I recall it, I feel as though I am burning inside," Munuo told the BBC.
This feeling resonates with farmer Juma Nasibu, who lives near the city of Mwanza on the shores of Lake Victoria.
He has not seen his 25-year-old nephew Juma Shabani since the unrest.
The young man had been at a cinema hall in the evening when his uncle later heard unconfirmed reports that he was amongst people rounded up and shot. His family have fruitlessly searched for him at hospitals, police stations and prisons.
"To date, what still pains me is that we were never able to recover the body," Nasibu told the BBC.
