Hundreds of GP practices lose online services after collapse of tech firm

Hundreds of GP practices lose online services after collapse of tech firm
- Published
Patients in many parts of the country have been left unable to access their GP surgery online after a tech firm went into administration.
Silicon Practice ran digital services, including websites, online booking and consultations, for around 500 practices in England – just under 10% of the total.
Practices across the country, including in London, Gloucestershire and Norfolk, have reported problems. Services in Wales are also affected.
GP leaders said the problem would cause huge disruption, given the scale of online booking that now takes places.
Patients in areas that are affected are being advised they will have to make appointments via the phone. The NHS app is working.
Since last year, all practices in England have had to offer online appointment booking. Currently, more than 40% of appointments are made that way.
An NHS England spokesperson said while "the majority" of GP practice websites were running as normal, some using Silicon Practice will be affected.
"If your GP practice website is unavailable and you need help, you should contact your practice by phone or in person as usual."
'Hugely disruptive'
Affected practices have been contacted by NHS England with advice on how to maintain business continuity and minimise the impact on patient care.
Silicon Practice ran the digital tool FootFall, which it advertised as reducing patient phone calls to practices by 30%, by working to "free your reception team from routine admin and manage demand more efficiently. Proven in 1,000+ GP practices across the UK".
Prof Victoria Tzortziou Brown, president of the Royal College of GPs, said: "GP practice websites are an increasingly important way for patients to access care, book appointments and find information about the services available to them.
"When websites are not working, it can be hugely disruptive for patients and place additional pressures on already stretched practice teams.
"It is vital that any disruption to practice websites is addressed promptly to ensure patients are able to access care."
She said affected practices must receive prompt, practical support from NHS England and local NHS organisations to restore their websites, minimise disruption and ensure patients know how to contact their practice and access the care they need in the meantime.

article:
Fighting returns to Kherson region after longest Ukraine war ceasefire

Fighting returns to Kherson region after longest Ukraine war ceasefire
- Published
Fighting has resumed in Ukraine's Kherson after a six-day truce brought quiet to the front-line region for the first time in years.
The ceasefire - the longest since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 - allowed hundreds of people trapped in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky and its surroundings to be evacuated.
On Monday morning, local authorities confirmed that strikes had resumed, saying Moscow had hit a medical facility in Kherson city centre. They also said a 62-year-old woman and a 73-year-old man were injured when a Russian drone attacked the car they were travelling in.
Ukraine also accused Russian forces of using the humanitarian ceasefire to strengthen their military positions, rotate units and deliver ammunition.
"The enemy used the humanitarian pause to set up their positions," said Ukraine's General Staff, adding they had recorded rotation of Russian units, expansion of anti-drone equipment on the roads, and delivery of ammunition.
The Kremlin appeared to corroborate this when spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was "reasonable to assume that the Ukrainian army also used this period for the necessary regrouping".
"It is a completely standard practice in such situations," he added.
The ceasefire had been brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump. Both Kyiv and Moscow thanked her repeatedly, though no details of her involvement were shared.
An unusual show of cooperation came from Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova and her Ukrainian counterpart Dmytro Lubinets. The pair oversaw the ceasefire, travelled into Oleshky and were filmed speaking to residents together. They publicly thanked each other for their work, often highlighting that no violations of the ceasefire had been observed.
Both Lantratova and Lubinets called for the initiative to be repeated elsewhere, and Ukraine repeatedly said it would be prepared to observe similar ceasefires on a national level too.
But many have questioned whether this will lead to more cooperation and further truces.
In fact, the Kremlin swiftly dismissed the idea even as the ceasefire was under way, calling Oleshky "an isolated case" which would not affect the "settlement process" – a euphemism for the stalled peace talks. "There are no similar plans or initiatives," Peskov reiterated on Monday.
And although last week the guns fell silent in Kherson region, elsewhere in Ukraine Russia's air strikes continued, killing scores of civilians and destroying crucial infrastructure.
The decision to observe an unusually broad and comparatively lengthy ceasefire in and around Oleshky was therefore a notable exception.
The ceasefire's observance appears, at least in part, to have been linked to Melania Trump's reported involvement. By violating the truce, Moscow would have risked undermining its own efforts to cultivate the crucial relationship with her husband, US President Donald Trump.
Some commentators have argued that Trump himself would be interested in presenting the Oleshky ceasefire as a foreign policy achievement scored days before the US midterm elections on Tuesday.
"I totally get why our official representatives need to 'play along' with the US first lady on Oleshky," said Artyom Sheynin, a prominent figure on Russian state TV.
"I understand why it's so important to create a 'success story' ahead of the elections for the US president, whose wife 'achieved a ceasefire' in Oleshky."
Kyiv, too, had its reasons to be fully compliant. Although relations with the US and its president are often fraught, Ukraine continues to rely heavily on US intelligence and US-made Patriot air defence missiles to counter Russian aerial attacks. Ahead of another tough winter of war, continued American support is essential to protect Ukrainian skies from Russia's assaults.
But though the ceasefire may have been born out of political calculation rather than purely humanitarian compassion, it also resulted in hundreds of civilians escaping.
There were emotional scenes when hundreds of Oleshky residents arrived in northern Ukraine on Saturday. Many were met by tearful relatives they had not seen in years. To the journalists waiting, the evacuees told of years of hunger and hardship in a destroyed town.
The hundreds of residents who decided to stay behind will receive monthly humanitarian aid deliveries, Lantratova said, adding that decision too was the result of Melania Trump's mediation.
Yet the troop rotations and resupply efforts show that neither side is expecting Oleshky to be a blueprint for lasting respite in the future.
As Kherson came under fire again, Ukrainian drones hit several energy facilities across four Russian regions. In Samara, residents reported hearing explosions and seeing black plumes of smoke rising into the sky as an oil refinery was hit for the fifth time in a month.
If the truce brought a rare moment of relief to Oleshky, it has done little to alter the wider trajectory of a war that grinds on for now.

article:
Supreme Court rejects Trump's request to stop California counting disputed votes

Supreme Court rejects Trump's request to stop California counting disputed votes
- Published
The US Supreme Court has rejected a last-minute request by the Trump administration asking it to intervene in California's midterm election vote count.
The justice department wanted 20,000 ballots to be set aside that it alleged may have been issued to non-US citizens in the state.
Two lower courts had already rejected the request. State election officials had questioned the federal government's claims - saying the process used to identify alleged non-citizens was inaccurate.
The Monday ruling comes on the eve of the midterms, which will determine which political party controls the US Congress for the last two years of President Donald Trump's second term.
The Supreme Court announced its decision in a one-line order, saying it was denying the justice department's request for an injunction.
"The application for injunction pending appeal presented to Justice Kagan and by her referred to the Court is denied," it reads.
Its means rulings made in lower courts will stand and essentially ends the Trump administration's bid to disqualify the ballots.
California is the most populous state in America with some 23 million people on its voting register. As of Sunday night, more than six million mail-in ballots had already been received, according to the California secretary of state's office.
- What are the US midterms? A simple guide 
  - Published5 hours ago
The justice department sent letters to the California secretary of state and Los Angeles County Registrar last month, demanding they set aside the ballots of 20,000 registered voters whom the Trump administration "believe" are "likely" non-citizens, according to court documents.
About a week later, armed officials from the Department of Homeland Security delivered letters to county officials and employees across California threatening criminal charges if they didn't sequester those ballots.
In a 22-page brief reviewed by the BBC, the justice department maintained that ballots cast by non-citizens could "debase or dilute valid votes".
On Friday, a federal appeals court declined the government's request to segregate the ballots.
California election officials have questioned the accuracy of the government's claims, and have said the list of names the government has provided is riddled with inaccuracies.
They have expressed concern that eligible voters could be disenfranchised and said segregating ballots whilst voting is underway is unfeasible.
The attempts are a part of a years-long campaign by Trump and his administration to fight alleged voter fraud that they believe is widespread, despite research showing that it is extremely rare.
President Trump has repeatedly claimed that Democrats steal elections by allowing immigrants to vote illegally, and he blames much of it on the so-called "mail-in" or postal voting that is permitted in many Democratic states.
Last week in a scathing ruling, district judge David Carter said the government's move in California was indicative of an "ongoing pattern of attempted election interference" on the part of the Trump administration.
The judge added that "never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the executive branch".

Jury in trial of man accused of Chloe Mitchell murder sworn in

Jury in trial of man accused of Chloe Mitchell murder sworn in

A jury of seven women and five men in the trial of man accused of the murder of Chloe Mitchell in Ballymena has been sworn in.
Brandon Rainey, formerly of James Street, Ballymena, denies murdering the 21-year-old on 3 June 2023 and preventing the lawful burial of her remains.
The 30-year-old defendant appeared in the dock wearing a grey tracksuit and confirmed his name and then replied "yes" when asked if he was ready for his trial.
The jury has been sent home for the day and the trial is set to begin on Wednesday.
More than 60 friends and family of Chloe Mitchell were in the public gallery.
Brandon Rainey's father was in court.
The process of jury selection began with the judge, Mr Justice Fowler, asking potential jurors to raise anything with him that they thought would affect their ability to try the case.
They were given some information about the case by a prosecution barrister – including that the alleged murder of Chloe Mitchell happened in James Street in Ballymena and that the defendant lived in that street at the time.
They were also given information about some of the witnesses who are expected to be called during the course of the trial, which the judge told them is expected to last about four to five weeks.
Jury selection lasted just under an hour and the judge then reminded all the jurors that they should not discuss details of the case with friends or family or read anything about the case.
He then sent them home for the day, with the first evidence in the trial due to be heard on Wednesday.
What happened to Chloe Mitchell?
Chloe Mitchell's remains were found days after she went missing.
The 21-year-old was last seen alive on CCTV in Ballymena town centre in the early hours of 3 June 2023 and an extensive search operation was launched by the PSNI.
Detectives investigating her disappearance later launched a murder inquiry after human remains were discovered in the County Antrim town.

MP facing voice loss after surgery shows recovery signs

MP facing voice loss after surgery shows recovery signs

The "whispering MP" who feared she may never be able to speak confidently again revealed she has seen signs of recovery after suffering nerve damage to her vocal cords during surgery.
Liberal Democrat Anna Sabine lost her voice for several months following a thyroid operation in June, which cut one of the nerves to her vocal cords, leaving her with a condition called vocal cord paralysis.
The MP for Frome and East Somerset said the loss of her voice had made her want to "hide" when Parliament returned in September.
But in a surprise turn of events, Sabine said she awoke a few weeks ago to find it had regained some of its natural strength and "broadly speaking, it's back to where it should be".

The 46-year-old said she first realised something was wrong when she woke up from surgery in hospital in Bath.
"I had been warned it might feel strange, so I was trying to reassure myself hopefully this was just what it was going to feel like," she said.
"But the next morning, my surgeon did come around and say, 'I'm really sorry, but there has been a mistake and we have caused permanent damage'.
"At that time I could speak, but only just. I was kind of whispering."
When Parliament returned after the summer, she had to use a microphone to take part in debates.
'I can't hide away'
Sabine said the experience had been a shock and had left her feeling quite lonely.
"Your voice is a really key point of who you are, whether you are an MP or not," she said.
"When I came back to work in September I really wanted to hide, I did not want to speak in the chamber with my voice, because it actually, at that point, when you stood up to speak, you weren't really sure what was going to come out."
She added: "But over that summer, I had heard from so many people because I'd done various radio and TV about it, and people had emailed me.
"I can't now hide away, so I kind of felt inspired by them really to stand up in the chamber, which I did feel really embarrassed about. Even though no-one made me feel embarrassed, it felt extremely exposing."
Sabine said she would be doing a campaign about getting more therapy for adults.
Her voice is now the closest since the surgery to how it was before.
"During recess, one morning I woke up and my voice was like it is now, and my family said 'Your voice is stronger'," she added.
"My friends would say I don't sound quite like I used to, and I can feel that my voice is still really wobbly. But, broadly speaking, it's back to where it should be."

article:
Tax thresholds remain unchanged - here's what it means for your pay

Tax thresholds remain unchanged - here's what it means for your pay
- Published
Income tax thresholds, which have been frozen under successive chancellors, will stay at current levels until April 2031 as planned. But after that they are expected to start to rise again with inflation.
John Healey may not have mentioned the end of this policy in his Budget speech - after all, it is still some way off - but according to the documents released by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) the freeze, which has been shaving additional tax off people's take-home pay for the past five years, is scheduled to end.
The proportion of your income that is taken in tax will continue to go up over the next four years in line with decisions made in previous Budgets.
But then the personal allowance - the point at which you start to pay tax - and other thresholds, where you tip into paying a higher rate of tax, will rise again with inflation, meaning you keep more of what you earn.
Freezing thresholds is often dubbed a stealth tax because, unlike raising the headline rates, it is not as obvious on your payslip.
It has been a useful way for chancellors from Rishi Sunak onwards to raise more money to help pay for things like defence, the NHS, schools and support for the sick, disabled and the elderly.
The amount of extra money brought in by freezing tax thresholds has risen steadily every year, and is due to reach £58bn by 2030-31, more than the UK government spends on transport and not far off current defence spending.
Who is affected by frozen thresholds?
They hit you hardest if your income is close to one of the tax thresholds, but anyone who gets a pay rise is affected, as long as you earn enough to pay tax. Only people earning under £12,570 - the personal allowance threshold - pay no income tax.
By 2031 an extra 6.8 million people will be paying tax who wouldn't have if the personal allowance had not been frozen, the OBR calculates.
The state pension is currently just below the personal allowance threshold, and pensioners looked set to be drawn into paying tax from next April, when the basic state pension rises to £13,036.
However, the chancellor is putting in place a new separate Pension Tax Allowance, which will ensure that low-income pensioners, with income up to the value of the full new state pension, will not pay income tax.
The personal allowance threshold is set for the whole UK, so people in Scotland will also be affected, although other tax bands there vary, external.
National Insurance Contributions (Nics) are levied according to the same thresholds.
- Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you 
  - Published5 days ago
- Budget 2026: Key points at a glance 
  - Published5 days ago
How does it work?
Wages usually go up year-on-year to cover the rising cost of living. Normally tax thresholds would also be raised in line with rising prices. Currently that isn't happening - the thresholds have been "frozen" at 2021 levels.
So, as your pay rises, a bigger proportion of it ends up above the threshold where you start to pay tax.
If the personal allowance had risen with inflation over the last five years, you would now be able to take home the first £16,070 of your salary without paying any income tax. Instead you pay 20% on anything you earn above £12,570.
Will I pay the higher rate?
As incomes rise, frozen thresholds also mean more and more people are dragged into the higher, 40%, tax bracket.
An extra 5.4 million will be higher rate taxpayers by 2031, thanks to the freeze, according to the OBR.
If thresholds had risen with inflation you would have had to be earning £64,470 this year before you tipped into the higher tax bracket.
As it is, with thresholds frozen at 2021 levels, you pay the higher rate on anything you earn over £50,271.
If you were already earning more than the threshold and you get a pay rise, a bigger proportion of your earnings will be taxed at the higher rate.
Almost one in four taxpayers will pay some of their tax at the higher rate by 2031, according to the government's official forecaster.
The same principle - that rising income can push you into a new tax bracket - applies to the additional, 45%, rate that is charged on a person's income over £125,140.
Will I be better off after 2031?
Wages have risen sharply to keep up with inflation in recent years, making the impact of the first five years of this policy quite noticeable, and that is set to continue.
The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) says if Healey had unfrozen the personal allowance this week, instead of keeping it in place until 2031, basic rate taxpayers would have saved up to £198 in tax a year.
Higher rate taxpayers would save £395 a year.
However, for people in the middle of the earnings range, a cut to Nics introduced in 2024 has offset the higher income tax bill.
How much of a difference "unfreezing" thresholds will make in four years' time depends on how fast wages are going up at that point.
There is no fundamental principle at stake, no point that is the "right" level for tax thresholds. Before the financial crisis the personal allowance was much smaller than today, and it was allowed to grow until the pandemic hit. Even in 2031 you'll be able to take home a bigger proportion of your earnings before income tax than you could back in 2008.

article:
British adventurer Karl Bushby completes 28-year journey

British adventurer Karl Bushby completes 28-year journey
- Published
British adventurer Karl Bushby has completed his 31,000-mile (50,000 km) journey from South America to Hull in the UK, reuniting with his mother at the family home 28 years after setting off.
In November 1998, the former paratrooper, then aged 29, set off from Punta Arenas, Chile, to complete an unbroken path back home, without breaking two self-imposed rules: not to return to the UK until the end of the journey, and not to use transport to advance.
Earlier, crowds gathered in Hull's city centre to welcome Bushby, before he set off to complete the final few miles home to his mother Angela Bushby.
Reaching the front door, he said: “It’s good to be home. It feels surreal."
Bushby's journey took him to four continents, with key moments including navigating through the dense jungles of the Darién Gap, crossing the frozen Bering Strait and, more recently, swimming the English Channel.
During a press conference that followed the reunion with his mother, he confirmed: "I'm hanging my boots up."
As they had agreed years earlier, Bushby's mother, Angela, waited for him at her home in Sutton Park, where she raised him.
He appeared almost lost for words, telling the BBC moments after the meeting: “It feels surreal. It’s the end of a 28-year journey.”
His mother, who had not seen him for a decade, told Bushby: “Where have you been?”
She told the media: “It’s good to have him home.
“I feel relieved.”
Bushby said he was "still processing" being home, admitting his head was "one big blurry mess".
Asked what is next for him, he said: "I have a story to tell."
As well as working with acclaimed German filmmaker, Werner Herzog, on a documentary, he confirmed he is working on a second book about his travels.
Bushby admitted he never expected such a homecoming.
Addressing a large crowd in the city centre, Bushby, when he was received by the lord mayor, Maria Coward, said: “There has never been a welcome home like this, I am sure. It's madness. An enormous thank you."
He added: "The biggest team - Earth - got me back here.”
On Sunday, when he crossed the Humber Bridge into East Yorkshire, he was met by his 36-year-old son Adam, his 12-year-old granddaughter whom he had never met, his father and brothers.
“It was amazing,” Bushby said of that reunion.
After returning to the UK, Bushby said he expected to struggle in the coming days and weeks as he readjusted to normal life.
"Everything that I am and everything that I know of me is going to go away," he said. "And that's going to be a problem. You're going to have the old identity crisis, because Karl is this [an adventurer] and has been for half his life.
"I think the old adage goes... the only thing worse than a man who can't fulfil his dreams is a man who's fulfilled his dreams... because then what?"
Bushby previously said he had always had a "wanderlust", and his opportunity to embark on this journey came following the end of his marriage, with his wife returning to Northern Ireland with their son.
Bushby said only about 15 of the 28 years were spent walking, with struggles obtaining visas, the 2007 global economic crash and Covid blamed for delays.
Bushby often retreated to Mexico, where costs are low, between stints.
Under the rules he set for his journey, he could not return to the UK to meet his family.
On rare occasions, he met his son and parents, who are divorced, in other countries.
Bushby said he set off as "penniless backpacker", often relying on handouts, or occasionally being forced to eat food discarded on roadsides.
He later secured sponsors and a book deal as well as a planned documentary.

Virgin Media O2 set to cut thousands of jobs to reduce costs

Virgin Media O2 set to cut thousands of jobs to reduce costs
- Published
Thousands of Virgin Media O2 staff are facing redundancy as the telecoms firm attempts to save money in the face of billions of pounds of debt and tougher competition.
The broadband provider has not finalised the number of roles to be cut but it is likely be a sizeable chunk of its 16,000-strong workforce, the BBC understands.
Virgin Media O2 has billions in debt on its balance sheet and is tackling both smaller providers as well as giants like BT, which has agreed a deal to acquire rival TalkTalk, which Virgin Media O2 has firmly opposed.
The company declined to comment. Prospect, a union which represents Virgin Media O2 staff, said the cuts were "disappointing and very unsettling".
Noel McClean. deputy general secretary at Prospect, said the union was "committed to supporting our members through what is a difficult time, as well as also working with employers to explore ways to mitigate the number of redundancies and ensure retraining and redeployment of staff affected".
The majority of the affected staff are in roles that are not customer-facing and a number of senior leadership changes are already under way, the BBC has been told.
Virgin Media O2 is also expected to review its use of contractors and suppliers in conjunction with the job cuts.
As of 30 June, Virgin Media O2's total liabilities stands at £27.2bn while it holds assets worth £45.9bn, according to the firm's latest accounts.
Meanwhile, the company is dealing with fierce competition from cheaper "altnets" like Hyperoptic, Community Fibre, Gigaclear and YouFibre.
Virgin Media O2 had attempted to respond to this growing threat by buying altnet competitor Netomnia for £2bn via nexfibre, a joint venture owned by Virgin Media O2's owners.
However, the Competition Markets Authority (CMA) has provisionally found competition concerns in the deal, external, with a final decision to come in December, sparking anger from Virgin Media O2.
'Stitch-up'
In October, Virgin Media O2 called the BT's agreed takeover of TalkTalk a "stitch-up" that had allowed its rival to "tighten its grip" over the market.
BT said its deal provided "a safety net" for TalkTalk customers as their broadband provider faced collapse without the takeover.
On Friday, BT's share price jumped 7% after the Financial Times reported Virgin Media O2 was close to agreeing a deal, external to use its rival's fibre broadband network.
The BBC has been told the deal was very close and that Virgin Media O2 was highly likely to announce it will stop all investment in fibre in its results on Tuesday.

article:
'Quiet quitting' could be hitting the economy - here's why

'Quiet quitting' could be hitting the economy - here's why
- Published
The so-called "quiet quitting" trend where workers do the basic requirements of a job but refuse to do anything more might be hitting the economy, analysis has found.
Over the last decade, Britons have become less engaged with the jobs they do and are less willing to put in extra effort, according to a Resolution Foundation report.
The thinktank said this could partly help explain the slump in productivity since the pandemic.
"This is self-evidently bad for workers, but it also doesn't bode well for productivity and labour supply, both of which are vital for lifting living standards in the years ahead," said Hannah Slaughter, principal economist at the Resolution Foundation.
Quiet quitting was popularised on social media shortly after the pandemic.
Frustrated by high demands, low pay, and a squeeze in living standards, many online posts said workers should only do what their bosses asked and nothing more.
So you still show up for work, but no more helping out with additional tasks or checking emails outside work hours, instead focusing on work-life balance and "acting your wage".
Yet, far from being just a talking point on TikTok, the Resolution Foundation said the findings in its report were "consistent" with the idea of quiet quitting.
- 'I was working 60 hours a week so I quiet quit' 
  - Published31 August 2022
The percentage of those surveyed willing to go the extra mile to help their employer has sunk from 69% in 2015 to 55% in 2025, according to their survey of 4,656 adults.
Meanwhile, those who were not even "fairly" satisfied with their roles has sank to one-in-four, the lowest level on record.
In addition, workers are less likely than 10 years ago to say they have an interesting job, with 63% of those surveyed saying so, down from 74%.
"Workers today are indeed a little less committed to their employers, and a little less intrinsically drawn to work in general, than workers were a decade ago," the report added.
This shift over the last decade "may have contributed to weak productivity growth", which has slowed since the financial crisis and weakened again after the pandemic, the Resolution Foundation found.
Workers were also more focused on pay than in the past, which it said was "perhaps unsurprising... given the flatlining living standards of the past decade".
Sir John Curtice, politics professor and co-editor of the report, said the analysis does not mean that young people have "become more 'work-shy', nor have workers in general become more reluctant to change jobs".
"But if workers are to be fully engaged in their work, it has seemingly become more important for employers to provide jobs that are both financially rewarding and have flexible work hours," he added.

article:
Green Party at 'crossroads', says former co-leader

Green Party at 'crossroads', says former co-leader
- Published
The Green Party is at a "crossroads" and needs to focus on its "core values", a former party co-leader has told the BBC, weeks after members adopted a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism.
Adrian Ramsay suggested the Greens need their policies to appeal to a majority of British voters if they want to bring the "environmental changes that we need" and advised against taking an approach that risks being "quite divisive".
Green Party leader Zack Polanski responded by saying there was "no environmental justice without social, racial and economic justice".
The motion, which Polanski did not take part in or vote upon, defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" that had led to the "disenfranchisement and destruction" of Palestinians.
- I would not have voted for Zionism motion, Polanski says 
  - Published9 October
It backed the creation of a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.
Members of the Green Party of England and Wales adopted the policy motion last month.
It led to a backlash from some Jewish groups, as well as criticism from senior Green figures, including Ramsay and other Green MPs.
Israel's foreign ministry said it had banned Polanski, who is Jewish, from entering the country.
The Equality and Human Rights Commission also wrote to the Green Party asking for more information about the motion after concerns were raised by dozens of Labour and Lib Dem MPs and Jewish campaigners.
Labour later said it would end power-sharing agreements with the Greens on local councils, unless its councillors disowned the policy.
Speaking to Newscast, Ramsay replied "no, it's not" when asked if he thought Zionism is racist before adding he agreed with Polanski and others in believing that what is happening in Gaza is "appalling".
The MP for Waveney Valley, who joined the party in 1998, said he does think Israel has a right to exist, something Polanski has stopped short of saying.
Ramsay also said he has made it clear he is "deeply uncomfortable" with the motion adopted and suggested there is an "opportunity to take some action in relation to the motion in the run-up" to the party's spring conference next year.
He said the question now is how Polanski and the party as a whole responds to the motion.
Ramsay said: "I think there's a real crossroads point for the party at the moment.
"One option is to sort of dig in more down this approach, not only in relation to this motion, but I think that there's a risk it brings with it - a quite divisive, a quite internally focused approach to politics."
Ramsay said this is "perhaps seen from small groups of people on the hard left of politics who go around different parties try to influence how those parties are run".
He added: "What I want to see is the party really focus back in on our core aims as a party and our core values."
Ramsay said this includes ensuring the party is "consensus-building in how we approach our politics" and that "we engage the grassroots of our membership".
He added the party needs to be "very externally focused, because we're only going to be able to bring the environmental changes that we need to have to safeguard our society for now and for the future if the majority of the British public come behind that".
Ramsay served as co-leader of the Greens from 2021 to 2025 alongside Carla Denyer, who is also now an MP.
He unsuccessfully stood on a joint ticket with fellow MP Ellie Chowns in 2025, with the pair losing to Polanski in the leadership contest.
Polanski, who missed the conference vote to unsuccessfully campaign for election in a Westminster by-election, previously said he wants to see the "imperfect" motion amended in future.
However, he said the "substantial part of the motion", that "the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people is clearly underpinned by a racist ideology" was "obvious". Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.
Under Green Party rules, motions supported by members become official party policy, but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election.

article:
'I live with a ghost' - inside the haunted homes attracting bargain hunters

'I live with a ghost' - inside the haunted homes attracting bargain hunters
- Published
From the moment Ryua first walked into her rental apartment in Tokyo she believed it to be haunted.
"When I visited the place for a viewing there was a man standing there, glaring at me," she says.
"Since the estate agent couldn't see him, I realised he must be a ghost."
While someone more squeamish would probably have quickly left the flat never to return, Ryua chose to go ahead and move in.
"I'm a bit of a contrarian, so I decided I wanted to become friends with this glaring male ghost," adds Ryua, who works as an aidoru, a young entertainer, and who doesn't wish to share her surname.
Four years later, and still in the same apartment, she says she continues to experience paranormal activity on a daily basis. She says she hears endless footsteps and the ghost talking.
Although Japan has increasingly marked Halloween, external in recent years, many Japanese people take ghosts seriously all year round. The country has a word, "yuurei", which means a lingering, troubled spirit.
These are the ghosts of people who died in violent or tragic circumstances - those who were murdered, killed themselves, or simply were lonely and died alone. If they died at home, then the belief is that their yuurei won't go away.
For house hunters who are not superstitious or squeamish it means there are big bargains to be found. There is a whole category of dwellings called jiko bukken, which means "stigmatised" or "incident" properties.
Under guidelines issued by the government in 2021, Japanese estate agents must disclose suicide, murder, death by fire, and any death where the body was not discovered for an extended period of time.
For rental properties this information must be disclosed for three years, and it must be revealed indefinitely for any property offered for sale.
By contrast, in the UK there is no legal requirement, external to reveal that a person died in a property. And in the US, it differs from state to state., external For example, in California you have to reveal if a person has died in the property in the past three years, while in Arizona and Oregon you do not.
Ryua was told that a man had killed himself in her apartment. It meant that she gets an almost 30% discount on her rent on her tiny, 25 sq m bedsit in the fashionable ward of Setagaya. She says she pays 45,000 yen ($285; £213) a month, instead of what should have been 62,000 yen.
While a house where there had been a murder or suicide would probably be harder to sell or rent out anywhere in the world, Tokyo estate agent Erik Oskamp says that Japanese people are particularly superstitious and averse to stigmatised properties.
"[Even] an apartment next to a cemetery will be difficult to rent out, especially if you can see the tombs from the kitchen," explains Oskamp. "The worst thing is if a suicide has happened in the apartment. Even if somebody has jumped from the roof, many renters will move out. Other issues are a serious crime or a lonely death."
The latter issue, that of a person dying alone, would not generally affect the price of a property in, say, the UK or the US.
But in rural Kagoshima, in Japan's southwest, it enabled Diane Tincher to buy a large three-bedroom house for about half of what would have otherwise been the asking price.
'If there is a ghost I'm thankful to her'
The 69-year-old American has lived in Japan for nearly 40 years, working as a tour guide. She says that the estate agent had been straight with her – there was a heavy discount as an elderly lady had died alone, thereby stigmatising the property.
Tincher paid 20m yen for the house, in a location where similar properties usually sell for up to 45m yen.
"I don't believe in ghosts. But I know that the Japanese are very superstitious," she says. "If there is a ghost I'm thankful to her every day... to live in such a splendid and affordable home."
Researching the house, Tincher had found it on a website called Oshimaland, which lists jiko bukken properties, giving details of the events that occurred. It was launched in 2005 covering Tokyo, before expanding across Japan and then internationally in 2011.
It is crowdsourced, meaning that members of the public add the homes and their details.
Teru Oshima, the founder of Oshimaland, says that in the past such properties were "not very attractive options" in Japan.
Yet as house prices have surged in the country in recent years, as well as a big increase in the wider cost of living, one 2025 survey found that more than half of Japanese people would now rent a jiko bukken if it was cheap., external
Back in Setagaya, Ryua says she is happy living with her ghostly flatmate. "I believe that ghosts were once living human beings, so they deserve our respect," she says.

article:
I've been stuck on a tiny Pacific island for years and can't get a transit visa to fly home

I've been stuck on a tiny Pacific island for years and can't get a transit visa to fly home
- Published
When Ruchira Ranasingha left Sri Lanka almost a decade ago, she could never have imagined she would end up stranded on a tiny archipelago in the South Pacific.
The 50-year-old has now been stuck in the Cook Islands for three years. She tells the BBC she is desperate to go back to Sri Lanka and has even offered to go "handcuffed, bound and gagged".
Ranasingha had been hoping to settle in New Zealand.
After seeking asylum there, she says she followed an immigration adviser's recommendation to temporarily exit the country to apply for a work visa. But once in the Cook Islands, her application was rejected. And by leaving New Zealand, she had breached the terms of her existing asylum-linked visa.
Now New Zealand is refusing to issue her a transit visa that would allow her to fly home to Sri Lanka.
Australia is refusing too. The only other international destinations she can fly to from the Cook Islands - Tahiti and Hawaii - require her to give biometric information in New Zealand before any visa can be processed.
As a result, she has no feasible way of leaving.
"My son - my only child - is getting married in November and I really want to be there for his wedding. My mother is so worried about what has happened to me that she is constantly in and out of hospital," she says through tears.
"I will do anything they ask of me - I just want to go home."
Ranasingha left Sri Lanka in 2018 after being forced to close her small T-shirt factory due to a loss of business. Struggling to repay loans, she moved to Hong Kong to work as a domestic caregiver looking after elderly people and children.
Her brother tells BBC Sinhala she had come under immense financial pressure. Her husband was a drug addict who died about seven years ago, he adds.
In December 2022, Ranasingha headed to New Zealand, where she says she lived with a cousin on a two-month visit visa. As it came close to expiring, she says an immigration interpreter helped her apply for asylum on the grounds she was facing threats from lenders in Sri Lanka.
She was granted an asylum seeker "open work visa", enabling her to work for almost any employer for a year. She found a job at a restaurant, she says, which ultimately agreed to sponsor an employment visa, which she believed would give her longer-term stability.
But as asylum seekers generally cannot apply for other visas while their applications are processed in New Zealand, it was declined.
That's when she got in touch with Immigration & Secretarial Services, a firm she claims told her a fresh application for an employment visa could be made from overseas. Email correspondence the BBC has seen shows its manager, Sylviane Gallant, saying she would initiate the process as soon as Ranasingha had left the country.
So she booked a short stay in the Cook Islands while the application was made.
It turned out to be a disastrous decision.
She was again refused the employment visa. And by leaving New Zealand, she had violated the terms of her existing visa. New Zealand authorities made it clear they would not grant her any future visas.
Gallant claimed to make various interventions on her behalf, including writing to politicians including Chris Penk, New Zealand's then-immigration minister. But ultimately, Ranasingha says Gallant admitted the situation was her fault and told her "there was nothing more she could do".
"She told me I was better off going home. There was nothing holding me there so I agreed to go."
But when she turned up at the airport with an Air New Zealand ticket to Sri Lanka in hand, she was told she couldn't board the flight without a New Zealand transit visa.
Three applications for a New Zealand transit visa were rejected. Authorities said they weren't convinced she would leave New Zealand. Four applications for Australian transit visas were rejected too.
In one of its rejections, New Zealand suggested she explore other routes. But both the US state of Hawaii and the French Polynesian island of Tahiti told her she would need to provide biometric information before any visa could be processed - and that could only be done in person in New Zealand.
Her latest application to New Zealand, which included all the details of the alternative routes she'd been trying, as well as her son's upcoming wedding and mother's failing health, was also rejected.
"I have lost so much money on tickets. For almost four years I have been just applying for visa after visa with nothing working out," she says, breaking down.
On a collection of islands known for their sweeping sandy beaches and rugged volcanic peaks, just four hours from Auckland, Ranasingha has been an involuntary guest.
She's luckier than others in her position, she says, with her hotel letting her stay free of charge in its staff accommodation and friendly locals providing her with food and clothing.
One of the hotel directors even gave her a sewing machine, she says, enabling her to make a small income.
"My mother always tells me I must have done something good, for me to be in a place like this where people have been so kind to me," she tells the BBC.
But it does little to ease the sense of being trapped.
Ranasingha says the stress is impacting her health. "I am scared something is going to happen to me," she says.
"I don't know what her solution is, to be honest," says Auckland-based immigration law specialist Alastair McClymont.
She had received "terrible advice" which "certainly" could not have come from a genuine immigration lawyer, he says, pointing to an industry of "so-called immigration consultants" who charge people to lodge applications without fully understanding the risks involved. Ranasingha says she has parted with thousands of New Zealand dollars in fees to Immigration & Secretarial Services.
The BBC reached out to Gallant but did not receive a response.
McClymont suggests New Zealand authorities will not grant the transit visa because, as far as they are concerned, she has no intention of returning to Sri Lanka having made an asylum claim saying her life was in danger there.
New Zealand co-ordinates with its neighbour Australia which means it won't want to let her transit either, he says, and France and the US are likely to reach similar conclusions.
To leave, "she is going to have to transit through somewhere and no-one will want to take the risk."
- Forty Iranian sailors stranded off Sri Lanka coast rescued 
  - Published26 October
Immigration New Zealand told the BBC it had received multiple transit visa applications from Ranasingha - all declined "as we were not satisfied she has a genuine intention to transit through New Zealand".
When asked why one couldn't be granted even when Ranasingha had offered to be handcuffed and escorted, a representative of the immigration minister's office said those measures do not prevent individuals from making an asylum claim.
Australia's Home Affairs department said it would not comment on individual cases. It said any non-citizens travelling to Australia "must satisfy the requirements of the Migration Act 1958 (the Act) and the Migration Regulations 1994".
Meanwhile, Ranasingha's family have been trying to see if the Sri Lankan government can help. Her brother says they have tried "every possible avenue... but so far we haven't been able to get anywhere on this".
Sri Lanka's foreign ministry told the BBC it was "taking all necessary steps to facilitate her return to Sri Lanka from the Cook Islands. Officials of the Sri Lankan High Commission in Wellington, New Zealand, as well as the relevant New Zealand authorities, are working closely with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on this matter."
But Ranasingha's brother is deeply worried.
"Her mental state is not good," he tells BBC Sinhala.
"One of the times we spoke, she told me that if they were not willing to get her back home alive, they might at least repatriate her body."
Additional reporting by Kethaki Masilamani and Julianna Khan

article:
Six dead after helicopter crashes in northern Indian state

Six dead after helicopter crashes in northern Indian state
- Published
Five pilgrims and a pilot have died after their helicopter crashed in the northern Indian state of Uttarakhand, officials say.
The aircraft reportedly took off from the Hindu pilgrimage site of Badrinath on Friday afternoon before losing contact.
The cause of the crash is not yet known but there had been reports of heavy rain and poor visibility in the region.
Uttarakhand, a Himalayan state which borders China and Nepal, is home to some of Hinduism's holiest shrines and attracts millions of pilgrims every year.
Badrinath is one of four sacred sites on the Char Dham pilgrimage circuit, alongside Kedarnath, Gangotri and Yamunotri. Many devotees travel through steep Himalayan valleys to reach the temples, which are open for only part of the year because of harsh winter conditions.
Uttarakhand's Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami said the helicopter came down near a village close to Joshimath in Chamoli district.
The local civil aviation authority later confirmed to Indian media that six bodies had been located.
Helicopter services have become increasingly popular among pilgrims seeking to avoid difficult mountain journeys, but their safety has come under scrutiny following a series of accidents.
Before Friday's crash, India's weather department had issued an orange alert for the area, warning of thunderstorms, hail and strong winds.
In June 2025, seven people were killed when a helicopter carrying pilgrims crashed near Kedarnath. Another seven died in a crash on the same pilgrimage route in October 2022.
Several other helicopter accidents were reported during the 2025 pilgrimage season, prompting aviation authorities to tighten safety checks and restrict some operations.

Mayor defects from Greens after Zionism motion

The leader of the Green Party on Cornwall Council has defected following the party's recent "Zionism is racism" motion.
Drew Creek joined the Labour and Co-operatives on Thursday after the policy motion was passed at the Green Party's conference earlier this month.
Creek, who is Mayor of Newquay and serves as a councillor for Trenance ward, said he had "huge respect" for Greens across Cornwall but the motion "crossed a line".
The Cornwall Green Party said it was "deeply saddened" by Creek's decision to join Labour and said it does not "try to impose uniformity of belief" among its members and elected representatives.
The motion backed by Green members at its party conference said Zionism was an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/or domination of the non-Jewish population".
It has been criticised by Jewish groups, as well as some Green MPs and opposition political parties.
Creek said he hoped the Green Party would step back from the stance – but said instead, "Zack Polanski and the leadership has doubled down".
"I can't stand behind that, and I won't pretend otherwise," the councillor said.
He added: "People in Newquay don't want politicians driving division. They want someone who'll fix the roads, protect our coast, fight for local services and bring people together.
"That's the kind of politics I believe in and the kind of politics Andy Burnham has shown.
"Newquay is my home and where I am raising my family. I came into politics for one reason, to stand up for this town and the people in it. Labour is where I believe I can do that best, and I'm looking forward to getting on with the job."
Councillor Kate Ewert, Labour and Co-operative Group Leader on Cornwall Council said Creek's decision "highlights the serious questions about Zack Polanski's leadership".
Noah Law, MP for St Austell and Newquay, added: "In this period of polarised politics, it takes great courage to stand up for what you believe in.
"Having worked with Drew since my election, I have always found him to be steadfast in his beliefs, easy to work with, and a good advocate for Newquay."
'Disagreements'
A spokesperson for the Cornwall Green Party said Creek had "done excellent work as a Green councillor" and they understood there were "different views within the Green Party on the 'Zionism is Racism' motion".
They said: "Disagreements over the wording of this one motion should not distract from the fact that the Green Party is united in its condemnation of the racist genocide and ethnic cleansing that Israel is perpetrating in Gaza and the occupied territories, and united in its demand for much tougher sanctions on Israel.
"Labour, by contrast, refuses even to recognise that what we are seeing is genocide, and continues to allow arms exports to and intelligence-sharing with the government that is committing it.
"It's hard to see how anyone who is serious about action on climate, action to end extreme inequality, and action to prevent an ongoing genocide could switch their support to a party that is not serious about any of these."

Jury in Russell Brand rape trial begins considering verdicts

Jury in Russell Brand rape trial begins considering verdicts
- Published
The jury has begun considering the verdicts in Russell Brand's rape and sexual assault trial.
The media personality, 51, has been on trial at Southwark Crown Court in London for three weeks, facing three counts of rape, three of sexual assault and one of attempted indecent assault.
He has pleaded not guilty to all the charges. Giving evidence, he told the court he had been "obsessed" with sex in the past, but insisted it was always consensual.
The charges relate to allegations from six women spanning a decade between 1999 and 2009. Prosecutors said the complainants described him as someone who "didn't listen" when they said no, and "didn't care".
On Tuesday, judge Mr Justice Bennathan told the jury of eight men and four women he can only accept a verdict they all agree on.
Brand was one of the UK's most high-profile comedians, presenters and actors during the 2000s.
At the trial, he admitted using his fame to "facilitate sexual access", which he now said was wrong, but denied ever doing anything criminal.
His barrister told jurors that Brand "had an immense amount of sex", but that "none of it was unlawful".
He also said none of the women reported the alleged incidents to police at the time, and that allegations in a 2023 TV and newspaper investigation had "poisoned the well of justice" by prompting women to come forward afterwards.
Meanwhile, prosecutors depicted Brand as someone who saw women as a "disposable commodity" who "didn't matter to him" and were simply a "means to an end".
Barrister Riel Karmy-Jones KC, for the prosecution, told the jury that the women said his personality changed "from charming to frightening to nasty" during the alleged attacks.
She said the women, who do not know each other, had been "haunted for years" by their experiences.
One woman accuses Brand of raping her after they had met at the Labour Party conference in Bournemouth in 1999.
She claimed he turned from "camp, friendly and effeminate" to "monster-like" before the alleged assault.
When asked if there was any truth in the allegations that he raped her, he told the court: "No."
Another woman claims that the entertainer grabbed her breasts at a bar in London in 2004 before dragging her into a toilet, where he allegedly orally raped her.
Brand said he remembered going into the toilet with the woman but did not drag or force her there, or force her to perform oral sex.
A third woman had a consensual sexual encounter with Brand and another fan in his dressing room at the Hammersmith Apollo theatre in London in 2009.
She accuses the star of later raping her after he invited her to his house in Hampstead.
She said she had agreed to vaginal sex but did not consent to anal sex. After he texted her six months later, she said she told him he had "treated me like an animal".
Brand told the court they had consensual sex, and denied committing anal rape.
The other allegations come from a woman who says she was pinned against a wall and groped; another who claims he put his head into her lap when she had been forced to give him a massage; and a complainant who says he tried to drag her into a toilet. Brand also denies these charges.
Brand's wife Laura gave evidence in his defence at the trial, describing him as "caring, kind and a wonderful father to our children".
Allegations of sexual misconduct against Brand were first made in a Channel 4 documentary and a Times and Sunday Times investigation in 2023.
He denied those allegations, which related to different women than those involved in the criminal trial.
Brand first rose to fame as a stand-up comedian and became a household name as host of TV shows such as Big Brother's Big Mouth, and with his own radio programmes on stations including BBC Radio 2 and 6 Music.
He went on to establish a Hollywood career, starring in films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him To The Greek. He was married to pop star Katy Perry from 2010 to 2012.
In recent years Brand has reinvented himself as an online social, political and religious commentator.

Why a US-Russia showdown left Morocco celebrating

Why a US-Russia showdown left Morocco celebrating
- Published
Morocco has welcomed the end of a decades-long UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara, after a diplomatic showdown between the US and Russia left the Security Council unable to agree on its future.
The council failed on Friday to renew the mandate of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (Minurso) after Russia vetoed a US-backed proposal. A rival Russian draft to extend the mission also failed to secure enough votes.
The decision raises questions about the future of Africa's longest territorial dispute and the fragile ceasefire between Morocco, which claims Western Sahara, and the Polisario Front which has been fighting for the territory's independence for more than 50 years.
Here is what you need to know.
Why is Western Sahara disputed?
Western Sahara, on Africa's north-west coast, was a Spanish colony until 1975. It has significant phosphate reserves and valuable fishing grounds along its Atlantic coast.
As Spain prepared to withdraw, both Morocco and Mauritania claimed the territory.
The International Court of Justice found historical ties of allegiance but no territorial sovereignty that overrode the Sahrawi people's right to self-determination.
Morocco's then King Hassan II responded by organising the Green March. On 6 November 1975 about 350,000 Moroccan civilians entered the territory in a mass demonstration intended to put pressure on Spain.
Days later, Spain signed the Madrid Accords with Morocco and Mauritania, agreeing to transfer administrative control. Morocco took the northern two-thirds and Mauritania the southern third. The agreement did not settle the question of sovereignty.
The Polisario Front, an independence movement founded in 1973, opposed the deal. It saw it as replacing Spanish colonial rule with Moroccan and Mauritanian control.
Mauritania renounced its claim in 1979, but Morocco continued fighting Polisario.
Algeria became Polisario main regional ally, providing military support and hosting its leadership and thousands of Sahrawi refugees in camps near the city of Tindouf.
The North African country says its position is based on the right to self-determination, while Morocco sees Western Sahara as an integral part of its territory.
Morocco and Algeria fought a brief border war in 1963 over disagreements about territory inherited from French colonial rule. Their relationship has remained tense, with Western Sahara at the centre of their dispute.
What was the UN's mission role?
After 16 years of fighting, Morocco and Polisario agreed to a UN-brokered ceasefire in 1991, with the territory divided by a sand wall, or berm, to keep the rival forces apart.
The UN established Minurso to monitor the ceasefire and organise a referendum on the territory's future. Sahrawis were meant to choose between independence and integration with Morocco.
The vote was scheduled for 1992 but never took place. The two sides could not agree on who would be eligible to participate, with disputes over voter identification becoming a major obstacle.
In 2007, Morocco put forward a proposal for autonomy, which would see Sahrawis managing their internal affairs, while Rabat retained control over defence and foreign relations.
The Polisario Front and Algeria rejected the plan, insisting on a referendum that included independence as an option.
Years of UN-sponsored negotiations failed to produce a breakthrough.
The ceasefire broke down in November 2020, when Polisario said it was resuming armed struggle.
But following a long diplomatic campaign by Morocco, the UN Security Council voted in 2025 in favour of a resolution backing the autonomy plan as the "most feasible" solution for the disputed territory.
While most Sahrawis live in the part of Western Sahara controlled by Morocco, tens of thousands are estimated to be in refugee camps in Algeria.
What happened at the UN?
The US proposed extending Minurso's mandate for another year, but its draft went beyond the usual renewal.
It would have removed the word "referendum" from the mission's name and made Morocco's autonomy proposal the sole basis for further negotiations.
The draft received the support of 11 of the Security Council's 15 members, including France and the UK but Russia vetoed it, arguing that it was too favourable to Morocco.
Russia then proposed extending Minurso's mandate without changing its terms. That draft also failed, receiving only two votes in favour.
Minurso's mandate expired at the end of Saturday, 31 October. The UN said the following day that the mission had entered a liquidation period, with a reduced team overseeing the transfer of military equipment and other assets.
UN Secretary-General António Guterres said the Sahrawi people's right to self-determination must be respected and warned of the risk of renewed hostilities.
The Polisario Front condemned the US proposal. Its representative, Sidi Omar, thanked Russia for vetoing it, saying it would "torpedo the foundations of the UN peace process" and threaten regional and international peace.
Morocco, meanwhile, said the mission's personnel and equipment should leave the territory in the coming days, arguing that Western Sahara issue should no longer be considered by the Security Council.
Minurso had 155 military personnel and was expected to cost $62m (£46m) in the financial year beginning in June, according to a UN report.
Why is Morocco celebrating the end of the UN mission?
Morocco's royal palace welcomed the failure to renew Minurso's mandate.
In Laayoune, the territory's largest city, footage showed people celebrating, waving Moroccan flags and displaying portraits of King Mohammed VI.
"The decision is an opportunity for Rabat to challenge what it sees as an international mechanism that has failed to resolve the dispute," Issam Laaroussi, a Moroccan expert in international relations, tells the BBC.
He said Morocco would now have more room to push its autonomy proposal and shift negotiations away from a referendum on independence towards autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty.
The decision does not, however, change Western Sahara's legal status or amount to international recognition of Moroccan sovereignty.
Western Sahara remains on the UN list of non-self-governing territories, while the African Union officially recognises its independence, as the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic (SADR).
But the decision comes after several countries backed the position of Morocco, which in recent years has made securing international support for its claim a central part of its foreign policy.
In 2020, the US recognised Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara as part of an agreement to establish diplomatic relations between Morocco and Israel.
France also backed Morocco's autonomy plan as the basis for resolving the dispute in 2024.
Morocco rejoined the African Union in 2017, more than three decades after leaving its predecessor, the Organisation of African Unity, in protest at the SADR's admission.
Since returning, Rabat has sought to build support for its position from within the organisation. At least 10 African countries have opened diplomatic missions in the territory in support of Rabat.
"Morocco is not necessarily seeking to abandon the UN process, but to change the framework for negotiations and draw greater support from regional organisations," says Laaroussi.
Addressing a special joint session of parliament on Monday, House of Representatives Speaker Ahmed Touizi hailed the end of Minurso as a victory for the country's diplomacy.
He said the country should now move from "managing the dispute to implementing its autonomy plan under Moroccan sovereignty, while pressing ahead with development projects in the territory."
Could this lead to a renewed war?
The fear is that Minurso's departure could lead to renewed fighting.
The mission has monitored military developments and helped reduce the risk of escalation.
Aid organisation Oxfam warned that losing its monitoring and de-escalation role could undermine stability, with serious consequences for civilians.
Laaroussi admits that the mission's departure could create security gaps.
"Minurso's departure does not create the original conflict, because the conflict is already there, but it could aggravate an already fragile security environment," he says.
The UN decision has also fuelled nationalist rhetoric online.
Several Moroccan users have shared AI-generated images of themselves in military uniform, declaring their readiness to fight for Morocco's sovereignty over Western Sahara.
In Morocco, Western Sahara is widely regarded as a national cause. Political parties that are often divided on other issues are united in supporting the country's claim to sovereignty over the territory.
Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita has said the end of the mission does not mean the end of the ceasefire, and that Rabat remains committed to it "within respect of its security and sovereignty."
Polisario has not said what it will do next.
Any resumption of fighting could well draw in Algeria, as tensions with Morocco remain high.
According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), both countries significantly increased military spending last year, with SIPRI citing their dispute over Western Sahara as a key driver.
Algeria spent an estimated $25.4bn, more than four time Morocco's $6.3bn.

Burnham says he wants to cut welfare bill 'as soon as we possibly can'

Burnham says he wants to cut welfare bill 'as soon as we possibly can'
- Published
Andy Burnham has said he wants to cut the welfare bill "as soon as we possibly can", but was unable to guarantee this would happen before the next general election.
Opponents raised concerns over the lack of details on welfare reform in Wednesday's Budget, after welfare spending was forecast to increase from £353bn this year to £431bn in 2031/32.
Asked whether he would seek to reduce the bill before the next election, Burnham told reporters: "We want to get the welfare bill down as quickly as possible, and we're working flat out to that end."
He warned against "crude cuts" and said he wants to get people into "sustainable employment". The Conservatives accused Labour of being "addicted to welfare".
- Budget 2026: Key points at a glance 
  - Published5 days ago
The prime minister faced questions about his approach after the Treasury disputed that Chancellor John Healey had suggested to the BBC that the benefits bill will be cut before the next election, which must be held by August 2029.
When Healey was asked by the Today Programme on Radio 4 whether there would be a cut in the bill before polling day, he said: "There will be, there will be a reduction in the benefits bill, we'll do that in a Labour way."
But several Treasury sources took issue with this being interpreted as a promise to do so by the next election. Downing Street later said it was "not setting an arbitrary target or timetable".
The prime minister's official spokesman would not say whether the government's ambition to cut welfare spending meant reducing it below its current level, or ensuring that future spending rises at a slower rate than is currently projected.
Further details about the government's proposals are expected after two major reports are published in November.
These include a review of disability benefits co-chaired by Labour minister Sir Stephen Timms and one on young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) led by former minister Alan Milburn.
The two reviews were announced by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer after his attempt to make significant changes to the welfare system, including restricting eligibility for some health-related benefits, resulted in a mass revolt of Labour MPs and an embarrassing climbdown in June 2025.
Speaking during a visit to Derby, Burnham said the "big next priority in front of us" is the publication of the Milburn report.
He said: "We just want to get stuck into supporting people to help people off benefits and into work. There's no delay there. We want that to happen as quickly as possible."
Pressed again for a timeline on his plans, the prime minister said: "We're working hard to cut the welfare bill as soon as we possibly can. But we're doing it in a way that supports people into work.
"If we just went and made crude cuts, in the end, that leaves people in crisis, and you spend more public money somewhere else, so it's about getting people into sustainable employment."
'Huge bonus'
Former Bank of England chief economist Andy Haldane said if the government could provide a plan to show "greater restraint" of the benefits bill, that would "play spectacularly well" with the financial markets.
Haldane, who has previously advised Burnham, told the BBC's Political Thinking with Nick Robinson podcast: "If the government could get that through I think it would come with a huge bonus."
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch responded to the Budget by saying the country was "overspent, overborrowed, overtaxed, and drowning in an out-of-control welfare system".
Reacting to government briefings and remarks on Thursday related to when a reduction in the benefits bill could take place, Badenoch said it "looks like foot in mouth syndrome is spreading".
She said: "Don't let anyone tell you this was a 'do no harm budget'. In doing so little, Labour have harmed our economic security and they've harmed our national security."
Welfare spending is forecast to rise this year by £19bn to £353bn.
Watchdog and forecaster the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) said this figure is expected to rise to £431bn in 2031/32, driven primarily by health-related and pensioner benefit spending.
Of the figure forecast for 2031/32, £209.8bn is on pensioners, including the state pension and winter fuel payments, while £110.7bn is on universal credit and legacy equivalents and £69.6bn is on disability benefits such as personal independence payments.
The government has already pledged to reform the existing state pension triple lock from 2030, and more proposals and changes to the welfare system are expected to emerge in the coming months.
