A Paralympian vs a former TV news anchor - and other US Senate races to watch

A Paralympian vs a former TV news anchor - and other US Senate races to watch
- Published
Millions of Americans are deciding the future of the Republican-controlled Congress in a midterm election that will have a significant impact on President Donald Trump's final two years in office.
All eyes are on a handful of Senate races that will decide control of the prized upper chamber.
A four-seat gain by Democrats would give them control - and with it the power to limit Trump's ambitions, reject his judicial nominations and investigate his administration.
Billions of dollars are being poured into the 35 races across the country, but only a handful could go either way.
For much of the race, independent elections analyst Cook Political Report, external has characterised seven Senate races as toss-ups.
Here, we profile the personalities making waves in these much-watched contests.
In a nutshell:
This race has been marred by controversy over the appearance of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot. The Republican senator of that name faces stiff competition from Mary Peltola and accuses her of introducing his namesake to confuse voters, which she denies.
Story of the race:
The race may ultimately be the tipping point state that decides which party controls the chamber if, as expected, Alaska is one of the slower states to reach an outcome.
Peltola, a former House member and the first Alaska Native to be elected to Congress, has run on a platform of "fish, family, freedom" and has attacked Sullivan's record as Alaska's natural resources commissioner.
Two-term senator Sullivan, a long-time Marine Corps reservist who also served as Alaska's attorney general, has accused Peltola's campaign of links to an effort to confuse Republican voters which led to a second man named Dan Sullivan entering the race.
The Peltola campaign denies any such link, though the issue is the subject of a state investigation and a justice department lawsuit, which on Sunday was rejected by a judge.
Alaska's ranked-choice system also adds uncertainty to the mix, and the state has historically been difficult to poll, with surveys historically underestimating Republican voters.
How they got here:
Sullivan, 61, only retired from the US Marines as recently as 2024, after a 30-year career that included deployments in to Afghanistan and the Middle East. Peltola, 53, grew up fishing salmon with her father, later becoming the first person born in the state to actually represent it in Congress.
In a nutshell:
One of the few Republican senators who voted to convict Trump when he was impeached in 2021, Susan Collins has consistently outperformed her party in this Democratic-leaning state, partly by presenting herself as a rebel. Her opponent Troy Jackson, who draws on his background as a lumberjack to persuade blue-collar Mainers he can relate to them, hopes that time is finally running out for one of the survivors of US politics.
Story of the race:
Collins is hoping her reputation as a centrist will persuade independent-minded voters in a state that reliably votes Democratic in presidential elections.
Now her campaign will test whether Republicans can win by distancing themselves from Trump.
Collins, who is seeking her sixth term, entered the midterm cycle as one of the most vulnerable incumbent Republicans seeking re-election.
But she has been helped by controversy on the other side of the aisle involving Graham Platner, who was ultimately replaced as the Democratic nominee by Jackson, a former president of the Maine state senate.
Both Jackson and Collins oppose Trump's tariffs on Canada, mindful of the impact they are having on this border state. Unlike Collins, though, he favours the abolition of the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency (ICE).
How they got here:
Collins, 73, began her political career fresh from college in the 1970s and she entered the US Senate in 1997. Jackson, 58, is a logger who became politically active when he helped to lead a protest to block lower-paid workers from Canada entering Maine.
In a nutshell:
James Talarico aims to end a decades-long electoral drought for the Democrats in Texas - and show that one of the Republicans' main strongholds could be in play for the 2028 presidential election. His match-up with Ken Paxton has become the most expensive Senate race ever.
Story of the race:
Republican Paxton knows his party has been winning statewide races in Texas for more than 30 years.
Texas State Representative James Talarico, a former schoolteacher and Presbyterian seminary student, is the latest Democrat hoping to break his party's long losing streak.
Texas Republicans are facing a daunting combination of headwinds. It is a challenging national political environment for conservatives and there are several state issues like data centre construction and aggressive immigration enforcement that have cut against their party. Added to that is a controversial candidate, Paxton.
The campaign has been acrimonious, with Talarico targeting Paxton's 2023 impeachment by the Republican-controlled state House of Representatives for alleged corruption, bribery and abuse of power. Paxton denied the charges and was later acquitted by the state Senate, calling the impeachment a "politically motivated sham from the beginning".
Supported by more than $170m in funds from tech mogul Elon Musk, Paxton has attempted to paint Talarico as a liberal who is out of touch with Texans on issues like transgender rights, law enforcement, immigration and energy policy.
A Democratic victory here might indicate America's second-biggest electoral prize in a presidential election could be within their reach in 2028 - a notion that could dramatically reshape the nation's political landscape.
How they got here:
Before he entered public service, Paxton spent 14 years launching and building his own law firm. He served in the state House and Senate before becoming the chief legal officer in Texas.
Talarico taught at a middle school in San Antonio, in a neighbourhood he has described as one of the poorest in the state. He has studied theology and names Pope Leo as a "spiritual hero".
In a nutshell:
This is one of the most bitter contests, with left-wing candidate Abdul El-Sayed aiming to keep this crucial seat in Democratic hands. He is up against Mike Rogers, a Republican former FBI agent who received a surprise endorsement from El-Sayed's defeated Democratic rival, only adding to the acrimony that has characterised this race from the start. The day before the vote, it was moved by Cook Political Report from "toss-up" to "leans Democrat".
Story of the race:
A doctor and public health official, El-Sayed is one of the most left-wing Senate nominees this election cycle.
He supports a government-run health insurance system and the abolition of ICE. His strong criticism of Israel has been a source of tension in the party.
Rogers, who emphasises his military and intelligence background, has managed to maintain Trump's support despite decrying his Canada tariffs and his Russia diesel deal.
He has also diverged from the president by calling for a quick end to the war with Iran. El-Sayed would be the first Muslim person ever elected to the US Senate.
As well as attacking him for his politics, Trump and Rogers have sought to link him to the Muslim Brotherhood; El-Sayed has denounced the organisation.
The president has also invoked 9/11 and even called him a "jihadist" without citing any evidence, prompting a backlash and accusations of Islamophobia.
How they got here:
El-Sayed, 41, was born and raised in Michigan before his medical studies in the US and UK and subsequent work in the sector. Rogers, 63, served in the US Army and in the FBI before entering Congress and emerging as a key advocate of US surveillance policies.
In a nutshell:
Trump made the trip to Iowa on his final day of campaign rallies, such is its importance. Polls have it as a toss-up between Republican and former TV news host Ashley Hinson and Democrat Josh Turek, who won gold at basketball at two Paralympic Games.
Story of the race:
Farms, tariffs and Trump have all emerged as key issues in the closely-watched race.
Hinson has slightly distanced herself from the president, urging him to end the war with Iran and breaking with him on easing beef tariffs, while at the same time defending Trump's broader tariff policies as important.
Meanwhile, Turek argues that Trump's tariffs have led to "farmageddon" in the largely rural state. He has also sought to convince voters that the war in Iran has led to rising fuel and fertiliser costs.
Hinson has cast Turek as a candidate who would vote as an "East Coast liberal".
The two have also clashed on issues ranging from taxes and social security to immigration. The last time a Democrat won a federal election in Iowa was nearly 20 years ago.
How they got here:
Hinson, 43, is a former local news reporter who says her journalistic background helps her understand the issues faced by the state's farmers and small businesses. Turek, 47, was born with spina bifida, going through multiple surgeries before representing the USA at wheelchair basketball at four Paralympic Games, twice triumphantly.
In a nutshell:
A Democratic victory in Kansas would upend 94 years of history - the last time this Midwestern state elected a Democratic senator was 1932. Senator Roger Marshall is the Republican trying to avoid a humbling defeat, while first-time candidate and Methodist pastor Adam Hamilton is the Democrat trying to break records.
Story of the race:
Marshall has closely aligned himself as a Trump-aligned, pro-farmer candidate.
Hamilton, who once considered running as an independent, has pitched himself as a candidate that can bridge the partisan divide. He has largely campaigned on a message of lower costs and protecting healthcare access.
Marshall has sought to attack Hamilton's record as a pastor, describing him as "too woke" for the conservative state.
Marshall, meanwhile, has been under scrutiny ever since reports emerged that he sued patients unable to pay their medical bills. He told Fox News the story was a hit job by the left media and senior Democrats.
The tight race is broadly seen as a potentially ominous sign for Republicans.
A Hamilton victory would be seen as a sign of increasing dissatisfaction with Trump's policies - particularly on economics - in territory that was once considered safe for the party.
How they got here:
Both Marshall, 66, and Hamilton, 62, highlight that they are fifth-generation Kansans who are in close touch with local issues. Marshall worked for 25 years as an obstetrician, delivering some 5,000 babies, while his rival Hamilton founded a church which became the centre of the largest United Methodist congregation in America.
In a nutshell:
Trump won this state with ease in 2024 and no-one a year ago considered it in play for the midterms. But Republican Senator Jon Husted finds himself neck and neck with Democrat Sherrod Brown who is running to get his old job back, having represented Ohio in the Senate for many years before losing his seat.
Story of the race:
Husted was appointed in 2025 to the Senate seat vacated by Vice-President JD Vance, and is now running to serve the rest of Vance's term.
He promises to use his business experience to bring jobs and growth to Ohio.
In a different election cycle he would probably be the favourite to win this onetime swing state that has become reliably red in the Trump era.
But Husted is facing a formidable challenge from Brown, who has high name recognition from three decades representing Ohio in Congress.
Brown is known as a champion of workers and was advocating economic populist policies long before others in his party.
The race is a referendum on Trump's economic policies, in particular his trade wars that have impacted the manufacturing and auto industries that underpin Ohio's economy.
How they got here:

Chris Mason: Home secretary to face scrutiny over changes to rules for legal migrants

Chris Mason: Home secretary to face scrutiny over changes to rules for legal migrants
- Published
At the heart of the debate around legal migration are contested notions of fairness.
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has talked of her parents coming to the UK from rural Kashmir. Now, this daughter of immigrants is responsible for reshaping the very system that brought them here decades ago – and doing so in a way that both her party and the country regard as fair.
"Fair to those who seek a new and better life here, like my parents did. And fair to those already here, including British workers, and especially the young," is how Mahmood put it in her speech to the Labour Party conference in September.
The debate has come at a time of huge legal immigration in recent years and during a period in which Reform UK have been particularly prominent in the national political conversation.
Both of these things are factors in Labour wanting to be seen to be taking people's concerns about the scale of arrivals seriously.
But her political opponents smell what they see as weakness and retreat, with parts of her original plan now being revised, as the BBC's Iain Watson reported over the weekend.
It is worth examining this policy throughout the last year or so, as it is instructive in how we have arrived at today's announcement.
- Mahmood to set out changes to settlement rules for legal migrants 
  - Published10 hours ago
In November last year, Mahmood set out a plan called "a fairer pathway to settlement".
The idea was opinions on her instincts would be sought in a consultation. And boy, were there plenty of opinions offered.
Around 200,000 people contributed to the consultation, of which 140,000 responses came from visa holders themselves I'm told.
"It's been a colossal exercise and a genuine one," is how one Whitehall source put it to me, claiming: "We have taken the time to get this right."
Or is the real truth that they have buckled under political pressure from their own side – and a change of prime minister?
Mahmood said last year that she felt compelled to act because "between 2021 and 2024, we have seen net migration of an additional 2.6 million people. Around one in every 30 people in this country today arrived in these four years." It is what critics have labelled "the Boriswave", named for the changes made under former Prime Minister Boris Johnson.
And, Mahmood argued, it was important to act with urgency, as very soon significant numbers of those recent arrivals would start qualifying for indefinite leave to remain, or ILR.
"Migrants on lower wages who bring non-working dependants and children are likely to present significant fiscal costs to the UK.
"It is therefore right that we apply more stringent controls for this group before they qualify for settled status," she said, adding: "Under our current rules, they will usually qualify for benefits payments and council housing five years after arrival.
"As the majority of this group began arriving from 2022 onwards, this is currently set to begin in 2027. We consult here on a separate baseline qualifying period, of 15 years, for this group."
But plenty within the Labour Party and beyond were uncomfortable – and yes, they cited fairness, or the perceived lack of it, in mounting their criticisms.
As the now Housing Secretary Angela Rayner put it in March, before she returned to government, the ideas were "un-British" because they involved "moving the goalposts" - migrants who had arrived in good faith under one set of rules would have their future in the UK determined by the new ones.
Associated costs
Just a few weeks before Rayner's intervention, Mahmood had doubled down on her plans. Addressing the centre left IPPR think tank, she said "in just four years, this country experienced levels of migration it had previously seen across four decades.
"It was not just the scale, but also the nature of that change that was so destabilising."
There was more, and with a big number attached.
"We have never, in the history of this country, had so much low-skilled migration in so little time.
"We estimate, based on findings from the Migration Advisory Committee, that the lifetime cost to the taxpayer will be £10bn. That figure would be paid for by working people in this country."
She added: "It is an affront to the idea of fairness within our migration system."
Incidentally, the £10bn figure is contested by some – or at least placed in a wider context.
The aforementioned IPPR argue that the original plans were "never in reality going to create a £10bn long-term saving, given they were meant to delay care workers' eligibility for ILR rather than prevent them from settling altogether.
"Delaying ILR would save money on welfare, whereas the £10bn figure includes much broader long run costs once care workers enter retirement, claim the state pension, and make greater use of health and social care."
Nonetheless, Mahmood's message in March left senior Conservatives privately agreeing with her – and struck by her willingness to be unflinching in her approach to the subject.
But around 100 of her Labour colleagues were not happy – and making their views known publicly.
By the time I found myself in the dusty car park of a sports club near Wigan in May, waiting to talk to an ambitious by-election candidate by the name of Andy Burnham, it was clear changes were highly likely.
He told me it was important to "work hard to get the balance right" but that the "broad thrust" of what the home secretary was doing "is right".
"Broad thrust" will be the words that account for the gap between what Mahmood used to say and what she is saying today.
The Conservatives and others will seize upon the change. The Tories will argue it amounts to an "excruciating U-turn" as one senior figure described it to me, claiming it would be "deeply personally embarrassing" for the home secretary.
They also ponder how the government will choose to make the changes, as they believe if primary legislation isn't used to do it – such as via an amendment to the Immigration and Asylum Bill currently before parliament – the plans could be successfully challenged in court.
Mahmood will argue she has tried to finally arrive at a policy the widest range of people may see as fair.
We will see and hear the range of reaction she provokes in the coming hours and days.

article:
DUP leader 'very sorry' Carla Lockhart has quit the party

DUP leader 'very sorry' Carla Lockhart has quit the party
- Published
Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Gavin Robinson has said he is "very sorry" that MP Carla Lockhart has quit the party.
Robinson said he would not be criticising the Upper Bann MP, who left the party on Monday over its response to the Drumcree parading dispute, and expressed hope they would continue to work together in the future.
Lockhart had been calling for the DUP to withdraw Stormont's deputy first minister to force Sinn Féin First Minister Michelle O'Neill from their joint office.
Speaking on Tuesday, Robinson said the disagreement was over strategy not sentiment.
O'Neill and several other senior Sinn Féin figures have been interviewed by police investigating the Garvaghy Road demonstrations, with unionists accusing the party of acting unlawfully.
Last week the DUP, which shares power with Sinn Féin in Northern Ireland's devolved government, announced it would block official engagements involving O'Neill in response to the fall-out.
But Robinson stopped short of Lockhart's call to force O'Neill from office.
Speaking on the Good Morning Ulster programme he said: "We share exactly the same sentiment - all of us are angered, all of us believe the position of Michelle O'Neill and her willingness to break the law, to ignore the courts, to breach her pledge of office requires sanction.
"So while we share the same sentiment, we have not been in agreement when it comes to how you deal with it.
"The Democratic Unionist Party is firmly of the view that it is Michelle O'Neill who should face the consequences of her actions, not the rest of the people of Northern Ireland.
"Northern Ireland needs a functioning government, Northern Ireland needs a budget - those important discussions will continue on Thursday I believe with the secretary of state."
Robinson said he believes "there is a role for this government to come forward with a sanctions regime that will punish those who break the pledge of office".
Speaking after a meeting of the Northern Ireland Executive, Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly reiterated DUP calls for "unionist cooperation" and warned that unionism was "weakened by infighting".
Little-Pengelly said the unionist community felt "anger and frustration" over Sinn Féin's response to Drumcree and the Irish republican party had "fractured" relations within Northern Ireland's power-sharing government.
O'Neill, the Sinn Féin vice-president, has defended her involvement in the Drumcree protests, saying it was the "right thing to do".
In an open letter to colleagues last week, Lockhart said forcing O'Neill from office was the "only one credible option" and any kind of "graduated response" would be "insulting to those who have trusted us".
In a statement posted on her Facebook page on Monday, the MP said: "My first responsibility remains to the people of Upper Bann.
"You placed your trust in me, and I will continue to work every bit as hard for you, your family and our community."
Lockhart said she was leaving the DUP on a "point of principle" and would continue in the House of Commons as an independent unionist.
"I cannot stand idly by whilst Sinn Féin wilfully ignores the rule of law and the promised profound consequences fail to materialise," she added.
Lockhart concluded that she would "look forward to working with all shades of unionism, elected or not, to advance the cause we love".
A local councillor has also quit the party.
Clement Cuthbertson, a councillor for Dungannon in Mid Ulster District Council, has been a DUP member for 30 years and will continue his elected role on the council as an independent unionist.
"I have reached the point where remaining a party member would mean asking people to accept a position I cannot defend," he said in a social media post. , external
A DUP spokesperson said: "We regret Clement Cuthbertson's decision to resign from the party and wish him well for the future."
The DUP MP for East Londonderry Gregory Campbell said Lockhart's resignation had come as no surprise and could prove a "pivotal moment" for the wider unionist family.
"Do we advance the cause of unionism by fracturing or closing ranks and uniting and trying to get people together to say 'what is the best way forward, what's the best way to set out a strategy what will maximise the pro-union voice?'," he told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme.
"Fracturing only assists those who are the enemies of unionism, uniting will thwart the enemies of unionism and that's what we need to do and I think that realisation is going to come home now in the next few weeks."
- MP Carla Lockhart quits DUP in Drumcree row 
  - Published21 hours ago
Speaking on the Good Morning Ulster programme on Tuesday, Traditional Unionist Voice leader Jim Allister said the DUP had "preferred to keep Michelle O'Neill and let Carla Lockhart go" and that would "hang over them and haunt them for some time to come".
He added: "I have both publicly and privately made it very plain that Carla would be very welcome in the TUV, but I understand Carla's position.
"When you've been in a party as she has and indeed as I was for 20 years and then you leave it, it's quite a step."
'Set party politics aside'
Also on Tuesday, Sinn Féin Finance Minister John O'Dowd said the DUP needs to "set party politics aside" as the executive works to agree a budget.
He was speaking after ministers met ahead of further talks with the secretary of state later this week.
O'Dowd said all ministers need to remain focused on the task at hand, and that he will present further options to them about what is possible in the coming days.
There is the prospect of strike action by health workers if they do not get a long-awaited pay deal that cannot be released without a budget.
O'Dowd said the primary task was to ensure strikes are avoided, adding: "We are reaching a crunch period in relation to the discussions around the executive table and the terms and conditions with the British government."
On the absence of a Stormont budget and further talks this week with the secretary of state, Little-Pengelly said that "we are in a better position than where we were" but there was "still a significant gap".

Brit North arts college plan given go-ahead

Brit North arts college plan given go-ahead
- Published
Plans for the north of England's first Brit School-inspired performing arts college have been approved.
Inspired by the world-famous arts academy in London which produced talents such as Adele and Tom Holland, Brit North is expected to bring more than 550 students and staff into the city centre.
The college will be housed on the site of the former Jacob's Well council building, which is currently a car park, and aims to open by 2028.
The project, which has been approved by Bradford Council, is spearheaded by the British Phonographic Industry (BPI) who are owners and organisers of the music showcase, the Brit Awards.
The authority said the school would boost the city centre's regeneration and "increase footfall and activity within the area".
According to the planning application, the building will have a theatre, set construction workshop, a multi-use games area, music performance spaces and a TV studio set as well as classrooms and college facilities, said the the Local Democracy Reporting Service.
The free-to-attend college was first proposed in 2023 with the Department for Education later approving the plans.
Following the approval by the council, BPI chief executive Dr Jo Twist said Brit North was "a cultural and educational initiative" but also "an important regeneration project for Bradford".
"It successfully brings together significant investment from the private sector and central government, working in partnership with regional and local leaders, with an ambition to deliver for the city and the young people of Bradford and West Yorkshire," she added.
"We look forward to celebrating more milestones in the coming months."
Mark Casci, head of policy and representation at West Yorkshire Chamber of Commerce, said the city was the "perfect location" for the college.
"Bradford's year as UK City of Culture demonstrated conclusively that the city is a significant national player as a cultural epicentre and is a region brimming with talent and creativity.
"Bradford is therefore the perfect location for Brit School North and will give our young people a significant springboard to performing arts greatness.
"This in turn will act as a magnet for talented people all over the UK who will hone their genius in the city and further enhance its prospects."

article:
Former Rangers player Kyle Hutton to stand trial over road death

Former Rangers player Kyle Hutton to stand trial over road death
- Published
Former Rangers player Kyle Hutton is to stand trial in 2028 accused of killing a woman in a road collision.
Hutton is said to have been "unfit to drive through alcohol or drugs" when he allegedly struck Victoria Cairns, 40, in Farmeloan Road, Rutherglen, South Lanarkshire, on 2 November 2024.
The 35-year-old denies the charges, which include going at excessive speed for the conditions at the time and not seeing the pedestrian.
Cairns died from her injuries in hospital four days later.
Hutton faces a charge of causing death by dangerous driving, and other charges of failing to co-operate with breath and drug tests and not providing two specimens of breath to determine his "ability to drive".
There is an alternative allegation that the fatality was as a result of Hutton - who played for the Ibrox club between 2010 and 2015 - being careless behind the wheel.
Prosecutors state Hutton failed to carry out "proper observations" and did not detect Cairns standing on the road.
It is alleged he then struck the woman, causing her to fall to the ground and that she was so badly hurt she died in hospital four days later.
During a hearing at the High Court in Glasgow Graeme Brown KC, defending, pleaded not guilty on Hutton's behalf.
The solicitor advocate added there was potentially upsetting footage which jurors may be shown as part of the evidence.
He also said Hutton's wife was likely to be called as a defence witness.
Lord Scott went on to set a trial, which could last about four days, for 7 February 2028.
Hutton, whose other clubs included St Mirren, Dumbarton and Partick Thistle, remains on bail meantime.

article:
'I was heading for a breakdown, then books saved my life'

'I was heading for a breakdown, then books saved my life'
- Published
International bestselling author Kit de Waal has told the BBC how a chance conversation changed her life after she left home at 16, struggled with drugs and found herself on the brink of a serious mental breakdown.
The Birmingham-born writer said she was "a couple of months away from a very serious breakdown" before a solicitor's reading recommendation changed the course of her life.
Speaking to BBC Upload, she said: "I found the world of reading, the world of imagination.
"I can honestly say it saved my life."
Born in Birmingham to an Irish mother and a Caribbean father, de Waal grew up in Moseley at a time when mixed-race families were rare.
"My father came over from the Caribbean in 1956 and my mother is an Irish immigrant," she said.
The family lived on the edge of a predominantly middle-class area, but de Waal said her childhood was marked by poverty.
"We were very, very poor. I was brought up in poverty, there's no other way about it."
She said those experiences later became central to her writing.
"What I learnt from it was difference, what it's like to be an outsider, what it's like to be poor, hungry, lost, not fit in, the damage that poverty does, the damage that racism does to children."
Yet she also remembers acts of kindness.
After her family moved into a largely white neighbourhood, one neighbour invited the children into their home to see their pet tortoise.
"I learnt from that the power of kindness and the profound effect it has when other people aren't being kind."
When she was six, her mother became a Jehovah's Witness.
De Waal left home at 16 after deciding she no longer wanted to follow the faith.
The years that followed were difficult.
"I was wild," she said. "I took a lot of drugs, drank a lot, did everything you can imagine."
The deaths of friends from heroin overdoses forced her to confront where her life was heading.
By the age of 21, she said her mental health had deteriorated badly.
"I was really very, very unwell.
"I would say a couple of months away from a very serious breakdown."
After returning home and finding work with the Crown Prosecution Service, an off-hand comment from a solicitor would prove life-changing.
Seeing her yawn during a meeting, he suggested reading to help with her insomnia.
At the time, de Waal said she disliked books and had never developed a reading habit.
The solicitor gave her a list of 10 novels, including War and Peace and Madame Bovary.
She bought them all.
"I've never cured the insomnia," she said.
"But I have found a world."
Reading became a lifelong passion and eventually inspired her to start writing herself.
Despite believing she could write a novel in a matter of months, de Waal said it took more than a decade of rejection and learning the craft before she was published.
Her breakthrough came with My Name Is Leon, the story of a young boy in the care system growing up in 1980s Birmingham.
The novel became an international bestseller and was later adapted by the BBC after Sir Lenny Henry, who narrated the audiobook, became determined to bring the story to the screen.
It is now studied in schools.
Yet de Waal said the most important lesson from her success was a simple one.
"If there's a lesson, it's write the thing you really care about."
Now one of Britain's best-known authors, she remains a passionate advocate for reading in all its forms, including audiobooks.
Despite an international career, she still credits reading with changing the direction of her life.
"I found the world of reading," she said.
"It saved my life."

article:
'She never forgot her roots' - hometown and school tributes to Ciara Mageean

'She never forgot her roots' - hometown and school tributes to Ciara Mageean
- Published
Former European champion and two-time Olympian Ciara Mageean has been described as "selfless" by staff from her former school.
Mageean, from Portaferry in County Down, was diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer in May 2025.
She died on Sunday morning, surrounded by her loved ones, a statement posted on her social media accounts said.
Marcelle Orsi, vice-principal of Assumption Grammar School in Ballynahinch, said the loss will be felt "by so many for many years to come".
"Everybody was so devastated and heartbroken with the news of Ciara's passing," Orsi said.
"She left 16 or 17 years ago but was a great advocate for all the sport here.
"If you think what we try to develop and foster within our own students - commitment, dedication, tenacity, compassion - Ciara Mageean was an Assumption girl through and through."
Orsi added that the school will remember Mageean as "the smiling, bubbly vivacious girl who was always willing to help anybody".
"That selflessness was there right to the end," she told BBC News NI.
She said Mageean will always be remembered in the school, with her photos displayed in the corridors.
"She lived and breathed this school and it was only fair we showed how proud of her we were. She brought us so much."
Eamonn Christie, who was Mageean's first coach, said the athlete's death will "never sink in fully".
Christie, who began coaching Mageean in 2006, said he knew she was a special talent "from her first race".
"In Ciara's prime she could be unbeatable," he said.
"She was a delightful person, she was great to work with. She was a great girl on and off the pitch."
Christie added that Mageean always made time for people, and that she will "never be forgotten".
Mageean's funeral will take place near her family home on Tuesday, with a ceremony at St Patrick's Church, Ballyphilip, followed by burial in the adjoining cemetery.
Her death comes less than three weeks after her marriage to her long-term partner Thomas Moran.
The athlete represented Ireland at the 2016 and 2020 Olympics and won gold in the 1500m at the European Athletics Championships in Rome in 2024.
She also represented Northern Ireland at the Commonwealth Games, winning silver in Birmingham in 2022.
'An absolute star'
One Portaferry resident, Maureen McCarthy, told BBC News NI she was "heartbroken, she was just such a lovely person, nobody nicer".
"She was a star, an absolute star and treated everybody the same, nobody was any different no matter who you were.
"Everybody is devastated, absolutely devastated."
She said Mageean's grandparents "were the first friends that we made whenever we came to Portaferry way back in 1989.
"So I remember when she was born, I remember when her mummy and dad were married, I was at their wedding."
Another Portaferry resident, Josephine McClurg, said she "just sat and cried" when she heard the news of Mageean's death.
"I couldn't believe it," she told BBC News NI.
She added that everybody in Portaferry "thought highly" of Mageean.
'Tears of sorrow'
SDLP Councillor Joe Boyle attended Mageean's wedding reception - held two weeks after the civil ceremony - in County Louth a week ago.
He said it had been a "fantastic day, Ciara in her element enjoying everybody's company, enjoying all her friends, those that were closest to her and had time for everybody, photographs with everyone.
"We had so many tears of joy to see Ciara eventually get married.
"She was very determined and whatever Ciara said she would do she would do.
"Lo and behold a week later and here we are, tears of sorrow and Portaferry as a community just cast into such sadness with such a dark cloud over it because everybody loved Ciara."
'Great fun'
Speaking to BBC Good Morning Ulster athlete Katie Kirk, who competed alongside Mageean, recalled her first experience of training with her at Mary Peters tracks in Belfast for a cross-country session.
"Even then she was great fun, very determined, focused".
Kirk commended Mageean's success saying "she achieved so much" even through "incredibly difficult" times.
"She still came out, she still spoke to people, she still took pictures with children and participated fully in life.
"That for me is just the essence of who she is," she added.
In many interviews that she gave following her diagnosis last year, Mageean spoke candidly about the symptoms she experienced which led her to seek medical help.
She also worked with a charity that promotes bowel cancer awareness.
Noticing blood in your poo - which may appear black or dark red in the toilet bowl - can be a sign of bowel cancer.
If there is no other obvious cause for the bleeding, such as piles, the NHS recommends that you ask for an appointment with your GP, external.
The NHS also advises a check-up if you notice changes in your regular toilet habits, such as having to poo more often, or a pattern of diarrhoea or constipation.
Abdominal pain or lumps, stomach bloating and unexplained weight loss are also among symptoms which should lead to a bowel cancer test.
Bowel cancer can also cause anaemia, the features of which include extreme tiredness and shortness of breath.
The earlier bowel cancer is detected, the easier it is to treat.

Suited and booted: How Joseph Kabila went from president to rebel leader

Suited and booted: How Joseph Kabila went from president to rebel leader
- Published
Joseph Kabila was a commander in the rebel alliance that brought his father to power in the Democratic Republic of Congo in 1997, went on to succeed him as president and now, at the age of 55, he is a rebel leader once again.
In an even stranger twist, the man he has sworn to topple is the very man he handed power to after 18 years at the helm, and with whom he had formed a coalition government after stepping down. While one of the rebel groups he had fought against as president is part of his new alliance.
His career reflects the ever-shifting nature of politics in DR Congo, where alliances are ephemeral, with the use of force a constant threat.
When Kabila was named leader of the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), earlier this month, it confirmed what many Congolese had long believed – that the former president was working with the M23 rebels, who last year seized much of eastern DR Congo, including the region's main cities of Goma and Bukavu.
Nevertheless, the confirmation sent shockwaves through DR Congo – a vast country two-thirds the size of western Europe, with huge deposits of gold, diamonds and even more importantly minerals used to make everything from the mobile phones to batteries for electric vehicles.
For Kabila, the alliance offers a possible route back to the power he had lost.
For the M23 rebels, his involvement brings the experience and networks of a former head of state to a movement whose military advances have yet to translate into broad national legitimacy.
But it is far from certain that they can achieve their stated goal of ousting President Félix Tshisekedi.
Policy analyst Henry-Pacifique Mayala told the BBC that Kabila had been left with few options for regaining political influence.
"He actually was left with no other choice," he said.
Facing a death sentence after being convicted in absentia of treason, as well as US sanctions over his alleged support for the M23, Kabila may have sought assurances that the partnership could serve his interests, Mayala suggested.
"I'm not sure that he is making this huge leap in the dark without having received considerable assurance," Mayala said, adding that the M23's military strength could give Kabila greater leverage in any future negotiations with the Congolese government.
Kabila's involvement also raises questions about whether the conflict could spread beyond the east.
The M23's territorial gains have been concentrated in the country's eastern provinces, some 1,500km (1,000 miles) from the capital, Kinshasa.
Kabila's political networks could give the rebellion a broader reach, but that does not necessarily mean it has the capacity to extend its military campaign across the country.
And it is not clear how far Kabila's national reach extends.
While he was in power, after being named following the mysterious assassination of his father Laurent in 2001, he was often seen as something of an outsider in Kinshasa. He was far more at home speaking Swahili, the lingua franca of eastern DR Congo, as well as east Africa, rather than the Lingala spoken in Kinshasa.
His father's rebel group actually walked across the country to Kinshasa, also starting in the east, over a period of seven months, before eventually seizing power in May 1996 and ousting long-time ruler Mobutu Sese Seko, who had governed the country as his own personal property for more than 30 years.
There is little suggestion that Joseph Kabila's FRN would try to repeat that feat but earlier this week, he likened Tshisekedi to Mobutu.
"You have a tyrant who wants to impose and dictate what he thinks is right and not necessarily follow the constitution, which is the supreme law of the land," he told Conspiracy Trackers Great Lakes (CTGL), a pro-M23 research group.
Kabila accused the government of using the death penalty, ending the moratorium introduced during his own presidency, to intimidate civilians, politicians and members of the military, as well as himself.
"This is personal," he said.
He framed his confrontation with Tshisekedi as a fight against authoritarianism, invoking Section 64 of the constitution, which calls on citizens to resist anyone who seizes power or exercises it in violation of constitutional provisions.
Tshisekedi is rumoured to be planning to change the constitution to allow him to seek a third term in office, with the C64 coalition of opposition parties named after that same section of the constitution, campaigning against such a move.
But in a sign that he may not get everything his own way, the C64 coalition this week refused to back Kabila's rebellion, saying that Congo's multiple security crises cannot be resolved by military means alone. Instead, it announced plans to seek direct talks with both Tshisekedi and Kabila in pursuit of what it called a "genuine and inclusive national dialogue".
Richard Moncrieff, a Great Lakes analyst with the International Crisis Group think-tank, said President Tshisekedi retained substantial advantages.
"Tshisekedi has strong American backing. He has a lot of money. And he generally controls the political system and, as far as we can see, the military system," Moncrieff said.
In his first public reaction to Kabila being named FRN leader, Tshisekedi was damning: "In my view, it's simply proof that he has never loved this country, and even less its inhabitants," he said last week.
And yet Kabila is widely believed to have helped ensure that Tshisekedi succeeded him, rather than Martin Fayulu, who was the true winner of the 2018 elections, according to leaked results provided by the Catholic Church, which had observers around the country.
Indeed, the former head of the electoral commission who announced Tshisekedi as the winner, Corneille Nangaa, has said as much.
Now one of Kabila's deputies in the FRN, he claimed that Kabila and Tshisekedi had reached a political agreement before the final election results were announced.
"I can confirm that I helped draft the deal," Nangaa told France 24 in September 2023. "Tshisekedi is a liar. He knows there was an agreement and he knows what was contained in the deal."
Tshisekedi has maintained that he won the election legitimately.
- What's the fighting in DR Congo all about? 
  - Published5 December 2025
- How Trump wants the US to cash in on mineral-rich DR Congo's peace deal 
  - Published28 July 2025
After the disputed election, Kabila and Tshisekedi entered a power-sharing arrangement that allowed Kabila's coalition to retain control of parliament even after Tshisekedi took office in January 2019.
The arrangement unravelled in December 2020, when Tshisekedi moved to break Kabila's parliamentary dominance and build his own majority. The former allies became rivals, and Kabila went into self-imposed exile in South Africa.
From exile, Kabila's criticism of Tshisekedi grew louder.
He returned to DR Congo in 2025 and appeared in rebel-held Goma. In September that year, a military court sentenced him to death in absentia on charges including treason and financing violence in eastern Congo.
At the time, he rejected the accusations.
Yet another intriguing sub-plot to the announcement is Kabila's relationship with Rwanda's President Paul Kagame.
In the early years of his presidency, ties were strained between DR Congo and Rwanda, which accused its giant neighbour of not doing enough to remove ethnic Hutu militias involved in the 1994 Rwandan genocide from its territory. Their presence in what is now DR Congo has been used to justify Rwanda's repeated military involvement in its giant neighbour, going back to its backing of Laurent Kabila's rebellion.
The M23 was formed in 2012, vowing to stand up for the rights of ethnic Tutsis and to protect them against these militias, but also battling the Congolese army, under the control of Joseph Kabila.
From the start Rwanda was accused of backing them. It has always denied these allegations, as it still does despite overwhelming evidence.
However, relations later improved and Kabila's government worked with Rwanda against the Hutu militias.
Alex Adams, Africa programme director at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said Kabila's appointment as rebel leader could bring his interests into alignment with those of Rwanda's president, even though their objectives differ.
"Kabila wants to recover political influence nationally, while Kagame is primarily concerned with Rwanda's security and strategic position in eastern Congo. This is an alignment of convenience rather than a partnership built on deep trust," he said.
Policy analyst Mayala said Kabila's involvement could help Rwanda counter accusations that it was interfering in Congo's internal affairs.
"This is a former president. It's finally a Congolese rebellion," he said.
Even before the announcement of Kabila as the rebellion's leader, fighting was continuing despite a peace accord overseen by Donald Trump last year.
Part of that deal saw the US sign an agreement to extract DR Congo's mineral wealth and the US has since seemed to side with Tshisekedi by imposing sanctions on various Rwandan officials and bodies, accusing them of prolonging the violence.
Elections are scheduled for 2028, but Tshisekedi has warned that fighting in the east could delay voting.
Against this backdrop, Kabila has questioned whether elections alone can resolve the country's political crisis.
"Does Congo need elections or a revolution?" he asked, arguing that lasting peace required a fundamental overhaul of the country's executive and legislature.
International security analyst Ovigwe Eguegu argues that Kabila is banking on military force to regain political influence, while Tshisekedi seems to be trying to extend his time in office beyond what the constitution allows.
"It looks like the Congolese people are going to lose either way, because neither of these two sides present a credible economic transformation plan for both the eastern Congo and the entirety of the country," Eguegu said.

Winter fuel cuts turned the Welsh against Labour, former leader Neil Kinnock says

Winter fuel cuts turned the Welsh against Labour, former leader Neil Kinnock says
- Published
Former Labour leader Neil Kinnock says the party's welfare policies turned disillusionment with Labour in Wales into "active dislike".
He said that UK government decisions on benefits and winter fuel payments had driven voters in Wales away from the Welsh arm of the party before the country's Senedd election in May.
Lord Kinnock made the comments as part of a Newyddion S4C, external YouTube special on Andy Burnham's first 100 days as prime minister.
Governing "at both ends of the M4" before Wales' parliamentary elections had presented an extra challenge for his party, he said.
- Winter fuel payments fell by 9.3 million before U-turn 
  - Published16 September 2025
He said: "If there is any opposition or resentment to the government on either end of the M4, the other lot are going to pay as well.
"There is no doubt in my mind," he said, that "alienation... had been creeping up".
"It could be a mixture of boredom. It could be a mixture of dislike," Kinnock said.
He said "what turned that into active dislike" had been things "like the withdrawal of the winter fuel allowance, the threats to the welfare system" and not scrapping a cap on two child benefits quick enough.
In June last year, the Labour UK government U-turned on its controversial decision to means-test winter fuel payments for pensioners in England and Wales.
Almost one year later, Labour lost power in Wales in a seismic election in May, returning just nine Senedd members after running the Welsh government for 27 years.
Lord Kinnock, who is the father of Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock, also said he had reservations about devolving justice to Wales - a key demand of the Plaid Cymru Welsh government.
Plaid ministers say it would allow for a more effective system tailored to Welsh communities and better integrated with health, housing and education.
Kinnock said there would no be "much of an argument" against the idea if it meant that "Wales was better protected, that the streets were safer" and "that the justice system was more efficient".
"But those guarantees are absent at the moment," he said.
"Until they exist, until they're in place, the upheaval of creating what would have to be effectively a new system with new management... with an introverted view of the justice system - there would be more downsides than upsides.
"Now that picture might change, but as I can see it now in October 2026, that's where we are, there are more disadvantages than advantages."

article:
New charity uses outdoors to improve mental health

New charity uses outdoors to improve mental health
- Published
A new charity hopes to use activities ranging from cold-water swimming and archery to hill walking and breathwork to improve men's mental health and reduce isolation.
Connect Outdoors is being officially launched alongside an International Men's Day event at the Venture Centre in Maughold, where organisers expect about 80 people to take part in a range of outdoor activities.
The charity said it wanted to gather research on what kind of support men are most likely to engage with, arguing that services have often been designed without asking men first.
Chief executive Kate Bergquist said it had grown out of years of work in social care, public services and outdoor wellbeing programmes.
She said: "We have this abundance of landscape on the island that is never used enough for health.
"This should be embedded into everyone's health and wellbeing routine every week."
'Blue and green health'
Activities on offer include high ropes, bushcraft, mindfulness, breathwork, yoga, archery, ice baths and guided walks, alongside informal spaces designed to encourage men to connect with one another.
The charity is built around what is known as "green and blue health", which encourages people to use natural environments such as forests, beaches and the sea to improve their health.
Bergquist said a key focus would be addressing men's mental health through activities that encourage conversation without making mental health the main selling point.
As part of Sunday's event, attendees will be invited to complete surveys that organisers hope will help identify which activities and approaches are most effective at engaging men.
Among those supporting the event is Gary Thomas, who runs Walking for Wellness and takes people on Manx hill walks where they can talk through any challenges.
The former serviceman and mountain leader said many people found it easier to open up outdoors than in a traditional counselling setting.
"It gives them that opportunity to feel secure and have that ability to open up in an environment that's not oppressive," he said.
"Nature's not clinical, nature's natural."
Thomas said group activities could also help tackle loneliness by creating new social connections.
"We've had people turn up and find their own circle of friends and common interests," he said.
"Then they go off afterwards and explore things together, which is brilliant."
Also involved in the event is Douglas barber Joshua Moore, who completed suicide prevention training through the Lions Barber Collective.
Moore runs Renegade: Cuts and Clobber, and said barber shops often became places where men felt comfortable discussing difficult issues.
"The barber chair is a very special place," he said.
"You can leave feeling a little bit better about yourself, whether that's having a nice haircut, but also just having the opportunity for somebody to listen to you."
Moore said he had seen first-hand the impact mental health struggles could have on families and communities, and wanted to support initiatives aimed at encouraging conversation and early intervention.
The International Men's Day event aimed to introduce men to new activities and point participants to support available to improve both their physical and mental wellbeing.

article:
'It's been killing me!' Celebrity Traitors winners relieved the secret is out

'It's been killing me!' Celebrity Traitors winners relieved the secret is out
- Published
- Spoiler warning: This story reveals details of The Celebrity Traitors final
The winners of Celebrity Traitors have said they are relieved that they no longer need to keep the biggest secret in British TV, as they reunited to celebrate their victory.
Actor Sebastian Croft and comedian Romesh Ranganathan were the last ones standing, with the two faithfuls splitting the £83,000 prize pot between their chosen charities.
"I am feeling good, it's so nice to finally be able to talk about it properly," Croft, known to pals as Bash, told BBC Newsbeat.
The second series of the hit BBC One show finished on Friday, after the original 21 celebs were whittled down to seven finalists.
Reuniting with Ranganathan on the comedian's BBC Radio 2 show on Saturday morning, Croft said they had been worried about being seen together in public before the final.
"We were having dinner and we're not exactly a likely duo and the whole restaurant was like, 'we like you on Traitors and hope you win'," he said.
Croft added that he had woken up on Saturday "with a light sense that I don't have to keep the secret anymore. It's been killing me".
Ranganathan, 48, started his show by saying: "Last night, I don't know if you're aware, was the finale of The Celebrity Traitors and I won."
He said he was "delighted to win" but admitted he probably wouldn't have done so without Croft convincing him to banish the last remaining traitor, King Kenny.
"It's taken the gloss off it slightly that everybody's saying, 'you better thank [Croft] every day for the rest of your life'," he added, with his typical deadpan-humour.
But 24-year-old Croft said he thought Ranganathan had played the game in a "lovely" way.
"People are seeing how smart you are and how you're actually so on it, and you're such a good judge of character," he praised.
The finale drew an average audience of 11.2 million live viewers, and that number will rise when fans catch up on iPlayer. Other recent episodes have been watched by more than 15 million, including catch-up.
"It's been a wild thing to be part of. To be on Uncloaked and sat with Romesh talking about winning was so surreal," Croft said, referencing the BBC's spin-off chat show.
"It's an out of body experience," he added.
- Celebrity Traitors comes to a climax in nail-biting final 
  - Published3 days ago
Croft said he "really wanted to be a traitor", but he turned out to be one of the strongest faithfuls after voting out Kenny - a tactical decision on how to play the show's famous endgame.
"The truth is, I didn't know for sure, but what you're trying to do isn't find a traitor, it's trying to get rid of everyone who isn't the most faithful," he explained.
"I think for both Maya [Jama] and Kenny there was no big thing where I was like 'they're obviously a traitor', but when you boil it down they haven't done anything that's really stuck out enough to make them obviously faithful."
Croft told Newsbeat that he gets why "people are obsessed with the show" and even his family had their own theories about how the game would go.
"So many people get so invested and it's lovely because it becomes so much bigger."
The final saw the celebs successfully banish the remaining traitors - Love Island host Maya Jama and YouTuber King Kenny.
But Kenny shocked viewers when he turned on his fellow traitor Jama at the final round table.
Asked if he's spoken to her since then, Kenny joked that "she's blocked me on everything", and then admitted that he had pre-warned her.
"I already told her that I was going to vote for her and she knew potentially that could be coming," he said.
"It was just too obvious, if I didn't go for her at that point, I think my time would've been coming even quicker than when I went out."
Kenny said he "experienced everything possible in the game" after starting out as a faithful, getting a shield to protect him from murder and then being recruited as a traitor.
But he said he "should have had a better plan for the final" and wasn't prepared for how hard it would be.
"There were so many times when I felt bad pinning stuff on people," he said. "It's a very draining thing to do as a traitor.
"There's moments when there is fun but lying to people for that long is insane, you build friendships as well and feel bad."
On his show, Ranganathan also asked fellow finalist, Little Mix singer Leigh-Anne Pinnock, about taking part in challenges while pregnant.
In the final episode, Pinnock was seen hanging off the side of a helicopter and lowering herself to the ground with a rope.
"I'm just super proud of myself," she said. "It's kind of just shown me that I really can do anything I put my mind to."

article:
Labour MPs pull their punches on immigration changes

Labour MPs pull their punches on immigration changes
- Published
Today's announcement has long been viewed in government as a potential political banana skin.
When the home secretary announced her first version of changes to the settlement system last year, many Labour MPs, including the housing secretary Angela Rayner, voiced their concerns about the plans.
But there was a feeling that Sir Keir Starmer's government was determined to plough on regardless. Shabana Mahmood herself repeatedly expressed how important she believed the reforms were.
But the change of prime minister over the summer gave renewed hope to those unhappy Labour MPs that they could force the Home Office into two changes.
Firstly, social care workers – under the original plans many social care workers would have had to wait 15 years before becoming eligible for settlement.
Secondly, the retrospective nature of the plans – some MPs were uncomfortable at the idea of someone coming to the UK and expecting to be eligible for settlement after five years, but then having to wait longer.
Angela Rayner described that as "un-British" and said the government shouldn't be shifting "the goalposts".
She returned to the cabinet under Andy Burnham as housing secretary and chose to repeat those criticisms in an interview during the Labour Party conference in September.
That was seen as evidence that a debate inside the top levels of government about whether to water down the plans was well and truly rumbling on.
For all the Labour MPs who wanted a change, there were others, particularly those in Brexit-supporting areas, who wanted the home secretary to stick the course.
Some inside government felt nervous about providing what they saw as catnip to Reform and the Conservatives.
All of that added up to one of the more difficult decisions that has had to be taken since Burnham walked through the doors of Number 10.
In the end ministers chose to water down the proposals for care workers – those who arrived before May 2025 and earn at least £25,000 a year will qualify for settlement in five years.
But the retrospective nature of the plans, the thing Rayner described as shifting "the goalposts", hasn't changed.
Despite that, the majority of Labour MPs pulled their punches when Mahmood made a statement in the House of Commons earlier.
Perhaps the strongest pushback came from Rachael Maskell, who is no fan of the retrospective element - but others on the left of the party, including John McDonnell and Diane Abbott, were critical without being scathing.
- Mahmood scraps settlement plans for migrant care workers 
  - Published10 hours ago
- What are the planned changes to immigration rules? 
  - Published2 hours ago
Outside the Commons chamber, the mood among Labour folk was pretty similar to what was said from the green benches.
One would-be critic said that while they personally still had concerns about the plans announced today, they believed the Home Secretary had successfully taken the political sting out of the situation for now.
They said the campaign by MPs and unions had led to a "big win" on settlement for social care workers, but said they were still expecting to hear from constituents negatively affected by the new rules.
One Number 10 source praised Mahmood's "take no prisoners" performance in the chamber, argued she had "found the right balance" and said the announcement had gone down as well as could be expected with Labour colleagues.
Of course, the home secretary will still need to deal with criticism from other parties.
Her opposite number for the Conservatives, Chris Philp, accused Mahmood of a significant U-turn.
Philp highlighted a claim she had previously made – that allowing care workers to reach settlement more quickly could cost the UK £10bn.
The social care workers plans announced today will see around 500,000 people have their path to settlement delayed, that number would have been around 800,000 under the original plans last year.
In an interview with the BBC, Mahmood wouldn't say what sort of financial burden her watering down would result in.
She also refused to confirm whether Burnham had directly asked her to water down the plans.
They are tricky questions that she will have to navigate over the coming weeks.
But the general view within government is that this is one political hurdle that has been successfully jumped.

article:
RFL backs Wilkin's £30m funding plea to Burnham

RFL backs Wilkin's £30m funding plea to Burnham
- Published
The new head of English rugby league has backed a call for Prime Minister Andy Burnham to approve a £30m five-year community funding plan for the sport.
Former England international Jon Wilkin has appealed directly to Burnham and Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy, both rugby league fans, to pledge government money to a rugby league-based social impact project.
Ian Nolan, the new chief executive of the Rugby Football League, has supported Wilkin's plea, issued on BBC Radio 5 Live on Monday.
Wilkin wants Burnham and Nandy to follow the lead of Australia's government, which in July announced it was committing A$250m (£130m), external over 10 years to the Pacific Rugby League Partnership.
That initiative is designed to help create sporting, educational and employment opportunities in Papua New Guinea, Tonga, Samoa and Fiji, and is being led by the Australian Rugby League Commission - the sport's national governing body.
Wilkin has argued that a similar plan for the north of England would benefit deprived communities.
He said: "Australia has recognised rugby league's potential as a vehicle for social change, committing hundreds of millions to developing communities, especially across the Pacific. Why shouldn't Britain show the same ambition for the north?
"The infrastructure already exists, the clubs, the foundations, the school and community relationships are already well established. What's missing is a coordinated strategy and meaningful government investment.
"The ask would be simple: For the government to establish a £30m five-year Northern Rugby League social impact partnership, bringing together the RFL, professional clubs, community foundations, local authorities and government departments.
"The programme would target disadvantaged northern communities."
Nolan, a former Manchester United executive who took up his role with the RFL on 1 October, suggested the social benefits of such an initiative would be felt more quickly because rugby league clubs are already established in their communities.
"When the government normally invest in community hubs and new things to generate something, they tend to be brand new," he said. "And it's really difficult then to attract people to go there because it's a new habit, it's a new place.
"But rugby clubs are already established in the most deprived towns in the UK. And that's the difference. People already go there. Families already rely on them for even just moving around."
BBC Sport has contacted the Department for Culture, Media and Sport for comment.
- The plan England's rugby league bosses hope avoids repeat of World Cup pain 
  - Published2 days ago
- The England team who can still win the Rugby League World Cup 
  - Published1 day ago
'A big opportunity to start a new Ashes-type series'
Nolan announced on Sunday that the RFL will be consulting English rugby league greats to map out a future for the national game under an initiative it is calling One Game, One England.
There is an acknowledgement within the governing body that the sport needs reform from grass-roots level upwards to ensure players of a high enough quality are developed to ultimately benefit the national team.
England's men and women have both exited the Rugby League World Cup at the group stage in the past few days - the first time neither team have reached the tournament's final four.
Wilkin has been highly critical of the set-up of the English game, arguing that an overcrowded Super League calendar - and the resulting lack of a mid-season international window - was a factor in England's disappointing World Cup.
Nolan is seeking ways to give domestic players higher quality fixtures, potentially in the style of the International Origin series - staged between 2011 and 2013, in which England played an Exiles team of overseas Super League players - or the War of the Roses, a representative fixture between Lancashire and Yorkshire, last played in 2003.
"I think there's a big opportunity for us to start to think of new Ashes-type series that we could play against the likes of Australia and New Zealand or even against France, or even domestically," Nolan said.
"We've had flashes with War of the Roses and even the Exiles games. Although they might not be international games, they're actually of an international standard.
"I think what we've done is we've always innovated and come up with these formats, but then we haven't given them a chance to really grow legs like State of Origin has in Australia. So I'm hopeful that we can come up with some innovations."
The World Cup is 'meant to be a festival'
International rugby league as a whole is facing intense scrutiny at present, with the men's and women's calendar largely squeezed in at the end of the club season, in October and November.
Former England international Ryan Hall told BBC Radio 5 Live that the men's World Cup had suffered for being cut down from 16 to 10 teams this year - with Scotland, Ireland, Italy, Greece, Jamaica and Wales all missing out.
That decision was made after Australia stepped in to stage the tournament, which was postponed for a year when scheduled hosts France pulled out for financial reasons.
"I don't think it is a World Cup," Hall said. "The essence of any World Cup in any sport is that it's a festival of the sport.
"Compare it to the football World Cup. Curacao were one of the 48 teams in the World Cup.
"I'm not saying rugby league could get 48 teams in the World Cup because that's not achievable, but [they could] certainly [have] more than 10.
"It's meant to be a festival and showcasing everyone of all levels of different countries who's eligible to play."
Wilkin, meanwhile, suggested that international rugby league's exposure has suffered because of a lack of a free-to-air live television deal.
Premier Sports is showing all the World Cup matches live, with the BBC providing live radio coverage, along with online highlights and live text commentaries on selected games.
Rights were awarded by the International Rugby League, the sport's world governing body. Its chair Troy Grant told the iPaper last week, external that it made the decision to go with Premier because the BBC did not offer enough money, saying he was "disappointed that the BBC didn't stump up". No other free-to-air broadcaster made a suitable offer.
Wilkin said: "The BBC Sport mantra has gone from showing live sport to clipping up digital assets. It's a digital format now.
"And I suppose we're now trying to compete in a market for those scraps of digital content with every other football club in the country. And that is alarming, isn't it?
"The World Cup should have been on the BBC. There is no doubt in my mind as a public service broadcaster, this had so many reasons to be a slam dunk home run to be free to air on the BBC. It had to be."
A BBC spokesperson said: "We must make difficult choices to deliver the savings required while continuing to serve audiences as effectively as possible."

article:
Scrum, foul play, TMO - what can we expect from refs this autumn?

Scrum, foul play, TMO - what can we expect from refs this autumn?
- Published
The number of tries in international rugby has rocketed from six to eight per match in the space of just two years as World Rugby looks to futureproof the game.
It has laid out a vision of a safer and more continuous sport, but with a desire to "embrace the contest" around the breakdown and set-piece.
As part of the manifesto, the sport's world governing body will ramp up fan engagement and has launched a study using biometric sensors to find out what excites and invigorates supporters during matches.
Before the return of the Nations Championship, the top 24 international head coaches met with World Rugby officials outside London to discuss how the game will look over the coming month.
According to World Rugby sources, the coaches highlighted a number of "grey areas"; for example the scrum and breakdown, deliberate knock-ons and foul play in the act of scoring.
However, the coaches were said to be broadly supportive with the number of tries and the increase in ball-in-play time across the international game, which referee insiders attribute to an increase in speed and a consistent approach to the breakdown from officials and players.
Other top referees believe there is now more fatigue in the game, with officials encouraged to form scrums and line-outs within 30 seconds - which has helped with space and scoring opportunities.
As well as a rise in the number of tries scored, the number of penalties kicked has dropped from 3.5 in 2024 to 1.5 in 2026. The data was collected from all Nations Championship and Nations Cup games in 2024, 2025, and 2026.
The day after the coaches summit, a wider group of World Rugby match officials met at a conference attended by BBC Sport. The refereeing of the scrum, foul play and the use of the Television Match Official (TMO) were all high on the agenda.
The scrum presentation was led by former Scotland and Wales coach Jonathan Humphreys, while feted Wales and British and Irish Lions boss Warren Gatland was also in attendance in his capacity as a World Rugby advisor.
Former Kiwi official Brendon Pickerill, who was part of the refereeing team for the 2023 World Cup semi-final, led on foul play and the role of the TMO.
- England's Mitchell ruled out of Nations Championship 
  - Published57 minutes ago
- Fixtures and standings as Nations Championship returns 
  - Published1 day ago
Special focus will be put on the following areas this November:
- Scrum: Both loosehead props must have their right shoulders out to encourage a fair and even contest. The hooker must have his brake foot grounded in the tunnel to ensure scrum stability.
- TMO: Will only come in for "clear and obvious" decisions. They will intervene in a "short window of opportunity" or otherwise will leave calls to the on-field officials. The TMO's remit will largely revolve around foul play and try-scoring situations.
- Foul play: Crackdown on "hip-drop" tackles, with the entry point for sanction a yellow card. This is where a defender grabs an opponent from the side or behind, swings or rotates around them, and drops their body weight directly on to the ball carrier's lower limbs.
- Reinforcement of the law around tacklers dropping to their knees before making a tackle.
- Red cards: As has been the case since its introduction, all offences around the tackle and breakdown deemed to reach a red-card threshold will result in a 20-minute red card. The Head Contact Process - the checklist officials use to sanction foul play - has been updated to include illegal acts at the breakdown.
- A permanent red card is reserved for egregious acts of foul play away from the ball.
The Nations Championship returns on Friday, 6 November as Ireland host Argentina in Dublin, and the tournament culminates in a finals weekend at the Allianz Stadium in Twickenham at the end of the month.
On finals weekend, all matches apart from the showpiece will use a "golden point" scoring system to determine the winner if the teams are level after 80 minutes.
