King to address slavery in Antigua as PM says he is open to possible UK apology

King to address slavery in Antigua as PM says he is open to possible UK apology
- Published
King Charles III is to speak with "unflinching honesty" and "sincere sorrow" on the lasting pain of the transatlantic slave trade during the final leg of his Caribbean tour in Antigua, Buckingham Palace has said.
The King will address Commonwealth leaders on Tuesday in a speech that will touch on the issue.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham earlier wrote in the Guardian, external that he was "open" to the possibility of the UK formally apologising for its role in slavery - a change in the government's stance.
It is understood the Palace was told in advance of Burnham's comments in an opinion piece on Friday night, and that the King has not made any changes to his speech in light of them.
The British government has never formally apologised for slavery or offered to pay reparations.
Burnham has previously stuck with the policy of his predecessors and stopped short of offering any consideration of reparation payments.
In an address to the nation to mark Antigua and Barbuda's independence day, Prime Minister Gaston Browne said the history of slavery was painful and "its consequences have not disappeared with the passage of time".
He said the country's pursuit of reparatory justice deserved "seriousness, sensitivity and sustained international engagement".
Browne went on to say that his government was having these conversations in bilateral discussions with the UK and other Commonwealth countries at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm).
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch described "endless talk about apologies" as a "distraction" from solving current problems.
She told BBC Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: "The transatlantic slave trade happened centuries ago. It is time for the Commonwealth to start looking forwards, not endlessly backwards."
The King will make his speech at the Chogm.
He "will not shy away from confronting the most shameful aspects of the past during this visit", a Palace spokesperson said.
"You may therefore expect him to address them in his speech with unflinching honesty, sincere sorrow and respect for the wider discussions that will be taking place between relevant governments on this issue at Chogm and beyond."
When asked about the King's reaction to the prime minister's comments, the spokesperson said it would "not be appropriate" for the King to address matters of policy relating to the government's position.
The Caribbean tour has again thrust the King into the difficult debates over the UK's colonial legacy in the region.
On his first stop in the Bahamas, the King delivered a speech in which he spoke of the "suffering of the past".
In Guyana, he visited the site of a Slave Rebellion, where hundreds of enslaved people were killed.
Buckingham Palace said it was a moment for the King to learn more about the history of slavery and resistance. His engagements have also covered the environment, opportunities for young people and trade relationships with the UK.
Royal sources have stressed that the decisions around making an apology were a matter for government, not the Palace.
"His Majesty is well practised on the diplomatic tightrope," a Royal aide said. "He is up for challenging visits with complex issues and relationships in play. He sees it as his role to bat for Britain, the Realms and wider Commonwealth."
In a piece for the Guardian published on Friday night, Burnham described the transatlantic slave trade as a "brutal and barbaric violation", and said Britain "must face up to the past".
His separate pledge in his article to strengthen the work of the Commonwealth as an organisation will be welcomed by the King, who views the collection of 56 countries as a powerful vehicle for change.
The King will be giving the opening speech at Chogm, which gathers leaders from those 56 states every two years in a different part of the Commonwealth.
The biennial meeting's official theme this year is Accelerating Partnerships and Investment for a Prosperous Commonwealth.
Queen Camilla is with the King in Antigua and, as the couple attended a church service on Sunday morning ahead of joining celebrations to mark Independence Day on the island, there was a reminder of what the intended focus of the week will be.
Bishop of North Eastern Caribbean and Aruba, Ernest Flemming, told the congregation the "prosperity" of the Commonwealth must be a "shared prosperity".
"True partnership requires mutual respect, it requires listening, it requires fairness."
A Buckingham Palace spokesperson said: "Institutions are under strain across the globe. The Commonwealth has scale and breadth, but is also small enough for leaders to know each other and co-operate together."
The King, they said, "contributes ideas and encouragement on a wide range of issues, delivering practical results which help improve the lives of millions".
Later on Sunday, the King was left drenched and without an umbrella when a torrential downpour interrupted an Independence Day ceremony.
The Queen was swiftly given an umbrella when the rain started, while the King was seen gesturing to be given one of his own.
It has been a difficult few months for the King, with developments surrounding his brother, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, and the publication of a book by his former brother-in-law, Earl Spencer.
In addition, his son, the Duke of Sussex, made a surprise move back to the UK with his wife Meghan and their two children in August.
Asked whether the King was confident that his approach to family matters had been the right one in terms of public attitudes towards the institution, the response was concise. "Yes," a senior aide told the BBC. "That is why he takes the actions he does - and has done."
On the serious allegations that have emerged about Meghan's father, Thomas Markle, the Palace did not want to get involved publicly: "We wouldn't comment on private family matters."
The King is also still being treated for cancer. He was diagnosed in early 2024 and the Palace says he remains on a "positive trajectory".
In hot and humid conditions, he will soon celebrate his 78th birthday and will have carried out about 36 engagements by the end of this nine-day tour of the Caribbean.

Cleft lip filler 'boosts confidence' - but expert warns of exploitation risk

Cleft lip filler 'boosts confidence' - but expert warns of exploitation risk
- Published
Two young women who have turned to dermal fillers after having cleft lip surgery say it has given them confidence after they were both left with scarring.
"Now I feel like I can just go out and talk to anyone, be more social and just be confident," Amber Dorgan, 20, from Neath, said of the treatment, which is offered by the NHS as well as by aesthetic clinics.
But experts and clinics have called for regulations to be introduced for aesthetic practitioners providing the service.
It comes as one psychology academic warned people with a cleft lip were being "deliberately targeted" by the aesthetics industry and "left vulnerable to potential harm and exploitation".
Aesthetics treatment for people with scars involves using filler to reduce their appearance, restore symmetry, and add volume after cleft lip surgery.
Dorgan was born with a cleft lip and has faced hearing difficulties, speech difficulties and bullying at school because of her scars.
She had five operations as a child, as well as regular hospital appointments for speech and language therapy.
Now she receives free dermal filler for life through The Welsh Centre for Cleft Lip and Palate based in Morriston Hospital in Swansea, something she feels extremely fortunate to have.
Dorgan said: "I've always been insecure about how I look, going out and about, I've always had anxiety and I just get nervous.
"Now the lip fillers have made me feel confident in myself a little bit more. It's helped a lot," she said.
Dorgan believes the treatment should be available to everyone with a cleft lip "because it makes you much more confident and happy".
"Before [filler] I was really shy, I wouldn't talk to anyone, I didn't want to leave the house."
What is a cleft lip and palate?
A cleft lip and palate is a condition which is present from birth, external when the upper lip, roof of the mouth, or both, fail to fuse properly during pregnancy.
It affects one in every 700 babies born in the UK and surgery to close the cleft is typically given when a baby is three to six months old.
A cleft lip and cleft palate can cause a number of issues, particularly in the first few months after birth before surgery is carried out.
This can include difficulty feeding, hearing problems, dental problems and speech problems.
The NHS offers lifelong care to those with the condition.
Emily Evans, 21, from Kidwelly in Carmarthenshire, is a stay-at-home mum to her two young children.
She was born with a cleft lip and underwent two surgeries, one as a baby to close her cleft, and one when she was 10 to smooth out her lips.
Growing up she always felt different, as her peers would ask questions about her scar.
"Nobody hates anything more than being different," she said.
"I would often joke I was bitten by a shark."
Evans was discharged from cleft services when she was 17. She was never offered filler treatment for her scars, but was told to keep in contact.
"When I was younger, I was seeing these people who all look perfect and the same, and I didn't," she said.
"So it sort of felt like I needed to sort of get something done."
Evans said she thought aesthetics treatments might help boost her confidence.
"I understand why people might not choose to have filler, it makes people unique, it's nice to have something that makes people different," she said.
But she added: "I think more people would choose to have it if it was a more well-known option."
Both women agree that seeing more people with a cleft lip in the public eye would help young people with the condition.
Evans discovered through social media that treatments were available and found aesthetic practitioners in England offering it to those with scars.
But she said she found a lack of practitioners in Wales.
That was until Evans discovered Summer Rose-Dorland, who runs a clinic in her hometown in Somerset and sometimes runs pop-up clinics in Wales.
After completing extra training she now works with non-profit organisation CleftInject, which help adults with scarring from cleft lip surgery find aesthetic practitioners who understand the condition.
According to Rose-Dorland, some practitioners associated with CleftInject "offer a majority of treatments free of charge", especially for people's first treatments.
She said: "A lot of my clients struggle with their scar, I have messages from people that say that they had to stand side on in photos or when they're talking to someone because they feel like they obviously have to stand a different way."
Some people may choose an aesthetic practitioner over the NHS, she said, as they believe they will have more choice about how their lips will look after.
There are currently no regulations in the aesthetics industry, and some people believe that practitioners like Rose-Dorland should not be allowed to offer and administer these treatments.
Rose-Dorland, who qualified four years ago and said she had since done 20 training courses, said: "I'm a non-medic and I stand for having regulation, I generally think we need it in the aesthetics industry.
"There are some people out there that just do things that are actually quite scary, but I don't think it should be that a non-medic can't practise.
"The person I trained with trains medics, so it's not just non-medic doing these trainings. There's doctors, nurses, midwives, they are all actually doing the same training as well."
Dr Neil Brierley is a consultant cleft and plastic surgeon in the West Midlands Cleft Service.
He said it was important for people who have had a cleft lip or have loved ones with a cleft to engage with NHS teams that provide lifelong support and care.
The surgeon said they could offer an "unbiased" opinion to come to "an appropriate decision between the individual that's seeking assistance and what we feel is their best and worst options".
"What we don't want is to have people who are potentially vulnerable who are looking for maybe a quick fix or a solution to feel that they don't have an option to come back to the NHS," he said.
"And they certainly do not have to, but we are here if they need us."
Brierley said everyone was entitled to their own choice about using aesthetic practitioners, but that it was important to be aware of how to deal with any complications.
"I think it's important to inform your cleft team because it may impact any further treatment that you might need," he said.
"For example if you were wanting revisional surgery, placement of filler in certain areas would prevent certain operations from being possible afterwards."
Brierley said the lack of regulations around injectables and cleft dermal fillers was also concerning.
"I know that there are a number of organisations, various world colleges and specialist societies [which] are trying to bring in regulation in line with government but at the moment the entire field is unregulated, he said.
"There will be many excellent practitioners out there, but it will be impossible to know in advance if there is someone who isn't following best practice."
Dr Nicola Stock is an associate professor whose work focuses on the psychological impact of appearance-altering conditions such as a cleft lip.
Alongside others, she has worked on a project at the University of the West of England's Centre for Appearance Research. They have looked into the use of dermal fillers for people with a cleft, the people who provide them, what experiences and qualifications they have, and how these fillers are being marketed to the community.
Stock said research suggested adults born with a cleft still had concerns with their appearance after surgery.
The research also suggested that more people born with a cleft lip were interested in aesthetics treatments like dermal filler.
She believes the way filler is being marketed on social media is fuelling this steady increase of people seeking out treatment.
"Within the general population, dermal filler has exploded in popularity in recent years, and it's now one of the most common non-surgical cosmetic procedures used worldwide," she said.
"And we believe that this is being fuelled predominately by the aesthetics industry and predominately on social media."
Stock said she was worried that adults with a cleft lip, who have a complex medical history, were being "deliberately targeted" and "left vulnerable to potential harm and exploitation at the hands of the aesthetics industry".
Until there are more guidelines in the sector, Stock recommended that anyone considering dermal filler should research their options and get in touch with their local NHS cleft team or contact the Cleft Lip and Palate Action charity, external.
If you have been affected by the issues raised in this story, information about available help and support can be found via BBC Action Line.

G20 'family photo' cancelled after protests over presence of Russian minister

G20 'family photo' cancelled after protests over presence of Russian minister
- Published
European diplomats have refused to stand for an official photo with Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov at the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting, leading to the American hosts cancelling the planned picture.
Two officials confirmed to BBC the cancellation of the "family photo" scheduled for Friday, which usually include representatives from all nations attending.
"Let me say this directly to the Russian Foreign Minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband later told his Russian counterpart at the summit, accusing his government of killing innocent civilians in Ukraine.
The meeting is being hosted in Atlanta by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Speaking with G20 foreign ministers on Friday, Miliband said that member countries must "work harder to secure just and lasting peace in Ukraine".
"Russia's war continues to cause colossal global harm - including the deaths of thousands of innocent civilians and disruption that hits energy and supplies and worsens food insecurity," he said.
"This war is not simply a test for Europe or for Nato - it requires all of us to apply economic and diplomatic pressure to deprive Putin of the revenues that perpetuate this barbaric war."
Ukraine is not a G20 member but has been invited to similar meetings in recent years. However, Ukraine was not invited to this meeting.
One British official told the BBC: "The UK has a longstanding policy not to have direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since the invasion of Ukraine and we are not about to change that".
Relations between Ukraine and the US have been particularly tense this month, with a diplomatic standoff between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and US President Donald Trump over Kyiv's strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.
A US official said the photo was cancelled "after it became clear some of the delegations were unwilling to participate in a joint photo".
"Rather than allow a ceremonial photo opportunity to become a diplomatic distraction, the US decided to forgo the photo and keep the focus on the substantive discussions," the official said.
In contrast to Ukraine, relations between the US and Russia appear to have partially thawed in recent weeks, as Trump waived some sanctions and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the American market.
The move comes as Trump attempts to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of midterm elections on Tuesday, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.
Ukraine and its European allies have heavily criticised Trump's deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Zelensky called it "a gift" to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged".
Trump said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table in the war between Russia and Ukraine.
Putin has said Russia, which introduced a ban on diesel exports earlier this year, is willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products.
Still, the US State Department this week said it had approved the sale of more than $2bn worth of Patriot missiles to Ukraine, a critically needed munition for the country's air defences to protect itself from Russian attacks.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and currently controls approximately a fifth of Ukrainian territory.
Moscow has in recent weeks intensified its deadly missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities.

article:
Libya's top religious authority rules against wearing Nike clothes

Libya's top religious authority rules against wearing Nike clothes
- Published
Libya's highest religious authority, the Dar al-Ifta, has issued a ruling banning Muslims from buying, selling or wearing clothing bearing the Nike logo.
The ruling, issued by the Tripoli-based institution, states that the US sportswear giant was named after the Greek goddess of victory and that its famous swoosh logo was inspired by her wings.
It argued that wearing clothing displaying the logo amounted to promoting symbols associated "with polytheism," or the worship of more than one god.
Libya is home to the ancient Greek city of Cyrene, where archaeological remains include a statue of the Greek goddess of the same name.
The religious committee also accused Nike of supporting Israel and called for a boycott of companies that back the country.
It referred to a statement issued by its Council for Research and Sharia Studies on 5 November 2023, urging Muslims to boycott Western companies it considers supportive of Israel during the war in Gaza.
The ruling, known as a fatwa, is a religious opinion on a matter of Islamic law. It was approved by Libya's Grand Mufti, Sadiq al-Gharyani.
The BBC has contacted Nike for comment.
The Dar al-Ifta is an influential religious institution based in Tripoli, in western Libya. The country is politically divided, with rival authorities and institutions operating in the east and west after years of conflict following the toppling of long-time leader Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.
Although its religious rulings can carry considerable social influence, they are not necessarily government orders or legally enforceable.
Last year it ruled against wearing jewellery and watches bearing the logo of French luxury jewellery house Van Cleef & Arpels, arguing that its four-leaf clover design was associated with Christian beliefs and the pursuit of good luck, which it said contradicted Islamic teachings.
The latest fatwa does not announce a state ban on Nike products or specify penalties for people who continue to buy or wear them.
Social media reactions were mixed, with some users welcoming the ruling, while others questioned its significance, describing it as ironic or a distraction from more pressing issues.
The ruling comes amid wider debates over the rise of religious conservatism in public life in Libya.
In 2025, authorities in eastern Libya announced restrictions on rap music, theatre and dance performances, citing concerns that some lyrics and performances violated public morals and Islamic values.
The measures were subsequently extended to western Libya.
The Dar al-Ifta has also previously issued religious rulings against music, although there is no clear evidence that it was directly involved in the restrictions on performances.
Nike does not operate an official store in Libya, however Nike-branded products are available through local sportswear retailers.
Sportswear brands such as Nike and Adidas are popular across North Africa.
In Libya, as in other countries in the region, counterfeit versions of popular sportswear brands are also sold in local markets.

How city became home of drum and bass and jungle

How city became home of drum and bass and jungle
- Published
It has been more than 30 years since Bristol with a "rebel" mentality ventured into the unknown, giving birth to the global phenomenon that is jungle and drum and bass music.
The city is still a heavyweight on the scene, inspiring generations of artists to continue pushing boundaries in dance music.
Jungle continues to be developed by artists across London and Bristol, but in its beginnings the sound from Bristol was more expansive and experimental.
It all started in the early 90s, with a DJ collective called Full Cycle, external. They were influenced by Jamaican sound systems, acid house and hip hop, which led to a new sound explosion in the city.

DJ Krust - who was part of the collective - said the music was about "finding expression through our artform which was DJing and producing".
"Rave culture was a huge factor in speeding the tempo up. Once it got to 160bpm and now it's 170bpm, that felt like home for us," he said.
The jungle music they had a hand in creating is still to this day characterised by its speed, syncopated rhythms, breakbeats and ragga, funk and reggae samples.
The Full Cycle collective showcased their new music on the streets at St Paul's Carnival and when they saw people liked it, they made more.
Krust said the beginnings of jungle and drum and bass were a partnership between the open mindedness of the city, the creativity of these DJs and their proximity to rave culture at free parties in the West Country countryside.
"We had to explore and dig deep to hear and see how this experiment can work in real time - that was huge to see," he said.
"When we finally figured out jungle we found our voice," he added.
The collective was made up of DJ Krust, DJ Die, producer Roni Size and DJ Suv - from Krust's original band Fresh Four, best-known for the top 10 hit Wishing on a Star, external.
By this time, Full Cycle had a show on commercial radio station Galaxy Radio - something Krust said became a really "pivotal moment" for the collective.
"It was like the calling for the youth - here you go, here's your new soundtrack, it's British and it's the sound of the streets," Krust said.
"You could feel it in the air that we'd got something and it was travelling through word of mouth - something was brewing and we could all feel it.
"This was the movement, this was the shift," he added.
In 1997, Full Cycle formed the live act Reprazent and released the album 'New Forms' which included the hit track Brown Paper Bag, external.
Later that year they made history by becoming the first drum and bass group to win the Mercury Prize - firmly putting Bristol, jungle and drum and bass on the musical map.
Jungle went on to become the precursor to drum and bass music which is also fast, but has a signature simple kick and snare pattern that sits over rolling basslines.
The two genres are sometimes used interchangeably, but both still have a distinct sound.
DJ Die, who was also a member of Full Cycle, said Bristol was at the heart of the movement because of its "rebel" and "do it yourself mentality".
"It hasn't seemed to have died yet, it's more healthy than ever. A lot of people move to Bristol for the music scene," he said.
"There's so many great producers here, there always have been - it's a hotbed for production," he added.
DJ Die attributed the longevity of the city's jungle scene to sound systems that have been passed down through generations and new talent inspired by Bristol's artists.
"You've got these grassroots soundsystems handed down from old ravers like Spiral Tribe," he said.
"You've also got to shout out St Paul's because that's had such a big influence and the Jamaican community there."
The scene is thriving now more than ever as new artists such as Nia Archives - who was discovered by DJ Die - make waves in the industry.
Nia's second album was shortlisted for the Mercury Awards, she headlined Bristol festival Love Saves the Day in 2025 and had also played a number of the biggest festivals in the UK, including Glastonbury.
'Rich cultural undertones'
Another artist continuing the city's legacy is Sherelle.
She said DJ Die and DJ Krust were direct influences on her high-tempo music, which includes a blend of footwork, jungle and drum and bass.
"If you were to separate Die, Krust and Roni from everyone, they have their own individual sound and when they come together, it also builds on another sound," she said.
"Bristol is such an off-kilter place. It's a place whereby exploration is so expansive.
"The city is rich in cultural undertones and you can tell that they're making music from the heart.
"There needs to be a lot of focus and emphasis about actually how special and important Bristol is to the current music, culture and climate that we've got now," she said.
Roni Size and Reprazent will perform their seminal album New Forms live across the UK next year to celebrate 30 years since its release.

article:
Why Scottish football is struggling to produce young talent

Why Scottish football is struggling to produce young talent
- Published
Calum Ferguson achieved what thousands of young footballers dream of when he played for his boyhood club, Inverness Caledonian Thistle, in the Scottish Premiership.
Yet the 31-year-old looks back on his career as proof of a difficult truth about youth development in Scotland.
Ferguson graduated from Caley Thistle's academy at 18 but played just two games for the first team before moving to lower league clubs and then to Canada and New Zealand to try to get top-flight football.
Now a development officer with Alba Football Alliance, he believes Scottish football continues to sell young players and their families the promise of a pathway from the academies to the first team, which for most will never be a reality.
"Parents believe their boy, or their girl, will get to the first team - that they will be a star in football," he told BBC Scotland's Eorpa programme.
"That is not the truth at all.
"You just fall away from the game and your life changes overnight."
His comments come as Scottish football wrestles with a growing concern over the number of homegrown players who are making it to the top of the game.
In September, all 42 SPFL clubs gathered in St Andrews for a summit to discuss why so few young Scottish players are making the grade at elite level.
Data presented to the clubs showed that Scottish players under the age of 21 made up just 4.1% of minutes played in the Scottish Premiership.
By comparison, in the Danish Superliga, a league of the same size, the figure was 15.1%.
In the first round of fixtures in the Scottish Premiership this season, 28% of the starters were born in Scotland.
A stark contrast to similar sized Norway, where homegrown players made up 72% of the starting 11s on their opening weekend.
This is because Norway has strict quotas.
Its league rules state that a club's full squad must include 16 homegrown players and a matchday squad can have a maximum of nine foreign players.
Nicklas Fuglestad is 20, and regularly plays for Viking FK, based in the Norwegian city of Stavanger. He believes quotas are good for the game.
"Everyone I know is very happy with how the Norwegian football league operates," he says.
"It makes it a bit easier for a young player to move up from the academy and make the step into A-league football."
Viking turned their focus to developing academy talent nearly a decade ago, after they were relegated to the second division.
After finishing champions last year, they have made it to the league stage of the Champions League, where they recently started eight Norwegians in their line-up, four of whom had been in their academy.
Another three from their academy came off the bench.
With both Viking FK and Bodø/Glimt in Europe's top competition this year, it could be said that Norway is going through a golden generation.
Their national team reached the World Cup quarter final – and that wasn't just down to man mountain Erling Haaland.
However, there's more to Norway's success than quotas, according to Håkon Grøttland, head of player development at the Norwegian Football Federation.
He says two big changes over the past 25 years have made a huge difference - the increase in the use of artificial pitches, and more resources being put into coaching and talent development.
Grøttland says artificial pitches allowed football to develop from a summer game to a year-round sport, turning Norway into a proper football nation.
Between 2016 and 2025 alone, 539 such pitches were built, with another 586 redeveloped.
Nearly all are open and free to use, so long as official games aren't taking place.
Made in Scotland
With Scottish football facing a talent crisis, Calum Maclennan examines the SFA’s youth development plans and discovers what Norway’s successful system can teach Scotland.
Grøttland says changes to player development have provided the second boost to the country's game.
"In the period 2010 to 2020 we used a lot of resources, hired a lot of talent coaches, and built some talent systems in Norway, where I think it's quite unique because it's a system that link grassroots football and top club football together," he says.
That talent system is Landslagskollen - or the National Team School (NTS) - that was established in 2013, following the country's failure to qualify for Euro 2012.
It's neither an academy nor a centralised school, but a national development structure connecting grassroots clubs, districts, top clubs and the federation.
Eleven of the 15 players who played in Norway's 2-1 win over Brazil in the round of 16 at this year's World Cup were part of the NTS pathway from under-15 or under-16s.
Despite a disappointing group campaign, a return to the World Cup after decades in the desert was a significant achievement for the Scotland national team.
The question now is whether the next generation can be developed.
The Tartan Army will not want to wait another 28 years.
At the meeting in St Andrews in September, the Scottish FA proposed quotas, as well as financial incentives, in an attempt to increase game time for young Scottish players.
The governing body put forward three suggestions:
- Two under-21 Scotland-eligible players to start in all Scottish Cup matches
- Two under-21 Scotland-eligible players to start in all Premier Sports Cup matches
- Clubs should field Scotland-eligible Under-21 players for an average of 60 minutes in each league game across all four SPFL divisions (6% of available minutes).
Two votes were to take place on the proposals.
The first, on the issue of Scottish Cup rule adoption, should have happened in October at the SFA's AGM, but did not take place.
The SFA now says it is expected to happen in mid-December.
The second vote is due to take place at the SPFL's annual meeting this month.
Adoption of the league and premier sports cup recommendations require 11 out of 12 top flight clubs to vote in favour – a high bar.
St Mirren manager Craig McLeish told the BBC he did not believe the proposals went far enough – although he said he didn't think they would get voted through if they were more extreme.
"It's probably a little bit unfortunate, the governance in this country, that we can't just be told by one power, look this is what's happening," the 36-year-old said.
The young manager came into his role on an interim basis in March, before landing a permanent contract in the summer.
By the time BBC Eòrpa interviewed him in September, he'd given out six debuts to homegrown players.
Having worked in academy football for years, he says he could not sit where he is now and not give youngsters opportunities if they are ready.
A common argument against playing young players is the jeopardy that comes with managing in the Scottish Premiership.
Managers don't want to risk untried young players when they know that a handful of defeats could cost them their job.
"Yeah, you've got a longer term contract but you know that can be short-lived," Craig says.
"It's results based and I'm totally fine with that. I don't fear the negative outcome that can come.
"I trust them," he says.
In recent years, top players such as Andrew Robertson, John McGinn, and Ryan Christie, have all had a significant grounding in the Scottish Premiership before moving on to greater things.

Elon Musk is a 'real genius', Putin says after satellite talks with SpaceX boss

Elon Musk is a "real genius", Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Wednesday after revealing the two are in "close" contact about satellite technology.
The remarks came during the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, during which Putin discussed Russia's own satellite internet project Rassvet, which provides internet connections to people from satellites.
"He's a genius, a real genius," Putin said of Musk, according to a translation of his remarks by the BBC. "We are in close contact with our American partners, including Mr. Musk."
Starlink is part of Musk's company SpaceX. The company did not respond to a request for comment.
Putin added that it was important for Russia to be in contact with Musk so Rassvet and Starlink satellites do not "interfere with each other in orbit".
"We and our American partners value this mutually, and despite all the political questions, we are working hard," he said.
Starlink has launched roughly 13,000 of its satellites, according to the company. By contrast there are only a couple of dozen Rassvet satellites currently in orbit, according to online satellite trackers.
The Russian Embassy in South Africa said on Wednesday Rassvet is "Russia's Starlink alternative" and "marks only the country's first steps in this field".
"Russia maintains close contacts with the US on space, including with Elon Musk," the embassy wrote.
Putin's comments about Rassvet and Starlink were made as the US and Russia appear to be growing closer, even as it approaches five years since Putin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Ukraine relied on Starlink internet in its efforts to keep Russia's forces at bay. But its military last week suddenly suffered Starlink connectivity problems, something Musk has admitted SpaceX did intentionally.
US President Donald Trump earlier this month said he'd struck a deal with Russia to import diesel in an effort to lower gas prices that have skyrocketed due to the US war with Iran.
Then Trump waived certain sanctions against Russia that were set to take effect.
Not long after, a US citizen was released from Russian custody, with US envoy Steve Witkoff referring to Putin as a "humanitarian".
Musk was born in South Africa and then immigrated to Canada before settling in the US. All of his business ventures, including Tesla, SpaceX and Starlink, are based in America, with most operating out of California and Texas.
The billionaire, and off and on again trillionaire, has been one of the biggest political allies and financiers of Trump and other Republican US politicians.

Chris Mason: Budget felt cautious despite its range of small measures

Chris Mason: Budget felt cautious despite its range of small measures
- Published
This was a Budget I would describe as a flotilla of small measures.
Westminster is poring over the 150 page Red Book, external in which the Budget is printed and also what is formally called the Economic and Fiscal Outlook published, external by the watchdog and forecaster the Office for Budget Responsibility, the OBR.
The Red Book sets out the measures the chancellor will implement and how much they will cost. There are 98 of them, considerably more than normal and more than in either of Rachel Reeves' budgets.
But nearly all of them are pretty small in terms of their impact on the Treasury's spreadsheets.
This gets to the heart of why those involved in compiling this Budget have been irritated by commentary in the build up to it suggesting there would be nothing to see in John Healey's address – but also why those suggesting that were arguably onto something as well.
Firstly, as expected, it was a much smaller Budget in overall tax and spending terms than plenty of recent ones have been. But there were plenty of measures here and there which the chancellor will hope enough people notice and value – and others that some will likely curse.
There are more taxes for savers and landlords, for instance, and too for banks.
When a government has promised, as Labour have, to not put up income tax, national insurance or VAT – the big revenue generators – they end up looking elsewhere if they conclude putting up tax is necessary.
That runs the political risk of choosing particular sectors who might respond rather noisily. Think of the plenty of farmers who were incensed by the changes to inheritance tax Rachel Reeves was keen on.
- Budget 2026: Key points at a glance 
  - Published5 days ago
- Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you 
  - Published5 days ago
- Chancellor begins to deliver his first Budget 
  - Published6 days ago
The central challenge for Healey, which he shares with his recent predecessors, is the public finances are in a mess and so are the personal finances of so, so many households.
And there is a recurring sense of déjà vu in the language of the OBR. "The UK's economic and fiscal position remains very challenging," it says, with a splash of understatement, adding that "there have been further adverse developments" this year with in the conflict in the Middle East.
As for what happens, next, well, frankly, who on earth knows. Or, as the OBR puts it: "The outlook for the economy and the public finances is uncertain, with significantly better or worse outcomes of broadly equal probability."
The Budget book argues that "the UK economy is showing signs of resilience" but it is also true that the national debt, tax burden, inflation and interest rates are high, going up or both – and there could yet be further economic shocks that make things worse.
What happens, for instance, in the Middle East, once the mid term elections are done in America and the result of the Israeli general election is clear?
In short, the chancellor felt constrained in his capacity to act and his capacity to make a noticeable positive difference is perhaps constrained even more so – because any intervention, even expensive ones, may merely make a grim situation a bit less bad, rather than things actually feeling better.
Mitigating the bad is arguably a noble political aim, but it costs money and potentially comes with little political upside.
Instead there is this fleet of smaller measures that the government will hope gives their MPs something to try to sell – while acknowledging that they are not world changing.
Luke Tryl, the UK Director of the More in Common think tank, says: "The softly populist tone of this budget is likely to land well with the public. The Chancellor targeted groups the public have little sympathy with - banks, landlords, gambling companies and vape shops - and turned it into cost-of-living support, rate relief for small businesses and ensuring the state pension isn't taxed."
He adds: "Crucially, the chancellor may have avoided the biggest potential trap of the Budget - being seen to offer energy support for those on benefits and incurring the ire of the squeezed middle, who think they work hard but are left to fend for themselves.
"Instead, by offering support to all of those on Council Tax bands A to D, he is able to reassure them that the government will support them too."
The reaction of the opposition parties, from a range of different political perspectives, amounts to a critique that this Budget was thin.
The government counters that it is one piece in the emerging jigsaw of detail from the new-ish prime minister and his chancellor – with a plan help young people into work and cut benefits before Christmas, alongside a big picture sense of what the UK's long term relationship with the European Union could look like and a 10 year vision from Andy Burnham.
In summary, this felt like a cautious Budget. One critical friend of the government suggested to me this would be a "Mr Sensible Budget" – their hope and expectation that it might be shorn of bells and whistles, but shorn of timebombs too. Let's see.

article:
Why has Caf abandoned plans to hold Afcon every four years?

Why has Caf abandoned plans to hold Afcon every four years?
- Published
After a shock announcement 10 months ago that the Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) would be held every four years, the governing body of football on the continent has reversed course.
The Confederation of African Football (Caf) will instead retain the tournament's traditional biennial staging, with its president Patrice Motsepe saying the U-turn was based on "advancing, protecting and promoting" the interests of the African game.
The first indication that the frequency of Afcon was being reconsidered came at Caf's strategy conference in Cape Verde earlier this month.
Questions are now being asked about the decision-making process and what this means for the future of African football.
Why was the planned change controversial?
Afcon has predominantly been held every two years since its first edition in 1957, barring two three-year gaps in the 1960s and one year between the 2012 and 2013 tournaments.
On the eve of the 2025 finals in Morocco, Motsepe announced all that would change from 2028.
The South African said the shift to a four-year cycle was, in part, to help the global calendar "be significantly more synchronised and harmonised".
In recent years Afcon has been staged midway through the European club season, leading to recurring disputes over the release of African players.
Fifa general secretary Mattias Grafstrom was sitting aside Motsepe when the plan was announced, and critics highlighted that the scheduling change favoured football's world governing body more than the African game.
"I think the general sentiment around the continent has been that the two-year cycle has served the continent very well," Football Association of Zambia (Faz) official Sydney Mungala told the BBC.
"The idea of pushing it to a four-year cycle was a bit of a surprise, maybe a concern, to the bulk of the African federations."
- Afcon to return to two-year cycle after Caf U-turn 
  - Published4 days ago
- Afcon to be held every four years from 2028 
  - Published20 December 2025
What were the benefits of the switch?
Afcon has developed into Caf's biggest revenue generator, with a profit of $114m (£85m) forecast for Afcon 2025, up from $75m (£56m) for the previous finals in Ivory Coast.
In its stead, an annual Africa Nations League involving all 54 countries on the continent was proposed. Motsepe described the ambition as creating a "world-class competition every year".
The idea was to move beyond Caf's heavy reliance on Afcon and develop a more sustainable commercial model which could support football development.
Yet the last time an ambitious alternative competition took place in Africa, it failed to deliver on its financial promise and was quickly ditched.
The Africa Super League, announced by Caf in 2022 to revolutionise continental club competition, and with projected annual revenues of $200m (£149m), was discontinued after just one edition.
Motsepe later acknowledged that commercial deals fell short of expectations.
"We didn't proceed as quickly because the partners that were giving us money were not giving us the deals we thought we would be happy with," he said.
Why the U-turn on Afcon?
The decision to move to a four-year cycle was taken at a meeting of Caf's executive committee last December - without being tabled at a general assembly where all member nations are represented.
"These kinds of decisions should be put to the general assembly, they should be debated and discussed for months at a time," Algerian journalist Maher Mezahi told the BBC.
"Afcon is the locomotive by which Caf funds all of its other competitions."
Caf subsequently asked its 54 associations to express a preference between proceeding with the four-year format or retaining the original schedule, and the executive committee eventually voted to restore the status quo.
Motsepe said the decision was in the "best interest of African football" and would contribute to the development and growth of the sport.
He also admitted misgivings about the new Nations League, with concerns it would require "several years" before it could make "the substantial financial and football development contributions" to help the continental game be "self-supporting".
How does Fifa fit in?
Fifa president Gianni Infantino first publicly proposed holding Afcon every four years in February 2020, an idea Motsepe rejected after he was elected as Caf president 13 months later.
That has not stopped the South African cultivating a close relationship with his counterpart and Infantino's drive to expand the Fifa World Cup to 48 teams - and in the process increase African representation at the tournament - has won him backing across the continent.
Yet the Swiss' position has been under threat since his plan to sell stakes in Fifa's competitions was leaked in July.
Since then Infantino has been busy shoring up his power base ahead of his re-election bid, including at Caf's strategy meeting this month.
"He came to Cape Verde to generate support and, by and large, Africa gave him that support," Mezahi said.
"But I think they did that in a quid pro quo - they gave him the support in return for some concessions.
"And I think the main concession was the return of the Africa Cup of Nations [to a two-year cycle].
"It shows that Africa is willing to assert its influence and look after its interests, even in the face of the global game's interest."
- Infantino says he is backed by 'vast majority' 
  - Published24 October
- Does Africa still back Infantino as Fifa president? 
  - Published6 August
Why is Afcon revenue so important?
Afcon is Caf's financial lifeline, accounting for a substantial share of the governing body's income.
Morocco 2025 was projected to generate $192m (£143m), representing 66% of Caf's total revenue from competitions across men's, women's and age-group football.
For many FAs, Afcon's importance extends far beyond the tournament because they cannot always rely on consistent government or corporate investment.
"We have 11 [Zambian] national teams and only two are partly sponsored by government," Faz official Mungala said.
"The rest have to be supported from the FA's coffers. We actually fund some of these programmes from the support that we get from Caf and Fifa."
What about upcoming Afcons?
The 2027 Afcon is scheduled to be held in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda from 19 June to 17 July next year.
Yet, on a visit to East Africa in September, Motsepe called for a "heightened sense of urgency" in order to make sure stadiums and supporting infrastructure are ready on time.
The following Afcon will be held just one year later in 2028 - a decision Caf made when planning for the switch to a four-year cycle and which it has stuck with.
An announcement on where and exactly when the finals will be held is yet to be made.
Subsequent tournaments will be held in 2031 and 2033 to avoid clashes with the World Cup.
The proposed kick-off date for the Africa Nations League, meanwhile, is September 2029.
Motsepe's latest statement suggests the new competition will also be held every two years - rather than annually as he initially announced last December – but that begs the question of how space will be found for the fixtures to be played in an Afcon year from 2031 onwards.
While debate continues around the game's congested calendar, Caf's U-turn on scheduling has at least protected the tradition of Africa's biggest sporting showcase.
It also exposes, however, the challenge of finding a workable financial model which benefits African football as well as the demands of the global game.

What is the Nations Championship?
The Nations Championship pits the northern hemisphere teams who compete in the Six Nations - England, Ireland, Scotland, Wales, France and Italy - against southern hemisphere giants South Africa, New Zealand, Australia and Argentina, plus invited sides Fiji and Japan.
All teams play each of the six nations in the opposing hemisphere once, with three rounds of fixtures having already been staged in July and now another three in November.

article:
A simple guide to the midterms

What are the US midterms? A simple guide
- Published
The midterm elections are under way in the US, as voters take part in a ballot that could have a major impact on the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.
What are the midterms?
Americans will choose members of Congress, which is made up of two parts - the House of Representatives and the Senate.
Elections take place every two years, and when they happen in the middle of the president's four-year term of office, they are called the midterms.
A key task of Congress is to create and pass federal laws - laws that apply nationwide.
The outcome of the midterms will decide which political party - Trump's Republicans or opposition Democrats - controls Congress and how easy it is for the president to carry out his plans.
The results are also seen as a measure of how happy people in the US are with the president's performance so far.
Who is being elected?
All 435 members of the House - the lower chamber of Congress - will be elected. They serve fixed terms of two years. The House is commonly where proposed laws are introduced and debated.
Meanwhile, 35 of 100 seats in the Senate, the upper chamber, will also be up for grabs. Senators serve six-year terms. Among other jobs, they approve or block proposed laws that have been received from the House.
On the same day, voters across much of the US will also choose state-level politicians. Governor contests in California, Florida, Georgia and Michigan will be among the most closely watched.
What are the key issues?
The US economy is on the minds of many voters struggling with the price of fuel, groceries, housing and healthcare.
Inflation remains above the level targeted by the US Federal Reserve, partly down to the war that the US and Israel started with Iran in February.
Democrats argue Trump's programme of trade tariffs has also pushed up prices for Americans.
Immigration is another key issue. Republicans say Trump has delivered on a major campaign pledge in 2024 by tightening the border and launching a widespread - and often controversial - crackdown on illegal immigration.
Concerns over AI have grown in urgency in recent weeks. Senior politicians from both parties have agreed on the need to regulate it - setting themselves in opposition to Trump, who has rejected the idea of laws to control development of the technology.
What is at stake?
Congress is one of the three branches of government, alongside the presidency and the judiciary. Control of it matters for the shaping of legislation.
Both the House and Senate are currently held by the Republican Party. But its majority is a slender one. They have 218 seats in the House, which is the minimum number needed to control it, plus one independent who votes with them.
In the Senate, they have 53 seats. The upper chamber will only change hands if the Democrats win 51 seats, which would overcome a tie-breaking vote by the vice-president - currently a Republican - in the event of both sides getting 50.
If opposition Democrats win back control of at least one chamber, they will gain power to bring their own laws to the floor.
Who might win?
Voters have tended to "punish" the party of the president in the past and vote against them.
Recent polling shows a low approval rating for the president. He began his second term as president with an approval rating of just over 50%, according to polling resource website Silver Bulletin, but in early October it was sitting at about 37%. Meanwhile 61% disapproved of him.
But not all seats in each chamber are competitive. Some are a safe bet for Republicans or Democrats.
The Cook Political Report, which analyses campaigns and elections, suggests that a limited number of districts are "toss-ups" that could be won by either party. Its latest update identifies 18 House districts, including in Florida and Michigan, and six Senate races, including in Alaska and Texas.
The vote is more unpredictable this year because of a battle between the two parties over the way voting districts in the House of Representatives are drawn.
Republicans tried to gain an advantage by creating more favourable electoral maps in certain states and Democrats followed suit.
What does it mean for Trump?
If the Democrats win either the House or the Senate then Trump will find it difficult to get any laws through Congress.
So his domestic plans could be frustrated, although he has found ways to exercise power without his wider party.
Democratic control of either chamber would also mean they could use committees to investigate aspects of the Trump presidency. Corruption allegations, the new White House ballroom and ICE tactics could be subject to scrutiny.
There is also a debate within the Democratic Party about whether to impeach Trump, which means to bring charges in Congress that will form the basis for a political, not criminal, trial.
If the Republican Party stays in control of Congress, Trump will be able to keep going with his plans for the remainder of his time in office.
What does it mean for the 2028 election?
The president's name is not on the ballot during the midterm elections, though Trump has urged Republicans to pretend that it is by voting for him as an endorsement of his actions so far.
Whichever way the results fall, commentators are likely to use them to make arguments about how voters feel about the direction of the country under Trump's leadership.
Trump cannot run to be president a third time. After the midterms, we can expect speculation to start building about who might be his successor as the Republican presidential nominee for 2028 - and who might compete against that person for the Democrats.

article:
Why MPs keep talking about an early election despite Burnham's denials

Why MPs keep talking about an early election despite Burnham's denials
- Published
Wander through Parliament at the moment, and there is one issue many MPs want to discuss: is there going to be an early general election?
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has nearly three years to go before he has to call an election and he has repeatedly and categorically ruled out going to the country early.
But the discussion persists - and many think it is a real possibility.
After Wednesday's Budget, that talk has only increased.
As one former Labour minister puts it: "Why would you sprinkle round a few politically smart (albeit small) giveaways now but delay all the really tough and unpopular decisions on welfare and defence to an autumn spending review if you weren't creating a window for a spring election?"
Others have also suggested to the BBC that Chancellor John Healey's plans felt like a pre-election programme.
They argue the Budget contained voter-friendly measures on the cost of living, such as £100 help for many with energy bills and extending VAT cuts on electricity bills. Young voters are to be offered help on to the housing ladder, through the Your First Home scheme.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has questioned why some-voter friendly measures announced by Healey will only be in place until the summer.
Could it be, she suggests, that the prime minister plans to go to the country before these measures run out?
(The counter-argument to this is that household energy pressures are less severe in the summer.)
Some MPs also point out the prime minister is popular at the moment and Labour is leading in most polls.
Reform, who had led the polls for some time, have had a difficult few months.
Will things ever look better for Burnham, they ask.
Then there are the difficult spending decisions faced by the chancellor.
How to find the money to fund an increase in defence spending? How to bring down the welfare bill? How to cut departmental spending to make the books add up?
"He is delaying all of the bad stuff until after a poll," reckons one Conservative MP.
The Liberal Democrats have claimed there is a 30% chance of a general election on 10 December. The party has been put on a "snap election footing".
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has said he thinks there could be a general election in May.
It is worth pointing out predictions of an early election are coming more from opposition MPs, some of whom might be keen to cause a bit of trouble.
An election has to be held by August 2029, but some Labour MPs have said they are so convinced an early election is on the way that they have told their staff to prepare for one in the first half of next year.
- Healey unveils £100 for energy bills and bank tax in first Budget 
  - Published5 days ago
- Burnham rules out early general election in next 12 months 
  - Published5 days ago
There are, though, plenty of arguments against a general election in the next year.
Firstly, the prime minister has repeatedly ruled it out in interviews.
On Wednesday, he said explicitly that there would not be an election in the next 12 months. Politicians can change their minds, but one veteran Tory concludes a change of heart, after emphatic denials, would be too damaging to "Brand Burnham".
Next – despite the chancellor's giveaways on the cost of living – the overall economic outlook is "pretty grim", in the words of the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).
Real Household Disposable Income looks set to fall in the coming months. Interest rates are predicted to go up. Nobody knows for sure what will happen next in the Middle East – and whether things could get worse before they get better.
Burnham has pledged a rewiring of the British state. He plans to set out a 10-year plan in the coming weeks. But without more detail, some wonder if voters will know enough to make a judgement.
On more than one occasion, Burnham has vowed to bring about the most significant change in British politics in four decades.
One former Labour minister could not detect much in this week's Budget to that effect, saying: "It's not an end to 40 years of neoliberalism is it?"
That message was echoed by another Labour MP: "It was too low key to be an election Budget."
"It was a disappointment, a play it safe, keep everything ticking over Budget… crumbs for all," said another.
"No early general election after that Budget. We would be toast."
Some argue Burnham would benefit from having his own mandate, with his own manifesto. But given the size of Labour's general election win last time, many MPs think it's inevitable that Labour will lose ground.
Others say that if Burnham's government does feel the need to break Sir Keir Starmer's manifesto commitments by increasing taxes, they should just do it, instead of holding an election.
"If we need an election to put up taxes then arguably that's easier to do now with our massive majority than to start an election campaign on the basis that we're calling it in order to put up taxes," said one Labour MP.
"People act like a manifesto is a legal document written in blood. Plenty of governments have broken lots of manifesto promises."
Remember too that the prime minister has promised a detailed plan on social care in England, which is some way off. He has also not decided how far he wants to go in taking the UK closer to the EU.
There is a lot for Number 10 to weigh up.
Labour might look back to Gordon Brown, who did not call an early election when he was prime minister and doing well in the polls. If he had gone to the country in October 2007, might Labour have stayed in power?
But there will be plenty of others who look to Theresa May. She opted for a snap general election in April 2017, after mulling the decision over on a walking holiday in Wales. Despite flying high in the polls, the Tories lost their majority.
So will Burnham do it?
He might be tempted. But there are plenty of risks that mean it would be far from an easy choice.

Young athlete and former minister among victims of Spain train crash

Young athlete and former minister among victims of Spain train crash
- Published
A 24-year-old athlete and a former government minister are among the victims of a deadly train crash that killed 69 people near Urda in central Spain on Wednesday morning.
The crash, between a high-speed Renfe train and a stationary Iryo train on the same track, also injured more than 100 people, many seriously.
The impact caused carriages to derail, and there are fears the death toll could still rise, with reports of family members searching for missing relatives in hospitals across the region.
The bodies of those killed have been taken to the main forensics institute in Toledo, where families have been giving DNA samples to help identify them.
The crash is the second rail disaster in Spain this year, and the worst in the country's history since 2013.
Who are the victims?
Julieta Gallego
Julieta Gallego, 24, was a Spanish long jumper who competed for Madrid athletics club, AD Sprint.
"The entire club is heartbroken," it wrote on Instagram.
The Royal Spanish Athletics Federation (RFEF) announced her death, external, expressing its condolences to her family, friends and teammates.
Gallego regularly competed in Spanish club championships, local media outlet ABC reported, external, and had a best jump of 5.9m (19ft 3in).
Raúl Chapado, president of RFEF, told the outlet that her death is a "blow that strikes at the very heart of the athletics family."
"Today, the sport mourns the passing of Julieta, a life ahead of her that has been unjustly extinguished".
Fátima Báñez
The death of former employment minister Fátima Báñez, 59, was confirmed by the Spanish Confederation of Business Organizations (CEOE), which she chaired.
"Her warmth, generosity, and commitment leave an indelible mark on businesses and the entire CEOE team," it said in a statement.
Báñez served in the government under former Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy from 2011 until 2018, and was the first woman to hold the role. In 2012, she introduced controversial labour reforms that made it easier for companies to fire people, sparking mass protests across the country.
Following news of her death, Madrid regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso paid tribute to her, saying she would be "deeply missed".
"Spain loses a great political figure," she said.
José Manuel Chacón
The Civil Guard confirmed the death, external of its officer José Manuel Chacón, 31, in a statement expressing its "deepest condolences" to his family, friends and colleagues.
Antonio Montero Domínguez
Finance and tax lawyer, Antonio Montero Domínguez, was remembered as a "meticulous professional" and "tireless worker" by legal news website, El Derecho, external.
His death was confirmed by Spain's tax authority, external, where he had been an inspector between 2012-2016.

article:
How the US midterm results could unfold - as millions of Americans head to the polls

Three scenarios for how the US midterm results could unfold
- Published
After months of campaigning and billions of dollars spent on the US midterms, election day is finally here.
According to the latest public opinion surveys, Democrats appear to have the upper hand - but polls haven't always been reliable, and this year could have its own share of surprising results.
In broad strokes, however, there are three possible outcomes after Americans have their say.
Here's a look at what they could be, what the early signs might be as results come in (which you can follow later on our results page) and what it could mean for the country.
1. A big Democratic wave
If history is any guide, midterm elections tend to favour the out-of-power party.
Add in what polls suggest is a historically unpopular president, a war with Iran that has driven up consumer costs and some controversial policies - like aggressive immigration enforcement and support for data centre construction - and you have the conditions for a so-called electoral wave.
In this first scenario, a huge wave is exactly what happens.
Democrats could not only take control of the House of Representatives but far surpass the 218 seats needed for a majority. They may win not only the dozen or so races that election analysts rate as too-close-to-call, they could also flip some seats in more solidly conservative terrain.
In the Senate, this scenario would require Democrats to win all or most of the current crop of races that are toss-ups, including some in traditionally conservative states. There would be at least one eye-popping victory in a place that hasn't elected a Democrat in a generation, Texas, or in nearly a century in the case of Kansas.
If this did happen, Democrats wouldn't just take control of the Senate, they would do so with a seat or two to spare. This might avoid any drama around a potential legal challenge by Republicans in Alaska where a judge dismissed a Trump administration lawsuit over two Dan Sullivans being on the ballot.
Democrats might accomplish this by boosting turnout of their voters and winning independent voters by sizable margins. This would reverse Trump's 2024 inroads with Hispanic voters and young men. Some Republican voters might also support the Democrats or just stay home.
This kind of a result would represent a stinging rebuke for Trump and his Republican Party, setting up two years of conflict between a newly invigorated Democratic Party with its hands firmly on the lever of legislative power and a president who seldom backs away from a fight.
Early signs as the results come in:
If Democrats hold targeted House contests in Florida and win some Republican districts in North Carolina, Michigan, New York, Virginia and Kentucky. If they flip the Senate seat in South Carolina, it's going to be a good night for Democrats.
2. A Democratic trickle
Maybe the polls won't be entirely wrong, but not entirely right either.
In this scenario, it could be that while they take enough of the low-hanging fruit in the US House contests to deliver a majority, it's not a sizable one.
This would mean Democratic leaders in the chamber would regularly have to wrangle with their fringe members on the left and the centre to ensure they have enough votes to pass legislation.
On the Senate side in this hypothetical, the Democrats would just flip a seat or two - North Carolina, for instance, seems all but assured - but the contests in the conservative heartland would prove to be out of reach.
Perhaps they're unable to unseat stubbornly resilient Republican Senator Susan Collins in Maine or left-wing candidate Abdul El-Sayed can't keep Michigan in the Democratic column.
Maybe the duelling Dan Sullivans controversy is enough to sink Democratic candidate Mary Peltola in Alaska.
For this "Democratic trickle" scenario to unfold, the big Democratic turnout we've seen in early voting would be matched by a Republican surge on election day.
Trump's efforts to rally his base in Republican red states could help his party avoid the worst-case scenario. The races that were at or near the margin of error in polls might provide a mixed bag for both parties.
The result would be a divided Congress - and that's a recipe for political gridlock.
Early signs as the results come in:
If Florida stays comfortably Republican across the board. If Democrats pick up some House seats in places like Virginia and Pennsylvania, but the Republican incumbents on more secure political ground across the country avoid getting washed away in a deluge.
3. A good night for Republicans
This scenario involves Republicans resiliently holding on to both chambers of Congress.
For this to happen, the polls - which have previously underestimated Trump's support - need to be wrong and the toss-up races to mostly fall the way of Republicans.
Not only would Republican voters have to turn out in unexpectedly impressive numbers, independent and Hispanic voters who had seemingly soured on Trump's policies would have also to break his way in the end.
In this scenario, control of the House, far from being a done deal for Democrats, could end up coming down to California and its extended days-long counting process for mail-in ballots.
In the end, Republicans might eke out a slim overall majority thanks in part to efforts to draw more favourable congressional district lines in places like Texas, Florida and North Carolina.
It could also be that Republicans win all the Senate contests in the conservative states and they also flip Michigan, a seat that was held by Democrats heading into the vote.
Even if Republicans don't hold North Carolina or win in Democratic-controlled Minnesota or New Hampshire - races just on the periphery of competitiveness in this year's elections - they may at least make the Democratic candidates sweat.
If this was to happen, Trump might on Wednesday morning claim a renewed electoral mandate and push forward with his domestic and foreign policy agenda with the continued support of a Republican Congress.
Early signs as the results come in:
If Senators Ashley Moody in Florida and Jon Husted in Ohio cruise to re-election. If Republicans hold their own in House races in Pennsylvania and Virginia, and they flip current Democratic seats in North Carolina, Ohio and Florida.

I was told I was too young to have cancer, it had spread by the time I was diagnosed

I was told I was too young to have cancer - it had spread by the time I was diagnosed
- Published
A woman who said she was told by a GP she may be experiencing "medical anxiety" after finding a lump in her breast was later diagnosed with cancer.
Beth Jenkins, 42, visited a locum GP at her practice with concerns that a lump on her right breast had grown significantly. But she said she was told she was "too young to have breast cancer" and it may be linked to postnatal depression instead.
However, it was lobular breast cancer, external, with a 5cm (2in) tumour and the disease had spread to three lymph nodes.
Practice 1 Keir Hardie Health Park said it could not discuss individual cases but encouraged patients to "make a second appointment" if they had concerns about their health or care.
The mum-of-two from Merthyr Tydfil first noticed a "small pea-sized" lump in her breast in 2018, but, after an ultrasound, she was told it was likely glandular tissue and no biopsy was carried out.
A few years later she had given birth to her daughter Robyn and, while changing her nappy, Robyn accidentally kicked the right side of her chest.
It was then that Jenkins noticed the lump had become "massive", so she visited her GP practice in October 2024.
She said, being 40 at the time, she was told she was "too young" to have breast cancer and the lump might be linked to an infection or "medical anxiety" as she had postnatal depression, and was prescribed antibiotics.
She said: "I haven't got medical anxiety, otherwise I'd be up the hospital and doctors' every week."
Two weeks later she returned to the practice while taking her baby for an appointment and decided to speak to a female GP about her concerns.
The GP reviewed her notes and advised her to submit an e-consult, saying she should have been referred straight away.
"So I went straight home, did what she said and the same locum doctor picked it up and he rang me," she said.
"He was like, 'you're still a bit anxious about this lump here.' I said, 'I'm not anxious. I said it's something, it's non-infection. I need to have it seen to'."
She was referred to a breast clinic and diagnosed on 14 November 2024. The cancer had spread to three lymph nodes by the time it was found.
"Me and my dad, we just sat in shock really. I didn't even cry, I didn't get upset," she said.
Despite the devastating news, Jenkins, a police officer, praised the specialist team, saying the consultant reassured her: "I promise you I will get rid of this."
At first, Jenkins had a mastectomy and initially told her eight-year-old daughter Fallon that she had a "boob job".
She laughed: "Her remark to me was, 'why did you just have the one boob done and not the other one?'"
Jenkins decided to tell Fallon she had cancer before starting chemotherapy and radiotherapy - which caused her to lose her hair.
She had further preventative treatment, but experienced serious complications including neutropenic sepsis, external.
"They said if I had gone there [to the hospital] 24 hours later, I wouldn't have survived," she said.
Jenkins is classed as having no evidence of disease but will be monitored for 15 years.
She said people have described her as "one of the lucky ones" but added: "Lucky would be not to have cancer at all, and not for my kids to see what they've had to see for the last two years."
Jenkins described GPs as "the gateway to the services" and stressed "if you can't get past the GP to get to that service, there's people dying".
In the UK, routine NHS breast screening is not automatically offered to 40-year-olds, as standard invitations begin at 50.
Dr Lee Campbell from Cancer Research Wales said, although uncommon, there were about 100-115 cases of breast cancer in women under 40 each year in Wales.
"Age should not be a deciding factor for referral for further investigations if symptoms present in younger women," he added.
Jenkins hopes sharing her story will encourage others to "keep pushing" for answers and to fight to be heard.
"If I hadn't had a voice, or if I'd just listened to that doctor, I could be sitting here now and they'd say, 'it's in your bones, in your brain'," she said.
"So many more people are sat in the house right now who should have been diagnosed and by the time they go back they're terminal.
"Cancer didn't care that I was a mother to a 10-month-old... cancer doesn't discriminate".
The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines state that people 40 and under should be referred for further investigation if they have an unexplained breast or armpit lump, with or without pain, or skin changes that could indicate breast cancer.
Research by Cancer Research Wales found "an inequity" on how GPs apply these - some follow them closely while others rely on experience or instinct.
Campbell said: "We are currently working with researchers and primary care centres across Wales to ensure guidelines are followed and best practice is pursued.
"With respect to cancer, this will enable GP practices to go from gatekeepers to case-finders and will ensure cases like Beth's are dealt with sooner and not readily dismissed."
Since raising concerns publicly, Jenkins said her GP practice had been "pretty forthcoming" and put out a statement on social media in July 2025.
It said a "serious diagnosis was unfortunately missed at first.
"Thankfully, she returned to see another member of our team who sent an urgent referral - but had they not, the outcome could have been very different. In the patient's own words 'trust your instincts'."
Jenkins said she had "tried to turn a negative into a positive."
To mark two years since her diagnosis, she decided to create Breast Fest, a charity event to raise money for Merthyr Cancer Aid on 14 November that has raised £6,000 from ticket sales alone.
"People are being so kind. It's gone really well and I'm hoping to raise a lot of money," she said.
