article:
From banshees to the big screen: Ireland's unique approach to horror

From banshees to the big screen: Ireland's unique approach to horror
- Published
As a "nation of storytellers" what separates the way we tell stories of horror and folklore, making it quintessential to where we are from?
The answer to that question could lie at this year's Belfast International Horror Festival, which is in its seventh year.
Having kicked off on Wednesday, running until Sunday, this year's event will showcase six horror movies across four venues in the city.
With Hollywood favourites on offer, there is also a rich vein of local talent competing in the festival's short film competition, with their own unique take on the genre.
Nathan Hughes from Belfast is one of the few short-film directors premiering his work, The Widow's Ring, at the festival on Friday.
Sharing the festival itinerary with Stanley Kubrick's The Shining and John Carpenter's The Fog, Hughes' film, a modern Irish ghost story rooted in local folklore, explores the Banshee, "which is probably one of the most famous characters within Irish folklore that exists".
Hughes said he was inspired by filmmakers like Aislinn Clarke and Damian McCarthy.
"There's so many great Irish filmmakers that are making films that have very dark subject matters that are often influenced by superstition or things that we've believed in within Irish culture like changelings, witches and spirits".
He said his film is "very heavily influenced by religion."
"In Ireland superstition and religion are very interlinked. In my film, the old widow says, 'he who does not believe is condemned already', which is a biblical quote.
"It also plays into superstition and folklore because if you don't believe in it and it's true, you're doomed."
"I think Irish filmmakers often tend to explore things in a very dark way and they're not as suggestible to having a nicely wrapped-up happy ending in their film," Hughes continued
The director added "a dark sense of humour" comes through in Irish films.
"We're quite prone to being able to laugh at ourselves and laugh at terrible situations that we're in."
Hughes decided to bring in Julian Simmons for a cameo, "not that his role was particularly funny", Hughes said, however Simmons "injects a sense of innuendo and dark comedy that is quite unsettling in the scene that he's in".
"It actually started out as a short film festival," said Jim McClean the lead programmer for the festival.
"We just showcased Irish filmmakers and wanted to give a platform for Irish directors, particularly within the horror genre."
Now in it's seventh year as a fully-fledged festival, the talent has expanded and progressed, with McClean saying what he loves about it is seeing "the kind of creativity within filmmakers".
"There's such a great kind of local industry here that has developed and now you can really see that it has its own voice and its own style."
'A nation of storytellers'
McClean, who is also editor-in-chief of a movie podcast, said those on the island of Ireland are a "nation of storytellers".
"We have that history with an Irish folklore of stuff like changeling and things like that. And we have seen directors, both in the shorts and features, playing with that," he said.
The people of the island of Ireland "have passed on, and travelled and with them their stories, so they will always be a people with those ideas of those stories", he added.
McClean also points to the growth of the film industry across the island, saying filmmakers now have more opportunities to tell their stories than they did 10 or 15 years ago.
He gives the examples of Lee Cronin's The Mummy Evil Dead Rise movies, as well as Damian McCarthy's Hokum.
A history of violence
Simon Aeppli is documentary filmmaker and lecturer in film production from Carrickfergus whose studies include theories of haunting and folk horror.
He said Northern Ireland's relationship to its history, religion and landscape play a pivotal role on our outlook on the horror genre.
His documentary - Operation Bogeyman - examines folklore, folk horror and black propaganda during the Troubles.
"Horror films allow us to look and deal with our relationship to a past, and often it's not a good past. It's a horrible past that rests beneath the surface, that is just waiting to explode, waiting to rise up," he said.
"We've got a long, contentious history of violence, obviously, in this country, which goes back centuries."
Aeppli said there has always been an appetite for horror in Northern Ireland.
Despite censorship attempts he said, during his research he was "surprised to uncover how many horror films were actually being shown" in places like Belfast, Londonderry and Newcastle in the early 1970s.
Aeppli asks the question: "Do we [in Northern Ireland] see these stories differently?
"I think yes, because of our relationship to folklore our relationship to poetry. There's a real dark poetry in the landscape of Ireland," adding that the Northern Irish "relationship to religion is really important" as well.

article:
Spanish footballer dies after collision with goalkeeper during match

Tenerife striker De Miguel dies after on-field collision
- Published
Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel has died after the 30-year-old suffered a serious injury during a Spanish second-division match.
The forward suffered head and chest injuries during a match against FC Andorra on Monday in a heavy collision with goalkeeper Jesus Owono, who was sent off for his challenge.
De Miguel's condition was described as 'stable but serious' on Monday but his health deteriorated on Tuesday morning, with the Spaniard dying at 07:00 GMT.
"Heartbroken, with a lump in our throats and unable to believe this is true, CD Tenerife announces the tragic death of Jesus de Miguel Alameda," a club statement said.
"There are no words of comfort; there is absolutely nothing that can lessen this overwhelming sadness. We stand with his grieving family, with his loved ones, with all of Tenerife who mourn this cruel loss today."
'There are no words'
Tenerife and Andorra were drawing 2-2 seven minutes into stoppage time when the incident occurred.
Owono ran towards the centre circle to clear a long ball when his knee appeared to collide with De Miguel.
The striker lay motionless on the pitch as medical staff treated him before he was taken by ambulance from Tenerife's Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez to hospital.
Players from both teams were visibly distressed by the incident, with a number of De Miguel's team-mates in tears.
The referee showed Owono a straight red card before abandoning the match.
The goalkeeper, who had over 30,000 followers on Instagram on Tuesday morning, has since deactivated his account.
Spanish media, including Marca, reported De Miguel suffered a cardiac arrest in the ambulance and was resuscitated by paramedics on the way to hospital.
Andorra, Tenerife's opponents on Monday, said: "With broken hearts and devastated, we want to send our most sincere condolences to the family of Jesus de Miguel, to all his team-mates, friends, and to CD Tenerife."
Former Barcelona defender Gerard Pique, who co-owns Andorra, said: "I am sorry with all my soul. Rest in peace, Jesus."
De Miguel's former club, Castellon, said: "It's hard to find words when reality strikes in such an unfair way.
"We join with all our affection in the grief of his family and loved ones, whom we embrace in these terribly difficult moments and to whom we extend our most heartfelt condolences."
Javier Tebas, president of La Liga, said: "Today, we all share the terrible pain of an irreparable loss.
"My deepest condolences to his family, loved ones, team-mates and the whole club."
Real Madrid and France striker Kylian Mbappe wrote on his social media: "Much sadness, there are no words."
Inter Miami and former Barcelona forward Lionel Messi said: "There are no words. My condolences and lots of strength to all his family and friends."
The Spanish football federation announced following De Miguel's death that Tuesday's Spanish Cup fixtures had been postponed.
Two fixtures in the first round of the men's Copa del Rey were due to be played, while Espanyol were set to take on AS Celtas in the women's Copa del Reina competition.
A lower-league player with an eye for goal
De Miguel, who was born in Madrid, started his career at Leganes in 2015 and went on to play for eight different clubs in Spain.
After spells with Lugo Fuenlabrada and Internacional Madrid, he returned to Fuenlabrada before stints at Union Adarve, Navalcarnero and Unionistas.
He joined Castellon in 2023 and scored 16 goals as the club achieved promotion to Spain's second division a year later.
The Spaniard joined Tenerife on a three-year deal in 2025 and scored 11 goals in 29 appearances for the side.
De Miguel is survived by his daughter, Carla de Miguel Fernandez, who was born in 2025.

Jeers again as home woes continue - Jaissle has big problems at Newcastle

Jeers again as home woes continue - Jaissle has big problems at Newcastle
- Published
If Matthias Jaissle was unsure what Newcastle fans thought of his team's latest error-strewn performance, he certainly knew at full-time after a second defeat by Everton inside a week.
Despite another miserable showing by Jaissle's side, the Toon Army had stuck by the team from start to finish before a chorus of boos echoed around St James' Park at the final whistle.
The frustration and anger from the stands came after a 1-0 defeat which included a goalkeeping howler by Lukas Hornicek, a red card for substitute Jacob Ramsey and another blunt attacking performance.
"Big frustration, big disappointment," said Jaissle after a fourth defeat in six Premier League games.
"After a performance like that I can understand the reaction from the fans. That's the reality and I am responsible for that.
"We need to work on the things we need to improve and after today that is a lot."
Newcastle's final game before the November international break is away to Fulham on Saturday (15:00 GMT), before facing leaders and defending champions Arsenal at home on 21 November followed by third-placed Brighton away eight days later.
"It's not my first time as a manager in this situation," added Jaissle, whose side sit 13th in the table and were eliminated from the Carabao Cup by Everton last Thursday.
"The only way is togetherness and showing unity."
Will the German - who became the Premier League's second youngest coach in the summer - find the solutions to get Newcastle's season back on track, with fans starting to run out of patience?

  - Published17 hours ago

  - Published16 hours ago
'I fear a little for Newcastle'
No Premier League side has lost more home games in 2026 than Newcastle (7), while they have now lost 16 of their past 18 league games when conceding first.
The unwanted stats do not stop there.
The Magpies have failed to keep a clean sheet in each of their past 14 home league games - the longest run in their league history.
It all points to worrying times, with former Red Bull Salzburg boss Jaissle just three months into a four-year contract.
"I fear a little for Newcastle," former Liverpool and England defender Jamie Carragher said on Sky Sports.
"They have a young manager and young players. You are always going to question the manager when the team is not winning.
"I think it is going to be a tough season. At home, especially, it feels flat and boring, and I never expected to say about Jaissle's Newcastle. You expected it to be front-footed and exciting, coming from the Red Bull model."
Newcastle are in the bottom half of the table, with 11 points from nine games.
It was always going to be a period of transition following Eddie Howe's exit, after five years in charge, and the arrival of 38-year-old Jaissle, after successful spells in Saudi Arabia and Austria.
In addition, Newcastle lost a number of key players in the summer including Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimaraes.
At the start of the year, Newcastle United's chief executive David Hopkinson said he could put them "in the debate about being the top club in the world" by 2030.
That now seems a long way off amid suggestions the ambitions of the club's Saudi Arabian owners, the Public Investment Fund, are running out of steam.
Jaissle was not helped on Monday by his goalkeeper, with Hornicek allowing a routine shot to squirm under his body for Thierno Barry to tap home the winner.
The Newcastle boss claimed Barry's winner should have been disallowed for a foul on Fabian Schar in the build-up, but he conceded his players had struggled to show the bravery required to get back in the game.
"It's almost like a negative spiral," he said. "I'm not happy with the referee decision.
"Unfortunately we couldn't deliver actually over the whole 90 minutes. It was not our game and our style of playing.
"That is something we are very frustrated and disappointed about. If you cannot deliver when it counts then you don't deserve to win.
"We were not brave enough in possession, too many long balls."
Jaissle admitted Newcastle are lacking belief in the midst of their miserable run.
"There are certain moments with not too much confidence, not only with the young lads but also with the more experienced ones," he said.
"It's a difficult period. We also know you can only overcome that as a unit. We worked hard and it looked good but unfortunately we couldn't deliver.
"We will analyse in detail and try and make things better against Fulham."
'You can sense nerves in the ground'
Newcastle have problems at both ends of the pitch.
While they have managed just 12 goals in nine league games, they continue to struggle to keep clean sheets.
They registered 17 attempts against Everton but only two of those were on target, and they have scored just once from their past 47 shots in all competitions.
Newcastle have faced the most shots of any Premier League team this season, including 15 or more in seven of the nine top-flight matches they have played.
While only Sunderland (6) and Hull City (5) have committed more errors leading to goals in the Premier League this season.
Meanwhile, this was Everton's first top-flight away win since February - when they won at St James' Park.
"I've been a fan so I understand the frustrations when they're not getting what they're expecting," said captain Dan Burn after the game.
"You can sense that nervousness in the ground.
"When you're not winning games there's always a lack of confidence. The fans weren't happy. That doesn't make it easy to build confidence when you're in that atmosphere.
"Between the boxes we do OK, but we're not ruthless enough going forward or defending our own box."
Jaissle cut a forlorn figure at full-time as the autumn rain fell on St James' Park and the sound of boos rang out around him.
"You have to stick together," he said afterwards when asked how he intended to get Newcastle moving in the right direction after an underwhelming start to the season.

'Like cutting up a Picasso': AI microdrama edit of Neighbours worries actors and crew

'Like cutting up a Picasso': AI microdrama edit of Neighbours worries actors and crew
- Published
Former Neighbours actors and crew have raised concerns about plans to use AI to help re-edit old footage and make mini episodes for mobile phone viewers.
Fremantle, producer of the now-defunct Australian TV soap opera, has partnered with US-based RoseBerry Media for the project that will use AI to "scan decades of episodes" to help make short vertical videos.
Footage of Margot Robbie, who played Donna Freedman from 2008 to 2011, will be the initial focus of the micro-drama.
Both companies say the move will bring the show - which aired its final episode last year - to new audiences. But some actors and crew say they have not consented to their images, voice or work to be re-purposed.
Robbie has yet to respond publicly. The BBC has contacted her agency for comment.
In a statement, the companies behind the project said the AI-assisted technology will "scan decades of episodes to map character arcs, storylines and standout moments, helping editors quickly identify the strongest material".
The micro-drama episodes will use "original, previously broadcast footage, dialogue and performances", according to Fremantle spokesman.
"It does not generate new scenes or performances, alter actors' faces or likenesses, or use synthetic voices," he said, adding that a human editor would be "reviewing and approving every stage of the editing process".
The mini episodes will likely feature Matt Werkmeister, 34, who joined the set of Neighbours in 2005 when he was 13 years old. He played a regular character, Zeke Kinski and shared many scenes with Robbie's character.
Now a Melbourne-based producer and director, Werkmeister says he hasn't been approached by the companies behind the micro-drama and is concerned what the episodes will feature.
"If they're creating a new micro-drama out of something that already exists, I feel there needs to be consent for using our image and voice as well as the writers," he said.
Robbie is "obviously a big draw card" and "it's nice to watch old clips from shows you used to watch," Werkmeister said, but when he signed his contract two decades ago, "streaming didn't even exist as a platform" so he's unsure of what his rights are.
That uncertainty is also at the forefront of Sam Clark's mind. He played Ringo Brown on Neighbours from 2006 to 2010, a character who later marries Robbie's fictional character.
Speaking from Los Angeles, Clark – now working as a producer and voice actor - said he hadn't heard about the micro-drama until a friend sent him an article.
"I don't have a negative view of the work that we did all those years ago getting a second life as long as it's not being manipulated into new storylines," Clark, 39, said.
"AI and social media obviously wasn't a thing when I signed my contract 20 years ago so I'm still trying to understand exactly what those parameters are."
Sound recordist Bruce Findlay, 68, has worked in the TV industry for close to five decades and Neighbours has a "special place" in his heart, having worked on the show from episode one.
Using AI to help make short episodes from old footage was "like cutting up a Picasso and rebuilding it".
"We worked so hard to get this product out… and now they're chopping it up into little tiny pieces, throwing it up in the air and putting it back together again using AI - it belittles the process".
Guy Hameiri, head of RoseBerry Media, said the project is the first time the company will use its in-house AI tool to sift through Neighbours footage - there are more than 9,300 episodes - to make "premium vertical television".
The project will "reimagine" the material, giving it "new audiences, new relevance and new value," he said.
The head of Fremantle's commercial and international arm, Jens Richter, has called the project "an exciting example of how technology and creative thinking can unlock new value" from their catalogue.
It's understood that Fremantle is in discussions with two unions on the issue and that residuals - ongoing payments for actors and writers when their work is re-aired or syndicated - will be paid, but this does not apply to crew.
The Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance, one of the unions, confirmed the talks.
"Workers should be consulted before their likeness or expertise is used in a way they could never had envisioned when they signed contracts decades ago," said MEAA's acting CEO Adam Portelli.

Concern over cut to young people's mental health crisis scheme

Concern over cut to young people's mental health crisis scheme
- Published
Concerns have been raised over the reduction of a specialist mental health support service for children and young people in the north west.
The Card Before You Leave scheme ensures young people experiencing a mental health crisis who present at a hospital's emergency department are given a written appointment with specialists before leaving.
The Western Health and Social Care Trust (WHSCT) said due to financial pressures the scheme is now only operating on a Monday to Friday basis and not at all on weekends and bank holidays.
Londonderry GP Dr Joe McEvoy said the reduction was a further "chipping away at an already threadbare service".
"It's already difficult for families when they're dealing with a young person who is distressed to know how they should manage it," McEvoy told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme.
In a statement, WHSCT said the reduction was introduced in August as "part of wider savings measures" and would remain under review.
It said the reduction in the scheme's operating hours applied only to young people "who present out of hours and are assessed as low risk".
"These patients are now assessed by Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services (CAMHS) on the next working day rather than the next calendar day," the trust said.
It added: "There has been no change to arrangements for young people assessed as high risk, who continue to receive the appropriate assessment and support based on their clinical needs."
The trust said it remains "committed to providing safe and effective mental health services for children and young people".
In August, Northern Ireland's health trusts announced proposals on how they intend to make savings of up to 12% over three years.
At that time the Permanent Health Secretary, Mike Farrar, said health and social care in Northern Ireland is facing enormous challenges, with a current funding gap of £800m.
There have been no changes to the Card Before You Leave scheme in the Belfast Health Trust, Northern Trust, Southern Trust and South Eastern Trust areas.
McEvoy said weekends and bank holidays are "the times when we actually see peaks in mental health distress in young people".
The reduction, he added, means "a young person in distress on a Friday evening will now have to wait until Monday morning on a normal weekend, Tuesday morning on a bank holiday weekend and maybe a Wednesday morning on a weekend which as two-bank holidays, such as Christmas or Easter.
"It's a small change but it is a significant one," he said.
Foyle DUP MLA Julie Middleton said the decision to reduce the scheme's operating hours should be reversed.
"We should be united on calling for the service to be reinstated and we have to acknowledge that while someone could be deemed to be low risk that could move quite rapidly," she told BBC Radio Foyle.
"We need to provide a pathway where they know it's okay to ask for help, that they've asked for help and the help is coming."
'Going to impact people'
SDLP MLA Mark H Durkan said the Trust's need to save money was directly "impacting on the services, not the services that people want, but the services that the population need."
He said parents should not be deterred from seeking help for their child.
"Any reduction in that service you know is going to impact people. We have to be sure the message goes out there that those deemed more at risk, even medium or high risk, that they won't be just sent home," Durkan said.

PM plans debt reset for Commonwealth nations as slavery apology talks begin

PM plans debt reset for Commonwealth nations as slavery apology talks begin
- Published
The prime minister will join the King at the formal opening of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua later - and begin talks with fellow leaders about the UK issuing a formal apology for the slave trade in the next year.
As part of the discussions, Downing Street said Andy Burnham would set out his plans for what it is calling a "debt reset" to support Commonwealth countries having to deal with the growing costs of paying interest on their debts.
The issue of reparations, compensation to those who were the victims of slavery, has dominated debate in the build up to this summit, in which representatives from 56 Commonwealth countries are meeting.
"Britain is bringing a new approach to this meeting," the prime minister said, in a tacit acknowledgement that the last Commonwealth gathering, on the Pacific island of Samoa two years ago, did not go well from a UK perspective.
The previous Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer had said prior to the meeting that reparations were not on the agenda, but other leaders insisted they should be.
This time, the new prime minister has sought to get ahead of the debate, and appeared to directly address the anger of some Commonwealth leaders after the last summit.
"For years, those members of the Commonwealth affected by the slave trade have asked for an honest conversation about the legacies of slavery, external. By sticking our heads in the sand, we have damaged the ability of the Commonwealth to function," Burnham argued in an article in the Guardian.
Burnham alongside the Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and the former Prime Minister Gordon Brown, are beginning conversations which, they hope, will help detoxify the debate about reparations.
They do so while insisting the UK will not pay them, but is likely to formally apologise for the slave trade for the first time next year, when the UK holds the rotating presidency of the G20 group of countries.
"A formal apology," Miliband said in a social media video, external, is something "the British government are open to".
He said this would be a "significant step" but added that "we don't believe financial reparations are the right or feasible answer to transatlantic slavery. We don't think the right response is to ask British taxpayers today to make financial payments for these historic acts."

The Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has urged the prime minister not to issue an apology for slavery, saying it would give countries a reason to ask the UK for reparations.
She said: "I don't think we should be giving any money to compensate people for the slave trade, and I don't think that Andy Burnham needs to be apologising because it is a lever to wedge open the door to ask for cash."
But British officials are hopeful, even confident, that the prime minister and foreign secretary's approach will create space in the next two days for a wider conversation with fellow Commonwealth countries.
No 10 said the UK would lead two new task forces - one focused on critical mineral assets and vulnerabilities in supply chains across the group and the other aimed at boosting trade and investment more widely.
Both will be set up by the end of the year and report back at the next leaders' summit, officials said.
British diplomats view the Commonwealth as a useful forum for conversations with developing countries, and, crucially, one that does not involve China, America or Russia.

Laura Kuenssberg: Healey risks breaking minimum wage promise for younger workers

Healey risks breaking minimum wage promise for younger workers
- Published
The Chancellor, John Healey, has suggested that younger workers might not receive the same minimum wage as others before the next election, potentially breaking a Labour manifesto promise.
In 2024, Labour said it would remove "discriminatory age bands", vowing to end the gap between the adult minimum wage and pay for 18 to 20-year-olds.
But in last week's Budget, Healey said that younger workers would see the same increase as older workers, leaving a gap between the two rates this year.
Pay for 18 to 20-year-olds in 2026 will rise to £11.27, while over-20s will be paid a minimum of £13.21 an hour.
In a BBC interview broadcast on Sunday, Healey was asked if younger workers would be paid the same as older workers, when it comes to the minimum wage, by the time of the next election?
"We'll take one step at a time," he said, suggesting that Labour might abandon its plan to close the gap before the next election.
It is a change that is likely to anger the unions and some on the left of the party.
Healey added that Labour was still committed to the ambition, but hinted the plan to equalise wages might be delayed, partly to encourage businesses to employ younger workers.
"There is no question about whether or if, it's a question of when - it's a question of how fast," he said.
"I want to make sure we can look hard at those trade-offs that are there between jobs and wages."
"I want to take business, I want to take trade unions with me, and with the government, because together we have to get into what at the moment is a moral shame on this nation. A million youngsters - written off without any prospect of being helped into work and making contributions to this country for the future."
The chancellor also suggested that he is willing to make potentially big cuts to some areas of public spending, to get the country's debt falling.
The budget documents spell out real-terms reductions to some government departments in the years to come.
The likelihood of the government following through was questioned by the respected independent number cruncher, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) this week.
But asked if he would make big cuts, Healey said: "We've already demonstrated we are prepared to take hard decisions about the priorities in government."
Pressed on whether he would make cuts of more than 2% a year to some government departments, he added: "We will carry that through to the 10-year plan and the spending review next year."
"But in the budget I also set out the ways that we're preparing and the work we've got under way to prepare for those spending review decisions."
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said the "bulk" of spending cuts should be from the welfare budget, describing it as containing "astronomical sums".
She also proposed reducing the size of the civil service and reducing budgets in departments such as the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport.
On whether she would support cuts pencilled in by the government, Badenoch told the same programme: "What exactly are they cutting? I'm not against what they're doing but there's no detail."
Badenoch said she did not want to see cuts in frontline services but said there was a need to "bring down the cost of government".
Reflecting on the Budget, she said: "The chancellor had 98 different measures, a lot of them very piecemeal, none will make a difference.
"So living within our means, absolutely, we've got to do that. That will require cuts to government, but we are setting out the things very clearly that we're going to change, the bulk of which is in welfare. Other departments will have changes too."

Analysis: Lockhart departure presents massive challenge for DUP and unionism

Analysis: Lockhart departure presents massive challenge for DUP and unionism
- Published
Within minutes of her resignation letter being published online on Monday, Carla Lockhart's photo and profile were stripped from the DUP webpage.
All traces of one of the party's most popular politicians were wiped away at breakneck speed.
The party she joined as a teenager wasted no time in moving on, issuing the shortest of statements regretting her decision to quit but making it clear such divisions in unionism only benefit Sinn Féin.
It was a parting swipe at its former Upper Bann MP in what was a bitter break-up.
Lockhart resigned from the DUP over its handling of the fallout of the Drumcree parading dispute.
Despite insisting she makes her own decisions, Lockharts's former colleagues remain convinced she is being manipulated by others.
They refuse to accept their one-time loyal MP could be fast-tracked out of the party without the influence of others.
Not so, says Lockhart, as she prepares to take her seat as an independent unionist MP at Westminster.
She leaves behind a party which has now just four MPs, falling from the high of 2017 when the DUP had 10 members of parliament.
It has also lost its only female MP and three of those left behind are in the twilight of their political careers.
Splintered unionism
Rebuilding the party's Westminister presence will be a massive challenge as unionism continues to splinter.
That fracture is now clearly illustrated on the green benches in the commons with no fewer than five different brands of unionism.
Two independents and three very different parties - the DUP, Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) and Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV).
No wonder the cries for unionist unity has grown louder in recent weeks.
So much so that alongside her resignation letter Lockhart published her own vision for the future of unionism.
The eight-page document set out her key principles and action plan for unity.
It was clearly timed and aimed at those who would accuse her of further dividing unionism with her departure from the DUP.
She wanted to have a positive to off set any negative narratives.
Wide support base
Her decision to remain as an independent MP and ignore any advances from the TUV was also well calculated.
As the only DUP MP elected with the support of TUV votes, Lockhart was in a unique position.
Upper Bann was the only constituency where the TUV opted against fielding a candidate in the last Westminster election.
As a result Carla Lockhart has a wide support base which she will hope to count on next time around and remaining as an independent will help her cause.
The DUP is also less likely to run a candidate against her as an independent and avoid the risk of splitting the unionist vote and possibly handing the seat to Sinn Féin.
Before then there is an assembly election to be fought in May and the new independent MP for Upper Bann will be under pressure to endorse candidates.
As the party which now shares her political outlook, the TUV will be hopeful of securing her support.

Popular Australian children's author jailed over child exploitation offences

Popular Australian children's author jailed over child exploitation offences
- Published
Australian children's author Craig Silvey has been sentenced to seven months in jail for possessing and distributing child exploitation material.
In handing down her sentence, Judge Hayley Cormann called Silvey's actions "repulsive" and "degrading".
In January, Silvey was arrested after police raided his home in Western Australia and seized several electronic devices. In May, the 44-year-old pleaded guilty to possessing and distributing child exploitation material and in October he was jailed pending his sentencing.
The father-of-three is best known for his award-winning young adult novel Jasper Jones and children's book Runt, both of which were later made into movies.
"You have devastated and betrayed the trust of thousands of people, and you've let entire communities down," Cormann said on Monday, according to WA Today.
Police said Silvey had online chats, in which he discussed child exploitation, open at the moment they turned up to raid his house.
In them, the court heard, Silvey had described himself as "extremely open minded" and "obsessed with taboos".
He'd discussed his sexual interest in children as young as five with another user of a pornography site, and detectives found images and videos of other adults abusing children on his devices.
He was initially charged with four offences, but prosecutors later dropped two.
Prosecutors said Silvey contributed to the "cycle of abuse" victimising the children in the images, and argued a harsh sentence was required.
However, the author's defence lawyer said he did not have a "sexual interest in children" and was seeking out "the most depraved material" as a form of "emotional" self harm.
"His behaviour provided temporary relief from psychological agitation," Eloise Barker said.
She said Silvey had displayed genuine remorse for his offending, and that his high profile and the resulting media scrutiny - which led to his former partner and children relocating interstate - was already a form of punishment.
Judge Cormann did not accept many of her arguments, and said Silvey's offending was extremely serious.
"These children, the victims of this type of offending, are real and are traumatised… the consequences for them from these abuses are long lasting and very, very traumatic," she said, according to The Australian.
Silvey was sentenced to seven months in jail, backdated to 22 October. He is eligible for parole.
Silvey's coming-of-age novel Jasper Jones sold more than half a million copies and was awarded the Book of the Year Award by the nation's peak publishing body in 2010.
The novel, set in Western Australia with two teenage boys as the main characters, was also shortlisted for the International Dublin Literary Awards and the Miles Franklin Literary Award.
It was later turned into a film starring Toni Collette and Hugo Weaving in 2017 as well as a stage play.
Another of his acclaimed works is 2022's Runt, about the adventures of an 11-year-old girl and her stray dog and set in the Australia outback. It was also adapted for film in 2024, featuring Celeste Barber.
Since his arrest, publishers and book shops have pulled his works from shelves while schools in some states have removed Jasper's books from teaching lists.

US urges Venezuela to release remaining political prisoners

US urges Venezuela to release remaining political prisoners
- Published
The US has urged Venezuela to release the remaining political prisoners being held in the South American country.
More than 1,000 political prisoners have been freed since US forces seized Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro in a military raid on Caracas on 3 January and took him to New York, where he faces trial on drug-trafficking and torture charges.
But Venezuelan prisoners' rights group Foro Penal says 322 people remain in detention.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio met his Venezuelan counterpart, Oliver Blanco, on Monday where he called for their release and discussed reforms aimed at laying the groundwork for free, fair, and credible elections, the US state department said.
The release of political prisoners has long been a demand made by Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado.
Machado, who was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2025, returned to Venezuela on 25 October after living in exile for almost a year. One of her first meetings was with relatives of political detainees.
Many of those in detention were arrested in the aftermath of the 2024 presidential election.
The National Electoral Council (CNE) - which is dominated by government loyalists - declared the incumbent, Nicolás Maduro, the winner of the election even though copies of the voting tallies collected by the opposition and verified by independent media suggested that the opposition candidate had won.
The Carter Center, which had sent independent observers to Venezuela, also said that the election "could not be considered democratic".
A UN fact-finding mission found, external that in the months that followed, the Venezuelan government orchestrated "a harsh repression against persons perceived as political opponents or simply because they express dissent or critical views against the authorities".
After US forces seized Maduro, his loyal vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, was sworn in as interim president.
While Rodríguez has the backing of the Trump administration, opposition parties within Venezuela have been expressing impatience with the slow pace of reforms.
In Monday's statement, the US state department stressed that it remained committed to US President Donald Trump's three-phase plan, consisting of "stabilisation, economic recovery and political reconciliation, and democratic transition".
A week ago, Rubio had told journalists that Venezuela's "election infrastructure" had to be replaced in order for fresh elections to be valid.
"Not in 10 years, not in five years, not in two years; it needs to happen quickly under the timelines that we've established," he insisted.
Days later, Rodríguez told Venezuelans in a televised address that "there will be elections" under a "renewed" electoral authority.
However, she did not give a timeline for when the election could be held.
Opposition leader Machado, on the other hand, has been pushing for elections to be held in 2027.
At one point she suggested 24 July 2027 - the anniversary of the birth of independence hero Simón Bolivar - but she has since returned to calling for a vote at some point in the next year.

article:
Tributes to 'inspirational' Olympian Ciara Mageean after death at 34

Tributes to 'inspirational' Olympian Ciara Mageean after death at 34
- Published
Tributes have been paid to former European champion and two-time Olympic runner Ciara Mageean, who has died at the age of 34.
Mageean, from Portaferry in County Down, was diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer in May 2025.
She died on Sunday morning, surrounded by her loved ones, a statement posted on her social media accounts said.
"A beloved daughter, sister, wife, friend and inspiration to so many, she will be deeply missed," it said.
Mageean's funeral will take place near her family home on Tuesday, with a ceremony at St Patrick's Church, Ballyphilip, followed by burial in the adjoining cemetery.
Her death comes less than three weeks after her marriage to her long-term partner Thomas Moran.
The athlete represented Ireland at the 2016 and 2020 Olympics and won gold in the 1500m at the European Athletics Championships in Rome in 2024.
She also represented Northern Ireland at the Commonwealth Games, winning silver in Birmingham in 2022.
'One of our own'
Olympic legend Lady Mary Peters said Mageean was a "wonderful lady" who was "gracious, beautiful, talented and inspirational to the next generation".
"We knew she was very ill and we knew that it was inevitable but we didn't expect it so soon," said the 1972 Olympic pentathlon gold medallist.
Lady Mary's charity the Mary Peters Trust, which supports Northern Ireland athletes, had helped Mageean in her athletics career.
"My charity supported her for as long as we could because she was so talented and we recognised that in her," said Lady Mary.
She said that Mageean had continued to inspire young athletes even while undergoing treatment for cancer and would be "sorely missed in the world of sport".
Sean Young, the secretary of Portaferry Gaelic Athletic Club, where Mageean played camogie in her younger years, said its members were in "disbelief and shock" at her death.
He said Mageean had been a "fierce competitor" who began her sporting journey at the club before pursuing athletics.
"Outside the sporting arena she is the most inspirational, humble person we have ever had within our club," he said.

Down Gaelic Athletic Association (GAA) said it was "honoured and privileged" to call Mageean one of its own, describing her as someone who never forgot her roots.
"She touched the lives of so many people and she helped change the lives of so many," it said.
"In her battle with illness she showed us courage, positivity and the value of life."
Her former school, Assumption Grammar in Ballynahinch, County Down, said it was "deeply saddened and heartbroken" by the death of its "cherished past pupil".
"Ciara's kindness, strength, faith and unwavering determination were an inspiration to us all," it said.
"She touched countless lives with her warmth, humility and generosity of spirit."
'A champion in every sense of the word'
Northern Ireland's First Minister Michelle O'Neill described Mageean as "a champion in every sense of the word and a role model for all athletes".
"She represented her country with pride and helped put Irish athletics on the map," said O'Neill.
She said Mageean had faced her cancer diagnosis with the same "bravery and determination" she had shown throughout her sporting career.
"Ciara's legacy will live on and she will continue to be an inspiration to many."
Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly said people across Northern Ireland had been "deeply proud and inspired" by the athlete.
She described Mageean as an "outstanding athlete and ambassador for her sport" who had spoken with honesty and bravery about her health battles.
Irish President Catherine Connolly said Mageean had stood out for "her strength and perseverance, for her clear speaking and for her determination to succeed".
"It was these qualities that led the public to appreciate her so much and to be so thrilled for her achievement in Rome," said Connolly.
"Since Ciara shared the news of her illness, the public have stood with her and their affection for her has only grown."
Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin said he was "deeply saddened" by her untimely death and extended his sympathies to her husband, family and friends.
Tánaiste (Irish Deputy Prime Minister) Simon Harris said Mageean had inspired people both through her achievements on the track and her openness about her illness.
"She gave so many others strength and hope," he said.
'Great fun'
Speaking to BBC Good Morning Ulster athlete Katie Kirk, who competed alongside Mageean, recalled her first experience of training with her at Mary Peters tracks in Belfast for a cross-country session.
"Even then she was great fun, very determined, focused".
Kirk commended Mageean's success saying "she achieved so much" even through "incredibly difficult" times.
"She still came out, she still spoke to people, she still took pictures with children and participated fully in life.
"That for me is just the essence of who she is," she added.
'Self-belief and commitment'
World Athletics described her as "an inspiration to many, on and off the track", highlighting her historic European gold medal in Rome in 2024.
Athletics Ireland, the country's governing body for the sport, said Mageean was "much-loved and inspirational".
"Her courage, warmth and spirit will leave a lasting legacy," the organisation said.
The Camogie Association also paid tribute to Mageean, with its president Brian Molloy describing her as a great friend of the sport, both as a player and a supporter.
"In her all-too-short life, Ciara touched the hearts of so many," he said.
"Her self-belief and commitment to her craft will always be inspirational and she will be fondly remembered by all who had the privilege of knowing her."
'A light has gone out in the world'
Mageean was named the 2023 BBC Northern Ireland Sports Personality of the Year after an impressive year, in which she broke national records and was fourth in a competitive World Championships final.
BBC Sport NI broadcaster Thomas Niblock, who interviewed Mageean in July for The GAA Social podcast, described her as a "one off".
"A light has gone out in the world. Authentic, talented, decent. Her kindness and wonderful personality was a joy to watch and see," he wrote on social media.
Niblock recalled how Mageean had received disappointing news the day before their interview but had insisted on going ahead with the recording.
"It's 90 minutes [co-presenter] Oisin [McConville] and myself will always treasure. She was the best of us," he said.
He also paid tribute to her husband and the wider Portaferry community.
"I've never met a person who met Ciara, who didn't love her," he added.
Patrick Kielty, who said it was a "privilege" to interview Mageean on Irish national broadcaster RTÉ's The Late Late Show, said "she wasn't just a champion on the track".
"She was a champion of others who showed us all how to live."
In many interviews that she gave following her diagnosis last year, Mageean spoke candidly about the symptoms she experienced which led her to seek medical help.
She also worked with a charity that promotes bowel cancer awareness.
Noticing blood in your poo - which may appear black or dark red in the toilet bowl - can be a sign of bowel cancer.
If there is no other obvious cause for the bleeding, such as piles, the NHS recommends that you ask for an appointment with your GP, external.
The NHS also advises a check-up if you notice changes in your regular toilet habits, such as having to poo more often, or a pattern of diarrhoea or constipation.
Abdominal pain or lumps, stomach bloating and unexplained weight loss are also among symptoms which should lead to a bowel cancer test.
Bowel cancer can also cause anaemia, the features of which include extreme tiredness and shortness of breath.
The earlier bowel cancer is detected, the easier it is to treat.

article:
Family of girl murdered by ex given law change hope

Family of girl murdered by ex given law change hope
- Published
The family of a murdered schoolgirl says the government has told them it plans to create a new law defining teenage abusive relationships because of their campaigning.
Micala and Lee Trussler met the Safeguarding and Violence Against Women and Girls minister Satvir Kaur at the Home Office in London on Monday, where they were given an outline of the plans.
Their daughter, Holly Newton, was 15 when she was stabbed to death in an alleyway in Hexham in January 2023 by her ex-boyfriend Logan MacPhail.
Kaur said: "Stories like Holly's are why we are deploying the full power of the state to halve violence against women and girls in a decade."
MacPhail was 16 when he killed Holly and could not accept the relationship was over. He had been controlling and stalked the teenager in the run up to her death.
Police recorded her murder as knife crime because the law does not recognise those under 16 as victims of domestic violence.
This is something her mum and stepdad, Micala and Lee Trussler, have been campaigning to change.
Lee said: "Without that classification they can't receive the help and guidance that they need to safely exit that relationship."
But Micala and Lee agree that a standalone definition for abuse in teenage relationships would be as effective as lowering the age someone can be classed as a victim of domestic abuse.
Micala said: "I think a stand alone definition is actually better than just lowering the age because it is actually giving teenagers better protection and also acknowledging teenage relationships can look a lot different to adult relationships.
"We've definitely felt really proud that we've got here because we have campaigned for so long. It's also quite emotional because we've still lost Holly.
"But I do feel like they've [the government] taken Holly's story seriously and they've realised the failings in her case. And we're now helping other young people get the support they really, really need."
Stabbed After School
The shocking story of how a teenage relationship ended in murder.
In January, a House of Lords select committee started a review of the Domestic Abuse Act 2021 to consider its impact and effectiveness.
Among the areas it examined was the definition of domestic abuse and The Act's recognition of children – like Holly - as victims. The move to explore a new definition for teenage relationship abuse comes as a result of this review.
In a statement, Kaur said: "Micala Trussler has shown incredible courage in campaigning in Holly's memory, following the unimaginable loss of her daughter.
"Stories like Holly's are why we are deploying the full power of the state to halve violence against women and girls in a decade."
The MP for Hexham Joe Morris who accompanied the Trusslers to see the minister said the government was taking the family's concerns seriously.
He said: "This is a major victory for Micala and her hard work and campaigning on this issue because Holly was failed, and I'm delighted to see the seriousness and the rigour the government is treating this issue, and I think it's a massive step in the right direction to get Holly's law on the statute book."
The government has not revealed a timeline for the proposals or said when the full review of the Domestic Abuse Act 2021 will be revealed.
Logan MacPhail was detained for at least 17 years in 2024 for carrying out the "vicious and brutal" stabbing.

article:
Mum says autistic son, 18, left abandoned and falling through cracks in system

Mum says autistic son, 18, left abandoned and falling through cracks in system
- Published
Cherisse Lanigan feels her son has been "abandoned and is falling through cracks in the system" because of a lack of support for young adults with learning difficulties.
Callan has autism and Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), as well as anxiety and other behavioural issues.
After recently turning 18, he took a test which found he has an IQ above 70. In Northern Ireland, this means he cannot access adult disability services, even thought he had been assessed as having special educational needs as a child.
The Northern Health Trust has said it recognises the approach "can present significant challenges" for individuals and families who do not meet the eligibility criteria.
Health trusts in Northern Ireland use a psychometric assessment to define if someone has a learning disability or not.
Cherisse, who lives with her son in Draperstown, County Londonderry, described his autism diagnosis as complex and said that he has "significant social and emotional support needs".
"My son's autism is so much more than his IQ, and he really struggles with the social aspects of being around people, but any help we had has now been taken away because of one test," she told BBC News NI.
"It just feels like he's being treated like he's not that important because without support, he's not going to make progress, so is he just expected to stay at home all his life?"
Callan was diagnosed with autism at the age of two. He was in a special learning unit in a mainstream school for most of his time at school.
He currently attends a further education college with support one day a week but his mother accompanies him to local youth clubs a few nights a week.
"Callan could tell you everything about a computer and how it was built, but he struggles with the social and communication aspects of everyday life," she said.
"But the system just seems to want to put all the emphasis on his IQ and it feels like everything else is less important and because he doesn't fit into a neat box or category, we're left in limbo."
How the system works
A statement of Special Educational Needs (SEN) ends with school, but in England a care plan is in place until a young person reaches 25.
There have been a number of campaigns in Northern Ireland in recent years to do more for young people with SEN after they leave school.
Earlier this year, the health minister said there was not enough time to introduce new ministerial policies for post-SEN support ahead of the next assembly election.
Northern Ireland's Independent Autism Reviewer says it is "indefensible" that adults with autism were being left to navigate "the most complex of systems" and as a result are often "left in crisis".
Ema Cubitt said: "Once that learning disability door is closed and that support is taken away, where do these families go?
"Those families who love and support people with the most complex needs are also navigating the most complex systems, and government are well aware of this problem and the issues these families are facing."
'Left to linger in a wasteland'
Sinn Féin MLA Emma Sheerin has previously raised Callan's case in the Northern Ireland Assembly.
"Callan has just missed that threshold by the tiniest of margins, he has fallen between two stools time and again, leaving him to linger in a wasteland," she said.
"I have previously called on the Department of Health to do something for people like Callan who do not just fit in the box."
She added: "I'm not saying that if Callan had the learning disability diagnosis and access to these services that it would solve everything, but he's being robbed of even being given the chance to try and see if it would help."
The Northern trust said it acknowledged the "frustration and worry" felt by Cherisse and Callan Lanigan, but said that it had to commission care through specific mental health and learning disability programmes.
A spokesperson added: "We recognise that this approach can present significant challenges for individuals and families who do not meet the eligibility criteria for accessing these services."
The trust said it would continue to engage with the Lanigan family, and Cherisse confirmed that discussions had started around getting her son more support.
In a statement, the Department of Health said it was aware that young people with autism can present with vulnerabilities similar to those with a learning disability and that further work was needed to meet their needs on a "regional consistent basis".
A department spokesperson added: "Work is underway within a financially-constrained environment to improve clarity, consistency and support for people as they move into adulthood."

article:
Reeves says UK's future should be inside the EU

Reeves says UK's future should be inside the EU
- Published
Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves has argued the UK's future should be inside the EU, and that Brexit has made the country "poorer, weaker and less secure".
In her first major intervention since leaving the Treasury, Reeves said she welcomed debate around the UK's relationship with Europe.
At the last election, Labour's manifesto said a Labour government would stay outside the EU and make Brexit work.
But Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said there needs to be an honest discussion about what the future relationship looks like.
The Conservatives have said there is no desire to rerun the Brexit debate and Reform UK's Nigel Farage has said there is no mandate to pursue closer EU ties.
Labour's 2024 election manifesto ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.
Burnham has said that any changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is next due by 2029.
In the Sunday Times, external, Reeves wrote: "No-one in the Treasury ever doubted where my instincts were. I do believe Britain's future lies in the European Union."
She said supporters of rejoining the EU had to "make the argument, demonstrate tangible benefits and to get the next steps right".
Reeves added that at the forthcoming UK-EU summit, she hoped for confirmation of the youth mobility scheme she has been pushing for since she was in office.
She also said she was hoping for "progress towards entry" into the Security Action for Europe (SAFE) scheme.
Announced last March, SAFE is part of an EU-wide effort to rearm after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
A defence pact agreed with the EU last May paved the way for UK-based defence companies to be part of projects funded by SAFE.
In her piece for the Sunday Times, Reeves also sought to defend her record in office.
She wrote about the need for governments to be "braver" in building big infrastructure projects and "clear eyed" about the risks and benefits AI would drive in advanced economies.
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said she "can't even believe we are reopening" the Brexit debate.
She told BBC One's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: "This is not something that is needed in order to cut welfare, in order to spend money on defence.
"We are having yet another Westminster bubble argument about the EU when it is time for us to actually start using the opportunities, fix mistakes that have been made and go into the future."
Badenoch added: "I do not want to indulge Andy Burnham's fantasies about redoing the referendum because he doesn't have a plan for what to do today."
Burnham told Badenoch during the most recent session of Prime Minister's Questions that he was focused on "getting a better deal for Britain, that is my responsibility".
The next UK-EU summit will take place in Brussels on 20 November.

Asian Cup postponed in wake of attacks on Saudi Arabia

Asian Cup postponed in wake of attacks on Saudi Arabia
- Published
The 2027 Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia has been postponed because of a series of deadly attacks on the host country.
The 24-team tournament was scheduled to take place from 7 January to 5 February but has been rescheduled to run from 23 December, 2027 to 21 January, 2028.
In October, a missile attack by Yemen's Houthi movement on Riyadh's airport killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.
A statement from the the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), external said the decision to reschedule had been taken "in light of the current exceptional circumstances arising from developments in the region, including substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions".
It added: "The new dates of the tournament will be presented to Fifa for approval."
The Saudi Pro League has postponed this week's round of fixtures following the rescheduling of the Asian Cup.
It says the rescheduling creates "additional flexibility" in the calendar to allow for a "more balanced distribution of fixtures" across the rest of the season.
A number of events in Saudi Arabia have been cancelled recently, including the Six Kings Slam tennis exhibition event, which was scheduled to be in Riyadh.
The Asian Tour has also indefinitely postponed it's season-ending golf tournament, which was scheduled to take place from 18-21 November.
This is the second successive Asian Cup to be postponed after the 2023 tournament was moved to 2024 and to Qatar from China because of the Covid pandemic.

  - Published13 October
The decision to postpone the 2027 Asian Cup means a number of Premier League players will not have to miss part of the current season.
Some of the players that would have been expected to be called up were Japan's Zion Suzuki of Aston Villa, Wataru Endo, who plays for Liverpool, and Daizen Maeda of Ipswich Town.
Leeds United's Ao Tanaka, Crystal Palace duo Takehiro Tomiyasu and Daichi Kamada, and Hull City's Hidemasa Morita also play for Japan.
Japan would have been one of the favourites for the tournament and Villa, who are in the Champions League, might have had to do without Suzuki for at least seven games if his country had reached the final.
Liverpool are also in the Champions League but Endo has yet to play for the Reds this season.
Brighton winger Kaoru Mitoma is currently injured but is expected to be back later this year and is also likely to have been called up by Japan.
Manchester City defender Abdukodir Khusanov, of Uzbekistan, and Hull City and Australia defender Lucas Herrington would also have expected international call-ups for the Asian Cup.

Davies hamstring injury deepens Cardiff crisis

Isaak Davies has become the latest player to be added to Cardiff City's growing list of injuries, with the Wales international forward ruled out for four weeks with a hamstring issue.
Head coach Brian Barry-Murphy revealed after Saturday's 3-0 Championship defeat at Wolves that there were fresh fitness concerns over defenders Will Fish and Perry Ng, as well as midfielder Alex Robertson.

Forward Callum Robinson was left out of the matchday squad for a third successive game at Wolves.
Barry-Murphy confirmed the Republic of Ireland international was not suspended but would not explain why he continues not to select him.
Asked if he could elaborate, the Cardiff boss added: "No. I'll always try and be as transparent as possible with every question that I'm asked on behalf of the supporters, but it's already been discussed."

article:
The elections that could define Trump's closing chapter

Americans head to the polls for elections that could define Trump's closing chapter
- Published
With two years of his presidency remaining, Donald Trump, who has dominated American politics over the past decade and transformed it in remarkable ways, is facing potentially pivotal elections.
And the midterm elections on Tuesday that will decide control of Congress come at a difficult moment for his Republican Party.
Voters overwhelmingly say they are most concerned about the cost of living. Food and fuel prices have soared in part due to the president's aggressive tariffs and unpopular war with Iran, so it will be top of mind as many head to the polls.
Trump, who has faced record low approval ratings in recent months, has been campaigning hard, headlining dozens of rallies across the country.
He made his closing pitch on Monday in front of the Reflecting Pool in Washington DC, which has been the subject of a controversial renovation. Looking back at the midterms campaign, he said Republicans "gave this a very strong shot".
But ahead of the vote, high prices are a concern for voters on all sides - which helps explain why he has been campaigning in previously safe Republican territory, appearing in Iowa and Kansas during a final weekend blitz.
His party has also poured hundreds of millions of dollars of campaign advertising into these traditionally safe contests, such as the Senate race in Kansas.
"When they start spending hard American dollars on political advertising in a state that they should be winning, that's how you know that they think they're in trouble," Carrie Dann, the managing editor of the Cook Political Report, which analyses campaigns and elections, told the BBC.
"The spending [in Kansas] is going to be far more than Republicans ever anticipated," she added. That points to a party that is approaching these elections on the defensive.
At many of his rallies, Trump has also made a plea to voters. "In this election, I'm asking you to pretend, please, that I'm on the ballot," he said last month. "Just pretend."
Of course, he is not on the ballot. But this plea - which he made again in Iowa on Sunday - gets to the heart of a critical question: Is he still an electoral asset for his Republican Party?
The answer to that is not as simple as it once was.
Trump returned to the White House as a formidable force following his crushing 2024 election win - and had the healthy approval ratings to match. Before that, during the previous midterm elections in 2022, his endorsement was courted by Republicans who saw it as vital to success.
Now, with the war with Iran dragging on and hitting many Americans in the pocket, his approval ratings have sunk. The price of a gallon of diesel - which was $3.75 before the war started in February - hit a record high of $6.52 in September.
"I literally just had my son drive across the country, and he called me in every state and told me the price of gas," one voter in Iowa told me. "And I was like - 'oh my gosh, this is horrible'."
Inflation has also ticked up from 3% when Trump took office to 3.7% today, and economists estimate it would have been lower without his sweeping regime of global tariffs.
There is concern among Republicans that this economic picture has left them vulnerable in typically safe races, in states such as Texas, Ohio and Kansas.
"The southern states, the midwestern states, the American heartland - that is where Republicans tend to thrive," said Stephen Hawkins, the global director of research at the pollster More in Common.
"But that is where the Senate races that are so interesting are playing out right now."
"Places where President Trump won by 10, 12, 15 points just two years ago in the presidential race are now states where Democrats have a very viable chance of taking a Senate seat," he said.
When I asked voters in Iowa, a state Trump won in 2024 that has been hit by soaring fuel and fertiliser costs, whether the president would make people more or less likely to back Republicans - the answer was revealing.
"With the current climate, I would think possibly less, believe it or not," Paul Ross told me outside a busy college football game. "As a Republican myself, I would think it might be detrimental."
"I think it definitely puts voters off, there's no doubt about that, and I do think it probably raises the Democratic side to a level that isn't always there, just because it's Donald Trump," added Zach Shimp.
"He's got us in the war," another voter, Rose Heming, said. "Prices and groceries [are] high - sky high - gas is sky high."
That is the story of this election. Many voters, including in solidly Republican states, are hurting financially and polls suggest they may want to make this known at the ballot box on Tuesday.
But it is too simplistic to think this backdrop of war, tariffs and soaring prices will usher in a thumping Democratic victory in the House, Senate and governors' races.
Many Republican voters are angry with the president, but not so angry that they would vote for a Democrat. It is a mistake to assume that Trump's weak approval ratings translate to increasing popularity for the other side.
In fact, final polls taken before the elections suggest Trump's approval rating is around 38%. That is low - but the same polls, including a national NBC poll released on Sunday, external, indicate that only 29% of voters view the Democratic Party positively.
Voter frustration is no guarantee of a willingness to switch sides on Tuesday.
"We like to stay out of people's business," Tim McKinnon, a Republican in Iowa who voted for Trump in 2024 told me last month. "And so [Trump's] world stage interventions time after time after time - we don't love it.
"We didn't expect him to necessarily be a perfect choir boy obviously," his wife, Michelle, added. "We voted for the underbelly of what he was standing for."
The Democratic Party cannot rely on voters like the McKinnons, who are frustrated with elements of Trump's recent agenda, to back them. They do not think Democrats will ever reflect their Christian, conservative values.
"One dollar more on gas is not going to change what we believe in," Tim McKinnon told me.
If Democrats do win a large swathe of seats on Tuesday night, it won't necessarily be because voters love them – they just hate them a little less.
The party, however, is already looking ahead to a 2028 presidential election in which they will have to unite behind a single candidate. That is easier said than done given their clear fractures - some of which spilled out publicly during this election cycle, including in Michigan over the weekend.
Democrats will be closely watching these results for lessons ahead of 2028. Can they really win in Texas? Can they tempt rural voters in deep Republican strongholds? And will some of their rising stars, such as Jon Ossoff in Georgia and James Talarico in Texas, live up to the hype?
If the answer to some of these questions is no, there will be much to ponder for the party over the next year. And the post-mortem may not be pretty.
"This represents an opportunity, really, for Democrats to expand a lot of their influence, not just in terms of numbers, but in terms of perception of where they can compete," Hawkins, from the pollster More in Common, said.
Republican attempts, including from Trump himself, to paint the Democrats as dangerous communists have not landed with all voters.
In Detroit, Michigan, Nicole Williams - who owns her own hairdressing salon - summed up the view of many people I spoke to. "Anything is better than what we have now," she said. "Socialist? Socialised? It don't matter to me. Lower my cost of living."
"People are just tired of the disrespect to Americans, because he is an American," Gwen Jackson, another Michigan voter, said, referring to the state's left-wing Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed who Trump has repeatedly attacked.
"People are just tired," she said. "They're ready to see a change."
Even when a sitting president is more popular than Trump, their party usually loses seats in the midterms. This, combined with the latest polling, means there is confidence among Democrats that they will at least win the House of Representatives.
"It's the cost of living, it's the undeclared war," Democratic strategist Mary Anne Marsh said of the key issues. "Every Republican who did not stand up to Donald Trump is about to realise the consequences of believing he was invincible."
If the Democrats do win the House, the party could try to block any legislation Trump wants to pass. That is unlikely to worry him, given he has already tried to bypass Congress as much as possible and rule by signing executive orders from the Oval Office instead.
Trump will be more concerned about the investigations Democrats will be able to launch if they take control of the House. They may also try to impeach some of his cabinet members, with Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth seen as a likely candidate due to the war in Iran.
Winning the Senate on Tuesday is likely to be a much harder task for Democrats.
Thirty-five seats are up for election, and they will need a net gain of four to win control. If they lose in Michigan - a battleground seat they already hold - they will need a net gain of five seats to win it.
Most of the battleground races are close and several sit within the margin of error for pollsters. The crucial Senate races to watch are in Michigan, Texas, Ohio, Iowa, Maine, Alaska and North Carolina.
This is, in reality, where these midterm elections will be won and lost.
There is, as always with American elections, an important caveat around the polls. They have historically overestimated the Democratic Party and underestimated President Trump, who appears convinced that he can once again defy them.
But if the polls are close to correct about the suggested surge of support for Democrats, then he could be looking at painful defeats in states that have been reliable Republican strongholds for decades.
How Trump may respond to any stinging losses is an open question. He has repeatedly questioned the integrity and security of these elections, and the possibility that he does so again as votes are still being counted or when results are declared is a very real one.
These elections, however, represent a hugely significant moment for Americans, many of whom want to see real change over the next two years.
For both parties, they will serve as the final electoral test before a 2028 presidential election that will determine what a post-Trump politics looks and feels like. And for the president himself, they are an opportunity for voters to cast judgement on how he and his party are performing.
As Trump looks to shape his legacy in the next two years, the question is whether a change in control of Congress, which he has largely bypassed, would really curb his presidency at all.

article:
Mahmood refuses to put cost on care worker settlement climbdown

Mahmood refuses to put cost on care worker settlement climbdown
- Published
The home secretary has declined to specify how much scrapping her plan to make foreign care workers already in the UK wait longer to qualify for permanent settlement will cost.
Shabana Mahmood had originally proposed doubling the wait from five years to 10 for most migrants, with some facing a 15-year wait, which the Home Office suggested could save £10bn.
But under revised plans described by the Tories as a "U-turn", some foreign care workers will continue to wait five years, and others will be able to seek a five-year extension.
While not detailing the cost of the revised plans, Mahmood told the BBC they would still save "billions" because workers in other sectors would have to wait longer.
In March, the Home Office said, external the net lifetime cost of care workers and their adult dependants expected to settle between 2026 and 2030 was estimated at £10bn under existing rules.
Mahmood was proposing to delay settlement for this cohort in response to concerns over record post-Brexit net migration figures under the previous Tory government - dubbed the "Boriswave" by critics.
She had previously argued that not delaying settlement for migrant care workers already in the UK would lead to a "£10bn drain on our public finances".
Following a backlash, Mahmood announced on Monday that care workers who arrived in the UK before May 2025 and earned at least £25,000 a year would continue to qualify after five years, alongside some other groups.
Foreign care workers who do not qualify for the five-year settlement will be able to apply for a new five-year visa, and then seek settlement.
Just over 500,000 people will now be delayed from gaining permanent residency, down from almost 800,000 before Monday's changes. Some 1.9m people will settle in the UK between 2026 and 2030, according to the Home Office.
Indefinite leave to remain (ILR), also known as settlement, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible. They can also use it to apply for British citizenship.
No new cost figure yet
Asked about the cost of her revised plans, the home secretary told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the detailed costs would be published when her department puts the changes before Parliament.
In an interview recorded on Monday evening, she said the changes overall represented "savings in the billions" to the Department of Work and Pensions in people not claiming benefits.
"The reason for that is the cohort that was most likely to fall upon the state is that cohort of care workers not doing care work at the moment - if they'd settled at five years, many more of those would have gone on to claim benefits.
"That will now not happen because they will not be settling at five years - those individuals get a second chance to make that contribution that they originally came to make," she told Today.
The Home Office's £10bn figure was based on an estimate by the Migration Advisory Committee of how much an average migrant care worker would cost the UK in benefits and public services throughout their lifetime.
While Mahmood would not give a new savings figure, Home Office minister Anna Turley told BBC Breakfast it would be "at least £1bn over the next couple of years in terms of welfare savings" but "we'll be doing more calculations" on the total.
The Conservatives said the "U-turn" would cost the UK billions of pounds.
The £10bn figure has been criticised by the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR), which found a £115bn addition, external to UK public finances under current settlement rules.
"Public debate has focused heavily on the costs of recent migration, but this is not the whole story," IPPR associate director Marley Morris said.
Mahmood also declined to say whether Prime Minister Andy Burnham had told her to change tack on her proposals, which she had put forward in November under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.
She told Today a public consultation had resulted in a "transformative package" that "strikes the right balance".
She has denied Monday's move was a U-turn, and said the revised plans meant some 500,000 people already in the UK would now have to wait longer than five years to qualify for settlement.
The exact wait will vary based on income and whether people arrived in the UK legally or illegally.
Mahmood had faced criticism within the Labour Party for proposing to retrospectively change the rules for migrant workers already in the UK.
Housing Secretary Angela Rayner had said it amounted to "chang[ing] the goalposts", while several MPs described the retrospective approach as "un-British" and warned it could worsen the UK's skills shortage, particularly in the care sector.
