China state broadcaster pulls La Liga matches following Mbappé joke

China state broadcaster pulls La Liga matches following Mbappé joke
- Published
China's state broadcaster CCTV did not air a Real Madrid match on Sunday, despite the club's star striker Kylian Mbappé's apology for his "ill-judged" remarks on the late Chinese leader Mao Zedong.
Mbappé drew huge backlash after saying the meme "that makes [him] laugh the most" was the one in which his face is superimposed on a "Chinese dictator" resembling Mao.
China Media Group, CCTV's parent organisation, said last Tuesday it would suspend broadcasts of Spanish football La Liga matches following the furore, which also led to Mbappé being dropped by several Chinese brands.
China's foreign ministry had said it took Mbappé's apology "seriously". Real Madrid and La Liga have also apologised.
China Media Group had earlier demanded apologies from the three parties, calling them "an absolute prerequisite" for moving past the incident.
It has acknowledged the apologies, but has not commented on how long the broadcast blackout will last.
Mbappé, who reportedly made his remark about the meme on French talk show The Bridge, apologised later on Tuesday.
"My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world," he had said.
The joke did not go down well in China, where Mao is revered by the Communist Party, despite his having overseen one of the bloodiest chapters in the country's past.
Mao, who led the Chinese Communist Party to victory in the civil war and founded the People's Republic of China, died in 1976.
During his rule he oversaw the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution, which led to a famine that killed tens of millions and unleashed violent purges across Chinese society.
This is not the first time Beijing has suspended sports broadcasts over political sensitivities.
It pulled NBA games for a year from October 2019 after Daryl Morey, the general manager of Houston Rockets, tweeted in support of Hong Kong protesters during widespread pro-democracy protests in the city.
Morey backtracked on his comment after fierce criticism from Chinese fans, sponsors and commercial partners.
"I have had a lot of opportunity since that tweet to hear and consider other perspectives," Morey later wrote.
"I have always appreciated the significant support our Chinese fans and sponsors...I would hope that those who are upset will know that offending or misunderstanding them was not my intention."
Real Madrid beat Racing Santander 3-0 in Sunday's match, with goals from Mbappé, Jude Bellingham and Yan Diomande.

Russian bombing kills 31 people at Ukraine aid centre, Kyiv says

Russian bombing kills 31 people at Ukraine aid centre, Kyiv says

At least 31 people have been killed after Russian bombs hit an aid distribution centre in Zaporizhia, the Ukrainian regional head has said, describing it as one of the deadliest attacks there since the start of the full-scale invasion.
Mykhailo Semikin said at least nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit the village of Komyshuvakha in southern Ukraine on Monday and the aid centre collapsed from a "direct hit".
"They had come for help - not to a military facility, not to a frontline position, but to a place where they were supposed to receive support," he wrote on Telegram.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the attack "utterly horrific" and said there were still people "under the rubble".
Zelensky posted a video showing a huge crater left after Monday's attack and rescuers searching for survivors.
However, officials say teams have at times been forced to halt their search because of Russian drone attacks in the area.
Zelensky said after the first strike on the local school "used for humanitarian needs", there was a second attack on the place where people were sheltering.
He earlier said that "the Russians could not have been unaware that the local residents who remained in Komyshuvakha received humanitarian aid there every week" on Monday.
The Russian military has not publicly commented.
Three days of mourning have been declared in the region.
The death toll has continued to rise on Tuesday. Earlier, when 29 people were confirmed to have died, Semikin said another 10 had been injured and 48 were reported missing.
Among the dead are two rescuers and four police officers, according to Ukraine's state emergencies service DSNS.
Zelensky said the attack was "yet another proof that Russia does not want any de-escalation".
He said that after a recent successful joint Russian-Ukrainian operation to evacuate civilians from the Russia-occupied southern city of Oleshky during a temporary ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, "there was a moment when the next steps could show that peace is possible".
"With such killings, Russia is sending the exact opposite signal - Russia is counting on further killings," Zelensky said.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Teams from Ukraine, Russia and the US are due to resume peace talks in Abu Dhabi, the United Arab Emirates, next week, US President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff said on X.
Since the talks were suspended in February, Moscow has stepped up attacks as Kyiv virtually ran out of Western-supplied interceptors to defend against missiles.
No major breakthrough is expected at the talks. Witkoff said the discussions would focus on "post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace".
Witkoff said US negotiators would also meet European and Nato officials this week in Brussels.

article:
The Indian chef who brought curry to America - then vanished

The Indian chef who brought curry to America - then vanished
- Published
One hundred and twenty-five years ago, in 1901, an Indian chef opened what was almost certainly the first Indian restaurant in the US.
Ranji Smile was one of the most colourful and enigmatic figures to shape the American food scene.
In the summer of 1899, Smile sailed from London to New York. We know hardly anything about his origins and early life, not even his real name.
"Ranji" was probably a nod to the Indian cricketing sensation KS Ranjitsinhji, then a star attraction at Test matches in Britain. "Smile" could have been an anglicisation of "Ismail".
Whatever his origins, Smile possessed an uncommon knack for reinvention. Once through the portals of Ellis Island, he appended a new name to his identity, something more in keeping with America's egalitarian promise: Joe.
Joe Ranji Smile arrived in New York to work at Sherry's Restaurant, a glittering new establishment on Fifth Avenue.
In London, he had been a curry cook at the Cecil and Savoy hotels. Here, according to an 1899 profile in Harper's, he was noticed by Sherry's owner, Louis Sherry, who invited him to bring his culinary skills across the Atlantic. Late Victorian London already boasted an Indian dining scene: as early as 1810, Sake Dean Mohamed, a native of Patna, had opened his Hindostanee Coffee House near Portman Square, plying customers with both curry and hookah.
Manhattanite tastebuds lacked much exposure to masala. There was, however, growing curiosity about India and its culture. Swami Vivekananda, the spellbinding orator and exponent of Hindu philosophy, enthralled audiences during his visits to the city in the 1890s. At the same time, more Indian sailors, students and professionals trickled into New York. This was probably why Louis Sherry decided to add a curry cook to his kitchen staff.
At Sherry's Restaurant, Smile joined one of the great culinary institutions of the American Gilded Age. Positioning itself as a rival to Delmonico's, New York's byword for fine dining, Sherry's catered to city plutocrats like the Astors and was famed for over-the-top dining experiences. During one such soiree, patrons marched their horses into a ballroom, saddled up and ate on horseback.
Smile, a skilled showman, thrived in this environment.
Customers soon flocked to taste his preparations of Bombay duck, a glutinous lizardfish that is a delicacy along the western Indian coast, and novel creations like "Lettuce Ceylon".
Cooking and serving became a performance. Dressed in a satin coat and blue silk turban, Smile salaamed in front of customers before enquiring, "Will you have the curry hot or mild, sahib?" Pictures of Sherry's curry chef were soon splashed across newspapers and magazines. One headline said it all: "New York women go wild over him."
As his fame grew, Smile decided in 1901 to leave Sherry's and set up his own establishment, one exclusively devoted to Indian cuisine. For financial backing, he leaned on Roland R Conklin, a prominent financier, external and the inventor of an early version of the motorhome.
Omar Khayyam, Smile's Indian restaurant, opened in late 1901 at 325 Fifth Avenue. This was prime real estate, a block away from the original Waldorf-Astoria Hotel where, 29 years later, the Empire State Building would rise. Smile adorned the restaurant with Indian draperies and hanging lanterns.
As the New York Herald reported, a fleet of Indian waiters in "voluminous turbans" staffed the premises, as did a group of Indian musicians. Now quite the embodiment of the American immigrant success story, Smile eagerly awaited his customers and fans.
Alas, they never materialised. Within a year, Omar Khayyam shuttered. The New York Sun claimed that people had "tired" of Indian fare, dismissing it as a passing fad.
Smile's stardom, which had blazed so brightly in the Big Apple, also began to dim. Unfortunately, his showmanship and flair for theatrics shaded into deceit and criminal activity.
Smile began claiming that he was, after all, not an everyday Joe but rather a prince, the son of the emir of Baluchistan, a fictional title. And, before opening Omar Khayyam, he made a quick visit to Bombay, where he pronounced himself to be a guest at the upcoming coronation of King Edward VII in London and recruited a retinue of staff: valets, a dancing girl, and "mahouts to drive his herds of elephants".
All of this was reported in New York newspapers like the Times because, as a subsequent federal case against him alleged, Smile illegally trafficked this staff into the US to work at his restaurant. Instead of becoming a pioneer outpost of Indian gastronomy, Omar Khayyam nearly got Smile deported.
"Prince" Joe Ranji Smile evaded deportation (many in his retinue were not as lucky) and went on evolving his invented persona, all while wooing and marrying a series of impressionable young American women. He began claiming that Indian food was a secret elixir for female beauty. "The eye will grow lustrous, the complexion will be yet so lovely," Smile promised, displaying his wives as clinching proof.
Meanwhile, he honed his performing skills at Indian cooking demonstrations across the country.
In Washington DC, Smile prepared dishes, including a dubious-sounding dessert called "bungalow", while a juggler and dancing girl entertained him. On his way to Chicago, as one newspaper in remote Idaho reported, he declared himself to be no longer the son of the emir but the brother of an even more fanciful figure, the "great Beglerberg of Baluchistan". If Smile was guilty of being a conman, then his American interlocutors were equally guilty of wide-eyed gullibility.
While Smile's theatrics and good food kept people entertained for a while, the tall tales and outright fabrications soon caught up with him.
Smile retreated from the public gaze, hurt by further brushes with the law which ranged from forcible confinement of one of his dancing girls to refusing to pay a bill at an Italian restaurant in Manhattan. By the 1920s, he apparently abandoned cooking entirely, listing his occupation as a merchant.
The final shred of evidence about Smile dates from 1937, when his fourth or fifth American wife approached the New York Supreme Court and filed for an annulment of her marriage to her now-absconded husband. Ranji Smile's last act of reinvention was to simply disappear.
Despite this inglorious end, Smile and his Indian restaurant did pave the way for the popularisation of Indian cuisine in America. Other immigrants soon tested the waters.
In 1909, Saint Nihal Singh, a peripatetic journalist from Punjab, introduced readers of the Chicago Daily Tribune to recipes for bhajias, puris, halwa, and "Fried Chicken a la Hindoo".
Aware of the unfamiliarity of many Indian ingredients amongst Chicagoans, Singh urged readers to look for them in the city's Chinese grocery stores. On another occasion, which might make contemporary chefs blush, he suggested that hamburger meat was an adequate substitute for preparing gosht pilau (a meat pilaf).
Not long after Ranji Smile was hauled to court for trafficking immigrants, a young man from Ceylon named KY Kira arrived at Ellis Island.
Like Smile, he had a talent for reinvention. Kira joined a troupe of Sinhalese dancers which performed for American circuses like Barnum and Bailey and Ringling Brothers. In 1913, he opened an Indian restaurant in Harlem, eventually called the Ceylon India Inn. Unlike Omar Khayyam, the Ceylon India Inn was a hit.
New York now had a much larger immigrant Indian population and the restaurant attracted expatriate nationalists and revolutionaries. But it also benefited from a burgeoning American interest in Indian culture and food. By the 1920s, Kira's restaurant, now located off Times Square, catered to Broadway and Hollywood stars. The Ceylon India Inn remained in business until the late 1980s, touting itself as the first Indian restaurant in America.
That, of course, was not the case. Ranji Smile might be long forgotten, but 125 years after the brief existence of his Omar Khayyam restaurant, his legacy lives on in the thousands of Indian eateries flourishing across the US.
Dinyar Patel is associate professor of history at SPJIMR in Mumbai

article:
How video game remakes tap the power of nostalgia

How video game remakes tap the power of nostalgia
- Published
The moment she saw footage from the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, Kacey Doran picked up her phone. She had to tell her sister.
"Have you seen this?" messaged Doran, excitedly.
Nearly 30 years ago, a 10-year-old Doran had sat in front of her family's TV, reading out the dialogue on screen to her sister, a year younger, as they inched their way through the original Nintendo 64 game's sprawling, puzzle-filled dungeons. Ocarina's fantasy-like story, and beautiful music, enthralled them both.
It was also the first game Doran ever completed. Now, countless memories rushed back to her as she devoured clips of the fully redesigned version, due to arrive on the Switch 2 later this year.
Doran's sister messaged back: "I'm not tearing up… YOU'RE tearing up."
This is the power of nostalgia – and a perfect example of how video games can trigger it. Doran now teaches an esports course at Rowan University in New Jersey. She says the original Ocarina of Time, released in 1998, had a "magical" quality that she hopes to rediscover, and also share with her sister's children.
The video games industry has long leaned on remakes. From Mario Kart to the Final Fantasy series, or even Pac-Man, some games just keep coming back in updated forms, as new generations of gamers emerge and as computer hardware improves, enabling more detailed graphics and increasingly expansive game worlds.
While the emotional hook may be the most significant draw, putting out a remake can be a double-edged sword. Some gamers are very protective of their favourite titles and new versions don't always meet certain fans' astronomically high expectations.
Nostalgia is an important but mixed emotion, says Tim Wulf, at the Centre for Advanced Internet Studies in Bochum, Germany. It has positive aspects but also a kind of sadness, too. Happiness in remembering things that were important to us, and also an awareness that that time is now gone.
"It's a social emotion because memories that induce nostalgia for us are connected to other people," he explains, adding that nostalgia can boost our self-esteem while highlighting key social bonds.
Video games, says Wulf, are notoriously good at triggering nostalgia because gamers can "jump into the same environment". In other words, games are like time machines for our emotions, and returning to fondly remembered places can feel stabilising or reassuring in an ever-changing world.
Doran, for one, notes that when you return to a favourite old game, there's something satisfying about deploying previously learned skills. You know what to do here, you're winning again. Just like the old days.
Putting out remasters and remakes has been a "really successful" strategy for the games industry, says Piers Harding-Rolls, head of games research at Ampere Analysis.
"Tying in with established audiences and building on existing content is quite a safe route for a lot of companies," he adds. In many cases, it is cheaper to update an existing game rather than create a new title from scratch.
Among other remakes that have found big audiences recently are those of Resident Evil 4 and Assassin's Creed Black Flag.
But Ocarina of Time perhaps stands out because, ever since its original release, it has been considered by many as one of the greatest games ever made. "The interest from all the Gen Zs that I work with is really high," says Harding-Rolls. The legend of The Legend of Zelda, as it were.
Clearly, nostalgia is not the only driver of interest in the remake, and today's audiences will expect a game that plays to today's standards.
Games companies must keep innovating when linking contemporary audiences to the past, says Wulf, in order satisfy their desire for fresh experiences. And although Wulf himself was a big fan of the original, he has no personal interest in the Ocarina of Time remake. "I want a new game – I don't want to play an old game," he says. Nostalgia isn't always enough for some.
Plus, critics often highlight a tension between originals and remakes. Which is the definitive version? In 2021, Square Enix released the bizarrely titled Nier Replicant ver.1.22474487139... – a remaster of a game first published in 2010. One reviewer wrote, external, "What we're left with is two nearly identical Niers each vying to be the true Nier."
Fans may react badly should a remaster or remake fail to do justice to the source material. And, in the gaming world, angry fan reactions can be serious.
"There's always going to be that fan base or group of people that are going to nit-pick," says Stephanie Ijoma, chief executive and founder of NNESAGA, a consultancy and creative agency.
Ultimately, games developers working on remakes have to "find the right balance" between appealing to fans and allowing themselves to be creative with the material, she adds. "You can't make art in fear, you can't create in fear."
Ijoma gives the example of Final Fantasy VII. First released in 1997, it got a highly anticipated remake in 2020.
This was a game Ijoma played back in the late 1990s and she was thrilled to be able to share it with younger players today.
Remakes enable this sharing of experiences because getting old computer hardware or video games consoles to work, while a pastime loved by some, is not possible for everyone.
"I've tried multiple times to play Silent Hill 2 because I'm interested in older games but it's such a difficult game to come into nowadays," says Niklas Hallin, a solo indie game developer who runs the studio Neckbolt. "They made a remake and it's so smooth, it just works. It works on your modern hardware."
Hallin did not play many games as a child so he says nostalgia isn't much of a motivator for him. However, in his own games, he likes to include subtle stylistic references to classic games because he knows that this appeals to gamers.
Indie developers often lean on retro games aesthetics not just because people respond well to them – but also because they are easier to achieve. "You can't compete with billion dollar budgets, super high-fidelity, Triple A graphics," he says.
One question remains. The visual difference, today, between games released years apart is, arguably, negligible. So will there be any point in remaking a game from 2026 in, say, 2038? Will technology have moved on so much by then that it's actually worth it?
Harding-Rolls predicts that games companies will still seek to connect new audiences with classic titles by offering updates.
Remakes might become less about graphical improvements and more about editorial adjustments. "Reinterpretations," he says. "Or versions with additional content."
It's never really "game over", is it?

Party Rock Anthem singer struggled with mental health before death

Party Rock Anthem singer struggled with mental health before death
- Published
A British singer who was a member of the girl group G.R.L took her own life, an inquest has found.
Lauren Bennett, 36, who also featured on LMFAO's 2011 hit Party Rock Anthem, was found dead in Kent on 29 May.
In a statement read out by an assistant coroner on Friday, her husband Kenny Wormald said she had been struggling with severe mental health issues before her death.
The court heard she told him she was going out for a walk on the morning of her death while he remained in bed half asleep.
When she did not return for a few hours and did not answer calls or texts from him and multiple other family members, Wormald and her father went looking for her.

He went to a rural location using Find My iPhone for Bennett's device where he found her body.
The professional dancer said the pair talked about everything and there was no indication she was going to end her life.
Her father, Richard Bennett, said his daughter had lived an "amazing life" in a statement read out by assistant coroner Jyoti Gill.
He said she signed a record deal at just 17 and moved to the US on her own.
Pages of farewell notes were later found at her home, Kent and Medway Coroners' Court heard.
Bennett had previously been diagnosed with Fragile X syndrome, a genetic disorder that can cause anxiety, mood instability and depression, it was also told.
In the January before her death, the musician did not sleep for a number of days and was admitted to hospital under a mental health section.
She had experienced "substantial psychological suffering" since this point, Gill noted.
Bennett was in the care of "special mental health services" at the time of her death.
She had reacted poorly to medication and did not think she was going to get better, the court was told.
No alcohol or illicit drugs were found in Bennett's system when she died.
Bennett's former musical group G.R.L. shared the news of her death on its Instagram account in July.
"Our hearts are broken, and we cannot begin to express how much she meant to us," they said.
Party Rock Anthem has been named the fifth most successful song of all time by Billboard after spending six weeks as the number one song on its Hot 100 in 2011.
Bennett also featured alongside LMFAO members in the song's music video, which has more than 2.5bn views on YouTube.
Aria Crescendo, who Bennett performed with in the band Paradiso Girls prior to G.R.L., told the BBC: "She was super talented, super beautiful and super funny.
"We're so in shock that this happened, honestly."

article:
Refugee athlete to make history for second time at Youth Olympics

Refugee athlete to make history for second time at Youth Olympics
- Published
When he started running, Yiech Pur Biel had to compete barefoot. Far from home in a new country, it was the first step towards rebuilding his life as a refugee.
"That's when I decided now it is time to depend on myself and also to start a new life with determination," he tells BBC Newsbeat.
In 2016, Biel made history competing in the 800m event as part of the first Olympic refugee team at the Rio summer Olympics in Brazil.
Ten years on, he's making history again leading the first refugee team for the Youth Olympics as their Chef de Mission.
Joining almost 3,000 athletes, the small team of six will be wanting to make sure their debut counts - but Biel says they're also hoping to send a message that "refugees still need our help".
Hosted in Senegal, Saturday's opening ceremony will launch the first ever Olympic sporting event on African soil.
Africa is home to nearly 45 million displaced people, out of almost 120 million globally, representing the world's biggest displacement crisis.
Biel says for the refugee team, the Youth Olympics is "a chance for them to tell the world and also to represent the population, especially the refugee population, in Africa".
"It's about representing the hope of young people who are living in a refugee camp, who have lost their motivation or their talent."
Biel was a child when he was forced to flee his home in South Sudan after his village was attacked.
He ended up in Kenya, telling BBC Newsbeat: "It traumatised me, starting a new life, being alone in Kakuma," referring to the major refugee settlement close to the border between Kenya and South Sudan.
"But I started a new life, I believe that school helped me a lot. It helped me to interact with young people who faced the same challenges."
The rest of his childhood was spent on the refugee camp where he took an interest in football.
After realising it wasn't the sport for him, he gave running a go during trials set up by the International Olympic Committee - where he raced without shoes.
It made him "believe that if I can work harder by myself, I can achieve", he says.
One of the athletes on the refugee team, Arno Yafunga Botay, also lived at Kakuma after fleeing his home in the Democratic Republic of Congo in 2017, when he was six.
Now 15, he will be competing in judo and told BBC Sport Africa he's promised to bring back a gold medal which he'd like to take to the refugee camp.
"I think if I achieve [a] gold medal, I can go there and teach them the value of judo," he said.
As for Biel, he says it's an honour to be chosen as the team's Chef de Mission.
"This is so important for them, to learn from my experience as an athlete and also as a refugee who is coming from a refugee camp," he says.
"So this role means a lot to me and also means a lot to those young athletes who are going to compete."
Competition at Dakar 2026 begins later, with the opening ceremony on Saturday.

The childhood promise that brought professional ballet to a post-industrial town

The childhood promise that brought professional ballet to a post-industrial town
- Published
Darius James remembers sitting before Gwent County Council at 10 years old and being asked the question: "Why should we give you money?"
He had earned a place at the Royal Ballet School, but his parents could not afford the school fees.
In response, he told the council he would go away and develop his skills and use them to help his community in Newport.
As James' Newport-based dance company Ballet Cymru marks its 40th anniversary, he hopes he has fulfilled that promise.
Growing up in Newport in the 1970s, James said it was "really, really unusual" for a boy to be doing ballet and that he was grateful for the support of his parents.
He said his father, a keen footballer who spent his life working at the Alcan aluminium factory in Newport, particularly embraced something that was so new to him.
"He didn't really understand at the beginning, but he loved it. And we work with a lot of young people now whose parents are not quite as understanding, even 40 years later, which is a bit depressing."
After years of training at the Royal Ballet School and dancing professionally, James returned to Newport and founded Ballet Cymru, originally called Gwent Ballet Theatre, in 1986.
He said the idea to start a ballet company in a post-industrial town was "totally crazy, but totally needed and logical".
"There is so much talent in Newport, so many brilliant, brilliant young people, and there's not the outlets you have in London or Cardiff."
After some initial backing from the Arts Council of Wales, he said Ballet Cymru went 13 years without any funding at all and 28 years without its own dedicated studio.
To help finance the company, James toured with other ballet troupes including Northern Ballet.
Amy Doughty, the company's co-artistic director and James' wife, joined Ballet Cymru as a dancer in 1996, and said they would rehearse wherever they could find space.
"We'd have to carry in all the ballet bars, all the equipment that we use, all the dance floors," she said.
However, with National Lottery funding in 2014, the company was able to renovate a warehouse into its current studio.
It sits on the same industrial estate James' father walked through to work each day.
In the early years, James said he would cover the word "ballet" on the van they took to do community workshops because he feared it would put people off before trying.
Doughty believes attitudes have changed since then, adding: "I think we've worked really hard in Newport to go into schools, to do shows here, to really develop people who understand what we're about."
However, James believes some barriers to participation in dance remain.
The directors identified seven boys through the company's Duets scheme who they believed showed talent, only to face reluctance from some parents.
"The dads will come in and say my son doesn't dance, he doesn't want to do ballet," Doughty said.
But the pair said the children had "absolutely loved it".
Established in 2012, the scheme runs workshops in Welsh schools where the company identifies children it believes have natural ability in dance but are not in any formal training.
Ballet Cymru then provides them with two years of free tuition. For Doughty, the financial aspect is particularly important.
She grew up in Australia as one of four children and said without scholarships, she would not have enjoyed the same career in dance.
Doughty feels that not being familiar with ballet can stop people from engaging with the art form.
"The reality is, we've got to take it to them. They're not going to seek us out, why would they?"
She said one way they try to do this is by giving free show tickets to children participating in the Duets programme and their families.
For some, she said, it can be their first time seeing live ballet.
Ballet Cymru marked its anniversary with shows at the Riverfront theatre in Newport on Thursday and Friday, before a tour to Leeds and Bangor.
Doughty said her hope was that she and James had built something that would last and grow beyond them.
Looking back at the council's decision to support him, James said: "They believed in me.
"If in the last 40 years we've reached one kid and inspired them to be better than they would have been otherwise, then surely that's worth it.
"I'm sure it's more, but just one would be worth it."

The Zombies' Rod Argent back on stage after stroke

The Zombies founding member Rod Argent has returned to the stage for his first live performance in two and a half years after suffering a stroke.
The 81-year-old keyboardist said he had felt "really nervous" before joining bandmate Colin Blunstone at St Albans Cathedral as part of the band's annual Begin Here Festival.
Founded in the Hertfordshire city in 1962, the band most recently became active again in 2004 before stopping after Argent's stroke in July 2024.
"I felt people were all trying to make me feel at home in the best possible way, and then after each song they all stood up and cheered... It was very emotional," he said.
Argent was welcomed to the stage with a standing ovation, with the audience rising again after each song.
Singer Blunstone said: "It was very emotional and I think the crowd felt it and we certainly felt it on stage... It was a wonderful reaction to him.
"They were a wonderful audience. They really, really were and they lifted us... It was very moving."
Argent initially thought he had suffered a transient ischaemic attack, external before hospital tests confirmed it had been a stroke.
The songwriter said: "In my head, if I'm just thinking through things, I've got absolutely no lack of fluency at all.
"But when I speak, sometimes I lose my thread, lose where I'm going... but it is getting better."
Argent also paid tribute to his wife for her support during his recovery, and said he did not want to tour again.
The songwriter – who also founded the eponymous band Argent – said: "Over the last two years she's been wonderful because she's got a few health issues herself, but she was with me when I had the stroke.
"I want to spend more time with my wife now really, because I was away all the time before."

Martha Stewart says she 'really screwed up' with homeless Halloween costume

Martha Stewart says she 'really screwed up' with homeless Halloween costume
- Published
Veteran lifestyle guru Martha Stewart has admitted she "really screwed up" by dressing as a homeless person for Halloween.
The 85-year-old US entrepreneur and personality has deleted a photo of herself wearing torn clothes and dirt on her face, holding a sign saying: "I am hungry help me!!"
She posted a statement on Sunday saying she was "distressed that my Halloween costume yesterday, which was intended to bring more awareness to the very serious subject of homelessness, has offended people, which was never my intention".
That was followed by a fuller apology. "It's hard to admit when you've really screwed up. My earlier statement didn't go far enough. I know many people are suffering economically. Wearing a costume like I did was insensitive and not funny. I am very sorry."
Stewart had captioned her original Instagram photo: "My QVC candles are perfect for Halloween!!!"
The post received a swift and sharp backlash.
"This sartorial take on a homeless person is a lot. Insulting? Demeaning? Confusing? All of the above," PR expert Molly McPherson wrote, external.
One person wrote on social media: "Why in the hell would you even think about wearing that as a costume?"
Another said: "Why would she do that? Who did she think would find that funny? Billionaires?"
Arguably the original lifestyle influencer, Stewart started a catering business in the 1970s and rose to fame in the 1990s when she started her own magazine, Martha Stewart Living.
She later became a billionaire, albeit briefly, when her media empire Martha Stewart Living Omnimedia was floated on the stock market in 1999.
But in 2004 she was sentenced to five months in prison after she was found guilty on a number of charges related to an insider trading scandal.
She has since attempted to rebuild her brand, starring in her own reality television show, expanding her food products and teaming up with rapper and friend Snoop Dogg for a television series.
In 2015, she sold Martha Stewart Living Omnimedia for more than $350m (£220m).

article:
Celebrity Traitors comes to a climax in nail-biting final

Celebrity Traitors comes to a climax in nail-biting final
- Published
- Spoiler warning: This story reveals details of The Celebrity Traitors final
We've had four weeks of suspense, suspicion and very suspect tactics, as some of Britain's biggest stars engaged in a battle of wits to win the most popular show on TV.
The second series of BBC One's The Celebrity Traitors reached its climax on Friday, with the 21 original contestants having been reduced to seven before the final.
They were then whittled down to two winners - with the faithful duo of comedian Romesh Ranganathan and Heartstopper actor Sebastian "Bash" Croft emerging victorious.
The players successfully banished the remaining traitors - Love Island host Maya Jama and YouTuber King Kenny - in dramatic fashion, and the winning pair shared the £83,000 prize for their charities.
The finale drew an average audience of 11.2 million live viewers, and that number will rise when catch-up is included. Other recent episodes have been watched by more than 15 million, including catch-up.
Kenny reached the final stage, the endgame, after turning on his fellow traitor Maya at the last round table.
Kenny, Romesh and Bash were joined by singer James Blunt in the climax of the endgame, where the remaining contestants gather around a fire pit to decide whether they think there are any traitors left.
When James and Kenny were tied in a vote for who was a traitor, Bash persuaded Romesh to banish Kenny instead of James - thereby securing victory for team faithful.
"Absolutely devastated. Almost scraped it," Kenny seethed. "I was so close, I smelled the victory."
However, he can take consolation from the fact his performance on the show has established him as a mainstream star.
In a further twist, James chose another round of voting and was subsequently evicted himself, leaving Romesh and Bash as the last men standing.
"This might actually be the best day of my life," said 24-year-old Bash through tears of joy.
He, too, can expect a major career boost.
Romesh reflected: "I just really hope my mum's proud. And also my youngest son Charlie, who wanted me to come on the show - dad won. Please show me some respect."
The pair will split their winnings between two refugee charities, the Refugee Council and Choose Love.
Earlier, actor Michael Sheen was murdered in the first action of Friday's episode. "I am incredibly disappointed," he said. "Gutted that I got so close to the end. It's been absolutely unforgettable."
When it came to the endgame, Little Mix singer Leigh-Anne Pinnock was swiftly banished after Kenny voted to remove her.
"I was thinking me and him had a mutual understanding, and now I feel so stupid," she raged.
"But I'm walking away feeling super proud and like I've really accomplished something here."
Meanwhile, James B was left rueing one final mistake in a long but valiant catalogue of misjudgements throughout the series.
The singer, who looked aghast when he was attacked by Romesh during the endgame, was then the only one to choose to banish again when it came to the final three.
James was unaware that Romesh and Bash had both chosen to end the game - meaning he too could have been a winner if he had done the same - but became the victim of his own choice to banish.
"I've loved trying to work it out, I've loved getting it wrong so often, I've loved the tiny moments when I've got it right," he said wistfully. "I've loved the game."
Celebrities who departed earlier in the series included ex-EastEnders actor Ross Kemp, model Jerry Hall, sitcom star Miranda Hart, comedian Joe Lycett, presenter Hannah Fry and former BBC journalist Amol Rajan.
This series is also likely to be remembered for the two contestants who made the unorthodox decision to reveal themselves as traitors, before being summarily dispatched by their fellow players.
First, actor Richard E Grant was so giddy to have received the tap on the shoulder that he blurted out his supposedly secret status in episode two.
Comedian James Acaster, meanwhile, was the most reluctant traitor in the history of The Traitors, and unexpectedly gave himself up when he came under pressure at the round table in Thursday's penultimate episode.
Aftermath of Acaster's admission
There have been reports, external that filming of the scene was paused and he was checked by welfare staff after he became anxious.
Asked about the reports, a BBC spokesperson said on Friday that the safety and welfare of those taking part was the "highest priority", and "players are closely monitored and supported throughout by production which includes a dedicated and experienced welfare team".
Speculation about the round table being heavily edited was fuelled when eagle-eyed viewers noticed, external a shot of Romesh reacting in shock - apparently to James A's initial confession - which in fact seemed to have come from a later moment, after Romesh had voted for James by writing his name on the blackboard.
In the episode, the sequence where the celebrities all voted for James in light of his admission was shown as a relatively quick and straightforward process, raising a question about what prompted Romesh's shocked look.
Acaster did not take part in Friday's edition of spin-off show Uncloaked, which reunited some of the celebrity contestants following the final.
'A bit dull?'
The comedian's bombshell the previous night did provide the programme with a twist to spark it to life after what some viewers saw as a mid-series lull.
On Thursday, the Hollywood Reporter noted, external that the show had achieved record-breaking ratings - before asking: "Why, then, has much of the consensus on social media been that it's all felt a bit dull?"
Some noted a shortage of true back-stabbing, double-crossing and explosive rows - the things, in other words, that viewers love the most - while the celebrities were more chummy and savvy than previous groups of castle dwellers.
And while there was no shortage of big characters, this season lacked an equivalent to Alan Carr, the hugely popular and apparently hapless comedian who lied and murdered his way to an unlikely victory as a traitor last year.
The drama ramped up in the final, though, and Friday's episode is likely to have been the most watched TV programme of the year.

University staff warned of 'difficult decisions' ahead over finances

University staff warned of 'difficult decisions' ahead over finances
- Published
Staff at Queen's University of Belfast (QUB) have been warned of "difficult decisions" ahead due to the university's finances.
Pay deals with staff, and childcare and gym fees for staff and students are under review while staff car-parking charges are going up.
The details came in an message to staff from the university's vice-chancellor Prof Sir Ian Greer.
His message came after the grant paid by the Northern Ireland Executive to universities had a "significant" cut in 2025/26.
What is the state of Queen's University's finances?
According to Greer, the university had a deficit of about £12.5m in the last financial year.
While the university hoped to reduce that, he said that a combination of cuts in funding from Stormont and a fall in student fee income meant the university had to "control costs".
There have been tougher visa requirements for international students coming to UK universities in recent years.
According to the university's annual accounts, the income QUB received from international student fees recently fell by around £5m - from more than £60m in 2024 to around £55m in 2025.
Greer also said that student recruitment income was expected to be around £7m "below target" in the current year.
He said that the university still hoped to deliver agreed pay deals to staff.
"However, given the Department for the Economy's position, we have no choice but to keep the position under review," he said.
Some other charges, including for staff car-parking on campus are going up.
Costs for university services that staff and students use, like childcare and membership of the university Physical Education Centre (PEC) are also under review and may rise.
However, plans for a new university heritage and visitor centre, external, to be built in the Quad on the site of the current administration building, are going ahead.
But there may be more savings measures to come.
"The University Management Board has agreed to identify approximately £10m of savings this year and, depending on the final position with public funding, further difficult choices may have to follow this academic year," Greer said.
How are students affected?
Greer said that due to a cap on student numbers, QUB had turned away "around 500 students who had the grades to attend Queen's".
The number of local students both QUB and Ulster University (UU) can admit is decided by Stormont's Department for the Economy and depends on available funding.
Current QUB students who use university childcare or the PEC may also face higher fees for the services.
But Greer said that "the student experience must remain central to our decisions".
What has the university said?
In a further statement to BBC News NI, a QUB spokesperson said that the university was "facing increasing financial pressures arising from reduced public funding, lower student recruitment income and rising costs".
"Our planned approach is centred on both stability and growth, to secure the university's long-term future while supporting our students and staff," it said.
"Strategic investment in projects such as the Public Engagement and Discovery Centre are part of a commercial growth strategy to help generate income while providing teaching and research space to further enhance the student experience."

article:
From Bitcoin to Binance: Crypto terms and what they mean

From Bitcoin to Binance: Crypto terms and what they mean
- Published
From the rapidly rising and falling values of Bitcoin to high-profile heists like the hacking of Binance, the world of cryptocurrencies is often in the headlines.
The world's biggest crypto exchange said hackers had gained access to $6.3bn (£4.7bn) worth of digital assets, and while it has frozen about half, many remained in the hands of the thieves.
These stories are full of specialist language that people outside the industry struggle to understand.
So if you're unsure what the blockchain or a crypto echange or even a cryptocurrency itself are, here are some key terms and what they mean.
Bitcoin
While many may struggle with the finer points of crypto, pretty much everyone has heard of its most famous product: Bitcoin. But what actually is it?
Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is to say a type of digital currency. Unlike traditional currencies, Bitcoin is not controlled by centralised financial institutions.
This makes it popular for people who think decentralisation can bring financial freedom, but it also makes it extremely volatile with it rising and falling in value at the whim of Bitcoin buyers and sellers.
Donald Trump has pledged to make the US the "crypto capital of the world" - backtracking on his previous claim that Bitcoin was a "scam".
Its price topped a much-awaited threshold of $100,000 in December 2024, then rose to $120,000 in July 2025 as US politicians prepared to debate bills to regulate digital assets.
In October 2025, Bitcoin hit an all-time high of around $126,000, buoyed by a continued wave of institutional investment and positive market sentiment. But it has been known to plummet in value just as quickly as it spikes.
In early February 2026, its price dipped below $65,000 to effectively wipe out gains achieved under President Trump.
Against the backdrop of these frequent price fluctuations, speculation continues about the true identity of Bitcoin's mysterious inventor known only as Satoshi Nakamoto.
Blockchain
Blockchain is the technology underpinning all cryptocurrencies, and many related products like non-fungible tokens (NFTs). In essence, it is a virtual spreadsheet on which all the buying and selling of crypto is recorded. They are arranged in blocks linked together in a giant chain - hence the name.
Every cryptocurrency transaction is individually recorded onto the blockchain by a huge network of volunteers verifying its authenticity by using computer programmes.
The incentive to do this for Bitcoin's network is that the first person to validate transactions is rewarded in Bitcoin. This potentially lucrative process, known as mining, is also controversial because of the incredible amount of energy, external used as people the world over race to be the first to successfully update the blockchain.
Crypto Exchange
A crypto exchange is the digital platform where investors can buy, sell and trade cryptocurrencies.
Similar to traditional investing, a crypto exchange acts as a brokerage where people can transfer traditional money, like pounds or dollars, in exchange for cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin or Ethereum. Most transactions are accompanied by fees.
Binance is the world's biggest, which is part of what makes the hack so monumental.
Crypto Wallet
A crypto wallet is a place where investors hold their cryptocurrency. There are two types, a hot wallet and a cold wallet.
Hot wallets are connected to the internet, and thus more accessible for quick transfers and easy access.
Cold wallets are physical devices like specially designed USB sticks that store crypto offline typically for safer and longer term storage.
Ethereum
Ethereum is used to describe both the second largest cryptocurrency after Bitcoin, represented by the Ether token, and the blockchain underpinning it. This supports an array of different applications and digital assets, such as non-fungible tokens.
It functions in a similar way to Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies, but in 2022 switched to a greener operating system requiring less computers and energy.
Exchange-traded funds (ETFs)
ETFs are portfolios that let investors bet on multiple assets without having to buy any themselves. Traded on stock exchanges like shares, their value depends on how the overall portfolio performs in real time. They can comprise a combination of gold and silver bullion, for example, or a mix of shares in both technology and insurance companies.
A spot Bitcoin ETF buys the cryptocurrency directly, "on the spot", at its current price, throughout the day.
While some ETFs already contained Bitcoin indirectly, the US approved several spot Bitcoin ETFs in January 2024. This allowed new investors, such as investment management firms like Blackrock and Fidelity, to enter the speculative world of Bitcoin without having to worry about digital wallets or navigating crypto exchanges.
Meme coins
Meme coins are a form of cryptocurrency used for fun and speculation.
They are typically created to capitalise on social media trends or viral memes - such as for internet-famous pygmy hippo Moo Deng.
But meme coins are heavily criticised for their speculative nature and the risk involved for investors, as they often have little prospect of accumulating value over time.
They can also be susceptible to "rug pulls" - where promoters of a cryptocurrency draw in buyers to raise the price of their coin, only to stop trading activity and make off with the money raised from sales.
Some celebrities have faced backlash after launching meme coins.
Stablecoins
"Stable" is the key word here - this cryptocurrency differs from others as it is intends to be less volatile in value.
This typically works by the price being linked to an existing asset, for instance currencies like the US dollar or pound sterling, which in theory should make them more stable in price than cryptocurrencies that are not backed by assets.
Stablecoins themselves are usually controlled by companies that provide them, with transactions recorded on digital ledgers. While held up by some as the future of finance, high profile price collapses of stablecoins have alerted regulators to risks for investors and prompted scrutiny over their supposed stability.
XRP
XRP is a cryptocurrency used by a platform called the XRP Ledger. It was created by the co-founders of financial services company Ripple Labs in 2012 as a cheaper, faster alternative to Bitcoin.
The cryptocurrency has a fixed supply of 100 billion coins, which were created when it launched. Much of it is held by Ripple and periodically released into circulation.
Unlike cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin, transactions made using XRP are verified through consensus - whereby the majority of validators on its peer-to-peer network must agree whether or not a transaction is valid before it is added to its blockchain.
This has been credited with allowing many transactions to take place simultaneously, at high speed and low cost - making it appealing to financial institutions or for processes like cross-border payments. But as with other cryptocurrencies, XRP has received regulatory scrutiny and seen sudden, sharp declines in value.

article:
When will we know the results?

When will we know the US midterms results?
- Published
Millions of Americans are voting in midterm elections that could reshape the balance of power in Washington. The outcome determines which party - US President Donald Trump's Republicans or opposition Democrats - controls Congress.
Once polls close, it is possible the results will not be projected for several hours, days or even weeks. Here's what you need to know.
When will we know the results and who controls Congress?
Congress is made up of two parts - the lower chamber, the House of Representatives and the upper chamber, the Senate.
To win a majority in the House, a party needs 218 seats. In the Senate, a party needs 51 seats for an outright majority. But if the upper chamber is split 50-50, the vice-president has a tie-breaking vote, which gives their party control of it.
First results will start to come in after 18:00 EST (23:00 GMT). They won't tell us much about the overall result because these races are in places considered safe bets for Republicans (Kentucky and Indiana) or Democrats (Vermont).
Throughout the night, BBC analysts will focus on the competitive races which will give an indication of how well things are going for Trump.
There are several tight Senate contests in the Eastern Time zone - like Ohio, where polls close at 19:30 EST (00:30 GMT) and Maine, where they shut at 20:00 EST (01:00 GMT). These could provide early indications of the electorate's mood.
Some key contests might start to be "called" by US media outlets. They use models to project which way a state has voted, even before the full vote count has been completed.
This happens when they believe a party or a candidate has gained a lead that cannot be beaten. But in some closely-fought states, outlets could take a long time to make their projections.
The overall timing of the result will depend on how tight the races are and which races end up being decisive.
When did we know the results in 2022?
In 2022, Republicans and Democrats were still in a tight race for control of the US Congress on 9 November, a day after the midterms.
While Republicans were favourites to win the House of Representatives, the fight for the Senate remained on a knife-edge.
The full picture took several days. CBS News projected Republicans had secured the 218 seats needed for a majority in the House on 17 November.
Counting in a crucial Senate race in Nevada took four days. The Democrats' narrow victory in the state brought them to 50 seats, allowing them to retain control of the Senate because then Vice-President Kamala Harris held a tie-breaking vote.
Georgia's Senate contest had to be settled by a run-off election because no candidate passed the 50% mark in November.
The results were not available until 7 December, when Democrats won this seat.
What are the key races to watch in 2026?
There are seven Senate races deemed to be a toss-up by independent elections analyst Cook Political Report, external - Alaska, Kansas, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas.
Of these, six are currently held by Republicans and one by Democrats. The Democrats would need to win four of those seats, plus four classed as likely or leaning Democratic, to hit 51 and take control of the Senate.
If Democrats fail to keep hold of their seat in Michigan, winning a majority in the Senate becomes much harder. Abdul El-Sayed, a left-wing political outsider, is up against Republican rival Mike Rogers, a Trump ally and former FBI agent.
But polls have suggested they have a chance even in Texas where former teacher James Talarico could become the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state since 1988 if he defeats Ken Paxton, the current state attorney general and close Trump ally.
The current Republican majority in the House, the lower chamber, is thin. They have 218 representatives, plus one independent who votes with them.
Some of the most closely-watched races in the House are in east-coast states, according to the Cook Political Report. These include New York's 17th District, Pennsylvania's 8th District and Virginia's 1st District.
When do polls close?
The results of a voter poll will be released at 17:00 EST (22:00 GMT), which will give us an indication of the issues at the forefront of voters' minds.
Then, at 18:00 EST (23:00 GMT), the first polls close in Kentucky and Indiana. After that, all eyes will be focused on the seven key battleground states:
- 19:30 EST (00:30 GMT) - Polls close in Ohio, where Republican Senator Jon Husted finds himself neck-and-neck with Democrat Sherrod Brown. Results from this state could give us a clue as to how the night might unfold
- 20:00 EST (01:00 GMT) - Voting ends in the tight Senate race in Maine between Republican Senator Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson and in most of Michigan, Kansas and Texas
- 21:00 EST (02:00 GMT) - Polls close in Iowa and the remaining parts of Michigan that sit in the Central Time Zone, as well as Kansas and Texas. In the hours that follow, a picture might start to emerge of whether things are going to plan for the Republicans - or the Democrats
- 01:00 EST (06:00 GMT) - Voting ends in Alaska, the last battleground state. A close Senate race between Democrat Mary Peltola and incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan has been making headlines over the inclusion of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot
How does the vote-counting work?
Each state administers its own elections and has its own rules for counting and processing votes.
Some states, like Florida, process early and mail ballots prior to election day, while others only begin tabulating on 3 November.
Local election officials verify, process and count individual votes, in a process known as canvassing.
Most states require a post-election audit that involves a manual count of ballots checked against machine totals, although rules vary across the country. Full hand counts are generally reserved for recounts.
Every state and locality has rules which specify who can participate in the canvass, the order in which votes are processed and which parts are open to the public, including how partisan observers can watch the count and, in some states, raise formal challenges.
What might cause a delay?
Tight races will take longer, and create the possibility of recounts being triggered and legal challenges.
Mail-in ballots take longer to count, as officials need to process envelopes and verify signatures.
More than 30 states allow ballots to be processed before election day, but other states do not. In California, all ballots must be posted before or on election day and will still be counted if they arrive within seven days of the election.
In Alaska, ranked-choice voting could mean that tabulations take considerably longer than elsewhere in the country and the controversy over ballots could mean that legal challenges can complicate things.
What happens if results are challenged?
Once every vote has been included in the final results, and after processes such as recounts have been completed, the election results are certified - first at the local, county, level and then state-wide.
The governor then typically signs the certifications for House and Senate winners to be sent to Congress.
Results can be challenged. Recounts can be requested by candidates in close races, and in some states recounts are automatically triggered if they fall within a certain margin.
Candidates can also file legal election contests alleging irregularities.
Congress has the final word. Losing candidates in both House and Senate races can file contests, with slightly different processes in each of the two chambers.
Both chambers can, theoretically, refuse to seat someone or order an investigation.
When do winners take office?
Outgoing members of Congress leave office on Sunday 3 January. Because that date falls on a weekend, the new members may take office on the same date unless Congress passes a law setting a different day., external

Danske bank to move 250 staff to Belfast city centre

Danske Bank is to move its Northern Ireland call centre staff into its Belfast city centre headquarters.

Future-ready

Don't get caught out by new Buy Now Pay Later rules

Don't get caught out by new Buy Now Pay Later rules
- Published
If you've bought something via Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) since the summer, then you'll have been tested to see if you can afford it.
BNPL has always been a type of loan, usually paid back in instalments, but it's only been officially regulated since July.
This means stricter background checks on your ability to repay.
If you fail, then your purchase via BNPL will be blocked. If there's a chance of this happening to you, here are some ways to approach the situation.
What are the new rules?
BNPL lenders - such as Klarna, Clearpay and others - must now have regulator approval to operate, giving shoppers more access to refunds and independent rulings on complaints if things go wrong.
But new affordability checks on each BNPL transaction could also leave you blocked from services for the first time.
There are different affordability checks for different purchases, partially based on how much is borrowed.
But, with the expensive festive season approaching, here's how to avoid being blocked when time and finances are tight.
How do I avoid being blocked?
Here are four things to consider if you find your account is closed or your borrowing limit has been massively reduced, from Sara Williams, a former volunteer debt adviser at Citizens Advice who posts tips as Debt Camel on social media.
- Slow down your purchases: is what you are buying essential or can you postpone it?
- Be more careful about what you buy to avoid needing a high credit limit to, for example, buy lots of clothes in different sizes
- Cancel subscriptions to escape the trap of having to use BNPL to make up for the cost of previous payments
- Talk to debt charities for help and access to food bank vouchers if you are using BNPL for essentials
Avoid getting into debt
If you are struggling to make repayments on any type of loan - BNPL or otherwise - you should seek help before things spiral out of control.
The government-backed, independent, MoneyHelper website, external has a guide to finding free debt advice near you, external.
It also suggests writing down exactly what you owe, to help plan how you will repay the money.
There are also tools to work out if you are receiving all the benefits and grants you are entitled to, and a bill prioritiser, external to show which payments to make first and what to do if you miss a payment.
You should also be sceptical of supposed debt solutions you might see on your social feeds.

article:
How the European question impacts on Scotland's future

How the European question impacts on Scotland's future
- Published
Rachel Reeves must have been smarting this week as the new Chancellor stood on the steps of No 11 Downing Street - but she's now using her former platform to make a clarion call for Britain's re-entry into the European Union.
Her former rank carries weight and adds fuel to the prime minister's arguments on re-opening the EU debate.
That also opens up a Pandora's box of inter-twining constitutional questions here in Scotland.
The Reeves argument is clear. From her position in His Majesty's Treasury, she saw a United Kingdom that was "poorer, weaker and less secure" post-Brexit.
She therefore believes "Britain's future lies in the EU".
Her intervention may leave many people questioning - why make it now, after leaving office?
- Reeves says UK's future should be inside the EU 
  - Published2 days ago
It has been up to the new prime minister to make the running, with Andy Burnham looking forward to an EU summit in Brussels on 20 November.
He's looking to lock-in deals on food and drink, emissions trading, and a youth mobility scheme.
It adds to the impression there has been almost seven years of the UK trying to patch things over with the EU, sector-by-sector.
Speaking on BBC Scotland's Sunday Show, the UK government minister Martyn McCluskey was asked when the people might be consulted about this?
He said: "I'm not going to get ahead of myself on process here. What we need to focus on is we're having a conversation.
"A conversation that was happening already in the country, that I think Andy Burnham has just said very clearly. It's a conversation we're all having, so we may as well have it in public about what the benefits are."
It's certainly clear that, after the summit, the prime minister wants to "explore options" for the longer-term relationship. But there will be no major changes before the next general election
All this rather horrifies the Conservatives.
Their leader Kemi Badenoch said on Sunday it was "yet another Westminster bubble argument".
Her Shadow Scottish Secretary Harriet Cross told the Sunday Show: "When we have a vote, that should be respected. That is the point of a democracy and it's incumbent on everybody to make that work and there have been benefits to leaving the EU".
What is particularly horrifying for the Conservative leadership is the prospect of re-opening the decades of Tory in-fighting on a matter they thought had been put to bed.
Far from horror, the SNP view the prime minister's European stance with some glee.
Brexit is so woven in with the issue of Scottish independence that it can be hard to unpick the threads.
The SNP's Westminster leader, Dave Doogan, told me he "really welcomed" Rachel Reeves' comments, and a majority of Scots had already known that leaving the EU was a "retrograde" step.
He said: "When you are sold a false prospectus, it's ok to go back to re-visit that after a reasonable period of time and I would say that, whilst that's appropriate for the European Union referendum, it's also appropriate for the referendum that happened two years prior to that in 2014 over Scottish independence."
The leader warned it would be "hypocrisy" not to re-visit the independence issue.
However, when the prime minister was in Glasgow on Friday, Downing Street was clear that a second independence referendum is "off the table".
It's unclear at this early stage what impact there could be on the SNP's "independence in Europe" argument if the UK does seek ever-closer union, or even re-joins the EU.
Given all these arguments, it is striking how often people outside the political bubble tell me they just want "certainty" over all these constitutional issues.
It's probably a very human reaction but their hope is maybe misplaced.
These arguments never really lie still.
For hundreds of years the relationship with our neighbours was fought in cross-border skirmishes or in battles across the English Channel.
Now, it's down to democratic votes and arguments in air-conditioned summit rooms.
With the prime minister re-opening this Pandora's Box, be prepared for plenty more constitutional debate.

Afcon to return to two-year cycle after Caf U-turn

Afcon to return to two-year cycle after Caf U-turn
- Published
The Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) will return to its traditional two-year cycle after a U-turn from the Confederation of African Football (Caf).
In December, Caf announced that the tournament would be held every four years instead, but that decision has been reversed after a review.
Under the new plans, the governing body was planning an African Nations League to replace Afcon as its biennial tournament, but acknowledged that it would take several years to generate the revenue required to become self-sufficient.
"The decision by the Executive Committee to reinstate the organisation of the Afcon every two years aims to advance, protect and promote the interests of African football and the 54 Caf Member Associations, as well as those of African players playing for clubs outside the continent," Caf president Patrice Motsepe said in a statement.
The biennial hosting of Afcon has long caused issues with the football calendar, with the vast majority of recent tournaments held midway through the European club season.
Fifa's expanded 32-team Club World Cup was held in June and July last year, which also forced Caf to opt for mid-season dates.
The next Afcon will take place in 2027, with Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda jointly hosting the tournament, followed by editions in 2028, 2031 and 2033. There will be no tournament in 2030 because of the World Cup.
The dramatic 2025 Afcon final saw Senegal crowned champions before they were stripped of their title three months later in favour of Morocco.

article:
'The internet's a less whimsical place' - YouTuber Jacksepticeye branches out

'The internet's a less whimsical place' - YouTuber Jacksepticeye branches out
- Published
The world's changed a lot since Seán McLoughlin, better known to 31 million subscribers as Jacksepticeye, began making YouTube videos.
He started uploading in 2012, in what many people consider to be the platform's "golden age" when vlogging, video game playthroughs and comedy escapism were all the rage.
Like many in the content creation space, he's been branching out in recent years, taking more acting jobs and getting involved in film production.
BBC Newsbeat caught up with McLoughlin to talk about his new role, his work on bringing one of his favourite video games to the big screen and why he misses the "whimsical" days of the internet.
McLoughlin got famous playing video games, and these days there's a good chance you'll see - or hear - him in one.
After a role in the 2025 superhero adventure Dispatch, McLoughlin's got a new role in Hitman, the successful "assassination simulator" from Danish studio IO Interactive.
He plays controversial content creator Finn Colton, known as Finnvictus.
Although the fictional character shares McLoughlin's likeness and voice, he says the "manosphere-adjacent influencer" is not based on him.
As the name of the game suggests, players aren't there to collab with him.
He's one of the celebrity "elusive targets" Hitman's developers occasionally place in the game to encourage returning fans.
"If you love me it'll be funny to play and you'll get to kill me in different ways," says McLoughlin.
"If you hate me maybe that's even more fun to play."
It's not the first time McLoughlin's worked with IO - he appeared, briefly, in their James Bond game 007: First Light earlier this year.
He'd hoped to watch other streamers react to the blink-and-you'll-miss-it cameo, but says many of his friends missed it.
"This time you're forced to interact with me," he says, even if that does involve thinking of imaginative ways to kill him off.
Earlier this year, McLoughlin was also unveiled as a producer on an animated movie version of Bloodborne, one of the highest-rated video games of all time.
Some parts of its passionate fan base reacted negatively to the announcement, questioning the YouTuber's credentials.
McLoughlin reassured them he's a huge fan of the games and has a tattoo of a Hunter's Mark - one of the game's key items - to prove it.
He's described himself as a "vibe-checker" and sees it as his responsibility to make sure the adaptation is done properly.
"If it feels off, especially with something like Bloodborne, people can feel it immediately, even if they don't know what they're pointing towards," he says.
"They know the game so well that if the atmosphere, or the world, or the vibe feels off, they'll pick up on it pretty fast."
McLoughlin says he's been trying to pick people for the project who have ideally played Bloodborne and "have a feeling" for what it's all about.
"I feel like I have good instincts on what works and what doesn't and what I like and what I don't like," he says.
"So the producing side of it fits a lot more naturally for me right now."
'Rise of anti-communities'
Screen adaptations are a big trend in video games at the moment, but they're not the only thing seizing the industry.
Hitman's new mission lands just weeks before the launch of the hugely-anticipated Grand Theft Auto 6.
It won't be released on disc at launch, a move that's arguably accelerated the game industry's move towards digital-only games.
McLoughlin, who fondly remembers PlayStation cases on a bedroom shelf and getting new games for Christmas, says "it would suck to see physical games disappear completely".
"Just in terms of the humanity behind it all, I think it would be a shame to see that stuff disappear because it's a magical experience," he says.
The use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in video game development is another hot topic at the moment.
Earlier this month, Epic Games, makers of Fortnite, announced a "pivot" towards using AI as a primary development tool.
Like many players, McLoughlin's opposed to its use.
So no chance of seeing a Jacksepticeye Fortnite skin any time soon?
"I think the chances of that happening were already zero before anything related to that even happened," he says.
"But now it's definitely, definitely unlikely."
Physical games, GenAI and content creators' career moves are sure to generate discourse, and conversations online are another thing McLoughlin thinks have changed since he started out.
He says there's been a "rise of anti-communities", where people will "rush to condemn a film or game before it's even been released".
"I'm just sad that the internet is such an angry place these days," he says.
"It's just zero to a thousand immediately. I think we're just not there in terms of having nuanced discussions about anything.
"But I think that's just endemic of the internet in general."
McLoughlin thinks that could be linked to people's real life worries.
"Right now, it's just people are angry in general, just at the world," he says.
"So it's harder to interact with stuff online these days.
"It's a less whimsical space. But hopefully that's something that can change."
McLoughlin's doing his bit to bring people together in December with his annual Thankmas event.
The fundraiser took a break last year but its returning to raise money for the Make-A-Wish Foundation.
"I think it's a nice little pinprick of light in the middle of everything else going on," he says.
And while he's not afraid to speak his mind, he says he is mindful of letting others do the talking sometimes.
"I'm trying to get better about not giving an opinion about absolutely everything any more," he says.
"Because I think there's too much of that in the world."

Uganda begins withdrawing troops from Somalia after 20 years

Uganda begins withdrawing troops from Somalia after 20 years
- Published
Uganda has begun withdrawing its troops from Somalia after nearly two decades of military involvement in the country.
Uganda's acting army spokesperson Chris Magezi on Monday said the first group of troops deployed to Somalia through a bilateral arrangement had already arrived back home and others would follow in a few days' time.
He said all forces, including those under the African Union (AU) mission, would exit by the end of 2027 in the phased withdrawal.
Uganda was the first African country to deploy troops to Somalia under the African Union Mission in Somalia (Amisom), established in 2007 to help protect the country's transitional government from attacks by Islamist militants.
A first contingent of 109 Uganda People's Defence Forces (UPDF) troops reportedly left the capital, Mogadishu, on Friday, following an announcement by Uganda's army chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba.
Last week, Kainerugaba said Uganda had begun pulling out its troops and would hand over security responsibilities to Somali forces.
"As we promised, we have started withdrawing UPDF from Somalia. After 20 years of a lot of blood and sacrifice, we are handing over security to our Somali brothers," he wrote on X.
On Monday, Magezi said this would mark the end of Uganda's operations in the Horn of Africa country, with Somalia expected to "assume full responsibility for security".
The withdrawal comes after Somalia President Sheikh Mohamud met his Ugandan counterpart Yoweri Museveni in Kampala last week.
The meeting was planned to discuss Somalia's security situation, as well as trade and economic ties between the two countries.
The Somali president reportedly sought to persuade Uganda to extend its military presence.
In remarks during the visit, Museveni urged Somali leaders and citizens to unite in the fight against the militant insurgency led by al-Shabab, which is part of al-Qaeda.
An estimated 4,500 troops are in Somalia under the Africa Union mission, alongside about 2,000 deployed through bilateral arrangements.
Somalia has been battling a prolonged and deadly insurgency for more than two decades.
After Ugandan forces were first deployed to the country in 2007, they played a key role in driving al-Shabab out of Mogadishu and other major towns.
They fought alongside the Somali National Army to recapture strategic territory and secure key government installations.
Ugandan troops were involved in successive Africa Union missions, including the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia (Atmis), which began with the aim of gradually transferring security responsibilities to Somalia.
This was replaced in 2025 by the African Union Support and Stabilisation Mission in Somalia (Aussom), which is focused on strengthening Somalia's security institutions and preparing its forces to take full responsibility for the country's security.
Aussom now faces uncertainty over its future funding, amid plans to wind down US and UN support.
A 12-month transition plan is due to begin in January, giving Somalia and the AU time to seek alternative sources of funding.
