I didn't know I was lacking in vitamin D until I collapsed at work

I didn't know I was lacking in vitamin D until I collapsed at work
- Published
Twenty-three-year-old Saskia Reeves-Priestley was at work when she suddenly collapsed.
"I just felt really dizzy, really nauseous, was having heart palpitations and was really hot," she says.
Saskia, a special educational needs teacher, was a keen goalkeeper who played football four times a week and felt fit and healthy. While her symptoms are not directly linked to vitamin D deficiency - she realised something was wrong.
Blood tests later showed her level was so low - it was "next to nothing".
In the UK, low vitamin D rates are increasing in some age groups, external - particularly in girls and young women.
According to data from the National Diet and Nutrition Survey, last year nearly a quarter of 11- to 18-year-olds were classed as deficient.
Vitamin D can come from our diet, in foods such as oily fish and meat, or supplements.
But most is made by our body when UV light in sunlight hits the skin. Lower levels of sunlight - depending on where in the world you live or the time of year - decrease the body's ability to produce it.
Covering parts of the body and wearing sunscreen also has an impact - despite their protective advantages.
Those with darker skin need exposure to stronger light to produce the same amount of vitamin D as lighter skin.
Doctors don't routinely offer blood tests to check for vitamin D deficiency, but will offer a supplement if a patient is concerned they might be high risk.
What are the symptoms - and their daily impact?
Vitamin D deficiency is linked to the bone disease rickets in babies and infants. In adults it causes a similar weakening of the bone called osteomalacia, external.
"They call it the silent disease," says Dr Suma Uday, a paediatric endocrinologist who wants to raise awareness of the problem.
She warns that vitamin D deficiency in young people and adults is difficult to spot and can be missed or misdiagnosed. Symptoms include fatigue and joint and bone pain.
Uday says: "It's basically silently eating away at the bones, leaving them softened and prone to breaks."
Amaka was in the middle of making dinner at her university house in Liverpool when she started shaking.
"I couldn't really see in front of me," she says. Her housemate took her to A&E - later she too would be diagnosed as vitamin D deficient.
Other than feeling tired, she says she had no symptoms: "I'm a 21-year-old student. I've got work and uni - I'm always feeling tired."
She remembers her mother suffering from low vitamin D but says she did not realise it could happen to her.
After taking supplements, Amaka feels a lot better, but she is anxious in case it happens again. "It was scary and I don't want to experience that again."
Lifelong deficit in girls
Uday joins other clinicians and academics who have formed a group - ACT NOW Vitamin D - calling for the threshold at which you are classified as deficient to be raised.
She says that would "catch" more people with low vitamin D and give a more accurate picture of how widespread the issue is. It would also mean they can treat the deficiency earlier, she says.
Uday warns of "a lifelong deficit" in women - in adolescence, then pregnancy, and then the newborn is affected.
"If you don't correct it from the very beginning," she says, "this is going to affect multiple generations."
"It's shocking," says Prof Martin Hewison, from the University of Birmingham.
He tells me that despite being 100 years on from the discovery of vitamin D "rickets hasn't gone away".
"If we have rickets in the community, there are going to be many more people who are vitamin D deficient."
He says the government should look into wider fortification of food in which vitamins are added to foods during production. Countries like Canada and Sweden have mandatory policies.
In the UK, some foods such as breakfast cereals and spreads are already fortified with vitamin D, but it is voluntary.
During the winter months, people start to lose their vitamin D levels.
"We might have to accept that for certain groups vitamin D supplementation is a matter of course," says Hewison.
Saskia is now taking vitamin D supplements regularly - and is back in goal.

article:
Sir Patrick Stewart remembered as 'Mirfield's finest'

Sir Patrick Stewart remembered as 'Mirfield's finest'
- Published
Sir Patrick Stewart once said he had to drop his Yorkshire accent for Hollywood, but he never forgot his roots.
The Mirfield-born actor, best known for his roles in Star Trek and the X-Men films, died at the age of 86 at his home in Los Angeles on Wednesday after suffering with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia.
His death has prompted an outpouring of love from the community he proudly called home, along with his beloved Huddersfield Town - the club he followed from childhood.
Stewart's friend and fellow legendary actor Sir Ian McKellen said Stewart "never forsook his origins".
He added: "Before everything else, Patrick was defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire, the proud county in the north of England which he loved to the end."
Referencing a trait often associated with people from the region McKellen said Stewart "told you what he thought and felt".
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was "very sad" to hear about Stewart's death, describing him as "one of the very best" who "never forgot his working-class Yorkshire roots".
In a TV interview with fellow Yorkshireman Michael Parkinson, Stewart said "we did toy" with using his regional accent when playing Captain Jean-Luc Picard in the Star Trek franchise.
But he added: "It was incomprehensible to the producers."
South Yorkshire-born actor Brian Blessed also paid tribute to Stewart who he first met as "young lads in Yorkshire, on a drama course in Calder Valley".
Posting on Facebook, he said that although Stewart was two years younger, he had "maturity beyond his years."
"His mysterious eyes and reserved demeanour broke open when he smiled, and lit the room," he wrote.
"Art was woven into his huge heart, and the shared passion bonded us at an early age."
Blessed, who hails from Mexborough, added: "Our bond never waned, and whenever we met, he would hug me as hard as when we were boys, never afraid to weep at the enormity of his emotions.
"We have always been connected, and always shall be.
"I'll see you up in space, my dearest friend. Patrick is not gone but merely on another journey."
In 2004 he became chancellor of the University of Huddersfield - a role he filled until 2015. A year later the university's drama building was named after him.
Speaking at the time, he said: "I'm thrilled. It still makes me a little self conscious to think there's a building named after me."
Bob Cryan, the Vice Chancellor of the university, said Stewart was "very proud" of being chancellor and his success never changed him.
"It's something he took very personally," he said.
"He saw it as a way of paying back to Yorkshire because he was very proud of the fact that he was given a scholarship from what was then the West Riding of Yorkshire, but he felt he had never paid back."
Born in Mirfield in 1940, Stewart attended Crowlees Church of England Junior and Infant School before moving onto Mirfield Secondary Modern School.
His mother Gladys was a textile worker. She was active in amateur dramatics and encouraged her three sons to take part.
His father was a former Sergeant Major in the Parachute Regiment, whose experience during the wartime evacuation of Dunkirk had badly affected his mental health.
Stewart's love of drama came at school when one of his teachers introduced him to Shakespeare and encouraged him to perform.
His first public performance was in a local church production of Cinderella.
He left school at 15 and eventually got a job as a reporter and obituary writer on the Dewsbury Reporter.
He later won a scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School launching a career that would take him from Yorkshire to the world stage.
Although he became one of Britain's most celebrated actors through roles including in Star Trek and Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men film series, Stewart spoke of his pride in being from West Yorkshire.
Childhood friend David Pinder described him as a "thoroughly nice man" and said the pair would meet up when they were both in Mirfield.
"I came back here when I retired from the Foreign Office and got into local politics," he said.
"We couldn't have been more different. He was very firmly old Labour and I at the time was Conservative, verging on Independent so we kept off politics."
Pinder said the men would have lunch in the town and added: "People would come and go.
"They'd know it was Patrick and of course by then he was internationally famous, but people were very good. They'd just say hello and not pester him."
Mirfield Free Grammar, which Stewart attended as a child, said he held a "special place" in its history.
The school said he had last visited in 2011, when he was presented with a commemorative plaque "made out of the very stage boards on which he made his first theatrical appearance".
In a tribute, the school said: "Staff and students who met him during his visit remember him as a warm, friendly, compassionate and charismatic gentleman who left a last impression.
"We feel privileged to have been part of his story."
Spen Valley MP Kim Leadbeater described Stewart as "Mirfield's finest".
Posting on X, the Labour MP described him as "an outstanding talent and someone who came across as a thoroughly decent and lovely".
Leadbeater said she had met the actor at Huddersfield Town football matches and corresponded with him several times, adding: "He was incredibly kind and he will be greatly missed."
A lifelong Huddersfield Town supporter, Stewart attended games when his schedule allowed and celebrated the Terriers' promotion to the Premier League at Wembley in 2017.
The club's chief operating officer David Threlfall-Sykes said: "Obviously it was Sir Patrick Stewart walking around so people would get star-struck, but he would get star-struck by seeing the players and the manager because they were his heroes.
"It was a weird dichotomy but it just shows how much this place meant to him, just like it does to everyone that comes here every weekend to fill the ground. He was no different in that respect."
For many, it was the combination of worldwide fame and his down-to-earth Yorkshire roots that made him such a star across the world.
Reflecting on his sense of humour, Cryan, of the University of Huddersfield, said: "He had a great sense of fun.
"I remember saying to him we were hosting a dinner for staff at the university to say thank you for all their hard work and we decided he and I were going to be waiters.
"You can imagine peoples' faces when Patrick served them their meal."
The statement announcing Stewart's death, which was shared on his Instagram account, ended with a quote from his memoirs: "Like me, Jean-Luc has lived an unusual life that has taken him far beyond the bounds of normal human experience.
"But he is also someone who remains true to his earthbound roots, for they are what gave him his identity. In the end, he feels the call of home, as do I."

article:
Democrats have high hopes for midterms - but are the polls right?

Democrats have high hopes for midterms - but are the polls right?
- Published
The Democratic Party has high expectations as it heads into these pivotal US midterm elections.
A historically unpopular Republican president, an American public unhappy with the rising costs of food and bills, and months of favourable polls point to a good night for them on Tuesday.
Democratic candidates lead in well over the 218 seats needed to flip control of the lower chamber of Congress, the House of Representatives, the polls suggest. And they are tied or narrowly ahead in the key Senate races.
A recent New York Times poll had the Senate race in South Carolina, a state Donald Trump won by 18 percentage points in 2024, as a tie. Recent CNN surveys put the Democrats ahead in Texas, Kansas and Maine.
But are the polls accurate?
Recent US political history is littered with examples where public opinion polls, even ones just days before an election, were off the mark. Trump outperformed predictions on his way to White House victories in 2016 and 2024. His narrow defeat in 2020 came after most surveys indicated a more comfortable win for Democrat Joe Biden.
Earlier this year, polls suggested Democrat Abdul El-Sayed was poised for a double-digit win in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary. Instead it was 1%. In Wisconsin's Democratic primary for governor, the candidate that had a polling lead that approached 20 points lost by a fraction of a percent.
- Democrats have an identity crisis - it won't be an easy fix 
  - Published4 days ago
According to Clifford Young, president of Ipsos Public Affairs, which conducts political and market research surveys, polling has become difficult in recent years because it's harder to reach Americans as they abandon their land lines and screen their calls. And many of those who pollsters do contact have become less willing to participate.
"Conservatives, especially those on the far right, are much more anti-establishment by nature," Young says. "And they don't participate in anything. They hate the system. That's the challenge."
If Republican voters are being undercounted in a systematic way, and polling companies don't take that into consideration when constructing their voting models, it could skew their data towards the Democrats.
That's one of the reasons why it has become trickier for pollsters to predict what the electorate will look like.
One explanation for why Trump overperformed in previous presidential elections is that his supporters – many of whom were not regular voters – flocked to the polls in higher-than-expected numbers.
That unpredictability is one of the main contributing factors to those notable recent polling misses, even if the margins in most reputable polls were only off by a few percentage points.
In a close race, those few points can make the difference between victory and defeat for a candidate. And this year, many of the key Senate races are within those narrow margins.
In recent years, midterm general election polls have proven to be more accurate, in part because Trump - and his unique ability to draw disaffected Americans to the polls - was not on the ballot.
In 2022, they suggested Democrats would defy conventional expectations and avoid an electoral wipe-out despite Biden's low approval numbers.
While the party lost control of the House of Representatives, the margins were slim and Democrats maintained control of the US Senate.
While this year's primary results did provide bigger surprises, Young says that nominating contests have historically been volatile, with voters more likely to make up their minds at the last minute. It shouldn't be seen as an indication that the current crop of general election polls are off the mark.
It's common for the party of the president to have a bad night in the midterms.
One of the most notable examples in recent years came in 2010 when Republicans flipped more than 60 House seats and made gains in the Senate.
It came off the back of an economy struggling to recover from the financial crash and conservative fears over President Barack Obama's healthcare reforms. A defeat had been predicted by the polls but not quite on that scale.
The roles are reversed this time, with the Democrats in opposition and the economy on the minds of voters. But there are a number of reasons why Democrats may not have as good a night as history might suggest or as some might expect, given Trump's low approval rating.
Firstly, much of the territory in play in this election Trump conquered with ease in the presidential election just two years ago. It's like a home game for Republicans.
Then there have been changes to House election boundaries over the years that have meant fewer seats switch between parties.
Thirdly, there are fewer swing voters due to the deeper polarisation of the country. Some experts describe the electorate as calcified.
There's also the cash advantage Republicans have enjoyed which has given them hundreds of millions of dollars to spend on attack ads in the final weeks.
Polling models try to capture shifting fundamentals. And a well-designed poll is built to anticipate issues that may make it less than reliable.
Individual polls do have a built-in margin of error – a statistical level of uncertainty based on the sampling size compared to the population as a whole. Taken as an aggregate, polling averages and not individual surveys can provide a more accurate prediction.
At the moment, even the kind of polling lean we saw in recent presidential elections would suggest Democrats are likely to have a good night on 3 November. And polling inaccuracies can go both ways. In last year's state and special elections, Democrats outperformed most surveys as it was their voters who turned out in unexpectedly larger numbers.
The sight of Trump holding rallies in the final days of the campaign in states he won comfortably in 2024 will have lifted Democrats' hopes that Republican internal polling has conservative candidates in trouble.
There's always the chance that voters change their minds right up until election day, however.
Sometimes there are late shifts that can alter the dynamics of a race. Sometimes undecided voters, which still account for a key segment of the electorate in many of these races, all break the same way.
In polling, there will always be some level of uncertainty – and managing that is the art that goes along with the science.
"I think we're doing a better job," says Young. "But part of the problem we always have is not just with the pollsters. Part of it is that we're dealing with humans. Humans are not easy."

article:
Christmas ad 'shock' for Fender's old school choir

Christmas ad 'shock' for Fender's old school choir
- Published
A chance encounter with an old music teacher ended with the "real shock" of Sam Fender's old school providing vocals for the John Lewis Christmas ad this year.
Without telling them Fender enlisted the help of current pupils at John Spence Community High School in North Shields to re-record the choir for his cover of the Rolling Stones classic You Can't Always Get What You Want.
Head of music at John Spence, Damien Grazzer, said the invitation was a "real shock" but it was an "amazing experience" for the children involved.
The singer also reunited with the Easington Colliery Band for the track after they worked together on his last album.
Fender said: "In the spirit of Christmas, we re-recorded the children's choir with the kids from my old school... and we arranged a brass section with the Easington Colliery Band."
Proceeds from the sale of the single, which includes Fender's 2020 cover of Winter Song, will go to the Teenage Cancer Trust and Action for Children.
Grazzer, who has worked at the school for more than 20 years, said the latest scholars became involved after he bumped into old boy Fender in the summer holidays.
"It came as a real shock to be honest," he said.
The pupils were not told what the recording was for and only had a day to rehearse, but Fender made an emotional appearance towards the end of the recording session.
"He even said just looking at the tie and the uniform really brought back his fondness for high school and his teachers," Grazzer said.
"What an amazing experience for those students, it's something that they'll never forget, it'll be there forever."
"Just to give something back like that I think is absolutely incredible."
Easington Colliery Band, who feature on the track Remember My Name on 2025's People Watching album, performed with Fender during his stadium tour last year.
Principal cornet player Dan Robson said the hardest thing was not being able to tell anyone about the latest collaboration.
"It's turned into a relationship more than just that kind of one job," Robson said.
"So when we got this phone call it was kind of like 'oh brilliant here we go again'."
He described the experience as "unbelievable", saying Fender "puts everything into everything".

article:
How the downfall of Serbia's Vučiċ mirrored that of Hungary's Orbán

How the downfall of Serbia's Vučiċ mirrored that of Hungary's Orbán
- Published
When they met in northern Serbia last November, Serbian President Aleksandar Vučiċ and Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán could hardly have guessed they would both be out of power within a year.
Both were ousted by popular movements - Orbán fell first, in April, defeated by Péter Magyar's Tisza party. Then last Sunday a student movement less than two years old won Serbia's parliamentary elections by a landslide.
The Tisza party in Hungary and the Student List in Serbia look very different - Tisza is centred on the personality and energy of its leader, while the students in Serbia insist they have no leadership.
But the huge turnout - 79% in Hungary and 69% in Serbia, was driven by tech-savvy young people in both countries. They used AI tools to crunch numbers, identify threats to the vote, and mobilise tens of thousands of election monitors to prevent intimidation and electoral fraud by the governing parties.
Mobilisation of voters, and the role of election monitors, played a big role in the opposition victory in both countries.
Last weekend, the DE civic action group in Hungary sent 70 election monitors to Serbia, to work with students' movement representatives, visiting polling stations in the northern Serbian province of Vojvodina.
During the summer, even before the election was called, they held workshops to share their experience and methods from the Hungarian election with the Serbian students.
A key technique was to identify "infected" polling districts in advance - places where the surprisingly high number of votes for the governing party at previous elections suggested that voter intimidation or "chain voting" techniques were used.
"From around 16:00 on election day, we noticed groups of masked hooligans - Vučiċ supporters - gathering near voting stations," Péter Klemm, a student activist from Subotica, told the BBC. "So we sent mobile teams, and started filming everything."
Combined with the "stationary" monitors already in place, 20 to 30 volunteers at each threatened polling station acted as a strong deterrent, he believes, and prevented intimidation or fraud.
Orbán in Hungary, Vučiċ in Serbia, both looked invincible. Both were powerful leaders, in office for 16 and 14 years, who had taken over state institutions and established business empires overlapping the two countries.
Orban chose cheese, Vučiċ meat, when they sat down to a quick lunch of traditional burek pastries at a small, popular town centre bakery in Subotica almost a year ago.
They continued to a local winery, to talk about oil and other business deals - the planned Hungarian purchase of a controlling stake in Serbia's NIS oil company. The two nationalist leaders found much in common, in business and politics, not least their friendship with Vladimir Putin in Russia and Chinese President Xi Jinping, and their strong support for Milorad Dodik, the separatist leader of the Bosnian Serbs.
A high-speed railway between Belgrade and Budapest is being built with Chinese finance and know-how.
The parallels between the fall from power of the two men are extraordinary. Aleksandar Vučiċ admitted defeat at exactly 21:30 on Sunday evening, just as Viktor Orbán did on 12 April. Few observers expected either leader to concede peacefully.
There has been speculation this week that Vučiċ spoke to Orbán twice on Sunday night to ask his advice - once before he conceded, and again at 23:15. And that Orbán convinced his Serbian ally not to use force.
Vučiċ denies that he spoke to Orbán before he made his announcement, but acknowledges the later conversation. Viktor Orbán, contacted by the BBC, declined to comment.
An hour before polls closed in Serbia, masked and hooded vigilantes took up position in central Belgrade. During voting, similar groups were photographed at many polling stations, and blocked by election monitors.
There is another strange numerical similarity. The Student List will have 140 seats in the 250-seat Serbian parliament, the same number Péter Magyar's Tisza party won in the 199-seat Hungarian parliament.
Magyar was the only European leader to ring the students directly to congratulate them that evening - and probably the only one who had their number.
"It is always good to hear that the story of Tisza could provide an inspiration for other nations," the Hungarian prime minister told the BBC.
"The result of the Hungarian election clearly showed us that what we are doing here is right," the head of the Student List, Ilija Srdanoviċ, said on the eve of the vote.
Srdanoviċ was one of those Péter Magyar spoke to that Sunday evening.
Orbán, 63, and Vučiċ, 56, may now both face prosecution for corruption and abuse of power.
The judicial machinery in both countries is similar. Serbia's special prosecution service for organised crime, JTOK, and Hungary's brand new special prosecutors, known as NVVH, have similar powers. They could prove useful to each other.
Hungarian companies close to Orbán were also involved in the Novi Sad railway station construction project. The collapse of the station's canopy on 1 November 2024 - blamed on corruption, as well as negligence - killed 16 people, and acted as the catalyst for the Serbian student movement.
"There was a perception in Europe that the longer the Orbán and Vučiċ regimes stayed in office, the stronger they got," Áron Timar, founder of the DE civic action group in Hungary told the BBC.
"In fact they got weaker. And once society found its voice and rose up, there was no way of stopping it."

article:
Gavin and Stacey actor hopes his band will be 'the next Stereophonics'

Gavin and Stacey actor hopes his band will be 'the next Stereophonics'
- Published
Gavin and Stacey fans will likely remember Oscar Hartland, or Neil the Baby, for his heartwarming performance of The Beatles' Blackbird in the sitcom's 2024 finale.
The episode was watched by about 12.3m people on Christmas day and saw Hartland's character serenade the crowd at the wedding of his on-screen dad Smithy, played by James Cordon.
But that was just the start for Hartland, now 17, who says his band is aiming to be "the next 'Phonics, or something like that".
He has recently released a new single and he and his fellow band members are on a "mission to create a new modern sound for Wales".
Hartland, from Machen, Caerphilly county, said his latest release, Wild Bull, was rooted in "being a bit crazy" and the challenges of growing up in the south Wales valleys.
The actor and singer went on his first tour in 2025 and said the past few months had been about "figuring out the earth behind the sound" with his bandmates Cayden Hughes on bass, Aiden Williams on drums and Deacon Ball on electric guitar.
"We've had lots of people say it's rocky, but it's Welsh and it's got lots of stuff behind it," he told Lucy Owen on BBC Radio Wales.
"Growing up, I was just a wild bull, I was just mental, you know, in school, just out and about, playing rugby, being wild, being crazy. I know loads of my friends who are just the same.
"It's very hard as a young lad, especially Wales in the valleys, to keep yourself contained, because there is so much trouble to get up to."
Lucy Owen with Oscar Hartland
Gavin & Stacey star Oscar Hartland aka Neil the Baby chats to Lucy about his new single
Hartland said he surrounded himself with music growing up and described himself as a bit of a "black sheep".
"I was playing the piano while everyone else was watching rugby," he said.
But he added the new single was all about "letting go and saying, 'this is me I'm a wild bull'."
Hartland said the response to the song, which was released on Friday, had been brilliant.
"People are loving it, the interaction is nuts... it's really nice.
"The biggest thing is trying to create a movement, that people can feel a part of."
At 14 years old, Hartland took part in The Voice Kids in the hopes of kickstarting his rock career.
His performance of Foo Fighters' My Hero impressed the judges and was also seen by Gavin and Stacey writers James Cordon and Ruth Jones, who approached him with the idea of performing in the series finale.
The Christmas day finale episode became one of the most watched scripted TV shows of the century, seen by 19.11 million people after seven days of catch-up viewing and beating the show's previous record of 17.92m for the 2019 Christmas special.
Nearly two years on, Hartland said it "blows his mind" that people are still talking about it.
"It's ageing well to be fair," he said.
Hartland added support was "always there" from his fellow Gavin and Stacey cast members, which was "lush".
"A lot of people don't really know what it would be like to be in our boots, I suppose, sort of, with the size of it," he said.
He said it was nice to see cast members pursuing "other adventures" too, such as Melanie Walters, who played Gwen, recently taking part in Strictly Come Dancing.
Hartland has been recording at Rockfield studios in Monmouth, which has also played host to the likes of Oasis, Iggy Pop and Queen.
"I want to record there all the time, because I just love what the place is about and I want that to be behind me as well," said Hartland.
"It's spectaular, you feel all of the presence of the past bands there looking at you like 'is he going to make a good song?'"
Despite his developing music career, Hartland said he would not rule out more acting in the future, as he is "just trying things out".
While he has not yet had a chance to cover the iconic Gavin and Stacey theme song, Run by Stephen Fretwell, he said he would love to in the future.
"It's iconic," he said, adding "that would be brilliant".

article:
When a wedding fell apart, 11 strangers helped create something unforgettable

When a wedding fell apart, 11 strangers helped create something unforgettable
- Published
When her fiance suffered a medical emergency and their planned elopement and relationship fell apart, she could have quietly drawn a line under the chapter.
Instead, Bridget Devaney turned to the internet with a proposal that sounded equal parts hopeful and improbable - come to Northern Ireland and celebrate the wedding that never happened.
What followed was a story that has resonated worldwide as 11 strangers answered the call and helped transform loss and heartbreak into an unforgettable week of connection, companionship and adventure.
For Bridget and her bevy of 'non-bridesmaids', the experience was a refreshing reminder that community is all around, "if you want to find it", she said.
Once associated with secretive romances and hurried ceremonies, elopements have evolved into destination weddings set against spectacular backdrops.
An increasing number of couples are choosing intimate celebrations as the way they begin married life, with many crossing the Atlantic to exchange their vows against the rugged Irish coastline.
Following her separation, Bridget - who is based between the US and Killarney in the Republic of Ireland - said she was "left reeling".
It wasn't until April of this year, when a photographer emailed to check in on her postponed wedding plans, that she realised she had to make a decision.
Spurred on by a friend, who suggested that she should advertise a female-only group trip on her anonymous social media profile, Bridget soon found herself overwhelmed by hundreds of inquiries.
"When these women signed up for this trip, they didn't know my name. They didn't know what I looked like. They didn't know anything about me," she told BBC News NI.
Janae Pettit, a design consultant from Utah, came across the invitation on 1 April.
"It was April Fool's Day, but Bridget was like, 'this is not a joke!'," she recalled.
"All the stranger danger we had learned growing up was just out the window."
Over the course of a few months, Bridget responded to questionnaires and set about organising the trip with women from the US, Canada and Wales offering to join her in Northern Ireland.
Each had their own reasons for wanting to join.
Janae said she discovered Bridget's post while approaching her 40th birthday and struggling with feelings she had not expected.
"I thought, this is a birthday present to myself. I'm going to go."
What began as a chance to travel soon evolved into something more meaningful.
"I wanted to go and meet these women and support this non-bride. I wanted to do something outside of myself," she said.
"I was sad because I was like, nobody cares about me. I'm unimportant. I'm finally entering middle age and I should do something for me."
For Shana Johnson, from Minnesota, the trip answered a different need.
Many of her friends were now focused on raising families and travelling with partners and children. When she saw Bridget's invitation online, she recognised an opportunity.
"I love to travel, I thought, 'what the heck? Let's see what this is all about'."
She found herself moving from one step to the next, signing up before she had fully thought through the reality of travelling to Ireland with a group of strangers - she hadn’t even cleared it with her partner yet.
The leap of faith paid off.
"It was kind of like we were all long-lost friends," Shana said. "We all got along really well."
Earlier this month, the group of women spent a week exploring the north coast, visiting the Giant's Causeway, the Dark Hedges and Londonderry.
Although many of the women had met online beforehand, seeing one another in person was different.
"I was so nervous. I [usually] can't remember anybody's face and name," Janae said.
But any awkwardness quickly disappeared as the group "all figured it out pretty fast“, she added.
For Bridget, the week became an opportunity to “reframe” and reshape memories attached to some of the places she had once planned to visit with her fiance, culminating in what became known as the "non-wedding day".
Epic Love Photography founder Rob Dight, who has spent more than a decade photographing couples escaping the pressures of traditional weddings, said the day was unlike anything he had encountered before.
With the deposit already paid for a photoshoot in 2024, Dight offered Bridget a two-year extension after learning that her fiance had been injured.
"Just me and a bunch of friends are coming over now", was how the project was later pitched, he said.
As the photoshoot progressed, he noted a deep sense of connection between the women and was "blown away" to learn, mid-shoot, that they had met just three days earlier.
"It was kind of a 'jaw-on-the-floor scenario'... It was just so wholesome," he said.
"Something clicked into place in my mind, like: 'Wow, this is really special'.
"I just did what I could on my end to encourage it, to let them have that time to shine and to celebrate being with each other."
'Not a dry eye in the room'
"There was such a level of uplift, like I could turn anywhere and get a hug if I needed it," Bridget said, recalling the photoshoot.
"Everybody was there for everybody that day."
Later in the week, the women took part in a wellness session focused on new beginnings, an experience Bridget described as particularly meaningful for the group.
"There was not a dry eye in the room," she said.
Weeks after returning home, the group's messages continue to flow, with future trips in the pipeline.
Bridget, who described herself as someone who in the past often overthought things and struggled to connect with others, said she had learned that "you can choose to do it that way, but you never have to”, when it comes to facing challenges alone.
The experience reinforced her belief that "there is community if you want to find it".
"There are people… even if it requires getting a little uncomfortable and vulnerable and putting yourself out there," she said.
"It could take a long time, but it's out there. You just have to keep trying."

Apple unsure when it will get more foldable iPhones ahead of Christmas

Apple unsure when it will get more foldable iPhones ahead of Christmas
- Published
Apple has said it does not know when it will get more of its new foldable iPhones back in stock as the company heads towards the key Christmas trading period.
The iPhone Duo sold out just over a week after its launch, despite being Apple's most expensive smartphone at a cost of nearly $2,000.
The company warned of "constraints" in sourcing key components and admitted it was "really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance".
Meanwhile, Apple's new chief executive John Ternus said the firm was seeing an "unprecedented" price rise in memory costs, including chips, as the artificial intelligence (AI) industry continues to invest billions of dollars in building data centres.
Ternus launched the Duo after he took over from previous boss Tim Cook in September.
It is the smartphone's first major design change in almost 20 years but some buyers have reported problems with the Duo's screen.
Last week, the company said it would replace any handsets that were affected by an issue that caused a "small number" to crack along the inside fold.
As it released its latest financial figures on Monday, Apple's executives did not mention any problems with the iPhone Duo.
Ternus said he was "thrilled" by the early reaction to the foldable phone. Chief operating officer Sabih Khan said the company was working hard to get the Duo "into the hands of our customers as quickly as possible".
Apple's results for the three months to 26 September did not include sales of the Duo, which was released at the end of October.
Nevertheless, Apple said it had sold more iPhones globally over the last year than ever before.
iPhone revenue for the quarter rose 17% to $57bn (£42bn).
Sales of Mac computers also grew over the three months by 27% to a record $10.7bn.
Overall, Apple's sales between July and September rose from $102bn to $114bn. Pre-tax profit also increased, from $32.8bn to $36.1bn.
However, sales for both the iPad and Apple's wearable products, including its headphones and watch, fell by 10% and 7%, respectively.
Khan said that most Apple devices were still experiencing supply constraints driven in part by difficulty in getting enough microprocessors with advanced nodes.
Those components are essentially computer chip technology that allow Apple devices to operate more quickly, most of which it has manufactured through TSMC, which is based in Taiwan.
Khan said the problem was expected to continue into next year, particularly impacting iPads and Macs.
The situation has been made worse by what the company has repeatedly insisted is "unexpected demand" for its products.
Ternus noted, too, that Apple is still seeing "unprecedented" cost increases for memory, or the ability of devices to store data like apps, photos and text messages.
Much memory storage runs through data centres, which have experienced a boom in demand for space as AI chatbots and platforms - including those developed by the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic - have become popular.
Storage prices have gone up for tech companies like Apple.
Earlier this year, Cook referred to a sudden increase in data centre costs as a "thousand year flood".
Apple has lifted prices on nearly all of its hardware products by around 20%.
Sunil Krishnan from Aviva Investors told the BBC's Today programme that Apple posted "a reasonably solid set of results" with a "pretty good performance" from its iPhone business.
While there were concerns over the company's guidance on profit margins and the cost of memory chips, Krishnan added that in the broader context, "margins well north of 45% for a very well-established company, I think, are pretty impressive".
However, Apple's share price fell by 1.8% in after-hours trading.

West Ham approach Parker after sacking boss Nuno

West Ham approach Parker after sacking boss Nuno
- Published
West Ham United are expected to appoint Scott Parker as head coach after sacking Nuno Espirito Santo.
The 52-year-old Portuguese head coach has paid the price for West Ham's disappointing start to the Championship season, having overseen their relegation from the Premier League last season.
BBC Sport understands that the club are in advanced talks with former Burnley, Bournemouth and Fulham boss Parker and he could be confirmed before Wednesday's Championship trip to Cardiff City.
The former England midfielder had four seasons as a player with the Hammers and led Bournemouth and Burnley to promotion from the Championship as a manager.
- Green backs 'proven' Parker for Hammers job 
  - Published2 hours ago
- What happens now at relegated West Ham? 
  - Published24 May
- Pragmatic Parker or a top flight contender? 
  - Published21 minutes ago
Widely seen as favourites for automatic promotion, the London side are currently eighth in the table, six points behind leaders Middlesbrough.
They have won two of their past six games and have lost back-to-back home matches - going down 3-2 to Southampton and then 3-1 to West Bromwich Albion on Saturday - losses that have seen them drop down from second place.
Assistant head coach Rui Pedro Silva and goalkeeper coach Rui Barbosa have also left the club.
Mark Noble, Steve Potts and Gerard Prenderville will take temporary charge of the side for their Championship trip to Cardiff City on Wednesday night.
"Following a thorough review of the start to the EFL Championship season, the board of directors believe that a change is necessary at this time in order to ensure that the club's objectives and expectations remain on track," a West Ham United statement read.
"West Ham United would like to thank Nuno, Rui and Rui for their hard work and commitment during their time at the club, and wish them all the very best for the future.
"The process of recruiting a new head coach is already under way."
The decision means West Ham are looking for their fourth permanent manager since David Moyes left London Stadium in May 2024.
His successor Julen Lopetegui was sacked after just six months in charge with the Hammers mid-table having won six of their 20 Premier League matches.
He was replaced by former Chelsea and Brighton boss Graham Potter, who oversaw a 14th-placed finish, but was sacked after only eight months in charge with the club 19th in the table.
The club opted to stick with former Wolves and Tottenham Hotspur boss Nuno despite him being unable to turn around the club's fortunes. They were relegated at the end of last season after finishing two points behind Spurs.
Despite that, this season had a troubled start for the Hammers - they failed to win any of their first three league matches and were 19th in the table.
A run of four successive wins in the first half of September, where they scored 16 goals and went top of the table, appeared to show they had adapted to the second tier, with a 6-0 win over Wrexham the highlight of the run.
Just two league victories have come since - a 6-0 win at nine-man Lincoln City and a 1-0 victory at Swansea City followed draws with London rivals Millwall and QPR.
A squad that Parker can work with?
Having posted losses of more than £104m, relegation meant West Ham had to sell players over the summer.
The departures of the likes of Mateus Fernandes, Crysencio Summerville, El Hadji Malick Diouf, James Ward-Prowse and Freddie Potts secured the club about £150m in transfer revenue.
They used some of that cash to pay Celtic a Championship record £22m for midfielder Arne Engels and spent a reported £12m on Norwegian winger Edvin Austbo.
Experienced campaigners Joel Veltman and Manor Solomon also joined on free transfers from Brighton and Tottenham respectively while they kept key players such as England winger Jarrod Bowen, Czech midfielder Tomas Soucek and Greek defender Konstantinos Mavropanos.
Soucek missed the first two months of the season with an ankle injury while some of their other signings have yet to deliver. Engels has three assists and no goals in 12 games while Austbo has scored twice and had two assists having started just two league matches.
It is a squad that is capable of turning things around, especially under a manager with Championship promotion experience such as Parker.
'West Ham's hierarchy feel Parker understands the club'
Analysis - Simon Stone, BBC Sport chief football news reporter
Given the estimated £200m loss in revenue it is imperative the club goes straight back up to the Premier League.
Two wins in six, a run which has dropped West Ham to eighth in the table, four points off second-placed Swansea in the final automatic promotion place, is not good enough.
Scott Parker is the obvious choice as replacement and West Ham are wasting no time in getting the deal done.
Parker made 129 appearances in a four-year stint with the Hammers. He won the club's player of the year award three times and was at West Ham when he was named Football Writers' Association player of the year in 2011.
West Ham's hierarchy feel Parker understands the club and the culture and is someone the fans can get behind.
Equally as important, he has already been promoted from the Championship three times, at Fulham, Bournemouth and Burnley.
West Ham will hope he makes it number four next May.
'The expectation is for an immediate return to the Premier League'
Analysis - Phil Parry, BBC Radio London sport editor
There were some who thought that Nuno would leave the club in the summer after they failed to survive their relegation battle, but the stability that he offered and his experience of guiding Wolves out of the Championship were seen as positive reasons to welcome his continuation at the helm.
The 6-0 thumpings handed out to Wrexham and Lincoln are contrasted with some disappointing home defeats, including the past two outings at London Stadium.
One of the major concerns has been the slow starts to games. They have conceded the opening goal in four of their past six in the Championship and have picked up just two points from those matches.
It has been suggested that the team just don't appear to appreciate the intensity and urgency of games at this level and are still a little too ponderous in the first half.
The Hammers have just been through a run of matches against teams who are in good form and are sitting high in the table, but losses in two of those games, both at home, have proven costly for Nuno.
With the squad at their disposal and the fanbase that backs them, it will be an attractive job for the next head coach, but whoever it is will be aware that the expectation at London Stadium is for an immediate return to the Premier League and falling short of that objective is risky for long-term prospects.

'I never enjoyed exercise at school as I was bullied' says DJ, ahead of 400-mile bike feat

'I never enjoyed exercise at school as I was bullied' says DJ, ahead of 400-mile bike feat
- Published
Radio presenter Owain Wyn Evans has admitted he "never enjoyed exercise at school" because of bullying, ahead of his four nations biking challenge for Children in Need.
The host of BBC Radio 2's Early Breakfast Show is set to cycle almost 400 miles over five days next week, setting off from Glasgow and finishing in Cardiff.
Evans, 42, who is originally from Ammanford, Carmarthenshire, begins his challenge in Scotland on Monday, 9 November, concluding the 643km feat in the Welsh capital on 13 November.
"Mentally, for me, it's been a challenge," said Evans. "Hopefully I'm going to inspire people to do exercise and realise that you can do this; you don't have to write off exercise forever."
'You can make a change'
"This is going to be really difficult for me personally, 100%," acknowledged Evans, who is undertaking his second challenge for the BBC charity fundraiser, following his 24-hour drumathon challenge back in 2021.
"I never had a good relationship with exercise when I was in school," the Welsh radio host said.
"I was bullied and I found going into a changing room, football field or rugby pitch... were places I didn't feel safe when I was growing up.
He said he hoped "people who are seeing me do this, understand that this is a tough one for me".
"And maybe there will be people watching this now who think, 'yeah when I was in school I didn't like PE…'," said Evans who remembered "never fitting in in some way".
"For me, as a 42-year-old man, who's had that experience for his whole life, I guess I am now realising that you can make a change in your life and you can make a difference."
"It's taken a while, but this challenge is what has helped me reach this point," he said.
"It's a four-nation, 400-mile cycle challenge… all of those things are alien to me," said Evans, who didn't even own a bike before the current challenge.
"I'm not a cyclist. I'm not an endurance athlete in any way, shape or form - and when I was asked to do this, of course I said yes, because I love Children in Need and have an existing relationship with them."
However, he added: "I did think - gulp - am I going to be able to do this? And that's been a bit of a recurring thing for me ever since.
"Am I good enough? Am I going to be able to do this? Will I succeed? Will I finish?"
He described Children in Need as "an incredible charity - we're so lucky to have it", but he stressed the extent of the support required, with the annual fundraiser only able "to help one out of the six projects that approach it".
Reflecting on his months of training, Evans said: "I think, for me, the hurdles are the hills. I think the distance stuff I'm kind of ok with, but you never know how long or how steep a hill is going to be.
"One of the worst things I did was look at the weather forecast for the challenge week, because it looks like it's going to be cold, wet and windy - famously not good conditions for cyclists.
"But it is what it is. Being a weather presenter for so many years - back in the day - I know there's one thing about the weather you can't do, and that's change it!"
'Hiraeth is very real'
The BBC said Evans' challenge would be the "greatest ever distance" covered in a Radio 2 endeavour for the charity.
After cycling through Scotland, Northern Ireland, England and Wales, Evans said bringing the challenge to a close in Cardiff will be "special".
"That was something I wanted to happen from the very beginning, so I think it will be a very emotional moment - arriving in Cardiff on that final morning."
Despite having worked all over the UK, he said: "I've always thought I'd like to return to Wales, because I believe we Welsh people tend to want to come back home.
"This feeling of hiraeth is very real, and I certainly felt it while I was away."

'Deal with dissidents' may need to be made to increase recruitment in PSNI - Denis Bradley

'Deal with dissidents' may need to be made to increase recruitment in PSNI - Denis Bradley
- Published
The first vice-chair of the Policing Board has said that it may be necessary to make a deal with dissident republicans in order to increase recruitment from young people from nationalist backgrounds to the PSNI.
Denis Bradley said "dissidency still retains the power to frighten people away," from joining the force.
Bradley's comments come before the 25th anniversary of the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI), which the Chief Constable Jon Boutcher said is a moment to look back on with "great pride".
While of the key objectives of the PSNI was to build greater community support for the police and increase Catholic officers Catholics remain under-represented in today's PSNI.
Bradley was speaking ahead of a two-day conference in Belfast marking the milestone, which is being attended by 160 delegates.
Jon Boutcher said the years had "not been without challenge" and repeated that the PSNI faces continued financial challenges, with a £1bn budget which has remained static for years.
"We have got to find a way to support policing by making sure the organisation is funded to do the job that all of us want it to do, to make sure we future proof for the next 25 years," he said.
'Residue of dissident activity remains'
A core goal of the Patten reforms was to increase Catholic and minority representation within the PSNI, speaking on Good Morning Ulster, Bradley said he finds it disappointing that it hasn't sustained.
He said a "residue of dissident activity" remained in communities.
He questioned how to get recruitment figures up and "how can young Catholics be expected to leave their homes, places of worship, local areas and join policing.
"While dissidence in some ways has faded to some great degree, it still retains a power to frighten people away" he said.
It can only be resolved by the two governments "making a deal" with the dissidents, "eliminating them" or "the dissidents themselves deciding to go away," he added.
Bradley was attacked by dissident republicans in 2005 with a baseball bat as he watched a football match in a bar. But he said that he thinks a "deal with the dissidents has to be made."
Bradley said that after some sort of political engagement, wherever it may be "policing becomes a vital cog within the wheel of change, within the wheel of peace"
He added that "policing hasn't been a complete success" but that "it has also stabilised the situation within our peace journey."
Speaking to the media on Tuesday morning, Boutcher acknowledged that the percentage of Catholic officers had "moved backwards" recently.
He said society, politicians and the police all needed to do more to encourage applications.
"Can I say when we will be truly representative? No I can't.
"Let's get our shoulder behind the wheel and then if we are still not making the progress we need, we will look at other options."
In March 2026, Boutcher said a return to 50:50 recruitment did not feel necessary, but "nothing is off the table".
Brendan Mullan, the chair of the Northern Ireland Policing Board, said the anniversary was a "significant milestone".
He said those who worked to establish the PSNI are owed "a huge debt".
The conference, organised by the PSNI and the Policing Board, is being held at Queen's University Belfast and Ulster University.
Entitled 'Foundations And Future: Policing 2026 And Beyond' it will consider progress made over the last 25 years and examine future challenges.
The PSNI was created out of the Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC) as a new beginning for policing, after work by Lord Patten, a former government minister.
In a video recording for the opening event, Patten, who was the last UK Governor of Hong Kong, said his work on policing was his most important job.
"I don't think there's anything I feel prouder of having done and I'm glad it has worked as well as it has," he said.

article:
Who are the real winners of Celebrity Traitors?

Who are the real winners of Celebrity Traitors?
- Published
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from The Celebrity Traitors final
In some ways, all the players on The Celebrity Traitors can be seen as winners.
They all got to appear on a hugely popular TV show, rubbing shoulders with other stars and gaining new fans along the way.
But there are certain celebrities, such as Miranda Hart, King Kenny, Maya Jama and Joanne McNally, who have been tipped by industry experts as getting the biggest career boost after the show.
Sebastian "Bash" Croft - who won the game, alongside Romesh Ranganathan - could also now be in line for greater roles.
We've taken a look at the breakout stars of the series and what might lie ahead for them.
Miranda Hart
After a spell of ill-health, the show has done wonders for bringing Miranda Hart back into the public eye.
There was that incredible “Little Mix Big Mix” viral dance moment, but Hart also displayed a level of vulnerability which stood out in a show where the stars don't really talk about their personal lives.
When her friend Joe Lycett was banished, her tearful reaction to his exit provided a rare poignant moment.
"Connection and laughter and joy are bigger than this game - and to meet someone and just play and laugh, it's all us humans need, you know?" she said.
When she was murdered, she also demonstrated genuine emotion in her response. "Ultimately, in my little personal story, this has been quite extraordinary," she said.
For culture journalist Natalie Jamieson, Hart's openness and relatability made her the "standout" star from this year's series.
And it could also lead to us seeing more of Hart on the small screen. According to The Sun, external, the BBC is looking to bring back her self-titled sitcom after her stint on Celebrity Traitors led to fresh interest in the show.
The BBC declined to comment on the possible return of Hart’s show.
But she’s not the only one who won hearts by showing real warmth.
The same could be said for Romesh Ranganathan - who, in a departure from his usual cynical, deadpan stand-up persona, seemed really to care about his fellow cast members. Jerry Hall also won viewers over with her charming eccentricity.
And then there’s James Acaster, who showed genuine vulnerability as he struggled to come to terms with being a traitor.
Social media users seemed split after his bombshell confession to being a traitor, with some totally exasperated and others saying they respected him for going out on his own terms.
Either way, he's definitely got the nation talking.
King Kenny
When it comes to celebrities who are most likely to see the biggest career boost, most experts say Kenny is King.
Going into the castle, the 29-year-old was best known to younger fans as a member of the popular British YouTube collective Beta Squad.
But Kenny will have been "the least familiar name to a mainstream audience," says showbiz journalist Nikki Onafuye.
That all changed as he was recruited as a traitor, bringing much-needed energy to the turret - and he made it all the way through to Friday night’s tense final.
Having shown he can hold his own alongside established broadcasters, actors and comedians, big things could now be in store for Kenny.
"He 100% has just been minted as a mainstream star now," said Marina Hyde, on The Rest is Entertainment podcast.
“The next steps could be panel shows, presenting roles, reality competitions or entertainment formats,” adds TV reporter Siobhan Synnot.
Maya Jama
Fellow traitor Maya Jama also sailed all the way to the final with her cool-as-a-cucumber persona making her a traitor to be reckoned with.
Despite being banished in dramatic fashion, she could now be in line to receive £1m per deal, according to a report in The Times earlier this week, external.
What Celebrity Traitors has done for Jama is allow her to reveal more of her personality than on Love Island, says Onafuye.
But TV reporter Synnot thinks between the two, Kenny has more to gain because he has introduced himself to millions of new viewers - whereas Jama was already one of Britain's best-known TV presenters before Celebrity Traitors.
"Maya's gain is subtler: she can emerge looking less like the presenter of Love Island and more like a genuinely versatile television star," she says.
Joanne McNally
Of all the comedians in the castle, Joanne McNally was initially the least well known, says Caroline Frost, TV editor at Radio Times.
But she flourished on the show, lasting right up to Thursday's semi-final.
"And she's taken her own path, ignoring the herd and making her own voting decisions, sometimes chaotically, but always with charm, wit and good humour,” says Frost.
The Irish comedian's podcast was already popular before the show.
But after her stint as the joker of the pack, bigger things could now lie in store for her.
Just a few days ago, it was announced, external that her stand-up tour has been extended into 2027, "due to phenomenal demand".
And her agents will be "fielding calls" for her to bring her star power to other shows, adds Frost.
Culture journalist Jamieson says some of the other female contestants - such as Sharon Rooney, Leigh-Anne Pinnock and Myha'la - also stood out for showing their wit and wisdom, which could serve them well in the outside world.
Things got a bit awkward in one of the episodes, when Sharon disagreed with some of the cast on a challenge, with some social media users saying she was acting in a "childish" way.
But others argued it was a classic case of women being drowned out by men.
"There's been a subtlety in the smartness of women on display here, alongside the frustration of not always being listened to in the game," says Jamieson.
Sebastian 'Bash' Croft
In the end, it was faithful duo Romesh Ranganathan and Sebastian ‘Bash’ Croft who emerged victorious.
Comedian Ranganathan was already a huge star, but the show has introduced Croft, 24, to a much wider audience.
He’s had previous acting roles in Game of Thrones and Heartstopper, but Traitors allowed him to show his own personality, "which as we've seen has endeared him both to other players and the huge watching audience", says Frost.
He is also building his career as a pop star, and he's had a strong presence on social media during the series, posting videos of his tracks.
His debut EP comes out later in November, perfect timing to capitalise on his Traitors win.
And what's in store for the others...
What's clear is that the true victors aren't necessarily the ones who get their hands on the prize pot.
Arguably, what matters most is the amount of screen time you get - and what you do with it.
On that note, spare a thought for those who left the show early, such as Amol Rajan, Julie Hesmondhalgh and Hannah Fry.
But all made an impact in their own way and, as Synnot points out, they get "a nice anecdote" for future interviews.
And what of James Blunt, who stole hearts with his military approach to the challenges and eccentric Top Gun-style outfits - and who came so close to winning the whole show?
Maybe he's the mystery man in contention for the new James B(ond) - although his hapless theories could mean he'll be in line to be the new Johnny English instead.

ACOTAR fans put real life on hold for latest release

ACOTAR fans put real life on hold for latest release
- Published
As I arrive at Waterstones in York shortly before 08:00, there is already a queue forming outside the bookshop.
Fans of Sarah J Maas's bestselling A Court of Thorns and Roses (ACOTAR) series are waiting eagerly to get their hands on the latest instalment.
Among them is Olivia Bray, 28, who has spent more than a decade immersed in the American author's fantasy world.
For Bray, the appeal goes beyond magic, romance and fantastical kingdoms. It is the feminism running through Maas's books that has kept her coming back.
And with the release of A Court of Splintered Harmony, Bray is prepared to put real life on hold, having booked an entire week off work to give herself time to recover from whatever awaits her between the covers.
"I'll be done [with reading] by tomorrow," she said. "I've just got the whole week off in case it's traumatising."
Set in the fictional world of Prythian, the series has amassed millions of fans across the world.
The series follows Feyre Archeron, a young huntress drawn into the dangerous world of the fae, where she navigates political intrigue, war and romance.
There have been five books so far, A Court of Thorns and Roses (2015), A Court of Mist and Fury (2016), A Court of Wings and Ruin (2017), A Court of Frost and Starlight (2018), and A Court of Silver Flames (2021).
A Court of Splintered Harmony, the sixth book in the best-selling series, was released on Tuesday - five years after fans last heard from the characters.
Another ACOTAR fan, 22-year-old Abigail Wright, hoped to finish the book on release day, which coincided with her day off, before returning to work.
She said the books were her "gateway back into reading" aged 19.
Like Bray, Wright believed the recurring theme of female empowerment was a key part of its appeal.
"I think it's so popular because, yes, the romantic side of it is very good, but the strong women you see in the books are just a way to make other young women feel really empowered," said Wright.
"It just gives them a sense of power and [makes them] see you can start from nothing, like Feyre does, and just make your way up… you don't need a man to do all these things for you, you have the power to do anything you want to do."
Gabriella Booth, 29, was introduced to the series in 2013, but attributes ACOTAR's explosion in popularity to both the pandemic and "BookTok" - a TikTok community dedicated to sharing what people are reading and writing.
"The characters in general are so easy to read about. You can relate in different parts to a lot of them, I find," said Booth.
"For me, I love the fantasy world - that's something I've loved reading growing up. So, to have that combined with the romance side of everything... there's something that's just so exciting to read about."
Booth has previously taken time off work to read new releases and plans to do so when the seventh ACOTAR book is published in January.
However, on this occasion, she hopes to finish A Court of Splintered Harmony after work.
Alice Boyce, a bookseller at Topping and Company Booksellers on Museum Street in York, said ACOTAR fans had made their way straight up to the science-fiction area of the store as soon as doors opened at 09:00.
"People are really enthusiastic; we've had emails saying, 'can you put a copy aside for me?', and last night we had people asking to put it on pre-order."
An ACOTAR fan herself, 26-year-old Boyce said she felt she could truly disconnect when she read the books.
"You can dive into books and just escape a little bit," she added.
Events were held across the UK, including in Wolverhampton and Northern Ireland, to mark the new book's release, with Waterstones on York's Coney Street hosting its first ever midnight release event.
Eighty ACOTAR fans, some of whom were dressed as their favourite characters, attended the event, while 100 members of the fandom flocked to a party in Wolverhampton.
Organiser Holly Fellows, from Redditch, told the BBC people were "ecstatic" when the book was finally released.
"The community was just lovely, it was so nice to see everybody come together and fan-girl over a book," Fellows said.
Fellows, who booked the day off work to read the book, said she was already through the first chapter.
"It sounds like it's going to be incredible", she said.
'Safe place'
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today Programme on Tuesday, Abi Fraser, owner of the Throne and Heart bookshop in Market Harborough, Leicestershire, where a release party was also held, said: "We had about 45 people in the bookshop to celebrate the midnight release.
"We had quizzes, we had games, we had a countdown to midnight - there is a real community vibe to the fandom... it's fantastic."
Elizabeth Vaziri, commissioning editor at Voyager and Magpie at the publisher Harper Collins, told the programme fantasy had "always been a portal for escapism".
Combined with romance, Vaziri said the "romantasy" genre had "given people a safe place to navigate relationships or sexuality".

Trump says US will stop providing aid to Israel after year-end

Trump says US will stop providing aid to Israel after year-end
- Published
President Donald Trump has said the US will stop providing funding to Israel at the end of the year, following a deal he struck with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
In a telephone interview with Fox News on Tuesday morning, Trump said that a deal had been reached "months ago" that will see the US stop providing $4bn (£2.98bn) each year.
"We've already agreed that by the end of this year we won't be paying Israel," Trump said. "Now we'll help Israel if they need it."
It is unclear what funds the president was referring to, although a memorandum of understanding that provides $3.8bn in military assistance to Israel expires at the end of 2028.
The BBC has contacted the White House for clarification. The Israeli Prime Minister's office has yet to comment.
Speaking to Fox News, Trump said that Israel no longer needs American funding.
"As far as paying Israel, Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal that we give Israel $4 billion a year, and we made a deal months ago that we're stopping," he said.
He also accused Democrats of weaponising US assistance to Israel as a "talking point" with which to attack Republicans.
Trump said that Israel can purchase weapons from the US if necessary. The contours of any new procurement or investment arrangement to help Israel's military remain unclear.
In a May interview with CBS, the BBC's US partner, Prime Minister Netanyahu said he wants to "draw down" US financial support to Israel "to zero" from the annual $3.8bn the country receives.
"Let's start now and do it over the next decade, over the next ten years, but I want to start now," he said. "I don't want to wait for the next Congress. I want to start now."
Israel has been the largest recipient of US foreign assistance since the end of the Second World War.
A Congressional report published last year put the total price tag at $174bn, non-inflation-adjusted.
The US-Israel relationship still has substantial bipartisan backing, but support has been softening among Democrats, particularly following the start of the war in Gaza in October 2023.
In July, Republican lawmaker Thomas Massie forced a vote on a bill to cut $3.3bn in security aid to Israel and he received support from 103 Democrats in the chamber. He was the only Republican to support the amendment. The measure was defeated by 314 votes to 104.
A September poll conducted by Quinnipiac University found that nearly half - 48% - of voters believe the US is too supportive of Israel, up from 16% in 2017.
Among Democrats, the figure stands at 67%, compared to 17% for Republicans.

The winner of the Voice UK says she decided "I was going to be Taylor Swift" as a teenager after being given a guitar, before busking on the streets of Cardiff.
Welsh singer Cate McHugh was crowned the winner of the show on Saturday, after being mentored by "the legend that is Sir Tom Jones".
McHugh, from Llantwit Major, in the Vale of Glamorgan, said Sir Tom was so warm and supportive that it felt "as if you've known him for years".
One of the standout pieces of advice he gave to her early on was to focus on the story being told in the song, she explained.
McHugh said that when she found herself getting "a little bit flappy and excited" while rehearsing Sir Tom would say "nope, what's the story?", and urged her to focus on that and "stay true".
The 32-year-old, who began her career as a teenager busking under the watchful eye of her parents, said she and Sir Tom had "really lovely interactions and a lovely comfortable connection" and that it was "just an honour to be in his presence".
The final was a poignant moment for Sir Tom as it was his last appearance on the show, having been a coach on and off since it began in 2012.
He made headlines in September after revealing that ITV had "made the decision" to "fire" him from the show's coaching panel.
McHugh said that in the moments before she was announced as the winner, she felt "super peaceful because I was so happy with where I'd come" in the show.
The singer, who has a six-year-old daughter and a 16-year-old stepson, said she felt confetti on her shoulder and "opened my eyes and thought 'oh my God, they said my name'."
She said she wanted to thank her family, including her husband Nathan, for surrounding her with "all of that love" and support throughout the show and during the final.
Recalling her early days of performing, McHugh said "I was the kid who was always singing and my parents decided very early on that if they didn't put me in singing lessons this was going to get really annoying really quickly".
She was gifted an acoustic guitar for her birthday around the time Taylor Swift released her album Fearless, and "decided that I was going to be Taylor Swift, I was going to learn the entire album from start to finish".
Aged 15, she told her parents she wanted to busk in Cardiff and "they did everything they could to fulfil that happening in the safest way which did mean, apparently, my father was lingering around on Queen Street, just keeping an eye on me".
Busking and taking requests from passers-by helped her to gain confidence and she has "paid my dues since then", including singing on cruise ships, McHugh said.
McHugh said that navigating losing her sight aged 22 due to degenerative macular condition Stargardt disease, external had made her more determined to succeed.
She said music had "always been an outlet, emotionally, as so many musicians will say, but for me, when I'm on a stage singing and the lights are down on the audience, it's the one place that I don't think about my sight loss".
McHugh said that "as long as I know the words and I'm not trying to read them off an iPad then I'm absolutely there in that moment".
She described her sight loss as "just a small part of me, it's not who I am".
McHugh added that while many people with differences and disabilities sometimes felt they had to make themselves smaller "so that you don't become a nuisance to people", she chose "to find a way to take up space and be bigger and that's where music took me".
She is now working on her first original song in a studio which should be released "relatively soon, hopefully, fingers crossed".
Footage shared by McHugh on social media after her win showed her laughing and smiling with family and friends screaming in delight as they celebrated her victory at a watch party in Cardiff.
She has won a £50,000 cash prize and a recording contract, with her first ever single, a cover of The Beatles classic Blackbird, now released.
