article:
What are the government's options for reducing welfare spending?

What are the government's options for reducing welfare spending?
- Published
Chancellor John Healey and Prime Minister Andy Burnham have both spoken of their desire for the benefits bill to come down, but the government has not yet laid out a timetable for any reductions.
Their political opponents have criticised them for a lack of detail on welfare reform in Wednesday's Budget, accusing the government of delaying difficult decisions over cuts.
Official forecasts released alongside the Budget indicate welfare spending is going to increase by £79bn in cash terms over the next few years.
BBC Verify has taken a look at the numbers behind this thorny political issue and some of the difficult options the government have to bring down welfare costs.
How much is being spent on welfare?
The official forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), estimates in its latest forecasts that the cost of the welfare system will rise, external from £353bn this year to £431bn in 2032.
The OBR's figures include spending on pensioners, which accounts for just under half of the total. The majority of this cost is on the state pension.
However, if we look at the size of welfare spending relative to the size of the overall economy the OBR's projections are less dramatic, increasing from 11.1% today to 11.3% of GDP in 2032.
Total welfare spending would also remain below the peak of around 12% of GDP in 2013 following the global financial crisis, leading some economists and researchers to question the idea that welfare spending is out of control., external
But there are some welfare costs that are rising rapidly.
Spending on health and disability related benefits, in particular Personal Independence Payments (PIP), is up sharply since the Covid-19 pandemic.
Accounting for inflation, spending on working-age disability benefits increased from £14bn in 2020 to £25bn in 2026, external.
Inflation-adjusted welfare spending remains lower than 2013 because several other working-age benefits, such as Universal Credit and housing benefit, were cut by Conservative-led governments as part of their austerity programme from 2010 onwards, external.
So spending in some parts of the system has come down while it has risen in others - and there could be a connection.
Some researchers think the post-2010 welfare cuts to benefits might have created an incentive for people to claim sickness and disability benefits instead to protect their living standards, external, therefore shifting costs around the system rather than generating lasting savings.
The problem of Neets
Many also see a specific problem regarding the growing number of young people in the welfare system claiming benefits, including PIP.
Official figures show the number of 16 to 24-year-olds who are not in employment, education or training (Neets) has risen, external by around 230,000 since 2019 to just under one million.
Former Labour health secretary Alan Milburn is leading an official review into Neets and is expected to recommend major reforms designed to get many off benefits and into work.
His interim report in May estimated that annual PIP expenditure on 16 to 24-year-olds rose from £1.3bn in 2020 to around £3.2bn in 2025, external. It also projected this cost would reach £6.5bn and cover 700,000 young people in five years' time.
PIP claimants can be in work, but official statistics show that only around one in five are, external.
What could cutting the benefits bill mean?
Politicians are often unclear about what they mean by reducing spending on welfare.
In March 2025, former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer's government presented a plan which it said would save £5bn a year from health-related welfare spending by 2030 by tightening PIP access and reducing the value of health-related Universal Credit payments.
But official forecasts made it clear that annual spending on health-related welfare in cash terms was still set to rise after the reform, external, just not as rapidly as the path it had previously been on.
However, at the time the OBR did forecast the plans would help put overall UK welfare spending on a "slightly downward trajectory" as a share of the economy, external over the medium term, rather than remaining flat as had been previously projected.
So this type of relative reduction in anticipated welfare spending, rather than a cut in absolute cash terms, could be what the government seeks to deliver.
Looming reports may offer options
The final Milburn report is expected in the coming weeks, as well as a separate final report from disability minister Stephen Timms into the options for PIP reform.
There has been speculation that these could recommend creating a new welfare system for people under the age of 25, external, so they are not eligible for PIP and receive lower payments than older people.
There are also suggestions Timms could propose a new PIP eligibility test to reduce access, external, although he was not specifically instructed to find savings.
Reforms along these lines could potentially make some savings to the welfare bill relative to the existing trajectory of rising spending, as well as reducing forecast welfare spending as share of GDP.
But some analysts argue that to be effective in delivering sustainable savings, such reforms are likely also to require the government to spend a lot more, external to enable young people in particular to get into and remain in work.
This was signalled by the interim Milburn report which noted that for every £1 the government spends on employment support for young people around £25 is spent on benefits, suggesting he could propose a significant increase in government spending on welfare-to-work schemes.
This means that any welfare savings could, in the near term at least, be offset by additional spending in other departments.
However, in the long term this approach could still deliver welfare savings if the employment support was effective.

article:
New pictures released ahead of The Other Bennet Sister Christmas special

New pictures released ahead of The Other Bennet Sister Christmas special
- Published
New images have been revealed ahead of the Christmas special of BBC series The Other Bennet Sister.
Inspired by Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice, the first series was filmed largely in Wales and attracted 6.5 million UK viewers in its first 28 days.
The series finale saw Mary Bennet, played by Ella Bruccoleri, agree to marry Tom Hayward, played by Donal Finn.
Filming wrapped on the three-part Christmas special at the end of August.
Little has been shared about the plot of the upcoming episodes, but the BBC teased: "With marriage comes a new identity and the question remains: who will Mary become as Mrs Hayward?" as fans eagerly await its return.
The first series of The Other Bennet Sister focused on Mary, the oft-overlooked middle sister in Pride and Prejudice, as she navigates the societal pressures of Regency England where marriage is both an aspiration and a necessity.
It was mostly filmed in south Wales at locations including Merthyr Mawr in Bridgend county, the Gower peninsula, and Brecon, in Powys.
The Christmas special has been produced by Cardiff-based Bad Wolf, and filming took place over the summer, also primarily in Wales.
Gavin & Stacey's Ruth Jones returns to the hit show as Mrs Bennet, who she previously described as "often quite cruel" to her daughter.
Other returning cast members include Ted Lasso's Tanya Reynolds as Caroline Bingley and Laurie Davidson as William Ryder.
Also resuming their roles are Poppy Gilbert as Lizzie Darcy, Maddie Close as Jane Bingley, Grace Hogg-Robinson as Lydia Wickham and Molly Wright as Kitty Buncock.
Nerys Amber-Stocks, best known for appearing in Out There and Mammoth, joins the cast as Mary's housemaid Lucy.
The stills also reveal another look at Bruccoleri and Finn, and the BBC teased: "Just as Mary begins this new chapter, an unexpected visitor from her past arrives at her door in need of her help..."
The show's producer Edoardo Ferretti had previously announced to fans on social media that the special had finished filming at the end of August.
He posted a short message on Instagram, saying: "And yet another wrap! Every time emotional, every time proud. This one is going to be so special!"
The three additional episodes, announced in June, will run for 30 minutes each and continue to be based on storylines from the original novel by Janice Hadlow.
It has been written by screenwriter Sarah Quintrell, who wrote nine of the series' 10 episodes, while Asim Abbasi returns to direct the special.
It will air in the UK on BBC iPlayer and BBC One, while in the US and Canada, it will also be available on BritBox.

article:
'Rok' solid recognition for Slovenian space scientist

'Rok' solid recognition for Slovenian space scientist
- Published
As a child growing up in Slovenia in 1999, Dr Rok Nežič couldn't have known that an asteroid that was discovered in New Mexico that year would be named after him almost three decades later.
The Orchard County may be best known for its apples, but for Nežič the real attraction was astronomy.
He first arrived at Armagh Observatory and Planetarium (AOP) in 2015 to complete his doctorate in space and climate physics, and has remained there ever since.
More than a decade on, he is one of two AOP employees to have recently been chosen to have a celestial body named after them.
Nežič, who works at the planetarium as a tours and outreach officer, said he thought it was "so cool" when he learned that asteroids can be named after people.
Speaking to BBC News NI, Nežič said he wished he "could get there some day" and, now that he has, he described it as "a dream come true".
"I'm not sure how to believe it myself,” he admitted.
He explains that an asteroid is "a smallish rock in space" compared to planets, and that his one is named (20560) Nežič., external
"That's its official name, so the number there tells you basically the order of discovery."
It is currently "sitting safely out in the asteroid belt and just going around the Sun, just like we are", he explained.
The naming process for small bodies in the solar system is governed by the International Astronomical Union, external. Asteroids can be named by their discoverers once their orbits are sufficiently known.
Nežič's asteroid is 10.9km across, while that belonging to his colleague Shane Kelly is 15.6km.
"They're both actually quite large as far as these asteroids that are named after people tend to be, because most of the really large ones were discovered first," Nežič said.
"So they were named a long time ago, and now we're finding smaller and smaller ones."
Nežič's asteroid was discovered by "one of the big missions", he said.
"This is an Earth-based mission in this case, which is looking for lots of asteroids, essentially, because the more we know about them, the more we know where they're going, the more we know which ones are not hitting us, including mine and Shane's."
To be considered for an asteroid namesake, someone must nominate you, and in Nežič's case, two people put his name forward.
He doesn't know who chose him for the honour - but his PhD supervisor, and a former astronomer from the observatory nominated him.
Nežič focused on comets with polarised light for his studies and years later is "still" talking about space.
The planetarium and observatory is "punching well above our weight", he said.
"Even though we're a small institution, people who work here can just focus on the research so much that we have really top researchers in the field."
The planetarium's neighbouring observatory has monitored the weather for more than than 230 years.
Shane Kelly, who is the principal meteorological observer at Armagh Observatory, was nominated by the emeritus director.
Since 1999, his role involves opening what is known as the Stevenson screen which holds sensitive thermometers, before noting down his readings for the day into the handwritten ledger.
His hand has entered far more lines of data than any of his 17 predecessors and his asteroid is called (7050) Shanekelly.
Kelly has been "doing this for 27 years", the institute's director said.
"He's probably observed the weather more than anyone else in the world, I suspect," Prof Michael Burton said.
"So this is in recognition of Shane's contribution to the observatory and to the measuring of the weather."
Kelly's asteroid was discovered in Chile, external in 1982.
Burton said it's "fantastic" that the two members of the team have been awarded in this way.
"There are now 29 asteroids which have some connection with the observatory and planetarium here in Armagh."
The AOP now plans on recognising their achievements with a new LED dome, which will show the asteroids and their orbits.

Wales face Denmark and Italy again on League A return

Wales will face Denmark, Italy and Iceland when they return to Nations League A next year.
Rhian Wilkinson's side were beaten twice by both the Danes and the Italians when they were previously in the top division in 2025.
The Welsh side also drew home and away with group winners Sweden, but finished bottom of the table and were relegated to the second-tier League B.
Wales now return to League A after topping Group B1 as part of the qualification process for the 2027 Women's World Cup, having been unbeaten in a campaign against Czech Republic, Albania and Montenegro.
Fixtures for the 2027 Nations League have yet to be confirmed by Uefa, but the competition will be played across the international windows in February/March, April and June.

Wilkinson's side will hope those Nations League games can form part of preparations for a first appearance at a World Cup finals.
Having beaten Albania 4-0 on aggregate in a World Cup play-off semi-final last month, they face a final against Norway, with a home leg at Cardiff City Stadium on Tuesday, 1 December before an away trip four days later.
However, victory against a side managed by former Wales boss Gemma Grainger may not be enough to guarantee a place in Brazil next summer.

The Nations League will have a direct bearing on qualifying for the 2028 Olympic Games, to be held in Los Angeles, USA, and the next Women's Euros in Germany in 2029.
The winner of each League A group will progress to the Nations League finals in October and will secure a place at the expanded LA Games, while the bottom side in each group will be relegated to League B.
Each third-placed side in League A will face a relegation/promotion play-off against a second-placed League B side.

article:
A thousand job applications, five interviews and still no job

A thousand job applications, five interviews and still no job
- Published
Casey Smith has been going to the job centre every few weeks since she was 16 but feels she's been "going round and round in circles".
The teenager, from Johnstone, Renfrewshire, is one of nearly a million young people in the UK classified as a Neet - not in education, employment or training.
After four years, she is desperate to work.
"I'm nearly 20 now," she told BBC Scotland.
"I at least thought by the time I was 18, 17 that I would have something and I don't.
"I'm very frustrated about it because the amount of pressure that is on young adults nowadays is absolutely insane."
The latest annual figures , external on young people's work status shows 93.6% of those aged 16-19 were in education, employment or training last year, up slightly on 2025.
It means around 8,500 young people in Scotland are not working or studying - and the activities of about 6,000 more are unconfirmed.
The problem is at its worst in Dundee, with 6.7% of young people lost to the labour market and education.
'Checking emails every day'
Those who are between 20 and 24 are more likely to be Neet than those aged 16-19 in the UK.
Casey is just about to enter that cohort. She says she is "constantly" applying for jobs.
"I think I've definitely applied to a thousand, maybe just a wee bit under that.
"You're waking up every day and you're doing the same thing, applying and applying, and you're not hearing anything.
"I've had roughly five interviews," she said.
She explained that as soon as she wakes up she is checking emails and applying for all sorts of jobs including in cleaning, retail and hospitality.
Casey hands in CVs and has phoned every store in her local area twice looking for work.
"If I had it my way I would be doing a nine-to-five every day. I would love to do that."
The majority of Neets in the UK - 60% - are economically inactive, meaning they are not searching for work or able to start work.
Former Labour health secretary Alan Milburn is leading an official review into Neets and is expected to recommend major reforms designed to get many young people off benefits and into work in the coming weeks.
For Casey, the current system at the job centre just isn't working.
"I go once every two weeks and you're supposed to be there for roughly half an hour and have a conversation about what you can do.
"I will sit in the waiting area for maybe 20 minutes and then I will be speaking to whoever it is I'm speaking to for no more than five.
"And it's honestly it's like seeing somebody in the street that you've not seen in a wee while: 'Hi, how are you, what have you been up to? Ok, see you later'."
She says she is sometimes referred to community projects for assistance.
"They will teach you how to do things like making CVs or there might be a couple people looking for young people to start working for them", she said.
"However, it never gets anywhere.
"They're telling me to go out and do these things which I have already done several times over."
'More feedback'
Job hunting for years can take its toll on confidence and mental health, she said.
"I think the pressure of it all is what really bugs me. Why is there so much pressure on me when you know that I try every single day yet I'm not getting anywhere with it?
"It's also embarrassing to talk about, because, I don't have anything, neither do my peers.
"And then when people who are older than us are like, 'Oh, have you got a job yet?'
"And it's just constant pressure, constant judgement."
Figures from Scotland last year revealed that 16-19 year olds from the poorest backgrounds were more than five times less likely to be participating in education, training or employment than those who lived in the least deprived areas.
Casey thinks there needs to be more feedback from employers when rejecting applicants and that those at the job centre could talk more about ideas for work, volunteering or experience.
"I know we have the job centre that's supposed to help us go out and get jobs and find work and things like that, but that's not working.
"That's falling to bits. I don't think it's going to be up and running in like the next 10 years.
"It's collapsing and nobody's doing anything about it.
"So once that crumbles and just does not work anymore, what do you expect us to do?
"We need a new system in place."
A spokesman for the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), which is responsible for Job Centres, said: "Every young person deserves the chance to build a future they are proud of.
"That is why we are investing £2.5bn to help more young people earn or learn, including through a Youth Hub in every local area, bringing together housing, mental health and employment support.
"And we are transforming Jobcentres to create a more personalised, modern and accessible service to support people across the country into work."

article:
Thousands of European troops to rehearse Ukraine deployment in event of peace

Thousands of European troops to rehearse Ukraine deployment in event of peace
- Published
Britain and France are to lead a military exercise to test a multinational force's ability to deploy to Ukraine, if there is a peace deal.
Nearly 3,000 military personnel from 12 European nations will take part in the rehearsal in neighbouring Poland this month.
Plans for a reassurance force for Ukraine were set out last year as one of the long-term security guarantees being proposed by European nations.
But there are still more questions than answers as to how such a military force might work in practice. Western officials stress that any force sent to Ukraine would not take part in offensive operations or be involved in peacekeeping or ceasefire monitoring missions.
Nor would they be operating under the command of Nato or on the front line.
Officials say their presence would be to provide reassurance to Ukraine and to help rebuild its armed forces.
The US has been involved in discussions, but is not contributing to the mission.
Russia has already voiced opposition to foreign troops being stationed in Ukraine and, last year, President Vladimir Putin said they would be "legitimate targets".
Western officials have declined to spell out the rules of engagement if any international troops were to be attacked in Ukraine. Though they say the force would be able to defend itself.
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the exercise showed Britain, France and their allies were stepping up preparation for the day when peace came to Ukraine.
He said: "This is not a hypothetical plan, it's a real force, ready to help Ukraine once the fighting stops."
Lt Gen Tom Bateman, the UK commander of the Multi National Force – Ukraine (MNF-U), said the exercise represented an important step in translating political commitments into credible military readiness.
He said it was a "real, capable, readily deployable force that represented a serious commitment from Coalition of the Willing nations to Ukraine's long-term stability and security".
Exercise Koalicja - which takes place from 9-22 November - will be a rehearsal of how to move, protect and supply a force in Ukraine. It will also be a test of their command and control to ensure troops from different countries can work together.
Some 2,800 military personnel will take part across land, sea and air, with the UK contribution including 300 troops and a pair of RAF Typhoons.
Fighter jets will simulate how they would reassure commercial aircraft once Ukraine's skies can be reopened.
Turkey has agreed to lead the maritime mission, with the eventual goal to clear mines and allow the resumption of trade in the Black Sea.
As well as the UK, troops will come from France, Belgium, Estonia, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Poland, Spain, Sweden, and Turkey.
However, Western officials could not comment on the final make-up and shape of the force that could be deployed to Ukraine if the fighting stops.
In the past, military experts have suggested that Western nations might have to send tens of thousands of troops to Ukraine to guarantee its security.
Officials acknowledge that the countries' commitment and contributions will depend on the circumstances of a cessation of hostilities and individual nations' political decisions.
It is also unclear what training role Western forces could provide to battle hardened Ukraine.
Ukrainian soldiers are already in high demand training Nato forces - passing on their expertise in drone warfare.
Above all, Russia has shown no sign of wanting to end its war.

article:
Sir Patrick Stewart: Actor who moved effortlessly between Star Trek and Shakespeare

Sir Patrick Stewart: Actor who moved effortlessly between Star Trek and Shakespeare
- Published
Sir Patrick Stewart, who has died at the age of 86, was a stage and screen great who balanced Hollywood stardom with an equally stellar career in classical theatre.
While many actors are typecast, he moved effortlessly from Shakespeare and Dickens to the command of the USS Enterprise and his famous wheelchair in X-Men.
In a career that spanned seven decades, Sir Patrick received multiple awards, a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame and a knighthood from Queen Elizabeth II.
One of the world's most versatile actors, he mastered both comedy and tragedy, science-fiction and historical drama - despite the entertainment industry's traditional dislike of bald heads.
Patrick Hewes Stewart was born in Mirfield in the West Riding of Yorkshire on 13 July 1940.
His mother Gladys was a textile worker. She was active in amateur dramatics and encouraged her three sons to take part.
His father was a former Sergeant Major in the Parachute Regiment whose experience during the wartime evacuation of Dunkirk had shredded his mental health.
"My father was a very potent individual," Stewart later recalled. "It was said that when he strode on to the parade ground, birds stopped singing."
But Alfred Stewart had become a quick-tempered man, suffering from what would now be called post traumatic stress.
He was prone to drink and often took out his frustrations on his family - although Patrick himself was never the target of his fists.
Young Patrick's love of drama developed at school when one of his teachers introduced him to Shakespeare and encouraged him to perform.
His first public performance was in a local church production of Cinderella.
He found the predictability of dramatic performances a welcome change from the turmoil of his home life.
He left school at 15 and eventually got a job as a journalist and obituary writer on the Dewsbury Reporter.
He also threw himself enthusiastically into the flourishing local theatre. "I used to recite Shakespeare from memory," he said. "I just learned all these big speeches."
But he found it impossible to concentrate on both his job and his acting. Eventually his editor told him to choose between journalism and the "foolhardy" acting.
Stewart picked up his typewriter and walked out.
At the age of 18, he had the traumatic experience of losing all his hair, a huge blow to an aspiring actor and self-conscious teenager - who worried that girls would no longer find him attractive.
He won a scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic and later joined the Royal Shakespeare Company - playing a variety of roles across the company's repertoire.
And when not appearing as Oberon or Enobarbus, he made his TV debut as a fireman in a 1967 episode of soap opera Coronation Street.
His Broadway debut came in 1970 as Snout in Peter Brook's critically acclaimed production of A Midsummer Night's Dream.
Over the next two decades, Stewart appeared in a variety of television roles without threatening to become a major star.
In 1974, he played Lenin in the BBC's 13-part drama series The Fall of Eagles.
He was a conspiratorial Roman soldier in the hugely popular I, Claudius and a Soviet spy in Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Spy and Smiley's People.
In 1984, Stewart left the RSC and moved to the National Theatre. By then in his mid-40s, he had only ever been unemployed for three weeks, but was rarely cast as a main character.
He had landed a number of supporting film roles: including playing Guinevere's father in Excalibur, a warrior-minstrel in Dune, and a riding instructor in Little Lord Fauntleroy.
And he was the voice of a small character in the animated film of Richard Adams' novel The Plague Dogs.
But even he described the first half of his career as "sound but never spectacular".
Then came the role of Captain Jean-Luc Picard.
A producer named Robert L Justman was intent on reviving the Star Trek franchise, and was looking for a successor to William Shatner's legendary James T Kirk.
He had hoped to find a sexy, hirsute Frenchman to play the role - but chanced upon Stewart giving a lecture to his wife's Shakespeare class in Los Angeles.
Justman turned to his wife. "I said I think I've found our new captain," he said.
Stewart was intrigued but sceptical.
He knew nothing about the original Star Trek and his great friend, Sir Ian McKellen, told him not to throw his stage career away on a wild goose chase into space.
But in need of a boost to his finances, Stewart signed a six-year contract, firmly believing the show wouldn't last and he'd be back on the boards before long.
"Everybody told me it would be a flop," he recalled. "A friend of mine said, 'Get a suntan, make some money, go home.'"
He was, however, pleased that the producers didn't mind his baldness.
He'd tried wearing a wig in early screen tests, but it looked ratty and - in the end - Star Trek's founder Gene Roddenberry told him to ditch it.
"In the 24th Century, they wouldn't care if Picard was bald," he said.
Stewart, who was billed by the New York Times as "an unknown British Shakespearean actor", found it hard adapting to his new job.
After his stage experiences, he found the 20 hours a day on set tiring, and he also struggled to work with a fairly laid-back and fun-loving US cast.
His decision to call his fellow actors together and give them a lecture about behaving more seriously failed to gain him popularity.
"It was really awful, being dressed down by the captain," said Brent Spiner, who played Data, the android. "We really thought, 'Well, please, get over it'."
Eventually Stewart softened, insisting that every member of the cast told at least one joke a day.
Despite his initial reservations, Star Trek: The Next Generation both survived and prospered - making its star a very wealthy man.
Captain Picard was supposed to be French, but displayed a surprisingly English regard for both Shakespeare and Earl Grey tea.
And, after playing all those Shakespearean princes and dukes on the London stage, Stewart became fiercely proud of him, and of the show's ability to connect with younger audiences.
In addition to the television series, Stewart played Picard in four Star Trek films. But while commanding the Enterprise, he managed to not neglect the theatre.
With his new-found celebrity, the parts he was offered improved greatly.
For years, he performed a one-man version of Charles Dickens' A Christmas Carol on Broadway - playing all 40 characters.
In 1995, he appeared as Prospero in a memorable performance of The Tempest and, two years later, he starred as Othello - who he presented as a white mercenary in a black African nation.
But his Star Trek success limited the roles that Hollywood was prepared to offer him.
"No director wanted to cast this grand, deep-voiced, bald English guy," he told the Times. "Because everybody knew he was Picard and couldn't possibly be anybody else."
Eventually, he took the role of Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men film franchise, essentially playing a telepathic Picard in a wheelchair.
His co-star was Sir Ian McKellen - the friend who'd warned him to avoid Hollywood - in the metal-bending role of Magneto.
Alongside his work in America, he won critical acclaim opposite Harriet Walter in Antony and Cleopatra in 2007.
And, in the same year, he played Macbeth for the first time - despite a 30-year age gap between him and Kate Fleetwood, playing Lady Macbeth.
But the critics refused to complain.
Critic Nicholas de Jongh decided it was "the best Macbeth I have ever seen", and hailed him as "one of our finest Shakespearean actors".
In 2010, Stewart was awarded a knighthood for his services to drama.
In 2009, he again teamed up with Sir Ian in Waiting For Godot.
It was a moment of personal fulfilment for Sir Patrick who, as an awed teenager, remembered watching Peter O'Toole in the play at the Bristol Old Vic.
His deep and authoritative voice made him much in demand for voice-over roles - including a reprise of his role as Captain Jean-Luc Picard on Star Trek video games.
One female interviewer once gushed that "just hearing him order breakfast is rather thrilling".
He also voiced a host of TV commercials both in Britain and the US.
Away from acting, he was a passionate political activist and a long-time supporter of the Labour Party, as well as a campaigner for victims of domestic abuse.
In 2013, he married his third wife - singer-songwriter Sunny Ozell - in Nevada.
Sir Ian McKellen officiated at the ceremony, which had to be restaged at a Los Angeles restaurant when someone discovered that his legal power to do so did not extend to the Silver State.
A year later, the two knights took their talents to Broadway, alternating performances of Waiting for Godot with Harold Pinter's No Man's Land.
Sir Patrick made a video for Amnesty International on the subject of domestic violence, referencing his father's brutality towards his mother.
Once named the third greatest Yorkshireman after Michael Palin and Sean Bean, he never lost touch with his roots - keeping a house in God's Own Country, and remaining a lifelong supporter of Huddersfield Town football club.
Forthcoming projects had included a final performance as Professor Charles Xavier in Marvel's Avengers: Doomsday, which will be released this Christmas.
And, if millions remember him only as the somewhat taciturn commander of the USS Enterprise, that prospect was not something that worried him.
"For huge numbers of people I will always be Jean-Luc Picard, and that's fine," he said. "I really believe we created an admirable individual."

Former Derry City striker Liam Coyle said that James McClean's exit from the club did not come as "any real surprise" after it was announced on Wednesday that his contract had been terminated by mutual consent.
The 37-year-old, who has not played since July, had previously described an earlier attempt by the League of Ireland club to terminate his contract as "incomprehensible" and said his exile from the squad was "one of the most difficult periods in my life, personally and professionally".
But in a joint statement released on Wednesday, the club and McClean said they are "satisfied with the outcome and are pleased to move forward constructively".
Coyle, who won two league titles with the Candystripes, believes it is a decision which suits both parties, especially with the club preparing for the FAI Cup final against Waterford on 8 November.
"Over the last three or four months there's been a real breakdown between himself and the club," Coyle said.
"The ex-manager and then the new manager has come in and it was always going to be on the cards that James was leaving at some stage. Maybe now, with the cup final, the club and him have decided it's the best course of action.
"I think it got to the stage where neither party was ever going to step down from what was said or what happened and once it got to that stage when the club felt James overstepped the mark a few times, there was no way back from it.
"Unfortunately, there's nobody bigger than any football club and James paid the price for it."

'It's a situation no one wanted to see'
Having started his career at Institute, McClean moved to Derry in 2008 and spent three years at the club before joining Sunderland in 2011.

"I don't know the ins and outs of it but I think the club have been steadfast in what they've done," he continued.

Uganda has arrested former deputy military chief and presidential adviser Peter Elwelu over allegations of involvement in activities aimed at destabilising the country.
Acting military spokesman Chris Magezi said Elwelu, whom he described as a "renegade" officer, was arrested on Monday evening and would be charged in court.
The arrest comes days after Uganda's defence chief, Muhoozi Kainerugaba, announced that he had stripped Elwelu of his lieutenant general rank and demoted him to a private.
Elwelu has not commented on the allegations.
Elwelu rose to prominence in 2016 when he oversaw a deadly military raid on the palace of a regional king accused of leading a separatist movement. He was subsequently appointed army chief.
He later rose to become the deputy chief of defence forces before being named presidential adviser.
In May 2024, the US government imposed sanctions on him over alleged human rights abuses, including extrajudicial killings committed by government forces. He retired from the military in August 2025.
On Monday, the military spokesman said security forces had recently recovered 15 guns in his possession, military fatigues, and two pick-up trucks.
"Elwelu has been on the run over involvement in subversive activities and plans to destabilise Teso," Magezi said, referring to an area in eastern Uganda.
Last week, Kainerugaba accused Elwelu of stockpiling weapons and organising activities against the government.
He ordered the former army boss to surrender, warning that anyone helping him evade arrest would face "serious consequences".
"We have recovered a lot of arms and ammunition from his house. He has hours to surrender before we declare him a rebel and deal with him," said Kainerugaba, who is the son of President Yoweri Museveni, as well as being the country's defence chief.
He also said that 20 former soldiers allegedly linked to Elwelu had been arrested.
Elwelu's family has rejected the allegations.
His wife, Patricia Apolot, told local media that her husband was innocent and could not contemplate starting a rebellion.
"He loves Uganda, and his dream is to have a peaceful country," Apolot said.

article:
'I could barely stand up straight with menopause after cancer'

'I could barely stand up straight with menopause after cancer'
- Published
A woman who went into medically induced menopause immediately after breast cancer treatment has described the experience as "horrible".
Rachel Bowman from Hove was 46 when she began treatment for breast cancer four years ago, but the medication put her into complex menopause, when symptoms happen abruptly and often more severely due to medical interventions.
"I could barely move. I could barely stand up straight. It was terrible," said Bowman.
A new pilot clinic to help breast cancer patients manage complex menopause after treatment has now opened in Brighton.
Dr Renske McFarlane who leads the project at the Royal Sussex County Hospital, said that for many women, living with the effects of treatment can continue for years.
"I felt we needed to do more to support women with that aftercare," she said.
Complex menopause happens abruptly due to medical interventions like cancer treatments, making symptoms such as hot flushes, joint pain and low mood much more severe and harder to treat.
Bowman said for her, complex menopause happened overnight.
"Your body has no time to adapt and it is like night and day.
"I had an ovarian suppressant injection one day - the next day I was dealing with 20 to 30 hot flushes a day.
"The onslaught of them was unbelievable and I was so not prepared for how I would feel and how horrific it would be," she explained.
Natural menopause is a gradual, natural, biological transition where hormone levels slowly decline over several years.
Treatments such as chemotherapy, ovarian suppression and endocrine therapies can trigger an early extreme complex menopause or cause menopause-like symptoms, including hot flushes, sleep problems, joint pain, fatigue, low mood and changes to sexual health.
To better support patients, University Hospitals Sussex (UHSussex) has launched the pilot clinic within its breast service.
A specialty doctor in breast surgery, Dr McFarlane said the pilot clinic was working to improve support for patients experiencing symptoms of complex menopause.
"Nationally, we're very good at screening, diagnosing cancers, operating and providing initial treatment," she explained.
"But for many women, living with the effects of treatment can continue for years.
"I was having more and more conversations with patients about how they were feeling, the impact on their confidence at work, their relationships and family life."
Patients can be referred to the pilot clinic by their surgeon, breast care nurse, oncology team or GP and there are plans to develop the service across Sussex.
Bowman now works with the charity Menopause and Cancer to personally try and improve support for women who have had a similar experience.
"Actually being able to speak to a clinician one-on-one and have a conversation about my personal circumstances really, really helped and really made a massive difference."

Elizabeth Taylor's suitcase up for auction after Richard Burton sent it to his sister

Elizabeth Taylor's suitcase up for auction after Richard Burton sent it to his sister

A suitcase once containing Elizabeth Taylor's unwanted clothes which was shipped by Richard Burton to his sister suggesting to give them to "old colliers" is up for auction.
Burton, from Pontrhydyfen in Neath Port Talbot, wrote to his sister Hilda from Switzerland saying "don't pass out but this is from me" as he sent her the clothes in 1971.
Burton was married five times, twice to Taylor with whom he starred in 11 films. Their relationship was born from an affair while filming Cleopatra together in the 1960s.
The suitcase the clothes contained and the letter Burton sent his sister are among a stash of Welsh memorabilia up for auction on Thursday.
Auctioneer Rogers Jones Co said the two items, along with a Pratesi shawl embroidered with "Hilda and David love Elizabeth" as a gift, are expected to be sold for up to £1,300.
The letter penned by Burton to Hilda suggested she give the clothes to a jumble sale or to "old colliers".
It reads: "Dear Hilda, don't pass out but this is from me.
"Chiefly it's to tell you that Elizabeth has found a lot of clothes that she doesn't wear anymore and wondered if you have a jumble sale or something or give them away to old colliers, or to do what you like with them.
"Some of them are out of style, but she says that a needle and cotton can work wonders.
"A large parcel will be arriving shortly, and all customs duties and carriage should have been paid. If not let me know and I'll create a fuss."
Burton and Taylor met on the set of Cleopatra in Italy in 1961, and were both married to other people but began a romantic affair.
They married in 1964 and their lavish lifestyle helped to cement their position as one of the most famous couples on the planet.
One of Burton's most extravagant gifts to Taylor was the sixty-nine carat pear shaped diamond that came to be known as the Burton-Taylor diamond. Burton is reputed to have paid $1.1m for the diamond in 1969.
The couple divorced in 1974 before remarrying for the second time eighteen months later in 1975. They divorced again in August 1976.
Screen legend Burton was born Richard Jenkins, in Pontrhydyfen in the Afan Valley, Neath Port Talbot, in 1925 and died aged 58 in 1984.
He was the son of a miner, and is well known for his alcoholism and turbulent love life.
As well as starring in Hollywood blockbuster Cleopatra, he was also known for his powerful performances in Dylan Thomas's Under Milk Wood and Shakespearean stage roles.
His rags-to-riches story, from poverty in a Welsh mining town to Hollywood fame, is one that continues to inspire.
A film telling the story of his formative years was released in 2025 - the centenary year of his birth.
Two blue plaques were unveiled that year in Port Talbot and Pontrhydyfen to commemorate Burton.

article:
What are the planned changes to immigration rules?

What are the planned changes to immigration rules?
- Published
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has set out plans to overhaul immigration rules.
Proposals for stricter requirements to qualify for permanent settlement in the UK were first outlined in detail in November 2025, when Mahmood was home secretary in Sir Keir Starmer's government.
She has argued that settlement should be "earned", rather than being granted automatically, with those who contribute more to the country able to settle fastest.
Following a consultation, external, Mahmood has now announced her final decision on what changes should be taken forward.
Elements of her original proposals have been revised following a backlash from some Labour MPs, with plans to make foreign care workers already in the UK wait 15 years to qualify for settlement scrapped.
- Mahmood scraps settlement plans for migrant care workers 
  - Published10 hours ago
- Labour MPs pull their punches on immigration changes 
  - Published6 hours ago
What is settlement and indefinite leave to remain?
Indefinite leave to remain (ILR) – also known as settlement – gives someone the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like.
Under the current system, people with ILR can also apply for benefits if they are eligible.
People who have lived in the UK for 12 months after being given ILR can apply for British citizenship, if they also meet other requirements, external.
How will the new rules affect migrants?
Under the government's plans, the standard length of time migrants will have to live in the UK to qualify for permanent settlement will double from five to 10 years.
Under this 10-year pathway, applicants must have earned at least £12,571 for five of the seven years immediately before being granted settlement.
However, there will be a shorter qualifying period of five years for certain groups, including:
- People who earned at least £50,271 for three of five years immediately before applying for settlement
- Care workers who earned at least £25,000 a year while meeting their visa conditions and arrived in the UK before May 2025
- "Skilled" public service workers in health and education, such as doctors, nurses, teachers and social workers
- Other health and education public service workers who fall below this skill level, for example nursing auxiliaries and teaching assistants, if they arrived in the UK before May 2025
- People from Hong Kong who hold British National (Overseas) status
People earning over £125,141 a year, as well as "highly skilled" migrants such as those on Global Talent or Innovator Founder visas, will qualify after three years.
Migrants who have claimed certain benefits or breached immigration rules will only be able to settle after at least 20 years.
Adults with a criminal record will be refused settlement, with discretion to refuse cases where the offence was committed when the applicant was under 18.
To qualify for settlement, migrants will generally also have to meet other conditions, including:
- Speak English to a high standard
- Owe no debt to the government, such as unpaid taxes
- Earn at least £12,571 a year for at least three years, aligned with the threshold for paying income tax
What about refugees?
There will be a different set of rules for refugees – people who have been granted asylum in the UK because they are unable to return to their own country as they fear persecution.
Refugees who arrived in the UK through an official government scheme will qualify for settlement after five years.
However, other refugees will need to wait 10 years and either work or study.
Those who do not work or study will need to wait 20 years.
Refugees who arrived in the UK by small boat or another illegal route will have to wait 20 years if they work or study, and 30 years if they don't.
Will migrants already in the UK be affected?
The changes will apply to migrants who are already in the UK but not those who have already been granted settlement.
What about family members?
A partner who arrives with someone who then applies for ILR will be able to settle at the same time, as long as they meet the relevant requirements.
However, a partner who joins later will need to complete the same qualifying residence period before they are eligible for settlement.
Eligible couples will be able to combine their earnings to meet the minimum income requirement.
The household income threshold will be £25,142 – twice the individual minimum income requirement.
Children under 18 will continue to be able to settle with their parents.
They will be exempt from the income, government debt, English language and Life in the UK test requirements, but will remain subject to the relevant suitability and criminality requirements.
Young adults aged 18 to 24, who remain dependant on their family, will also continue to be able to settle alongside them.
They will be expected to meet all the adult mandatory requirements but not the individual income requirement.
Someone who is aged 25 or over when their family becomes eligible for settlement will be expected to qualify independently.
Eligible partners, parents and children of British citizens will continue to qualify for settlement after five years.

article:
Grit and glory - Mageean's career in pictures

Grit and glory - Mageean's career in pictures
- Published
Tributes have been pouring in for European champion and Olympian Ciara Mageean, who passed away on Sunday aged 34.
On the track, she represented Ireland and Northern Ireland with great distinction and she became European 1500m champion in 2024.
Mageean was diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer in May 2025, but continued to be a shining light with her courage.
From her grit and determination to her medal moments, BBC Sport looks back at Mageean's career in pictures.
- Two-time Olympian Mageean dies aged 34 
  - Published2 days ago
- Tributes to 'inspirational' Olympian Ciara Mageean after death at 34 
  - Published1 day ago
An energetic child who loved to play camogie as well as to run, Mageean had a decorated junior athletics career.
She was third for Northern Ireland at the Commonwealth Youth Games in India in 2008, and the following year she won the European Youth Olympic Festival in Finland and was second at the World Youth Championships for Ireland.
Mageean announced herself to senior athletics at the Odyssey Arena by winning the National Senior Indoor title when she was just 15.
In 2010, Mageean was second at the World Junior Championships in Mocton in Canada and she had another breakthrough moment the following year, when she claimed a silver medal at the European Junior Championships in Tallinn.
Mageean missed out on the chance to race at the London Olympics in 2012 through injury, and had surgery on her ankle the following year.
The Portaferry runner bounced back to win the Irish 1500m title in 2014 and things were even better at the European Championships in 2016, when she won a 1500m bronze medal in Amsterdam.
After the highs of a European medal, the Olympics in Rio proved to be disappointing for Mageean after she missed out on a place in the 1500m final.
The following year, she split with long-time coach Jerry Kiernan to work with Steve Vernon in Manchester.
As well as on the track, Mageean often represented Ireland at cross-country level.
Here, her all-or-nothing approach was on show was she emptied the tank at the 2016 European Championships in Italy.
Before Mageean's arrival on the athletics scene, the majority of Ireland's middle-distance record were held by Olympic medallist Sonia O'Sullivan.
Now, she is the Irish record holder in the 800m, 1,000m, both the indoor and outdoor 1500m and the mile.
Mageean finished fourth at the European Championships in 2018, but she went one better the following year at the European Indoors in Glasgow, when she finished in third place behind Laura Muir and Sogia Ennaoui.
There was more disappointment for Mageean at the delayed Tokyo Olympics, which took place in 2021 due to the Covid-19 pandemic.
She injured her calf in the build-up to the Games, and failed to qualify from her heat.
Now coached by Helen Clitheroe, Mageean was back on the podium at the 2022 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.
She finished second behind Muir, who won gold for Scotland, in what was a long-running rivalry that year.
In a successful year, Mageean collected her second European medal in Munich.
Muir again won gold, but Mageean won a silver medal to add to her bronze from 2016.
In another battle with Muir, Mageean came out on top in the 1500m at the Diamond League event in Brussels in 2022.
Not only did she win the race, but her time of 3:56.63 took 3.6 seconds off Sonia O'Sullivan's Irish 1500m record with represented her first sub-four minute run.
So near, yet so far.
A World Championship medal evaded Mageean in her career, but she did finish fourth in the 2023 final in Budapest as Kenya's Faith Kipyegon won gold.
After her bronze in 2016 and silver six years later, Mageean completed the set of European Championship medals when she won a dramatic gold in 2024.
She was boxed in on the final lap behind GB's Georgia Bell and Jemma Reekie, but burst through a gap to win in a time of 4:04.66.
The elation on her face as she crossed the line said everything as she picked up the biggest win of her career.
After she missed the 2024 Paris Olympics through injury, Mageean was diagnosed with stage four cancer the following year.
But just like in her running career, she showed remarkable courage in the face of adversity.
Here, she is presented to the crowd at half-time of the All-Ireland Hurling Final at Croke Park in July.
No matter what she achieved on track, Mageean's connection with her fans and the next generation of runners always shone through.
At the Irish National Championships in July, 400 young athletes from clubs around Ireland joined Mageean in a 'Run with Ciara' celebration in Dublin.
Her smile and enthusiasm will leave a lasting memory.

Glasgow's Citizens Theatre wins best in Britain award

Glasgow's Citizens Theatre wins best in Britain award
- Published
Glasgow's Citizens Theatre has been named as Britain's top theatre in a new nationwide award.
The inaugural Great British Theatre Awards were hosted by the Theatres Trust, an advisory body for the stage industry, to mark the organisation's 50th anniversary.
"The Citz" was named as the Great British Theatre of 2026 and was also praised for the "remarkable transformation" that brought it back into use after seven years.
After originally closing in 2018 for a three-year renovation, the theatre went through several years of uncertainty as costs spiralled and work was delayed by the Covid-19 pandemic.
It reopened for community events in August 2025 before welcoming its first production the following month.
The refurbishment aimed to preserve the theatre's Category B-listed sandstone auditorium and its Victorian-era stage equipment while also improving the space's accessibility and modernising its facade, backstage area, foyer and bar.
The Great British Theatre Award judges said the Citizens "embodies the spirit of the awards".
It also scooped the award for "Great Renovation", with its conservation being highlighted alongside its role in providing an open community hub for the rapidly redeveloping Laurieston neighbourhood, south of the river Clyde.
The building's history as a performance space dates back to 1878 when it was built as the Southside's first theatre.
It gained its current name in 1945 when the Citizens Theatre Company relocated there.
In 1977, a fire at the neighbouring Palace bingo hall rendered some of the building unsafe, resulting in its iconic neo-classical facade being torn down.
This also saw the removal of one of the most famous aspects of the original design – six statues of William Shakespeare, Robert Burns and four Greek muses.
After deteriorating in storage, a lengthy and difficult restoration process has allowed them to now be returned to the theatre's roof.
A new 150-seater studio theatre has also been created in the renovation, allowing smaller productions to utilise the space.

Sir Ian McKellen has led tributes to Sir Patrick Stewart following his death at the age of 86, calling him "the most respected and beloved actor of his generation".
Tributes to the renowned British actor have poured in since his death at his Los Angeles home after "a brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy Body Dementia was announced on Thursday.
"He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and, in my case, love," Sir Ian, Sir Patrick's X-Men co-star, said.
Famous for his role as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek, Sir Patrick was a versatile actor who won multiple awards, balancing Hollywood roles and a career in classical theatre.
- 'RSC was where Sir Patrick Stewart felt at home'

William Shatner, who also helmed the USS Enterprise in Star Trek, said Sir Patrick brought "intelligence, grace and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did".
"Captain Picard stood for the best of us and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work," Shatner added.
Stewart depicted Picard in more than 170 episodes of the hit sci-fi TV series between 1987 and 1994, as well as in four feature films. He returned to the role for Star Trek: Picard in 2020.
Dame Judi Dench said she was "shocked" and "very sad" to hear of Sir Patrick's death, adding: "He's never been one of those actors who never felt like it that night, he was always very, very committed... He'll be much missed and he was much admired."
George Takei, who played Hikaru Sulu in Star Trek, said the actor "inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity".
Sir Patrick would later be celebrated for his portrayal of Professor Charles Xavier - most commonly known as Professor X - in the X-Men film franchise.
Hugh Jackman, who starred alongside him in the franchise, called him a "tremendous friend and man", saying: "We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today."
Sir Ian, a longtime friend of his X-Men co-star, who officiated his wedding in 2013, said Sir Patrick was "defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire".
"You could hear it in his accented voice and in the stern honesty with which he told you what he thought and felt. Yorkshiremen have no truck with half-truths or avoidance of big issues."
Sir Ian recalled first meeting Sir Patrick as young actors in the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC) and how he had expressed caution over him taking on the Star Trek role.
"He took the risk and thank goodness for us all that he did," said Sir Ian, who appeared with Sir Patrick in a 2009 theatre production of Waiting for Godot.
He added that while the US had become Sir Patrick's "adopted home", he "never forsook his origins" growing up in Yorkshire, and said "the proudest achievement of the most respected and beloved actor of his generation on either side of the Atlantic, was his appointment as chancellor of Huddersfield University".
Sir Ian noted that Sir Patrick's final film appearance will be as Professor X in the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday film. Marvel Studios described him as "a singular talent, a generous collaborator and a true gentleman".
The Academy dubbed his voice "unmistakable", adding: "Whether commanding the bridge of the Enterprise or guiding a generation of young mutants, Sir Patrick Stewart brought a tenderness to his characters that made us feel we knew them."
Sir Patrick died on Wednesday "in the loving care of his wife", a statement from his family said. "We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace," it added.
The veteran actor is survived by his wife, Sunny Ozell, as well as by his two adult children from his first marriage, Daniel and Sophie Stewart.
'One of greatest stage actors ever seen'
Born in the town of Mirfield in 1940, Sir Patrick's love of drama began at school where he was introduced to Shakespeare and his first public performance was in a local church production of Cinderella.
He threw himself enthusiastically into the flourishing local theatre. "I used to recite Shakespeare from memory," he said. "I just learned all these big speeches."
When Sir Patrick was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010, he said he owed "literally everything" to his former English teacher who first encouraged him to perform.
His first foray into professional acting was when he joined the RSC in 1966, going on to play King John, Oberon in A Midsummer Night's Dream and Henry IV.
The RSC described him as a "colossus of both stage and screen", remembering him as "one of the finest classical Shakespearean actors of his generation" whose contribution to the company was "beyond measure".
Dame Harriet Walter, who first met Sir Patrick in his theatre days more than 40 years ago, said his passing was like a "huge giant tree has fallen in the forest".
"He had fire in his eyes and you were absolutely in the room with him," the Succession actress told BBC Newsnight. "I've never heard a bad word against him. And I think the world's going to be very poor without him."
Theatres in London's West End will dim their lights for two minutes on 3 November in his honour.
Hannah Essex, co-chief of the Society of London Theatre and UK Theatre, called him "one of the greatest stage actors this country has ever seen".
As well as having roles in films such as Safe House, Robin Hood: Men in Tights and the original Dune, Sir Patrick continued to appear on TV throughout his career, making guest appearances on Frasier, Futurama and the Simpsons.
US actor and animator Seth MacFarlane, who grew up as a fan of Sir Patrick, said he was "gifted the privilege of becoming a colleague and friend" as they worked together on Family Guy, American Dad! and Ted.
MacFarlane described him as a "rare actor who could take any bit of dialogue and elevate it, making a good writer sound great and a great writer sound masterful".
Comedian Ricky Gervais, whose BBC programme Extras Sir Patrick guest starred in, described him as a "legend".
Sharing a video of the pair giggling in a set of bloopers for the series, Gervais said: "I still can't believe he agreed to do this scene. And he didn't even mind when I ruined every take."
Sir Patrick was a lifelong supporter of English Football League club Huddersfield Town, which called him a "titan of his craft".
"Fiercely proud of his Yorkshire roots, Sir Patrick was a Terrier in every sense, and we're proud to have counted him as one of our own," the club added.
Alzheimer's is the most common type of dementia, while Lewy Body Dementia is another common form caused by abnormal protein deposits, which cause a loss of cognitive function.
The Alzheimer's Society CEO Michelle Dyson said Sir Patrick was an "extraordinarily talented and much-loved actor, admired by millions around the world", adding: "His death is a heartbreaking reminder of the devastating impact dementia has on people and families across the globe."
The actor became a campaigner on domestic violence in later life, including becoming an ambassador for domestic abuse charity Refuge in 2007, after witnessing his mother suffer violence at the hands of his father.
Hetti Barkworth-Nanton, Refuge's board chair, said it had been a privilege to "watch his endless devotion" to the cause, adding that he "broke down barriers and taboos on the subject".
Andy Burnham considered Sir Patrick to be "one of the very best" who "never forgot his working-class Yorkshire roots".
"He brought joy to millions," the prime minister's spokesman said on his behalf. "He always stood up for what he believed in, including through his campaigning to help those affected by domestic violence.

Award-winning actress Gabrielle Creevy has told how she loved being able to play "a very Welsh assassin" in the upcoming new season of spy thriller Black Doves.
Creevy plays the role of Eleanor in the Netflix drama, starring alongside actors including Keira Knightley, Sarah Lancashire and Ben Whishaw.

article:
'One heck of a rollercoaster' - foster carers urged to come forward

'One heck of a rollercoaster' - foster carers urged to come forward
- Published
For almost 24 years, Beverly Craig and her husband have had 14 "wee ones" – or foster children – through their doors.
And despite the "emotional rollercoaster" of nurturing a child destined to leave sooner rather than later, she would not change a thing.
"There isn't one that has come through our door that my husband and I weren't able to love very much and take them like our own," she said. "It's just been a joy."
But with record numbers of children in care, more foster carers – like Beverly - are needed.
It is not a new problem. In recent years, Northern Ireland has not had enough carers to cope with demand.
But it appears it is becoming more acute, with the Fostering Network, a charity that supports foster carers and children, saying the number of children in need of care has been going up at a time when the number of carers is going down.
"We are not really keeping up with the level of recruitment that we need to see to ensure that every child who becomes looked after has the right opportunity to be placed with a fostering family," the charity's chief executive Sarah Thomas said.
For Beverly being a foster carer with children's charity Barnardo's is challenging but rewarding.
"Well, I suppose you are giving up your whole life, it's 24/7 so you do need to think about it very carefully," she said.
"But when you do it, it is amazing you'll not regret it."
If foster carers have room in their homes and "the capacity to love other people's children like your own" the rest "comes naturally", according to Beverly.
"The children come through your door and it is amazing - you are on one heck of a rollercoaster."
Colin Jamieson is also a foster carer with Barnardo's and said it was hard to pinpoint why more people do not come forward.
"I suppose sometimes there is a bit of bad press around," he said. "But we've got to remember we are talking about young, vulnerable children who just need someone there to support them."
He said there were a lot of people "quite capable of doing that".
"Those are the people we need to come forward, just to support these children and to give them what they need and that real start," he added.
Hilary Armstrong, operations manager at the charity, has suggested a number of reasons why people are not coming forward to foster.
"The cost of living is always a big factor for families and we know things have got very expensive," she said.
Armstrong explained there were financial supports available.
Another obstacle to fostering is societal change in families, she said.
"So it's things like young adult children that are remaining at home for longer," she said.
"Or perhaps they are going off for a period of time after school, but they are coming back home again to save for deposits for maybe having their own house in the future," she said.
"I think 10 or 15 years ago there was less of that around."
Health Minister Robbie Butler has first-hand experience of providing foster care and said he would like to encourage people to come forward to foster.
"My wife and I provided foster care for maybe around 17 years," he said.
"We had two kids of our own, both of us were working full time while we fostered children.
"I get a little bit embarrassed sometimes by people saying 'oh you were really good', but what we provided was short term respite and emergency."
Butler said his family were able to provide "a safe, loving, stable environment for children, for a short period of time".
"As health minister what I want to do is drive that awareness to help foster families," he added.
What do we know about a lack of foster carers?
As of the end of March, 4,287 children and young people were in care in Northern Ireland, according to the Department of Health (DoH).
This was the highest number recorded since the introduction of the Children (Northern Ireland) Order 1995.
The DoH said even though there had been an increase in health trust-recruited foster carers, there were still significant pressures in providing a placement for every child who needs one.
In England, the number of children in care increased by 17% from 2015 to 2025, while in Wales the increase across the same period was 26%, according to official statistics, external.
In Scotland there has been a decrease of 23% in the same time period.
The DoH said within the wider children's social care services reform programme, a draft strategy for fostering recruitment and retention had been developed.
Work is under way to start to implement the plan, although this is challenging within the current financial situation - with the department previously stating it is facing a projected deficit of between £800m-£1bn this financial year.
The department added it was committed to ensuring fostering was an attractive and valued option, with recent developments including uplifts in care allowance and the progression of a new regulatory framework.
How do I become a foster carer?
If you are interested in becoming a foster carer, contact your local fostering service.
This can either be the social services department in your local health trust, Health and Social Care (HSC) NI Adoption and Foster Care, or an independent fostering agency.
They will explain what is involved and will help you decide whether fostering is right for you and your family.
Further information and advice is also available on the BBC Bitesize website.

article:
Judoka determined to prove refugees belong at Dakar 2026

Judoka determined to prove refugees belong at Dakar 2026
- Published
Arno Yafunga Botay was six when his family fled the Democratic Republic of Congo after threats to his father's life culminated in an attack on their home which claimed the life of his seven-month-old sibling.
Following a spell living in the Kakuma refugee camp in north-west Kenya, the family settled in Nairobi. There, Arno used to watch his father Arnold practising judo and eventually asked him to teach him the sport.
Now, having coming through trials in East Africa, he will compete for the Refugee Olympic Team in the under-55kg category at the Dakar 2026 Youth Games.
"I didn't expect to be selected," the 15-year-old told BBC Sport Africa.
"I was so excited. I was crying tears of joy."
This is the first time that a team of refugees will appear at a Youth Games.
"It [means] a lot to me to represent other refugees, represent my community," Yafunga Botay added.
The family have been in Kenya since they were forced to leave DR Congo in 2017.
"There were people who wanted to kill me," Arnold said.
"At the time, I was detained somewhere when people came to our house and attacked my family. The situation led to the death of my child."
- All you need to know about the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympics 
  - Published26 October
- Africa prepares for historic Olympic moment at Dakar 2026 
  - Published23 July
After finding safety, Yafunga Botay and his elder brother Christian would watch their father training before he headed out to work as a labourer.
Yafunga Botay began receiving instructions in judo rules and techniques at the age of seven.
However, life in their adopted East African nation provided its own challenges.
"I [did] not have the judogi clothes or transport fees for local competitions," he explained.
"It's been difficult going to school. There's no money for school fees.
"My father has no work. He needs to go to work and give us money to go and pay the school fees.
"And here we don't have support. As a refugee, to stay in Kenya, you need to have documents.
"[Thankfully] the IOC (International Olympic Committee) came with this programme of helping refugees achieve their dreams."
An Olympic first for refugees
The Refugee Olympic Team was first introduced at the Rio 2016 Olympics and Cameroon-born boxer Cindy Ngamba won the team's first ever medal at Paris 2024 when she claimed bronze in the women's 75kg category.
In a double first, the team will now make its Youth Olympics debut at Dakar 2026, which is the first Olympic event hosted on African soil.
"As a refugee, we have a right to compete," Yafunga Botay said.
"A refugee is a human being like other people."
Father Arnold says the team serves as a message of hope to people around the world who have been displaced.
"Being a refugee does not mean your life is over," he said.
"Refugees can also do things that surprise people.
"My message to fellow refugees is don't give up. Keep pushing until the end."
The six-strong team competing in Senegal is being mentored by two-time Olympic marathon champion Eliud Kipchoge.
"He teaches us [to] respect the coach, focus on what you are doing," Yafunga Botay said.
"I promised him I'll bring the gold medal [back] so he can see [what] I achieved."
Discipline and respect
Judo has become a central part of life for the family.
Arnold still coaches Yafunga Botay and Christian, now 17, occasionally serves as his younger brother's sparring partner.
The teenager describes his father as "strict" even at home, with a firm focus on the importance of discipline.
"Maintaining his weight is not easy. He [Arno] has to keep training consistently," Arnold said.
"Judo teaches him respect and helps him interact with others, whether at school or at home.
"Those lessons follow him everywhere. In judo, every time you fall you gain the strength to keep going."
The owner of the dojo in the Kenyan capital where Yafunga Botay has trained since 2020 says his selection for Dakar 2026 has "changed perceptions" of judo in the community.
"It is helping parents understand that judo is not just a fighting sport - it has real value," Lawrence Karisa Nyundo told the BBC.
"I have received calls from parents who want to enrol their children.
"It is a big achievement for this club that one of our athletes is going to compete at the Olympics. We are praying that he performs well."
After Dakar, Yafunga Botay hopes other refugees can benefit from his experience in the future.
"In Kakuma, there are good judokas.
"I think if I achieve [a] gold medal, I can go there and teach them the value of judo."
Competition at Dakar 2026 begins on Friday, with the opening ceremony a day later and judo events running from 1-3 November.

article:
David Bowie's Scottish links celebrated in new exhibition

David Bowie's Scottish links celebrated in new exhibition
- Published
As musician Nile Rodgers once noted, David Bowie did not just make art - he was art.
So it is apt that his life and work should be celebrated in the V&A Dundee, within earshot of the first venue he played in Scotland under his new stage name.
David Bowie and the Buzz were not even the headline act that night at the Palais de Dans in 1966, but it was the start of a relationship with Scottish fans which continues today.
David Bowie: On Tour is the first exhibition to showcase items from the singer's archive, which was acquired by the V&A in London in 2023.
Many of the 100 items selected from the 90,000 housed in the David Bowie Centre, which was built to contain the sprawling archive, have never been seen in public.
Among them, his first instrument, a saxophone, which his father bought him for Christmas in 1961, the stopwatch he used when songwriting, his 1988 passport and an advance copy of The Velvet Underground's 1967 record I'm Waiting for the Man.
It also includes a letter of complaint from his London neighbours in December 1973, addressed to a "Mr Bowy".
The curt missive reads: "We would be very grateful if you would be considerate enough to have the music played much more softly and stop at a reasonable hour."
Leonie Bell, director of the V&A Dundee, said: "It offers something very special, the chance to encounter personal and intimate objects which reveal how David Bowie thought, worked and continually reinvented himself."
Bowie meticulously saved everything from the early portion of his career, charting his rise to one of the world's most enigmatic and influential musicians.
He later worked with professional curators to document and order it so he could use his own personal archive to rework projects he had previously abandoned.
Bowie also used it to fill in gaps where his personal items had been given away or lost.
The show also examines Bowie's many Scottish concerts and the impact they had on fans.
John Reilly was only 11 in May 1973, when the legendary Ziggy Stardust landed at the Caird Hall in Dundee.
Images of Bowie in a striking Kansai Yamamoto bodysuit take centre stage in the exhibition above a case of Polaroid photos and memorabilia from the show.
Despite gathering much of it, self-confessed super fan John, a former Dundee United footballer, did not join the 2,500 fans inside.
He went on to right that wrong by seeing Bowie live 49 times before his death in January 2016.
But the Dundee gig remains the one that got away.
"I thought it would be like a football match, and I'd just crawl in under the turnstiles behind my dad," John, now 64, recalled.
"I've got a couple of pals who were there and frequently remind me of what I missed out on but I like to think I made up for it after that."
John gave his children the middle names Bowie and Dalglish to represent his two great loves.
He said the chance to see Bowie's legacy return to his home city would be an emotional moment and a reminder of the "escape" his music provided.
"The girls in my class would save pictures from their Jackie magazines and I'd collect them in scrapbooks," he said.
"Then it was records and posters and tour programmes.
"I've made friends from all over the world and something like this brings the whole Bowie family together.
"Only this time, instead of travelling around to see him, I can get the bus into Dundee and the bus back home again and see it all on my own doorstep."
Among Bowie's most famous Scottish performances was a night at the Glasgow Apollo in June 1978.
In an interview for Reporting Scotland, Bowie told reporter Fidelma Cook that it was one of his favourite venues because of the "exceptionally excited audiences, intoxicated with the idea of a theatrical show".
But much of that theatricality was learned in Edinburgh a decade earlier from choreographer Lindsay Kemp.
A programme in the exhibition from January 1968 saw him appearing alongside Kemp in a performance of mime, music and dance called Pierrot in Turquoise, which had first been staged in Edinburgh.
Two years later, the show was filmed at Edinburgh's Gateway Theatre for Scottish Television as The Looking Glass Murders.
He also brought Ziggy Stardust to the capital, although fans had to wait until 23:30 for the gig to start as staff at the former Empire Theatre - now known as the Festival Theatre - emptied the bingo hall which provided its main source of income.
Much later, Bowie would draw on the imagery, dressing as the character of Harlequin in the video Ashes to Ashes.
By then, he was much better established and able to commission Muppets creator Jim Henson to create life sized dolls, rather than borrow dolls from the Museum of Childhood.
"He played in Scotland multiple times in his career," said curator Svetlana Panova.
"While researching the Dundee performances we were struck by how vividly they still live in the hearts and memories of local fans who have proudly held onto their keepsakes."
Svetlana added: "Their dedication has made it possible to tell the cherished story of 17 May 1973 as part of the legendary Ziggy Stardust tour."
