Outlander celebrated with special Bafta Scotland award

Outlander celebrated with special Bafta Scotland award
- Published
The team behind the historic-fantasy TV series Outlander are to be honoured by Bafta Scotland for their contributions to the industry.
Sam Heughan, who played Jacobite soldier Jamie Fraser, is one of four members of the show's production team who will get the Outstanding Contribution to Television award at a ceremony later this month.
Outlander ended in the summer after a 12-year run spanning eight seasons.
The awards body said Outlander has had an "undeniable" impact on Scotland's screen industry while also providing opportunities for local talent.
Throughout the show's run, more than 170 trainee roles were created through an initiative led by the production team.
Scotland's tourist agency has also heralded the impact of the "Outlander effect" for boosting the country's image on the world stage, with thousands of visitors now saying they have come to Scotland to see the landscapes seen in TV and film productions.
Alongside Heughan and his co-star Catriona Balfe, who played his time-travelling love interest, two other executive producers will be given the special Bafta award.
Ronald D. Moore will receive it for his role in adapting the story from Diana Gabaldon's original novels into the TV format.
He said: "It has been a tremendous pleasure to work with our Scottish crew, to utilise the Scottish locations and to learn more about Scottish culture and history.
"It's been a huge joy for all of us on the production."
American showrunner Matthew B. Roberts added: "When we first landed in Scotland, we were outsiders – Sassenachs – strangers in a strange land telling a very Scottish story.
"What we found was a country that opened its doors and a crew that opened their hearts.

article:
Glasgow 2026 generated £233m - is it a blueprint for future games?

Glasgow 2026 generated £233m - is it a blueprint for future games?
- Published
More than a million people attended the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow this summer, and 510 million sports fans watched from around the world, according to a new report.
The Glasgow 2026 impact evaluation also found that it generated £233m in economic activity across Scotland, with £158.6m of that in the host city itself.
Glasgow stepped in to host a scaled-down version of the event, which featured fewer sports and athletes, after the Australian state of Victoria pulled out due to rising costs in 2024.
Organisers promised it would cost the taxpayer nothing and the figures in the new report show they achieved this.
Some 2,749 athletes across the 74 Commonwealth nations took part in 10 sports and six para-sports.
Over 11 days in July and August, six world records and 152 Commonwealth Games records were set.
The overall cost of the games was less than £160m, according to the report.
The majority of this money, about £100m, was funded privately by the Commonwealth Games Federation (CGF), with the remainder coming from a range of commercial revenues such as ticket sales, broadcast rights, commercial sponsorship and merchandise.
And it found that community activity linked to the games reached all of Scotland's local authorities.
The games also supported 2,400 full-time equivalent years of employment, with 82 students securing games-time roles.
Phil Batty, chief executive of Glasgow 2026, told the BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast: "Glasgow has demonstrated that there is a template for designing an event differently.
"I think what is really unique here is that we have used the assets of the place. The amazing venues, the skilled workforce, the communities that must came alive through the course of the 11 days. That's the key here.
"So yes, it has been done for less than £160m but there's so many benefits for that."
A report into the 2014 Commonwealth Games,, external held in Glasgow 12 years earlier, found that version of the event cost a considerably higher £543m.
The Scottish government and Glasgow City Council provided £425m towards the bill, while the rest came from ticket sales, sponsorship and other commercial sources.
The report found this year's event cost 85% less to stage than the average of the previous three Games.
The 2014 games featured nearly 5,000 athletes who competed in more than 17 sports.
Before the 2026 Games, organisers said 500,000 tickets had been made available for sale across the programme, compared with 1.2m for Glasgow 2014.
Analysis:
Glasgow 2026 was never going to have the same look or feel of Glasgow 2014 - it was never meant to.
This was a stopgap Games - an event that was designed to provide life support to an organisation fighting for survival and relevancy.
This impact report makes a compelling case that it was mission accomplished but questions still remain from a local and global perspective.
In terms of cold hard cash, Glasgow 2026 promised it would cost the taxpayer nothing and the figures show they achieved this.
It's always more difficult to properly quantify the financial impact for the wider economy.
Economic activity isn't the same as economic profit and headline figures often reflect spending rather than long term financial gain.
Local legacy is also something that can be difficult to determine. Glasgow 2014 left bricks and mortar in the form of new venues and housing.
Glasgow 2026 can only leave a hope that the city can continue to attract global sporting events.
What the event has generated is a blueprint for what these Games might look like if the Commonwealth Games is to have a future.
It's now up to the cities of the future to decide if they actually adopt it.

A man died days after getting trapped in barbed wire while on a mountain walk, an inquest heard.
Malcolm Kitts, 92, had celebrated his birthday with a family party just days before setting off from his home in Cwmdare, Rhondda Cynon Taf, in September on one of his daily walks.
But Kitts, who was described as a "physically active" granddad who had been diagnosed with dementia, did not return.
He was found on Maerdy mountain the following day where he had likely fallen, with his leg tangled in a barbed wire fence.
Kitts was airlifted to hospital, but later died due to complications caused by his injuries, with his dementia described by the coroner as a likely "significant contributing factor".
Coroner Graeme Hughes said despite his "advancing years", Kitts was "physically active and mobile".
"He suffered with dementia which had on previous occasions led to him becoming confused and disorientated," he said.
Pontypridd Coroners Court heard Kitts' family dialled 999 when he failed to return home on 21 September.
A search party involving mountain rescue teams was launched and he was discovered on the mountain the following day.
Kitts was suffering hypothermia and was airlifted 31 miles (49km) to hospital in Cardiff by helicopter. However, he died on October 1 despite treatment.
Hughes concluded that Kitts died "due to the complications of a likely, but unwitnessed fall, or collapse, leading to leg entrapment and the complications of a long lie."
Kitts' immediate cause of death was listed as pneumonia and acute renal failure.
Speaking after he was found and taken to hospital, Kitts' wife Joyce praised police, mountain rescue team, volunteers, air ambulance and hospital staff for caring for him, and said: "I am forever grateful to everyone."

Launched in the early days of YouTube with homemade videos featuring emerging artists, online music channel SBTV went on to shake up the music industry.

As the channel marks its 20th anniversary, it is set to bring back some of its freestyle formats in the hope of discovering a new generation of rappers.
His sister has been keeping his legacy going by taking over as CEO of SBTV.
Tanisha, who is also a singer-songwriter and producer, feels in a world where algorithms influence what we listen to, it's important to still have platforms curated by music lovers.
"I know how it feels as an artist and trying to put yourself out there and break through those doors," she says.
"So I think it's very key to still have a platform that does want to help up-and-coming talent, that does want to go to places on the map that you wouldn't mainly really go to."
A host of the artists who were platformed on the channel, including Tinie Tempah, Lady Leshurr and Tinchy Stryder, are also set to perform at a one-off show held in London's O2 arena next week to mark the 20-year milestone.

Tanisha says being able to honour her brother's legacy "means everything".
"Obviously he's not physically here with us," she says.
"But to be able to carry on his name and carry on the work he did and be able to push his message of self-belief.
"And finding the next generation of talent, working with all these artists that he's previously worked with... I just feel really grateful, honoured and blessed that we're able to continue his name and legacy in such a way."

'It took years to get pain-relieving surgery - I hope a robot means others won't have to wait'

'It took years to get pain-relieving surgery - I hope a robot means others won't have to wait'
- Published
Like thousands of women in Northern Ireland, Colleen Crothers waited decades for medical help to treat chronic endometriosis - and, now thanks to an all-island first, she's hoping her long road will be a thing of the past.
"Robotic surgery came too late for me," she said. "I hope other women won't have to wait as long."
She is talking about a new breakthrough for female patients in Northern Ireland - the da Vinci gynae robot at Belfast City Hospital.
Operated by humans, the robot's wrists can twist and turn in tight pelvic spaces and it is said to be more precise at complex surgery than a human hand because it is steadier.
Belfast's da Vinci robot is the first of its kind on the island of Ireland and one of only a few across the UK.
It has the potential to massively reduce complex gynaecological surgical waiting lists in Northern Ireland, which affect thousands of women's physical and mental health and their ability to have children.
With an average wait of about seven years for complex surgery, which involves several specialities, delayed treatment means some women require a hysterectomy, like Colleen at 41.
She has lived with chronic endometriosis all of her adult life, having first begun to experience chronic period pain aged 14.
But it took another 22 years before she was referred to gynaecology and a scan confirmed she had both adenomyosis and endometriosis.
"I missed out so much of family life due to daily pain - pain that went on for years," she said.
"I can't have children - I have had to have a hysterectomy and I'm in early menopause.
"To be told you can't have children is hard to swallow," she said.
An urgent case, Colleen missed out on a da Vinci operation by just weeks earlier this year.
She knows the robot's arrival could mean a much better outcome for girls and women coming behind her.
"This type of technology is fantastic and it's amazing that it is now here.
"If anything like that can help another woman, I'm happy she won't have to suffer like I have."
And while her surgery was conventional rather than by a robot, finally getting the treatment she needed has been a relief.
"The outcome was good - my tummy feels lighter, and compared to before I am more or less pain free."
'It's really exciting'
da Vinci became part of the Belfast City Hospital's gynaecology team in May.
It cost £2.4m and was funded through charitable donations for gynaecological services within the trust.
To date it has performed 130 surgeries - 105 of them being on women with complex endometriosis - and four consultants have been trained to use the robot.
It means that complex gynaecology cases are being treated as a priority and are not being bumped when other surgical cases, including cancer cases, come in.
BBC News NI was given access to see the da Vinci in action - and, like a real-life sci-fi creation, it has multiple towering robotic arms that hover over the patient.
While humans are also in the theatre, it gives the surgeon a digital boost with incisions more precise and less invasive.
Dr Hans Nagar, a consultant gynaecological surgeon and oncologist, is one of the surgeons trained to operate da Vinci. He said women with complex endometriosis had previously been ill-served in Northern Ireland.
"They require complex surgery involving different specialists and now da Vinci lets us do that," he said.
"It will take some time to bed in but I believe it will make a big difference and there will be other robots going elsewhere in Northern Ireland.
"That encourages young staff to either stay or to return after a time in Canada, Australia, the UK and the Republic of Ireland," Nagar added.
New regional endometriosis centres
On Monday, endometriosis services across Northern Ireland are to get a financial boost when the health minister is expected to announce an investment of £1.95m to improve services.
That includes a £700,000 investment in two regional endometriosis centres located within the Belfast City and Altnagelvin Area hospitals, which will help develop specialist services for women with complex endometriosis problems.
Each health trust will also receive £250,000 as part of a phased investment for those women with less complex symptoms.
Ahead of the announcement, Health Minister Robbie Butler said the investment marked an "important milestone in efforts to improve women's health services" in Northern Ireland.
"By strengthening specialist and local services, reducing variation and expanding access to modern treatment options, it will help ensure more women receive the care they need, when they need it," he said.
Although Colleen has had her operation, she continues to need specialist care for endometriosis.
The symptoms she lived with for years included heavy bleeding, severe cramping, pelvic pain and tissue growing and getting trapped in the wrong places.
A night in the emergency department - where she was screaming with pain - brought things to a head and her consultant advised surgery as soon as possible.
In June, she had surgery, which included a hysterectomy and a full bowel shave to try to remove endometriosis tissue which attached her womb to her bowel.
She said the pain felt like she was being stabbed in the stomach - pain that has now been relieved thanks to surgery.
What is endometriosis?
Endometriosis is a condition where tissue similar to the lining of the womb grows in other parts of the body, most commonly around the ovaries, fallopian tubes, and pelvis.
The problem with endometriosis tissue is that it behaves exactly like the womb lining but it is trapped in the wrong place.
Lauren Best, a theatre nurse, said the arrival of da Vinci and a dedicated endometriosis centre was what women in Northern Ireland needed.
"I know how important it is for women to get back on their feet as quickly as possible and I am seeing that happen as da Vinci means less scarring and quicker recovery time - that's good for patients," she said.
Nagar said he hoped all those who gave donations that led to the purchase of da Vinci could see the money had gone to good use.
"I want to say thank you to everyone who donated to all the patients, their families, including those who have lost a loved one - their donations are helping others, and we all very grateful," he said.
Four months on from surgery, Colleen is also grateful.
She is back to work, walking her dog and said she is finally getting her buzz back.
While she is having to deal with early menopause and knowing she will never be a mum, the fact she is pain free is, at present, enough.

Christmas 2026 stamps unveiled by Royal Mail

Christmas 2026 stamps unveiled by Royal Mail
- Published
Royal Mail has unveiled its Christmas stamps for this year - featuring scenes from the Nativity.
The series of five stamps have been jointly created by graphic designer Gareth Howat and illustrator Rebecca Sutherland.
The stamps depict familiar scenes of Mary and Joseph travelling, baby Jesus, an angel, the shepherds and the Three Wise Men.
This year's collection marks the 60th anniversary of the first-ever Christmas special stamp.
Sutherland said it was an "absolute honour" to be given the opportunity to illustrate the Christmas stamps for the Royal Mail.
She said she has loved stamps since she was a child and had even collected them. "Being asked to create a set myself feels incredibly special," she added.
The Christmas stamps from recent years have featured snowy scenes of UK cathedrals, or lyrics from famous carols - although 2025 also showed scenes from the Nativity.
The first Christmas stamp collection came out in December 1966 after a children's art competition was announced by the then-postmaster Tony Benn.
David Gold, of Royal Mail, said: "We hope this year's Christmas stamps will add an extra touch of festive magic to the millions of greetings sent to family and friends at home and around the world."

article:
'Never too old to start' - meet the late starters shining in new sports

'Never too old to start' - meet the late starters shining in new sports
- Published
Stanley Hamilton is among the most highly-decorated arm wrestlers in Northern Ireland, but what makes his success all the more remarkable is that he only got to grips with the sport in his 40s.
His rise to the top has been rapid, from absolute beginner to a world beater in less than a decade.
It is more common for people to achieve peak performance in their youth, but Stanley is far from alone in discovering a competitive edge later in life.
From marathon running to roller derby, older generations are finding new sporting passions, and sometimes unexpected talents, well beyond the age they might once have thought possible.
Old dog, new tricks? The arm wrestler
For Stanley, he had spent more than two decades playing rugby, but needed a change.
"I got to 40 with a lot of injuries. A lot of broken bones. I thought, right, I need something low impact," he said.
The 47-year-old always had a passive interest in the sport of arm wrestling over the years but decided to train competitively after hanging up his boots.
"It looks simple. You grab a person's hand and you drag them to the pad, but there's so much going on there.
"I realised after the first session I know absolutely nothing about arm wrestling.
"I trained for five months before I did my first competition, and by the end of my first year, I was British novice champion."
He has gone on to win three world championship medals, clinching bronze in his left arm and silver in his right in 2022 and another silver in 2023.
"Everybody starts somewhere, but whether you start at the bottom rung or you start three rungs up, nobody starts as a champion.
"Don't be afraid to be useless."
The marathon champion
From novice runner to Dublin Marathon triumph in just four years, Judith Storm says her remarkable achievement is proof that success can come later.
"It's never too late to start something new," the 39-year-old told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme.
Her journey into running began during the Covid-19 pandemic, turning to exercise after giving birth to triplets.
Just four years ago, she lined up for her first race.
"I didn't really do much exercise until my 30s, so I started off just riding a bike in my garage during the pandemic and then when we later moved to Derry I didn't set up the bike that time and just thought I'll just start running," she said.
Beyond her marathon success, Judith hopes her success will encourage other women, particularly those who have had children, to make time for themselves and discover the benefits of running.
"I have got up early and I have fitted in the training around the kids so it's hard work, but for anybody you know resetting your own limitations is really powerful.
"I have such a busy life and running is just the time I dedicate to me, and I do prioritise it and sometimes as woman we can feel selfish for taking an hour here or there, but I am such a more patient and better mother when I have been out on a run, and my kids can attest that I am like a battle axe if I don't."
She described running as like being in her "flow state" and encouraged others to find something they love and go out and do it.
"Especially as mothers you can sometimes juggle so much, and sometimes you have to give yourself back that time so just start, nothing is impossible."
The roller skater
When people decide to take up a new sport, they typically choose more obvious options such as running or padel.
But Bangor woman Sarah McMillan chose roller derby, a full-contact sport played on skates.
Each team has five skaters consisting of one 'jammer' and four 'blockers'.
The aim is for the jammer to score points by lapping opposing blockers, who in turn try to prevent the opposing jammer from getting past, whilst also helping their own jammer score.
Sarah got into the niche sport in her 30s and is still going strong in her 50s.
Prior to this she had dabbled in sports such as hockey and running.
"I didn't find anything that really excited me," she said.
As the sport grows, people are getting involved from a much younger age. She has played against others where she's jokingly thought "I could have been their grandmother".
However, she thinks there's an advantage to picking up a new sport later in life.
"In the same way that if you are a mature student going to university," she said.
"I think your head is in the right place and you are there because you want to be there."
She has since represented Team Ireland at two Roller Derby World Cups and is hoping to line out at next Autumn's European Roller Derby Cup.
"Give it a go. What have you got to lose? Put yourself out there and try it."
'Feeling you are good at something'
Dr Gavin Breslin, a sport and exercise psychologist at Queen's University Belfast, believes people's experience of sport at a young age can influence activities they pursue in life.
"That stems from our childhood. In terms of making decisions about what activities and behaviours to be involved in," he said.
"If you get rewarded, either verbally or non-verbally, then you're more likely to keep going with that."
But discovering an activity that you enjoy, even at a later stage in life, helps motivate people to continue.
"A key thing here is their competence or actually feeling that they're good at something," he added.
"As a result, they're keeping going with it because their basic psychological need of competence and feeling good that they can actually achieve something is being met."

Bonnie Tyler Christmas single to be released as husband says he misses her every day

Bonnie Tyler Christmas single to be released as husband says he misses her every day
- Published
Bonnie Tyler's husband said it has "been a heartbreaking year" following her death and that he misses her "every single day".
Tyler, born Gaynor Hopkins, died in July aged 75 after undergoing emergency intestinal surgery in Portugal earlier this year.
The Total Eclipse of the Heart singer's last studio recording, Love, Light and Peace, will be released as a Christmas single on 13 November 2026.
Tyler's husband of 50 years, Robert Sullivan, said: "Gaynor never stopped working. She loved singing, she loved her fans, and she poured her whole heart into these songs."
Tyler was born in a Neath council house where she grew up with a love of music before being discovered by talent scout Roger Bell in a Swansea club.
After finding fame she was dubbed "the female Rod Stewart" for her husky vocals, and launched a career that spanned 50 years.
In August, fans travelled to Swansea to line the streets as a celebration of life service was held for Tyler at Swansea Minster.
"The only time she ever had off was during Covid, and even then she was still on Zoom doing interviews all the time," said Sullivan.
"Between live shows she would stop by David Mackay's studio to work on all these new songs.
"I know she would want people to hear them and I am so proud of everything she left behind."
After her last record contract expired, Tyler began self-releasing songs, with Yes I Can released on New Year's Day 2025, and then Only Love in March 2026, shortly before she became unwell.
Love, Light and Peace was written by Chrissie Hammond and 2026 Songwriters Hall of Fame inductee Terry Britten. It was produced by Britten and Mackay, who both worked with Tyler at the start of her career.
Tyler first worked with Britten in 1977, when he played guitar on her debut album, The World Starts Tonight.
Nearly 50 years later, he returned as a writer and producer of the last song she recorded.
November would have seen Tyler in the middle of her Jubilee Tour across Europe, celebrating 50 years since her song Lost in France broke her into the UK Singles Chart in 1976.

Irish police assaulted in Dublin and threatened with 'imitation' gun

Irish police assaulted in Dublin and threatened with 'imitation' gun
- Published
An investigation is underway after gardaí (Irish police) were threatened with what is believed to be a "realistic imitation firearm" in Dublin on Saturday.
Gardaí had been attempting to arrest a man when a struggle broke out which also resulted in a garda being assaulted.
Commissioner Justin Kelly said the incident "demonstrates once again the potential dangers that our members face every day".
An Garda Síochána (Irish police) said searches are ongoing for the gun, adding they are appealing to anyone who witnessed the incident to come forward.
Gardaí had been on active patrol on Abbey Street in Dublin city centre shortly before 05:00 local time.
The man, who had been riding a bike, was pursued by two uniformed Gardaí and a trainee Garda.
The man had thrown the firearm into the River Liffey as he fled from the scene.
Police said a magazine from the weapon was recovered and sent for forensic examination adding "preliminary examination of the magazine would indicate the weapon is a "realistic imitation firearm".

A man's body has been found in a burned-out van on an industrial estate in Renfrewshire.
